First Chapter: The Ritual for Worship at the Western Door.
I shall now describe the worship of the West, whether in the Niṣkala (undifferentiated) or Sakala (differentiated) form.
And in the mixed [age], it is appropriate for householders to perform sacrifices for the sake of others. || 1 ||
For the sake of increasing the kingdom and the realm, and for bestowing the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation,
one should perform the necessary morning purification and then carry out the ritual bath.

Having drunk water during the three junctions of the day with the mantras beginning with "sūryaśca," he should likewise perform the ritual rinsing (saṃmārjana) with those beginning with "dadhikrāviṇṇe."
Then, with the mantra beginning "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he should offer three handfuls of water with joined palms;
then, reciting that same mantra ten times, he should lead [the deity] forward.
This must be performed daily for the sake of attaining the status of the twice-born;
it is the practice that brings about the perfection of the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and other scriptures. (5)

Whether it be for a necessary rite, purification, bathing, or even sipping water; at the twilight prayer, in worship, or likewise in the offering of libations and the performance of fire-sacrifices; || 6 ||
Whatever else is prescribed for the twice-born, such as domestic offerings and the like—
whether it should be performed or not— is considered mandatory for the Śaiva.
Having performed the propitiation with the twilight mantras and other rites according to his own scripture,
and having performed the washing of his feet, he should proceed to the temple and so forth.
Having sipped water and entered within, seated upon his own seat and facing north,
he should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with thick, white ashes.

Then, having performed the ritual placement (karanyāsa) and visualizing the syllable *huṃ* blazing within the hollow center of the body, one should restrain the vital breaths (prāṇas) while remaining motionless.
Ending with the syllable *phaṭ* and accompanied by that very *recaka* [exhalation],
one then pierces the five knots and returns from there.
Having grasped the vital breath (jīva) with the Mūrti-mantra at the head of the syllable *huṃ*,
one should lead the upward-moving wind, joined with the *kumbhaka* [retention], upwards.
One should unite [the self] with that very Śiva residing at the *dvādaśānta*; this is the "union of the self" (*ātmayojana*). Thereafter, one should purify the elements and so forth.
Having understood that the elements, beginning with *nivṛtti*, abide pervading the entire temporal path (*adhvan*), one should purify them.
The burning away of the elements, or their mutual purification,
conjoined with the mandala and other rites, is here declared to be the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having contemplated that which is to be purified as being free from the external (parāga), established as a mere fraction [of light],
one should lead it to the immersion in nectar for the sake of the divine body.
Having meditated upon the Śakti Kuṇḍalinī, whose sole nature is nectar,
one should contemplate the divine Kalā sprinkled by the streams of nectar arising from her.
Having meditated on the seat within the heart, one should cause the self to enter it in the form of the deity;
then, having performed the ritual ablution once more, one should begin the ritual placement upon the hands (karanyāsa).
One should purify the back of the hand with the Astra-mantra while it is smeared with sandalwood paste;
having placed the Brahma-mantras on those two [palms], one should place the Netra-mantra on the palm of the hand.

Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of Śiva along with his limbs (sāṅga), one should again place Śiva there; then, having protected [him] with the armor-mantra (kavaca), one should employ him in all rites.
The ritual placement on the hands (kara-nyāsa) has been fully described; now the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅga-nyāsa) is being told:
one should place the Brahmans of the limbs beginning from the head down to the feet. (21)
Or, the wise one should install the thirty-eight *kalās* of the root *Brahmamantras*;
he should place Śiva in the heart according to the proper location, and install the Heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) and the others in their respective places.
Having placed the *netra* [mantra] upon the eyes, one should place the *heti* [mantra] in the directions;
then, having performed the *mahāmudrā*, one should recollect the *śiva-mantra*. (23)
The mahāmudrā consists of the two hands facing each other, touching from the lotus-feet up to the head; with the thumbs interlocked and the fingers of the hands extended.
This Mahāmudrā is the supreme joy for the wise in the act of perfection;
this is declared to be Mahāmudrā, which brings together what is deficient and what is excessive.
One should employ this mudrā in the rite of summoning the deity.
Having set aside the placement of the thirty-eight kalās, one should perform the placement of the Brahmans;
thereafter, one should perform the placement of the letters (lipinyāsa) endowed with the power of Rudra.
One should perform the placement of the syllables (akṣaranyāsa) together with Śrīkaṇṭha and the others,
or the placement of the Mātṛkās alone, or even without that.
Having thus assumed the body of Śiva, one should then proceed to the internal worship (antaryajana).
Worship, fire-oblation (homa), and meditative absorption (samādhi) should take place in the heart, the navel, and the forehead.

This is declared to be the purification of the self; after that follows the purification of the place, which is considered to consist of clapping the hands, the binding of the directions, and the invocation of the weapons.
Having taken up three vessels arranged in the shape of a tripod,
one should prepare the triad beginning with water for the feet (pādya) within them according to this procedure.
Sandalwood, uśīra, white mustard, dūrvā grass, saffron, and water combined are declared to be the best *pādya*; that which lacks saffron is considered middling. (29)
Water mixed with sandalwood and uśīra is called the *kanyasa* (inferior) *pādya*;
that which is joined with varāla, uśīra, camphor, *truṭi*, nutmeg, and cloves [is the superior].

The excellent water for sipping (ācamanīya) should be prepared with *mura* alone, combined in equal parts with cardamom (*elā*), cloves (*lavaṅga*), camphor (*karpūra*), *mura*, and jasmine (*jāti*). || 31 ||
The smallest [vessel] should contain cardamom, cloves, and camphor along with water;
it should also be joined with water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, barley, unbroken rice, and sesame seeds.
The best [offering] is combined with *śāli* rice and white mustard;
that combined with barley and black mustard is middling; and that joined with *śāli* rice grains is declared to be the lowest.
The *arghya* is prescribed for the youngest [deity], and it is described otherwise as well;
the *pādya*, moreover, consists of white mustard seeds, sandalwood, *uśīra*, and *dūrvā* grass. (34)
One should offer this water for sipping—consisting of cardamom, cloves, camphor, and excellent fruits—as part of the sacrificial rite. (35)
And what has been stated here may be adopted, or what has been said there may apply here as well;
protection is achieved with barley, mustard, and the grains of excellent rice.
Rice grains joined with unbroken rice are proclaimed as *akṣata*;
this *arghya* may consist of five ingredients, or three, or even just one.
One should perform the visualization with the heart-mantra; furthermore, the *saṃhitā-mantra* is used for the *arghya*.
Having sprinkled the ritual substances with the *astra-mantra*, one should conceal them with the *kavaca-mantra*.
Having consecrated each [item] with the heart-mantra, one should seal it with the mudrā called Amṛta;
then, having applied sandalwood paste as a tilaka, one should place a flower upon the head.
This shall be the purification of substances; the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
This shall be the purification of the mantra. (40)
Having taken up the general offering (sāmānyārghya), one should worship the Bull at the entrance,
Gaṇeśa, Bhāratī above, and Nandin together with Jāhnavī.
One should worship Mahākāla at the Yamunā on the left and right;
and one should worship Vimala and Subāhu on the two pedestals in due order.
Having entered with the left foot upon the threshold, one should worship the Astra-mantra;
then, having honored Vāstoṣpati, one should perform the worship of the Paryuṣita.
Having removed it from the liṅga, he should offer it to Caṇḍeśa;
then the wise man should wash both the pedestal and the Śiva-liṅga with water.
This is declared to be the purification of the *liṅga*; five purifications have been enjoined.
Alternatively, having worshipped the gatekeepers, one should perform the fivefold purification.
The seat of purification, joined with the refinement of ritual accessories and the aggregates, is the worship of the God of gods, which accomplishes all desired aims. (46)
Purification has been described previously; now the seat (āsana) is being discussed.
[One should worship] Gaṇeśa, the Guru, Śakti, Ananta, and those facing toward Dharma.

Upon the lotus pericarp, which has Adharma as its primary element and possesses infinite coverings, one should worship the nine mandalas beginning with Vāma and beginning with Sūrya, together with their presiding deities.
And at the end of that, one should worship Śivāsana while recollecting its respective mantra;
for this, consisting of five seats, is declared to be a single seat. (49)
From the two powers of Ananta and Ādhāra, there arises the infinite seat (āsana),
accompanied by the groups beginning with dharma and adharma, together with the two coverings (chadana).
This is declared to be the lion-throne (siṃhāsana); yoga is called the lotus of Māyā;
the lotus is the Vaiṣṇava lotus-maṇḍala, the stainless seat.
At the time of bathing, invocation, and other rites, one should prepare these separately;
having thus prepared the seat, one should place the image upon it.
Having placed the Brahmans within that [body], one should then place the thirty-eight kalās;
or alternatively, one should perform the lipinyāsa, or that which is joined with the śīkaṇṭha-mantras and so forth.
One should place the five Brahmans, endowed with the thirty-eight kalās;
then, having performed the placement of the body of knowledge (vidyādeha), one should thereafter invoke Śiva.
One should perform the placement (sthāpana), the proximity (sannidhāna), the confinement (sannirodha), and the immobilization (kuṇṭhana);
one should then install the heart-mantra and the others in their respective places in due order. 55.
Having placed Śiva upon that, one should bring about their unification;
or else, an incitement [to practice] should be performed by means of the application of Mahāmudrā.

One should present water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya) along with dūrvā grass and other items; these ten consecrations (saṃskāras) are renowned, and one should worship Śiva with these ritual services (upacāras).
One should offer incense, such as sandalwood and the like, according to one's desired measure;
one should arrange various kinds of fresh flowers. (58)
Incense is said to consist primarily of the resin of *laghucandana* and other such substances; one should provide lamps prepared with oil or ghee according to the desire of the performer. (59)
One should likewise imagine the lamps as being unextinguished;
the oblation is said to consist of an invocation, such as mung beans and the like, along with *āḍhaka* measures and so forth.
Then, having offered ornaments and other gifts, one should again present incense,
accompanied by auspicious songs and all kinds of musical instruments.
One should please the Bull-bannered Lord with various dances,
and then offer the *ārātrika* lamp at the conclusion of the incense offering.
Having rotated ashes mixed with fragrance with the tips of the thumb and ring finger, and then having released them, one should cause the *tilaka* to be applied upon Śivā.
One should show a mirror, and present a parasol and a fly-whisk;
at night, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) at the conclusion of the offering of lamps.
At the conclusion of the offering of the great oblation (mahāhavis), one should perform the bali and homa rites;
or, at the time of the invocation and the oblation, one may perform either the bali or the homa.
One may imagine both [the bathing and the singing] in both places, or one may conceive of them separately;
at the time of the bath, there may be chanting with mantras, or singing with a lute, or even singing otherwise.
Whether it be the study of the Vedas or the recitation of hymns and the like,
one should perform the chanting in the Gauḍī style and other such modes above that, ending with the offering of incense.
Above that, there is singing accompanied by dance in the Dravidian languages and others, whether in Sanskrit or its vernacular corruptions (apabhraṃśa), endowed with various musical notes.
One should arrange the song arising from the eighteen languages,
and one should arrange the dance produced in various regions.
Especially on festive occasions and the like, one should perform the perpetual festival (nityotsava), accompanied by many Gandharvas and attended by various women.
If women endowed with beauty and youth, who have been declared my handmaidens according to the desire of the agent, become Rudra-maidens (rudrakanyās), [they attain that state]. (71)
Their number shall correspond to the population of the village's layout;
at the conclusion of that, there should be a festival according to the rules for a perpetual festival.
The best of those who know the ritual procedures should arrange eight recitations of the Vādaka hymns;
at the end of that, there should be pure dancing, and at the end of that, a handful of water.
Then one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*), or else perform the dissolution-limb (*layāṅga*) placement;
and for the sake of success, the practitioner should withdraw the worship from the *liṅga*.
Having thoroughly purified the liṅga once again, one should worship Śiva with perfumes and other offerings;
however, this should not be performed every day, but rather at the conclusion of the ritual objective.
My worship is of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
That which is performed solely with the pure mantras declared by Śiva is called the superior. (76)
The middling [rite] is considered to be performed with mantras originating from the Śaiva Vedas, while the lowest is considered to be performed with Vedic mantras;
this procedure is proclaimed for both the obligatory (nitya) and the occasional (naimittika) rites.
There is no mantra equal to the Śaiva mantra here in the three worlds;
even among those, the root mantra, which is the essence of the seed-syllable, is said to be the most excellent. (78)

Those mantras which begin with the Praṇava and consist of a hundred thousand or more syllables, as well as those originating from seed-mantras (bījamantra) such as the Rudrādhyāya and others; || 79 ||
For that purpose, one should employ the seed-mantra (bījamantra) in its proper place;
there is no other thing equal to a seed-atom that brings me such great delight.
All of this, however, is common to the lingas facing east, south, and north,
as well as to the sakala and mixed lingas.
O lords of the wise, listen to the specific detail regarding the western gate:
everything else has been indicated as before, yet a certain distinction is intended here. (82)
One should visualize the god with his face turned upward, facing the door;
and Manonmanī should be installed either to the left or to the right.
Joined with a face like that of a god, endowed with two hands and a single face,
one should worship her in the northeast or in the southwest.
One should contemplate the Puruṣa in the eastern direction or the western;
or likewise, one should contemplate him in the southern or northern directions as having many forms. || 85 ||
The Guru should meditate on Vāmadeva in the north or the south;
meditating on Sadyojātamukha in the west or the eastern region, he should perform the placement (nyāsa).

One should assign the heart in the direction of Agni (southeast) or alternatively in Vāyu (northwest); the head in Īśa (northeast), and the tuft (śikhā) in Nairṛta (southwest) and Vaiśravaṇa (northeast).
One should arrange the armor (kavaca) in the direction of the wind (northwest) or in the southeast;
one should worship the weapon (astra) in the east or the west, or indeed in all four directions.
One should worship the enclosure of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) either from the east or from the west;
one should worship the enclosure of Gaṇeśa beginning from the north or from the south.
The world-protectors (lokeśas) should be as before, and Vajra and the others are likewise considered [to be placed] there;
in front of the deity is the bull, the trident, the position of the banner, and the gateway (gopura).
One should perform the worship of the retinue beginning from the eastern direction;
or alternatively, the worship of the retinue may proceed from the western direction up to the southwest.
The Nāla should be made on the left side so that it faces the Moon;
Caṇḍeśa should be in the northeast (Īśa) region, and Vighnarāja is prescribed for the east (Pitṛ).
921/2 All else shall be the same as the worship of the eastern door.
Thus ends the first chapter, the procedure for the worship of the western door, in the Great Tantra known as the *Uttarakāmākhyā*.
The foolish person, having abandoned the milk-rice held in his hand, licks his elbow.
[The ritual placement of the limbs is as follows: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva.*
Oṃ hoṃ, homage to the head of Īśāna;
oṃ heṃ, homage to the face of Tatpuruṣa;
oṃ huṃ, homage to the heart of Aghora.
Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva, the secret one; Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta, the form;
Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the body of knowledge.
Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to the eyes;
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the heart;
Oṃ hīṃ, salutation to the head.
Oṃ hūṃ, homage to the crest-lock; Oṃ haiṃ, homage to the armor;
Oṃ haḥ, homage to the weapon.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the armor;
Oṃ hāṃ, vaṣaṭ to Śiva.
This is the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa).
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva;
oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Śiva; oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to the head of Īśāna.
Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to the face of Tatpuruṣa;
Oṃ huṃ, obeisance to the heart of Aghora; Oṃ hiṃ, obeisance to the secret of Vāmadeva.
Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to the form of Sadyojāta; Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the body of knowledge (vidyādeha);
Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to the eyes.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the heart;
Oṃ hīṃ, svāhā to the head; Oṃ hūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock.
Oṃ haiṃ kavacāya huṃ;
oṃ haḥ astrāya phaṭ;
oṃ haḥ astrāya huṃphaṭ.
Oṃ haḥ astrāya phaṭ;
Oṃ hāṃ śivāya vauṣaṭ. [I offer] water for the feet to the pair of lotus-feet, and water for sipping to the face.
One should offer the arghya water, flowers, dūrvā grass, and unbroken grains (akṣata) upon the head of the deity.
In the Suprabhedāgama,
it is declared that water for the feet (pādya) consists of these four substances combined: uśīra, sandalwood, dūrvā grass, and white mustard seeds.
Cardamom, clove, camphor, rose-apple, jasmine fruit,
and nutmeg— these six substances combined with water constitute the water for sipping (ācamanīya) for Śiva.
Water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, rice, jasmine flowers,
sesame seeds, barley, and white mustard seeds— this is declared to be the eightfold *arghya*.
[He saw] the lotus-born Brahmā seated upon a lotus whose petals were fashioned from the syllables designated as ba, bha, ma, ya, ra, la, and sa— a sight that brings happiness.
One should contemplate the Source of the Universe as having two hands displaying the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, holding a mallet and a rosary.
Upon the supporting lotus joined with the syllables *va-śa-ṣa-sa-da-la*, one should meditate on the youthful Gaṇeśa, who has a reddish complexion, an elephantine face,
hands displaying the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, and who holds aloft a beautiful noose and goad.
One should contemplate the Lord of Obstacles as non-different from one's own pair of hands.
One should meditate upon Hari, seated upon a lotus whose petals are fashioned from the consonants beginning with *ḍ* and ending with *pha*;
he is the primordial Person, unborn Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, possessing the luster of the sun,
holding in his lotus-like hands the mace, discus, and pure conch, clad in yellow garments and adorned with the Kaustubha gem.
One should meditate upon the one who deludes the world, marked with the Śrīvatsa and accompanied by the lotus-born Lakṣmī.
Upon a lotus whose petals are fashioned from the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṣṭha*, [I meditate on] the beloved of Pārvatī,
who resembles ten million moons of splendor,
radiant with his matted locks, peaceful, holding an axe, a deer, the gestures of fearlessness and the granting of boons in his hands, and adorned with bracelets.

One should meditate upon the Lord, who bestows the fruits of desired objects, residing within the lotus of the heart; though formless, he is established within the limbs of the [meditator's] physical form— tranquil, with the luster of snow,
pervaded by a multitude of qualities that encompass all moving and non-moving beings, and enveloped by [the devotee’s] devotion.

One should directly contemplate the supreme Jīva— the stainless light, comparable to a lamp, which is both manifest and unmanifest, yet possesses manifold forms— within the divine sixteen-petaled lotus surrounded by the letters *ha* and *kṣa*, the cause of the universe.

One should meditate with devotion upon the omnipresent and eternal state of the Guru—the form of the imperishable One who is manifest before the eyes; who transcends the universe, yet assumes various bodies by his own will through his own desire; who is stainless and independent, appearing in the body of his respective teacher according to the particular yoga [of the disciple].
The mahāmudrā consists of the two hands facing each other, touching from the lotus-feet up to the head; the thumbs are interlocked and the fingers of the hands are extended.
The wise declare that this Mahāmudrā is the supreme joy in the act of transformation;
this Mahāmudrā is taught as that which brings together what is deficient and what is excessive.
One should employ this mudrā in the rite of summoning the deity.
In the second chapter, the procedure for the worship of the southern door:

I shall describe the worship of the southern face; it is traditionally held to be of three types, considered as being performed either upon a *liṅga*, or upon an image (*pratimā*), or upon a *mukhaliṅga*.
If the image faces south, it is designated as the "best of the best";
if it is mixed [in orientation], it is called "middling"; and if it faces west in the case of a linga, it is considered "inferior."
O twice-born ones, regarding the image, that worship of the southern face is especially desired for the Dancing Form, as it is considered exceedingly auspicious. (3)
The supreme linga faces west, while the image (bera) is said to face south.
The unmanifest linga bestows liberation, whereas the manifest one grants prosperity.
Having thus understood that the mixed [type of practice] bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
one should perform purification, sipping water, bathing, and the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana).
Having offered the *arghya* for Śiva with his hand, he should take recourse at the southern door;
having sprinkled the door with the Weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), he should worship the gatekeepers in due order.
One should worship Gaṇapa, Bhāratī on his head, Gaṅgā in his right hand, Nandin, Yamunā, and Mahākāla, in due order, with perfumes and other offerings.
Having entered within the site and worshipped the Lord of the Site (Vāstupati),
the worshipper, facing the east, should worship Śiva, who is endowed with the six qualities.
If the worship of the Liṅga is to be performed as before, one should properly worship Īśāna in its own proper place, or likewise Aghora or Puruṣa in the south.
One should worship either Aghora or Sadyojāta in the western direction;
however, one should worship the face of Sadyojāta or Vāmadeva in the northern region.
One should worship either Puruṣa or Vāma in the eastern direction;
one should place Īśāna in the south-eastern quarter and Manonmanī in the east.
The heart and the other [limbs] are established in the directions of the Pitṛs, Vāyu, Agni, and Īśa;
or else, as before, they may be so arranged starting from the south for the Vidyeśvaras.
Gaṇeśa is proclaimed to be in the eastern direction, or as previously described;
starting from the east, Śakra and the others, as well as Vajra and the others, are likewise considered to be situated there.
The bull facing south, the sacrificial pedestal, the banner, and so forth, should be prepared exactly as before; all else should be performed with a concentrated mind.
The worship of the deity may be performed through a *liṅga* or, alternatively, through an image (*bera*).
O best of sages, listen as this is now explained in brief. (15)
Whether it be made of iron, stone, clay, metal, or gemstone—
provided it is a stone image devoid of painted details— one should perform the rites as for a primary *liṅga*.
On the desired day, one should perform the purification of the image— whether it be made of jewels, metal, baked clay, or unbaked clay— until the image becomes covered with ash.
On an auspicious day, it is considered meritorious to perform the cleansing with cloth and the ceremonial bathing;
this applies to the ritual image, as well as for others, such as the jewel-liṅga or the pedestal.
Alternatively, one should worship [the deity] in a Bāṇaliṅga or in a mirror and so forth;
[one should worship] the one called Ādhāra, Ananta, and the tetrad beginning with Dharma.
The body is the fourth [element], with the lower and upper coverings on the pericarp of the lotus;
there, the group of nine beginning with Vāmā and the solar mandala and so forth are together with their presiding deities.
Having worshipped [the deity] within the cavity of the heart, one should meditate on the body of the Vidyā;
one should meditate on Īśāna at the top of the head and Puruṣa in the face.
Now, furthermore, it may be the same as the worship of the Śiva-liṅga;
however, the ritual placement of the parts (kalānyāsa) is specifically prescribed for images.
The characteristics of the image have been declared; now let meditation (dhyāna) be observed here.
One should apply the sixth seed-syllable to the western letter from the heart-seed (hṛdbīja).
One should join the three measures (mātrās) and apply the bindu at the crown;
having uttered this mantra, one should invoke [the deity] into the heart of the image.
Having established [the deity] by means of the ritual placement (nyāsa) and having performed the rites of presence (sannidhāna) and confinement (nirodhana),
one should thus offer water for the feet (pādya) at the feet with the heart-mantra (hṛd).
O twice-born ones, it was prepared with siddhārtha, sandalwood, uśīra, and dūrvā grass;
and it was fashioned with cardamom, cloves, camphor, and excellent ālaphala fruit.
One should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya) into the mouth of the one named Tatpuruṣa,
accompanied by milk, white mustard seeds, grain, Indra-seeds (indrayava), sesame, rice, and akṣatā.
One should offer the *arghya* water, accompanied by *kuśa* grass and flowers, upon the head;
protection is ensured by means of barley, mustard seeds, and the grains of excellent rice.
That which is joined with rice grains is proclaimed as *acyuta*.
Indeed, these five items beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*) are used both in the *sakala* and *niṣkala* rites. (29)
Even when [the ritual] is mixed, it should be performed during worship, bathing, sacrifice, the taking up of the *pavitra* grass, and so forth; or one may perform what has been prescribed.
That which is endowed with all the substances is called "excellent" (śreṣṭha);
that lacking one is "middling" (madhya), while that lacking two is "inferior" (kanyasa). || 31 ||
But that which is deficient by three is low; it is suitable for all doors.
[One should offer] fragrance, flowers, incense, a lamp, and indeed food offerings. || 32 ||
One should offer betel-leaf to the Supreme Lord with the root mantra;
and one should perform the offering of oblations, the fire sacrifice, the festival, and the dance at the appropriate times.

The twilight rites, the half-tithi period, the hour-measure (nāḍī), the ritual bathing, worship, the offering of food (naivedya), the bali-offering, and the fire-sacrifice— this procedure, as prescribed for daily practice, continues until the conclusion of the festival.
According to the sequence of pure dance,
with the eyelashes of the channels [nāḍīs] slightly opened like moons in the sky,
perform the worship of the half of the number of the arrows of Smara (five) using these ritual components as they are.
Or else, there may be channels (nāḍīs). || 34 ||
If the worship is of the highest-of-the-high (uttamottama) grade, it should be performed during two watches (yāma);
for the middling grade, it should last ten nāḍīs; and for the lowest grade, it should last for only one watch.
Dividing the interval into eight parts, one should designate nine divisions of time for the rites beginning with the plowing and ending with the consecration, as well as the annual festival.
The ritual of ascending the purifier (pavitrārohaṇa), the monthly worship, the sowing of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), and all such rites as the daily worship are expounded in this Tantra. (37)
Having reflected upon what is to be performed regarding Śiva, both with parts and without parts, the teacher, having investigated by this very method and principle, [should proceed]. (38)
O gentle one, the best of preceptors should perform the worship of Vaktraśa today;
however, the inner space in the eastern direction is especially distinguished. (39)
O best of the twice-born, what is the use of saying more here? Whichever direction faces whichever deity, that direction is determined to be the East for that particular deity. (40)
On account of that, those who know the directions must always postulate the other directions.
Thus ends the second chapter, the procedure for the worship of the southern door, in the great tantra named the Uttarakaumika;
[followed by] the twilight rites, the purification of the channels, bathing, sacrifice, the offering of food, the bali-oblation, and the fire ritual.
This ritual procedure, ending with the festival as prescribed for the daily rite, follows the sequence of pure dance;

it should not be diminished by less than half the number of the arrows of Smara (five) multiplied by the sages (seven)—that is, thirty-five—of the constituent parts of worship, [provided] the channels are not split apart like the eyelashes of the moon in the sky. Or rather, it may be so.
If it is the supreme-superior worship, the time is two watches (yāmas);
for the middling, it should be ten nāḍīs; and for the inferior, it is by a single watch.
Having divided the interval into eight parts, one should designate nine divisions of time.
Facing the east, one should worship Śiva, who is endowed with six qualities: 1. omniscience, 2. complete contentment, 3. beginningless awareness, 4.
sovereignty, 5. unimpaired power, and 6. infinite energy.
In the third chapter, the procedure for the worship of the Sakala [form]: I shall now describe the worship of the Sakala, which bestows all desired fruits.
[It consists of] purification, sipping water, bathing, the twilight prayers (sandhyā-vandana), and libations (tarpaṇa).
Having entered the palace and performed the washing of his feet,
he properly sipped water for purification and took up sacred ash along with water.
Having applied the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) according to the rule and having performed the ritual placement of the hands (karanyāsa),
one should respectfully unite oneself with Śiva by means of that hand.
O Lord, [perform] the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the immersion in nectar (sudhāplāva), and the invocation of the Self (ātmāvāhana),
as well as the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) and the ritual placement (vinyāsa) preceded by the Brahmās.
One should perform the ritual placement of the *kalās* upon one's own body; placing Īśāna on the head, and Puruṣa, the All, on the face, while recollecting the *malamantra*.
The rest would be the same as before; one should place the thirty-one kalās.
Having thus performed the internal sacrifice (antaryāga), one should then proceed to the purification of the locations (sthānaśuddhi).

Having prepared the special *arghya* water combined with fragrance, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, and having performed the purification of the ritual materials through the four rites beginning with *īkṣaṇa* as before,
one should worship oneself and then perform the purification of the mantra.
Having sprinkled the door with the Astra-mantra, one should worship Vṛṣa in front,
or likewise Gaṇeśa and Sarasvatī on both sides of the door.
Having worshipped Nandin, Mahākāla, Gaṅgā, and Yamunā as well, and having entered the weapon into an udumbara tree, he should enter the inner apartments again.
Having offered flowers to the Lord of the Site (Vāstveśa) and then having offered water for the guest-offering (arghya) upon his head,
one should remove the garland and other ornaments from Śiva using the Īśāna mantra.
Having performed the purification according to the prescribed rite, either with cloth and other materials or with water,
one should [visualize] Ādhāra, Ananta, and likewise Dharmādharmādi.

Then, while recollecting the seat of Śiva— which consists of a mass of powers upon the pericarp of the lotus, extending both downward and upward, and accompanied by the Heart-mantra beginning with "vāma"— one should meditate.
Having invoked the form within that [liṅga], one should fashion the body of knowledge (vidyādeha);
for Sadāśiva, Maheśa, and Rudra are the three abodes of consciousness.
That which is called the body of Śiva is said to be the body of knowledge (vidyādeha);
it is that pure power of Śiva which is inherent in him. 141/2.
For the sake of accomplishing those three bodies, one should first fashion a form;
having joined it with the heart-enclosure (hṛt-sampuṭa), one should deposit the Brahmās within it.
Thereafter, one should perform the deposition of the *kalās*; the procedure for that is stated here:
thirty-eight *kalās* are prescribed for the purpose of perfecting the body in its proper location. (211cd–212a)
Thirty-one kalās are considered for the bodies of Rudra and Īśa;
the placement (nyāsa) of the thirty-eight kalās has already been explained previously.
In the ritual placement of the thirty-one kalās, a certain distinction is maintained:
in Maheśa, whose form is that of Rudra, there is only one head and one face. (231ab)
There, with this eastern face, which is Īśāna and endowed with all [the other faces], one should likewise imagine it as distinguished by its impure nature, just as before.
Having meditated upon that form of Sadāśiva, which is joined with the fourteen [vowels], endowed with the sixth vowel, and adorned with the Bindu and Nāda; || 251/2 ||
Having formed the heart-cavity with the syllable *sāntaṃ* (the *saṃ* and *anta*), one should fashion the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*).
One should perform this likewise for an image (*bimba*) of Sadāśiva, or even for a linga.
Meditating upon the peaceful visualization of Maheśa’s dancing form and so forth,
one should contemplate Maheśa as endowed with the mantra, according to the characteristics described for the image.
Meditating upon the fierce form beginning with "the slayer of the elephant of the end of the eon" (kalāntakagajaghna),
one should fashion the body of knowledge (vidyādeha) accompanied by its mantra.
And in the form of Maheśvara-Rudra, the mantra Sādāśiva is prescribed for the sake of the body of knowledge (vidyādeha), for he is Śiva himself in every respect. (291)
Having invoked [the deities] as previously described in the extraction of the mantras,
one should then invoke Śiva into the triad of bodies by means of the aforementioned method.
One should perform the rites beginning with *sthāpana* (establishment) and ending with the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*) to the Supreme Lord;
likewise, one should offer fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings (*naivedya*).
One should present everything together with betel-leaves, as in the worship of the Niṣkala [form],
within the enclosures of four, three, two, or one [circles] combined with the five enclosures.
The Guru, having joined it with the desired coverings according to the previously stated procedure,
should perform the *balitaraṇa* (offering of oblations) therein, provided it is accompanied by a retinue.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) or the daily festival (nityotsava) when one's own [deity] is the principal;
and whatever pure dance (śuddhanṛtta) has been mentioned, one should conduct all of it according to the natural mode (prakṛti).
One should perform all the rites, including the worship of the gatekeepers, accompanied by offerings (bali) and fire oblations (homa),
or else, omitting the pure dance, one may perform the entire ritual action.
At the beginning of the evening and other times, one should perform the rite of *nīrājana* for Naṭeśa,
as well as the festival, the ceremonial bathing, and the rite of ascending with the *damanaka* plant.
The proper performance of the Pavitrārohaṇa rite, the Kṛttikādīpa festival, the writing of the calendar at the beginning of the year, and that festival known as Vasantotsava. // 371.2 //

O most excellent gurus, [you have taught] the monthly festival, as well as the practice of offering forest-grown food every month, expiation for the decayed, and the restoration of those [images]. (381/2)
One should perform everything exactly as spoken by the God, and likewise for the Goddess;
furthermore, in the month of Āṣāḍha or Aśvina, during the conjunction with the asterism Pūrvaphalgunī.
O best of the twice-born, the rite of filling (pūraka) should also be performed for Ādiśakti;
in that same location are the forms of Gaurī and Maheśvarī, as well as Manonmanī.
One should fashion the form of Manonmanī by means of the Manonmanya-ṛṣu;
and that of Gaurī, endowed with twenty-six kalās, by means of the Gaurī-mantra.
With the primordial power-atom (ādiśakty-aṇu), one should worship the primordial power within that [vessel]. || 42 ||
Thus ends the third chapter, the procedure for the complete worship, in the great tantra named the Uttarakāmika.
[He who is] moon-like, five-faced, and endowed with ten arms.
The trident, the excellent axe, the ink-pot, and the thunderbolt shall be without fear.
Holding a noose, the gesture of granting boons, a goad, and a jewel in his left hands,
he has the white lotus as his seat and the nature of Sadāśiva.

4. In the fourth chapter: The Ritual for Ablution. Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the ablution of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), [to be performed] on the eighth or fourteenth lunar day, or at the equinoxes and solstices.

On the day of the moon's eclipse, during the month and lunar mansion, under the constellation Ārdrā, on the two junction days (parvan), during an auspicious conjunction, on a Sunday, or for three days at the conclusion of a festival. || 2 ||
On the birth star of the performer, or on his own daily natal star, or on the king’s coronation star, during a famine, or when there are ill omens; || 3 ||

During an earthquake, the burning of the quarters, affliction by fever, Āryās, and the like; at the conclusion of a consecration, during a portent, upon the outbreak of all diseases, and during a drought.
One should cause the bathing of Śaṅkara to be performed for daily, occasional, and optional rites;
that bathing may be of many kinds according to one's means.
At the beginning of the rite of the great consecration bath (mahāsnapanakarma), there should first be the offering of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa),
either in the previously mentioned pavilion (maṇḍapa) or even in a place devoid of an altar (vedikā).
Alternatively, however, in the case of what was previously determined, there is no dependence upon that [subsequent] measurement and so forth.
Whether it be five cubits up to six or seven cubits in height, or endowed with four limbs up to eight limbs as desired; || 71.2 ||
Or even one endowed with archways adorned with every kind of ornament,
accompanied by dance, instrumental music, and the like, and filled with the sound of singing.
One should purify the ground with the Astra mantra and smear it with the Vāmadeva mantra;
the laying out of the lines (sūtranyāsa) should be performed with the Aghora mantra at intervals of one palm's breadth.
The Śivakumbha is two tālas high, the Vardhanī is one tāla;
the measurement of the Karṇikā is three tālas—this is declared to be common to all.
Alternatively, when the position of Karaka is in the northern path (uttaravīthī),
then the measurement of the pericarp (karṇikā) is declared to be two tālas.
Just as there is a four-petaled [mandala] for the placement of the five jars in the cardinal directions,
so too there should be that called "ninefold" in the intermediate directions, surrounded on all sides by a single enclosure.
O twice-born ones, it is surrounded on all sides by those numbering up to twenty-five,
forty-nine, and one hundred and eight.
One should visualize that [maṇḍala] joined with two enclosures; outside of that, one should arrange twenty-five jars situated in the center.
Having avoided [the obstacles] on all sides, one should construct a path for the two [deities] or for one; it should be provided with eight gates, and outside, there should first be three enclosures.
In the middle [circle], there should be the number of lunar days (tithis), arranged within the nine corners;
however, in the middle [of those], one should omit the central triad.
This [total] is one hundred and eight; if it is one thousand and nine, there would be forty arrays (vyūha), or they may be separate as twenty-five. || 171/2 ||
An alternative arrangement is recorded as being formed with one, two, three, or four [additional] sections;
specifically, there should be eight fire-pits surrounding the central arrangement on all four sides.
One should arrange the deities according to their respective numbers in an even formation for the purpose of the fire offering;
having invoked them within the path, the "Vīthi" (procession) is thus described in the scripture.
One should leave a space of exactly sixteen [units] all around the array of Śiva;
this is declared to be the laying out of the lines (sūtranyāsa), though it may also be done otherwise.
In the middle [circle] known as the one of one hundred and eight, there are twenty-five;
but in the corners outside the path, the number is twenty-one.
With the remaining [measures], it is further stated that there are four doors in the cardinal directions;
one should then lay down two lines running east-west and two lines running south-north.
The walkway outside should be fourteen in number, with an interval of one and a half cubits, or even just one cubit in measurement, according to the sequence.
Outside of that, a fire sacrifice (homa) is desired, performed in either the four directions or the eight directions;
the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) should be one puruṣa in size, and this [mound] of four prasthas is best.
Three *prasthas* is proclaimed as the middling [size], while two *prasthas* is called the inferior;
that which measures one *prastha* is designated as the lowest of the low. || 251/2 ||

Therefore, one should never employ this *śālimāna* for inferior purposes; if it were used for lower ends, such as for malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), it would certainly bring about that result—of this there is no doubt. (261.2)
Starting from that, increasing by one double at each step up to ten times the size, such shall be the measure for the Śiva-kumbha; above that, it is considered to be one cubit (hasta) in height.
One should know that half a *vrīhi* is a *taṇḍula*; half of that is the measure of a *tila*. Half a *tila* is the measure of a *lāja*; and in a thousand [of these], there are eight *droṇas*.
In the assembly of Śiva consisting of eight [deities], the one possessing rice (Śālimān) is proclaimed;
one should install the *mūrdhan* with the Heart-mantra and set down gold and other materials. 291/2.

By increasing the measurement from Śiva onwards by one prastha, the measure for the Śiva-pitcher (śivakumbha) shall be twenty-seven [prasthas]; half of that is considered the measure for the Kara-kema.
The pitcher, filled with four, three, two, or one *prastha* measure [of grain],
should be wrapped in turn with three, two, or zero threads.
Alternatively, there is a triple encirclement by means of the Vyomasūtra;
that is prescribed with the Varman [mantra], and thereafter follows the placement of the Kumbha with the Hṛdaya [mantra].

One should arrange the *kuśa* grasses up to thirty-six principles, as well as the *tryādi* [mantras], and place the *kūrca* bundles with the Vaiṣṇava mantra; one should deposit the ritual substances with the root mantra.
Gems, sapphire, lapis lazuli, coral, and pearl constitute the five jewels; in their absence, gold is considered an acceptable substitute.
A gold coin (niṣka), a quarter, a half-quarter, ten māṣas, or eight māṣas;
half of those, or half of that again, or a single māṣa for one who is extremely poor.

Therefore, the ritual action should be performed by the officiant; the substances, the jars, the intoxicant (madya), the water for sipping (ācamana), the offering (arghya), and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) [should be arranged] in the four directions.
First, fragrant water or pure water is prescribed;
then there shall be water with kuśa grass, milk, warm curd, and ghee.
Or else, one should place eight portions of scented water in the corners in sequence;
this is declared as the second installation, and now the third is being described.
Honey, parched grain, powdered excrement, powdered parched grain, turmeric, *bhūti*, sugarcane juice, plantain, sesame, mustard, and *pānasa* [fruit]. || 391/2 ||
Bhasita, tilasāra, plantain, sesame, mustard seeds, coconut, two types of oranges, and mātulaṅga; || 401½ ||
Furthermore, outside [the circle], there should be pomegranate, betel nut, black gram, ginger, jackfruit, mango, plantain, coconut, and mustard. (411)
Beyond those, sesame and bilva are prescribed; then a mātuluṅga fruit; after that, two oranges, followed by barley, wild rice, and parched grain.

At the beginning or at the end, honey is said to be used; then follow kuṣṭha, gulma, milk, mustard, and cloves. (431) Lavaṅgakam || 431/2 || [Note: This appears to be a section marker in the source text.]
Takola, ocean foam, and sandalwood; sesame, ushira-root, ghee, and cow dung; parched grain, coconut, and likewise powdered turmeric. || 441½ ||
Thus, within the threefold wheel, there is a triad of the twenty-five;
however, one should abandon the intermediate enclosure within those twenty-five.
When this is done, there are sixteen jars here;
and in the four cardinal directions and the corners, the eightfold set beginning with water for the feet (pādya) is prescribed.
In the intermediate spaces, the number eight beginning with the middle is proclaimed;
above, fifty-nine is recited in sequence.
Gulacandana, loha, kuṣṭha, kaccola, puṣpaka, patra, karpūra, nīra, dānta, māṃsi, muranta, and tṛṇa. || 481/2 ||
Śamī, dūrvā, white arka, bilva, campaka, śaṅkhinī, apāmārga,
then viṣṇukrānti, and that which is known as dhūrtūra.
The *nandyāvarta* and the white lotus [are included], making forty-nine;
or else, that same [number] is stated again in another manner. (501/2)

The lotus, water for sipping (ācamana), and the arghya offering, as well as the products of the cow— milk, curd, clarified butter, and honey— should be placed in the directions starting from the east and in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast.
Takola, resin from the *bhasmaniryāsa* tree, the flower-cluster of the *haribera*, coconut, *bilva*, *jambuka*, *cocola*, and *pāṭalī*.
One should designate sixteen weapons: the Punnāga, the Śaṅkhapuṣpa, Lakṣmī, Vyāghranakhī, as well as those known as Siṃha and Dhūrtūra. (531ab)
Sadūrvā, sarṣapa, āmra, nāraṅga, panasa, īmata, kadalī, śatapatra, dhātakī, and śvetalodhaka. || 541½ ||
Sugarcane juice, parched grain, campaka, fragrant oil, wild rice, saffron, sesame, māñji, uraja, and fine flour; || 551/2 ||

O best of the twice-born, in the preparation of the five [ingredients], one should exclude the *mātulaṅga*, *malayaja*, *malayaja*, *agaru*, *śīra*, and *rātrija*, while including the *brahmāṇi* and excluding the *aiśāna*.
The eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) should be arranged on the outside, and the Lords of the Embodiments (Mūrtīśvaras) in the directions;
within, there are twenty-five [deities] beginning with Vāmadeva.
Likewise, there are eight lords of the Gaṇas on the outside, headed by Aṅguṣṭha;
then the Krodhas and others, numbering eight, or alternatively, the Śatarudras and so forth.
But for the bathing of fifty [deities], it is the opinion of the gods that one should take thirty-six steps with the remaining one,
and then set aside a four-part portion.
There should be thirty-two positions; one should arrange the *pādya* and other offerings there, beginning from the southern half and ending with the northern half.
Now, that which has not been mentioned here is considered to be similar to the forty-nine [topics]. (61)
I shall describe the one hundred and eight [substances], which are said to be of three kinds:
sandalwood, agallochum, and kuṣṭha; kaccola, flowers, and betel leaves.
Camphor, nutmeg, ivory, māṃsī, uśīra, and tṛṇa—these are indeed the twelve substances situated in the third enclosure. (63)
Campaka, sahadevī, śatapatrī, and rocanā;
bilva, barley, śamī, dūrvā, and the plant known as megha—takkola. (64)
Dhātrī, mocaphala, lakṣmī, bhūmyaravindaka, rāsnā, vyāpalāśa, śvetārka, and karavīraka. || 65 ||
Dhātakī, droṇa, dhūrtūra, lodhra, apāmārga, kārjuna, plekṣa, ibha, pippalī, viṣṇukrānti, and nṛpāhvaya. (66)
In the fourth [offering], the substances are said to be the aśvattha and the nāgapuṣpa;
furthermore, tulasī, tagara, turuṣka, and tejanī.
Bilaka, jīraka, kṛṣṇajīraka, hareṇuka, śrīveṣṭaka, gandharasa, phalinī, and red sandalwood (raktacandana). || 68 ||
Sauripaka, vyāghranakha, vallakī, svarṇapuṣpaka, dārvī, śukti, nakha, dāru, sitāhva, kuṭa, and naṭa [are synonyms]. (69)
Guggulu, mṛdvīkā, sitā, girikarṇikā, vaṭaśṛṅga, indriyāhva, phaṇi, jambu, and manaḥśilā; || 70 ||
Śaṅkhinī, Bhṛṅgarāja, Nīvāra, Gairika, Āmramocarasā, Jāti, Pāṭalī, and again Mārjana; || 71 ||
This is indeed the fifth enclosure, though it is described otherwise [in other traditions]:
the Śamī, Dūrvā grass, Arka, Bilva, Campaka, and Śaṅkhapuṣpaka flowers. (72)
Likewise, apāmārga, viṣṇukrānti, and dhuttūra;
then nandyāvarta is proclaimed, and after that, śvetapadma is considered [to be used]. (73)
The punnāga, the jasmine flower, the pāṭalī, and the sahadevikā. || 731/2 ||
The hundred-petaled lotus is Lakṣmī; the earth-lotus is Dhātakī; furthermore, Tulasī, Karavīra, Kṛṣṇavallī, and Mallikā [are likewise]. (741/2)
After *gokṣura* and the others comes *śatāvarī*; after that, *kṛtāñjalī*, *mahādroṇa*, *punardroṇa*, *mahābhadra*, and *bhadrikā*.
Indravallī, rudraparṇī, and dhātrī, followed by harītakī;
vyāghranakhī, mañjiṣṭhā, sarala, and bhadrakoṣṭhaka. (761)
Navanīta, Drāviḍāhva, Sajja, and that known as Takkola; Cañcalā, Atibalā, Balā, Siṃhī, and Priyaṅgu. (771)
Loghra, keśara, nāga, and first jambu and kapittha;
aśvattha, guggulu, lājīra, and black cumin.
Sesame seeds, saffron, *megha*, agallochum, black *rocanā*, *śrīveṣṭaka*, fragrant resin, long pepper, and elephant pepper.
Then black agallochum, catagara, realgar,
that which is called red sandalwood, cloves, and the powder of turmeric.
At the end, one should set aside the decoction and the cleansing water with the heart-mantra (hṛdayāṇu).
It is called a "decoction" (kaṣāya) because it is produced from the bark of four milky trees.
The application of the bark of the mango, rose-apple, and peepal trees is prescribed;
furthermore, the sprinkling [of water] with tips of dūrvā grass, sesame seeds, and kuśa grass is declared.
When the eighty-one jars are established, the Atibalānta [rite] is desired;
one should offer water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya offering, as well as products of the cow (gavya), in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
One should place curd, ghee, honey, and milk starting from the fire;
then sesame, the leaf of the Śrīvṛkṣa tree, sandalwood, and that which is called "cloud" (megha).
Campaka, haribera, sarṣapa, nāgakesara, takkola, the fruit [of kakkola], kuṣṭha, kaccola, and that which is known as loha. || 851/2 ||
One should place sixteen cloves, leaves, and camphor on the outside;
in the third enclosure, one should place groats in the fire and in the jars of the spirits.
Ashes and night-powder, as well as cow-dung powder, in due order;
and the *dhātrī*, coconut, *likuca*, and *mātulaṅga*.
Outside of that, one should place Lakṣmī, Sahadevī, and Viṣṇukrāntī in sequence within the seven corners beginning with the southeast.
One should place [the substance] combined with *rudraparṇī* in nine and four [parts];
[the measure] for the water for the feet and other limbs ranges from a *guñjā* up to a *niṣka*.

One, two, three, four, or five *prasthas* of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth is declared to be the medium measure; likewise, one-quarter or even one-half [of that] may also be used.
One should likewise determine the quantity of ghee and oil;
let the desired measure of camphor, saffron, and other such substances be given.
In the center, the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) are to be worshipped, while the Hundred Rudras are considered to be outside;
thus, according to this threefold method, the number is held to be one hundred and eight.
With ninefold arrays numbering nine, situated between two pairs of directions and joined with eight gates, the eighty-one [deities] are worshipped.
Now, that which is called the "One Thousand and Eight" is being proclaimed here:
the finest camphor, cardamom, cinnamon, cardamom, and nutmeg. (941.2)
One should fill the *kumbhas*, the *vardhanīs*, and the *kalaśas* with that very auspicious water, which has been joined with these [mantras] and consecrated by the *śiva-mantra*. 951/2.

One should place the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), the respectful offering (arghya), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), water with kuśa grass, as well as milk, curd, and ghee in the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa).
Having placed honey, barley, molasses, kuśa grass, as well as the fruit of the rambhā plant, mustard seeds, the coconut, turmeric, and citron; 971/2 ||
Parched grain, pomegranate, flour, jackfruit, and ash-powder—
these sixteen substances are situated within the twenty-five.
The seed-syllables of the jewels, metals, and minerals, along with scented water, should be known as situated in the eastern [quarter], excluding the two corners. (991.2)

The cleansing with earth, the cleansing around the face, and that combined with leaves and flowers should be known as performed on the south and west; it is joined with water containing the "honored" weapons and fruits.
Furthermore, it is stated that in the north there is water enriched with astringents;
in the northeast is lovely root-water, the Brahmakūrca, and the water for pacification in a bark garment.
Ruby, sapphire, pearl, lapis lazuli, diamond, topaz, coral, crystal, and likewise emerald. || 1021/2 ||
It should be known as the "Five Jewels" (pañcaratna): the first is the primary substance, the second is called "jewel-water," and after that is "iron-water. (1031.2)
Gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, lead, brass, and then bell-metal combined with bronze— these are the supreme metallic waters.
Saurāṣṭra-mañjana, śyāmā, haritāla, manaḥśilā, gairika, and rocanā— these are considered the "mineral waters" (dhātūdaka) at the end [of the list].
Rice, *śāli*, *kodrava*, *nīvāra*, *priyaṅgu*, sesame, mustard,
black grain (*śyāmāka*), and barley— these are declared here as the eight seeds and seed-water (*bījodaka*).
Fresh butter, camphor, along with cinnamon, cardamom, and clove;
sandalwood, laghukuṣṭha, varā, uśīra, and mustaka.
Saffron, nutmeg, camphor, and jasmine—
when these are combined in powdered form, it is known as fragrant water (gandhodaka).
On a mountain, on a riverbank, at an anthill, in a hole dug by a crab,
on the horn of a bull, in a sacred field, in the ocean, or on an elephant’s tusk— 1091/2.
Water mixed with clay and eight [herbs] is highly praised;
namely, gokṣura, sahadevī, viṣṇukrāntā, and kṛtāñjali.
Śirīṣa, indīvara, and rātri—by these, cleansing is prescribed;
as well as dūrvā sprouts, the tips of kuśa grass, and white mustard seeds.
That which is joined with palms folded auspiciously is called the proper measure;
likewise for the Tulasī leaf, the Bilva leaf, and the Tamāla leaf, O ascetic woman. (1121/2)
Water from the leaves of the *apāmārga* plant is prescribed here;
thereafter, the lotus, the red water-lily, the *pāṭalī*, and likewise the *campaka*.
The *punnāga*, *kurava*, *nāraṅga*, and *nandyāvarta*, along with *mallikā*, white *arkī*, and *vakuḷa*—these are said here to constitute "flower-water. (1141cd)
Kuṣṭha, kuṭannaṭa, iron, sandalwood, and saffron,
combined with camphor and uśīra— this is declared here as the water for honoring.
A trident, a skull-tiger, a Pināka bow, an axe,
as well as a noose and a rosary made of gold— by means of these, the water for the weapons (astrodaka) is prepared.
Then the jackfruit, the coconut, two citron fruits, two oranges, plantains, and so forth—this is called "water with fruit" (phalodaka) in this context. || 1171/2 ||
Water decocted with the barks of *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *māyūra*, *plakṣa*, *pāṭalī*, and *jambū* is declared to be a *kaṣāya*.
Afterwards, the three types of mica and then the three types of honey,
combined with the three fragrances, are known as "āḍhyatoya" (the rich water).

The sun-gem (sūryakānta), the magnet (ayaskānta), the lodestone (bhrāmaka), the moon-gem (candrakāntaka), and the spearhead (nikunta)—that which is joined with these five is known as kāntodaka. || 1201/2 ||
Uśīra, haribera, pīvarī, puṣkara,
and śrīkaṇṭha— water mixed with these five is known as mūlodaka.
Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass—
when combined with these substances, it is traditionally known as the *brahmakūrca*.
Peacock crest, birch bark, yellow pigment, and *bhṛṅgarāja*— these five, combined with water from a tree-bark vessel, should be held with palms joined in reverence.
From the southeast corner, one should sequentially place oil, milk, curd, and ghee;
these are declared to be the substances for the forty jars situated in the center.
Lakṣmī, Bhadrā, Kuśodānta, Nīvāra, Campaka,
Vibhītaka, Gokṣura, and so forth— these eight are considered to belong to the inner enclosure of the womb.
The red lotus, the *śamī* tree, the lotus known as *surasa*,
the *nadyāvarta*, the *apāmārga*, the *dūrvā* grass, and the *karavīra*.
Barley, *droṇapuṣpa*, *viṣṇukrāntī*, and *mallikā*;
*jātī*, *bilva*, white *arka*, and the single-petaled lotus.
These sixteen substances are to be arranged in three successive rows;
next, I shall describe the circular sequence, with the Śiva-pitcher placed in the center.
To its left, the *vardhanī* vessel is to be known; one should place the eight jewels [therein], and the ruby (*māṇikka*) together with the five gems should be placed in the *śiva-kumbha*.
One should place the *karṇikā* in the outer region, or within the petals in the eight directions;
then, one should sequentially arrange the thousand [deities] for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth outside of that.

One should place water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), the respectful offering (arghya), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), water with kuśa grass, milk, curd, and ghee in the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa). || 1311/2 ||
In the second enclosure, there is gold at the sixteen steps;
at the twenty-fourth step, there is a coconut fruit on the outside.
In the thirty-second [vessel] it is said to be sugarcane juice; in the fourth, the essence of sugarcane; in the fifty-sixth vessel it is said to be honey; and in the fifth, honey is proclaimed.
The sixty-fourth is proclaimed as being outside with various flowers;
the seventy-second is associated with all seeds in the seventh.
In the eighty-fourth [square] of the eighth [row], one should place the fruit of the plantain tree;
in the ninety-sixth of the ninth [row], the ash immediately follows that.
In the tenth [case] joined with a hundred, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are prescribed;
in the case of a hundred joined with four, the five products of the cow are used in the eleventh part.
One hundred and eight [applications] of decoction water are prescribed for the exterior;
thereafter, one hundred and sixteen [applications] of mineral iron water are used.
When one hundred and twenty [vases] are used, it is taught that soft water should be used for the outer ones;
furthermore, one should place all types of fragrances into every vase.
In the middle [section], however, one should arrange twenty-five [vessels];
or else, forty in number, either jars (ghaṭa) or pitchers (kalaśa).
For the sake of the *vardhanī* vessels, one should properly place gold together with cloths, brushes (*kūrca*), and so forth; or else, one should arrange the ritual substances individually.
O best of the twice-born, one should know that both are excellent when the ritual deposition of substances is performed;
indeed, if everything is obtained according to the prescribed paths, it is proclaimed as supreme.
With half [of that measure], it is declared to be the middle; with a quarter, it is called the smallest.
In the middle [mandala], the gods are the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas); elsewhere, however, there is indeed Śiva alone.
And that [Lord] is especially recited by means of thousands of names;
or, while reciting them, one should worship the Lord either with the names of Śiva or with the name of Śiva alone.
Combined with the *kūṭākṣara* syllables and so forth, endowed with the dative case ending, ending in *svāhā* or concluding with a salutation (*namaskāra*), and preceded by the *praṇava*. || 1441/2 ||
The Guru should discard the outer enclosure after one thousand and eight [recitations];
there, he should perform the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha) situated in the corners beginning with the southeast.
One should establish [the fires] for the purpose of the directional oblations within the four internal corners on the exterior of the Śivavyūha, in the spaces between them.
Outside of that, the sixteen arrays are established as before;
everything else remains the same, and there would be five hundred and eight.
One should arrange two hundred bricks in the middle, joined with the number eight;
outside of that, one should fashion twenty-five [bricks] in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Externally, one should take those numbered sixteen located in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
thus, in that state, it shall possess the stated number of eight arrays.
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, the measurement of substances is stated according to their breadth; gems are auspicious when they possess their own characteristic forms.
The iron-measure is increased tenfold by the addition of the [other] metals;
likewise, the stone-measure is increased by the addition of metal. (1511/2)

The measure of seed-weights begins at one *niṣka* and increases by that same increment until it reaches the *pala*; the measure of rice and likewise the measure of sugar are considered to be of the same extent. (1521cd–1522ab)
However, up to the point of *nandapāla*, the measurement of the *guḍa* should be doubled;
the quantity of fragrant substances is proclaimed to be like that of the metallic ores.
Fruits, powdered leaves, parched grain, and roasted flour; sesame, mustard, turmeric, cow dung, and ashes—each of these in equal measure.
The five products of the cow (pañcagavya), curd, and milk should be equal in measure to the quantity of ash;
the ghee should be half or a quarter of that, and likewise one pala of honey.
In the absence of fruits, one should fill the remainder with water according to what is available. || 157 ||
The quantity of oil should be like that of ghee, or one may bring a full vessel;
the flower should measure half a pāda, a quarter, or half of that, or it may be the size of a hand.
The medicinal herb is said to be equal to that, and its measurement is likewise considered to be so;
the measurement of the vessel is the same, while the measurement of the root is like that of the fragrance.

The measurement of dry flowers, fruits, and the like is said to be like that of fragrant substances; the measurement of clay has been declared as before; other [substances] should also be inferred in this same way. (159)
The diamond is the foremost among all gems; fire is the presiding deity of metals;
barley is the chief among all seeds; and yellow orpiment is the foremost among minerals.
In the absence of medicinal herbs, however, Sahadevī is recommended;
among fruits, that which comes from the plantain tree, and among leaves, the Bilva leaf.
Among flowers, the blue lotus is prescribed as the best;
among all fragrances, sandalwood is supreme; and among earths, those produced from the roots of darbha grass are the most excellent.
Bark made from the *aśvattha* tree is prescribed [for the skin], while *kuṭannaṭa* is for the roots;
in the absence of sugar, jaggery is prescribed, and that same applies in the absence of sugarcane juice or honey. (163)
But in the absence of fruit, flowers, and so forth, one may use even their leaves and such;
all these materials should be deposited with the root mantra.

Having covered [the vessel] with the primary seed-syllable using either shallow bowls or sprouts, and having offered various garments with the heart-mantra (hṛdayamantra), [one should proceed]. || 165 ||
Having avoided those that are excessively black or inferior,
one should offer perfume with its own name-mantra, as well as flowers and incense.

Accompanied by a lamp, the mantra-practitioner should display the liṅga-mudrā; then, having enveloped [the deity] with the armor-mantra (kavaca), he should commence the rite of fire-offering (homa). || 167 ||
In the *sahasrakalaśa* rite, one should perform five hundred oblations in either a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on an altar (*sthaṇḍila*), provided it is endowed with all the required characteristics.
Having performed the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and other rites according to the path prescribed for the fire-ritual (agnikārya),
one should offer fuel-sticks (samit), clarified butter (ājya), cooked rice (anna), parched grain (lāja), and sesame seeds (tila) in due order.

The *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *vaṭa* trees are situated in order starting from the east; the *śamī*, *arjuna*, *ādira*, *māyūra*, and *śrīvṛkṣa* trees are situated starting from the southeast (the fire quarter). 170.
In the case of eight sides, one should discard the fuel-sticks at the four corners;
in the case of five sides, however, one should discard those fuel-sticks that arise from the *śamyā* and other such parts.

In the performance of the four oblations, however, whether in the primary or the preceding rites, the root-oblation is proclaimed to consist of one hundred, fifty, or twenty-five [repetitions]. || 172 ||

O beautiful-eyed one, having performed the fire-oblation (homa) starting from the root mantra up to the ten parts of the limbs, and having entered within after performing the worship of the door, [one should proceed].
Having entered the inner sanctum and purified the liṅga as before,
one should prepare the seat upon the pedestal, invoke the form [of the deity], and perform worship.
Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa with the Brahma-mantras, one should then project the body of knowledge (vidyādeha).
Having offered the triad beginning with water for the feet, along with fragrance, flowers, incense,
and a lamp accompanied by musical instruments, one should offer them while reciting the root mantra.
It was accompanied by dance and song, joined with the sound of conchs,
endowed with the resonance of Vedic hymns, and filled with the ringing of bells.
Having lifted up the auspicious jar (kumbha) and the vardhanī vessel accompanied by shouts of victory,
and having carried them before the deity, one should place them upon a tripod.

Having offered the three items beginning with water for the feet (pādya) to the Goddess for the deity residing in the jar, and having likewise prepared perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, and the respectful offering (arghya); || 1781/2 ||
Having removed that lid with his right hand, the preceptor,
while reciting the Śiva-mantra, [should hold] that which is enriched with kūrca-grass, flowers, and water.
Having gathered [the mantra], one whose mind is fixed on reality should place the mantra upon the top of the *liṅga*;
one should also install the Goddess of the Gods to the left of the God.
While recollecting the Śiva-mantra, one should bathe Śiva with the water from the pitcher;
while recollecting that mantra, one should bathe the Goddess who is embodied as the pedestal (piṇḍikā).
Having offered water for the feet with the mantra *jāta*, one should apply it to the feet and [water] for the mouth into their mouths,
employing the five [mantras] beginning with Īśāna and ending with Sadyojāta.
One should cause the water of honor (*arghya*) to be offered upon the head at the end of the tonsure ceremony of the preceptor,
accompanied by the great sound of a bell, following the consecration with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other rites.
One should place incense associated with the ritual attendance;
indeed, the attendance must necessarily take place within the enclosure accompanied by incense.
If various fruits, products of the cow, and the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) are available,
then one should bathe the Supreme Lord with them.
Having cleansed it with fragrant water, one should respectfully bathe the liṅga;
having worshipped it thoroughly according to the prescribed rite of worship, one should conclude the ceremony accompanied by burnt offerings (homa).
If, however, it is a complete bath, it should be performed as described for the complete installation;
having prepared a seat, one should contemplate the mantra of the form within this jar.
Having made those parts into Brahmabhissakas, one should place them there.
Having projected the body of the Vidyā and meditated upon Sadāśiva in that respective form,
the Guru, having performed the bathing and other rites as well as the offering of water for the feet and so forth, should offer [the oblation] with the heart-mantra.
Having offered perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, and the water of honor (arghya), and having displayed the liṅga-mudrā, one should veil [the deity] with the kavaca-mantra. || 190 ||
Having worshipped Gaurī with the *vardhanī* vessel and displayed the *yonimudrā*,
one should then conceal [the deity] with the armor-mantra (*varman*), as well as the Rudras stationed in the surrounding enclosures.
Having invoked according to the previously stated procedure, one should worship by means of the sequential invocation [of the following]:
the entire [deity], the proximity, the seat, and the form itself. (192)
Having formed a mental resolve and performed the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa*, while recollecting the mantra of the Vidyā-deha,
one should then perform the bathing and other rites, and offer the three items beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*).
One should present perfume, flowers, incense, and a lamp;
then, having taken the water-pot and the ritual vessel as before, one should place the mantra upon the heart.
One should place the mantra of each respective goddess into the heart of the Goddess;
having bathed her in due order, one should offer the water for the feet and other items in two or three portions.
Having offered [the portion] to the God, one should present what remains to the Goddess;
or, having set it aside separately, one should consecrate the Queen of Gods.
And one should sprinkle the base of the deity's feet with perfumes and other substances;
one should bathe [the deity] with paintings and mirrors, etc., as prescribed for the ritual bathing. 197.
If the bathing of the Goddess is performed in the center, one should place either a jar or a water-pot;
there is no difference here among the substances, though a distinction among the deities is intended.
In the arrangement of five, there are Śānti and the others; in the arrangement of nine, there are Vāmā and the others;
and in the great directions, there are Dhārikā and the others, which have come under the influence of the three-fold recitation.
Ananta and the others, numbering twenty-eight and designated by names such as Ādi,
beginning with Earth and ending with Pradhāna, are the deities there on the left side.
The deities of the upper [worlds] have been declared, and they are said to end with feminine gender terminations.
O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe the ritual bathing (snapana) of these very deities with milk and other substances.

With milk, curd, ghee, and honey, especially with flowers from coconuts, and with water accompanied by excellent fruits, [one should worship] using jars and other vessels filled with these substances. || 202 ||
With powders of turmeric, especially with flowers from coconuts, and with water containing fine fruits, kept in excellent jars and other vessels. || 203 ||

With perfumes and other substances combined with medicinal herbs, with pure water from fragrant oils, and with waters originating from the Gaṅgā and other sources, according to the previously mentioned procedure. || 204 ||
One should bathe the Supreme Lord for the removal of all defects, for the attainment of all desired objects, and for the sake of victory for kings. || 205 ||
For the sake of constant success in agriculture, especially for the sake of longevity, for the attainment of all prosperity, for the sake of strength, and for the cause of splendor. (206)

For the destruction of famine and ruin within the kingdom, for the removal of the wicked residing therein, and especially during national disturbances, the occurrence of portents, and the appearance of evil omens; || 207 ||

For the purpose of bringing all people under one's influence, for the successful acquisition of elephants, horses, and so forth, for the destruction of their diseases, and as a cause for the non-arising of diseases. || 208 ||

When one's own army is prepared for battle, for the sake of its strength and for the sake of immortality, it is for the purpose of instilling fear in the enemy army, for their destruction, and for the purpose of causing them confusion. (209)
It is specifically for the purpose of destroying the diseases of men, women, cattle, and so forth;
likewise on one's birth-star day (janmarkṣa), or at the coronation of kings. || 210 ||

Or on the eighth lunar mansion of each respective moon, or during his [the deceased's] time of destruction or cremation, or at the solstices, the equinoxes, or during eclipses, installations, and so forth.
During a festival, on a sacred occasion, or even at the time of offering the *damanaka* flower;
under the constellation Kṛttikā, when the lamps are lit, or under any other lunar mansion in the month. (212)
Especially on the eighth, the fourteenth, or the fifteenth day;
and particularly during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, when the moon is in the constellation Ārdrā.
This should be performed during expiatory rites, in the act of offering the ninefold oblation (navanivedya),
at times of auspicious birth, and for the purpose of protecting men.
And during the time of special worship, as well as at the festivals of the devotees, or at the time of the deity’s circumambulation, and especially during the hunt; || 215 ||
O best of gurus, one should perform this daily, or at the three junctions of the day;
or one may have the ritual bathing performed at two junctions, or even at a single one, O Śivā.
A certain distinction regarding that is stated by way of the previously mentioned path:
either by means of a single jar, or by a vessel equal in number to the sky. (217)
With [the ritual] joined by the previously mentioned substances, or accompanied by the *vardhanī* vessel,
[one should perform it] with five jars presided over by the lords of the five Brahmās, or with the *kalaśas*.
Alternatively, [the substances] may be joined with a single substance, or accompanied by the *vardhanī* vessel;
the desired substance should be placed in the center, or else whatever other [substance] is held in the hand. (219)

The water for washing the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), and the water for respectful offering (arghya) may consist of a single substance or different substances placed in the four directions; alternatively, they may be the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). || 220 ||
In the ritual for the nine jars as well, the procedure is considered to be similar;
or there may be a single substance, or in the deficient [case], the water for the feet and so forth in the various directions.
This procedure has been described for a vessel made of gold or other such materials;
and this aforementioned triad is specifically intended for the daily obligatory rite (nityakarman).
Even that which is numbered as twenty-five is established in the eternal [mantra];
for the highest of the high worship, it extends up to one hundred and eight.
Alternatively, the ritual bathing (snapana) should be performed as prescribed for the daily recitation;
that occasional rite (naimittika) follows after it, as previously described. || 224 ||
Regarding the number twenty-five and so forth, up to the limit of eight thousand,
some specific distinction is stated concerning the intermediate obstructions.
Having abandoned the four [lines] situated at the corners, or their radiance,
one should indeed bathe the Lord of the Gods with northern [substances], just as previously described.
In a place endowed with excellent worship and other requisites, the rite should be performed preceded by the ritual bathing;
one should likewise perform that [specific] action and abandon inferior rites.
The best of the twice-born do not perform excellent rites for inferior purposes;
bathing is considered to be of three kinds: obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya).
One should perform obligatory and occasional rites with the desire to ward off transgression;
