for the sake of desired results, one should perform rites for specific desires, but one must not practice what is prohibited. (229)

When a doubt arises as to whether something should be done or should not be done, it should be understood that excellence results from performing it; otherwise, a fault is incurred by performing it. (230)
If a rule is declared by both worldly custom and the sacred scriptures to be equitable, it should be followed;
however, if it is prohibited by those very same two, one should abandon that which is doubtful. (231)
It may arise through the distinction of ritual action (*kriyā*), mantra, and so forth, or through the distinction of the scriptures;
since there is a division of the tantras according to the distinctions of ritual action, mantra, and so forth, [the classification follows]. (232)

Therefore, in that matter, one should perform what is declared in the Śaiva [scriptures] and not that from other scriptures; nor should one resort to another scripture merely because it is praised or recommended therein. (233)
When no such rule has arisen there, this [rule] is prescribed even in that case;
when penance and so forth have not been stated in one's own scripture, they are taken from another scripture. (234)

But when the meaning of the scripture is being practiced, its ancillaries—such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and so forth—should be accepted either as established by one's own scripture or as declared in another scripture. (235)
That best of kings who, having first considered a single [instance], causes [this] to be made, shall in a short time become the sovereign of all. (236)
Whatever lifespan, health, and mental resolve he may have, all that shall be realized for him; devotion to Śiva arises within him. (237)
Even upon seeing perverse actions, he who remains indifferent incurs ruin; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. (238)

Therefore, by that preeminent teacher— who abides within the five spheres of perception, who has reached the further shore of thorough knowledge of the Śaiva Āgamas, and who is devoted to ritual action— (239)
In order to accomplish his ritual duties and for the prosperity of his own kingdom,
he should accept as his preceptor the best of gurus, one who is highly learned in the Śiva scriptures.
O best of sages, one should have the bathing and other rites performed by that very person;
by means of him alone should the special worship be conducted for the attainment of desired success. (241)
Having bathed the Lord Īśvara with milk, curd, ghee, honey, and other such substances, one should rub the Lord together with his pedestal using fine flour paste and similar materials.
Having bathed Śiva with scented water, one should wipe him with a cloth; having anointed him with sandalwood paste and other unguents, one should adorn him with silk garments and other ornaments.
Immediately thereafter, one should fumigate with incense, flowers, and the like;
then, one should offer a lamp combined with camphor wicks and perform the ārātrika ceremony.
Either an offering of five colors, or milk-rice (pāyasa), or even pure [grains], combined with various side-dishes and accompanied by various fruits. || 245 ||
At the conclusion of that, he should offer betel-leaf accompanied by mouth-perfumes,
combined with the powders of cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg, and kakkola.
This mouth-perfume, mixed with pieces of madder (mañjiṣṭhā), shall be used.
Having prostrated and received permission from the one to be entreated, he should resort to the sacrificial pit for the purpose of the fire-oblation.

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations consisting of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (caru), and sesame seeds, one should perform the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) at the end.
Therefore, having taken up the ashes, one should cause them to be given to the patron;
and having requested the desired rite, one should prostrate again and again. || 249 ||
Beginning from a single day, one should perform it for up to seven days;
or it may be performed for double, triple, or four or five times that duration.

Whether numbering six or seven times [the usual amount], performed specifically for the sake of accomplishing ritual actions, this is known as the "Exalted Worship," which bestows the fruits previously described. (251)

The occasional rite (naimittika) should be performed at the conclusion of the obligatory rite (nitya), provided there is no contradiction; however, when an occasional rite occurs while the obligatory rite is already in progress, [the latter must be completed]. || 252 ||
Having completed [the daily rites] in a short time, one should perform the obligatory and occasional duties;
if the time for the latter half of the twilight (sandhyā) has arrived, provided it occurs during the former half.
Occasional rites (naimittika) should be performed at their proper time without hesitation;
one should also perform the twilight worship (sandhyā) for even a short duration during the latter part of the day.
One should perform the ritual practice in both cases according to the Tantra;
that is, the daily rites (nityakarman) ending with incense, or alternatively, up to the food offering (naivedya). || 255 ||
Having performed that which is required by the time, one should then perform the occasional (naimittika) rite;
for if the occasional rite is a major one, it should indeed be commenced at its own proper time.
Having completed the remainder of the twilight rite from the first enclosure up to the end,
one should bathe [the deity] at the conclusion of the twilight with all the water-pots according to the prescribed method.
When two optional rites (naimittika) arise simultaneously, one should perform them starting from the major (mahat) and proceeding to the minor;
however, if they are of equal status, let there be freedom of choice (kāmacāra).
The time for the occasional [rite] is also proclaimed to be of two kinds, distinguished as small and not small; for the small [rite], it begins with the solstice (ayana) and so forth. (259)
The period from the commencement of the eclipse until the Great Time (māhākāla) is very brief;
one should perform [the rite] while the sun is being eclipsed, and when the moon is being released.

One should perform the ritual bathing and other rites during the southern transit (dakṣiṇāyana), once the northern transit (uttarāyaṇa) has passed, at the equinox (viṣuva), and during the middle period. || 261 ||
One should perform [the rites] at the end of Virgo, Gemini, and Sagittarius;
and one should perform them at the beginning of Leo, Scorpio, Aquarius, and Taurus. || 262 ||
In rituals such as ritual bathing and others, one should perform them for half [a watch], one [watch], two [watches], or even for a single *yāma* or a *ghaṭikā*, at both the beginning and the end.
Thereafter, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings;
as well as the materials used in the sacrifice, such as gold, clothing, and so forth.
It should be given to the preceptor and not intended for the enjoyment of others;
this includes whatever materials remain from the sacrifice, as well as the ornaments of the pavilion.
A sacrificial mound, a cloth, gold, a water-pot or a jar and the like, an archway, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the eight auspicious symbols, and the nine gems. (266)

Whatever remains of that oblation, cooked rice, and food offering, as well as the circle of the pavilion, the water-stalls, and anything else used [for the ritual], other than myself—[all this is for you]. (267)
It should be given to the teacher alone who abides within the five spheres of perception;
the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the instructor is considered to range from one niṣka up to ten niṣkas.
For one of inferior status, the lowest share shall be one-eighth less than the standard; for one of even lower conduct, it shall be half of that.
In the case of a minor offense involving inferior behavior, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall be divided into nine parts.
But in the case of a permanent [offering], one should provide an increase as well as that which satisfies the mind.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Chapter on the Ritual of Consecration (*snāpanavidhi*), in the great tantra known as the *Uttarakāmika*.
[The ritual] may be performed for [liṅgas] measuring five cubits and so forth, up to six or seven cubits.
Whether it consists of four limbs and so forth, or even up to eight times eight limbs;

The placement of the threads should be gentle, with an interval equal to the measure of a palm; just as a decoction is produced from the bark and pith of a tree grown in milk-water, so too is it astringent.
Alternatively, the essence of the bark from the mango or rose-apple tree is proclaimed [as a substitute].
Sprinkling with water from a vessel containing *dūrvā* grass, sesame seeds, and the tips of *kuśa* grass is what is called "mārjana" (sprinkling purification).
[This is] "jewel-water."
Gems of ruby, sapphire, pearl, lapis lazuli,
topaz, coral, diamond, and pieces of crystal.
Emeralds and gems—these are the nine gems, consisting of five types.
This should be known as the "five jewels"; in the absence of the first, the second is used.
Iron water consists of gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, lead, brass,
and then bell-metal; this is considered the supreme iron water.
Mineral water, Saurāṣṭra clay, collyrium, Śyāmā, yellow orpiment, realgar, red chalk, and gorocanā— this is considered the final list of mineral substances.
Rice, kodrava, nīvāra, priyaṅgu, sesame, mustard,
śyāmāka, black gram, barley, and seeds— this is declared here as "seed-water" (bījodaka). 106.
Scented water, fresh butter, camphor, along with cinnamon, cardamom, and cloves; sandalwood, *laghukuṣṭha*, *varāla*, *uśīra*, and *mustaka*. (107)
Saffron, nutmeg, camphor, and jasmine—when these are combined as a powder, it is known as "scented water. (108)
[One should collect] clay and water from a mountain, from a riverbank, from an anthill, from a crab’s hole,
from the horn of a bull, from an excellent field, from the ocean, and from the tusk of an elephant.
And clay mixed with water is proclaimed to be endowed with eight [qualities].
With *mārjanodaka*, *gokṣura*, *sahadevī*, *viṣṇukrāntā*, *kṛtāñjali*,
*śirīṣa*, *indīvara*, and *rātri*— by means of these, the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) is performed for liberation. 110.
A measure of water,
a blade of durvā grass, a lotus, the tip of a kuśa blade, and a white mustard seed—
when these are held together with palms joined in reverence, that is called a *parimāṇa*.
Water with leaves, tulasī, bilva leaves, tamāla, and the ascetic’s plant (tapasvinī),
combined with apāmārga— this is declared to be "leaf-water" (patratoya).
Puṣpodaka, padma, red utpala, then paṭalī, campaka,
punnāga, kurava, nāraṅga, nadyāvarta, and mallikā.
Flower-water mixed with white arka and bakula flowers is prescribed here.
Kuṣṭha, kuṭannaṭa, iron filings, sandalwood, saffron, camphor, and uśīra— these, combined with water, are prescribed here as the *māḍa*.
The weapon-water consists of a trident, a skull, a deer-skin, a Pināka bow, an axe, a noose,
and a rosary made of gold; with these, the weapon-water is prepared.
The fruit-water consists of jackfruit, coconut, the two types of citron,
two oranges, plantain, and so forth; this is what is declared as "fruit-water" in this context.
Decoction water (kaṣāyodaka) is said to be prepared from the barks of the palāśa, udumbara, aśvattha, māyūra, plakṣa, pāṭalī,
and jambū trees, combined together.
First, the three types of water from the Āṅga; then, the three types of water from the Abhra; finally, the three types of water from the Akṣa.
When combined with the three fragrances, this is known as the Āḍayatoya.
Sūryakānta, ayaskānta, bhrāmara, candrakāntaka,
and nikunda— water endowed with these five is known as *kāntodaka*.
Root-water is known to consist of five ingredients: uśīra, haribera, pīvari, puṣkara, and śrīkaṇṭha.
Bark-water consists of peacock feather, birch bark, gorocana, and bhr̥ṅgarāja;
when these five are combined, it is known as bark-water, offered with palms joined in reverence.
Cow’s urine, water, Lakṣmī, Bhadrā, Kuśa grass, Dānta, Nīvāra rice, Campaka, and Gokṣura— these eight are prepared, along with water infused with the bark of Lodhra.
Just as there is a four-petaled [lotus], so too is the placement of the five jars in the cardinal directions;
in the intermediate directions as well, there should be that which is called "nine," surrounded on all sides by one.
In the ritual directions as well, there should be that which is called "nine," surrounded on all sides by one.
It is surrounded on all sides by that which extends to the number twenty-five.
In the [maṇḍala] known as the one with one hundred and eight [squares], there are twenty-five in the center;
in the corner outside the path, there are twenty-one; and with the remaining [squares], the four gates are formed in the directions—this is further stated for the thousand[-square maṇḍala]. 108.
The height of the Śiva-kumbha is two tālas, that of the vardhanī is one tāla, and the measurement of the karṇikā is three tālas; this is declared to be the standard for all.
Alternatively, it may follow the subsequent procedure; just as the position of the *karaka* [is prescribed], so too is the measurement of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) stated to be two *tālas*.

Just as there is a four-petaled [lotus], so too is the placement of the five jars in the directions. Even in the [other] rites, there should be that which is called "nine," surrounded on all sides by one;
ending with the number twenty-five, it is likewise surrounded on all sides.

O twice-born ones, there are forty-nine [syllables] in number, one hundred and eight, and forty; these constitute the Vyūha. Furthermore, another Vyūha is recorded as consisting of twenty-five, or of one, two, three, or four words.
One should arrange eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) around the center of the formation;
in a symmetrical formation, one should designate them according to their respective numbers for the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa).
Having invoked [the deities] within the path, the "path" (vīthi) is thus described in the scripture.
One should leave a space of exactly sixteen [units] all around the Śivavyūha; this is declared to be the laying out of the lines (sūtranyāsa). It is also described otherwise:
O twice-born ones, the number is forty-nine, one hundred and eight.
14. One should visualize that [maṇḍala] outside [the central one], joined with two enclosures;
twenty-five jars are situated in the center. 15. Having avoided [the space] all around, however, [one should place] the jar for the traveler with either two or one [jars].

It is provided with eight doors, and there are three enclosures on the outside. (16) In the center, there should be fifteen [squares] arranged in a nine-cornered [figure]; however, one should omit that central triad within the center.
If this [measurement] is one thousand and eight or one thousand and nine,
one should lay down two threads running east-west and north-south,
with an interval of one and a half cubits or even an interval of one cubit.

There may be fourteen [units] in number outside the path (vīthi), and in sequence beyond that, the homa is desired in the four directions or the eight directions. 10. Two tālas for the Śiva-kumbha, and one tāla for the vardhanī.
The measurement of the pericarp is said to be three tālas, which is common to all [mandalas].
Alternatively, as there is an upper procedure for the placement of the *karaka* vessel, so too the measurement of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) is declared to be by the measure of two *tālas*.
(11½) Just as there is a four-petalled [lotus], so too is the installation of five pitchers in each direction. (11½)
Just as there is a four-petaled [mandala], so too the placement of five vases should be in the cardinal directions;
in the intermediate directions as well, there should be that which is called "nine," surrounded on all sides by one.
In the intermediate directions as well, there should be that which is called "nine," surrounded on all sides by one.
It is surrounded on all sides by that which extends up to the number twenty-five.
In the intermediate directions as well, there should be what is called the "ninefold" [arrangement], surrounded on all sides by one;
ending with the number twenty-five, that is surrounded on all sides by the number forty-nine,
O twice-born ones, and by one hundred and eight.
13. O twice-born ones, one should arrange one hundred and eight [pots] numbering forty-nine;
14. one should arrange them outside, joined with two enclosures, with twenty-five pots situated in the center.
Having avoided [the center] on all sides, one should draw the path with two or one [lines]; it is joined with eight doors, and outside there are three sets of eight.
In the middle, there should be numbers equal to the lunar days, arranged in nine corners.
In the middle [repetition], which consists of the number of lunar days (fifteen), one should abandon that triad in the middle.
This total is one hundred and eight; if it is a thousand plus nine, then in the middle repetition known as one hundred and eight, there are twenty-five [per day].
In the corner outside the path, there should be twenty-one [deities];
with the remaining [deities] in the directions, it is further stated that there are four doors and one thousand [deities].
There should be a fortyfold array, and separately, a twenty-fivefold one.
But a different arrangement (vyūha) is recorded as being formed by one, two, three, or four words.
One should arrange eight fire-pits around the center of the array;
in an even-numbered array, one should designate them according to their respective numbers for the purpose of the fire-oblation.
Having invoked [the deity] within the path, the "street" (vīthi) is described in the scripture;
one should leave a space of exactly sixteen [units] all around the array of Śiva (śivavyūha).
The arrangement of the Sūtras has been fully explained; it is also described in another way.
One should lay down two threads extending from east to west and from south to north,
with an interval of one and a half cubits or even just one cubit.
There may be fourteen pathways (vīthī) counted in sequence on the exterior;
outside of that, the fire-oblation (homa) is desired to be performed in the four directions or the eight directions.
In the fifth chapter: The Procedure for the Daily Festival.
I shall now describe the procedure for the daily festival, which is the supreme limb of the daily worship.
[One should perform it] either in front of Śiva, or to his left, upon a pure patch of ground.
Or, having smeared a palace, pavilion, or similar structure with cow dung,
and having sprinkled it with the Astra-mantra, one should place there a vessel endowed with the proper characteristics.
It may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even fashioned from bell-metal;
beginning with fifteen finger-breadths (tithi-aṅgula) and increasing by one finger-breadth (vyoma-aṅgula) at each step.
The measurement of the vessel is declared to be thirty-two finger-breadths;
it should be circular, provided with a desired thickness, and adorned with a pericarp and petals.
In that vessel, divided by seven, eight, nine, ten, or eleven [parts],
the pericarp shall consist of one, two, three, four, five, or six parts.
By what remains, the petals are declared; the eight-petaled [lotus] is considered to have modifications.
The height of the pericarp (karṇikā) should be one and a half measures, or two measures.
In the same way, it should be provided with eight defects, or be merely a vessel starting from two *kuḍupas* up to one *āḍhaka*.
One should prepare rice for the purpose of the food-liṅga or for the sake of unbroken grains;
or one should place food mixed with honey and ghee into the center of the vessel.
Therefore, the food-liṅga should be made according to the measure of one's own body;
its length should be from one finger-breadth up to eighteen finger-breadths.
Starting from three finger-breadths, the width should be equal to the lunar days (tithis); it may be two, three, four, five, or even six finger-breadths at the tip.
The food-liṅga is prescribed for the sake of occasional rites as well as for daily rites;
or else, the food-liṅga may be offered at the three times of day, or at the morning and midday.
At midday or in the forenoon, the Puṣpa-liṅga is prescribed;
at dusk, there should be an Akṣata-liṅga, wherein one should worship the Pāśupata.
The Pāśupata is to be known as threefold—conjoined with Candraśekhara, devoid of Him, and mixed—as well as the peaceful (śānta) and the causeless (agrahetuka). || 13 ||
Gentle, endowed with gentle eyes, and possessed of two or four arms. || 131/2 ||
White like a garland of lightning, adorned with a crown of matted hair,
he holds the gesture of fearlessness and a rosary in his two right hands, and the gestures of granting boons and a noose in the other two.
Or he may have hands granting boons and fearlessness, endowed with all the auspicious marks;
or, having set aside the rosary and the noose, he may hold a lotus and a bell in sequence.
One should employ the gentle form; now the fierce form is described:
[the deity] has the base of a trident and the gestures of protection and fearlessness in the right hands, and the tip of a trident and the gesture of granting boons in the other two.

One should worship while recollecting the threefold fierce form: having a wrathful gaze, flaming hair, and holding a trident with hands crossed, or else holding a trident and an eye in his hands. 171/2.
Thus, the fierce [form] may be mixed; [he] bears an axe and a trident in the right hand, while the noose and the deer are in the left, or it is described otherwise.

The trident and the gesture of fearlessness are on the right, while the noose and the bestowing of boons are on the left; thus the Pāśupata mudrā is described as twofold in its mixed form. || 191/2 ||
He should be worshipped with flowers, unbroken rice grains, and cooked food upon liṅgas using his own mantra; or else, an image should be fashioned according to the prescribed measurements.
One should worship him upon a pedestal in the shape of a sphere, or even without a pedestal,
in the form of a food-liṅga, with its width equal at the base and the top.
Or one should worship [the deity] at the end of the measurement of the hand-span, endowed with all auspicious marks, together with the measuring-stick for the pedestal. || 221/2 ||
The image of the Lord whose crest is the moon should be fashioned according to the characteristics of an icon;
from that [base size], the sandals may be three finger-breadths, increasing by one finger-breadth at a time.
The length of those two is proclaimed to be the measure of a lunar day (tithi).
According to that length, the height should be made half of the width. (241½)
The middle measurement extends up to eight parts, while the ninth measurement is the highest;
between these two, either Vṛṣabha or Ananta is proclaimed as the one to be worshipped.
The guardians of the world (Lokapālas) are to be worshipped on all sides at the beginning and end of the worship;
then, one should conduct the daily festival accompanied by a liṅga made of fresh grain.
One should then perform a perpetual festival endowed with all of these,
using two, three, or four [verses] during the forenoon and at dusk.
At midday, the Lord known as Pāśupata is to be worshipped alone,
either on a stage, in a palanquin, or upon the heads of the attendants.
Having mounted it, adorned with deities and accompanied by attendants, provided with umbrellas and chowries, and endowed with various banners; || 291 || 2 ||
Accompanied by song and dance, joined with the sound of musical instruments,
and provided with incense and lamps, one should perform the circumambulation.
One should perform the first circumambulation accompanied by the *tāla* of Bhṛṅgin;
for the Bull, the *tāla* shall be that of Brahmā, and for Agni, the *tāla* shall be that of Bhṛṅgin.
For the Mothers, there should be the Caṇḍa-instrumental; for Vighnarāja, the Ḍhakkarī;
for Ṣaṇmukha, the Udghaṭa; and for Jyeṣṭhā, the Kuñcita-tāla.
A blow from Durgā upon the bank, marked with uneven signs,
[is auspicious] whether in a village, a city, or even on a rampart.
For this second circumambulation is the circumambulation of the Great Seat (Mahāpīṭha);
it may be performed once, twice, or thrice, accompanied by Śabarī.

Alternatively, one should perform two circumambulations: the first accompanied by the *brahmatāla* rhythm at the sacrificial pedestal (*balipīṭha*), and the second joined with the *gaṇatāla* rhythm. || 351½ ||
In the case of the Paiśāca [rite], there should be only one [offering] thus, combined with *cavarī* and *tāla*;
or at the city gate (*gopura*), it may be without musical instruments or accompanied by the sound of conchs.
Indra’s [mudrā] should have its palms joined together and be combined with the Gāndhāra note;
Agni’s [mudrā] should have the fingers bound and be accompanied by the Kolligāna [note]. (371–2)
To the south is Bhṛṅgiṇī with Tāla accompanied by Kauśika;
this is declared to be the Mallatāla in the Naṭṭa dialect in the southwest (nairṛtyāṃ).
In the west is Navatāla, joined with the sound of Kāmaradhu;
in the northwest is Balitāla, joined with the tone of Takkeśī.
In the north-eastern direction, Koṭika is said to be endowed with tarkarāga;
in the north-west, Śālā is joined with pāṇi, and Ḍhakkarī is considered to be in the north.
Having thus performed the circumambulation, one should enter the third abode;
with their feet washed, all should enter the temple of Śiva.
Alternatively, having worshipped the pedestal situated within the pavilion and the images with offerings such as water for the feet (pādya) and other services, one should cause them to enter.
Having summoned the deity from the *liṅga*, one should install him within the right *liṅga*;
the two sandals, representing the left and right feet of Śiva, are to be worshipped.
For other gods and goddesses as well,
one should perform the private recitation (svādhyāya) using either their primary image or another form that has been perfected for the purpose of the perpetual festival.
Having accomplished that, one should always perform the perpetual festival;
then that weapon, along with its own vehicle, should be worshipped upon the food-liṅga and other such supports.
The pair of sandals should be worshipped; everything else is the same.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the procedure for the daily festival (*nityotsava-vidhi*), in the great tantra named *Uttarakāmika*.
In the sixth chapter, the procedure for the great festival (*mahotsava-vidhi*):
I shall fully explain the festival according to the proper sequence.
The ritual action beginning with the raising of the banner and ending with its lowering is called a festival (utsava). || 1 ||

The Dhvajāṅkura should be at the base of the flagpole; one should lead it from the front of the flagpole, having first determined the asterism of the sacred ford (tīrtharkṣa), either to its east or at a distance three times that [measurement].
One should begin the hoisting of the flag on the second day of the lunar fortnight or on that very day;
the month-star (māsabha) and the constellation Ārdrā are auspicious for all months.

The birth-star and death-star of kings, or indeed their consecration-star, as well as the end of the sixth [tithi] in the month of Māgha, and the end of every lunar festival (parvan) in all months; || 4 ||

The period for those at a sacred ford (tīrtha) lasts until the equinox or solstice, or until an eclipse; for others, it lasts until the fourteenth or eighth day of the lunar fortnight, or until the conclusion of their respective festivals.
On the third or second day, or on that very day at either dawn or night,
the preceptor, preceded by the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), should raise the banner.
O twice-born ones, one should determine the length of the flagstaff to range from five cubits up to a *viśva* (ten thousand) cubits; this measurement is declared to be between the head and the tail.
Or else, that [measurement] combined with it should be taken, up to a maximum of four or seven [units];
having divided this into parts, the width of the cloth is said to be one part.
The tail is equal in width [to the body], or it is said to be three-quarters or half [of it]. The head should be known as half the width [of the body], provided with two tails.
One should draw two reed-banners joined together, and in their center, a bull endowed with auspicious long-life signs (āyādi), either standing or reclining on a bed.
Whether white, red-colored, or yellow, it should be possessed of hair;
likewise, it should be endowed with red horns and provided with hooves.
The bull, facing toward the village, should be depicted as wandering through the village and other areas,
with Viśvāmitra and others positioned upon its thirty-six mātrā-high hump.
Endowed with the portions of the [five] elements, possessing three colors and three eyes, joined with all auspicious marks, and adorned with a golden garland. || 13 ||
The banner-staff (dhvajadaṇḍa) should be made of one māna and two fingers;
it should be adorned with a cloth and a bull, joined with a lotus-seat and accompanied by two lamps at its sides.
It should be joined with two chowries, its head covered by a parasol,
and likewise provided with a full water-pot or a trident.
Having thus consecrated the bull, or having performed the ritual of opening its eyes,
one should sprinkle it with water from the Astra-mantra, either in front of Śiva or within the pavilion.
In a delightful place or another location provided with two sacrificial altars (sthaṇḍila),
one should place a vessel resting upon a tripod atop a cooking pot.
One should place a banner, a new water-pot, cloth, gold, jewels, and a brush,
along with a lid and a thread, upon the lordly bull in the middle [of the mandala].
It was surrounded by eight water-pots, each with its lid and cloth,
containing the world-protectors along with sacrificial grass, and preceded by the bull.
Having uttered the four [mantras] known as Ādhāra, Ananta, Dharmādi, and Vṛṣāsana-pada— each ending in the dative case and joined with the Heart-mantra (hṛt)— || 20 ||
Having first uttered the syllable *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*, one should here perform the sprinkling and seating;
then, having encased the letter *vṛ* within the heart, one should fashion the form of the Bull.
Having placed the Brahmamantras in the upper [parts], one should place the root-mantra imagined for those [locations];
then, one should sequentially install the heart and the other [limbs] as they were conceived.
One should install the forms and the lords of those forms,
preceded by the invocation (āvāhana) and other rites, starting from the root of the bull.
Having performed [the rite] with the Vṛṣabha-gāyatrī, one should worship [the deities] in sequence with perfumes and other offerings;
having worshipped [the central deity] in the central jar as well, one should sacrifice to the world-protectors (lokapālas) all around.
We meditate upon the Bull, who has sharp horns in his form, whose feet are the Vedas;
may that Bull inspire us.
In either a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), prepared as previously described,
one should duly fashion the Śiva-fire through the purificatory rites beginning with inspection (nirīkṣaṇa).
Then, having invoked the Bull (Vṛṣabha) in the midst of that [mandala], one should satisfy him along with his limbs by means of a hundred and eight oblations of ghee and sacrificial porridge (caru).
Immediately thereafter, one should offer oblations to Tatva, Tatveśvara, and the others; having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the root mantra, which fulfills all desires.

Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should present an offering of mung-bean rice to the Bull who resides in the cloth, who resides in the water-pot, and whose form is the seat.
In the morning, having worshipped the cloth and the pitcher in due order with perfumes and other offerings,
one should offer mouth-perfume and betel-leaf to the Bull.
Again, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) accompanied by all auspicious rites, joined with all musical instruments, and provided with dance and instrumental music; || 30 ||
Having placed the bull-bannered Lord upon a chariot or a palanquin,
accompanied by the Lord of Gods who is equipped with the trident.
Having led the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the village, he should enter toward the temple;
afterwards, he should install the staff endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
On the day of hoisting the banner, or even on the day of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa),
[the height] should be equal to the height of the temple, or twice or even three times that.
With a staff of six, seven, or eight cubits, one should strike three times below the navel.
Either up to one *tala* (story) or even up to the *gopura* (gate-tower).
Or it may be measured by a number of handspans equal to twice that of Rudra;
if the excavation is deeper than the middle or the smallest [measurement], it is considered excluded from [the proper] exterior.
Or any tree mentioned among those suitable for all types of stakes, such as the *tvaksāra*, the betel nut palm (*kramuka*), and so forth. || 351/2 ||
[The sacrificial posts] are made of Palāśa, Khadira, Aśvattha, Vaṭa, and Candana wood. || 36 ||
Or it may be made of *sālāmādhūka* wood, or even of *sārāmraka*.
It should be made from bamboo, or from the Jāti tree, or likewise from Śamī or Bilva wood.
Or it may be made of *campaka* wood, joined with twice eight [sixteen] or more days up to a threefold limit,
combined with its own natural number of days, and fashioned from trees with hard wood and bark.
The flagstaff (dhvajadaṇḍa) is thus described, and it is also called the flagpole (dhvajayaṣṭi).
Having determined the length of the staff by dividing it into nine parts starting from two parts, || 39 ||
O most excellent gurus, the flagstaff should be made according to a single proportion,
beginning at five finger-breadths and extending up to sixteen finger-breadths.
One should determine the circumference of the upadaṇḍa (the upper staff) to be proportionate;
having established the girth of the base as being from one-fifth to one-twelfth [of the total height]. || 41 ||
The tip [of the flagpole] should be one part less than the total length; likewise, the tip of the staff is prescribed.
The staff is said to be made of bamboo or of a tree suitable for a flagpole.
Then, for the sake of achieving the union of both, one should bring forth three heaps;
two of these heaps should be twelve finger-breadths in measure.
One should determine the length of the aggregate (skandha) up to a maximum of thirty-six finger-breadths,
beginning from seven finger-breadths and extending up to the number of syllables of the Gāyatrī (twenty-four).
The expansion of the *skandha* (trunk) is taught to be three parts from the base to the tip, or half, or three-quarters; it may be shaped like a ladle, as the case may be. (45)
Alternatively, their measurement is proclaimed to be four, three, or two finger-breadths.
At the edge of the lower trunk, there is a half-cavity at the tip of the staff.
It should be provided with a hollow at the base and the top, in accordance with the dimensions of the staff.
At the edge of the lower trunk, there is a half-circular hole at the tip of the staff.
A ring should be fixed either at the end of the staff or on the shoulder itself;
for one with broad shoulders, it should occupy one-third of the length, measuring three-quarters of the [staff's] thickness.
Beginning from six finger-breadths and increasing by six finger-breadths at each step,
the measurement for the trench of the staff extends from the tip of the staff down to the base of the circle.
Half of that, from the top of the base-ring upwards, is proclaimed as the tip of the staff;
the measure of the portion entering the ground is the length of the staff at its tip. (50)
Whether it be large or small, if a pit has been excavated,
one should place the ring-shaft (valayaskandha) there, extending as far as the tip of the staff (daṇḍāgra), provided it is situated outside that [pit].

O twice-born ones dwelling on earth, the measurement of the ground should be made by increasing [the width] by three finger-breadths at a time, starting from twenty-five units up to double that amount.
Beginning with one finger-breadth and increasing by a quarter-measure (pāda) up to a limit of three measures, the enclosures (valaya), provided with stakes (kīla), should be constructed.
This is either the space within the ring, or it is according to the strength of the ring;
there may be a rope in the middle of the ring, joined with a cord of one or more fingers in length. (54)
It should be endowed with a length suitable for the act of hoisting a banner;
it may be made of three strands as prescribed, or, in case of inability [to procure such], it may be a binding-cord.
Having thus prepared the cord and established the purification upon the staff,
one should wrap it entirely with garlands of *darbha* grass from top to bottom in due order.
One should place a tuft made of a hundred blades of darbha grass upon the tip of the staff;
having sprinkled it with water while reciting the Astra-mantra, one should deposit the principles (tattvas) beginning with Śiva-tattva.
Having divided the staff, which measures five plus one [six] units, into three parts from the top in sequence,
one should worship the Sun in those very same [parts] within the three sections of the circle.
The rope is declared to be Śakti, and Śiva shall be the staff-leader (daṇḍanāyaka).
One should worship the deity with perfumes and other offerings, and then commence the installation.
Then one should perform the placement of jewels;
one should install either a tortoise or a bull at the base of the staff.
Emerging from Haimaguñja and other places, it reaches the face of the temple of Mānanda.
O twice-born ones, one should place the staff, which has been worshipped with its respective mantras, upside down;
then, one should place another staff above it so that there is a handle at the top.
The staff [of the banner] should have its face toward the temple, positioned either at the tip of the bull or behind it;
likewise, it may also be placed near the gateway (gopura) or close to the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha).
From the center of the middle gopura of the inner maṇḍala hall and so forth,
there should be nine, five, or one daṇḍa [in length] toward each of the four cardinal directions.
The principal [deity] is situated in the eastern region; the banners are measured by that same number.
Furthermore, the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) are in the eight directions, and the [gods] beginning with Nara are in the four cardinal directions.
The lords of the quarters are declared [to be placed] on the cloth-paintings, and indeed the bull itself [is placed there].
At the base of the staff, however, an altar (vedikā) should be constructed, which is of many kinds.
Starting from one cubit (*hasta*) and increasing by three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) at a time,
the width of the altar (*vedikā*) is considered to extend up to a maximum of two cubits.
The pedestal (vedikā) is proclaimed to be equal in height to the base, or three-quarters of it, or seven or five-eighths, or four or three-eighths, or half as high as the base. 671/2.
Alternatively, it may be provided with three girdles, each measuring eight finger-breadths;
or else, the measurement of the girdles is stated to be reduced by two or three finger-breadths respectively.
On a pedestal devoid of a girdle (mekhalā), there should be a small platform (upavedikā) at the base;
according to the rule, it should increase by two finger-breadths (aṅgula) for each subsequent level, up to six finger-breadths.
The heights are proclaimed to be equal to one and a half, one-quarter, and three-quarters of a *pāda* respectively.
Above the altar, a lotus should be fashioned with a measurement of four *aṅgulas*.
The height of the lotus is declared to extend up to eighteen finger-breadths by increasing the space by one finger-breadth at a time; its width is equal to that of the pedestal.
The procedure for the Rudra-measure consists of an entry of one finger-breadth per unit;
this is known as the Padma-entry, wherein there should be a lotus complete with a pericarp.
The emergence of the pericarp from the stalk should be made by increasing one part at a time along a single path, up to a limit of three finger-breadths; this is called its height.
One should fashion a lotus with four or eight petals, or even one with spreading petals; it may be circular or square, and it should be encircled by a border.
Likewise, it may be provided with a pedestal or even without one;
having prepared the seat in this manner, one should have it fashioned by a craftsman to his satisfaction.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited, and having sprinkled the altar with the Astra-mantra,
one should encircle the staff, the bull-pitcher, and its cloth with darbha grass.
Equipped with a trident and adorned with auspicious sprouts,
having led it around the sanctuary by way of circumambulation, one brings it into the presence of the staff.
One should place the one called Ādhāra and Ananta within the tortoise;
and in the center of the corners, one should arrange Dharma and the others, as well as Adharma and the others.
Having worshipped Vāmā and the others on the eight petals, Manonmanī in the pericarp, and Sadāśiva on the staff, with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in due order; || 791/2 ||
And that [image], endowed with the three aims of life (trivarga), should be worshipped according to the procedure prescribed for the ritual bathing. || 80 ||
Having tied the bull-cloth with a rope while reciting the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra, and having attached a small bell while recollecting the weapon mantra (śastramantra), [he should proceed]. 81.
Having taken the seed from the pot while recollecting the form of the bull, the Guru,
having placed it upon the heart of the lordly bull, should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
The preceptor should quickly mount the bull by means of the root-mantra of the bull;
having first touched it himself, he should then cause another to mount for the purpose of ascending.
When the bull is facing downward on the ground, there is peace for the king, especially;
when the cloth is held upward, there is victory for the king and satisfaction for the gods and ancestors.
When the moon is in conjunction with the asterisms beginning with Ārdrā and ending with Svātī, the departure of Dhvaja is auspicious;
security, health, victory, and nourishment are declared to be the results in successive order. (85)
Death through austerity and a great disease will be the result from the southeast; one should know that there is danger from the northwest, and the same results apply to the tail as well. (86)
If the cloth is obstructed during the mounting due to a fault of the instructor,
one should then effect the pacification of that defect while recollecting Bahurūpa.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice into the sacred fire;
then, one should sprinkle the base of the staff with water contained in a bull-shaped vessel.
The Guru should sprinkle the eight petals in the directions starting from the east with the waters of those [deities], namely the eight Lords of the Vidyās of the Bull (Vṛṣavidyeśvara), in due order.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should offer food along with sweets;
beginning from that auspicious day (puṇyāha) until the offering of the food (naivedya).
Accompanied by all musical instruments and endowed with the sound of singing,
one should perform dancing in the four directions, especially pure dancing (śuddhanartana).
From this point until reaching the holy ford (tīrtha), ending with the descent,
one should worship the Bull (Vṛṣa) once, twice, or thrice a day.
In whatever kingdom this installation of the flagstaff is performed,
there is no untimely death nor misfortune, even among those who have committed sins.
Therein, there was no fear of calamities, nor any confusion regarding the arrival of others;
even for those who were ill, contrary thoughts did not arise for the most part. 94.
The rain-cloud pours forth at its proper time, there is abundance of food, and the king is victorious;
all evils are pacified, and the milk-yielding cows are full of milk. 95.
An ungrateful person, a killer of a Brahmin, or a killer of a cow— upon seeing the encampment of the banner-bearer—
attains liberation from sin for both families of the performer of the sacrifice.
The sounding of drums at night should be performed according to the prescribed rule;
one should prepare two sacrificial altars (sthaṇḍila) in the presence of the God of gods.
The supreme gurus should fashion the sixfold seat as the trident-drum;
one should place the trident in one spot and set the drum in its vicinity.

Having first caused the proclamation of an auspicious day for a trident that is oriented from east to west, situated in the east, and endowed with faces turned toward the south, one should install the deity upon it. (99)
Rudra should be in the middle leaf, Brahmā on the right leaf,
and having invoked Viṣṇu on the left, one should place Pārvatī in the *pālikā*.
Senānī is at the region of the frontal globe (kumbha), while Vighnarājaka is at its mouth;
Bhāskara is to be known as being at the tip of the staff (daṇḍa) in Madana, and at the middle of the staff.
Caṇḍeśa is at the base of the staff, Lakṣmī is at the tip of the eastern petal,
the seven Mothers are on the right, and Jyeṣṭhā is on the petal in the western direction.
Kātyāyanī, however, is considered to be in the north at the base of the trident;
these are the eighteen groups consisting of the Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and the two Aśvins. (103)
Having summoned them and pronounced blessings, one should install the deities of the drum;
having wrapped the drum with cloth, one should worship Rudra in its center.
One should worship Brahmā on the right face and Viṣṇu on the left face;
one should worship Sūrya on the right armlet and Candra on the other.
Having placed the Mothers upon seven pegs, the nine Planets upon nine pegs, the Rudras upon that same number [of pegs], and Vāsuki upon the leather thongs; 106.

During the sixth watch, the preceptor should first worship Ṣaṇmukha on the head with separate substances such as perfumes, flowers, and so forth, ending with food offerings, while reciting the heart-mantra.
One should strike the drum while recollecting the mantra of the weapon;
the first blow is made once, and the second blow is made twice.
Having struck the third [drum] three times and the other three with a single stroke,
he should sprinkle the player while recollecting the five-syllabled mantra.
One should place the garment, the perfume, the garland, the upper cloth, and the thread into his hand, while recollecting that mantra. (110)
Then, having cast a flower upon the drum with the permission of the preceptor,
one who is skilled in all rhythmic measures should place the drum upon Skanda and cause it to be sounded.
Endowed with musical notes such as Gāndhāra and others, accompanied by rhythmic measures such as Sama-tāla, joined with song and dance, and provided with an offering of food and a liṅga. || 112 ||
Having taken up the King of Weapons (Astrarāja) together with a statue, or else accompanied by Caṇḍeśvara, and provided with a canopy and an umbrella; 113.
Accompanied by incense and lamps, and joined with the sound of the bell,
one should enter the city and so forth, proceeding in order from the station of Brahmā.
Or else, one should offer the bali-oblation from the station of Indra and so forth, using one's own name;
at the conclusion of the bali-offering, however, it should be accompanied by the sound of the tāla rhythm.
One should have it performed with dancing in their respective directions;
for the Brahmāṇīs, there should be the *brahmatāla* accompanied by the melody of the *megharāga*.
Samatāla, Gāndhāra, Kollī, and Baddhāvaṇa; then Bhṛṅgiṇī, Kauśika, Naṭṭa, and Mallatālaka in the Bhāṣā [language]. || 117 ||
The offering of a sacrifice (*bali*) to her hair was performed by one named Śrīkāmaranava; with a brilliance like ten million suns, she reached the hall with her hand. 118.
Aligned with the directions starting from the east, just as in the case of the eastern tāla,
the hoisting of the banner should take place at the beginning of the festival on the third day.
If the beating of the drum occurs first on that day, it is considered to be double [the merit];
having prepared four sacrificial altars (sthaṇḍila) in the presence of the deity.
Having first placed the form of the Weapon (astra), one should then set up the cloth-painting (paṭa) before it;
before that, there should be a bull and a water-pot (kumbha), accompanied by the Bull (Vṛṣabha) and the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśvara).
One should place the drum, endowed with all auspicious characteristics, in front of that;
having worshipped these [deities] in sequence with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in due order.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) either within the hollow of a kettle-drum or upon an altar (sthaṇḍila);
having worshipped according to the previously stated rule, one should then install the principles (tattvas) and so forth.
Having performed the invocation of the deity upon the trident by the previously mentioned method,
one should strike the drum and take hold of the trident accompanied by the bull.
Equipped with the various liṅgas and accompanied by all musical instruments,
having performed the circumambulation of the village and including the invocation of the deities, [he should proceed].
At the conclusion of the time for offering the oblation,
the preceptor shall enter the place of the banner and perform the hoisting of the banner according to the previously stated procedure.
At night, one should perform this proclamation preceded by the beating of drums;
and during the day, one should carry out the circumambulation of the consecrated banner.
At the time of invoking the deities, one should avoid the confusion regarding the bull;
thereafter, the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) is prescribed at night on the day the sacrifice begins.
For that purpose, one should perform the ritual of the sprout (aṅkura), or else omit it;
however, the circumambulation of the village and the rite for the sacred water-sprout (tīrthāṅkura) are considered mandatory.
One should cause all others as well to perform [the rite], or one may avoid it;
however, prior to the offering of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), at the time of evening, [one should take] earth.
Having collected [the seeds], one should sow them at night for the sake of the success of the sprouts;
this is prescribed on that very day, preceded by the beating of a drum.
Everything else has been fully described as being preceded by the offering of the ritual sprouts;
however, the commencement of the sacrifice to Śiva must be performed on that very night.
On the ninth day there shall be the Ketv-aṅkura, and on the seventh day the Utsavāṅkura.
Having thus resolved, one should worship the King of Weapons (the Astra-mantra) on the preceding day;
thereafter, one should construct the sacrificial hall either in front [of the temple] or at its front and sides.
Likewise, in each of the five halls located in the desired place on the left side,
and especially in the central hall, according to the measurement of five cubits.
By increasing by one cubit [at a time], the rule for the [mandala] measuring eleven cubits is established;
it is joined with three rows or provided with five rows.
Or they may be of equal rows by increasing one part from the measure of the *mātrā*;
however, there are five additional rows according to the measurement up to nine *aṅgulas*.
It may also be joined with a single row [of pillars], or it may be very large with four doors, or even provided with a single door, arranged in the form of a pavilion (maṇḍapa). || 1371/2 ||
Or it may resemble a heap of grain, joined with nine or five fires, or even joined with a single fire, and provided with a canopy and banners. || 1381/2 ||
It was adorned with a garland of *darbha* grass, hung with strings of pearls,
provided with coconut fruits, and decorated with every kind of ornament.
In the middle [section], it should be provided with a pedestal (vedikā) and measure one cubit (vasu) in size;
by increasing by one finger-breadth (aṅgula), it extends up to twenty-eight fingers.
The height of the altar (vedikā) is prescribed as one-third of its width;
alternatively, it may be according to the measure of a row, provided with secondary deities.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should measure one muṣṭi, one ratni, or one kara;
it may be either quadrangular or circular, and should be provided with three girdles (mekhalās).
One should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) for the sacrifice in a pavilion or in a flower garden and the like;
having thus completed everything, one should carry out the dismissal of the artisan.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should at the conclusion perform the *vāstuhoma* sacrifice,
or else the ritual for seizing the ground (*bhūparigraha*), which is joined with the head of all sacrifices.
One should construct an altar-platform in the center, endowed with the proper characteristics,
increasing from one *droṇa* up to nine *droṇas*.
It should be provided with half as much rice, combined with half as much sesame;
likewise provided with parched grain, and combined with half as much sesame.
It is endowed with a variegated pericarp, adorned with blazing petals,
enriched with lines of sesame seeds, parched grain, and other offerings, and encircled by darbha grass.
Increasing by one starting from five, according to the number of the final element among the principles (tattvas),
one should place within that [space] the jar named Śiva, accompanied by the Vardhanī vessel.
Accompanied by the eight Lords of Knowledge (Aṣṭavidyeśvaras) and joined by the enclosure of the water-pots (Kumbhāvaraṇa),
all [the deities] are adorned with threads and garments, and embellished with golden lotuses.

Provided with lids and water-strainers, possessing the luster of ripe bimba fruits, they were endowed with the correct proportions established by the perfection of meditation during the ritual bathing.
One should place nine gems in the vessel called Śiva, five gems in the Vardhanī,
and gold in the vessels of Lokeśa and the others, as well as in the external jars.
A wealthy person should perform it in this manner; for one of middling means, there should be a pair of garments, as well as arches, door-pots, and the jars of the world-protectors.
Having set aside Śiva, who is accompanied by the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa) and endowed with Śakti,
one should install the ten weapons together with the eight auspicious objects (maṅgalāṣṭaka).
Having thus completed everything, one should perform the rite of the *pratisara* (protective cord),
using a thread made of gold, silver, or even cotton.
The cover, made of gold or silver, should correspond in circumference to the width of the image’s chest; it should be slightly larger in measurement and adorned with the hoods of the serpent kings.
That thread joined with its tail and provided with the form of a banner is placed upon the head of the deity, either on a golden or a silver [pedestal]. (1561/2)
For the sake of accomplishing all desires, there should be a single thread;
it is said that when knotted and provided with a ring-grasper, it is the most excellent.

If that which is described in the sūtras as consisting of linen cloth and so forth is composed of the three principles (tattva), it is traditionally held to consist of the [sixteen] kalās for the sake of pacification, and for the sake of victory.
The ritual act, consisting of the nine principles, should be performed according to the authoritative rules for the sake of health;
if it includes the six limbs and the subsidiary limbs of the Mūrti-pāṅga, it bestows the fruits of sons and long life.
Having corrected the circumference according to the appropriate measurement by adding one, two, or three finger-breadths,
and having likewise washed it with water and smeared it with sandalwood paste.
One should place the ashes upon the support for the ashes while recollecting the Eye-mantra in the center;
having prepared a separate sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) for each, one should place them above that, upon the yantra.

Having placed the vessel and filled it with rice resembling stars, measuring between two *prasthas* and not less than that, up to a *droṇa* and so forth, while recollecting the Heart-mantra; ||| 1621/2 ||
In the middle of that, one should place a thread provided with a support for the ashes,
together with an unbroken pair of smooth betel-nut kernels.
One should place upon the sacrificial mound betel leaf that has not had its root cut, accompanied by water, a face-cloth, and a thread. 1641/2.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should sprinkle [the site] with water while reciting the *Hṛdaya* mantra.
One should worship Śakti upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and the three principles (*tritatva*) within the yantra.
The principle of Pradhāna is in the vessel; the rice-grains are considered to be like the staff. Umā is said to be in the receptacle for the ashes, and Lakulīśvara is in the ashes.
In the ritual manual, one should worship Ananta and the others in sequence with perfumes and other offerings;
having covered the vessel with silk cloths and the like, one should place a garland upon it.
Adorned with all ornaments and accompanied by all musical instruments,
he should circumambulate the village or the temple from left to right.
One should have [the image] made, or else one should avoid it; then one should worship the Lord of Gods.
Having taken hold of the thumb and the ring finger of the left hand, (one should perform the rite). 1691/2.
One should apply ashes mixed with a thread from between the two fingers of the right hand,
while recollecting the *Netra-mantra* in the *anuṣṭubh* meter on every forearm joint.
There, one should bind the deities and apply the sacred ash;
for all the goddesses, with one's whole being, either on the left or on the right.
Likewise,
the preceptor and the others should give betel nut along with fruits, cakes, and coconut fruits to the people.
One should give to the deity and to the devotees, or cause them to be given, or one should avoid it;
whether Skanda is present along with him or Skanda is absent, [this applies] to the moon-crested Lord Śiva.
Whether joined with or separated from the Goddess, especially in the form of a dance;
or Umā seated comfortably on the left side of Maheśvara, while Maheśvara [is seated] on the right.
And one should fashion another [image] of gentle form for the festival; the auspicious thread (kautuka) is prescribed for one, two, three, or all of them, according to one's desire.
If the rite of circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa) of the village and other sites has been performed as a preliminary act,
this procedure is proclaimed for the day of commencing the sacrifice.
On another day, during the middle of the festival,
or on a desired day, the *kautuka* (auspicious thread) should be applied to the image during the preceding night.
Whether the image (bera) is fierce or peaceful, the ritual is prescribed for one who is a devotee of Śiva;
it may be performed on a trident, on the middle petal [of a lotus], or even upon the hand of the deity situated therein.
The binding of threads for all ten weapons is prescribed;
one should perform it either on the day before the commencement of the sacrifice or on that very day. (1791) 2.
The preceptor, having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon his body, should first prepare the sprout for the sake of the sacred ford (tīrtha) together with the image-makers.
Having performed the worship of the door and entered the sacrificial hall,
one should again perform the sacrifice to Brahmā, the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), and the ritual of integration (sakalīkaraṇa).
Having performed the threefold rite beginning with the water for the feet (pādya), one should sprinkle [the area] with the water of the arghya offering;
then, having prepared the seat of Śiva upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) on the altar (vedikā).
Having fashioned the form in the Śiva-pitcher, one should project it by means of the Mūrti-mantra;
having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the five Brahmans, one should conceive of it as consisting of those [five] Kalās.
Having conceived the body of knowledge (vidyādeha), one should install the auspicious Praṇava;
then, having installed the heart and other limbs, one should worship it with water for the feet and other offerings.
Having thus performed the nyāsa of Manonmanī, one should worship her with the Śakti-mantra;
having worshipped the Vidyeśvaras all around, one should then fully worship the Lokapālas.
Then, having worshipped the weapons, one should worship the mirrors and other items;
they may be placed either on the outer edge of the altar, or upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or even on a flat surface.
Or, having worshipped [the deities] in the eight directions, two by two in the cardinal directions,
one should worship the King of Weapons (Astrarāja) at the end of that, stationed upon the sacrificial altars (sthaṇḍila) in the eight directions.

Having worshipped in this manner in due order, the Guru should go to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa); having consecrated the pit according to the rite, he should bring forth the Śiva-fire according to the prescribed method.
Having divided [the site] ninefold or fivefold and having placed [the deities] in their respective fire-pits (kuṇḍa) according to their own directions,
one should invoke Śiva along with his limbs (aṅgas) and Brahmā as a limb, and then offer libations (tarpaṇa).
In the four cardinal directions there should be those beginning with Nara, and in the intermediate directions those beginning with Hṛdaya;
one should satisfy them with all the mantras, each according to its own primary mantra.
Bamboo shoots, bilva fruits, or barley, as well as groats with milk,
barley-sized pieces, sesame, mustard seeds, or mung beans, are prescribed for the rite of fire-oblation (homa).
Or with *brahmaśāli* rice and barley, or with *māṣa* beans, *śāli* rice, and barley;
likewise sesame, mustard, and mung beans, as well as parched grain flour, bamboo shoots, molasses, and honey.
O lords of sages, the materials for the oblation have thus been declared to be fourfold;
one should offer fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, and parched grain within these four categories.
One should perform one hundred and eight oblations with Śiva and his limbs at a tenth part [of the total];
then, for the sake of the *kalā* (sixteenth part), they should offer oblations in sequence into the other primary fire-pits.
In some Śiva-āgamas, mantras are indeed taught according to the distinction of substances;
however, in this [system], no differentiation of mantras based on such distinctions is prescribed.

One should offer the oblation either at the conclusion of the *homa* or at its beginning; the offering of the *bali* should take place at the end of that. The procedure for this is now described here.
Having fashioned a linga made of sacrificial oblation (havis) according to the rite of perpetual festival, and having worshipped there the King of Weapons accompanied by the trident; || 1971/2 ||
Equipped with the ten weapons, provided with incense and lamps,
accompanied by the sound of the bell, and joined with the materials for the bali offering.
Accompanied by various umbrellas and provided with various musical instruments,
the preceptor or the disciple himself shall enter the city and so forth.
At the place where the deities are invoked, one should offer the bali-oblation in due order:
sweetmeat balls (laḍḍuka), sugar-coated sweets (modaka), mung-bean cakes (maudga), molasses (guḍa), and parched grain flour (saktu) to Gaṇeśvara.
Milk-rice, powdered at night, lotus flowers, and parched grain— this, which is dear to Brahmā, is to be offered on the second day as prescribed.
On the third day, kṛsarā rice mixed with ghee and combined with plantain fruit should be offered as a cause for the gratification of the spirits (bhūtas).
Combined with the powder of *rātri* and provided with coconut fruit, it should be administered on the fourth day; this is indeed beloved by the Gandharvas.
Ghee combined with priyaṅgu and endowed with indravallī should be administered on the fifth day; it will become pleasing to Indra.
On the sixth day, bamboo-seed food mixed with ghee and accompanied by jackfruit should be offered for the sake of pleasing and accomplishing the aims of the sages.
On the seventh day, rice mixed with ghee and combined with the fruit of the *bṛhatī* plant should be offered; this will be pleasing to Śrī.
On the eighth day, rice mixed with black gram, combined with ghee and goat meat, should be offered for the sake of pleasing and accomplishing the purpose of the Rākṣasa.
Pure rice, curd, barley meal, along with parched grain and flowers, should be placed in a new vessel; this shall be pleasing to Śiva.
Alternatively, the substance for the deity is described in another way:
pure rice mixed with curd, combined with sweetmeats and cakes.
Fruit combined with molasses is dear to Gaṇeśa;
likewise are fruit, the powder of turmeric, ghee-rice, curd, and parched grain flour.
Kṛsara is prescribed for the bhūtas; therefore, an offering (bali) should be made to them with that. || 211 ||
One should offer an oblation to the sages consisting of lotus roots, tips of kuśa grass, rice mixed with ghee, and combined with plantain fruit. || 212 ||
Indravallī, haridrā, and priyaṅgu, combined with ghee,
should be offered on the fourth day for the satisfaction of this Śakra.
On the fifth day, milk-rice (pāyasa), powdered rice, lotus flowers, and parched grain should be offered; this shall be pleasing to Brahmā.
On the sixth day, rice mixed with ghee and combined with the fruit of the *bṛhatī* plant should be offered for the sake of increasing the pleasure of Viṣṇu. (215)
Kṛsarā rice mixed with ghee and coconut fruit should be offered on the seventh day; this shall be pleasing to Śiva.
For the sake of accomplishing the propitiation of Īśvara, bamboo-seed food mixed with curd and accompanied by plantains and jackfruit should be offered on the eighth day.
On the ninth day, pure food mixed with curd, along with parched grain and flowers, should be offered for the sake of pleasing Caṇḍeśa.
O twice-born ones, the articles for the deities regarding the nine days have been described;
hereafter, those pertaining to the twelve-day rite are being told.
On the first day, one should offer food made of mung beans, sweetmeat balls (laḍḍuka), clarified butter, plantains, and jaggery, while recollecting the mantra that dispels obstacles.
Red rice mixed with meat, combined with kṛsarā and cakes, joined with ghee and fish, and accompanied by japā flowers. || 221 ||
On the second day, one should offer milk-rice, barley meal, and flowers, including lotus blossoms, while reciting the Paiśāca mantra.
On the third day, while recollecting the Brahma-mantra,
one should offer kṛsarā-rice, ghee, parched grain flour, and sweetmeat balls.
On the fourth day, one should offer [the oblation] while reciting the Gandharva mantra:
Indravallī, turmeric, rice, ghee, and parched grain.
On the fifth day, one should offer food made of jujube fruit mixed with ghee and accompanied by coconut fruit, while recollecting the Bhūta-mantra.
On the sixth day, recollecting the mantra of Skanda,
one should offer the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass mixed with ghee, along with pure food combined with curd.
On the seventh day, reciting the mantra of the sages,
one should offer milk-rice and rice flour mixed with pieces of sugarcane.
On the eighth day, recollecting the mantra of the Nāgas,
one should offer curd-rice mixed with molasses, as well as citron fruit.
On the ninth day, recollecting the mantra dedicated to Indra,
one should offer food made with molasses mixed with clarified butter, accompanied by plantains and jackfruit.
One should offer ten oblations while recollecting the mantra of Viṣṇu;
[the offering should consist of] red food mixed with meat, and cakes combined with sesame powder.
On the eleventh day, one should offer [the food] while reciting the mantra for the Rākṣasas:
rice mixed with curd, combined with jaggery and sugar-candy.
On the twelfth day, one should give [the gift] while recollecting the Śiva-mantra;
or on the seventh day, or the fifth, or the third, or on the night of the sky (the new moon).
Having first abandoned the former, the supreme [deities] have been proclaimed; O best of sages, the deities of the daily materials and the materials for the daily oblation have been described. (233)
First, there should be an offering (bali) to the gods, beginning with Brahmā, using these substances;
for the sake of satisfying the Lord of the Day (the Sun), pure rice mixed with curd [should be offered]. (234)
For the sake of satisfying the Lords of the World, one should offer [oblations] to the Lokapālas and others with their respective mantras,
in due order, to the retinues beginning with Vṛṣa, to the banner, and to those beginning with Brahmā.
Having offered the bali at that point, one should then offer the bali in sequence upon the bali-pīṭha;
from the banner (dhvaja) up to the end of the bali-pīṭha—this is declared to be the bali. || 236 ||
Or [the offering] may extend from Brahmā down to the base of the pedestal (balipīṭha), or from Śakra down to the base of the pedestal;
or there may be an offering at the base of the pedestal for the respective presiding deities of the days.
Or a bali offering with pure food may be made for the satisfaction of the gods of the day and others;
or a bali offering to the lords of the world (lokeśas) may be placed to the left of the gods of the day.
Alternatively, an offering (bali) may be made to the world-protectors (lokapālas) with the substances used for the daily deity-offerings;
furthermore, for all the days, there should be two offerings per day.
One should perform instrumental music for one of those two, or on both days of the bali-offering;
one should present the bali in the evening and in the morning, or at that specific time or at its conclusion.
The pilgrimage must be undertaken; the sequence of the journey is described here:
in the first [stage] there should be the bull-vehicle, and in the second, that suitable for wandering.
The swinging apparatus (ḍolāyantra) should be in the third [position], and after that the horse-apparatus (vājiyantra);
the lion-apparatus (siṃhmayantra) is declared after that, and then there should be the lamp-apparatus (dīpayantra). || 242 ||
Then the ram-mechanism is to be known, and after that the chariot-mechanism;
O best of the twice-born, these beautiful forms should be fashioned one after another.
Various other forms have been described at the conclusion of that;
at the end of that, there should be an offering of oblations (balidāna) accompanied by a sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha).
It is joined with the *annaliṅga* and endowed with a trident;
it is equipped with the ten weapons and united with the *golaka-liṅga*. || 245 ||
At the end of that [procession], one should place Gaṇeśas mounted on chariots, and then Nandikeśvara,
either on a chariot or in a palanquin, adorned with all ornaments.
Deprived of all these [qualities] and endowed with fierce and weak limbs, at the end of that [period], he will subsequently be a loud-mouthed actor for the sake of mere livelihood. (247)
At its end was the chariot of the Lord of the Gods, beautiful in all its parts,
and especially adorned by two figures stationed at the front of the chariot.
He was resplendent, flanked by my two daughters holding fly-whisks made of ghee,
with a white umbrella of the brilliance of the nine gems held over his head.
He was accompanied by a Śaiva teacher who had come into my presence, standing behind me and intent upon his duties for me. (250)
By my devoted and heedless attendant, with hands bound by a noose fashioned from lotus buds. (251)
He was adorned by the daughter of Rudra, who bore a human form,
as well as by my maidservant Sarvāṅgasundarī and the chariot.
At its end is the chariot of the Lord of the Gods, adorned in the same manner;
and at its end is the [pedestal] of Caṇḍanātha, either separate or provided with another.
There are the sixteen images and others belonging to Śiva;
and for those who are renowned as devotees of Śiva, there are many kinds of colors.
O best of the twice-born, those [plants] that grow in front or behind [the sacrificial post] are not to be taken;
however, whatever among them is desirable should be accepted as a portion for the *bali* offering, excluding the *kautuka*.
It was provided with various musical instruments, accompanied by elephants, horses, and camels, equipped with the sweeping of the streets, and attended by the sprinkling of water. || 256 ||
The house was provided with applied plaster, powders, and various paintings; it was endowed with auspicious sprouts, beautiful lamps, and water-pots for prosperity.
It was joined with plantains and betel-nut trees, adorned with fine silken cloths and the like, provided with garlands of *darbha* grass, and decorated with strings of pearls. || 258 ||
Above and below, from level to level,
one should place lamp-stands if there is a row of lamps at night.
The decoration of the house is prescribed even in a place devoid of a house;
it should be provided with various banners and accompanied by various musical instruments. || 260 ||
It was endowed with various musical instruments, accompanied by various dances,
provided with various umbrellas, and joined with peacock-feather fans.
One should perform this daily, both by day and by night during the great festival, providing it with palm-leaf fans and accompanied by incense and lamps.
Whether on a chariot or a palanquin, or upon the heads of attendants, betel-leaf and various fruits should be offered at the time of departure. (263)
Having given edible items such as cakes and roots, as well as a screen-curtain and so forth, one should,
according to the distinction between the worthy and the unworthy, [offer] objects that are either burnt or fresh in due order.
Everything is considered burnt by the twice-born, while for a Śūdra it is considered moist;
[the food] should be prepared with its skin removed or with its essence extracted, and purified through ritual inspection and other means.
Accompanied by the sound of conchs and provided with water for the feet and for sipping,
one should remove the concealed cloth once the removal of the faded garlands has been performed.
Having given offerings to all my devotees in due order, one should likewise give to other guests according to their respective degrees of devotion. || 267 ||

Having entered the sanctum and offered water for the feet and other services daily to Śambhu seated upon his throne— beginning with the primary peak-shaped seat— and having performed the ritual bath accompanied by the peace-offering (śāntihoma), [one should proceed].

The ritual action is for the sake of pacifying the touch of chariots and the like that have been handled by carpenters and others, and especially for the purpose of removing the defects caused by the sight and touch of a Caṇḍāla. || 269 ||
O most excellent gurus, this must be understood as an essential requirement for every undertaking;
however, in the event of inability, one may perform a ritual bath (snapana) instead of the peace-offering (śāntihoma).
Furthermore, when my vehicle has been prepared outside the fivefold enclosure, one should perform the ritual ablution provided it is accompanied by five khāris [of offerings]. (271)
One should reverently bathe the deity with forty bhāras of water, or half of that, or a quarter, or even less than that.
One should especially perform the rite of bathing during a hunting expedition;
this, when performed at its proper time, is proclaimed to be the bestower of desired fruits. (273)
The daily worship at the morning twilight, entering the sacrificial pavilion, ascending the chariot and other vehicles, and thereafter the midday worship. (274)
In the case of a chariot, the ritual ends with the offering of incense; in the temple of Śiva, it ends with the food offering (naivedya);
thereafter follows the ceremonial bathing for the festival, and then the occasional worship (naimittikārcana).
At the end, there is the viewing of the diversion, followed by worship at nightfall;
then again the performance of the oblation and the settling [of the deity], and thereafter the circumambulation of the village. || 276 ||
The ceremonial bath for the sake of the journey, worship, the viewing of dance, song, and so forth, then the entry into the temple and the settling down together with the Goddess. || 277 ||
When sixteen units of time had elapsed and half a watch (yāmārdha) was completed,
these deities performed their prescribed rites at the Kṛtasaras lake.
These rites, when performed at their proper time, accomplish all objectives;
however, there is lack of nourishment when the planet is in the preceding sign, and inauspiciousness when it is in the subsequent sign. (279)

Therefore, one should perform everything with every effort at the prescribed time; for even if performed at one's own convenience, there may be a fault, whereas it should be performed at the subsequent time.
At the time of the vehicle, at the time of the offering (bali), or at the initial time,
one should perform [the rite] upon the bali-pīṭha according to the path described for the retinue.
The seat may be made of cotton, wood, or iron, or it may be smeared with clay;
one may either enter the sacrificial pavilion or enter the inner chamber. || 282 ||
In that regard, one should either avoid the offering of betel leaves and such, or perform it;
if it is abandoned at the prescribed time, one should perform a propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma). || 283 ||
At night, the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) should be performed at the conclusion of the incense and lamps;
furthermore, abundant sacrificial food (havis) should be offered at the conclusion of the time for the procession.
One should perform this every day; however, the specific details are now being stated.
[This should be done] either within a village or outside it, in a constructed pavilion or similar structure. (285)
Having led the deity and propitiated him, and after providing entertainment and sights,
one should then enter the temple or lead him to the entire village.
One should perform the ritual in exactly this same manner upon entering [the city], or at the onset of rain, or even when there is apprehension of future rain, or in great darkness. (287)
