The pacification oblation (śāntihoma) should be performed at the beginning of the rite, during the remaining circumambulation, on the day the sacrifice begins, or even on the day of the gift at a sacred ford (tīrtha). || 288 ||
If one should cause the entire village to circumambulate [the image], no expiation is prescribed;
however, if the circumambulation of the village is omitted, one should have the fire-oblation (diśāhoma) performed.
When the sky is clear and the moon is visible, one must certainly perform the procession of the image (berayātrā) and constantly offer oblations (bali). || 290 ||
On the fifth day of the holy site (tīrtha), or on the preceding fourth day,
one should perform an oil massage, or one with powdered substances at night on that same day.

The offering of betel-leaf, together with other rites, should be performed in sequence for the deity, the devotees, and others; likewise, the raising of the banner should also be done in the leftward manner.
One should place the oil before the deity upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) on top of a yantra;
having sprinkled it with the Astra-mantra, one obtains [the fruit] through the Saṃhitā-mantra.
Then, having protected [it] with the Kavaca mantra, one should worship it with perfumes and other offerings using the Hṛdaya mantra.
One should gradually place oil mixed with the *śivatattva* and other [mantras] joined with the root mantra and ending in "namaḥ," along with flowers and night-powders, upon the head.
One should perform [the ritual] on the goddess from the forehead down to the feet and arms, or down to the throat;
having performed the bath either there or elsewhere, one should offer the food of the Maudga [grains].
One should perform the circumambulation of Naṭeśa on the day before the Tīrtha festival, or even on the day prior to that; half of it may be performed during the preceding night.
One should have a festive rite performed according to the previous procedure for the sake of the dancing image,
which is adorned with all ornaments and especially honored.
Therefore, elsewhere— whether on a dais, in an arena, or in a pavilion for the assembly—
having performed the circumambulation of the temple while adorned with all ornaments, || 2981/2 ||
O best of the twice-born, having caused the God of gods to enter [the temple] either at that time or at dawn, one should also arrange for the viewing of entertainments.
Having performed the morning bath and other rites, one should adorn [the deity] with ornaments worthy of adorning;
and [one should offer] various fragrant incenses mixed with camphor.
Having performed a circumambulation of the temple, accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments.
Having placed it upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
then, having sprinkled it with the water of the arghya offering, one should consecrate it with the Astra-mantra and the Śarva-śambara mantras.
Having worshipped [the deity] with perfumes and other offerings, one should enclose it with the Kavaca mantra;
[one should offer oblations] with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, caru-rice, sesame seeds, parched grain, or jaggery.
There should be a hundred oblations with the root mantra, and from this point on, there may or may not be oblations with the weapon mantra;
the oblation performed in conjunction with the consecration of the five fires accomplishes all purposes.

Having performed the expiation with the Aghora mantra accompanied by the Pūrṇāhuti, one should touch [the object] with the Sadyojāta mantra and cause the fragrant substance to be offered with the Mūla mantra. || 305 ||
For the satisfaction of the preceptor, one should give a cow with its calf, gold, a bronze vessel, fine garments, sesame seeds, clarified butter, or other such items. (306)
This gift for a journey is considered to be accompanied by the offering of water;
alternatively, it may consist of turmeric, salt, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds.
Betel-leaf, rice, fragrance, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and oil—this is known as the "Gift of Śiva," which bestows the desired objects upon the performer. (308)
For yogins engaged in meditation who understand the meaning of the knowledge of Śiva, the offering of worship to them would be as desirable as it is for all living beings. (309)
The *uṣṇīṣa* and other [offerings] should be presented on special days;
however, a counter-offering should also be given, and it must be accompanied by water. (310)
The Uṣṇīṣa and other [empowerments] should be bestowed; the wise one should bestow them upon the Ācārya.
The Ācārya is indeed Śiva himself; there is no difference whatsoever between these two.
He who perceives a difference between these two shall attain a downward course;
[he who knows] one who is learned in all the scriptures, peaceful, and devoted to the worship of the Śiva-liṅga.
The alms-food, which is free from censure, is prepared for the sake of Śiva, joined with daily fire-oblations and the like, and accompanied by offerings to the planets and other rites. (313)
O twice-born ones, what is the use of much speaking in this matter? When such a guide is present, wherever he is satisfied, there lies the attainment of the goals of human life.
Truth, truth, and again truth—truth alone is indeed the triple truth.
He by whom that wealth has been seized is called a thief of the three worlds. (315)
Even after hundreds of millions of eons, one cannot escape the consequences of stealing from a deity;
therefore, having fully understood the various kinds of evil, one should avoid them, especially that which pertains to the teacher.
That which is given should be accepted with faith, and it should be heard as the means of crossing over [saṃsāra];
therefore, one should offer this gift for the sake of the journey, such as the food offering (naivedya) and so forth. || 317 ||
It is approved for use at the beginning of the installation of a liṅga and other such rites;
furthermore, it should be performed elsewhere as well for the sake of the victory of kings.
For this is the supreme among all gifts; it is distinguished by its reception and so forth, being endowed with all ornaments and accompanied by a face. (319)
Having placed [the image], accompanied by a Śaiva preceptor, upon an excellent palanquin, one should perform a circumambulation either within the five enclosures or outside of them. || 320 ||
Having performed the prescribed sequence of the procession, which is endowed with all auspiciousness, accompanied by men dressed in royal attire and engaged in various dances; || 321 ||
Accompanied by those mounted on skillful palanquins, carrying flowers and scented waters,
and performing service both in front and behind.
Or else, one should avoid the face of those wearing royal attire;
having first caused them to enter the palace, one should afterwards establish [the image] by the previously mentioned path. || 323 ||

Having discarded the *kautuka* (protective thread), one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; at the conclusion of that, the procession of the image (*bera-yātrā*) and so forth is proclaimed, or it may be performed prior to it. || 324 ||
At the end of the night, having mounted the god of gods, Naṭeśvara, upon the chariot,
he should perform the circumambulation of the villages and other places according to the same sequence as the previous procession.
Having performed [this], one should cause [the image] to enter within, and then perform the ritual bathing again;
this same procedure is considered applicable to other images as well. || 326 ||
O best of the twice-born, on the day preceding the day of the *tīrtha*, or even on the day before that, [the account] should include the commencement of the battle and conclude with the hunt. (327)
Furthermore, for another purpose related to a festival, one should have [the image] recast;
specifically, its ceremonial bathing (snāpana) should be performed according to the previously mentioned procedure.
On that night, one should perform the auspicious rite for the sake of the sacred ford (tīrtha) according to the previous procedure;
for the sake of the sacred ford, one should prepare nine water-pots during the night.
[The vessels] should be provided with threads, lids, and kuśa-grass bundles along with sprouts;
they may be covered with cloth or left uncovered, or else a cloth may be placed only on the principal one.
Or one may accomplish the pilgrimage at night, or even at the time of bathing;
however, one should perform the rites of the pilgrimage in the morning, prior to sunrise.
Having reached a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) and performed purification on the surface of the earth,
one should prepare two sacrificial altars (sthaṇḍila), one for the trident and one for the water-pot (kalaśa).
One should place the trident in the west and set the water-pots at its tip;
then, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), one should first invoke the deities.
One should worship the trident, which contains all sacred fords (tīrthas) and is endowed with all the Durgās,
together with Manonmanī in its center, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should bathe the afflicted area with those waters after entering into a river or similar body of water;
one should perform the collection of sacred waters by means of the invocation of the Gaṅgā and other rivers.
O Goddess Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Narmadā, and Sarasvatī; O Sindhu, Godāvarī, and you, Kāverī, [come] to this reservoir of water! || 336 ||
This supreme place is for the purpose of a sacred ford (tīrtha) where Śarva is ever-present;
it serves for the purification of the sins of all holy sites until the setting of the sun.
In the midst of that collection of sacred sites (tīrtha), one should bathe a trident placed with its point facing east in the waters, while recollecting the Śiva-mantra.
Having emerged from the water, one should place the trident on the bank;
having performed the ritual collection of the sacred water (tīrthasaṃgrahaṇa), [one should place it] either at a holy site or in a temple.
One who is unable to submerge [the image] should carry it to a reservoir of deep water;
then, adorned with all ornaments, one should enter the temple. || 340 ||
Having performed the fire-oblation (homa) and the offering of oblations (balidāna) according to the previously mentioned method,
one should then conduct the powder festival (cūrṇotsava) in the pavilion for the deity's assembly.
On the sacrificial ground, one should prepare two [marks] in the presence of the God of gods;
one should place a trident here in the west and a mortar in the other.
One should place the Night [powder] in the middle of that for the sake of perfecting the powder;
or, having wrapped it in cloths, one should throw the Night powder into the middle of that.
Having first worshipped the trident, one should then perform the overnight consecration (adhivāsana).
Having made the ritual resolve (saṃkalpa), one should conceive of the pestle as Śakti and designate it as the support (ādhāra).
Having worshipped the Lord on the pestle, one should perform the offering of ghee to the head with rice grains, husks, and the like, accompanied by *dūrvā* grass and flowers. || 345 ||
The *śūla* (trident) of the Lord is proclaimed to be either facing forward (*sammukha*) or turned away (*vimukha*);
likewise, the *musala* (pestle) is described, and the *ulūkhala* (mortar) is to be understood in the same way.
Whether covered with cloth or uncovered, it is proclaimed as the pestle (mūsala).
Having first worshipped the pestle, one should thereafter worship the mortar (ulūkhala).
The offering of *dūrvā* grass should be performed either starting from the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*) or starting from the principle of the Self (*ātmatattva*), by the Guru or by the initiate.
Then the king, the queen, the high-souled men appointed by them, those headed by the domestic priest, and the people devoted to Maheśvara must give it. (349)
This must be performed by my daughters and female slaves in the presence of the king; otherwise, it shall be done by those appointed by the king or by unmarried maidens.

Then, by the command of the preceptor, the offering of durvā grass should be performed in due order by female servants, or by male attendants, or by other suitable persons who are knowledgeable. || 351 ||
On any other occasion for the amusement of the God or the Goddess,
at the beginning of that event, such as the time of the ritual bath, this should be performed for the sake of auspiciousness.
At the end of that, one should grind [the materials] for three nights while reciting the *astra* mantra;
one should diligently grind [them] for the duration of the night in the proper sequence, beginning with the taking up of the *dūrvā* grass.
Having recollected that mantra, one should take that powder from there and place it into various kinds of vessels intended for the liṅga or the image. (354)
One should designate one portion for the festival image, specifically for the trident, and one portion for the retinue, in due order. (355)
And for the sake of the remaining people, one should collect [the substances] in jars and other vessels; or one may prepare pure scented oil separately in individual containers. (356)
Having sprinkled [it] with the *hetimantra*, one should thereafter worship it with the *hṛnmantra*.
Having consecrated it as nectar (*amṛtīkṛtya*), one should offer it preceded by betel leaf (*tāmbūla*) with *gostanī* [betel nut];
and the night-powder (*rātricūrṇa*) should also be given, O twice-born ones, according to the previously mentioned procedure.
One should cause the powder festival (cūrṇotsava) to be performed with a trident in the village and even in the temple,
using capable attendants who move with swift speed.
A great holy site (mahātīrtha) should be established in a vast body of water such as the ocean;
it must not be established in shallow water, nor should it be treated like a mere ceremonial pool (kautukatīrtha).
However,

[it should be] provided with the *bera* (image) and the consecrated water-vessel (*prapādi*), adorned all around, equipped with the placement of the ritual jars (*kalaśa*), and joined with the invocation of the deities.
O best of the twice-born, a vessel should also be prepared for the purpose of visiting a sacred ford;
however, one should not enter the water before first collecting the [sacred] earth of that ford.
Having performed the collection of the sacred sites (tīrthas), one should carry out the great rite of the sacred site;
having released all the auspicious thread (kautuka) and having bestowed it upon the devotees.
A great sacred site (mahātīrtha) should be established, provided with a phallic image (śūlabera),
or even accompanied by a trident (triśūla), [constructed] with materials brought from various temples.
Or one should perform it together with tridents accompanied by deities;
or alternatively, one should perform it together with a lotus and a wheel.
One should resort to a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) at night when it is joined with Mahāmoṭi;
during the day, a tīrtha should be performed, and at midday, the tīrtha is most excellent.
The middle bathing place (tīrtha) is in the forenoon, while the lowest would be in the afternoon;
however, excluding the lunar eclipse, bathing at night is also considered excellent.
And that [science] combined with [the science of] moṭi is considered the most excellent of the excellent;
the Sāmudrika is primarily concerned with lunar days, while the other is primarily concerned with the right hand.
The conjunction of a lunar day (tithi) and an asterism (nakṣatra) is said to be difficult to obtain;
it may occur either in the forenoon or in the afternoon, when the lunar day and the asterism coincide.
Or else, it should be performed at midday by the sea or at a river and so forth;
however, the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) or even the lunar day (*tithi*) should be selected during the daytime.
When a lunar mansion or a lunar day occurs twice within a single fortnight, or when two auspicious constellations (tīrtha-ṛkṣa) coincide in one month, that is most excellent. (3701/2)
In that case as well, if one is engaged in yoga, it should indeed be undertaken at the same time as before;
specifically, in whichever month and under whichever lunar mansion the pilgrimage was previously performed.
In that month and under that asterism, one may perform it even later;
provided it is for a self-manifested (svāyambhuva) linga, or one made by the gods (daivika), or one made by the sages (ārṣika).

O best of the twice-born, the rites for the holy ford (tīrtha) should be performed during the month and asterism of Mānuṣa, or in the second month and asterism, or even on the specific lunar day (tithi) of that asterism.
Then, the most excellent preceptor should cause a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) to be made in the midst of the water;
immersion is said to be of two kinds, according to whether the image is joined with or separated from the pedestal.
At the time of separation, on the bank of the river, one should have the bathing of the image performed, or indeed the bathing alone;
afterwards, one should worship it with offerings such as perfumes and other services.
One should cause an offering of food (naivedya) to be presented there, or else at a temple or a grove; thus one should satisfy the Lord of Gods with all auspicious things.
It may be accompanied by the circumambulation of the village, or one should avoid that;
it may be attended by all the devotees, or it may be devoid of them.
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) accompanied by all auspicious rites,
he performed a circumambulation of the temple along with his pure attendants.
Having caused the Lord of Gods, accompanied by the Goddess and the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), to be grasped [in meditation],
he should duly install him in the inner sanctum upon the pedestal of the Liṅga in the proper sequence.
Having installed the God and the Goddess, one should install the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) all around them;
having sprinkled each with their respective waters, one should bathe the Lord with pure water.
Then one should worship the deity with extensive offerings according to one's means;
the lowering of the banner on that night is declared to be most excellent.
On the third, fifth, seventh, or ninth day,
or on the eleventh day under a Viśva constellation, or on the fifteenth day, one should perform [the rite].
One should perform it on the seventeenth day, or even on the nineteenth day.
One should perform the directional fire-oblation (diśāhoma) following the image-oblation (mūrtihoma);
this applies if the period lasts for a number of days beginning from the flagstaff (dhvaja) up to the sacred bathing place (tīrtha). || 384 ||
Starting again from the festival until the conclusion at the sacred ford (tīrtha), one should perform everything;
on the lunar mansion of the lowering of the flag (dhvajāvaroha-ṛkṣa), one should conduct the bath known as the "Pure" (śuddha).
One should perform the ritual bathing (snapana) of the Liṅga, the Bera, the Śūla, and the Dhvaja;
having worshipped them thoroughly as prescribed for worship, one should adorn the abode with garlands.
Beginning from the inner sanctum (garbhageha) up to the gateway (gopura), one should fumigate the temple of the deity with incense made from black aloe-wood (kālāgaru) according to one's capacity.
One should offer various kinds of food oblations (naivedya) and devoutly satisfy the God;
thereafter, one should perform the worship of Caṇḍa together with the fire-oblation (homa).
Then one should offer the village oblation (grāmabali), accompanied by a linga made of food, joined with a trident, and associated with Caṇḍanātha. || 389 ||
At the time of the offering (bali), there should be the sounding of kettledrums, together with clay drums, joined by tabors and trumpets,
and accompanied by conchs and sandalwood incense.
Having performed this, one should dismiss the gods beginning with Brahmā who reside in the village;
first, one should offer a bali-oblation at the banner, and at the end, the banner again.
Having brought down [the deity] from the cloth, one should join it with the bull upon the bull;
an offering is prescribed either at the beginning or at the end of the lowering of the banner.
The performer should honor the preceptor with garments, gold,
and rings at the time of the offering of sprouts and at the time of hoisting the banner.
At the commencement of the fire-sacrifice (homa) following the consecration for the sacrifice, during both twilights, or at the beginning or the conclusion of a single twilight; || 394 ||

During the festival of the dancing form, at a sacred bathing place, and at the time of the pure ablution, one should subsequently cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given; that [fee] is considered to be of three kinds.
The fee for the preceptor should be known as follows: five niṣkas is the lowest, double that is the middle, and triple that is the highest. (396)
In the sequence of the inferior [initiation], the fee is said to be half that number;
however, for the superior [initiation], it is said to be double, or else it is described otherwise.
A daily sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of one niṣka, half a niṣka, or half of that is prescribed;
thereafter, one should perform a feast for the devotees either at the end of the fortnight or even before it.
Whether at the beginning or in the middle of a festival, it is considered a festival for the devotees;
this occurs whenever a monthly festival takes place during the period of the annual festival. (399)

Whether joined with the *bali* offering, the *homa*, and so forth, or accompanied by the procession of the image (*bera-yātrā*) and other rites, one should either perform them all or at least conduct the procession of the image alone. (400)
When two monthly festivals coincide, one should perform the rites in this very same manner;
O twice-born ones, what has been described here as a monthly festival is actually a single-day festival.
One should perform that festival for one month, either as a single event or multiple times;
or else, one may perform it preceded by the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa), or even without that.
One should hold a festival for one day, preceded by the beating of drums;
having prepared two sacrificial altars (sthaṇḍila), one should place the trident on one of them.
One should place the drum in front of that [image] and then cause the proclamation of "an auspicious day" (puṇyāha) to be recited;
having worshipped both the weapon-mantra and the drum, one should strike the drum in the proper sequence.
Then, having bound the *pratisara* on the deity upon the trident in the proper sequence,
and having performed the circumambulation of the temple, he enters the sacrificial hall.
The preceptor should place the trident upon the auspicious sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) above the altar;
he should then set down the Śiva-vessel together with the Vardhanī vessel.
Then, one should place eight jars or pitchers all around;
having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day, one should sprinkle [the area] with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra.
One should place a golden lotus, wrapped in cloth, into both the water-pot (kumbha) and the prosperity-vessel (vardhanī);
both should be provided with a thread, a tuft of grass (kūrca), and a lid.
One should worship Śambhu together with Manonmanī, accompanied by fruits and sprouts, in the central jar;
one should worship the eight Vidyeśvaras in the vardhanī vessel and in the other jars.

Having worshipped the doors and the door-keepers headed by Nandin, either in the water-pots or upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should adorn them with arches and the eight auspicious symbols.

Whether accompanied by [the ritual] or devoid of it, or provided with the ten weapons—or even nine—one should perform the rite of homa either in a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). || 411 ||
Then, in five or even one [vessel] provided with the previous substances, one should offer the village-oblation (grāmabali), either together with the image or not. || 412 ||
Thus one should act during the night; at dawn, one should worship the Lords of Sacrifice (Yāgeśvaras).
Having performed the fire-oblation (homa), one should present the ritual offering (bali) together with the sacred image (bera). || 413 ||
Having entered the Ālaya at the conclusion, the Guru should perform the powder festival (cūrṇotsava).
Thereafter, the Tīrtha rite should be performed; what is not mentioned here is to be done as previously described.
In the morning, one should have everything performed except for the beating of the drum;
having performed the immediate consecration (adhivāsana), one should carry out everything else as previously described.
Or one may perform this rite even without the powder festival;
it may take place in the temple, at the great offering site, or excluding the sacred bathing place (tīrtha). || 416 ||
The procession of the image should be performed in the evening or at nightfall;
however, if the procession is to take place above the sacred site (tīrtha), it should be done from another image at the time of the bali offering.
Or else, the pilgrimage may be performed in another manner, as it is described:
either by omitting the offerings, fire-oblations, and so forth, or by wandering alone. || 418 ||
One should perform the consecration ceremony for the deity on these days as well; this has been declared.
Or rather, this is considered to be determined at times established by the desire of the agent;
or [it may be performed] on the birth-star of the agent, or on the star Ārdrā.
On the fourteenth or the eighth day, on both fortnights' festival days, during the solstices, the equinoxes, an eclipse of Rāhu, or on a festival of [the deity's] awakening; 4201/2.
[It is used] during the Pavitra and Māsa-pūjā rites, at the lighting of the Kṛttikā lamp,
for the drawing of the lines at the beginning of the year, and also at the Navatoyāga sacrifice.
During the Pūrvaphālgunī nakṣatra, at the rite of offering fresh food (naivedya),
or during any other auspicious undertaking, a wise person should perform a single festival.
In this manner, it should be conjoined with the respective year for the sake of enjoyment; otherwise, it serves for liberation.
The worship of the day (vāra-pūjā) and other rites should be performed starting from Sunday in successive order.
Or one should bathe [the deity] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the nectars (amṛta) as part of the bathing ritual;
one should worship the Supreme Lord with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings according to the prescribed proportions.
Sthalapadma, apāmārga, śrīparṇa, tulasī, gokṣura, bilvapatra, and viṣṇukrānti— these [are used] in sequence.
One should employ these leaves on the days beginning with Sunday;
on Sunday there should be a ruby, and on Monday a pearl.
Coral is [auspicious] on Wednesday, while emerald occurs on Thursday;
topaz should be used on Friday, and diamond is traditionally prescribed for Venus.
Sapphire is suitable for a Saturday, as are all other [gems] whatsoever;
it is the established rule that they are appropriate for all days for the purpose of ornaments.
And one should offer flowers and garments that possess the same colors as those [deities]. || 429 ||
One should offer the food oblation (naivedya) of the respective colors at each respective gate;
and at the conclusion of the worship of the day, one should then perform the festival of the day (vārotsava).
Or one should perform the Arkavāra festival for the attainment of desired goals, especially for the destruction of afflictions caused by the planets and for the sake of health. (431)
For the sake of destroying the agitation of the world and for the purpose of warding off [evil] through a planetary influence,
worship on that specific day should be performed, accompanied by a festival on that very day.
Through the distinction of the various days of the week, or through the perception of scents and other objects,
the annual festival is proclaimed, as well as the monthly festival.
O best of Brahmins, the specific rule for the Vāra-vrata festival is now being told:
it is for Brahmins in the forenoon, and for Kṣatriyas at midday. (434)
In the evening for the Vaiśya caste, and at midnight for the fourth [caste],
one should perform the hoisting of the banner, preceded by the ritual of raising the banner.

Either preceded by the beating of a drum, or preceded by the sowing of seeds, [the initiation] may be for the three classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, or for a Śūdra, it may be preceded by the appearance of sprouts. || 436 ||
In a city, it is preceded by a banner; in a village, by a drum;
and in a town, by a sprout; likewise, it is proclaimed for the Śūdra.
O best of the twice-born, beyond four thousand [yojanas], in a larger village or in a city and so forth, no confusion regarding festivals has been declared by Vipaśyin.
One should construct the pedestal of the banner using seven, six, or five *tālas* with *vādya*, *aja*, and *daṇḍaka* measures; for Śūdras and others, it should be done in reverse order.
One should not set up a banner other than a banner; rather, a bull-banner should be established.
O twice-born ones, during festivals, one should not perform any festival other than the desired Śaiva festival.
The commencement of the flag-raising and other rites is most auspicious when performed under a constellation favorable to all;
white, red, and yellow [garments] are prescribed for the three classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. (441)
For a Śūdra, yellow is prescribed; for all [castes], white is also proclaimed.
The commencement on the cloth begins at the head and ends at the tail. 442.
At the time of circumambulating the banner, the Guru should go in front or not;
Gāndhāra should be in the eastern part, while Kauśika should be in the south.
Kāmarāja is to be known in the west, and Tarkarāga in the north;
in this manner, one should assign the vowels according to the division of the directions.
At the time of hoisting the banner, however, even if only one of these four [rites] is performed—
whether it be from the hoisting of the banner up to the end of the ritual at the sacred site (tīrtha), or the village offering (grāmabali) at night.
Alternatively, there may be an offering (bali) for the gods at the base of the banner,
either in a place where there is a constant festival or elsewhere during a festival.

In the case of a single-fire ritual, one should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) starting from the north and proceeding in a clockwise direction, according to the divisions beginning with the Brāhmaṇa and so forth.
A celibate student (brahmacārī) assuming a fierce form and eating well-prepared food,
having meditated upon himself as being like Caṇḍa, should sever the staff of the banner.
One should arrange either a festival (utsava) or a purificatory rite (pavitra), or indeed both;
the festival-consecration (ketv-aṅkura) should take place on the ninth day, while the festival-consecration (utsavāṅkura) should be on the seventh day.
In that number of holy sites (tīrtha), everything is considered auspicious everywhere;
at midday, one should perform the worship of the banner (dhvajapūjā) or [the offering] of water into the Soma-vessel.
Then, the depositing [of the image] and its worship are performed at night;
or else, for one who has had the *kautuka* ceremony performed on the image, the departure from that village is prescribed.
O best of the twice-born, at the times of hunting activities, the year is declared to be of two kinds—solar and lunar—in the Kāmika Āgama. (452)
The solar [day] is declared here to be the best; the lunar is said to be middling; the civil (sāvana) is declared to be the lowest, and therefore it is not desired for ritual purposes. || 453 ||
During times such as festivals, one should not perform the installation (pratiṣṭhā) and other rites;
rather, having performed a propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma), one should proceed with the installation and so forth. || 454 ||
Alternatively, the festival may be performed in another manner:
having raised a single banner, preceded by the hoisting of the banner. || 455 ||
On that very day, O Brahmins, when the sun has grown dim,
one should have the day of the holy ford proclaimed while mounted upon an elephant or similar vehicle.
A Caṇḍāla, together with his wife and accompanied by a drum, should perform it;
it must be done on that very night, preceded by the beating of a kettle-drum.
Having invoked the gods as before at the tip of the trident, he should announce the day of the pilgrimage site, excluding the village and other such offerings. (458)
Having thus performed [the rite] within the sanctuary itself, the most excellent gurus should then go to a body of water and prepare two sacrificial altars on the bank.
One should place the trident in one spot and set down the jars in another;
one should bathe the trident with groups of nine and immerse that trident [in the water].
Having entered the abode of the deity, on that very day or within ten days,
one should again commence the sacrifice, preceded by the ritual offering of the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa).
One should perform the village offering (grāmabali) conjoined with a single oblation (ekahoma),
as well as the procession of the image (berayātrā), every day and night throughout the entire day.
On the fifth day, one should scatter sand consecrated with mantras throughout the entire dwelling, both inside and out, as prescribed.
When the eighteenth day arrives, one should perform the sowing of seeds;
for the sake of the sacred site (tīrtha), one should do so at night in the eight directions of the temple precinct.

Having raised eight banners marked with the vehicles of the World-Guardians (Lokapālas), or bearing their weapons or the bull-emblem, he should be accompanied by the presiding deities of the images (mūrtipatis).
From that time forward, the specific rite of fire-oblation (homa) must be performed;
at its conclusion, there should be the offering of the bali-oblation accompanied by the procession of the image (bera).
Having performed this for nine days, one should conduct the pilgrimage on the tenth day;
that night, there is the lowering of the eight banners.
Having performed this, starting from that day, it should be accompanied by various musical instruments, joined with various songs, and provided with various dances. || 468 ||
Having performed a circumambulation of the village, one should carry out the sequence of serving food.
Having done this for seven days, at the end, one should go from there to a body of water.
Having prepared two sacrificial altars on the bank of a body of water, the most excellent Guru should place the trident in one and set down the ritual jars in the other.
One should bathe the Śūla with nine [vessels] and immerse that Śūla;
having entered the place of the deity and having set aside all musical instruments.
Having maintained silence for seven days thereafter,
one should lead Caṇḍeśvara in front and subsequently perform the procession of the image.
If, however, the bali-offering and the fire-oblation (homa) are omitted, one should perform them for seven days;
the rite should be accompanied by the worship of Caṇḍa, the fire-oblation, and the ceremonial bathing (snapana).
At its conclusion, one should cause a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) to be made, provided with a trident;
one should perform the lowering of the banner that night according to the previous procedure.
Or, even without going on a pilgrimage, one should perform this rite;
or else, having fashioned a linga from fresh grain, it may be done for the sake of the weapons of the guardians of the quarters.
Or one may perform the offering of oblations (balikriyā) with a trident in a village or similar location;
or one should arrange ten perpetual festivals and lingas.
Or else, the flagstaff should be installed at the end of twelve years;
if there is a defect such as decay, one should discard that staff and install another flagstaff.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the procedure for the Great Festival, in the great tantra known as the *Uttarakāmika*.
O twice-born ones, one should determine the length of the banner (*dhvaja*) from five cubits up to a *viśva* (ten thousand) cubits; this measurement is declared to extend from the head to the tail.
That [measurement] should be taken as combined, with a limit of four times seven;
having divided it into parts, the width of the cloth is said to be one part.
The tail is equal in width [to the body], or it is said to be three-quarters or half;
the head should be known as half the width, provided with two tails.
One should draw two reed-bundles joined together, with a bull depicted in their midst;
it should be endowed with auspicious dimensions such as length and so forth, and be either standing or reclining.
It should be white or red in color, and possessed of yellowish tail-hairs.
It is likewise endowed with red horns and similarly possessed of hooves.
The flagstaff should be made of wood one *mātra* and one finger-breadth in measure;
it should be joined with a lotus-base and accompanied by two lamps at its sides.
It is joined with two chowries, its head covered by a parasol,
and it may be accompanied by a full water-pot or not by a trident.
Having thus consecrated the bull and performed the ritual release of the bull's eye, [he should proceed].

Having fashioned the length of the staff from two parts up to nine parts, using either a tree mentioned by all the world, such as the *tvaksāra* (Butea monosperma), or the *kramuka* (Areca catechu) and so forth;
O most excellent gurus, the flagstaff should be determined as a single proportion;
beginning from five finger-breadths (aṅgulas) and increasing by one aṅgula, it may be up to sixteen aṅgulas.
One should determine the circumference of the lower staff to be as much as [the length];
having established the thickness of the base as twelve parts out of five.
The tip [of the flagstaff] should be reduced by one part; likewise, the tip of the staff is prescribed [in that manner].
The bamboo or tree mentioned for the staff shall be the same tree used for the flagpole.
For the sake of accomplishing the yoga of both, one should extract the three clusters.
7. In the seventh chapter, the ritual of *nīrājana*:
I shall explain the ritual of *nīrājana*, and it is performed at night; or it may be performed at the beginning of the evening twilight, or at the conclusion of the incense and lamp offerings.
It should be performed at festivals and other auspicious occasions;
for that purpose, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or construct a mandala.

One should sprinkle [the materials] with the Astra mantra in the inner sanctum (garbha), or in the half-pavilion (ardhamaṇḍapa), or in the area in front of it called the bathing-chamber (snapanaka), or in the kitchen, or in any other [suitable place]. || 3 ||
Having brought pure vessels provided with lamp-holders,
the vessels should be prepared according to the procedure prescribed for the offering vessel (balipātra).
One should cause lamp-stands to be made in their center with a single measure;
according to the rule, they should increase by a quarter-inch (pādāṅgula) up to nine inches.
Its width is said to be equal to that, or even half of it;
when the earth is divided into nine parts, this measurement is declared for the central portion.
The lip measures two barley-corns at its base and increases by half a barley-corn until it reaches the end of the *mātrā*;
the thickness of the bowl is half its width, and it is provided with a hollow cavity in the middle.
Or one may fashion it in the shape of a lotus, resembling the base of a *pālikā* vessel,
or in the form of a *dhūrtūra* flower, or even in the shape of an arrow.
It should be provided with four or eight petals and endowed with all ornaments;
there should be one lamp-stand in a single vessel, or five.
Or he should have nine of them made, either joined together or with intervals between them;
or else, for the sake of the deity, he should make lamp-holders out of flour or cooked food.
For the sake of the Goddess and for the sake of the image—especially for one in the form of a dancer—one should place sesame seeds in one spot and mustard seeds and salt in another. (11)
Cotton seed elsewhere, or even cow dung ground into a paste; colored rice, sacrificial food (haviṣya), and the waters from the bathing of a banyan tree or a horse.
One should arrange them in sequence in the four cardinal directions and the intermediate corners;
or one may arrange five lamp-vessels in the center.
One should place incense, the water of honor (arghya), flowers, and ashes in the southeast corner;
or, in every case, one should arrange nine brightly burning lamps.
One should place [the offerings] moistened with ghee and mixed with oil, together with the limbs of Brahmā;
the world-protectors along with Viriñca, or the deities of the forms (mūrtis) along with the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās).
The Vasus joined with the fires, the supreme Śaktis beginning with Vāmā, the Kalās, the elements, the gods, and the lords of the causes beginning with Brahmā. || 16 ||
The vessels are declared to be deities, and the fire is the deity of the lamp;
their increase is said to begin from a *prastha* and a quarter thereof, up to the limit of an *āḍhaka*. (17)

The quantity of sesame seeds and other materials for the vessels depends on the desire of the performer; having consecrated them with all the common purificatory rites (saṃskāras) according to the prescribed sequence, [one should proceed]. 18.
Having recollected the seed-syllable of fire (Raṃ), one should join the lamp with the lamp,
accompanied by all musical instruments and joined with the sound of the conch.
One should maintain those lamps, accompanied by village dances, in their proper sequence; or else, one should have them carried by women or by attendants.
Having placed it before the deity, one should worship it upon a tripod;
having offered water for the feet with the Ajāta mantra, one should offer water for sipping with the Hṛdaya mantra.
One should worship all [the deities] with fragrance and other offerings using their respective seed-syllables and the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) and so forth;
one should then cause them to revolve three times or once above the head of Śiva.
Having taken those lamp-vessels with both hands, one should worship them;
then, with the mantras beginning with the Ātmatattva, one should place them in the lotus-hand of the disciple.
He too, having taken that lamp, should place it with a respectful salutation,
immediately after [the ground] which is white, pure, fragrant, and free from sand.
Having taken [the ashes] with the hand smeared with ashes and having whirled them over Śiva, one should then cast them into the midst of the lamp three times. || 25 ||
With the thumb and the ring finger, one should apply the *tilaka* on the five faces;
sequentially on the foreheads, and then in order on the heart and the two arms.
One should also apply a tilaka on the pedestal; if the Goddess is of manifest form, the tilaka should be placed in the region to her left.
If the Goddess is of unmanifest form, the tilaka should be in front.
One should bring [the deity] to the region of the throat with the root mantra, or else with the heart mantra;
one should apply a tilaka-mark on the body at the forehead, the heart, and the region of the arms.

Having collected that ash, one should cause it to be given to one's own devotees, such as Caṇḍeśvara and others, as well as to other devotees who have fashioned images out of iron and other materials.
Then the preceptor,
having brought forth the vessels as before, should first give them, adorned with all ornaments, to the devotees.
Then, taking [the embers] both with flames and without flames from the temple of Śiva,
[he should place them] either in front of the pedestal, on the side of the bull, or near the gateway.
Or else, he should deposit those substances in due order at the base of a bull or elsewhere;
he should give them to the preceptor or burn them with fire and wind.
The quantity of sesame seeds and other materials is proclaimed to be according to one's desire;
this should also be performed by kings, though in that case, Agni is the presiding deity.
For the sake of victory, the king should perform [the rites] at the beginning of the consecration ceremony and so forth;
however, even in the consecration of the preceptor, it should be performed excluding the lamps.
Rice grains are placed there, and if it is night, it should be accompanied by a lamp.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the Ritual for the Lustration Ceremony (*nirājana-vidhi*), in the great tantra named *Uttarakāmika*.
In the eighth chapter, the Ritual for the Garland of Kṛttikā Lamps:
"O best of the twice-born, listen as I proclaim the ritual for the garland of lamps."
In the month known as Kārttika, under the lunar mansion named Kṛttikā.
Or, during the full moon or when it is in conjunction with that [asterism], for the sake of accomplishing all desires,
one should perform the ritual of ascending the lamp at the time of sunset.
The examination of the eighth house from the natal ascendant and other such factors regarding defects of the ascendant,
as well as the examination of the "rain-destroying" asterisms and so forth, is considered appropriate in that context.
The time prior to sunset, ending with the last quarter of a watch (yāma), or the time thereafter, up until half a watch, is indeed the proper time for [the ritual]. (4)
Having thus determined the time, one should perform the rite of sowing the seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa);
on the preceding day, one should begin the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) consisting of the worship of lamps.
One should place the staff before the deity, or at each gateway;
it may be placed in the eight directions, the four directions, in three, in one, or in two.
The measurement of the lamp-post is like that of the flagpole;
that pole may be made of coconut, palm, betel-nut, or bamboo. (7)
Alternatively, one may use a staff of the same length as that prescribed for the flagstaff;
there, one should fix the stakes, beginning at twelve finger-breadths and increasing by increments of one finger-breadth (the measure of space).
The emergence of the kila from the staff occurs at the end of fifty finger-breadths;
starting from two mātrās, it increases by one quarter (pāda) until it reaches a limit of six aṅgulas.
The thickness of that [pillar] should be one-third, one-half, or three-quarters of its width;
or else, the pillars may be fixed in the ground or set upon a base.
Starting from the ninth peg and increasing by one peg up to the twenty-seventh peg, one should apply them to a single direction.
In this manner, one should likewise install stakes in the other directions;
it is desired that there be three stakes or four stakes, accompanied by the mental visualization of the sacrificial ground.
One should place that [wheel] at the front specifically for the purpose of supporting the vessel;
one should join together the wheels made of wood as if they were pegs.
One should arrange lamps numbering two, twelve, or sixteen;
or alternatively, one may place them outside with dry materials such as coconut leaves and the like.
Or else, one should cover the wheels so that there are no gaps;
it should be one cubit in width and twice that in length.
One should fashion the door on the south for the sake of accomplishing the ascent of the staff;
this primary ritual (kalpa) has been fully explained, and now the secondary ritual (anukalpa) is being stated.
Having set aside all the disks, one should fix the lamps;
the ritual preparation should be performed, excluding the homa-pile.
Having set aside the staff, that which is arranged is called "akalpa";
one should lead it from the lamp-pile toward the cardinal and intermediate directions, as well as within that interval.
One should cause many lamps to be prepared and offered;
or one should set up many lamp-stands arranged in the form of a garland.
Or having fashioned many [lamps] in the shape of archways, or in a circular form,
or in the shape of rays of light, one should place lamps therein.
In a palace, a gate-tower, a hall, in the dwellings of attendants and the like, in a pavilion,
at the sacrificial altar and so forth, or even in a well or a house.
One should arrange lamps in the bull-stall, the kitchen, and within flower-pavilions; or alternatively, one may arrange them outside, even throughout the villages and all surrounding areas.
This festival of lights (Dīpāvali) should be performed preceded by the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana);
one should purify the staff with the Astra-mantra and worship it with the Praṇava.
One should prepare a pit in the ground measuring six, four, and five tālas;
having established it on the previous day, one should lead a sacrificial altar (vedikā) to its base.
Just as the Goddess [is placed] upon the flagstaff, or alternatively, together with a lotus;
having released the artisan at the end, one should then cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
One should worship the staff with a lamp, together with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; having tied a protective cord (pratisara) and entered within, one should perform this rite.
In the Ālaya, or in a pavilion, or indeed in a sacrificial pavilion, or elsewhere in a pleasant and auspicious place smeared with cow dung. (27)
Having prepared a sacrificial mound there, the Guru should sprinkle it with water using a ritual vessel;
he should then place either nine, five, or one vessel upon it.
In the rite of lustration (nīrājana), all those deities are likewise honored;
one should worship the syllable Om (praṇava) in the vessel with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
One should prepare either a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) or a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to the east of that;
having established the Śiva-fire there, one should satisfy Śiva along with his limbs (attendants). || 30 ||

Then, one should perform [the rite] with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge; subsequently, one should perform it with cotton seeds, milk, or [with these materials] a hundred times, or fifty times, or half of that.

Meditating upon the fire-seed syllable (vahni-bīja), one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with the root mantra and its limbs according to a tenth-part ratio, and having performed the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) at the end.
Then, having dismissed the deity along with his limbs, the preceptor should offer lamps,
filling the vessel with either oil or ghee while meditating upon him as the soul of all.

Having recollected the seed-syllable of fire (raṃ), and having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in sequence from the center and the other directions, one should dismiss the Śiva-fire.
Then, taking the central vessel together with its lamp,
the Guru [should take] the lamp called "Taruṇa," which is adorned with all ornaments.
One should place [the deity] upon the staff or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with the heart-mantra;
at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, one should perform the rite for the lamp-staff or the marriage-thread ceremony (kautuka).
Then, on the second day, [he constructed] a structure provided with four archways in the four cardinal and intermediate directions, and endowed with four peaks.
The peaks should be five, four, three, two, and one cubit in height, with the intervals between them being one cubit;
or else, one may lead a single peak toward the east or the southeast.
One should erect archways (toraṇas) as is appropriate according to one's desire;
everywhere, the archway should be adorned with a pinnacle, garlands of darbha grass, and other ornaments. (39)
Having thus prepared everything— adorned with all ornaments and accompanied by plantains and betel-nut trees— at the time when the sun has grown dim, (40)
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), one should worship the staff with perfumes and other offerings;
then, one should wrap the base of the staff with a pair of garments.
One should place a vessel made of gold or other precious materials upon the top of the staff;
it should be joined with cotton seeds and heartwood, and combined with oil and clarified butter.
The wise one should employ [the ritual] upon altars, in sacrificial pits, or on leveled earthen mounds;
he should perform the fire-oblation together with the preliminary consecration oblation.
The preceptor should perform the fire-oblation (homa) either in the fire or in the *kūṭa* [of the mantra];
[the deities are] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. || 44 ||
In this context, the presiding deities of the oblations are declared: Sadāśiva resides on the staff of the lamp;
furthermore, all [the deities] of fire are [represented by] the Palāśa, Vaṭa, Śamī, and Arka trees.
O best of the twice-born, after the offering of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and ornaments, along with all the lamps.
Having unified [the elements] with the heart-mantra, one should place them in the vessel by means of the seed-syllable of fire;
[the deity] is endowed with all ornaments and adorned with auspicious sprouts.
It was provided with canopies and banners, equipped with parasols and chowries, accompanied by various musical instruments, and attended by diverse dances. || 48 ||
And accompanied by the *bera* [image], the *bera-yātrā* (procession of the image) should be performed nine times;
while standing before the deity, the celibate student (*brahmacārī*) should hold a lamp in his hand.
Having quickly mounted the staff, one who possesses a gentle countenance should ignite it at its upper end; then, having lowered it from that vessel above, [he should proceed].
At that time, one should inform the Great Lord of those who stand upon the discus;
then, one should place lamps beginning from the head down to the feet.
The wise preceptor, standing facing north, should honor the attendant who has lit the lamps with garments and other offerings. (52)
Having recollected the Jyotirliṅga, one should burn the four peaks;
or else, having omitted the burning of the peaks, one may perform everything else.
One should lead the deity beneath the archway, performing three circumambulations around the lamp-stand; having done so, one should lead it through the village accompanied by lamps.
Having performed a circumambulation of the palace, one should lead [the deity] to the assembly pavilion;
then, one should install lamps everywhere in the palaces and other structures.

Having entered the abode of the deity, one should proceed with the sequence of serving [the offerings]; one may or may not perform the ceremonial bath (snapana) for the *bera-liṅga* according to the prescribed rule.
Having offered abundant sacrificial oblation, one should present betel leaf;
one should cause flattened rice to be offered to the deity along with coconut fruits.
One should perform this rite either with black pepper and cumin, combined with the essence of molasses, or even without the offering of sprouts.
One should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, and immediately thereafter to the Hotṛ priests.
Whatever materials are required here, such as the heap for the oblation (homakūṭa) and the staff (daṇḍaka), [should be provided].
Then one should cause another limb to be given to the guide;
this ritual action should also be performed in the dwelling of kings.
O twice-born ones, this should be performed in villages and similar places, in sacred sites dedicated to Brahmā and elsewhere,
as well as for other mortals and even when there is a loss of vehicles.
Especially in a cow-pen, for the sake of curing their diseases, on whichever lunar day the sun rises, [that day should be observed]. (62)
O best of the twice-born, that lunar day (tithi) is to be known as complete in both the bright and the dark fortnights.
Whatever [constellation] the sun reaches when it sets—
all that has been stated regarding the zodiac signs should likewise be understood for the lunar mansions as well.
Knowing this, O best of the twice-born, one should apply oneself to all ritual actions.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, the Ritual for the Kṛttikā Lamp-Procession, in the great tantra named the *Uttarakāmika*. One should fix the stakes there according to the dimensions prescribed for the flagpole;
beginning from twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), they increase by one *vyoma* (zero) finger-breadth at each step.
The emergence of the kila from the staff extends up to fifty finger-breadths;
however, with an increase of two mātras per step, the limit is six aṅgulas.
The width should be one-third of its thickness, or half, or three-quarters;
or the pillar-logs may be fixed by being passed through a shaft, or joined by being wedged together.
Starting from the ninth peg and increasing by one up to the sky-peg (the twenty-seventh), one should apply them in a single direction.
One should place a tripod or a quadrupod, provided with a sweet-smelling measure,
before that [deity], especially for the purpose of holding the vessel;
one should attach wheels made of wood to each prong.
For each wheel, however, there are eight, twelve, or sixteen lamps.
One should prepare the gateway on the right for the successful accomplishment of the staff-climbing rite.
In the third [chapter], titled "The World," the examination of defects regarding the ascendant, such as the eighth house from the ascendant or the natal sign of the agent,
as well as the observation of the Viṣṭi periods and the destructive constellations (vaināśika-ṛkṣa), is considered therein.
The Karaṇa-doṣa is Viṣṭi on the fourth; others say Viṣṭi is on the eighth from the first half [of the lunar month];
on the eleventh it is Viṣṭi in the latter half; and on the full moon, it is in the former half.
On the third lunar day, it is on a black cloth; on the seventh, from the eastern part;
on the tenth, in the west; and on the fourteenth, in the east, it is destructive.
The twenty-second birth asterism is known as Vaināśika.
In the ninth chapter, the procedure for the ghee-bath in Mārgaśīrṣa, the swing-ride in Pauṣa, and the honey-worship in Puṣya is described.
In the month known as Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship Śiva at Ārdroḍuka,
accompanied by a bath with ghee, according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Or, having especially performed a complete ritual bathing,
one should worship the deity with perfumes and other offerings, and gratify him with various songs.
Having led the deity around the village in a clockwise direction, one should install him in his abode;
or else, he may be so installed at night or even during the day, accompanied by offerings and oblations.
Having performed circumambulations to the right, adorned with all ornaments,
and having consecrated the sacred bathing place (tīrtha) accompanied by the powder festival (cūrṇotsava), one should enter the temple.
Then, O twice-born ones, one should perform the swinging ritual (ḍolārohaṇa) at the time of evening.
Having likewise fashioned two pillars adorned with all ornaments and endowed with the characteristics of pillars, one should fix a staff between them.
In the middle of that, one should place a swing measuring four cubits,
provided with four arms and equipped with an upper canopy.
Adorned with various ornaments, endowed with two arms,
seated upon a single swan-throne, and accompanied by the sprinkling of the "Auspicious Day" (Puṇyāha) rite.

Having sprinkled [the area] with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (astra), one should prepare a seat as prescribed; one should worship Haṃsa upon a wooden plank with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), and worship [him] on the Haṃsa-seat.
One should worship Brahmā on the right arm and Hari on the left arm;
having worshipped Rudra on the seat, one should worship Śiva above the plank.
Having worshipped the Goddess on the left, one should sacrifice to the General in the center;
or else, one should worship the Goddess with perfumes and other offerings upon a wooden plank.
Then, accompanied by various songs, provided with various dances, and endowed with various musical instruments, she should please Hara.
Furthermore, the mounting of the swing (ḍolarohaṇa) should be performed elsewhere as well, for it bestows desired results;
or it should be practiced daily for the sake of accomplishing all goals and purposes. 121/2.
Swinging the image on a swing and ascending it [to a higher place] are desirable;
in this month, especially under the constellation of the Pitṛs (Maghā), [the rite should be performed] accompanied by clarified butter.
One should cause milk-rice (pāyasa) to be offered to Śambhu and also to the Goddess, as it is approved by them both. || 14 ||
In the month of Puṣya, under the Puṣya asterism, one should perform the consecration with honey;
at the conclusion of the offering of the great oblation, one should arrange for the procession of the image.
By means of the previously described procedure, the performer shall obtain the desired fruit.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the ritual procedure for worship in the months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Puṣya, in the great tantra named Uttarakāmika;
O twice-born ones, one should then perform the *ḍorāroha* ceremony at the time of evening.
Having likewise adorned both pillars with all manner of ornaments.
One should fix a pole between those two pillars, joined with the characteristic marks of a pillar;
in the middle of that, one should place a swing measuring four cubits.
Endowed with four arms and provided with an upper garment, she was adorned with various ornaments; then [she appeared] endowed with two arms.
[She is] endowed with a single swan-throne and accompanied by the sprinkling of the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha).
In the tenth chapter, the procedure for the worship of the "Ghee-Blanket" (ghṛtakambala) in the month of Māgha:
one should indeed perform the Ghee-Blanket rite in the month of Māgha under the Maghā asterism.
The clarified butter should be exclusively from a tawny cow (kāpila) and free from worms, insects, and the like. || 1 ||
The preceptor should place hairless, fresh, pure, and fragrant [wood];
he should cast it into water with a weapon, while reciting the seed-mantra of Varuṇa.
Then, having prepared that clarified butter like a *piṇḍa*, it should be consecrated with saffron and agallochum,
and also with the powders of turmeric and camphor.
Having placed it in a vessel made of gold or other precious materials and having fumigated it with incense,
one should then consecrate it with the five Brahmans, the six limbs, and [the mantra of] Śiva.
One should perform a special ablution with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the nectars;
having performed a special worship, one should finally place clarified butter upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
The wise one, correctly reciting the heart-mantra, should worship with the *gaṇa* and other [mantras];
then, on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to the east of that, the wise one should satisfy the fire of Śiva.

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations consisting of palāśa wood fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, sesame seeds, and parched grain, and having performed the final full oblation at the end; || 7 ||
Having performed the oblation of the remnants into the clarified butter (saṃpātahoma) by way of the insertion of the purifiers (pavitrāropa),
one should first place [the vessel] upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) together with its lid.
Then, having enveloped [the deity] with the Kavaca mantra, one should worship the Lord as before at either morning or midday, accompanied by the rites of bathing and so forth.
Having honored [the deity] especially, endowed with all ornaments,
and having performed a circumambulation of the temple while reciting the Śiva-mantra.
Having smeared the liṅga and all the pedestals up to their bases with [unbroken rice] and other substances,
and having worshipped them with perfumes and the like, one should wrap them with a woolen blanket.
In this manner, one should offer an oblation to Śambhu accompanied by betel leaf.

On the following day, or within the interval of the twilight, having avoided [the use of] blankets and such, one should worship the Deity as before; at that time, one should also fully honor the Guru.
One should cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given for him according to the extent of one's wealth;
or one may perform this preceded by the offering of sprouts, or even without it.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, the ritual procedure for the worship of the "Ghee-Blanket" (*ghṛtakambala*), in the great tantra known as the *Uttarakāmika*.
Now, in the eleventh chapter, the ritual procedure for the worship on Śivarātri in the month of Māgha:
O twice-born ones, I shall now explain in detail the vow of Śivarātri.
Listen, O you who are self-restrained, to the most excellent of vows. 1.
They performed that which was formerly practiced by the Goddess and practiced by others as well;
sporting joyfully together with me, they attained their desired goal.
By the command of Yama, they are not tormented by the servants with cruel eyes;
they do not even behold Yama, nor do they go to the hells. (3)
Listen indeed to that procedure, which is approved by all:
on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, [there occurs a specific rite].
That night shall be Śivarātri, which brings all merit and auspiciousness; on that very night, one should perform the worship of Śiva upon a Śivaliṅga in a temple of Śiva.
On the preceding day, the practitioner, having performed his bath and fast, being self-restrained,
should perform the ritual service together with faith.
Having first performed the fivefold purification according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should then prepare the seat of Śiva (śivāsana) and therein the form consisting of the body of knowledge (vidyātanu).
Having invoked and brought Śiva into close presence, one should worship him with water for the feet and other offerings;
having worshipped him and rubbed him with scented oil and flour paste, one should cleanse him.
One should sprinkle [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to their respective methods;
one should also sprinkle [him] with scented water according to the ritual procedure, using clarified butter and other substances.
One should perform [the purification] with the five purifiers and the five limbs in due order;
then again, having rubbed [the body] with flour and likewise with an *āmalaka* fruit.
One should purify [the site] with powder, with ground turmeric, with incense,
and indeed with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra.
Thereafter, one should consecrate him with coconut water alone;
then one should consecrate him with scented water while reciting the root mantra, the limb mantras, and the Brahma-mantra.
Having wiped it with a pure cotton cloth,
one should cover the liṅga with a pure garment such as one from Devāṅga.
One should worship each watch separately with various substances such as perfumes and so forth,
using sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and other materials in their proper order.
One should worship properly with jasmine, blue lotus flowers, jasmine flowers, and bilva fruits, as well as with dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains, and sesame seeds.
One should fumigate with the resin of guggulu, agarwood, and the essence of sarja;
and one should light a lamp with a very white wick soaked in clarified butter.
In the first watch, milk-rice; in the second, rice with sesame; in the third, cow-meat; and in the fourth, pure food.
And after that, having offered [the food] together with all its condiments,
one should offer betel-leaf along with ghee and molasses.
Having offered incense along with the *ārātrika* lamp to Śiva,
one should perform a special fire sacrifice (*homa*) either in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).

In a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), a ritual vessel (kalpa), or a bowl (pātra), having first performed the consecration of the pit and having envisioned the Śiva-fire within the fire, one should envision the seat of Śiva within the heart.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods there, one should offer oblations into the blazing fire with clarified butter,
sacrificial offerings, parched grain, and sesame seeds, using the root mantra, the limb mantras, and the Brahma-mantras.
For other mantras, the offering should be one-tenth of that for Śiva;
it increases by ten-fold increments until the offering reaches fifteen oblations.
Having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* with Śiva alone, which brings about a flawless completion, and having offered salutations and then bowed down to that Lord of Gods who is smeared with ashes; || 23 ||
One should worship in this manner again and again at every watch;
if one is unable to perform it oneself, one may have another perform it for one's own sake.
Having kept a vigil during the night, then at the clear dawn,
having performed his daily obligatory rites, he should thereafter perform the ritual bathing according to the prescribed rules.
Having worshipped the deity as before, one should then proceed with the worship of the Guru;
thereafter, one should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), avoiding any stinginess regarding one's wealth.

Having properly completed the worship, one should honor with devotion and according to one's capacity those who bear the sectarian marks (liṅgins), devotees of Śiva, Brāhmaṇas, and guests as well. (27)
Having returned to his own home together with his kinsmen, the practitioner, having washed his feet and hands, should perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa). || 28 ||
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the procedure for the worship on the Śivarātri of the month of Māgha, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
In the twelfth chapter is the procedure for the worship with fragrances in the month of Phālguna.
In the month of Uttara-phālguna, one should worship with all kinds of perfumes,
accompanied by a special ritual bathing and a special sacrifice.
The measurement for sandalwood is said to begin from one *pala* and increase up to a thousand *palas*;
the measure for agallochum (*agaru*) shall be half of that.
The saffron should be one-fourth or one-half of that [measurement], or half of that again;
the border should be one-eighth of the foot-measure, or half of that, or even just one foot-measure.
Or, having ground camphor even twice as much, one should incense everything;
it should be perfumed with fragrant flowers and consecrated with all the mantras.

Having consecrated the linga along with its pedestal by means of the path of the ghee-woolen-blanket and the path of the fire-oblation, one should smear it with fragrances while reciting the Śiva-mantra.
One should adorn the linga and its pedestal with fragrant flower garlands;
everything except the woolen blanket should be treated as if it were made of ghee-wool.

In the event of the outbreak of all diseases, for a miracle, for the attainment of desired objects, or for the removal of the fault caused by malevolent magic, one should perform this ritual procedure.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, the ritual for the worship with perfumes in the month of Phālguna, in the great tantra named Uttarakāmika.
In the thirteenth chapter is the ritual for the worship with *damana* in the month of Caitra.
I shall describe the offering of *damanaka* flowers, which bestows the fruits of the month of Caitra.
In ancient times, one known as Damanaka was born from the wrath of Hara. || 1 ||
By him all the gods and the mighty Dānavas were subdued; then, being pleased, Śiva said to Viṭapa: "Become a tree upon the surface of the earth. (2)
Having attained a state of being tamed, you shall become an object of enjoyment for me;
and those mortals who worship you with sprouts and other offerings, [they too shall attain my state]. (3)
Those men who shall again perform the Damanaka festival will go to the supreme abode through the power of Damana.
Having gone to the presence of Damanaka on the seventh or the thirteenth day, I have bestowed upon them the fruit of merit arising from the month of Caitra.
Having purified it with the Astra-mantra, one should worship it with the Saṃhitā mantras;
then, the knower of mantras should awaken the cord with the words of Śiva.
May you attain the presence of the mantra obtained through the grace of Śiva;
for the sake of Śiva’s work, you must be led [there] by the command of Śiva.
Having thus addressed Evandamana and protected him, he should go to his abode;
for having brought [the plant] from afar along with its roots and accompanied by earth... (8)
Having placed it back [in the fire] and poured water into a vessel filled with clay,
the wise man should perform the invocation of the planets according to the previously stated procedure.
When the time of evening has arrived,
one who has performed the auspicious rites such as bathing should bring the sacrificial materials and perform the consecration (adhivāsana).
Having worshipped the Sun, Śaṅkara, and Agni according to the prescribed rite,
one should take the root of that God of gods together with earth from the western side.
It is kindled by the Sadyojāta mantra, or by the Heart mantra, or by the Vāma or Śiras mantras; thereafter, one should worship Nālandhātrī with the Uttara mantra.
To the south, he should place the vessel of ashes, either with the Śikhā-mantra or the Rūpinī-mantra;
or, to the east, the tooth-stick along with flowers, using the Puṃ-mantra or the Varman-mantra.

Having placed the five limbs [of the mantra] along with fruit and root, joined with fragrance, in his cupped hands in the northeast according to the Gāyatrī, he should offer a garland accompanied by flowers and unbroken rice grains.
One should inform the Lord of the World regarding the mounting of the goad:
"O Lord of Gods, O Master, you have been invited by me at the time of dawn. (15)
"And whatever may be obtained, it must be performed in its entirety by the command of the Mountain";
having thus informed the God, he offered a handful of flowers upon His head. (16)
Having joined it with the Śiva-mantra, one should perform the recitation (japa) and other rites;
having poured the remainder into a vessel, one should cover it with a second [vessel].
One should envelop it with the *kavaca* [mantra] according to the ritual procedure for the *pavitraka*. Having thus rendered it well-protected, one should offer it to Śiva. || 18 ||
Thereafter, one should consume the sacrificial offering, or else subsist on air alone;
having performed a vigil before Śiva with meditation, chanting, recitation, and other rites. (19)
Having bathed in the morning, one should worship the Lord of the World with eight flowers,
having performed both the regular and occasional worship in a special manner.
One should worship the God with *damanaka* flowers, even if they are broken into five parts;
then, taking the remainder in the hollowed palms along with *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
Meditating upon the god Sadāśiva, who faces [the practitioner] and possesses five faces,
[he meditates] by means of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Śiva and ending with Īśvara— namely, Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva.
One should worship Śiva in due order according to the rite of the *pavitraka*,
using the previously mentioned principles of the self (*ātmatattva*) and so forth, accompanied by two, four, and six vowels respectively.
One should perform the purificatory rite with the peaceful mantras accompanied by nasal drops (bindus).
The mantra for the fourth añjali consists of the Praṇava and the Śiva-mantra.
One should perform the repetition of "O Lord of Sacrifice, complete the sacrifice," ending with the name Śūlapāṇi in the dative case followed by the word of salutation (namas). || 25 ||
Having prostrated before Śiva and worshipped the Fire according to the prescribed rules,
one who knows the ritual should then petition Śiva, the bestower of the fruits of desired objects.
O Blessed One, whatever I have done that was either excessive or deficient,
may all of that become complete for me on this Dāmanaka festival.
Having thus performed the rite of binding, one should perform the worship of the Guru;
thereafter, one should satisfy those who have been initiated with that which brings them complete satisfaction.
Whether he be a householder or a celibate student, whoever performs this rite—
consisting of worship, recitation, and so forth— obtains the fruit arising from the month of Caitra.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, the procedure for the Damanaka-pūjā in the month of Caitra, in the great tantra named Uttarakāmika.
In the fourteenth chapter is the procedure for the Vasantotsava festival in the month of Caitra.
In that month, the desired Vasantotsava festival was to be observed;
on the preceding day, having tied the marriage-thread (kautuka) amidst a grove filled with various trees, [he entered].
It was strewn with various garlands, variegated with various fruits, endowed with various songs, and accompanied by various musical instruments. || 2 ||
It was filled with various dances, equipped with various mechanical devices, strewn with diverse kinds of flowers, and endowed with manifold fragrances. || 3 ||
It was strewn with banners, illuminated by blazing lamps,
provided with an assembly pavilion, and equipped for water-sports.
When the sun has grown dim, one should lead the deity, adorned with all ornaments, to the divine garden accompanied by a circumambulation of the village.
Having performed the circumambulation around him, one should especially worship the deity with ritual offerings such as perfumes, incense, meat, and so forth.
Recalling that the Flower-Weaponed One (Kusumāyudha) has come for the sake of service and is dwelling there,
one should [worship him] on the right and left of the Deity with various perfumes and other offerings in due order.
One should worship those two [deities] in two water-pots provided with gold, cloth, and other offerings,
or else upon two sacrificial altars (sthaṇḍila) adorned with various flowers.
Having covered the food offering with a cloth, one should present the milk-rice (pāyasa);
at the end, one should offer betel nut and especially satisfy the two of them.
Having dispelled [the obstacles] with divine songs accompanied by dance and instrumental music,
O Lord of Gods, he should thus lead [the deity] back to the temple at that time.
One should cause the ceremonial bathing (snapana) to be performed and worship Śiva with special offerings;
thus one should respectfully worship the god Śiva with special offerings.
Thus, the mortal who performs this shall attain all desires. || 111.2 ||
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the procedure for the Spring Festival of the month of Caitra, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
In the fifteenth chapter is the procedure for the Cold Vase (śītakumbha) of the month of Vaiśākha.
Thereafter, I shall describe in detail the cold-water jar (śītakumbha) in its proper sequence;
it is prescribed for the month of Vaiśākha under the asterism Viśākhā, or during a drought.
For the purpose of destroying all misfortunes and for the cessation of all portents,
