one should employ [this rite] in matters such as expiatory ceremonies (prāyaścitta) and in events such as the burning of a village.
When the time for the four-legged disease arises, or when fever, Āryā, and other ailments occur,
the ritual of the cold water-pitcher (śītakumbha) should be performed to eliminate those respective defects.
Having fashioned a tripod from trees suitable for sacrifice and placed it upon the top of the liṅga,
one should begin at eight finger-breadths and increase by one finger-breadth up to the length of a cubit.
Having performed the *antara* rite in that manner, the Guru should wash [the disciple's feet] with water,
cover them with a cloth, and worship Brahmānanda on the right side.
One should place Viṣṇu on the left, the bull on the back, and the deities on the three legs;
one should install Mahāmāyā above, and [the other deities] all around the body of the fruit.
Having done this, one should place the three-legged stand upon the top of the liṅga;
then, having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the pavilion with eight droṇas or more of śāli rice.
One should place a water-pot there filled with rice, sesame seeds, and parched grain;
it is best when full of four *droṇas*, though three *droṇas* is also acceptable.
The medium [liṅga] is one filled with a khārī measure;
the smallest is wound with thread, shaped like a ripe bimba fruit, covered with cloth, and provided with a tuft of wool.
It is joined with a golden lotus, auspicious with five gems within its interior, provided with a hollow at the back, and endowed with a golden stalk. || 10 ||
It is joined with one, two, or three feet, fashioned according to the measurement of a niṣka,
with a length of four finger-breadths, and possessing a hole as fine as the tip of a needle.
It is provided with a lid, equipped with a sprout,
and at its front, near the jar, it is joined with cloth, gold, and other such items.
One should place it on its right side, provided that the back opening is absent;
then, having prepared a seat, one should invoke the deity's form into the jar.
One should fashion the body of knowledge (vidyādeha) with Brahma-mantras endowed with their respective kalās;
having invoked Śiva with the Praṇava, one should worship him properly with perfumes and other offerings.
One should perform this rite at the principal [image] and at the upakumbha;
or one may employ scented water, honey, milk, and so forth for all purposes. || 15 ||
When another expiation has occurred for the sake of destroying misdeeds,
one should pour in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or even pure water.
One may prepare sandalwood paste mixed with ashes as the fragrant substance,
or else simply the prepared fragrance itself for the purpose of the water for sipping (ācamanīya).
One should place hairless and insect-free substances into the vessel near the jar;
having worshipped it with perfumes and other offerings using the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should then perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*). || 18 ||
In the nine, five, or one sacrificial pits, [the oblation] should consist of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice,
combined with sesame seeds and parched grain, and further joined with honey, grains, and Indra-seeds (priyaṅgu).
The fuel-sticks (samidh) should arise from the añjula-tree, accompanied by all the mantras dedicated to Varuṇa,
as well as by the Āpya mantra, the Amṛtabīja, the Saṃpuṭa, and the Śiva mantra.
One should perform the oblation for each substance either a thousand times accompanied by the Āpyāyana mantra, or a number equal to that [specific requirement], or one hundred and eight times.
One should mutter the root mantra that many times as there are water-molecules within the casket; likewise, those desiring success through ritual offerings should mutter the Varuṇa mantras.

The mantra "Āpyāyasva" should be recited with reverence by the twice-born who are masters of the four Vedas, who have performed their ablutions, who are humble, and who subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣya). || 23 ||
With undistracted minds, tranquil, and obedient to the commands of their preceptor,
all were endowed with the initiation of Śiva and were longing for rain.
One should sprinkle the entire temple with water day and night;
at that time, one should especially cause milk to flow from the udders of cows.
If there should be a thousand in number, endowed with half that number [of attendants], and if the protectors are a hundred in number, there will be prosperity and rain. (26)

O best of the twice-born, this should be performed every day at the time of the fire-oblation (homa), during worship, and when the rite is completed; O brahmins, one should then perform the Varuṇī concentration (dhāraṇā).

Having meditated upon it as consisting of nectar while reciting the root mantra ending with "vauṣaṭ," one should perform the rite accompanied by the sound of a conch; and one should practice in this manner every day.
At the conclusion of the daily worship, one should commence the occasional rite;
however, if the occasional rite is a major one, one should perform it at the beginning of the major [daily] rite.

Having installed the Lord of the gods of gods with cool waters endowed with various fragrances and accompanied by the ritual of placement (sthāpanā), while recollecting the immersion in nectar (amṛtāplāvana).
With abundant sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron, and with many fragrant flowers that were instantly awakened [into bloom], the Guru [was honored]. || 31 ||
With incense produced from black agallochum, prepared for a joyful kingdom;
with lamps using camphor wicks; and with abundant milk-rice offerings—in an instant. (32)
With food offerings prepared in nine vessels made of rice, with cool drinking water, fragrant scents, and delicious foods served in new vessels. || 33 ||
With betel leaves, fragrant white leaves produced from the *kramuka* tree, and mouth-freshening substances, accompanied by songs, musical instruments, and dances; || 34 ||
With hymns endowed with the nine dramatic sentiments, even in the melodies of the Vedas, by those chanting, with shouts of victory, and with prostrations performed many times; || 35 ||
One should worship the deity every day until the desired fruit is attained;
at its conclusion, the daily fire-sacrifice (homa) should be performed according to the prescribed ritual.
On the first day there is this special rule: at the end of the full [period], having caused two jars to be taken—either from the mouth or from the head—one should circumambulate them clockwise.
Having performed these two [rites] in a beautiful vessel within the Sudhāman [temple],
under a lunar mansion favorable to both the preceptor and the patron.
On a Saturday or at an auspicious moment (sulagna), one should plant [the tree] while reciting the mantra of Śiva;
into that [hole], one should pour water contained within a new jar that has a small hole in it.
Having recited the Śiva-mantra and meditated upon the stream of nectar,
one facing north should pour it into the center of the tripod.
One should always carry the remainder of the water until the ritual action is completed—whether for seven days, twice seven days, thrice seven days, or for a month. (41)
For two or three months, one should not practice [the rite] in this manner;
first, one should worship the preceptor with garments and ornaments consisting of five parts.
O King, at the beginning one should cause sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) such as ten niṣkas to be given;
and at the end, O men, the worship and the sacrificial fee should be double.
To all others as well, he should give gold, garments, and finger-rings, accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of one niṣka, endowed with faith.
Every day, for the sake of their food, the king should provide them with rice accompanied by side dishes and betel leaf, endowed with faith.
Food must be provided daily for the devotees and even for the yogis; likewise, food should be given every day to the poor and the helpless. (46)
At the conclusion, one should have the ceremonial bathing performed and cause abundant sacrificial offerings to be given.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the ritual for the cold-water jar in the month of Vaiśākha, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
Having fashioned a tripod from trees suitable for sacrifice, one should place it upon the top of the liṅga.
Starting from the *vastvaṅgula* and increasing by one *aṅgula* at each step, it extends up to the *ākara*.
Having performed the intermediate rites in that manner, and having washed his feet with water and covered them with a cloth, he should worship Brahmā to the south.
One should install Viṣṇu on the left, the bull on the back, and the deities of the Great Illusions (Mahāmāyās) upon the three feet and the upper plank with their respective mantras.
Having done this, one should place the tripod upon the head of the liṅga;
it should be filled with four *droṇas*, or preferably with three *droṇas*.
The medium [liṅga] is one full khārī in measure;
the smallest is wound with thread, shaped like the stem of a ripe bimba fruit, and provided with cloth and a tuft of hair.
It is joined with a golden lotus, auspicious with five gems within its interior,
provided with a hollow at the back, and endowed with a golden stalk.
16. In the sixteenth chapter, the procedure for worship and the fruits [obtained] in the month of Jyeṣṭha:
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, under the Mūla asterism, one should worship with sweet fruits, accompanied by a special bathing ceremony and endowed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). || 1 ||
It is accompanied by special worship, provided with milk-rice (pāyasa),
and joined with a special fire-oblation (homa) consisting of sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice.
Having filled [the vessel] with substances endowed with various fruits,
one should fill [the body of the deity], from the pedestal up to the top of the *liṅga*, with fruits while reciting the root mantra.
Having made the linga disappear, or having filled it from the outside,
one should wrap both the linga and the pedestal with two cloths while reciting the armor-mantra (kavaca-mantra).
Therefore, one should lead them outside during the interval between twilights or on the following day;
at the conclusion of the rite, the performer should honor the preceptor with garments and gold.
Whatever is desired as a fruit for the agent, that shall quickly come to pass.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the ritual for worship and the fruits of the month of Jyeṣṭha, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
In the seventeenth chapter, [the ritual for] the month of Āṣāḍha and the asterism Pūrvaphalgunī.
The ritual procedure for worship should be performed in the month of Āṣāḍha under the lunar mansion known as Pūrvaphālgunī,
or else in the month of Āśvayuja. || 1 ||
One should tie the protective amulet (kautuka) at night according to the previously mentioned procedure for the Goddess;
and in the morning, one should bestow gold and other gifts upon the maidens for both the God and the Goddess.
Having offered clothing and food, one should present milk to the Goddess;
then, adorned with all ornaments, one should perform a circumambulation of the village.
At that time, one should cause to be offered sprouts of mung beans endowed with auspicious characteristics;
before the circumambulation of the village, one may or may not cause an offering of food (naivedya) to be presented.
Having led [the deity] to the assembly pavilion (āsthānamaṇḍapa), one should proceed with the sequence of the ritual offering;
this includes the nocturnal powder (rātricūrṇa) and oil, according to the prescribed rules for the powder festival (cūrṇotsava).
Immediately thereafter, one should offer to the God and the Goddess, as well as to the Jayas,
betel-leaf along with various side dishes and rice.
Or, having abandoned the task of grinding [the powder] and the offering of rice and other grains,
one should lead the Goddess, accompanied by the trident, to a river or similar location.
The preceptor should prepare two sacrificial altars with rice according to the prescribed rite;
having first established the trident of the Goddess upon one, at its front.
Having properly established those jars according to the procedure prescribed for the ritual ablution,
the Guru should worship them with groats mixed with fruits, as if they were lakes.
Having bathed that trident with them, one should perform an immersion;
then, together with the people, one should enter the temple situated in the midst of the sacred ford.
Or, having abandoned the rites for visiting sacred sites, until the end of wandering through villages and the like,
or on this very day, [one should worship] with a garland that does not fade, [visualizing] the lamp of Nirvāṇa.
One should perform this every year accompanied by the offering of oblations (bali),
or else joined with both oblations and fire-offerings (homa), whether by night or by day.
Having performed circumambulations, adorned with all ornaments, together with various devotees and various sweet fruits, (he departed). || 13 ||
The preceptor should cause parched grain flour mixed with pieces of jaggery to be given,
together with various cakes and accompanied by various fruits.
Having offered molasses, fruits, parched grain flour, and other oblations on the bank of the water before the God of gods, one should then release [the bull] at the holy ford in the fresh water.
Alternatively, having fashioned [the image] as simple as possible or provided with a trident,
one should then lead it to the temple and perform the ceremonial bathing along with worship.
At the conclusion, one should respectfully worship the Guru with abundant offerings of oblations and with betel leaf accompanied by mouth-perfume.
One should cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of garments, gold, rings,
and so forth to be given for the sake of destroying all sins and for the cessation of all misfortunes.
For the sake of accomplishing all desired objects and for the success of every undertaking, this ritual procedure, which causes the satisfaction of the Goddess, must be performed. (19)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, the ritual procedure for the worship of Pūrvaphalgunī in the month of Āṣāḍha, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
In the eighteenth chapter is the ritual procedure for the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
O bulls among sages, listen as I describe the Pavitraka rite for the purpose of destroying the sins committed throughout the year. 1.
A mantra-practitioner who fails to perform expiation due to transgressing the prescribed rules suffers a fall from accomplishment; such a teacher shall become a partaker of disease.
A son attains enjoyment through birth alone, but by restraining [the breath] for a single lifetime;
whereas one who merely abides by the rules (samayī) does not attain it at all, even while remaining established in the rules, because he lacks the *pavitraka*.
One must strive by whatever means possible, through every manner of activity of speech, mind, and body, to ensure that [this] is accomplished daily. (4)
Because it protects one from falling, this is therefore called *pavitraka*.
The three months beginning with Āṣāḍha are classified as superior (*jyeṣṭha*), middling (*madhyama*), and inferior (*kanyasa*).
The months of Āśvina and Kārttika are likewise proclaimed;
however, the Pavitraka rite should be performed on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āṣāḍha.
And during the other months, on the fourteenth and eighth days of both the bright and dark fortnights, one should perform the Pavitraka rite according to the prescribed rule.
After the Kṛttikā festival, the Pavitraka rite should not be performed;
for a householder it is in the bright fortnight, and for an ascetic in both fortnights.
Whether or not an auspicious constellation is favorable for the one who performs the rite or the one who causes it to be performed,
the thread should be made of linen or cotton, or, if those are unavailable, of muñja grass.
Having gathered either *darbha* grass or [grass] grown from its own kind, one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*).
Having tripled it and then folded it threefold, one should purify it with the *astra-mantra*.
The preceptor should wash the woolen cloth and other materials with pure water while reciting the Astra mantra;
having dried it, he should then have the purification performed over it with the Hrdaya mantra.
The nine powers, beginning with Vāmā, are considered the presiding deities of the nine threads;
the strands in the hand are double that number, increasing by ten in sequence thereafter.
One hundred and eight of those threads is the most excellent of the excellent;
with an increase of twelve each, there are twelve [varieties] ending at that point.

Or else, the threads are fully established in the lower attainments (siddhis) such as the "Kanyasa" and others; for the younger ones, they are numbered by their digits (kalās), while for the middling ones, they are characterized by their colors.
In the case of the superior [liṅgas], the number of threads is considered to be ten in human-made liṅgas,
as well as in those made of self-manifested stone (svāyambhuva), Bāṇa-liṅgas, or those made of precious gems.
Whether on a sacrificial mound, in a mandala, or upon mobile or stationary images,
all the numbers— whether even or odd— should be collected.
O lords of sages, the householder is indeed equal toward his family members, gods, and others, as well as toward those of meager wealth and those who bear the outward marks of asceticism.
The threads increase one by one starting from one up to twelve;
the knots are considered to be equal in number to the threads, fresh, and having smooth cores. (18)
Or else, according to one's desire, the knots may be established everywhere with equal intervals; in this scripture, the measurement of a knot is said to be from one to three finger-breadths.
Then, the wise should apply knots and wraps around the region of the abdomen using red sandalwood, saffron, red ochre, agallochum, and sandalwood.
Combined with kuṣṭha and camphor, and joined with turmeric and black fragrance,
one should dye it with the heart-mantra itself, or else with red thread and so forth.
A triad consisting of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva should be placed upon the top;
the fourth sacred thread, however, should touch the pedestal and be entirely composed of the principles (tattvas).

The garland known as the *yajñasūtra* and the arm-garland (*bāhumālā*) should be placed upon the face-linga thereafter; or alternatively, they are considered appropriate for the *sakala* [liṅga] as well. (23)
It should be beautifully manifest up to the knees, joined with its own desired thread at three points before;
it may be the size of a mechanical liṅga or measured according to a flower-liṅga.
In the case of a small liṅga, the purifier (pavitra) may be according to one's inclination on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and so forth;
for a bull, there should be one [ring] reaching to the horns and another reaching to the hump and the hooves.
"Let a single purifier (pavitra) be prescribed for all those who are enveloped [in ritual];
however, one each must be given to Caṇḍeśa and Kṣetrapāla. (26)
One should circumambulate clockwise a single thread around the fields, the boundaries, the world-supporters,
the sacrificial hall, the bull-pen, the temple, and the dwellings.
One should wrap all the ritual implements with a triple-stranded thread;
having thus resolved, one should begin the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) on the preceding day.
Either at the front of the palace, or to its left or right, in a pavilion measuring from five cubits up to twenty-four cubits; (29)
It should be provided with sixteen pillars, or even joined with twelve pillars;
it should have a central altar and be endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
Or, in a previously prepared pavilion measuring three parts in length and joined with twenty pillars, or one with an altar twice as long [as it is wide].
Around that, nine, five, or one well-arranged sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be prepared; or else, on an altar (sthaṇḍila) of that same number, or even upon a raised platform (vedikā).
One should prepare the mandala in the west and place the sacred thread in the east;
having performed purification, ritual bathing, the twilight worship, and the libations. (33)
Having performed the daily worship, the practitioner of mantra, accompanied by the worship of the Sun,
being pure and with his body armored by the mantra, should not dismiss the Sun.
Having taken hold of the ground, the door, the door-keepers, the lord of the site (vāstunāyaka), Lakṣmī, Yāgeśa, Vardhanī, the world-protectors (lokapālas), Gaṇapa, and the gurus; || 35 ||
Having performed the sacrifice and offered prayers, he then worshipped Śaṅkara within the maṇḍala according to the prescribed rites; O Lord, he then sat upon his own seat near him.
Beginning with the worship of the seat, one should perform the ritual up to the invocation, provided with the five nectars and accompanied by the special ablution. (37)
Having performed a special worship provided with various perfumes and various kinds of food, both hard and soft, the Guru goes to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Beginning with the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa-saṃskāra) and ending with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa),
offering fuel-sticks (samit), clarified butter (ājya), cooked rice (caru), parched grain (lāja), sesame seeds (tila), and grains (sasya), together with Indra [or indrāṇī].
The Palāśa, Udumbara, Āvattha, and Vaṭa trees should be placed in the directions starting from the east;
and the Śamī, Khadira, Śrīvṛkṣa, and Plakṣa trees should be in the south-eastern corner.
In the primary pit according to the Prādhānika view, the altar for Śiva should be one hundred or fifty palas;
for the ancillary deities, it should be one-tenth the size of that for Śiva.

Half of that [quantity] should be placed in the other sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) for the human beings and others; having prepared the oblation of cooked rice (sthālīpāka), one should divide that clarified butter into three parts with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra).
One should prepare the portion for Śiva and the portion for Agni mixed with honey and clarified butter,
but one's own portion should be made with clarified butter alone.
Having worshipped the portion of the deity with his heart and taken it, he should go into the presence of Śiva;
having fully honored the Lord of Gods, he should offer the constituent parts of the vow.
The knower of mantras should place the tooth-stick in the east while recollecting the Puruṣa as prescribed by the rules;
the knower of mantras should place the ashes in a pure vessel to the south with the Aghora mantra.
Afterwards, one should offer pure clay while recollecting the *Sadyojāta* mantra;
then, one should present five *dhātrī* fruits, water, and edible food in the east.
O lady of beautiful countenance, all the materials for the fire sacrifice along with kuśa grass are on the left;
the staff, rosary, loincloth, and alms-bowl are on the right.
Rocana, saffron, oil, a hair-cleansing probe, a mirror, a small knife, a toothpick, a nail-cleaner, and collyrium. (48)
One should offer another vessel while recollecting Vāmadeva;
one should offer betel-leaf mixed with ashes while recollecting Tatpuruṣa. (49)

In the northeast, having consecrated the seat, the parasol, the sandals, and the yoga-band upon the sacrificial mound near the thread, or having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) around it; || 50 ||

One should offer to Śiva that armor which has been sprinkled with the Astra-mantra, sharpened, worshipped at the heart, turned into nectar by the Dhenu-mudrā, and which is a portion of Śiva himself. || 51 ||
Then, O God, the priests should bring purifying materials for the deity;
there shall be a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) upon the altar made with eight *droṇas* of rice.
Then the preceptor should place the purifiers in that vessel, accompanied by half as much rice and provided with sesame seeds and parched grain.
If [the deity] is situated above the altar in the mandala, or even here near the water-jar (kumbha),
one should install [the image], sprinkle it with the arghya water, and touch it while reciting the Saṃhitā-mantra.
Having covered it with a deer-skin and other such materials, one should place it near the fire—
the imperishable witness of all rites, whose nature is the year.
Recalling the auspicious Brahman, who is the protector, the refuge, and the cause for attaining the fruits of action, [he should meditate] upon the six-limbed Śiva through the Śiva-mantra.
Then, one should likewise offer oblations twenty-one times;
having given fragrant purifiers to the Sun and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the preceptor [proceeds].
One should encircle with the thread and the armor-mantra the five agents— the sacrificial ground, the bull-station, the temple, the fire, and the refuge.
One should offer the fragrant purifier (pavitra) to Nandin and the others while circumambulating;
then, having entered within as before, one should offer the purifier to Brahmā.
"Therefore, O Blessed One, these purifiers have indeed been consecrated; I offer them to Śiva residing in the jar and I pray to him. (60)
Having offered the fragrant purifier (gandhapavitraka) to those [deities] for their protection,
or first having given it to the water-pot (kumbha) and the vardhanī vessel, he should proceed toward the presence of Śiva.
One should offer the fragrant *pavitraka* to one's own image and to the row of gurus;
it should be fashioned from fine threads and provided with a single knot. (62)
The Guru, taking up incense and flowers joined together in his cupped hands, offers that consecrated vessel,
which is the "invitation-purifier" (āmantraṇa-pavitra) and is made delightful by the "nectar-seal" (sudhā-mudrā).
Having placed [the deity] upon the head of Śivā with the exhalation (recaka) and the Śiva-mantra,
one should recite the mantra consisting of invocation in the presence of the Lord of Devas.
O Lord, for the sake of filling every gap in the entire ritual procedure,
I address you, the one who brings about the fulfillment of your own will.
O Lord of the conscious and the unconscious, know that the success of one who sacrifices [to you] is thus;
O Śambhu, may there be salutation to you in every way and at all times—be gracious to me! 66.
Having recited [the mantra], offered [oblations] to the deity, praised him, and bowed down, one should ask for forgiveness;
then one should give the purificatory thread (pavitraka) to the guardians of the directions and to their weapons.
Having offered a third portion of the sacrificial oblation (caru) to the deity residing in the fire,
the preceptor should perform the invitation (āmantraṇa) and offer the purificatory thread (pavitra) for that very deity as before.
Saying "Indrāya saṃgṛhāṇa," preceded by the syllable Om,
and likewise for the others with their respective forms, one should offer the external bali in due order.
Having offered [the oblation] to the Kṣetrapāla in the northwest and sipped water,
the Guru should again offer the bali, then perform the expiatory rite (prāyaścitta), and finally offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One should perform oblations with the words *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*, both individually and collectively;
then an offering to Agni, one to Soma, and the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation to both of them.
Having first offered oblations with the previously mentioned mantras ending in "svāhā" while holding a lamp,
he should then [unite] Śiva residing in the fire with Śiva residing in the maṇḍala.
One should join with and meditate upon Śiva by means of the path of the union of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna-mārga).
Having offered the sacred thread (pavitraka) to one's own guru and to the book of the Siddhānta, [one should perform the rite]. || 73 ||

Having departed from the sacrificial site and performed ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the pure preceptor should, in due order, partake of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the sacrificial porridge (caru), and the tooth-cleansing stick (dantadhāvana).
Having sipped water (ācamana), he should sleep again at the end, recollecting Śiva.
Then, in the morning, having performed the necessary bath, the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), and the libations (tarpaṇa).
Without having received permission from the Lord of Gods, one should remove the sacred threads (pavitra).
O Lord, one should arrange them upon the mandala and in a vessel for the sake of Caṇḍeśa.
Having offered the eightfold flower-offering to the deity, one should bid farewell to the Lord from the liṅga;
then, having sipped water and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), the Guru should hold the general arghya vessel.
Having properly performed the daily rites and sipped water, the one whose body is the mantra,
having worshipped the doors and the lords of the doors, enters while offering the weapons into the two jars.
One should perform the worship of the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) and their weapons in due order;
seated upon one's own seat prepared with lamps, one remains standing with the face turned toward the east.
The mantra-body, endowed with the purification of special offering substances (arghyadravya),
and having envisioned the hand of Śiva, one should likewise prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) as before.
One should worship Śiva in a special manner, accompanied by a special ablution, provided with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and joined with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). 81.
Having performed the recitation (japa) and reported it, the Guru should go to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having sprinkled the pit with the weapon-mantra (astra), [he should likewise sprinkle] those situated on the girdle (mekhalā) and the enclosing sticks (paridhi).

Having worshipped the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and consecrated the clarified butter according to the rules, the knower of the ritual procedure should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), invoke the deity, worship him, and gratify him with libations.
Then, having performed the expiation, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
having offered the purifier (pavitra) to the Sun and sipped water, one becomes endowed with a subtle body.

Having offered the *pavitra* to Nandin and the others, and having entered within, one should present the *pavitraka* to Brahmā and to the water-jar (*kumbha*) and the *vardhanī* vessel in due order. (85)
Having gone into the presence of the deity and sat down well upon his own seat, he performed a special worship according to his means. || 86 ||
Having placed the thread upon his own body and in the row of gurus while recollecting Śiva, [he should contemplate] the form consisting of the year,
season, month, fortnight, day, nāḍī, breath, and so forth.
The sole cause for the functioning of all the senses, the body, and their objects;
the unique witness to deeds performed, left undone, and abandoned, as well as to afflicted karma. (88)

With a pure mind, desiring the grace of the Lord, and holding the purificatory grass (pavitra) in his hand, he should address the all-pervading Lord Īśāna, the protector of the field, the refuge, and the pure-minded one. 89.

O God, whatever has been seen by you in the form of Time within my ritual procedure—whether it was performed, corrupted, omitted, stolen, or concealed, even if done by me—[let that be rectified]. (90)
O Śambhu, by Your will, let all that has been done— whether afflicted or unafflicted, performed or nourished, and even if done disrespectfully— become purified through this, Your entirely holy self.

Having uttered "pūraya" (fill) twice, and then the phrase "makha-vrata-phalam" (the fruit of the sacrificial vow), he should recite the words "niyameśvarāya" (to the Lord of Observances), ending with "svāhā. || 92 ||
One should also recite: "Obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of the reality of the Self," as well as the mantra known as Tatva-vidyā-śiva, which is the locus for those desiring liberation.
Having placed three purifiers upon his head, he who enjoys those [purifiers] should first utter "Śiva" and so forth;
then, having first uttered the atom (aṇu) of Śiva, he should again utter that which consists of Śiva and Vidyā.
One should offer the Gaṅgāvatāraka [image] to the Lord of all principles (Sarvatattveśvara);
then, with hands joined in a hollowed gesture of flowers, one should address the Lord with devotion. 95.
You are the refuge of all beings, the established state of all that is mobile and immobile;
by moving within all beings, you are the witness, O Supreme Lord.
In deed, thought, or word, my devotion is directed nowhere else;
whatever has been performed by me that is deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in material offerings— [may it be accepted]. (97)

O Maheśvara, whatever daily rite of yours has been performed by me devoid of recitation, fire-offerings, and worship, or whatever has been left undone along with the failure to speak [your] words— please fulfill that.
O Lord of the Gods, you are supremely pure, a purifier, and the destroyer of sin;
by you, the entire world—both the immobile and the mobile—is sanctified. 99.
O Lord, whatever has been broken by me through the occurrence of deficiencies in my vows—may all that become whole again, bound together by the thread of your command. (100)
Having performed the recitation (japa), having offered it to Him, and having praised the Lord and received the rule from Him,
one should, bowing with devotion, undertake [the vow] for four, three, two, or one month.
For half a month, or seven days, or five days, or three days, or even for a single day, one should maintain the observance until the completion of the rite once it has begun. (102)
All such practices as eating once a day and so forth should be performed with devotion toward the Lord;
having undertaken the vow, it must be observed until the descent of the thread.
Having considered the thread from the scriptures and the lords of the directions as situated in the fire,
the Guru, having offered the fourth purifier (pavitra) to Śiva with the vyāhṛtis, [proceeds].
Having restrained the fire, performed the rites up to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, and entered within,
he should worship the deity, as well as the preceptor and the book according to the Siddhānta.

Having offered the purifier (pavitra) and the oblation to the guardians of the directions, and having sipped water (ācamana), the preceptor (deśika) then offers the expiation (prāyaścitta) and the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) which fills all deficiencies.
Having worshipped the deity situated within the mandala, one should then ask for his forgiveness;
at the conclusion of that, [one should honor him] with food, clothing, and other such requisites.

Having worshipped the initiated ones, he should say: "May Sadāśiva be pleased with me. This is done when the removal of the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) from the sacred thread (*pavitra*) on the *liṅga* has been performed. || 108 ||
Having bathed and worshipped [the deity], and having mounted it, one should not dismiss it day after day;
at the conclusion of the vow, having worshipped Śiva as before and according to the procedure for the past days.
Having declared the vow, he should say: "May its fruit be for me, the practitioner";
likewise, one who desires worldly enjoyment as a practitioner says: "May there be desire, which binds one to karma. (110)
Having performed the ritual of satiation with mantras up to its conclusion, one should perform the rite of atonement;
then, having paid homage to the ashes, one should unite that which resides in the fire with Śiva.
Having withdrawn the mantras of the fire and led them to the dvādaśānta,
one should establish the fire within the heart and release it from the seat of the opening.
Having offered oblations to the enclosing sticks (paridhi) and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the pure preceptor,
having withdrawn the mantras of the Śiva-pitcher, the weapon-mantra, and the vardhanī-vessel, should join them together.

Having thus addressed the Lord with words of dependence, saying "Forgive me," one should dismiss him, as well as the guardians of the directions accompanied by their weapons and the door-keepers stationed at the gates. (114)
Then, having dismissed the one who was reciting [the mantra] and having taken the purifiers from Maheśvara,
one should offer the purifier to Caṇḍeśa when he is present.

If other items such as the remains of offerings (nirmālya) or other purificatory objects have not been prepared, one should perform the Aghora mantra a hundred thousand times along with its enclosure, and then perform the fire oblation (homa) for one-tenth of that amount.
One should prepare the perpetual purifier (pavitra), which is an essential limb of daily worship, using flowers and other materials;
or, once the perpetual purifier has been offered, one may perform the annual rite.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, the procedure for the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrārohaṇa*) in the month of Śrāvaṇa, in the great tantra known as the *Uttarakāmika*.
In the nineteenth chapter, the procedure for the nine food offerings (*navanaivedya*).
Henceforth, I shall describe the characteristics of the nine types of food offerings (naivedya),
excluding the months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Āṣāḍha, and Māgha.
In all other months, one should present fresh offerings;
having determined an auspicious lunar mansion (nakṣatra), one should perform the rite of germinating seeds (aṅkura) on the day preceding it.
Even without the ritual of sowing seeds, on an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction, amidst the sounds of conchs and drums and the auspicious performances of song and dance, || 3 ||
Adorned with various banners and canopies, and provided with incense, lamps, and sprouts,
it was accompanied by my devotees and endowed with the trident.
The wise one should enter the sacred field (devakṣetra) accompanied by Caṇḍeśvara, or even without the weapon of Caṇḍeśa, having gone to the field.
One should offer an oblation (bali) to the beings with sacrificial food mixed with curd,
likewise accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, in the eight directions beginning with the east.
Facing either the east or the north, and recollecting the mantra of the weapon, he should [cut] with a sacrificial blade that possesses the proper characteristics and has been duly consecrated.
Having plucked the awn, one should place it upon a pair of small earthen mounds;
that [grain], joined with its awn and combined with fresh rice, [is prepared]. (8)
It was provided with rice, combined with various side dishes,
accompanied by coconut fruits, and endowed with fresh betel nuts.
It was provided with sugar-cane pieces such as *marīca* and *gulaka*,
along with various vegetables and diverse side dishes.
With such various materials for worship consisting of diverse roots and fruits,
as well as other wondrous things accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments.
Accompanied by dance and song, provided with various banners and various parasols, they entered the city and other such places.
Having circumambulated the village clockwise, he should enter his residence,
which is provided with full water-jars and accompanied by fragrant lamps.
Having bound it with plantain stalks and adorned it with various auspicious items,
one should separate the grain from the husks and dry it indeed in the sun.
In a vessel made of cane or other materials, or even on the bare ground,
or on ground smeared with cow dung or decorated with flour-paste, one should place it together with a lamp.
Having flattened [the grains] according to the procedure taught in the sequence for the powder festival (cūrṇotsava), one should discard the husks and so forth;
then, having collected the pure rice grains, one should wash them.
Combined with black pepper and cumin, and endowed with the essence of molasses.
One should first prepare rice together with coconut fruit;
then one should perform the ceremonial bath for the deity and adorn him with ornaments worthy of such decoration.
When the auspicious moment has arrived, having strewn rice upon the ground and placed the cloth upon it,
one should arrange plantain leaves over it.
Having sprinkled it with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra while recollecting Mṛtyuñjaya,
one should place rice there and sprinkle it with water mixed with molasses.
Having veiled [the deity] with the Kavaca mantra at the end, the Guru should worship [it] with the Hṛdaya mantra;
having rendered it nectar-like by means of the Dhenu-mudrā, [he should do so] with the Brahma-mantras or the Puruṣa-sūkta.
One should offer the food oblation and water to the Supreme Lord in due order;
with those same mantras, one should present betel-leaf to the God of gods.
The Guru should also present [an offering] accompanied by nine areca nuts to the Goddess, according to the previously mentioned procedure for all the deities in their entirety. (221.2)
Alternatively, one may offer [the oblation] from all [the vessels] into a small dish;
then one should complete the rite of fire-offering (homa) for the retinue beginning with Vṛṣa.
At the conclusion, one should cause the food offering (naivedya) to be presented and offer betel-leaf;
this is followed by the presentation of guests together with the offering of sacrificial oblations (bali).
Having offered rice and cooked food, the fire-oblation (homa) should then take place;
at its conclusion, one should perform the festival, or proceed even without it.
Having abandoned the offering to the field, or having abandoned the activity of the mortar, everything else shall be the same; at the end of that, one should worship the Guru.
Then one should cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given consisting of garments, gold, rings, and so forth;
the mortal who performs it in this manner shall attain a meritorious state.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, the procedure for the ninefold food offering, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
In the twentieth chapter is the procedure for initiation into the specific commitments (samaya).
Now I shall explain the initiation (dīkṣā) based upon the rules of conduct (samaya).
The preceptor, having performed his daily rites and having offered libations with mantras and other substances, [should proceed].
Having performed the worship of the Sun, being purified, and having undertaken the mantra-recitation,
one should enter the sacrificial pavilion after preparing the general offering water (*sāmānyārghya*).
Having sprinkled the doors with the weapon-mantra (astra), one should worship the guardians of each door;
first, [one worships] the digit of peace (śāntikalā) with the mantra: "Obeisance to the door of sound."
Having recited [the mantras], one should worship the eastern gate;
the southern is called Vidyā, the western is named Nivṛtti, and the northern is declared to be named Pratiṣṭhā.
Nandi and Mahākāla are in the east; Bhṛṅgi and Vināyaka are in the south;
Vṛṣa and Skanda are in the west; and Devī and Caṇḍa are in the northern direction.
One should worship [the deities] in sequence, beginning with the syllable Om and ending with "namas," using the dative case;
one should worship those situated at the archways, those in the jars, and even those on the walls.
Having taken recourse to the western gate and performed the rite of scattering flowers,
he then struck three blows with his heel upon those who had fallen to the ground using the Astra-mantra.
Having formed three *tākas*, the mantra-practitioner should, by means of three snaps of the fingers, drive away the obstacles from the sky and expel them outside the sacred abode.
Lifting his right leg, he should enter while resting on the left branch;
having cast a flower upon the udumbara post with the Astra-mantra, he should do so toward the center of the sanctuary.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, saying "To Vāstoṣpati" and also "Salutation to Brahmā," one should imagine the construction of a protective wall of weapons.
Having protected the sacrificial hall by covering it with armor and other means, the preceptor,
seated and facing north, should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and completed the internal worship, the Guru should then prepare the special arghya with barley, white mustard seeds, and unbroken grains.
Having sprinkled that with water mixed with sesame seeds, tips of *kuśa* grass, milk, and flowers,
one should sprinkle one's own head while holding those substances.
One should envelop all of that with the armor-mantra (kavaca);
having consecrated each item individually with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), one should apply the sandalwood mark (tilaka).
Having consecrated the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta) and placed it upon his head,
he [should take up] the sword of knowledge (jñānāsi), consisting of either twenty-four or fewer principles (tattva).
One should fashion a blade of *darbha* grass one span in length and consecrate it with mantras;
then one should prepare the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the procedure for which is stated here. (16)
In an auspicious part of the pavilion, on a site divided into nine squares and upon the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the five elements, one should arrange five vessels.
In the Vidyā called Śivasaṃdā, at the time of the Puruṣa, the Guru [should contemplate it] as well-established, perfectly tranquil, radiant, and composed of the elements. || 18 ||
Having consecrated the "jewel-water," one should place milk, curd, and ghee,
as well as cow dung and cow urine, while reciting the mantras beginning with Īśāna.
Having consecrated the water of kusa grass with one, two, three, four, five, or six recitations [of the mantra],
and having worshipped it, one should practice oneness with Śiva.
Having sprinkled the pavilion with that [water], one should consecrate the scattered offerings (vikira):
parched grain, sandalwood, white mustard seeds, ashes, flowers, kusha grass, and unbroken rice grains.
These seven weapons should be arranged mixed together with missiles;
having stood in the Nairṛtya corner of the pavilion, one should perform the consecration of the pavilion itself.

The Guru, facing the northeast, should perform the consecrations such as *vīkṣaṇa* (inspection) and so forth for his own mouth [face] just as he did previously for the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), consisting of eighteen [rituals].
Having scattered the scattered offerings, O Sovereign, one should collect them on a seat of kuśa grass,
either upon the altar, or in the pavilion, or in the northeast or the west.
Having brought one of the jars made of gold or other materials, it should be filled with water that has been strained,
provided with sprouts, and joined with gold, cloth, and so forth.
Having performed the withdrawal of the scattering missiles (vikirāstra), one should establish the movable and immovable seat;
then, having conceived it through the Mūrti-mantra, one should place the pitcher which has become manifest as the form.
One should place the Vardhanī vessel, filled with water and joined with cloth, thread, gold, and so forth;
it should be consecrated with the Weapon-mantra (Astramantra) ending with the Bhūta-mantra, and provided with a stalk of reed (nāla).
Having worshipped the water-pots, the weapons, and the preceptors with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
[they worship] Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, and likewise Varuṇa.
One should worship Vāyu, Soma, and Īśāna starting from the eastern direction; likewise, one should worship Viriñci situated to the right of Īśa, and Viṣṇu situated to the left of Nirṛti.
The Guru should worship [the deity] residing in a small jar (ghaṭa), a water-pot (kalaśa), or a large pitcher (kumbha);
likewise, he should also worship the ten weapons, beginning with the Vajra and Śakti.
O Śakra, by the command of Śiva, you must remain vigilant in your own quarter until the conclusion of the sacrifice in order to pacify all obstacles. || 31 ||
Having thus addressed all the world-protectors (lokapālas) in this sequential manner,
one should proclaim the command of Śiva and cause the pitcher to be circumambulated while holding the weapon (astra) in front.
Immediately thereafter, one should place the water-jar (kumbha) and the vardhanī vessel as before;
having worshipped the firm seat (sthirāsana), one should worship the deity and the weapon-mantra (astra).

Having worshipped Śiva— who possesses a body consisting of form and knowledge (mūrti-vidyā), along with his limbs (aṅgas), coverings (āvaraṇas), and weapons (astras)— one should contemplate the unity of the two [the worshipper and the worshipped] by means of the bhaga-mudrā.
The left fist is Umā, the thumb is the Liṅga, and Hara is the thumb itself;
for the sake of prosperity, one should first touch the water-pot with the joint of the thumb.
Thereafter, one should touch the *vardhanī* with the fist at the heart and the anus;
and for the sake of liberation, having first touched the *vardhanī*, one should likewise touch it with the fist alone.
Likewise, he should touch the final jar with the tip of his thumb,
[offering it] to Umā, who has the form of the *bhaga*, and to Him who bears the form of the *liṅga*.
Having praised him with "Salutations to you, Śaṅkara," and having offered approval, [he said]:
"For you are indeed the Lord of this sacrifice; this mountain is your immutable form. (38)
Take up this sword of knowledge, your own weapon;
let this sacrifice, which has been inaugurated by me as a performer of rites, proceed. (39)
"For you must indeed protect this until its completion;
having thus placed the burden of protecting the sacrifice upon him, the Teacher [departed]. (40)
Then, having prepared the vessel for the *arghya* offering, the Guru should offer the *arghya* with water;
likewise, he should place that vessel there for the purpose of confinement (*nirodhana*).

One should contemplate the demarcation of the ground as having all obstacles removed from every side by means of the weapons arising from the *vardhanī* and *vikira* mantras within the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*).
One should worship Śiva either in a mandala, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or in a linga;
one should also worship Śiva in the fire, accompanied by special offerings.
O Blessed One, having entered my body out of compassion,
you should bestow your grace upon those disciples whose minds are purified.
Having thus made this request and received permission from Śiva, saying "I shall do so," the Guru [takes] a white, auspicious [flower] consecrated seven times with the root mantra.
Having placed the uṣṇīṣa upon the head, one should contemplate oneness with Śiva;
he is the witness of all rites, present within the maṇḍala. (46)
Established in the auspicious pitcher (śivakumbha) as the protector of the sacrifice,
Sadāśiva resides within the fire as the locus for the oblation (homa).
But in the body of the disciple, the God who effects the liberation from the bonds of that disciple and bestows grace is established within my own body. 48.
I am that very Lord Sadāśiva, possessing fivefold attributes;
one should meditate upon Him as non-different from the selves and as possessing qualities equal to theirs. (49)
There is no doubt that my heart and other organs are also means of accomplishment;
having conceived [this] as absolute freedom itself, one should inform Śiva. || 50 ||
"O Lord, these very animals for whose sake this sacrifice of yours was undertaken stand at the door, pacified and restrained. (51)
Having long ago understood [the truth] through your rays, which dispel the activity of darkness by means of non-contradictory signs and are impelled by you; || 52 ||
Having performed their necessary duties, bathed, and completed their daily rites,
they wore white garments as upper cloths, desiring to behold your lotus feet.
O Śaṅkara, grant me the favor for their entrance;
I shall lead these very people into the presence of your lotus feet.
"O auspicious one, carry out my word for the sake of entry," so was I addressed by Śiva; having honored him accordingly, one should then cause the disciples to enter. || 55 ||
Having established the disciple right there, facing the door outside upon a *kuśa*-grass mandala at the *praṇava*, he himself should stand facing north.
The Guru should gaze with the eye of the knowledge of reality from the tip of the crest-lock down to the tips of the toenails, and from the tips of the toenails up to the crest-lock. (57)

This self is worthy of attaining the state of Śiva, its bonds having been loosened; and by the power of the Lord, the multitude of fetters is brought under my control for the sake of its immersion [in that state]. (58)
Then, impelled by Śambhu, I beheld this [mantra], which has the appearance of copper, which is fit for the arising of its own qualities, and which resembles a touchstone-manifesting gem.
Having purified it through contact, like gold in no time,
I shall make it endowed with virtues and a crest-jewel for the virtuous.
Then, having sprinkled [him] with water using a blade of *darbha* grass, he should apply ashes to the head;
using both the root and tip portions of the *darbha*, he should apply them to the regions of the heart, below and above.
One should draw the continuous chain of nooses, which is oriented toward the active instrument (pravṛttakaraṇa);
having performed the ritual of totalization (sakalīkaraṇa) upon that disciple and having bound his eyes.
The preceptor [should proceed] with a weapon consecrated by mantra, with armor that has been blunted [of its power],
with the root-mantra duly recited, and with a white cloth.
Having caused [the disciple] to enter and having made him perform the scattering of flowers, one should show him [the mandala];
then, as before, one should lead him to the mandala situated to the right of the Śiva-maṇḍala.

Having established the Praṇava there, and having purified the disciple’s upright body through meditative concentrations (dhāraṇā) and other means, he should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon that body.
Having perfumed it with fragrance, [he should hold] his own right hand-creeper, which is presided over by Śiva together with his body and his teaching. (66)
Having meditated upon it as the Hand of Śiva— both with and without expectation—
one should lead it from the region of the heart up to the region of the eyebrows, and indeed to the end of the crest-lock.
Simultaneously with the utterance of the *prāsāda* mantra, which pierces all knots,
one should place [the seed-syllable] upon the head, bestowing the attainment of the station of Rudreśvara.
One should perform a touching of all the limbs of the disciple, especially so;
then, [one should place] into his joined palms [a substance] perfumed with flowers, scents, and incense. (69)
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with his whole being, he should pray to Śambhu as He stands there,
gradually removing the cloth that covers His eyes.
O Īśāna, beheld all at once, let this limb of mine, which has gone toward the lotus-face of Śiva, be released; it is like a flower offered before Śiva.

In a place indicated by its falling, which was previously marked by the word "śiva" followed by "pada," there appeared a mass of white lotuses as if they were the passion for the worship of Śiva made manifest. (72)
The name of a Brahmin should be determined as consisting of the words *deva*, *kaṇṭha*, and *gaṇa*;
for those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, and for women, it should end with the word *śakti*.
Then, having taught the eight-limbed prostration with circumambulation to all, he declared that everything is everywhere considered to be the name of Śiva. (74)

Having led [the disciple] to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit, he should establish the disciple on his own right upon a seat of the Praṇava, and place the root-end of a blade of Darbha grass into the disciple's hand.

The preceptor, having joined the tip of his own *dharma* [channel] to the joint of his own calf, causes it to emerge spontaneously from himself through the *piṅgalā* situated in the middle of his body and enters the disciple. (76)
The Guru, having offered three oblations for the purpose of joining the channels, should contemplate [the disciple's] own channel as being dissolved [into his own] by means of the root mantra. (77)
The entry and exit [of breath] should be performed for the sake of grasping consciousness;
having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should indeed offer to Śiva and the ten limbs.
Having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Śiva-mantra itself for the purpose of expiation,
one should then offer one hundred and eight oblations with that same Śiva-mantra.
Even those of the Śūdra caste may become Brāhmaṇas and the like through their qualities;
one should uplift them by first elevating them from their Śūdra birth and so forth, using the root mantra ending with "svāhā."
Having offered three oblations, one should afterwards address Śiva [as follows]:
"Due to the defects of food and state of being, and from the womb, seed, and body... (81)
"O Blessed One, O Supreme Lord, may my self become a pure twice-born;
even for the purpose of attaining a portion of Rudra, one should likewise perform these three oblations. (82)
"O Blessed One, by your grace, may this Rudra become my very self.
Having made this prayer, one should perform the sprinkling and the striking.
Having entered the body of the disciple by means of the exhaling breath (recaka) of his own self, the Guru effects its disjunction and severance with the Astra-mantra and that called the Aṅkuśa.

Having drawn the consciousness of the disciple by means of the mudrā to the end of the twelve [fingers], and having brought it there, one should worship it with the Dhruva mantra from the top of the disciple's head.

Having entered [the disciple] into one's own heart by means of the withdrawal gesture (saṃhāramudrā) and inhalation (pūraka), and having recollected the state of equal flavor (samarasa) of the child [disciple] through retention (kumbhaka), [one should proceed]. 86.
By means of the practice of exhalation (recaka), having led Keśava, Īśāna,
and Sadāśiva [within], and having turned oneself back, one then [places] Śiva at the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta).
The Guru should unite [the deity] with the disciple's body by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*;
he should then bestow the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), consecrated with the root mantra.
Having offered a hundred or a thousand oblations, one should present the final offering with the mantra of Śiva.
Thus, he who is endowed with the consecration of the pledges remains engaged in the worship of Śiva. (89)
O sages, by staying at home, by studying, and even by hearing the mantras, a human being becomes fit [for liberation] and attains the state of Rudra. || 90 ||
Then, the twice-born shall become qualified for initiation into Nirvāṇa;
for even after initiating a Śūdra according to the very same rite as that for the first-born (the Brāhmaṇa), [he attains this]. 91.
He too attains the status of a Śūdra by giving initiation; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, the procedure for initiation according to the specific commitments (*samaya*), in the great tantra named *Uttarakāmika*.
In the twenty-first chapter is the procedure for the cooked oblation (*sthālīpāka*).
I shall describe the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* (pot-cooking) rite for the preparation of the food offering (*naivedya*) and the sacrificial rice (*caru*).
One should take a vessel made of copper or clay, provided with the proper characteristics.
Having washed the vessel, veiled it with the *astra* and *kavaca* mantras;
having gazed upon it, sprinkled it, bathed it, struck it, and smeared it with fragrant substances.
Having wound around his neck a silken cord in the form of armor,
he stood upon a mandala smeared with cow dung and sprinkled with water consecrated by mantras.

Having performed the ritual of the sixfold arising seat (ṣaḍuttham āsana) upon a vessel protected by armor and strewn with darbha grass consecrated by mantras, one should install that [deity] in the form of an image.
Having invoked Śiva together with his retinue there and worshipped him, one should dismiss him;
then, having anointed the flowers and other offerings with clarified butter, one should place milk purified by a cloth.
Having delineated with the *cullīmāstra* mantra, sprinkled it with water, and veiled it,
and having swept and smeared [the site], one should then worship the two, dharma and adharma.
One should place Śivāgni in the middle of the two arms situated on the right and left;
having made the Praṇava the seat, one should cause her to ascend upon it.
The wise one should prepare the fourth portion, consisting of śāli rice, grains, and so forth, measuring either two prasthas, one āḍhaka, or five prasṛtis.
Having performed the shaking and opening with the Astra-mantra while recollecting the Aghora-mantra,
one facing the east should cook [the substance] so that it becomes properly cooked in the center.

When it is hot, there should be an offering of warm substances; when it is cold, an offering of cool substances, by means of a collection of mantras ending with "svāhā," O Śiva, carrier of the oblation, in the past.
At the end of the oblation, having uttered "ha," he should also say, "become well-cooked.
Thus there should be a sprinkling over the heated [mixture] in the second mandala.
Even when it has been worshipped and provided with sprinkling and other rites,
one should likewise cause it to descend [into the fire] with the mantra "Become very cool," using the *vauṣaṭ* syllable and a sprout.
The sprinkling with cool water should likewise be performed with the conjunction of mantras;
and having cleansed the vessel with clay and water using the *surabhi* mudrā, [one should proceed].
Having rendered [the site] immortal, in the eastern mandala to the west of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
one should worship it with the heart-mantra and offer oblations to each of the limbs (aṅgas) in sequence.
One should perform one hundred and eight oblations with the *śiva-mantra* as before; it is prescribed that the *homa* should be performed with the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) thus prepared. (15)
Then, one should always cook the sacrificial oblation (caru) with rice and water;
or alternatively, it is considered that the rite of oblation (homa) should consist of a fourth part of the sacrificial offering (havis).
The remainder of the oblation should be diligently given to the preceptor,
who is established in the five spheres of perception and is a knower of all the Agamas.
If what remains is given away by another, the oblation is indeed fruitless.
If the oblation of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) is performed without a remnant, that oblation brings about undesirable results. (18)
In the rite of oblation, one-twentieth part of the sacrificial offering is for the caru;
the first portion is declared to be for the deities, while the second is for the act of homa.
The third [offering] should be for the retinue, and the fourth indeed for the Preceptor;
if there is a separate sacrificial porridge (caru), one should offer all the food offerings (naivedya) to the Lord.
The Prāṇāgnihotra must be performed by practitioners who desire its fruits;
if these are otherwise, everything becomes otherwise.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, the Ritual for the Sthālīpāka, in the great Tantra known as the Uttarakāmika. In the twenty-second chapter is the ritual for the study of dreams.
Now, O best of the twice-born, I shall explain in detail the chapter on dreams;
one should observe an excellent dream prior to initiation or for the sake of a desired object.
For if a dream should occur there during the first watch of the night,
O best of the twice-born, one should perceive that one will partake of its fruit at that very time.
If [the practice is performed] during the second watch of the night, success shall come within a year;
if during the third watch, success shall come within six months.
If [this is practiced] during the fourth watch of the night, success shall be attained in just one month;
his fruit will manifest very quickly, of this there is no doubt. || 4 ||
[He saw] the radiant Vivasvat, the moon surrounded by stars,
the blazing agnihotra fire, and a lamp exceedingly brilliant.
If a man sees his mother, father, wife, sons, brothers, or friends in a dream, he shall obtain abundant prosperity.
By swallowing the moon, the sun, and the stars, as well as by wiping them away,
eating them, and holding them, a man shall attain sovereignty.
From seeing garlands made of white flowers, white birds,
and golden-winged birds, one obtains prosperity.
By seeing or reaching a city of the Gandharvas, or by beholding the women of the gods and Gandharvas in a dream, one shall obtain abundant prosperity.
A parasol made of gold adorned with white garlands, and the sight of auspicious trees such as the mango tree bearing fruit—[these are signs]. (10)
The mounting of them, the gathering of their fruits, and the eating of them—these are recommended for mountains, palaces, horses, and elephants. (11)
Beholding and mounting cows, lions, and bulls is auspicious; likewise, ascending a lion-throne, a four-tusked elephant, or a palanquin is auspicious. (12)
Beholding the sun, the moon, fire, the ocean, the sky, the earth, and the mountains;
and crossing rivers, the sea, forests, and water. (13)
The act of milking is highly praised for female buffaloes and cows,
as well as for lionesses and female elephants within one's own household among kinsmen.
Or rather, their procreation is remembered as a sign of prosperity, just like the playful drinking of milk by a cow with white spots on her face. 15.
O best of sages, the eating of curd, uncooked meat, excrement, and milk-rice (pāyasa), as well as the acquisition of these very things, is highly praised.
The drinking of nectar, blood, or wine; the eating of fish;
or even the sight of these, or bathing with blood—[these are forbidden]. (17)
Anointing with water, or with water flowing from the horns of cows, or with water flowing from the moon, is desired as an auspicious consecration for kingship. || 18 ||
There will be the acquisition of cattle, lions, and elephants, especially in battle; furthermore, there will be the teaching of scriptures and the smearing with food. (19)
He has a navel produced from grass and wood, and flowers and water;
he has external heads, hands, and the state of being white garlands and ointments.
The wearing of white garments by a Brahmin, the sight of auspicious blessings, and [the sight of] a white fruit, a fan, or a banner; 21.
Of a lotus, an umbrella, jewels, a mirror, a lamp, a fly-whisk, a weapon, and a water-lily. (22)
The sight of pure water and gold is auspicious;
likewise, the sight of a king and conversation with him are considered to bestow good fortune.
Upon seeing a temple with its image, or even a white cow,
or the ocean or rivers filled with water, one shall obtain prosperity.
By the sight of these as well, a man may attain sovereignty;
likewise by seeing a conch shell, an ornament, a white garment, or even a man [in such attire]. (25)
A man, having seen even such a woman endowed with beauty and youth, or likewise having seen supreme prosperity in a dream, attains that very same prosperity. (26)
Upon seeing a prince, a serpent, a bull, or an elephant, one shall obtain a son;
likewise, one shall find abundant grass, grain, and a house endowed with fire. (27)
Having seen [these] in a dream, one obtains prosperity; likewise, having seen the banner of Śakra, the swallowing of earth and water by an enemy, and the act of slaying enemies.
Having achieved victory in disputes, legal cases, and the like, as well as triumph in battle, one attains prosperity and establishes a dwelling upon the earth, O Moon. (29)
Having seen the cloudless sky, and likewise having seen the attainment of boiled rice and death;
having made a collection of fire and obtained the insignia of Vairāja—30.
A man obtains happiness by playing upon stringed instruments;
likewise, crossing over those two [rivers] and weeping bring about auspiciousness. (31)
Likewise, there is the gain of another's wife as well as her embrace;
imprisonment with fetters, grain, and likewise the burning of one's own body. (32)
Having cut off his body, casting it toward the quarters is considered auspicious; likewise, being welcomed by a serpent or even being devoured by a lion is likewise auspicious. (33)
The sight of crops in the heart, the head, or the belly is auspicious; likewise, eating from a vessel made of gems or silver is highly recommended.
Or eating curds or food from a golden lotus leaf;
or hearing the sounds "lābha" (gain), "āhaya" (challenge/call), "jaya" (victory), or "bhukṣva" (eat). || 35 ||
O twice-born ones, the sight of mudrā, honey, and rain is auspicious;
likewise, oil-cake, cow dung, and one's own house rising high are praised.
He saw himself surrounded by kinsmen, blazing while staying within his house, as well as auspicious sprouts, seeds, and the arrival of the Vidyādharas. (37)
If one sees oneself with feet smeared with blood at the navel, one quickly attains sovereignty and obtains many sons. (38)
He whose right hand is severed and bloody in a dream shall quickly obtain a son who is long-lived and illustrious. || 39 ||
He who sees his own head severed and drenched in blood in a dream quickly attains health, and his wealth increases. (40)
He whose body is shattered in a dream by golden forms attains wealth and grain, adorned with all kinds of ornaments.
If one sees oneself as a merchant in a dream, one should know that there will be prosperity for him and his lifespan will increase. (42)
By drinking from the wheel, the full pitcher, the śrīvatsa, the svastika, and likewise the soma-vessel, one obtains the desired fruit. (43)
The hearing of words such as "Śiva-āgama" and the like shall be a bestower of wealth; likewise, the arrival of a wise teacher and the sight of a scorpion are auspicious. (44)
Conversation with gods, brahmins, and the wives of the gods is considered most auspicious;
likewise, betel, collyrium, bilva leaves, and saffron are auspicious within the sacred circle. (45)
One should observe the performance of sacrifices and other rites, as well as the construction of walls and cow-pens; the creation of gardens and groves is said here to bestow auspicious results.
The arrival of the groom, the approaching of him, the binding of all her limbs, the joyful rubbing by her kinsmen, and the taking of the maiden by her husband—this is indeed auspicious. (47)
Bathing, worship of Śiva, libations to the sacred fire, beholding the virtuous, [worship of] the Gaṇas and the gods, drinking nectar, and traveling through the sky. || 48 ||
Such visions as these in a dream indicate auspiciousness:
the acquisition of land and garments, reclining on a couch, and the burning of one's clothes. (49)
There was the burning of his seat, as well as his boarding of a boat;
he wore new white garments and likewise ate pure rice. (50)
The production of honey from a lotus, one's own destruction, and the acquisition of the treasures of the conch and the lotus—this is declared to be an auspicious dream. (51)
Furthermore, the non-attainment or the loss of these very things, even though they have been seen or somehow acquired, indicates undesirable matters in a dream. (52)

From the breaking or similar damage of the *liṅga* or the image, the death of the king occurs; from that of the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), the death of the queen; and from that of the temple, the ruin of the kingdom. (53)
The destruction of kinsmen, the loss of sons, and entering the fire;
fruit crushed by the hand, and jujube vegetables—these are inauspicious. (54)
Traveling abroad, coarseness of character, affliction by disease, protruding teeth, ruin, and impurity due to lack of purification. || 55 ||
The appearance of gold, silver, charcoal, mud, or poison is inauspicious; so too is the sight of powders on the head, of bell-metal vessels, of nakedness, or of soiled garments. (56)
Anointing with oil, falling down, and climbing onto a high swing bring about undesirable results;
so too does the sight of red-flowering trees, outcasts, or hunters. (57)
The eating of cooked meat, oil, and blood;
dancing, swallowing, marriage, and singing. (58)
Playing musical instruments that lack strings, immersing oneself in a river current, and bathing with cow-dung water; || 59 ||
Or else, there is an inauspicious entry into the mother's womb due to mud;
or perhaps ascending onto a funeral pyre, or the falling of Indra’s banner. (60)
The falling of stars from the sun and the moon, as well as the appearance of celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial portents, portend misfortune. (61)
The wrath of gods, brahmins, and other elders, as well as kings;
embracing virgins, and sexual intercourse with men. (62)
There is indeed a wasting away of one's own limbs, the performance of purgation and emesis, traveling toward the southern direction, and likewise being overcome by disease. (63)

There shall be the falling of houses, as well as the collapsing of dwellings and their sweeping away; furthermore, there will be affliction caused by piśācas, carnivorous beasts, monkeys, and even men.
O twice-born ones, there is defeat by others and from that arises calamity; likewise, there is the wearing of saffron-colored robes and sporting with women. (65)
Drinking unctuous substances, immersion baths, red garlands and ointments, play, licking, eruptions, hunger, thirst, and fatigue. (66)
The movement of the stars, of banners, and of flowing streams;
the snapping of a rope; and the shaving of the beard and hair—these may be performed during the *pratipad*. (67)
Longing for the length of a fingernail, or even consorting with a woman;
having one's body massaged by an ugly man, or even during a festival; (68)
The playing with domestic animals or birds, or the floating of one who is paralyzed or dead, as well as the breaking of a vehicle, will lead to inauspiciousness. (69)
O twice-born ones, playing and dancing in a lake, carrying a vessel of lac, the loss of wealth, separation from friends, and wearing dark-colored garments [are the omens]. (70)
The cutting off of the hands, the removal of the lotus, the wearing of tattered garments, and the descent from the peaks of palaces and mansions are not desired [as auspicious omens]. (71)
And whoever obtains cotton, sesame roots, and so forth, or metals, when used for wrapping or binding around the ears, nose, and other parts [of the body] like the coils of a serpent; || 72 ||
One who is healthy meets with disease, and one who is diseased meets with death;
seeing a broken banner or an excessive number of broken banners, or seeing a broken umbrella, one shall obtain inauspiciousness.
Likewise, it is declared that one should hold a single lotus;
similarly, one should laugh while eating boiled rice together with sesame seeds. 74.
Her head was downward as she bathed in oil, which caused her teeth to fall out;
it was like the burning of an elephant by fire or the scorching of the earth by the god of flame.
O twice-born ones, he was established upon a seat of black iron amidst terrible mountains;
his appearance was dark-hued as he stood upon a chariot yoked with donkeys.
The vehicle, the neck-binding, the riding upon the *śiṃśumāra* and the serpent, and the inferior dancing and assemblies—these occur in regions other than the navel. (77)
The arising of grasses, trees, and animals—even through play—[occurs], as well as enjoyment by means of donkeys, monkeys, camels, serpents, and fierce beasts. (78)
For other beings, the smearing of the body with oil, cow dung, mud, or turbid water would be undesirable. (79)
It is not desired to lick the tongue or the arms, nor to tear at the hair with the nails; climbing upon a serpent is not desired, and smelling it is not approved.
He who is violently sniffed at by beasts of prey with distorted faces,
and likewise he who is submerged in mud, undergoes great suffering.
Furthermore, there is the embrace of those who have departed as ghosts or even of renunciants, or being dragged away by the messengers of Yama, who are the lowest of outcasts. (82)
What man, possessed of strength, could climb a silk-cotton tree, a *kiṃśuka*, a sacrificial post, a sacred fig tree, a *paribhadraka*, a flower-laden tree, or a *kadāra*? || 83 ||
Drying therapy (śoṣaṇa), known as "boiling" (kathita), and the drinking of water are for those suffering from urinary disorders (prameha);
likewise, the consumption of turmeric is for one afflicted by jaundice (pāṇḍuroga). || 84 ||
He who drinks blood or sees blood shall perish;
likewise, one who sees a broken vehicle or a tree falling in a dream will experience misfortune. (85)
If the sun, the moon, or the stars should fall from the sky out of devotion—becoming soiled and disfigured—or if a lotus, an oblation, or a maiden should do so; (66)
One should predict the death of a king even from the seizing of the planets, or from the sight of inauspicious ones, or from their very embracing [of one another]. (87)
Upon seeing a crow, a vulture, a hawk, a piśāca, or a rākṣasa, or even a falling statue, one shall encounter misfortune. || 88 ||
If a banner, a mountain, or a bull falls while being raised, or if a large house or a principal wall collapses, it shall be a primary cause of death. (89)
Upon seeing a lamp-bearer, a washerman, a leper, a gambler, a barbarian, or even an outcaste, as well as one with black teeth or a foul mouth; 90.
If one sees in the end of a dream a man or a woman dressed as a madman carrying a skull-bowl, or a black woman with a spear, one meets with immediate death.
And likewise, upon seeing oneself slain by those two, one may see a horse, a camel, a donkey, a buffalo, or even a dog. (92)
A jackal, a buffalo, oil, a person of ill complexion, a crow, a wolf, a bull, a boar, a cat, an owl, and a black serpent. (93)
If one should see a black insect or a black cow, one will encounter fear;
likewise, upon touching, seizing, or stepping upon these [beings], [the same occurs]. 94.
Even the sight of a golden tree portends death; likewise, the breaking of fire-vehicles, chariots, umbrellas, and the like [is a bad omen]. (95)
The sight of widows as well as the loss of wealth through association with them;
one’s own self becoming smoky and the shaving of the head. (96)
If one should see [the moon] bound by others or obstructed, one will encounter fear; or if one sees it as gruel or fermented rice-water (māranāla), it portends the destruction of wealth. (97)
Seeing cooked rice or meat amidst husks, charcoal, or saline soil, or seeing mung beans, black gram, black pepper, or mustard seeds, is inauspicious. (98)
Falling into a pit or similar place is undesirable, as is the scattering of hair;
likewise, the application of ointments and unguents with substances such as oil, sesame, and the like [is forbidden]. 99.
