He dwells in darkness or travels upon the great highway; as a renunciant, he enters into cremation pits and similar places together with hungry ghosts.
One may eat a crane or even consume a corpse;
however, any substance that is red in color or black is not praised.
That which is impure is declared to be black;
however, this excludes blood, the lotus, the palāśa flower, and red sandalwood. (102)
Likewise, if he should see a washerman, a dog, a gambler, a barbarian, or even heretics, no auspiciousness arises for him. (103)
Seeing an anthill, seeing a withered poisonous tree, hearing the wailing of spirits, and the sudden falling of trees—these are not auspicious omens. (104)
Whatever deities, twice-born brahmins, ancestors, yogis, or kings tell a man in a dream, that shall indeed come to pass. || 105 ||
A dream is the sign of future karmic fruition, whether auspicious or inauspicious, as ordained by destiny; it never arises from a disorder of the bodily humors.
Whatever element is one's natural constitution, or by whichever element one is afflicted, one indeed perceives its transformation as if it were directly present in a dream. (107)
And for one who is asleep, having attended to an object—whether seen or heard—the continuous stream of thought regarding it appears as if directly perceived in the dream state. (108)
In this scripture, that twofold dream-consciousness is not intended;
it is like a cognition of something distant seen by one with impaired vision, for it is subject to deviation even while being manifest. (109)

Therefore, whatever auspicious or inauspicious one sees in a dream while in the state of meditative concentration is true, provided it is free from intentional resolve; otherwise, it is not so without distinction.
One should report an inauspicious or auspicious dream to the teacher, according to one's status as a twice-born, or by virtue of age, or by wealth. (111)
O Brahmins, whoever possesses preeminence through conduct, dharma, or knowledge, one should present that person at the very beginning of all [the rites].
Then, in this very sequence, each person should report their respective dream;
or else, by the permission of the preceptor, seniority among them is proclaimed.
A Śūdra who is endowed with the sacrament known as the Brāhmaṇa-samaya and joined with the initiation of Nirvāṇa shares in the same portion as these two [the twice-born]. (114)
He for whom there is an appointment (niyoga) among them should resort to that very guru;
even when there is an initiation (dīkṣā) by an equal [guru] at the outset, it is so where [this applies]. || 115 ||
That child, being appointed [to the office], should first pay homage to the most excellent guru;
even when there is equality of birth and so forth, and even when there is equality of sacramental rites. || 116 ||
The appointment belongs to the instructor, and he should first take refuge in a guru;
even in the case of mutual salutation, this same sequence is prescribed. (117)

Even if he is the eldest, because of his [inferior] refinement, he must not be honored with salutations and the like by those who have received the sacraments, even with the permission of their own guru, for the sake of [the seniority of] their guru. || 118 ||
The conduct for disciples has been fully described;
what is the use of saying more here than that which has already been stated by the Teacher? (119)
That alone should always be performed by disciples who desire their own welfare.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, the procedure for the study of dreams, in the great tantra named Uttarakāmika.
In the twenty-third chapter: the procedure for the initiation into nirvāṇa.
I shall proclaim the initiation known as Nirvāṇa, which bestows supreme liberation.
The preceptor, having performed his daily rites and having offered libations with mantras and other offerings, [should proceed]. (1)

Having performed the worship of the Sun, being pure, having consecrated his body with the kalās, holding the general arghya water, and being joined by the worship of the door-keepers at each entrance. || 2 ||
Having entered the sacrificial hall by way of the western door,
and having performed the worship of Brahmā, he— being purified— should provide protection for the sacred field according to the prescribed rule.
The knower of ritual procedures, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the placement of mantras (nyāsa), and the special arghya offering,
and having prepared the sword known as "Knowledge" (jñāna-khaḍga) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Then, having consecrated the scattering materials (vikirān) and performed the purification of the ground,
one should scatter those materials and collect them back with kusha grass toward the northeast (īśa).

Having worshipped the water-pot (kumbha) and the secondary vessel (vardhanī) there, the Guru should then worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) all around and cause their permission to be proclaimed.
Having brandished the water-pot weapon and worshipped the sword of knowledge,
and having honored the Lord of Gods within the mandala, one should satisfy the mantras in the fire.
O Blessed One, having entered my body, please grant your grace out of compassion; you should bestow favor upon these disciples whose minds are purified.
Having made this request and received permission, he should place the *uṣṇīṣa* upon his head;
for Sadāśiva, residing within the maṇḍala, is the witness of all ritual acts.
He is the protector of the sacrifice, the cause of the oblation in the fire-pot;
he is the destroyer of bonds for his disciple and the liberator from bonds within my body.
The Lord consists of five bases; you and I are indeed Sadāśiva.
Those mantras which are the causal principles of Śiva, beginning with the Heart (hṛdaya), [are these bases]. || 11 ||
In this matter, you likewise possess full autonomy over yourself;
therefore, having reflected upon this, you should entreat the Lord with your vital breaths situated both within and without.
This Parīkṣit, who has appeared for the sake of liberation, is capable;
he is of noble birth, a portion of the Lord, and established in his duties at the proper times. || 13 ||
Therefore, let confidence be placed in me for the sake of this liberation;
having fulfilled my intended purpose, I am supported by the teachings of Śiva.
Having begun from the sacrificial site, one should enter facing the fire,
and having placed the disciple's entry on one's own left side.
One who knows the practice of joining the channels should perform the satiation together with the full [breath],
and then correctly carry out the kindling of the mantras beginning with Śiva.
Having formed the *aghora-sampuṭa*, one should [visualize] Śiva along with his limbs, ending with *phaṭ*, joined with curved eyebrows and endowed with a straight face. (17)
Three oblations should be offered, as well as the kindling of the mantras;
a thread spun by a maiden, tripled and then folded three times over.
Having sprinkled the armor with the Astra-mantra and blunted it with the root-mantra,
one should worship it and bind it upon the crown of the child’s head.
One should cause that thread to extend down to the tip of the big toe;
having meditated upon the thread as being of the nature of the *suṣumṇā* within the body of the disciple. (20)
Saying "Salutation to Suṣumnā," he should grasp [the thread] and apply it to this [image];
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, he should protect it with the *varman* mantra. || 21 ||
One should offer three oblations with the root mantra for the sake of bringing [the deity] into proximity;
then, having sprinkled the region of the disciple's heart with flowers while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Having struck his heart and entered it through the exhaling breath (recaka),
he utters the syllable "huṃ" and [extracts] the consciousness of that person, which has the form of a star.
Having severed the knot of the heart with the weapon-mantra and grasped it from its root,
one should place the disciple’s life-force, encapsulated by the heart-mantra, at the end of the twelve.
Having uttered the peaceful seed-syllable (*bīja*), one should join it to the thread with the *saṃhāra-mudrā* and protect it with the armor-mantra (*varma-mantra*). || 25 ||
Having offered three oblations into him from the very root for his purification,
[he offers for] the impurity consisting of karma and māyā, which arises from the body of the enjoyer and the enjoyed.
One should distribute the [deities] beginning with Śāntyatītā according to their respective mantras in the Sūtra.
[One should worship] Śāntyatītā, ending in the dative case, followed by *hūṃ phaṭ*, starting from Śiva. (27)

Having struck with the Flower-Arrow (puṣpāstra) alone, and having drawn forth Śiva—who resides upon the head of the disciple—by means of the withdrawal gesture (saṃhāramudrā), preceded by the Praṇava; || 28 ||
Having uttered the syllable Śāntyatītā ending in the dative case and joined with the word *namaḥ*,
one should apply it to the thread, which is marked by the space between the eyebrows.
Then, by this very sequence and according to the path taught for the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi),
one should perform the striking, seizing, and joining within the four digits (kalās).

The wise practitioner should establish the relationship of pervader and pervaded, extending from the throat, the navel cavity, and the interior of the knees, down to the tips of the big toes. || 31 ||

Mantras, words, and phonemes, as well as the principles (tattvas) and the worlds, are the objects to be pervaded; [the subjects] are the pervaders, bound by the fetters of karma, impurity (mala), and māyā. || 32 ||
Vyāpinī, Amalā, and the others are also pervaders (vyāpaka), and they are known as Kalās;
therefore, by the inclusion of these, all [the principles] are indeed accepted here.
Even those who have been established today become pure through those who were established long ago;
therefore, the purity of all must be ensured, and thus that purification is required.
And their illumination should be performed with [mantras] beginning with Oṃ and ending with Phaṭ, as well as the Aghora seed-mantra, the root-mantra, and the Śāntyatīta-kalā. (35)
Having uttered [the name] ending in the dative case and pronouncing the syllable *huṃ*,
one should lead [the deity], abandoning the root-mantras of others while recollecting its own respective seed-syllable.
Having offered three oblations, one should perform the binding of the fetters;
then, striking the head with the Astra-mantra while recollecting the Śiva-mantra three times.
O Blessed One, that which is called Śāntyatītā is endowed with impurity (mala) and karma;
it is pervasive and is the bond (pāśa) of the two states of bondage for the principles beginning with Śānti. || 38 ||
Having uttered [the mantra] ending with *huṃ phaṭ*, one should tie a knot in the thread;
[this consists of] the word *śiva* enclosed by its respective seed-syllable (*bīja*) and the word *bhagavat*. (39)

Having uttered the four parts of the noose (*pāśa*), namely *mala*, *tattva*, and so forth, which pervade [the soul], one should then utter the words *bandha bandha* (bind, bind), accompanied by *huṃ phaṭ* at the end. || 40 ||
Having recited [the mantras] individually, one should tie a knot in the thread;
then, taking that thread, one should place it within a pair of shallow bowls joined together.
Having performed the *asaṃpāta-homa*, he should present that thread to the presiding deity of the mandala and place it near the Śiva-pitcher for its protection.
And having caused [the disciple] to perform prostration with the Śiva-kumbha,
the preceptor, together with the disciple, emerges from the sacrificial pavilion.
One should offer the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the sacrificial oblation (caru) to them at the Dandhadāvana,
in a pure, secluded place on the ground that has been smeared and enclosed by a screen.
For those situated in separate mandalas, [the deities] on the eastern faces are for prosperity with regard to enjoyment and liberation, while those with gentle countenances are for liberation. (45)
To those who have washed their feet and hands, who are purified, who sit with knees tucked within [the arms], and who hold kuśa grass in their right hands, [he should offer] in due order.
Having drawn up [the water] with the right hand alone,
which holds the pavitra grass, one should offer a single handful of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) accompanied by the heart-mantra.
Having drunk that, he should then give a second [portion] in the same manner to those who have restrained themselves;
having also given another mouthful (culuka), he should then offer the sacrificial pap (caru).
The measure should be eight mouthfuls in a cup made from the Brahma-tree (Ficus religiosa),
prepared with leaves of the Pippala tree for those seeking liberation as well as for those seeking worldly enjoyment.
O twice-born one, after consuming this, one should again perform the touching [of the body] with pure tooth-sticks produced from milk-producing trees.
It should be as thick as the little finger, straight, succulent, and without blemishes;
it reveals the linga that bestows both liberation and worldly enjoyment, being the size of the auspicious thumb.

If that which was chewed by the pincers of the tips of the king’s teeth and washed before him falls upon a particular spot when thrown, one should know from that place whether it will be auspicious or inauspicious.
The falling of fire, meteors, or *palāśa* leaves in the cardinal directions or the northwest is not auspicious;
however, their falling upon his face in the remaining directions is auspicious, depending on the nature of the actions performed.
Having understood this, once they have sipped water for purification and are composed,
one should put them to sleep at night while protecting them by means of the very same dream-inducing rite.

And on beds that have been touched by the ground, or by those who have come into contact with me while engaged in yoga, one should touch them with kusha grass and ashes, provided they are oriented toward the east, south, or north.
On the sides, where [the beds] were not touching one another and were provided with pillows, and which were protected by the weapon called *caturdaṇḍikā* and free from darkness; (56)
Having placed them upon the heart after they have been protected by the Astra-mantra and consecrated one hundred times with the Astra-mantra,
and having bound the tufts of hair with the Śikhā-mantra, [one should proceed] with those consecrated by the Varma-mantra.
Having covered the disciples with garments and having projected three lines on the outside using sesame, mustard seeds, and ashes consecrated with the Astra-mantra; || 58 ||
Then, having instructed them in the mantra of the "Dream-Boy" (Svapnamāṇavaka),
he offered the external oblation to the lords of the directions in their proper order.

For the pacification of desired obstacles and adverse conditions, one should kindle a fire of uneven flames and offer oblations of cooked rice (caru) and tooth-sticks (dantadhāva), etc., one hundred times for each.
Then, having performed the expiation by offering one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra,
and having washed his feet and hands and sipped water for purification, he should bathe in water.
Having either dissolved [the image] with ashes or covered it with white cloth,
and having meditated upon Śiva whose body consists of the entire path (adhvan), one should contemplate Him as the one whose very form has been made Śiva-like.
Having first partaken of the *caruka* and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), he should use the tooth-stick;
then, having become purified as before, being himself pure, he should sleep.

Then, on the second day at dawn, having performed his daily obligatory rites, the Guru shall ask the disciples about their dreams during the night; if any were bad dreams, he should perform a rite for their pacification.
One should perform a hundred oblations with ghee, dūrvā grass, madhuka, milk, and the products of a tawny cow;
then, as before, one should carry out the auspicious rites such as the entrance of the disciple.
Having summoned his disciples to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit on his right side,
he should cause them to hold that thread which has been consecrated upon the bodies of the disciples.
"O God, I shall bestow grace; let the child strive," [he says]. Having received permission, he should place the Śakti in the form of the Foundation (Ādhāra) within the fire.
One should place the *nivṛtti* [kalā] within the *śakti*, conjoined with its *kalās* and *tattvas*;
the *pṛthivī-tattva* and the letter *kṣa*, along with the *hṛdaya* and *sadyojāta* mantras. (68)
The Kālāgni-ratha, Kumāṇḍa, Hāḍaka, Brāhma, Vaiṣṇava, and Raudra—these six worlds are situated within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). 69.
Kāpālīśa, Aja, Buddha, Vajradeha, Pramardana, Vibhūti, Avyaya, Śāstṛ, Pinākī, and Tridaśādhipa. || 70 ||
Agni, Rudra, Hutāśa, Piṅgala, Khādaka, Hara, Jvalana, Dahana, Babhru, Bhasmāntaka, and Kṣayāntaka. || 71 ||
He is Yāmya, Mṛtyu, Hara, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and he who is designated as the Creator (Kartṛ); he is the uniter and the disuniter, as well as Dharma and the Lord of Dharma (Dharmapati).
Nirṛti is the slayer and destroyer, of cruel gaze and terrifying aspect;
he has hair standing erect, deformed eyes, and smoke-colored, reddish fangs.
Bala, Atibala, Pāśahasta, Mahābala, Śveta, Jayabhadra, Dīrghabāhu, and Jalāntaka—[these are the eight]. (74)
Meghanāda and Sunāda are proclaimed as the tenth;
[the others are] Śīghra, Laghu, Vāyuvega, Tīkṣṇa, Sūkṣma, and Kṣayāntaka. || 75 ||
The ender of the five, the five-crested one, the one with matted locks, whose vehicle is the clouds;
the lord of treasures, beautiful in form, auspicious, possessing a gentle body, and wearing matted hair. (76)

The bearer of Lakṣmī, the bearer of jewels, the bearer of Śrī, the gracious one, the destroyer of the pride of the wicked, the lord of the masters of knowledge, the omniscient, the enjoyer of wisdom, and the one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas. || 77 ||
Sureśa, Śarva, Jyeṣṭha, Bhūtapāla, Balipriya, Vṛṣa, Vṛṣadhara, Ananta, Krodhana, and Mārutāśana. || 78 ||
Grasana, Uḍumbara, Īśa, Phaṇīndra, Vajradaṃṣṭrin, Śambhu, Vibhu, Gaṇādhyakṣa, Triyakṣa, and Tridaśeśvara. (79)
Saṃvāha and Vivāha, as well as the three-eyed Lord seeking to grasp the sky,
Vīrabhadra, and Bhadrakālī— above all these are two worlds.
Kapālīśa and the others are in the east; Agnirudra and the others are in the southeast;
Yamya and the others are in the southern quarter; and Nirṛti and the others are in the southwest.
In the western quarter are Balā and the others; in the northwestern quarter are Śīghra and the others;
in the northern quarter are Nidhīśa and the others; and in the northeastern quarter are Vidyādhipa and the others.
Vṛṣa and the others are in the lower portion, while Śambhu and the principal deities are situated in the sky;
one should thus arrange one hundred and eight worlds.
In the eighty-one squares, beginning from the final *praṇava* and proceeding in reverse order,
one should place two *namaḥ*s, a *praṇava*, and thereafter the six-syllable mantra.
Then there are Sarva and Daśa; likewise the pair Śarva and Śiva-sūkṣma;
likewise the pair of sounds, the pair of knowledges, and the pair of Piṅgas.
The *pataṅga* should be practiced twice; it consists of two pairs of *turu* steps, followed by two pairs of *sākṣi* steps, with the former remaining in its original position thereafter. (86)
"Recite 'astuta, astuta' (praise not, praise not)"; thus, being honored and yet unhonored, he is devoted to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, and is the cause of the presence of all.

Then [follows] "bestower of happiness upon all beings" (sarvabhūtasukhaprada) and "the state arising from existence" (bhavodbhavapada); likewise, the pair "Bhava" and the pair "Śarva" constitute the first two. (88)
"Muñca muñca" is the word; "yogādhipate" is also a word; "mahātejaḥ" is a word; and "sadbhāveśvaram" is proclaimed as a word. (89)

One should meditate upon the station of Mahādeva, followed by twenty-eight stations; one should contemplate the path beginning with the principles (tattvas) as pervaded by Nivṛtti through its power (kalā).
Having uttered "hlāṃ, obeisance to Nivṛttikalā," preceded by the Praṇava and ending with "namaḥ," one should extract the Nivṛtti [kalā] from the thread and place it upon the vessel.
One should perform three oblations ending with "svāhā" for those [deities] to be invoked.
Impurity (mala), action (karman), and that which is called Māyā—born of the enjoyer, the enjoyment, and the body—are [the objects of these rites]. (92)
Meditating thus, one should visualize the infinite wombs residing within the wombs of the goddesses;
having invoked Vāgīśī, who pervades them all, one should worship her.

Having first offered three oblations with the mantra beginning with the Praṇava and preceded by "Namaḥ" to Vāgīśvarī— specifically "Vāgīśvaryai namaḥ"— and ending with "Svāhā," one should subsequently [proceed].
"Be present, O Goddess of gods, for the act of bestowing grace upon the bound soul (paśu).
Having thus entreated [the deity], he should sprinkle the disciple with the Astra-mantra and strike him in the heart.
With the weapon-mantra ending in *phaṭ* and preceded by the *praṇava*, and having entered his body through the exhalation of one's own self, [one should perform the rite]. 96.
Having performed the severing of the heart with the weapon-mantra and the goad-mudrā,
one should draw [the deity] forth and perform three oblations with the root-mantra.
Having meditated on [the disciple] as being like a drop on the tip of a blade of grass, encased by the *praṇava*,
and having uttered the seed-syllable ending with the letter *sa*, [one should perform the rite for the child] with the *saṃhāramudrā*.

Having established [the breath] in one's own heart by means of inhalation (pūraka) and having performed retention (kumbhaka), one should remember one's own root-mantra and join it at the end of the twelve fingers (dvādaśānta).
Therefore, having taken that consciousness by means of the mudrā known as Udbhavā,
one should simultaneously effect the union of the child with all wombs.
One should offer three oblations with the root mantra ending in "svāhā," [saying]: "O Blessed One, O God, Lord of Gods, in all wombs of this child... (101)
Perform the conjunction here in this initiatory rite that bestows liberation;
for the successful completion of all the internal essences, one should offer three oblations with the root mantra.
"O Blessed One, let this disciple bring about the perfection of the womb right here;
O twice-born ones, he should lead [the soul] through all wombs with the words 'do it, do it'. (103)
Then, for the sake of birth, one should offer three root oblations, saying:
"O Blessed One, perform the birth of all embryos. || 104 ||
Having spoken thus for the sake of the animal's birth and for its very growth, and having offered three root-oblations (mūlahuti), one should address Śiva as follows: || 105 ||
"O Blessed One, bring forth the activity of the bodies of the disciples; bring it forth!
Thus saying, one should perform three oblations with the root mantra for the sake of acquiring [the power of] karma. 106.
"O Blessed One, grant various enjoyments to yourself;
having recited thus for the acquisition of merit, there is a distinction in the worldly dharma. (107)
Perform the acquisition of dharma-nature through past karma and future karma, according to place, time, body, and sense object. (108)
Recalling that enjoyment is manifold through the distinction between what has been accumulated and what is yet to come,
one experiences the sensation of pleasure and pain within the person (puruṣa), who is characterized by the state of being an enjoyer.
Having offered three root oblations, one should pray to Śiva as follows:
"O Blessed One, bring about the accomplishment of enjoyment everywhere for us, O Doer! (110)
Recalling the form of supreme bliss within enjoyments,
one should offer three oblations to Śiva, which are the very embodiment of supreme bliss.

And perform the dissolution (*laya*) and the act of making [the soul] do [it] for the child during the rite of liberation (*nirvāṇa*), for the sake of purifying the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of birth, lifespan, and experience, and for the expiation of the body. (112)
Having offered one hundred oblations with the heart-mantra, one should offer three oblations with the root-mantra;
perform purification and expiation in all rites for both the agent and the recipient.
"O Blessed One," [he says], for here the separation of the subtle self from enjoyment occurs due to the absence of experience;
one should lead it outward in a form free from desire, while remembering it as being bound by the noose of *māyā*. (114)
Afterwards, one should perform three root-oblations (mūlahuti) for the removal of impurity;
then, recollecting the agency of impurity and the state of being an enjoyer, one should offer oblations for the sake of purification.
Having first offered ten oblations with the heart-mantra, one should subsequently offer three oblations with the root-mantra;
in this way, the dissolution of impurities occurs, which is called the "dissolution of karma."
Having recollected here the separation of karmas, which is of the nature of absolute non-existence, one should offer three oblations while reciting the root mantra.
O Blessed One, here in this world, the fruit of one's own illusion consists of karma;
effect its disjunction from these [karmas] for the sake of the conditioned state of nirvāṇa.
Then, for the sake of purifying the pervasive bond of withdrawal (nivṛttipāśa) within the impurities and so forth,
one should offer three oblations with the Astra-mantra from the root [mantra].
Having offered three oblations, and having requested the command, "O Blessed One, perform [the rite] here," one should indeed proceed with the cutting of the *nivṛtti* [line]. 120.
Having contemplated the oneness of the self through the destruction of all bodies without exception,
one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Śiva-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
Having invoked [the deity] with "Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā," and having worshipped him, one should offer libations with the mantra:
"O Brahmā, accept sound and touch here; Svāhā! (122).
Having offered three oblations, one should then proclaim the command of Śiva: "O Lord of Causes, by you [is granted] the stainless state of this Creator. (123)
This command of the Supreme Lord must be carried out as a restriction:
having first dismissed Brahmā, who is situated at the forefront of the pure principles (tattvas). || 124 ||
Having meditated upon [the deity] as liberated from the bonds of worldly existence (nivṛtti-pāśa) and resembling pure crystal,
one should offer three oblations while reciting the root mantra.
"O Blessed One, perform the extraction of this self from the noose of *nivṛtti* by means of inhalation (*pūraka*) and the *saṃhāra-mudrā*. (126)
Then, having established that [thread] within oneself, one should fix it upon the thread with the armor-mantra (kavaca).
One should offer three oblations with the Śiva-mantra for the stability of the disciple.
Having worshipped her with the mantra "Salutation to Vāgīśvarī," one should then satisfy her;
her dismissal from the fire should be performed with three oblations.
Then, for the sake of purification, one should contemplate the foundation in the Sūtra-mantra:
the twenty-three principles, namely water, fire, air, and space. (129)
Smell, taste, touch, sound, the organ of generation, the anus, the feet, the hands, speech, the nose, the tongue, the eyes, the skin, and hearing. || 130 ||
The mind, ego, and intellect—beyond that is primordial nature (prakṛti).
Thus, O best of the twice-born, the principles beginning with "la" and ending with "ṭa" have been described. 131.
There should be twenty-four syllables for Śiśu and likewise for Vāma;
the mantras for Aghora are fifty-six, and there are nine cities.
Amareśa, Prabhāsa, Naimiśa, Puṣkara, Avadhi, Ḍiṇḍimuṇḍi, Bhārabhūti, and Lakulīśvara. (133)
Hariścandra, Śrīśaila, Jalpeśa, Āmrātakeśvara, Madhyameśa, Mahākāla, Kedāra, and likewise Bhairava. (134)
Gaya, Kurukṣetra, Nākhalo, Nakhala, Vimaleśa, Aṭṭahāsa, Mahendra, and the one known as Bhīma. (135)
Vastrāpada, Rudrakoṭi, Vimukta, Mahālaya, Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Svarṇākṣa, and also Sthāṇu. || 136 ||
Jhagalaṇḍa, Dviraṇḍa, Mākoṭa, Maṇḍaleśvara, Kālañcara, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sthūleśvara, and Sthaleśvara. || 137 ||
The Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yākṣa, Gāndharva, and Aindra; likewise, the Saumya, Prājāpatya, and Brāhma [forms] should be known. || 138 ||
The Akṛta, the Kṛta, the Bhairava, the Brāhma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Kaumāra, the Auma, and the Śraikaṇṭha—these indeed constitute the eight [tantras]. (139)

Amareśa and others are in the principle of fire (tejas-tattva); Hariścandra and others are in the principle of fire; Gayā and others are in the principle of air (vāyu-tattva); and Vastrāpada and others are in the ether (vyoma).
In the egoity of the *jhagalaṇḍa* and so forth, the mind is established as the *paiśāca* and other [states];
likewise, in primordial nature (*prakṛti*), there are the uncreated and so on—thus, there are fifty-six ancient cities.
There are twenty-one words beginning with Maheśvara and ending with Arūpin;
the first word is Maheśvara, and the second is Paramātman. (142)
Then the word "śarva" is uttered, and after that, "śiva";
then the one known as Nidhanodbhava, and after that the word called Nidhana.
The word *anidhana* is likewise [the first], and after that the word *oṃsvakṣa*;
then another word, *oṃbhuvaḥ*, and after that the word *oṃbhūḥ*. (144)
Then another [mantra] is formed from the four *dhū*s, followed by various and diverse *pada*s;
then there is another *pada* beginning with *anāde*, and then the *pada* "abhasma. (145)
Then there is another word, "without smoke," and from that, the word "without fire";
another word is "formless," and likewise "light, light. (146)
"Tejas-tejaḥ," "padaṃ proktuṃ," "prathama," and "prathamā"—these constitute two word-pairs of formless [names] and twenty single words. (147)
One should contemplate that all this is pervaded by the power of installation (pratiṣṭhākalā);
thus it has been stated, along with the syllables, words, and mantras of the three worlds. 148.
Having recollected that [deity] who is pregnant with the embryo, and having partaken of the continuous stream of bliss,
one should remember the pure and light bond, as well as the heavy one to be purified between these two.
Having likewise uttered the designating [mantra], one should observe the purification of that which is to be purified;
this has been taught, O twice-born Śivas, for the sake of the yoga of all unions. 150.

Having first uttered "Oṃ Hrāṃ Hrīṃ," followed by the two parts [of the mantra] in the dative case and ending with "namaskāra," one should offer three root oblations at the conclusion of the worship. || 151 ||
However, one should perform everything beginning with the re-establishment of the ritual form as before;
the preceptor should then offer an expiation by means of a hundred oblations starting from the head.
Having bestowed the white essence of Hari, one should take refuge in the digit (kalā) which is knowledge (vidyā).
Pervaded by that digit of knowledge, the person becomes the primordial one. || 153 ||
Passion (rāga), necessity (niyati), knowledge (vidyā), limited agency (kalā), time (kāla), and the deluding power (mohinī)—these are the seven phonemes from *ña* to *dha* in reverse order. (154)
The ancient mantra here consists of twenty-seven syllables;
[the deities are] Vāma, Bhīma, Ugra, Bhava, Īśāna, and Ekavīra. (155)
Pracaṇḍa, Umāpati, Aja, Ananta, Ekaśiva, Krodheśa, Saṃvarta, Jyotis, and Piṅga shall be the first [group]. || 156 ||
Pañcāntaka, Ekavīra, Śikheda of great splendor, Vāmadeva, Bhava, Udbhava, and also Ekapiṅgala. || 157 ||
Ekeṣaṇa, as well as Aiśāna, and likewise Aṅguṣṭhamātraka;
thus there are six, five, pairs, pairs, and twos, twos. (158)
There are eight [syllables] beginning with *puruṣa* and ending with *māyā*, for these are indeed the cities;
there are twenty *pada*s, and the word "vyāpin" occurs twice. (159)
In the Vyomin-vyomin [state], the word "paścāt" (afterwards) becomes insentient;
O Supreme Lord, the word "parāya" likewise occurs again. 160.
The name Jyotirūpāya and also Sarvayogādya, as well as the word Anidhanāya, and the word Goptre are proclaimed [as names]. || 161 ||
"Salutation after salutation to the secret and the most secret;
here, the five words beginning with Sadyojāta follow in sequence. (162)
The word "śivāya," then "sarvaprabhave," followed by the word "śivāya," and finally the syllable "oṃ. || 163 ||
The terms "meditation," "food," "non-perception," and "words" are proclaimed;
having performed the reconnection as before, one should place the vidyā into the fire.
Having offered expiation with the crest-lock and performed one hundred oblations, one should offer white [substances] to Rudra while reciting: "O Rudra, take away form and fragrance. (165)
This state called "existence" (bhava) is within the scope of the three kalās;
however, the Self that has transcended existence stands above the principle of the Self (ātmatattva). || 166 ||

Desiring to cause [the disciple], who is possessed by the impurity of office and is a vessel for emergent sovereignty, to enjoy the experience that is the means for purifying the senses, the teacher [proceeds]. (167)
Having perceived with the mind that tranquility which is favorable, unconfused, and free from attachment, as well as the internal states contained within it; 168.
O best of the twice-born, the three principles are Vidyeśa and Sādākhya;
the phonemes are said to be Ga, Kha, and Ka; and the two mantras are Vaktra and Tanucchada.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, Kalavikaraṇī, Balavikaraṇī, and also Balapramathanī. || 170 ||
She who subdues all beings is indeed Manonmanī; she becomes supreme.
Within this Vidyā, there are nine cities, and the one known as Ananta is subtle. || 171 ||
Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrtika, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍin—thus is the group of eight [forms] of Īśa. (172)
Within the Sādākhyabhuvana itself, there are eighteen cities;
furthermore, there are eleven stages known as those of the eternal yogins.
Then there may be another beginning with *yogapīṭha*; then the word for the eternal (*śāśvata*), the word for the fixed (*dhruva*), and then the word for the non-dependent (*anāśrita*). || 174 ||
The word "to the protectorless" (anāthāya) is proclaimed, and then the word "to the infinite" (anantāya);
then the word "to Śiva," and thereafter the word "to the all-pervading" (sarvavyāpine). || 175 ||

One should offer a hundred oblations with the *kavaca* mantra for atonement to the one whose form is the void of space and so forth, and whose station is likewise the void of space and so forth. (176)
Everything is as previously indicated; the intellect (buddhi) and the ego-sense (ahaṅkṛti) have the pure (śukla) as their object.
The Lord (īśvara) is the Lord of Causes (kāraṇeśa); everything beyond this is as before.
In the kalā beyond peace (śāntyatīta), however, the Śiva-tattva is established;
its seed-syllables are sixteen, and the mantras are the three: Āstreśa, Īśāna, and Śiva. || 178 ||
The single syllable "Om" is to be known as consisting of fifteen worlds:
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and the ethereal (Nābhasī). || 179 ||
Beyond this, five cities are further proclaimed here which I shall bind:
Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, and likewise Mocikā. (180)
Likewise, there is the upward-moving [power], as well as the worlds arising from the *nāda*;
then follow the Pervasive (*vyāpinī*), the Space-formed (*vyomarūpā*), and beyond that, the Infinite (*anantā*).
The one called Anāthā is likewise described, and the fifth is said to be Anāśritā;
indeed, the five worlds of Śakti have been thus declared.
Having recognized her as pregnant by these [signs], one should bring about the union with a pure [woman], while reciting the two kalās ending in the dative case: *hyauṃ* and *hauṃ*. (183)
Having worshipped him with a focused mind, one should offer three root oblations;
then, one should perform everything beginning with the re-establishment of the *kalā*s as previously described.
For the expiation, one should perform a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra;
having set aside the Astra-mantra, one should offer oblations with a lamp for the purpose of severing the bonds.
Then, in the seedless initiation (nirbījadīkṣā), at the conclusion of the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should cause this to be performed;
[the teacher] should impose the rule (samaya) and the practice of the rule (samayācāra) upon the empowered [disciple], who is otherwise of the nature of bonds.
"O Maheśvara, perform the purification of the disciple's commitment (samaya) and the bond of the conduct of that commitment," having said "Do so," one should offer a white [flower]. || 187 ||
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Śiva and then the word "Sadāśiva," one should perform three oblations with the mantra: "mano hṛhāṇa svāhā."
Having dismissed it as before and having gathered the stainless thread of the self, one should, by means of exhalation (recaka),
establish it within the body of the disciple.
Having placed a drop of water on his head, he should worship Vāgīśvarī;
having satiated her while she resides in the fire, he should then make this request: || 190 ||
O Goddess, you have been fatigued for the sake of the sacrificial animal; go now to your own domain, having meditated upon the digit Śāntyatītā as dissolved within the Śakti-tattva. 191.

Having established the reality of the self (ātmatattva) up to the end of Māyā, the supreme gurus [should perform the rite] beginning with the reality of the self (ātmatattva) ending in the dative case and accompanied by the root mantra. (192)
Having uttered "namaḥ" joined with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and having performed worship in its presence,
one should [offer] according to the *śivamantra* ending in *svāhā* for the sake of purifying any deficiency in the ritual procedure.
Having offered one hundred oblations with sound, one should [offer] the Vidyātattva in a whisper;
having approached up to the end of the Sadeśa, one should offer one hundred and eight [oblations].
Due to a deficiency in the pronunciation of the mantra, one is purified by the Śiva-mantra;
having established the Śiva-principle (śivatattva), one should mentally contemplate it as extending to the end of Śakti.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the Śiva-mantra even if there is merely a deficiency of mind, one is liberated; then one should commence the cutting of the topknot (śikhā).
Having meditated upon the crest-lock (śikhā) situated within the paths, pervading all paths, and being the cause of the paths— standing at its tip like pure crystal— 197.
Having intentionally reflected upon the consciousness of the disciple, one should touch the *kartarī* with the crest-lock;
one should cut the crest-lock with the crest-lock, and thereafter bathe Śiva.

Having sipped water and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, the preceptor, having offered an oblation into the fire, should offer a full oblation with the crest-lock situated at the tip of the sacrificial ladle while it is encircled by cow-dung.
Then, having gone outside and washed the *sruk*, *sruva*, and the knife, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) to become pure, one should worship Śiva and say this: || 200 ||
O Blessed One, O Supreme Lord, by Your grace I have performed the purification of the paths and the severing of the topknot, until this [soul] reaches the supreme abode.
"I shall now unite this disciple; let the command be given.
Thus authorized with the words "Do so," the eminent Guru, holding the arghya vessel, [proceeds]. (202)
Having summoned the child, he, accompanied by his disciple, should proceed toward the fire;
then follows the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of the disciple and the rite of sakalīkaraṇa.
Then follows the internal sacrifice, the joining of the channels,
and the satiation of the mantras by offering one oblation for each of the mantras that have been fully empowered.

Having performed the purification through the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, the preceptor, who is the locus of the Vidyātattva, seated upon a throne fashioned from the Bindu, should unite [the disciple] with Śiva.
Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, and likewise Mocikā, as well as Ūrdhvagāminī—these are considered the subtle [nādīs], along with Sūkṣmā and Sukṣmāmṛtā. || 206 ||
O twice-born ones, the power of the Bindu is thus declared, and the power of the Nāda is the Kalā; by these Kalās, the body of the supreme teacher is fashioned for the sake of the Age (Yuga). 207.
She is considered pervasive, of the nature of space, infinite, and indeed the Unsurpassed (Aparā);
she is the "Lordless" (Anāthā) and the "Unrelied-upon" (Anāśritā), conjoined with the external organs. || 208 ||

That which is conjoined with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is fashioned by the samanā; O Śarva, it is endowed with a body completely filled by the Unmanā state of the reality of the Self (ātmatattva).
Having performed inhalation and retention, with the tongue joined to the palate,
with the face slightly turned away, he should not let his teeth touch one another.
With his body properly erect, having united the child with himself, he should contemplate the *suṣumnā* channel as being made one with the vital air known as *prāṇa*. (211)
Having contemplated the consciousness of the disciple as being like a pure crystal, one should utter the mantra through the yoga of abandoning the causal [condition]. || 212 ||
One should unite the disciple with Śiva by means of the full breath-retention (kumbhaka),
for one whose mind has been turned away from the self consisting of the powers of the vital breath and the faculty of giving.

Having placed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles nearby, one should take up the deceased person’s individual soul (*pudgala*) from the fire using the *saṃhāra-mudrā*— a soul that is pure, with its crest raised, and resembling a flame.
One should join him to his own body with the seed-syllable of the weapon, as before;
yet, even though joined by that, he has not been made equal in qualities. || 215 ||
To whatever extent one has set forth, there is the attainment of reality, just as a prince achieves his purpose even upon attaining a vast empire. (216)
Even a hundred kings who are ignorant of the sixfold policy do not shine;
therefore, for the manifestation of one's own virtues, one should offer these six oblations of clarified butter with the sacrificial ladle.
The wise preceptor should perform the fire-oblation according to this ritual application:
"Become omniscient, eternally awakened, independent, and fully satisfied. (218)

You, whose infinite power is never lost, [should be worshipped] with the mantra preceded by *hrasvaprāsāda* (the short Praṇava), joined with the word *ātman*, ending in *svāhā*, and accompanied by the lamp. || 219 ||
Thus has been described initiation, which liberates one from all sins;
it applies to the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, as well as those considered to be of the anuloma (natural order) classes.

Those who are eligible for initiation—whether born of a formal lineage or born of a secret lineage—and those such as a son-in-law or the husband of one’s father’s wife, are fit provided they desire liberation. || 221 ||
Since Śiva is their initiator (dīkṣākarta), they do not have a son as their officiant;
nor does an outcaste serve as their Hotṛ priest, but rather one who possesses the power of vision (cākṣuṣī).
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, the procedure for the initiation into Nirvāṇa, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
In the twenty-fourth chapter is the procedure for the consecration of the preceptor (ācāryābhiṣeka).
Now I shall explain the consecration by which one becomes a teacher on earth:
he should be born in Āryāvarta, illustrious, and endowed with all the auspicious marks.
Where there are Brahmins of virtuous conduct, ascetics whose wealth is their austerity, as well as gods and the Vedas, that region is known as Āryāvarta. || 2 ||

This region has been described, though it does not extend into the middle of the Vindhya mountains and the ocean; however, for the sake of context, that which is devoid of the eight *kakāras* is also mentioned here.
Karṇāṭa, the one called Kaliṅga, Kaccha, the one named Kāśmīra,
Koṅkaṇa, Karahāṭa, Kukkuṭa, and Kāṅka are thus declared.

One born into a family of the Ādi-Śaivas would be the most excellent for the rites of installation and so forth; furthermore, the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas are also qualified for their respective duties.
In the initiation of all mortals, at the installation ceremony, during festivals, in the ritual bathing, in the sprinkling, in other rites, in expiation, and in consecration; || 6 ||
O Brahmins, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, at the beginning of an exposition or during the worship of all the gods, the foremost Śaiva guru is the one who is praised.
The three castes beginning with the Brahmins [are authorized] for initiation and installation;
among Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and so forth, the Kṣatriya [is authorized] for the Śūdras and Vaiśyas. (8)
In the initiation of a Śūdra, a Vaiśya is desired even for one's own caste;
likewise, these three [castes] are permitted for the installation of a mobile Liṅga intended for one's own benefit.
Even a Śūdra may [perform the rites] during the initiation of a Śūdra, for his own sake, or when the rite is designated as "movable" (cala),
or even upon seeing a Bāṇaliṅga, provided he is a lifelong practitioner (naiṣṭhika).
Ācārya, Gaulaka, Dayita, Parivartaka, as well as Pāravettṛ, Devala, and Punarbhava; || 11 ||

One who eats what is unfit to be eaten, a *kuṇḍa*, one marked with ashes, one with sprouts [on the head], one with a skull-topped staff, one with black teeth, one who has ascended [to a high place], or one who has fallen; 12.

Likewise, one who is lazy, a low-born man (vṛṣala), a fallen person (vrātya), the husband of a Vaiśya woman, one who has composed false scriptures, a eunuch, one who is diseased, and one with deformed nails. || 13 ||
Furthermore, one should avoid those who are addicted to vices, those who commit adultery, the husband of a low-caste woman, as well as painters, singers, and dancers.

One who is a servant of a foreign kingdom, one of impure intellect, a practitioner of secret spells (tāntrika), one habitually inclined toward slandering others, and likewise one covered with many scars; || 15 ||

One who has recently given birth, a lustful man, a physician, one established in fallacious reasoning, as well as one who is difficult to reach, those devoted to Buddhist and other scriptures, a renunciant, and likewise one observing a vow— [these should be avoided].
Fickle, associating with the deceitful, living solely for the sake of profit, yet devoted to pure deeds and indeed to the systems of Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika. (17)
[He studied] Sāṃkhya with its various divisions, Māyāvāda, the doctrine of the Arhat, Buddhism, Lokāyata, and especially the Mīmāṃsā scriptures. (18)
Even in other false paths, such as the Kāpāla, the Pāñcarātraka,
or the Somasiddhānta, as well as in the Eastern Tradition or the Western [Tradition], (19)
In the Bhairava and Kaula scriptures, in all other unrecorded traditions,
and in the entire web of established objects of knowledge, he has constantly placed his hope.
A man who is constantly devoted to poetry and drama, who has practiced the science of erotics (kāmaśāstra), and whose speech is characterized by poetic deviation (padavyutkrāntaka). || 21 ||

One should abandon a person who is intent on the knowledge of astrology, whose mind is devoted to the ancient lore (purāṇas), and who has exerted effort toward those goals that are not the true purpose of human life.
One should carefully avoid that person who, out of delusion, considers the Śiva-knowledge beginning with the Kāmika, as well as the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas, to be equal.

And in the knowledge-yoga and ritual actions fully established in the Śiva-siddhānta, as well as in the conduct (caryā) whose objects of knowledge are perfectly established and spoken by Śiva himself. (24)
Having abandoned constant deliberation regarding the body and its worldly purposes for the sake of Śiva,
the man who performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) here should avoid all wicked-mindedness.
One should avoid one who misappropriates the property of Śiva through unjust means, one who is like a murderer, those who are deficient in learning or prone to anger, and one who is deformed. (26)

Likewise, O Ambaṣṭha, one should avoid an astrologer who is devoid of the ability to deliberate and resolve doubts, as well as one who belongs to the same lineage or has a family connection, and one who holds a rosary of flowers (kusumākṣa). || 27 ||

On a day when the rising of the ascendant is pure, one should perform the consecration for one endowed with the aforementioned characteristics, preceded by the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa). || 28 ||
Either in the east, or in the northeast, or in the western direction;
in the pavilion, O gentle one, which is adorned with a canopy and faces the north.
Likewise, two altars (vedikā),
each four cubits in width and extending toward the south and north, should be made with a height of half a cubit and shaped like a yoke (four-cornered).
Having demarcated the ground with a svastika colored in the four directions and adorned with lamps, one should worship Śiva in the fire within the pavilion.
If a disciple whose ritual duties have been neglected is consecrated by initiation,
one should perform this procedure after offering the outer and inner oblations.
Having cleansed [the area] with sour gruel, rice, earth, ashes, dūrvā grass, cow dung, cow urine, white mustard seeds, curd, and water, immediately thereafter—
Either ninefold or fivefold, or in every way, he should place all the grains arranged [therein],
along with jars or pitchers, together with their *kūrca* grass-bundles and their lids.
He [offered] rivers with their waters, endowed with perfumes, jewels, and excellent gold,
featuring mango, *aśvattha*, and *palāśa* trees, and bearing *bījāpūra* fruits.
One should consecrate it with this mantra along with the lords of knowledge (vidyeśas) and the nine or five purifiers (pavitrakas);
in the case of five, one should consecrate it with the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti.
Or else, one should take jars that have been obtained in a hundred ways by Śiva, consecrated, and fit for the ritual bathing; or even a single jar associated with Śiva.
Having established [the deity] on the southern altar, one should place the child on the northern one,
upon an auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) presided over by Śiva together with his limbs (sāṅga).
Having properly honored him with a suitable seat, according to one's means, or with vessels of colored rice and water, having cleansed [the vessel] with water; || 39 ||
Having bathed him with pure water, he was then, in another place, provided once more with a changed set of garments,
including an upper robe and a lower garment.

Having brought him whose limbs are smeared with white sandalwood and likewise dusted with ashes, one seated upon the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha) situated on the southern altar (dakṣavedi). || 41 ||
Having worshipped the deity facing east with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should perform the *ārātrika* ceremony with burning lamps provided with wicks that have been fully kindled.
Then the preceptor should give to the disciple a pair of compasses and a pair of scissors, as well as a balance, a *sruk* ladle, and a *sruva* spoon, accompanied by the *uṣṇih* and other meters.
The preceptor [should offer] darbha grass, books, a rosary, a crown, sandals, a fly-whisk, an umbrella, an elephant, a palanquin, and so forth. (44)
At that time, endowed with faith, one should offer other royal insignia, and with faith, the preceptor should likewise accept the command from this day forward. (45)
Having understood the initiation, the exposition, and so forth, and having examined them according to the rule,
I have thus performed [this] for the sake of the God of gods and for the teacher.
"By your grace, may he perform his office without obstacles"—
thus the preceptor should request, having then approached the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

One should offer separate oblations for the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti using their respective mantras; then, having performed the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), [one should place it] in the right hand.
One should mark [the disciple] with the five limbs, beginning with the little finger, using the tip of a blade of *darbha* grass;
then, having conceived him as the hand of Hara, one should surrender one's own authority to him. (49)
For that purpose, one should perform the expiation according to this rule, using the mantras of Śiva’s throne and limbs, and with the names of the deity to be worshipped. (50)

Having offered ten oblations with the limbs [of the mantra], and ten oblations at the end with the word "Śiva," one should offer the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with that same [mantra] and ask the Blessed One for forgiveness.
In this very manner, one should also consecrate the practitioner;
however, his consecration should be performed with jars obtained from a person engaged in the practice (sādhya).
The initiated one is called a *putraka*; he who has been consecrated is a *samayin*. He who is a common *samayin* is remembered as a *māheśvara*. (53)

He who is devoid of the extraction from his caste (jātyuddhāra) is merely an ordinary initiate (sāmānyasamayin); however, one endowed with that [extraction] belongs to the special class, as are those known as the Cākṣuṣīs and others. || 54 ||
Those who are joined with those [lower] initiations are called "attendants" (paricāraka);
they are not fit for the worship of the Liṅga, much less for rituals such as initiation.
If he is the bestower of curses and favors, he should initiate the preceptors and others;
those born of the Śiva-dvija lineage are indeed the people devoted to Maheśvara.
All of them were previously initiated by Śiva at the beginning of creation;
their initiation is intended for the purpose of worshipping me and for the sake of their purification. (57)
Since it is a bond for the body, one should perform atonement;
he who is thus initiated in many ways shall swiftly attain Śiva.
The *bhautika* celibate student may be a teacher for householders;
the *naiṣṭhika* student should be among those who seek lifelong commitment (*naiṣṭhika*), because they lead respectively to worldly enjoyment and liberation. (59)
One who accepts [disciples] for the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment and liberation is desired as a Guru;
such a Guru, who always bestows grace upon all, is declared to be a *sāntānika* (one belonging to a lineage). 60.
It may follow the direct order, but the reverse order is not desired;
he should be joined with a woman, and equipped with matted hair, rudrākṣa beads, and a staff.
He who is free from the loincloth and the girdle is declared to be a householder; he may be shaven-headed or possessed of matted locks and the like.
One who observes the vow should likewise be separated from his wife and subsist on alms;
he who is capable of the vow and offers the vow according to the prescribed rite is truly a practitioner of the vow.
After he has performed his marriage, one who bestows vows is desired here;
those such as Kauśika and others who were initiated during the period following the creation of the world [are also intended]. (64)
By means of Śiva, the twice-born belonging to that lineage become Śaivas who perform rites for peace;
they are to be known as the Ādiśaivas (Original Śaivas), whose desire is to bestow grace upon all.
Among them, some are considered to be devoted to the conduct and vows of the [four] castes, while others are regarded as being devoid of those;
one should sleep on the ground during the three fortnights, eating only at night and always subsisting on sacrificial porridge (caru).
The Guru, observing silence, bathing at the three periods of the day, and worshipping Śiva, the Fire, and the Preceptor,
should practice the worship of Śiva along with His form and His limbs according to his capacity.
This vow of the teacher is the highest of all vows.
The teacher is one [type], while the practitioner (sādhaka), the spiritual son (putraka), and the initiate (samayin) are others.
One should worship the primary linga daily; no other is prescribed for occasional rites (naimittika).
That which is to be performed every day is proclaimed here as "daily" (nitya). (69)

The bathing festival, rites for peace, and so forth, are considered occasional (naimittika) rituals. One has the qualification for these [occasional rites] when they arise from one's own regular (nitya) duties or from an expiation (prāyaścitta). (70)
A son who is fit for his own purpose and for occasional rites, but not for others— if those two are indeed for the sake of progeny, then he is also fit for occasional rites.

Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, in all rites such as the installation (sthāpanā) and so forth, which are performed by an authorized preceptor (ācārya) and are devoid of [the need for] formal installation and the like; || 72 ||
Therefore, at the beginning of the fire-offering (homa) and other rites, those two [disciples] become fit by the command of the preceptor for the subsidiary parts such as the installation,
as well as for auspicious acts like the sowing of sprouts and so forth.
The authority over these two resides with the preceptor;
it shall belong to the ascetic who is fit for everything, provided he be a member of the lineage. (74)
And the practitioner who has become such is praised for all rites;
those who are Mahāśaivas and others, being worthy and initiated, are fit for the daily ritual.
If that which was performed by them as an occasional rite (naimittika) is deemed a fault, [the remedy is this]:
the best of gurus, a master of a hundred thousand chapters, is the bestower of the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One who knows half of that would be middling, and one who knows a quarter of it would be inferior;
or else, one who has mastered the Saṃhitā through instruction, having studied a hundred thousand verses, [is excellent].
The Saṃhitā shall consist of four quarters and begin with the Kāmika;
Śaiva is declared to be of four kinds: namely, Śaiva and likewise Pāśupata. (78)
The Soma-siddhānta and the Lākula are fourfold;
they originated from the four faces of Maheśa, arising from the mouths beginning with Puruṣa.
Previously, that which is preeminent due to its prior qualities was described; therein, it is fourfold, and each of those is said to be threefold according to the division of left and right. (80)
Among those, the Siddhānta is said to be the most excellent;
even within that, the Śaiva Siddhānta is indeed the highest of all. (81)
The Siddhānta consists of Mantra-tantra; the Atimārga is inferior to that;
the Adhyātma is lower than that, and the Vaidika is even lower than that. (82)
The worldly is inferior to the Vedic; Brahmā and the other five deities are the speakers of the worldly and so forth. Their distinctions are stated here. (83)
Emerging from the Sadyomantra, he was named Brahmā, the seer of all things;
by him indeed was the worldly scripture brought down into the mortal world.
Grammar, poetics, etymology, and prosody; the Arthaśāstra of Kauṭilya, the Mahābhārata, the science of astrology, and the works of Vātsyāyana and others. || 85 ||
The science of longevity, the science of archery, and indeed the Ayurveda of trees; likewise Lokāyata, Sāṃkhya, and the doctrine of the Arhatas. (86)
Mīmāṃsā, Daṇḍanīti, and Vārtā are considered worldly;
Viṣṇu, born from the Vāma-mantra, is the second Lord of Causes.
By him, the eighteen Purāṇas were indicated, as well as the Dharmaśāstra, Vedānta, Pāñcarātra, and Bauddha. || 88 ||
Rudra emerged from Aghora and established his own inner self (svādhyātma), as well as the systems of Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, and Sāṃkhya with its Lord (seśvara), which he composed. (89)
Īśvara, born from Puruṣa, established the Atimārga,
which consists of the Pañcārtha, the Lākula, and likewise the Pāśupata doctrine.
The Lord Sadāśiva indeed protected the Mantras and Tantras, as well as the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharva Vedas, and the Puruṣa-sūktas and others born from them. || 91 ||
The western one is known as Vāma; to the right of Vāma is Uttama;
to the right of Dakṣiṇa is the excellent Kaulaka, and beyond that is Mahākaula.
The Pūrvāmnāya is superior to that, and therefore the Siddhānta is the highest;
there is no knowledge higher than the Siddhānta—this is the certainty of the scripture. (93)
Those who are liberated in other tantras are considered bound souls (paśus) in the Siddhānta;
the Siddhānta is the essence of the Veda, while anything else is excluded from the Veda.
The conduct prescribed by the Siddhānta is called Vedic conduct;
it consists of the rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and ending with the funeral offerings (śrāddha). 95.
In the meantime, one should perform either Vedic or Śaiva rites;
for him also, initiation and the rites such as the birth ceremony (jātakarman) must be performed.
If a woman is joined with the vow (samaya) and a man with initiation (dīkṣā),
then that very conception in her womb is indeed endured by him who is joined with initiation.
Likewise, the Śaiva rites beginning with the *puṃsavana* are considered essential;
and for his son as well, the rites beginning with the *jātakarman* must be performed. (98)
Ritual actions must also be performed by him for the sake of accomplishing the goals of human life;
they should be performed either at the beginning of Vedic rites and the like, or at their conclusion, according to worldly convention.
If the wife is devoid of initiation, then for her and for their son—both of them—the Vedic rites must be performed, even if the husband is initiated. 100.
Vedic rites are not desired for those of low caste or born of inverse unions;
however, having abandoned [the need for] a gold coin and an astrologer, Vedic rites may still be performed. 101.

That which is conjoined with Śaiva ritual action is "Śaiva," while that which is purely Śaiva is independent; furthermore, there is that which constitutes the practice established by the Vedas, the Smṛtis, and so forth. (102)

Whether it be for the obligatory rite, purification, bathing, or even sipping water; or likewise for the worship of the twilight devotions, the libation, or the performance of the fire-sacrifice (homa). || 103 ||

Whether it be at the rites of conception and so forth, or at cremation, or at the performance of śrāddha, or even at the performance of the aṣṭakā, or at both the obligatory and occasional rites; || 104 ||
Whether it be the refinement through Vedic study, or the Soma sacrifice and so forth, or whatever else is prescribed for the twice-born at the commencement of Vedic study and the like; || 105 ||
All that ritual action must be performed, but not necessarily that which pertains to Śiva;
for even this undesirable [action] must be done if it does not conflict with the rites of Śiva.
If something is contradictory, it should be abandoned; however, one must not abandon that which pertains to Śiva.
Everything Vedic should be accepted provided it does not contradict the words of Śiva. (107)
It is said that Śaiva is indeed Vaidika, or Vaidika is indeed Śaiva;
for Śaiva is not outside of Vaidika, nor is Vaidika outside of Śaiva.
Nevertheless, the Śaiva [tradition] is superior to the Vedic; there is nothing higher than the Śaiva.
Among the Siddhāntas, that which begins with the Kāmika is supreme; there is nothing more excellent than this. (109)
Śaivism shall be the fundamental source, from which the four Vedas have emerged; even so, it is because of such statements as "the Vedic [tradition] is the essence of the Vedas. (110)

And it is stated everywhere in the Śaiva [scriptures], O lords of sages, that by explaining its meaning, the nature of being the body of Śiva is maintained for all the [Tantras] beginning with the Kāmika. (111)
That Śiva is said to be twofold, intended as both creation and withdrawal.
From the *Kāmika* up to the *Vātula*, and from the *Vātula* back to the end of the *Kāmika*. (112)
The crown above is Kāmika; that born of Yoga is called Puruṣa. The Aghora crown should be meditated upon, and Vāma would be the causal [crown]. || 113 ||
The Ajita [form] has a crown of skulls, a blazing face of Īśāna, a subtle face of Puruṣa, and a thousand faces to the south. || 114 ||
Aṃśumān is the left face, Sadyojāta is the excellent mouth, Vijaya is said to be the ear, and Niśvāsa is called the throat. (115)
The Svāyaṃbhuva heart is here, and the navel should be Anala;
Vīra is the region of the hips, and Raurava is said to be the anus.
The crown should be the region of the thighs, and Vimala would be the left side; Candrajñāna should be its tip, while the other discus (Bimba) is situated on the right.
Prodgīta occurs when the right knee is extended; Lalita occurs with the left foot. Siddha is said to be the position of the shank, while Saṃtāna occurs when it moves to the left. || 118 ||
The tip of the shank is as declared by Śarva; Vāmaka is Pārameśvara;
Kiraṇa is said to be Tala; and Vātula is Vāmaka-tala.
Śiva is said to be the emanation, while the reverse is withdrawal.
The sages said:
"In the initial descent of the Tantra, however, the pair of feet [of the scripture] was the Kāmika. (120)
"O God, such things as these have been spoken regarding mutual opposition. The Lord said:
"O Brahmins, you have attentively heard what has been told by you in many ways. (121)
My crown is everywhere, as are my eyes and likewise my other limbs;
at that time, so too are my feet and hands—yet how can one meditate upon them as distinct? (122)

O my elder brothers, my body, which is the embodiment of knowledge, is being divided by me through the path of creation and dissolution for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 123.
Cognition would be formless, yet from the worship of that [form], there is confusion;
thus it is contradicted by those of dull intellect who hold these views to be mutually contradictory. (124)
Whatever statement possesses authority is considered worthy of worship by the most excellent;
neither a human statement nor a divine one is [so regarded] by the sages. (125)
The word of a Vaiṣṇava Brāhmaṇa is never contradicted by the gods or by Brahmā;
nor is the word of a Śaiva ever contradicted by Viṣṇu.
The progressive superiority of all [the tantras] has been proclaimed;
those beginning with the Kāmika and ending with the Ajita have emerged from the mouths of Īśa.
Those beginning with Dīpta and ending with Suprabheda do not arise from the Puruṣa-narration;
these five, ending with Vijaya and Vīratantra, belong to the face of Aghora.
From the face of Vāmadeva arose [the systems] beginning with Raurava and ending with Mukhabimba;
and the eight Tantras beginning with Prodgīta originated from the face of Sadyojāta.
In the *Tantrāvatāra*, Īśa and the others are considered to be denoted by the words Sadyojāta and so forth;
he who knows the twenty-eight tantras along with their sub-divisions [is a true knower]. (130)

That guru should be Śiva himself; one should listen to him with great effort. If [the rite] has been commenced by another guru, his (the disciple's) eligibility for it [under that other guru] would cease. || 131 ||
When a rite has been commenced by a superior [teacher], one who is inferior lacks the qualification;
when commenced by an inferior, it is said that even a superior lacks qualification for the ritual action. (132)
In the event of a distinguished death or similar occasion, there may be the appointment of another guru;
yet, if a qualified one is already present, it is done by an ignorant person through sheer force. (133)
There will be great distress, a multitude of calamities, and blindness and deafness;
because of that, there will be fault for the king and fear for the kingdom as well. (134)
It brings fault upon the one who performs it, the one who causes it to be performed, and even the village;
yet, even a tiny gift given to a teacher renowned for his learning in the world [is meritorious]. (135)
It makes the substance auspicious and brings forth fame equal to that of all the world;
therefore, that gift of the king should be known as the most excellent of the excellent.
He by whom that wealth was seized is a sinner and is evil-minded;
he should be known as the lowest of men, excluded from all the worlds. || 137 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, the procedure for the initiation of the preceptor, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika;
[followed by] the procedure for the initiation of knowledge.
I shall now proclaim the initiation of knowledge; listen, O best of the twice-born!
It should be performed on an auspicious day, in a favorable fortnight, and especially at a propitious moment.
In a secluded and solitary place at the commencement of midnight,
a true teacher should especially bestow awakening upon his worthy disciples.

Seated comfortably in a pure place— whether in a temple of Śiva, the abode of a Guru, a sacred seat of Śakti (śaktipīṭha), a monastery, or a house— one who has renounced the five objects of the senses [should practice].
Seated upon a seat of darbha grass, a tiger skin, or a six-legged stool in the center of the altar—
the pleasant abode of the true gurus— he should dwell there while recollecting the supreme knowledge.
Having worshipped [the deity] in the center of the yoga-pīṭha with services such as bathing, as well as silk garments, ornaments, perfumes, flowers, and so forth, || 5 ||
One should offer milk-rice, cakes, and betel-leaf,
and worship the feet of the Guru with the sixteenfold service (ṣoḍaśopacāra).
The most excellent and true teacher should especially perform the initiation of knowledge (jñānadīkṣā);
he should offer his body, wealth, and vital breath to the true gurus.
One who is shameless should prostrate with a long staff in the presence of the guru;
however, toward a virtuous disciple, the teacher should especially bestow awakening.
Having stood with the fragrant lotus upon the head of the disciple,
the compassionate teacher should place the worshipped foot in the middle of the disciple's head.
Thereafter, one should awaken the disciple to the true existence of knowledge:
first, the nature of reality (tattva), and second, the vision of reality (tattvadarśana).
The third is the purification of reality, the fourth is the characteristic of the self,
the fifth is the manifestation of the self, and the sixth is the cleansing of the self.
The seventh is called Śivarūpa, the eighth is Śivadarśana,
the ninth is Śivayoga, and the tenth is Śivabhogaka.
Through the fourfold [categories] each divided into three, the triad of the Lord (pati), the bond (pāśa), and the bound soul (paśu) is revealed;
by the mere word of the Guru, this reveals the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
For this purpose, the group of ten is prescribed for him by way of the path of knowledge. || 131/2 ||
In the twenty-fifth chapter, the procedure for determining the *gotras*:
I shall declare the determination of the *gotras* even for all the sages (*ṛṣis*).
There are thousands, tens of thousands, and hundreds of millions of *gotras*.
The number of these great ones here shall be forty-nine:
Kauśika, Kāśyapa, Bhāradvāja, and Gautama; || 2 ||
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Agastya, Jāmadagnya Bhārgava, Aṅgiras, and another, Manu—these are proclaimed as the two kinds [of sages]. (3)
The sages who are endowed with Śiva’s creation, yet devoid of that [other], and those who are joined with Śiva’s creation, are initiated into the five faces. || 4 ||
The sages beginning with Kauśika were all initiated everywhere;
yet for them there was no lineage resulting from initiation, but rather their own [original] caste.
For Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, however, the lineage (gotra) is derived from the teacher; for a Śūdra, there is no lineage at all. Such is the established view regarding the rules for lineage.
Just as it is considered in the Ādiśaiva, so it is regarded in the Anuśaiva;
however, it is devoid of initiation and excluded from the creation of Śiva.
O twice-born ones, in the Kali age, the wise must avoid a marriage based on birth; alternatively, both [birth and conduct] must be observed, or else such a marriage is not desired.
O best of the twice-born, the principal sages are first mentioned:
the Kauśikas, the Lihitas, the Raudras, the Viśvāmitras, and likewise the Katas.
Then the Dhanañjayas, the Vājas, and the Aśvas are proclaimed;
as well as the Aghamarṣaṇas, the Kauśikas, and those preceded by Indra.
From them proceeded the Pauraṇas, Kāśyapas, Rephas, and Śāṇḍilyas;
then the Lokākṣayas, Bharadvājas, and the Raukṣāyaṇas are considered to have followed. || 11 ||
The Bhārgavas, the Śaradvantas, and the Kaumaṇḍas are considered to follow from that;
from them, the Dīrghatamasas are to be known, and from them, the Kāreṇapālayas.
Uśanas, Vāmadeva, Atri, the Vārddhakya, and the Gaviṣṭhira; the Mudgala, the Vasiṣṭha, the Kuṇḍina, and the Upamanyu [lineages]. || 13 ||
Then there were Parāśara, Agastya, those known as Sāmbavāhana, and those known as Somavāhana; after them, the Yajñavāhas are considered to have followed.
The Vatsas, Bidās, Ārṣṭiṣeṇas, Yaskas, and likewise the Mitrayus;
the Vainyas, Śunakas, Viṣṇuvṛddhas, and after them the Kaṇvas. (15)
The Hāritas, the Saṃkṛtis, and later the Rathītaras are considered;
those born of Mudgala are declared to be exactly forty-nine.
I shall first describe the Kauśikas: the Kuśikas, the Pārṇajaṅghakas, the Pārakyas, the Audalis, the Māṇis, the Ālaviras, and the Bṛhadagnagas. || 17 ||
Likewise, the *ghaṭṭi*, the *tathāpatti*, and then the *āpādyavat* are considered;
as well as the *kāntaka*, the *bāṣpaka*, the *vācyukita*, the *lomaka*, and the *dhana*. (18)
The Sāṅkāyanas, the Gauras, the Lokās, the Saugatayas, the Yamadūtas, the Ānabhiññas, and then the Tārāyaṇas are considered [the branches]. || 19 ||
Caulakāyana and Jābāli are considered [the teachers] of Udumbara; Daṇḍa, Bhuvana, Yājñavalkya, and Sauśrutaya likewise [belong to that lineage]. || 20 ||
The Śyātāmaya, Bhrāṣṭaṣaṭka, Deha, Niściti, Asaṃjñaka, Śālāvata, Mayūra, and likewise Udutsarit—these are the [names]. 21.
The Citrayajñas, the Saumatis, and those known as the Śvetundāyanas; then the Manuvatas and the Māntavas are likewise proclaimed. (22)
Those who have reached the ultimate limit of the quarters are therefore called Bālavas;
they are also known as Rālavas, Unmanas, and Kauśikas. (23)
Five ancestral lineages have been specified, and likewise Viśvāmitra;
in the *pravara*, there are three sages: Devarāta and Dadhīci. (24)
The Daṇḍakas, Cakravarmāyaṇas,
Jakṣayas, Prājñakas, and Vājijayas are recorded as being Lohitas.
The Kuśikas, these [others], and the Tryārṣeyakas are in the lineage;
Viśvāmitra, Sṭaiṣakaya, and the Lohitas—these three are they.
The Pravaryas are declared to be the sages; from them, the Raukṣas are considered to have arisen.
These Māṇas and Udvahalas are regarded as the Kuśikas. || 27 ||
In the Pravara, there should be three ancestral sages (triyārṣeya): Viśvāmitra, Raukṣaka, and Māṇi; these three are sages, the best among munis.
From him came Viśvāmitra, then Devaśravas, Paribhrama, Śraumita,
Devatarasa, and Kāmakāyanika.
The Kāmakāyanas—these are proclaimed as the Viśvāmitras;
they are designated as having three ancestral seers (ṛṣis), with Viśvāmitra being the first among them. || 30 ||
The Devaśrāvasas, ending with the Devatarasas—these are the Kaṭhas; along with them are those known as the Svairandhris, the Cakarabhas, and others.
From Vājāyana came the Kaukṛtyas, and from them the Jāṇāyanas are considered to have descended;
from the Kaukṛtyas came the Śaiśiras, and from them Udumbarāyaṇa.
Then there are the Piṇḍigrīvas, the Nārāyaṇas, and those known as the Nāradyas;
these are declared to be the Kaṭhas, who are proclaimed to have three ancestors (tri-ārṣeya). || 33 ||
The Viśvāmitrakas, Kaṭhas, Aṣṭilas, and other accumulators of wealth; the Āśvavītas, Kāriṣayas, Mayūras, and Saindhavāyanas. || 34 ||
The Talavyas, the Mahākṣas, and those who are the Puṣṭas are the Dhanañjayas;
they are declared to have three ancestral seers (triyārṣeya) in their lineage (pravara), O lords of sages.
Viśvāmitra, Madhucchandas, and Dhanañjaya—these three are [the first]; then Ājāyana is proclaimed, and Ekavatsa is likewise esteemed. (36)
Those of three ancestral seers (triyārṣeya) have been specified; likewise Viśvāmitra, Madhu, and Saja—these are the three seers of the Pravargya rite.
Then the Aghamarṣaṇas and the Kauśikas are considered;
these belong to three gotras: Viśvāmitra, Aghamarṣaṇa, and [Kauśika]. || 38 ||
These three eminent sages are the Kauśikas who are to be initiated into the Pravargya rite;
thereafter, the lords of sages are said to be the Kauśikas preceded by Indra (the Vasiṣṭhas). || 39 ||
Those belonging to the lineages of Viśvāmitra, Indra, and Kauśika are to be known as having three *ṛṣis*;
these three sages are declared to be the *pravara* in the sacrificial rite. (40)
The Pauraṇas and others shall have two ancestral seers (dvyārṣeya); they are considered Kauśikas. Their two recognized seers are Viśvāmitra and Pauraṇa. || 41 ||
Likewise, all ten Kauśikas do not follow the lineage;
now I shall speak of the Kāśyapas, for you, O Kāśyapa, are their first.
From him are to be known the Aṅgirasas, the Māṭharas, the Ātiśāyanas, the Ābhūtyas, the Vaiśipras, the Dhūmas, and the Dhūmrāyaṇas. (43)
The Dhaumadhaumrāyaṇas are considered to be the Audhapracurāgrāyaṇas;
their pravaras are Rudra and Agni, and others are the Paimbakayas.
The Kāyatāyas, Akāpāyas, Nikāmauṣanikas, as well as the Kādrāyaṇas, Oujvalayas, and those known as the Rohitāyanas; || 45 ||
Piṅgākṣi, Mitakumbha, and Mārāyaṇaya,
as well as the Vaikarṇeyas and the gods known as Dhūmalakṣmaṇayas, were then proclaimed.
The Kauṣītakeyas, Vātsyas, Agniśarmāyaṇas, Kāmijaṅghodaras, Gaurīvāyanas, and Daukṣakāyanas are considered [to belong to this group]. || 47 ||
The Vaitambas, the Devayātās, those known as the Mahācakreya, the Paiṭhinasas, the Bāndhrepras, and then those named the Mālandas. || 48 ||
The Vṛṣagaṇas, the Pānadhya, the Dākṣapāyana, the Harita, the Gākhamitraya, the Pañcāvā, and the Svairika; || 49 ||
Jāramaṇḍa, Vāyu, Svantivarṣa, Gaṇāyana, and the one known as Vaiśampāyanākṣa—these are remembered as the Keśāyatas. || 50 ||
From them came the Aukāyanis, then the Mārjāyanas, and further on the Kāṃsāyanas;
also Deva, Hotasūcī, Āsthūṇa, and likewise the Bhāguras.
Then there were the Pāthikāryas, the Kharebhas, and after them the Gomayātās; then the Hiraṇyapāpas, the Musalas, and after them the Āviśreṇyas.
Agnideva, Saumya, and Śūlabhinda—these are counted from the north;
beyond them is Mantravaikarṇaya.
These Naidhruvas of the Kāśyapa lineage are proclaimed to have three *ṛṣi* ancestors:
