Kāśyapa, Āpavatsāra, and Nidhruva—these are the three sages.
Likewise, those with three *ṛṣis* and who possess the letter *r* are remembered as the Kāśyapas;
Kāśyapa, Capavatsāra, and Rephakṣa are the three sages [of this lineage]. (55)
The Śāṇḍilyas, the Kaulahas, the Pāyakas, and then the Pāyikas; Rabhi, Avyaya, Somānu, and Vanasa joined with Kareyu. (56)
Kākuṇḍeya, Kāreya, and then the two considered as Ṣṭaiṣikayas;
Mahākāya, Jāṇavaṃśa, Kauśreya, and Kārdamāyana. || 57 ||
Then there are the Kāmaśayas, followed by the Mahaujakyas;
then the Mauñjāyanas are mentioned, and after them the Gāṅgāyanas are considered.
Those called Vātsabhālayas are then known as Gomilas; from them the Vedāyanas are to be known, and from them the Vāśyāyanas are considered to have arisen. || 59 ||
Those with many bellies are thus described; Bhāguri, Vārdatī, Mukha, Hiraṇyabāhu, Tedeha, and Gomūtra are considered to follow thereafter. (60)
Likewise, Vākyaśuṇṭha, Jānan, Dharin, and Dhanvantari; these are declared as the Jālandharis. The Śāṇḍilas, however, have three ancestors (tri-ārṣeya). || 61 ||
Kāśyapa, Apavatsāra, and Śaṇḍila—these are the three;
or alternatively, Kāśyapa, Kṣāpavatsāra, and Asita—these are the three.
Śaṇḍila, Asita, Agni, Devala-pravara,
Kokākṣaya, Maitravādi, Veho, and Dārbhāyaṇa followed thereafter.
The Cairaṅghris, the Paśus, those known as the Payaṇāyanas, the Kalayas, the Kāpuṣṭis, and the Laugākṣayas are thus remembered. || 64 ||
The Kāṃsapatras have been mentioned, as well as the Vālukāyanis; the Kaunāmīs and Sautayas have also been named, and there are the Parastāvirodakīs. (65)
Saitakiṃṣṭi, bheroniṣṭi, ṣṭaiṣiki, sausuki, and then yauthakālakikāleya, as well as lokākṣaya. || 66 ||
These Yaudhavas and Yājapas are known as the Logākṣayas;
the Vasisthas are for the day, while the Kāśyapas are for the night—these are the three-lineages (tri-ārṣeyas).
Kāśyapa, Āpavatsāra, and Vasiṣṭha are the three sages;
they are esteemed by the previously mentioned perfected ones (siddhas) of the Kāśyapa and Vasiṣṭha lineages.
Then there are Bharadvāja, Māgaṇḍa, and those considered the Kṣāmyāyaṇas;
then the Devāśvas, the Udvahavyas, and thereafter the Prāgvāśayas are considered.
Then there are the Vāhalavas, the Dvayaugas, others known as the Vāsināyanas, the Ājās, the Aumās, the Taudehas, and those designated as the Pariṇaddhedhas.
The Śaikheyas, the numerous Rūḍhas, the Śauddhyas, the Khārigrīvas, the Vayokṣibhedas, the Aupaśayas, the Agniveśyas, and the Śaṭhas as well. (71)
The Śvelakas, Tanakarṇas, and Gaurivāyanas shall be courtesans; as well as the Ṛkṣas, the Māṇabhidyas, and those known as the Kāmbojas. (72)
The Pailas, the Saujjvalayas, the Kārūṇas and others known as Śugas, the Bhāruṇḍeyas, the Iṣumatas, and likewise the Vaudodameghayas; || 73 ||
The Saurabhas, the Bhādrapathas, and the Devamatis are proclaimed; then there are the Kalmāṣas and the Sadopakṛts.
The *pravāhaṇeya*s are to be known; from them, the *stambha* and *stambhin* are considered to arise.
Also, the *vārāhya*s, the *devavelā*, and the *valabhīgaya*. (75)
Those known as Bhadrāṅgagata, Śālāhalaya, Nṛtyāyana, and Mahāvelā are considered to be the Śālālayas. (76)
From them, the Śārdūlas are to be known, as well as the Kākṣalas and the Bāṣkalas;
then the Krodhāyanas, the Kauṭilyas, and after that the Saiṃhyakendras. (77)
Likewise, O King, the pillars of Brahmā and the pillars of the [other] kings are proclaimed to be the axle;
they are preceded by Soma, Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, Indra, Yama, Viṣṇu, and Āpa. || 78 ||
Then there are other pillars, ending with Stambha; these are desired as Aruṇa and Sindhu.
Then there would be Kaumudagandhi, Śakti, and Kautukāyana. (79)
And the Ātreyas, the Māmaṇḍas, the Dhūmagandhas, as well as the Dhūmras, the Kaukṣeyakas, the Nitutayas, and also the Dābhyas. (80)
Then there were the Matsyakrodhas, the Śyāmeyas, those named Kṣokṣeyas,
the Kāblyas, the Kārupathayas, and those known as the Kāriṣāyaṇas.
In the forest of Bharadvāja, however, there are two sages who are highly esteemed;
all these Bhāradvājas are proclaimed to have three ancestral seers (triyārṣeya). || 82 ||
They are remembered as the Aṅgirasas, the Bārhaspatyas, and the Bhāradvājas;
Raukṣāyaṇa alone is proclaimed to have five ancestral seers (pañcārṣeya). || 83 ||
Bharadvāja is to be known as Aṅgiras and Bṛhaspati; Māta-vacas shall be Vandana, and then the Gargas are proclaimed.
Those known as Sāṃbharāyaṇas, as well as the Yaugandharāyaṇas, the Bāhulakas among friends, the Bhraṣṭayas, and the Bhraṣṭubindavas; || 85 ||
Then there are the Kroṣṭakas, the Sauyāmunis, the Kāṇāyanas, and the Munis;
they are called Bhājitākṣayas and are also known as Gotrāpacayas.
Those known as Satyāpacayas are designated as Jāṇapakvalas;
those possessing Palāśa branches are designated as Markaṭāyanas. || 87 ||
Then there were the Saṃgrahatulyas, the Vaidhūhyas, the Kārirotayas, the Tristrotas, the Kāravalyas, the Rājyas, and the Pailayas. || 88 ||
The Gargas are said to consist of thirty-five Munis; likewise the Bhāradvājas, the Āṅgirasas, the Bharadvājas, the Bārhaspatyas, and the Śainyakas. || 89 ||
Garga, Pravarya, Aṅgiras, Śainya, and Gargaka—these three sages are declared to be the Pravaryas in the Tripakṣaka [lineage]. (90)
The three Bhāradvājas as well do not follow the path of synthesis (samanvaya). Now I shall speak of the Gautamas; after them are the Āyāsyas and the Tauḍinis.
The Āṇīcayas, the Mūḍhas, and the Bādhyas are considered to be from Kācākṣa;
likewise, the Sātyakāyas, the Taidehas, the Kaumārās, and the Sātyamugrikas [are from him].
Vyāpyāpi, Nānāriṣṭi, Ṣṭaiṣaki, Devaki, Kaṭhori, Kāruṇi, and Kīlālaya—these are known as the Pārthivas. || 93 ||
These Kāśivājas are to be known as belonging to the Āyāsya Gautamas;
O best of sages, their lineage (pravara) consists of three ṛṣis.
The Pravaryas are known as the sages of Āṅgiras, the Gautamas of Asya, the Śaradvantas of Rohiṇī, and those of Abhijit are likewise considered [to belong to these lineages]. || 95 ||
Then there are the Kṣīrakambhas, and then the Saumucayas are considered [to follow];
likewise the Sauryāmunis, the Aupabindavas, and the Rāyaṇas are considered [to follow]. || 96 ||
The Rāhūgaṇas, the Māṣaṇyas, and these Śaradvantas are considered [to belong here];
they are to be known as Gautamas and are traditionally remembered as having three ancestors (triyārṣeya). || 97 ||
Aṅgiras, Gautama, and Śaradvant—these three;
then Kaumāṇḍa, Māsurākṣa, and thereafter Māmānyareṣaṇa. || 98 ||
The Payantyas, the Yanas, and then the Kāṣṭeyas; from them came the Paśus.
These are to be known as the Ūrjāyanas and the Gautamas, O best of the twice-born. (99)
The five *ṛṣis* are considered to be Aṅgiras, Ucathya, Kākṣīvata, Kaumāṇḍa, and Gautama; from them, Dīrghatamas is reckoned as the fifth. || 100 ||
They are to be known as having five ancestral seers (pañcārṣeya), yet they are also agreed upon as having only one; namely, the Āṅgirasas, the Aucathyas, the Kākṣīvatas, and the Gautamas. 101.
Then Dīrghatamas—these five lineages are recognized; likewise Kāreṇupālaya, Vāstavya, and Udīvasta. (102)
The Bṛhadukthas, the Pauñjiṣṭhas, those known as Rājagandhis, and those designated as Auduñcāyanas—these are the Kāreṇupālas. || 103 ||
O Gautamas, you have three *ṛṣi* ancestors: Aṅgiras, Gautama, and then Kāreṇupāli;
these three belong to the lineage of Uśanas. || 104 ||
The Sahas, Diṣṭas, those called Praśastas, Surūpākṣas, Mahodaras, Vikaṃhatas, Subuddhis, and the Nihataguhas [were also destroyed]. || 105 ||
These Gautamas, possessing three ancestral seers (triyārṣeya), were declared by Uśanas;
Aṅgiras, Gautama, and Auśanasa are recorded as their sages. || 106 ||
The Saha-diṣṭas, the Praśastas, the Surūpākṣas, and the Mahaujasas,
as well as the Vāmadevas— these are the Gautamas who have three *ṛṣis* as their ancestors (*triyārṣeya*).
Aṅgiras, Gautama, and Vāmadeva—these three are [the first];
now I shall speak of the Atris, among whom three are considered to be at the beginning. (108)
The Bhojas, those known as Ādityas, the Cāndras, the Īśīs, and the Pārvas;
the Kāmāṅgulis, the Śaivas, the Chagālas, and likewise the Chāgalas. (109)
And thereafter, Tṛṇabindu and likewise Bhāgantaya are considered [the kings];
then Mālaruka is proclaimed, and thereafter Vyākalaya is considered [the king]. (110)
The Śāmbavyasanas and the Kārmaryāyanas are considered [the branches];
from them arose the Dākṣis, the Taidehas, and also the Gāṇispatayas. (111)
Auddālaki, Droṇa, Bhava, Gaurīgrīva, and Āyata; from him Gaviṣṭira is said to have arisen, and from him Śiśupāla is considered to have descended. (112)
Then there are Gaurātreyas and Kṛṣṇātreyas, headed by Āruṇa;
and the fourfold Ātreyas, headed by Śveta, Nīla, and Mahāśyāma. (113)
The Hāleyas, Vāleyas, and Hneleyas are considered [the first];
then the Vāmarathinas and Vaidehas; and the Vājas are considered superior to them. || 114 ||
From them came the Kaudreyas and the Kaupamānas; from them were remembered the Kālatapas; then those known as the Anīlāyayanas, and from them the Aṅgirasas are considered to have arisen. || 115 ||
Gauraṅgi, Sauraṅgi, Mānaṅgi, and Puṣpayas are considered [the lineages]; Śaileya and Sāketāyana are proclaimed [as others]. (116)
The Bhāradvājāyanas, Indrātithi, and Atri are considered the three ancestral seers (triyārṣeya); the Pālikas and the Atreis are likewise declared [to have these same three]. (117)
These three sages are declared as Arcanānas;
likewise, they are to be known as Vāgbhūtakas, or in that regard, they are considered to have three ancestral seers (triyārṣeya). || 118 ||
Atri, Arcanānas, and Vāgbhūtaka are the three sages; from them, Gaviṣṭhira is to be known as the fourth. Thus, the Atris are those who have three ancestral seers (tri-ārṣeya). || 119 ||
Atri, Arcanānasa, and Gaviṣṭhira—these three;
then Mudgala, Vyālasandhi, Cūrṇavā, Bodhavājaki, and [the last]. || 120 ||
Vaita and Bhāvaya—these are considered the sages from that [lineage].
Then came Śālimat, Gaurīmat, and then Brāhmīmat. (121)
Then the Gaurakayas, the Vāyupūrakas, and the Sāyanas;
these are proclaimed as the Mudgalas who have three ancestral seers (triyārṣeya). || 122 ||
The three views held by Arcānānasa, Pūrvādi, and Tithi—
though fourfold in total according to Ātreya— are not in accord with the principle of systematic integration (samanvaya).
Now I shall describe the Vasiṣṭhas; among them, Vaikali is considered the first, followed by Vāṭharaki, and also Gaurīśravas.
Those known as Āśvalāyana are the Gaviṣṭhas; from them come the Āśvalāyanas, then the Śaucivṛkṣas, and from them the Vyāghrapādas. || 125 ||
Auḍulomi, Jatūkarṇa, Vāṣṭavya, Vāhyakāyani, Kolāyana, Ko, Bhoji—after him, the Paulāyanas are considered [to follow]. || 126 ||
Sunda, Harita, Kāṇḍeya, and Vidhi—these seven are renowned as the Vasiṣṭhas, the best among the twice-born. || 127 ||
These [descendants] shall have only one ancestral seer (ṛṣi); that single one is Vasiṣṭha himself.
The Pravara has been prescribed for them, and from him they are considered to be the Kuṇḍinas. 128.
Then the Guggulayas are mentioned; after them, the Lohāyanas are considered [to follow]. Āviśva, Aśvattha, Vaikarṇi, Rājīva, and Khadira are recorded [as the next]. || 129 ||
The Peṭhakas, the nine villages, as well as the Āśmarathyavāhas, the Somaraṅgalinas, the Kokas, and then the Kāpaṭavas are considered [to be there]. || 130 ||
Also Hiraṇyākṣāyaṇa, Pulābhakṣa, Mādhyāndini, Śānti, and Saupadārtha Kauṇḍina. || 131 ||
Those belonging to three *ṛṣis* have been designated; Vasiṣṭha is thus praised.
These three—Vasiṣṭha, Mitra-Varuṇa, and Kuṇḍina—are [the lineage]. 132.
Upamanyu, Aupagava, and Maṇḍalekhya; Jālāgata, Jaya, and Lokas—these are then declared to be the Kapiñjalas. (133)
The Traivarṇa, Vaivaśāgāri, Sārakṣa, and those known as Rakṣas; the Śailālaya, Mahākarṇa, Anaya, and Bālaśikha are considered [the remaining types]. || 134 ||
From them were considered the divisions of the Auddāhamānayas;
from them arose the Unmāyanas, the Saṃjñas, and the Kuṇḍodarāyaṇas. || 135 ||
Then there are the Lakṣmaṇeyas, the Kācas, the Vayalākulas, the Anṛkṣaras, the Vasasaṃjñas, the Kāpilas, and the Vayas. (136)
These should be known as the Kapikeśas, who are the descendants of Upamanyu;
they are Vasiṣṭhas with three *ṛṣis*, namely Vasiṣṭha, Abharadvasu, and [the third]. || 137 ||
Indrapramada—these three are the Parāśaras of the west; or else, another triad is proclaimed, remembered as Bharadvāja, Vasu, and [the third]. || 138 ||
Bhaimatāyana, Vājin, Gopāli, and then the fifth, Kṛṣṇa; these are declared to be the Parāśaras, and thereafter the Prārohayas are considered [the lineage]. || 139 ||
Kaumudī and Plākṣaya, then Vaikali is considered [the third];
Hāryaśvi is the fifth among them—thus the Gaura Parāśaras. (140)
The Khalvāyanas, the Gopayas, the Kārkayas, and the Śvetayovāruṇis—these are proclaimed as their fifth [group]. || 141 ||
The Parāśaras, the Aruṇas, and then those known as the Bhālukyas; likewise the Bādaris, the Gargas, the Vanas, and the Kaukasas and others. || 142 ||
Thus these five are declared as the Prāṇilās and Parāśaras;
then there are the Saudhavasānas and those known as the Ālaṃbhāyanas. (143)
The Svaryas, the Kākukṣatas, the Lomādya-s, the Pūrṇakāyanas, those known as the Colakāyanas, and likewise the Vārṇavalkas. || 144 ||
Furthermore, those known as the Devanaga are called Śraviṣṭhāyanas;
after them come the Vāśavayas, and immediately following those, the Pañcavājayas.
Those called Ādyakṣāyatas, as well as the Pūtimāṣas,
the Kaimīyatayas— these five are the Nīla-Parāśaras.
Then there are the Kṛṣṇājinas, the Kaviśubhas, and those considered to be the Śyāmāyanas;
then the Pauṣkarasādins and also the Śvetayūpayas. (147)
The Śvetas, the five Parāśaras, Vātsyāyana, the Śyāmeyas, the Pārṇayas, Sahacauli, and Saubudha; || 148 ||
These six Śyāmas and Parāśaras are declared to have three ancestral seers (tri-ārṣeya):
Vasiṣṭha, Śakti, and Parāśara—these three. || 149 ||
All these Parāśaras are mutually unrelated;
therefore, I shall speak of the Agastyas after them, for among them, the Agastyas come first. (150)
And Śālādyākhya, Kulmāṣa, Daṇḍi, and Kalāyana; likewise Aupadaha, Dhāvaṇi, and then Lāvaṇi. || 151 ||
Lāvya, Arbuda, Vairaṇaya, Budha, Adara, Bodari, Śaivarataya, and thereafter Śyāmātaya are considered [the teachers]. || 152 ||
Then there are the Mauñjikiyas, the Pāṇḍūrudhiras, the Mausalyas, as well as the Gaurīdīpas and the Rohiṣyas; these are the Triyārṣeyas.
Dṛḍhacyuta, Agastya, and Idhmavāha—these three, known as the Sāṃbhavāhanas, are the Triyārṣeyas among the Agastis. || 154 ||
Dṛḍhacyuti, Agastya, and Sāṃbhava—these three are known as Somavāhana; they are the Agastyas who have three ancestral seers (ṛṣis). || 155 ||
Dṛḍhacyuti, Agastya, and Somavāha—these three are known as Yajñavāhana; they belong to the lineage of Tryārṣeya, with Agastya as the third seer.
Dṛḍhacyuti, Agastya, and Yajñavāha—these three are the Agastyas; these four follow after us. (157)
Now I shall speak of the Jamadagnis; among them, Vatsa is said to come first, followed by Mārkaṇḍeya, Māṇḍūka, Māṇḍavya, and then Kāṃsya.
From them, the Ālekhanas were proclaimed, as well as the Dārbhāyaṇas;
then the Śārkarākṣas, the Devatāyanas, and the Śaunakāyanas. || 159 ||
The Māṇḍūkeyas are the Pārṣikas, and they are remembered as the Sāṅkaprabhāyanas; those known as the Paiṅgalāyanas, the Pailas, and then the Dādhreṣayas.
Then there are the Bāhyakayas, the Vaiśvānaras, and the Vilohitas;
then the Bāhyāgas, the Aṣṭāyanas, the Ṣṭaiṣakas, and the Pāṇinayas.
The Vādbhūtakas, the Kāśakṛtsnas, the Ṛtabhāgas, the Śāyanas, the Vaihīnarayas, the Vālmīkis, and the Sthaulapiṇḍyas. || 162 ||
Then there are the Dadhīcayas, the Vāpāṇis, and those considered the Śaikhāvatās; then the Vākāyanas, the Saukṛtas, and the Bālāyanas are recognized. || 163 ||
Sauviṣṭayas and Māṇḍavis are considered to follow them, then the Hastāgnis;
thereafter the Śauddhakayas are to be known, as well as the Vaikarṇas and Droṇajihvas. || 164 ||
Then there were Jānāyana, Aurakṣaya, Kāmbarodara, Kaṭhorakṛt, Virūpākṣa, Devamati, and Bhairavi. || 165 ||
Also Vṛkāśvārkāyaṇa and Uccairmanyava, as well as Mārkāyaṇa, Śārṅgarava, and Vāyavāpanaya. || 166 ||
The Kāhvāyanas, the Kārabayas, and those considered [descendants] of Candra; likewise the Nopeyas, the Gāṅgeyas, the Yājñikas, and the Parimaṇḍalis. || 167 ||
The Bāhumitrāyaṇas, the Āpiśalayas, and the Rohitāyanas;
from them came the Vaiṣṭapureyas, and others are considered to be the Uṣṭrākṣas. || 168 ||
From him came the Rājitas, the Vāhas, the Śāradvatāyanas, the Nālāyanas, the Vāsas, and those known as the Vānas and the Vātyas. || 169 ||
These five Vatsas are remembered as the descendants of Ṛṣis, belonging to the lineage of Jamadagni: Bhārgava, Cyāvana, Ārṣeya, Aurva, and Āpnavāna, who are the Jamadagnyas. || 170 ||
The five sages renowned for their role in the sacrificial rites are Vidas, Śailas, Śailas, Avaṭas, and Pulastayas. (171)
The Prācīnayogas are to be known as the Vainabhūtas;
from them the Abhayajātās arose, and likewise the Kāṇḍarathayas.
Likewise, there are the Ārkāyaṇas, the Nāṣṭrāyaṇas, and from them the Kārkāyaṇas;
then the Krauñcāyanas, the Jāmālas, and the Bhujāyanas are mentioned.
These five, known as Vidas, are considered the descendants of Jamadagni;
Bhārgava, Cyavana, Aurva, Āpnuvāna, and Vida—these are the five.
The Ārṣṭiṣeṇas, the Nairathayas, and the Grāmyāyaṇas;
then the Kaṇāyanas, the Cāndrāyaṇas, and the Pauṭhikalāyanas. || 175 ||
The Gaurāmbhis, the Āmbhis, the Siddhas, the Sumanāyanas, and the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas—these five are considered the ancestral lineages (ārṣeya) of the Jamadagnyas. || 176 ||
Bhārgava, Cyāvana, Āpnuvāna, Rathītara, and Upa—these five sages are considered the foremost ancestors (pravaras) by the lineage of Ārṣṭiṣeṇa. || 177 ||
It is declared that there is no marriage between the Vatsas, the Ārṣṭiṣeṇas, and the Vidās with one another; thereafter, the Bhṛgus are described.
Then there were the Yaskas, the Maunas, the Mūkas, the Vādhūlas, and Bhāskara;
then the Varṣas, the Puṣyas, the Vāleyas, and the Rājitatāyanas.
The Durdinas, the Mādhyameyas, and others known as the Daivantāyanas; the Kauśāmbeyas, the Vākalayas, and the Vāsayas are thus proclaimed. || 180 ||
Sātyaki, Citrasena, the Kauṭilyas, then the Aukthakas; then the Bhāgantas, the Vārkāśvakas, and the Bhṛgus who subsist on nectar. || 181 ||
From them shall arise these groups of enjoyers (bhogacitayas), who are known as the Yaskas;
they are to be understood as having three ancestral seers (triyārṣeya) and are proclaimed as the Bhārgavas. || 182 ||
Bhṛgu, as well as Yaska, and Divodāsa—these three;
then the Mitrayus, the Ramyāyaṇas, and then the Dākṣāyaṇas.
From Sāpiṇḍina came Mahāvālya, Mālya, and those known as Yāvālya;
from Purābhināya they were born, and from them the Rākṣāyaṇas are said to have descended. || 184 ||
The Kaitavāyanas, Māñjāyanas, and Mādāyavas are recorded;
these are declared to be the Mitrayus. However, the Bhārgavas have three *ṛṣis* as their lineage. || 185 ||
Bhṛgu, Mitrayu, and Divodāsa—these three are declared to be the Pārthas of Vainya; they are the Bāṣkalas known as the descendants of Vainya. || 186 ||
These best of the twice-born Bhārgavas are known as having three *ārṣeya* lineages; Bhṛgu, Vainya, and Pārtha are the three principal *ṛṣis*.
The Śunakas, Saugandhayas, Yajñapayas, and Gārtsamadās;
the Gāṅgāyanas, Matsyagandhas, and Ikṣus shall be the Khārdamāyanas. (188)
The Śrotriyas and the Taittirīyas—these are proclaimed as the Śunakas;
these Śunakas are also proclaimed as having a single ancestral seer (ekārṣeya). || 189 ||
Even a single dog was called Bhārgava; and among the Yaskas, the Maitreyas, and the Vainyas, there was likewise [the same usage] toward one another.
And it is understood that a connection with the Śunakas must be established;
now the Aṅgirasas are mentioned, of whom Viṣṇuvṛddha is the first. (191)
The Bhadraṇas and the Bhadraṇāśas, those known as Śaṭhamārṣaṇas, those known as Śābarāyaṇas, the Sātyakis, and the Sātyakāyanas; || 192 ||
Those known as the Bādarāyaṇas, those known as the Vātsaprāyaṇas, the Āruṇyas, the Vaihoḍhas, and those known as the Naitudyas; || 193 ||
These, ending with Devasthānaya, are proclaimed as the Viṣṇuvṛddhas;
these are declared to be the Aṅgirasas and are remembered as having three ṛṣis (triyārṣeya). || 194 ||
Aṅgiras, Viṣṇuvṛddha, and the three Viṣṇudāsas;
Vairudhya, Rurudhya, and Trāsadasyu—these are the three. (195)
The Kanvas, Śailas, Valkalas, Halinas, Mojayas, others, as well as the Mauñjis, Māñjayas, and those known as the Markaṭāyanas. || 196 ||
Then Mauñjigandha is proclaimed; then Vājaya and Vājayas;
and Mārgaśravasa—these are the Kaṇvas who have three ancestral seers (tri-ārṣeya). || 197 ||
Aṅgiras, Ajamīḍha, and Kaṇva are the three sages;
then there are the Hāritas, the Kautsas, the Sāṃkhyas, and likewise the Dārbhas. (198)
Śaivāṅga, Śarmanāyu, Lābavedara, Mahodara, Naimiśreya, Haimagava, and then Miśrodara. (199)
The Kautapas, the Kaulayas, the Kārīṣayas, and the Paulayas; as well as the Pauṇḍalas, the Mādhūpas, the Māndhātās, and the Māṇḍakārayas. || 200 ||
Thus these Haritas have been declared; they are remembered as having three ancestral seers (tri-ārṣeya):
Āṅgiras, Ambarīṣa, and Yauvanāśva—these three. || 201 ||
Then there were the Saṃkṛtas, Taṇḍi, Śambhu, and Malakas; then Paunya, Śaibhava, Tāraka and others, as well as Paribhāva. (202)
Then there are the Hāridras and the Vaitaleyas; thereafter are considered the Śrotāyanas; then the Cārāyaṇas and the Pūtibhāṣas; and after that, the Āgrāyaṇas are recognized. || 203 ||
Cāndrāyaṇa, Cāpa, and Ṛṣaya, as well as Avagrāpaya—these are declared to be the Saṃkṛtis, and they are proclaimed to have three ancestral seers (triyārṣeya). || 204 ||
Aṅgiras, Saṃkṛti, and Ambarīṣa are the three sages;
from them come the Rathītaras, the Kāhvāyanas, and the Naitirakṣayas.
The Śailālayas, the Laibhis, and from them the Lībhāyanas are considered [descendants]; the Maikṣavāhas, the Sauvāhavāhas, and the Hastivāsayas [are likewise]. (206)
Then these were the hundred Hemaśatas, the Rathītaras who have three ancestral seers (ṛṣis):
Aṅgiras, Ambarīṣa, and Rathītara—these three. || 207 ||
Aṅgiras, Virūpa, and Pṛṣadaśva, as well as Mudgala, Hiraṇyākṣa, and Mitākṣa were the sages thereafter. || 208 ||
The Ṛgyas, the Ṛgyāyanas, the Dīrghajaṅghas, and those proclaimed as the Jaṅghas; then the Toraṇas, the Bindus, and these who are celebrated as the Mudgalas. (209)
The Triyārṣeyas are specified as Kavaca, Taikila, and others; Hamyāśva is also specified, followed by the Kapayas and Vaitalas.
Aitiśāyana, Saṃjña, Tarasvin, Patañjali, Miṇḍi, Bhojasi, and then Śārṅgarava. || 211 ||
Then Karaśikhaṇḍa, then Mauṣītaki is considered;
likewise Sāṃśaya is mentioned, and after that Pauṣpayas are regarded as the next.
These Kapayas are to be known as having three ancestral seers (triyārṣeya);
they are proclaimed to be the triad consisting of Aṅgiras, Kapittha, and Ambarīṣa.
Viṣṇuvṛddha and all the others would be non-yogins with respect to one another. I shall now describe those of kings and vaiśyas: Manu, Caila, and Purūravas. (214)
Then the [sūtras] for the Kṣatriyas were proclaimed; thereafter, indeed, the Lauhandana and Kilas; the Vātsapra and Audaka for the Vaiśya, as well as the Nārāsātya and others.
Ātreya, Vādhreya, Vādhūla, and Saṃkṛti;
Vasiṣṭha, Śunaka, Kaṇva, and Yaska—these are the eight. (216)
The Nārāśaṃsas are proclaimed [as their ancestors], or Manu is the *pravara* here;
furthermore, for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, the teacher (*ācārya*) may also be the *pravara*. (217)
Having ascertained that the *gotra* and *pravara* are the same, one should establish a relationship;
however, one should never choose a girl who shares the same *gotra* and *pravara*. 218.
Just as one would protect a sister who has been married with the same care as a mother,
so too must her protection be ensured through food, clothing, and other necessities.
For the sake of purifying the defect of marriage, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow,
provided that any [sexual] union was performed with her through negligence.
He shall always be one who performs penance; the rule for that is stated here:
upon a single occurrence, he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One thousand oblations with the Aghora mantra should be performed twice, and two thousand on the second occasion;
thus, the increase in the number of oblations is prescribed here in accordance with the advancement of yoga.
After one month, he should perform the Kṛcchra penance together with the Cāndrāyaṇa;
from six months up to a year, he should perform everything as previously described.
After that, for up to three years with great hardship,
there is the initiation called Nirvāṇa, which liberates one from the cycle of existence.
Those sons born of them are all considered twice-born by the twice-born;
indeed, in the case of contact with their sons and grandsons, the expiation is exactly that same one. (225)
Then, fasting, bathing, consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), recitation (japa),
and burnt offerings (homa) thus completely destroy for men all that arises from intermixture of castes.
At evening, at the beginning and end of the day, and at midday and during the night—one who is devoid of these four meals is traditionally known as one who observes a fast (upavāsa). || 227 ||

Or he may be deficient in three times, occurring respectively during the night and the day-and-night; or he may be deficient in two times, being diminished for those who are emaciated and weak of spirit. (228)
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, the procedure for determining the lineage (*gotra-nirṇaya-vidhi*), in the great tantra named the *Uttarakāmika*.
In the twenty-sixth chapter is the procedure for the hundredfold consecration (*śatābhiṣeka-vidhi*).
O best of the twice-born, I shall here describe in brief the Śatābhiṣeka rite, which destroys untimely death and increases longevity and health. (1)
In ancient times, it was beheld by a thousand moons for those initiated [into the rite], bestowing increase of wealth and grain and causing the proliferation of sons and grandsons.
During the period of the northern solstice, especially during the bright fortnight,
on an auspicious day with a favorable planetary hour (lagna), an excellent weekday, and a propitious lunar date (tithi).
The preceptor, being tranquil and endowed with all auspicious marks, should perform the ritual bathing in a well-decorated pavilion provided with auspicious sprouts.
On a mountain peak, or at a water-shed, or in a pure and delightful place,
measuring between five and fifty-five cubits in extent.
Or else, it may have twelve faces and be provided with four gates,
adorned with one to five rows of niches (bhaktis).
O twice-born ones, [one should initiate] a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra; especially one born in the natural order (anuloma), such as a king.
The Śiva-brahmins [may approach] a king's wife, or a feudatory, a minister, or a domestic priest,
or a woman born of those respective castes.
Adorned with the five ornaments, one should perform the consecration;
prior to the day of consecration, on the night before, the binding of the auspicious thread (kautuka) should take place.
One should have the Garuḍottamas fashioned and fastened on the right hand of the sacrificer,
and on the left hand of his principal wife.
If there are many principal wives, one should prepare [the rites] for all of them;
having drunk milk that night, they should lie upon their beds covered with blankets and the like.
Once it has been consecrated, he should sleep there with his head toward the south;
then, having constructed a pavilion according to the previously mentioned procedure, he should remain restrained.
After dismissing the artisan, the preceptor should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made;
he should then lay down the measuring-line of Manu, extending from east to west and from north to south.
One hundred and sixty-six, clearly joined with the term *nanda*, should be [the total];
having taken twenty-five of those quarters from among them. (14)
One should abandon the surrounding area, including the eight gates, by removing two squares from each of the four directions, leaving a single square at the center. 15.
The wise should prepare one hundred and eight squares here;
in the center of that, an altar (sthaṇḍila) should be made with śāli rice measuring one droṇa.
The measure for the *vardhanī* should be half of that; in the *kalaśas*, it should be one *āḍhaka*.
One [āḍhaka] is declared to be the lowest [measure], while double that would be the middle.
One should know that three times [the standard amount] is the best; this is declared to be the sequence for the most excellent.
For one who is poor, it may be one āḍhaka, half of that, or even half of that again.
O best of the twice-born, this minor procedure has been declared regarding the measurement of rice;
in the absence of śāli rice, one may use ordinary rice, or one may add half as much husked grain (taṇḍula).
One should throw half of that amount of sesame seeds, or a fourth part;
for one whose wealth is diminished, one should throw an eighth part for the purification of the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila).
In the center, however, is the Śiva-kumbha filled with thirty-two prasthas;
the Vardhanī is filled with half of that, both being filled with [the essence of] Śiva.
The external jars are to be known as being filled with an āḍhaka;
there should be wrapping with three threads around the jar and two threads around the karaka.
All the others as well, each one individually, are wrapped with a single thread, provided with separate garments, and endowed with separate pieces of gold. (23)
Water from a river mixed with a paste of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, kuṣṭha,
and uśīra is recommended for filling the auspicious jars and other vessels.
Combined with various fragrances, endowed with various seeds, combined with various minerals, and endowed with various metals. || 25 ||
It was provided with medicinal herbs from various regions, endowed with various fruits,
joined with various flowers, and accompanied by various products of the cow.
Having established the entire water-pot, one should worship it with leaves and flowers;
then, one should recite the names of the hundred and eight Rudras.
The supreme preceptor should honor [the deity] with various substances for offering;
having wrapped both the Śiva-kumbha and the Vardhanī vessel with a pair of garments.
The wise one should place the nine and five kinds of jewels upon Śiva and Śakti,
and in the first enclosure, he should place the eight metals and so forth.
One should place gold, silver, copper, brass, lead, iron, tin, and bell-metal, as well as the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras).
And in the second enclosure, one should likewise place these elements:
agallochum, sulphur, orpiment, lac, and realgar.
Mercury, the two types of mica, red ochre, and collyrium; nutmeg, saffron, vermilion, blue vitriol, and the two types of vimala. || 32 ||
One should place these sixteen beloved ones in the second enclosure;
one should assign them to the twelve squares of Indra and to both sides of the gate.
[The ladles] are made from the palāśa, khadira, mango, plakṣa, and nyagrodha trees;
likewise, they may be produced from bilva, śamī, śirīṣa, and aśvattha. || 34 ||
The bark of the Audumbara, the Nāraṅga, and those originating from the Mātuluṅga—these are considered the inner [barks] of trees, beginning with the Vāmā. (35)
In the southeast, one should properly place nine other types of earth:
from a riverbank, a cow-pen, an anthill, and an elephant's tusk.
In the ocean, in a lake, in a field, on a mountain, and at the root of an Aśvattha tree;
likewise, two of the blue lotus (utpala) and two of the red lotus (paṅkaja). || 37 ||
The *vakula*, the *karavīra*, the *pāṭala*, and likewise the *kurava*, as well as the *mālatī*, the *munipuṣpa*, and the *nandikāvarta*. (38)
The Guru should place these twelve items, including the campaka, on the right side:
sandalwood, uśīra, kuṣṭha, saffron, and likewise nara.
Takola, agallochum, leaf, and clove are to be known as being in the group of nine in the southwest; now that which is in the west is described.
The Vaiṣṇava [should offer] black gram, wild millet, wheat, and barley;
as well as Apāmārga, sesame, mung beans, Priyaṅgu, and mustard seeds.
One should place a māḍhaka of śyāmāka grain in due order;
likewise, lakṣmī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, viṣṇukrānti, and haṃsinī.
Tulasī, Sahadevī, Indravallī, Padminī, and Sūryāvarta are declared to be the nine plants considered appropriate for the northwest direction. (43)
Likewise, the five products of the cow, milk, curd, and cow urine, as well as cow dung, coconut, and the fruit of the citron; || 44 ||
Then, an orange, a bilva fruit, a jackfruit, a mango, and one produced from the pomegranate tree should be placed there in successive order.
Then, having likewise placed fragrant water and the other substances in all nine jars in the northeast, one should worship Śiva and the others in sequence.
The preceptor, having performed his ablutions together with the image-keepers and being well-adorned,
shall wear new garments, a turban, and an upper cloth.
Adorned with the five ornaments as well as a finger-ring, one should perform all the rites, beginning with the worship of the gateway, within the pavilion. (48)
One should worship Śiva, complete with all his limbs, in the central pitcher;
and if she is a devoted wife, one should worship Manonmanī in the Vardhanī vessel.
If there are many [images], there should be many [offerings]; among them, one should worship that very one [which is the primary].
If he is already initiated, it is so; if not, then at that time he should be initiated.
One should arrange [the fire] in the eastern direction of the maṇḍala,
or in the northeast, or in the north or south, provided it is joined with a fire-pit (vahnikuṇḍa).
Alternatively, this [mandala] may be abandoned once it has been placed in a vessel dedicated to Śambhu;
having performed the ritual of throwing flowers and so forth, one should especially perform the fire-oblation (homa).
With perfumes, flowers, lamps, incense, and especially other offerings,
one should arrange either nine fires, five fires, or even a single fire.
The wise one should offer, in sequence, fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, sesame seeds, bamboo shoots, and mung beans— whatever materials are suitable for the oblation.
The Udumbara, Vaṭa, Aśvattha, and Plakṣa trees should be placed in the directions starting with Indra (the East),
and the Śamī, Khadira, Māyūra, and Śrīvṛkṣa trees should be in the intermediate directions.
The *palāśa* tree is primary; O Śiva, [the oblation] should be offered with the marks of Brahmā in due order.
One should offer all substances as the primary offering for the Goddess as well. (56)
One should offer one hundred, fifty, or even half of that [number] oblations with the root mantra;
however, for the Brahma-mantras and the limb-mantras, one should offer separately a tenth part [of the number of oblations].
Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) in due order and having passed the remainder of the night,
the supreme guru should perform their initiation (dīkṣā) in the principal fire.
If the performers are uninitiated, one should worship Śiva in the Śiva-pitcher; however, this should be done with the five-syllabled mantra alone, or even with "Śivāyai namaḥ. || 59 ||
One should worship Gaurī in the *vardhanī* vessel and in all the jars;
one should likewise worship Rudra himself with the five-syllabled mantra.
For the purpose of initiation, one should indeed prepare this hundred-fold mandala known as Sarvatobhadra for the sake of vision and for liberation from all sins. (61)
For the sake of accomplishing all desired goals, [he is] composed of divine and non-divine dust;
his limbs are smeared with the morning bath and he is adorned with ornaments worthy of decoration.
Adorned with all ornaments, he should be brought to the vicinity of the pavilion;
having performed the washing of his feet and the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), his mind shall be tranquil.
One should bring [the deity] to the southern gate, having sprinkled it with water while reciting the *praṇava*;
likewise, one should perform the offering of a handful of flowers, circumambulation, and prostration with that same mantra.

Then, having had [the image] fashioned, the preceptor, once Śiva is established within a pitcher, situated upon a mandala, or likewise placed within a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), installs it upon the bathing altar.
On a seat made of *bhadra*, or born from the *payovakṣaja* tree, or produced from the *vāmra*, or from the *pānasa*, or from the *bilva*, or from the *jambu*, or from the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree.
If it is for the consecration of kings, it should be endowed with a thousand streams;
for all others, however, it may be performed with a hundred streams or even a single vessel.
O King, it should also be made of gold, or one of those two [silver or copper],
endowed with all ornaments, and at the end, with *āmalaka* fruits and the like.

Having bathed with other substances as well, one should smear [the body] while wearing clean clothes; and having changed the water on the limbs as well as the garment and so forth, [one should proceed]. (69)
Having smeared it with sandalwood paste and other substances, and adorned it with fragrant flowers,
the Guru [should place it] in another auspicious location that has been smeared and decorated.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should place upon it an auspicious seat (bhadrāsana) covered with tiger skin,
cloth, and a golden lotus.
Having seated the consecrated one together with his wife in the center,
and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) up to the end of the mantra-body, [he should worship] with perfumes and other offerings and with a garland for the arms.
Having adorned it with perfumes and flowers and endowed it with all ornaments,
one should then cover it with a great cloth upon a smeared surface before it.
In that place, having placed all kinds of grains along with a honey-pot containing gold, one should present a milch cow together with her calf.
He was honored by his kinsmen, who were joyful, with garments, gold, and finger-rings;
and with golden flowers and other offerings, accompanied by songs and instrumental music. (75)
Having placed [the body] upon a palanquin or similar vehicle and performed a circumambulation of the village,
one should place it before the door of the house on ground smeared with auspicious unguents.
Having placed him upon a plank joined with a full water-pot and provided with lamps,
one should perform the washing of his feet with milk and water.
Then, having had it performed by women with a stream of colored water and accompanied by lamps, one should cause three circumambulations to be made.
Then, having stepped upon the sandals, one should enter toward one's own home;
this is the excellent path, or else [one may proceed] with forty-nine jars.
One should perform the consecration by means of twenty-five, nine, five, or even a single water-pot. || 80 ||
And he gave the teacher a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) appropriate for the highest and other grades [of initiation],
consisting of female and male slaves, land, cows, and household utensils.
At the conclusion of that [rite], for the image-protectors (mūrtipāḥ), and at its conclusion also for those who recite [mantras],
and for the devotees who offer hymns of praise, there shall be a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as previously described.
One should worship and perform the ritual for the sake of following the form of wealth;
the mortal who causes this to be done in such a manner shall have his mind fixed upon dharma.
In this very world, one becomes wealthy, prosperous, possessed of sons, and victorious;
having enjoyed long life, health, and beloved women, one attains the supreme goal.
In whatever kingdom this sequence of the consecration rite is performed, there is no untimely death, nor is there misfortune, even among those who commit evil deeds. (85)
Therein, there is no fear of calamities, nor any disruption of the traditional scriptures;
the rain-cloud pours forth in its proper season, there is abundance of food, and the king is victorious.
All beings are peaceful; they are full of milk, bearing milk. || 86 ||
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, the ritual for the hundredfold consecration, in the great tantra named Uttarakāmika.
In the twenty-seventh chapter: the ritual for the funeral rites.
O best of the twice-born, I shall now fully describe the funeral rites for those who have been initiated—
whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or those born of anuloma unions.
Whether they be teachers, practitioners, or spiritual sons established in the observance,
when their life-force has departed, the funeral rites must be performed by those who have received initiation.

For the triad beginning with the Ācārya, the funeral rite (antyeṣṭi) shall be accompanied by the purification of the paths (adhvaśuddhi); for the others, it shall be devoid of the purification of the paths.
If these three, beginning with the preceptor, are devoid of proper conduct and do not perform penance, then at the time of their death, the funeral rites (antyeṣṭi-karma) [must be performed].
And for those who, through the purification of reality, have properly performed their obligatory duties and the like,
and have avoided what is forbidden— those who are thus free from negligence— (verse 5).
Setting aside the purification of the principles (tattvaśuddhi), the final rite (antyeṣṭi) alone is prescribed;
or else, for those who have performed the practice, there is the "immediate departure" (sadyotkrānti) by means of piercing the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
And for those whose time of departure from life has arrived, the purification of their reality is not described by those who know the sacrificial rites. || 7 ||

Having performed the fire-related ablution (āgneyasnāna) with his body armored by mantras, and likewise having fashioned the body of the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) into a form of mantras related to fire; || 8 ||
Having worshipped the Lord with the eightfold offering of flowers for the sake of one seeking liberation,
[one should anoint] oneself or others with sandalwood paste and other substances using one's own hand or both hands.
Having established Maheśvara in the form of a *liṅga* within his heart,
and having touched his joined palms to his head, he caused him to be present there.
For that purpose, he recited this verse in the presence of the Lord of Gods:
"O God, this man has been initiated by you; he is an observer of the command of Śiva. (11)
He shall attain the state of Śiva without delay after the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite;
having thus informed the Lord of Gods, one should establish him in his own place.
One should perform this rite either once or many times;
at the time of departure from the body, one should recite it while keeping it close to the ear.
Especially the Śiva-mantra or the five-syllabled mantra—indeed, all of this must be performed by either the preceptor or another [qualified person]. (14)
Whether by a member of that family or by another, the rite to be described hereafter—
originating from a sacred ford (tīrtha)— should be performed for the sake of bathing that man whose life has departed.

If he is a householder, he should have the image bathed with water taken from a hundred jars and other vessels by those who have themselves performed a thorough ablution, combined with the customary worldly bathing rites.
Having thus prepared the jars or even the pitchers according to the instructions for the ritual bath,
one should bathe [the deity] using only water from the *vardhanī* vessel, excluding the other [consecrated] waters.
It should be richly provided with a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), along with cloth, gold, and a tuft of grass (kūrca);
it should be joined with a lid and unbroken grains (akṣata), and worshipped with the limbs and heart-mantras of the Vidyā. || 18 ||
One should bathe it, or take it up, or perform this rite even in a cremation ground;
or else, having carefully bathed the image associated with the fire-god (Āgneya) along with the ritual bathing ceremony.
Having performed the withdrawal through the path of reabsorption, he likewise put on a loincloth as his garment,
and adorned himself with the rosary and other ornaments worthy of such finery.
Then, for those who have been initiated, as well as for others who uphold the teaching of Śiva and for others [of other classes],
one should appropriately provide the night-powder mixed with oil.
Then, one should cause everything, including betel leaves, to be given to the people;
one should bring forth a throne made of sacrificial wood or other blameless woods.
And for those striving to reach the human [size], by increasing it by six finger-breadths, the length should be three cubits, or three, four, or five parts [of that]. || 23 ||
Having placed her upon a seat that is very spacious, endowed with splendor,
and provided with a supreme, wide cushion, one should perform the rite at the top of the peak and its lower part.
[He saw] another Śiva-yogin standing with his gaze fixed upon a canopy fashioned from red garlands and garments, while he himself was poised for the departure of the vital breath (utkrānti).
Having removed all his ornaments with auspicious rites,
one should bring a pure palanquin of this kind and place Śiva upon it.
He was cheered from behind by a procession of those established in their vows, led by a loud-sounding musical instrument being played with great resonance. || 27 ||
Accompanied by the sound of conchs and endowed with the sound of singing, his kinsmen should follow him with their heads uncovered. (28)
Restraining the tears from their eyes, those who have contemplated the worthlessness of saṃsāra should join the right hand to the head and bind it with both thumbs.
Having encircled it with a cord of *darbha* grass, one should lead it toward the northeast direction,
accompanied by those initiated who are of the same lineage and wear their sacred threads over the right shoulder (*apasavya*).
While others recite the Astra-mantra, one should cause [the image] to be carried along with water;
and by another person, a smoky fire should be placed in front of it, situated at the three parts of the waist.
One should slightly direct [the breath] toward the southern end of the resting place for the object,
upon the perfectly pure surface of the earth, with the deceased's head facing south.
Whether he be observing a vow or not observing one, whoever carries a Brāhmaṇa initiated into the Śiva-rite who has met his end, for him there shall be no untimely death.
Having gone there, bathed, and offered water for libation,
the cultivated soul attains his desired happiness both in this world and the next.
Nevertheless, one must not follow after a person of low caste who has abandoned his vows;
having followed him, one should bathe in water and mutter the *Sajātīśa* mantra a hundred times.
He who takes away a Śiva-yogin who has passed away— being without companion and without protector—
and performs the funeral rites for him, shall be liberated from all misfortunes.
This same principle is prescribed for the other three castes beginning with the Vaiśya.
Now, a place for water that is nearby, level, and pure— || 37 ||
Having reached a peak or a water-shed, and having thus prepared that interior space,
one should construct a single girdle (mekhalā) with a height of six finger-breadths and eight corners.
Having constructed a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) one cubit in size according to the prescribed rite,
and having consecrated a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) made from its earth, one should likewise prepare a funeral trench four cubits in extent.
The preceptor, having thus prepared the triad, should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to the south, two cubits in width and eight finger-breadths in depth.
Then, having smeared the ground situated near that [altar] with cow dung,
the Guru— pure, bathed, with his body consecrated by mantras, and having performed the *astrālukīkaraṇa* rite— [proceeds].

Having proceeded by way of circumambulation to the edge of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) facing north, he should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) in reverse order and be protected by the weapon-mantra (hetimantra). || 42 ||
Having performed the internal sacrifice with the Astra-mantra and having touched the vessel that increases the power of the weapons (astravardhanī),
he should perform the worship for himself, having consecrated the ritual substances with water sprinkled from that vessel.
Having repeated the Saṃhitā mantras in the order of withdrawal, the preceptor, having dissolved the [elements] together with their causes, Brahmā and the others, into himself, [proceeds]. (44)
Having formed the *saṃhāra-hara* hand gesture and having remembered Śiva even once,
one should scatter there *vikiro* offerings— namely, *kuśa* grass, ashes, and sesame seeds.
Having gathered [the materials] according to the rule, one should worship the site upon the funeral pyre;
when the field has been divided into five parts, there are twenty-five compartments.
One should install the deities of the site (vāstudevatās) upon a ground variegated with five colors according to their respective forms, using materials such as bamboo and cords.
There, in the center, one should worship Brahmā together with Bhū on five squares;
and in the southwest, Viṣṇu, accompanied by Vāri, on four squares.
In the southeast, one should worship Rudra together with Agni within four squares;
and in the northwest, within four squares, one should worship Īśvara together with Vāyu.
In the four corners of the northeast, together with the sky,
one should worship the four beginning with Śakra in the Vedic squares starting from the east.
One should offer the bali-oblation with one's own name, a prostration, and the word "svāhā" at the end;
having worshipped the Pāśupata weapon in the northeast direction upon the vardhanī-vessel.

Having placed the weapons beginning with the trident and ending with the thunderbolt in the eight directions, one should worship [them], as well as the Lotus and the Enemy of the Lotus, above and below.
One should properly worship Bhava within a mandala made of sesame seeds and darbha grass;
having provided a seat of sovereignty and so forth in the center of a lotus with its stalks [and petals]. (53)
One should worship the wheel of powers (śakticakra) beginning with Manonmanī and ending with Vāmā;
having thus worshipped Śaṅkara along with his limbs (aṅgas), after first honoring the seat in reverse order (vyutkramāsana).
Having consecrated the sacrificial pit as before and having worshipped the Śakti there,
one should cast into it the fire from which the portion for the flesh-eaters has been removed, while circumambulating counter-clockwise.
Having worshipped Śiva with the five ritual acts (saṃskāras) within the heart-lotus—just as one would on the sacrificial ground—and having offered libations with black sesame seeds; || 56 ||
Then one should pile the funeral mound with full vessels containing clarified butter and other offerings;
or alternatively, having dispensed with the mandalas produced from the five colors.
With consecrated jars at the extremities and with consecratory rites such as inspection and so forth,
one should then draw the city of Mahendra upon the funeral pit and the pedestal.
In the middle of that [space], one should apply the two deities of the fire (the black-pathed one) with dust and red [pigment]; then, one should plant stakes at the corners.
In the southeast and other directions, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), he should drive stakes made of dry wood—
obtained by reciting the Astra-mantra once each— with their roots upward and their tips downward.
One should wrap it with armor made of five-colored thread, or else encircle it on all sides with red thread. || 61 ||
The oblation for Śiva should be offered into the fire of Śiva for the sake of protection from the Rākṣasas;
there, the bier for the corpse should be thickly strewn with sacrificial wood.

Having worshipped [the image] with sandalwood and agallochum mixed together, covered with an inverted cloth, and with kusha grass, flowers, and sesame seeds, using the King of Weapons mantra; || 63 ||
Having fashioned an image of the deceased, rubbed it with clay and cow dung mixed with water,
one should bathe it and fumigate it there with ash from a newly prepared fire-pit.
Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder and disregarding his previous caste status,
having worshipped Śiva in the southeast, he should sit upon a kuśa-grass seat to the south of the fire.
Then, for this mantra-body which has been purified through the [five] purifications beginning with *vīkṣaṇa* and by means of the five *dhāraṇās*, [it is placed] within the hollow of the heart-lotus.

Having withdrawn that subtle body (liṅga), which is unattached to the latent impressions of karma to be experienced and has not yet reached a supporting physical body, one should dissolve it by means of the Great Net (mahājāla).
"Oṃ hūṃ hāmatha haṃ hāṃ hūṃ; this is considered the Great Net (Mahājāla).
Having spoken thus at the end, the Guru, meditating upon it, should utter the name of the deceased initiation ending with an obeisance. (68)
Having withdrawn those five kalās from that body into the *vidyādeha*,
and having performed the nyāsa of Śiva along with his six limbs, one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra.
Then, for the purpose of bringing consciousness into proximity, one should purify the principles (tattvas), taking up the [kalās] beginning with Nivṛtti either simultaneously or in succession. (70)
Then, one should worship those Kalās along with their presiding deities in the southeast as before;
having extracted the possessor of the Liṅga from the Liṅga by means of the various methods such as striking (tāḍana) and so forth.
Therein, as before, one should apply [the analysis of] birth, karma, and qualification,
as well as the experience, dissolution, and purification of the principles (tattvas) and the currents (srotas).

The concealment of the state of being a bound soul (paśutva) occurs through the severing and breaking of the fetters; its burning away by means of transgressive rites, or the liberation of the bound soul from its cause, constitutes the [teacher's] duty. || 73 ||
Having separated the sacrificial animal from that previous bond by means of the rite of extinction (nirvāṇakarman),
one should likewise purify the other fetters (pāśas) above it.
Having addressed them thus with the ritual manual (karmapaddhati) up to the level of Śiva,
one should extract them from the fire at the conclusion of the oblation and unite them in the stainless state.
When he has been thus instructed, the atom (the soul) shall never again be dependent on another;
having worshipped the Lord until all bonds are completely severed, he should then abandon even Him.

Having withdrawn the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) into that [physical] body, the Guru [dissolves it] into his own state; likewise, having withdrawn even the Lord of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍileśāna*) into his own state, the Guru [rests]. (77)
Having approached the corpse and placed it upon the bed covered with *kuśa* grass—
with its head toward the south and its feet toward the north— one should provide it with a pearl, a *struk*, and a *sruva* ladle.
The preceptor and the practitioner, as well as anyone other than those two who has abandoned them—
[one should worship these] with turuṣka, agaru, karpūra, candana, and uttaradāru.
Having covered and brought the fire from the sacrificial pit, one should place it at the region of the head;
then, having poured honey, sesame oil, and clarified butter into the blazing fire, [one should proceed].
Having lifted up a sacrificial ladle (sruk) filled with clarified butter, honey, and milk, and having honored it,
the Guru stands at the head of the bed, facing the northern direction.
Uttering the words, "One should cast the stream into the mouth of the purifier," he said:
"O Agni, you are the southern time; [cast her] who has been brought forth by Time itself. (82)
Take this great oblation, purified by mantras, upon the śāvyā ladle;
immediately thereafter, cast both the sruk and sruva ladles there with their openings turned downwards.
Having appointed four [assistants] skilled in the rites of consecration, the preceptor,
taking up the sword and the vardhanī vessel, moved counter-clockwise.
Having lifted and placed [the water] upon his left shoulder with his head covered and his face turned away,
he should release the stream while remaining composed and circumambulating clockwise those established in their own duty.

Having performed the rite with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), one should turn that *vardhanī* vessel upside down and cast it back toward the place from which that vessel for increasing the weapons was originally taken.
Then, having gone to a body of water and bathed, and having spread out excellent kuśa grass,
he should thereafter, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), first recite the Praṇava and the Hṛdaya mantra.
Addressing him as "O Pure-Souled One," one should employ names beginning with Īśa and ending with Śānta;
or else names beginning with Skanda and ending with Gaṇeśa, or ending with Bhava. (88)
Having spoken thus, the minister should again offer libations three times with the word "svadhā" at the end, according to what is appropriate;
then, having bathed once more with a serene countenance, he should [recite] the Śivasaṃhitā.
They may be all [the missiles] without exception, or even a hundred of them in embodied form;
likewise, those who give the shoulder-bearer (skandha) are twice as many, as are those who burn it.
Having thus performed the impurity due to death, they should enter their own homes after chewing neem leaves and remaining self-restrained at the door of the house.
Having sipped water (ācamana), they should then touch fire, water, cow dung, and white mustard seeds;
then, having stepped upon a stone slowly, they may enter.

For one who is disciplined, abides by the conventions, is humble, and whose mind is fixed on me with the thought, "The initiation into Nirvāṇa must be performed for me," the initiation into Nirvāṇa should be performed by means of the higher initiation.
Even for one who has failed, that final rite of purification of reality (tattvaśuddhāntyeṣṭi) is prescribed here;
it may be performed with water, fire, or weapons, especially by means of an elephant or a lion.
By tigers or other creatures, or by falling from trees and the like;
or by being struck or cut down by one's own hand, or by being bound with ropes and cast down. (95)

By others, for those whose death occurs as previously described—namely, for those whose bodies are no longer present or whose bodies are incomplete—the funeral rites are performed in the same manner. (96)
For those whose bodies are afflicted by consumption, leprosy, cholera, and other such great diseases,
one should perform all ritual acts upon a body fashioned from kuśa grass and similar materials.

One should burn a man who has died with deficient limbs or suffering from diseases such as smallpox either in the sacred fire alone or in a common fire without reciting mantras, or else one should bury him.

If one desires merit, it is accepted that one may cast [the image] into holy places such as the Gaṅgā, or perform the entry into fire and so forth; having understood this, one should carry out the rite accordingly. (99)

One should fashion an effigy made of flour paste, using *kuśa* grass, *darbha* grass, or leaves from the *palāśa* tree provided with threads, and drench it thoroughly with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Or one should have an image made from cow-dung according to the desired measurement;
and upon this, the ritual should be performed just as previously described.
However, O auspicious lady, one should burn that image when it has been sprinkled with ghee, honey, and milk,
under the Tripada constellation, during the periods of Venus, Mars, or Jupiter.
For those whose cremation is the cause of the destruction of their lineage,
for that very purpose, one should again perform the cremation with due respect.
For those men whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed who have died, the rite of digging a pit is prescribed;
for them there is no cremation, nor indeed an offering of bali, nor the rite of water libations.
For men, cremation or the rite of digging a pit may take place within four days; however, if a child dies before reaching two years of age, there is neither fire nor the water-rite.
For ascetics or even for those possessed of knowledge, the ritual act should be the rite of filling the pit,
accompanied by the pouring of salt, but without offerings of food, water, or boiled rice.
For one whose tonsure ceremony has been performed, the cremation should be accompanied by the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) and water;
for one who has reached adulthood, there should be an annual rite with abundance, whether in the offering of a rice-ball or in the ritual of water.
In the case of a ten-year-old, the period shall be ten days, and specifically for those older than that;
furthermore, whatever rite is performed for a body placed in a pit, purification is achieved once it has been smeared with [ashes].
Having spread a layer of sand and laid darbha grass with the tips pointing northward upon it,
one should place [the body] in a palanquin or similar vehicle at the cremation ground on pure ground.
One should dig the earth to the depth of an arm-span, making it equal in length and width to the bed;
having placed [the image] there and offered unbroken rice and other items, one should worship it silently with perfumes and other offerings.
Having placed the skull of the deceased there facing south, one should fill it with earth;
or, for yogins, one should dig a pit measuring one staff (daṇḍa) in depth, or half a staff.
Or else, having filled it with salt, one should place there, in its vicinity,
either a pedestal (pīṭha) joined with a temple, or indeed a linga.
Having assumed or established one's own form, one should perform worship;
in that regard, neither the piṇḍa nor the water-śrāddha, nor anything else, is desired there. (113)
O best of sages, both the binding of his thumb and the spitting of betel nut are not permitted for these devotees.
She should have the bodies of those who have died by lightning, fire, water, or other causes cremated.
But if her husband has gone to another country and no news of him has been heard for a year, [she may remarry]. (115)
Having passed twelve years, she should observe the vow of widowhood;
for if he is entirely unknown—whether dead or not dead—[she should do so]. (116)
Having fashioned a circle of the Vedas and Āśramas, one should place husks in the middle of the vessel there, above the three stakes, and burn them until the fire-sparks have ceased.
For the purpose of cremating the deceased, one should indeed collect fire in this manner, combined with the clarified butter remaining from the *homa* and rice mixed with milk. || 118 ||
At the regions of the ears, eyes, mouth, hands, navel, and heart, one should perform the casting of golden chips at the nine apertures with the *hṛdaya-mantra*. (119)
One should cast rice mixed with milk while reciting the Vāmadeva mantra;
one should perform the binding and cutting of the thumb while reciting the Aghora weapon mantra.
Then the sapindas, together with the brothers, should perform the throwing of the garland;
at that time, they all circumambulate it while holding the edge of a cloth.
Having taken up a full water-pot that produces heat and having performed three circumambulations to the right,
one should cast it to his left with the Astra-mantra.
One should pour water from a broken vessel onto the vital points;
or, at the conclusion of the bath, having drunk the five products of the cow or clarified butter, one should mutter the Śiva-mantra.
Then, having given a gift according to one's ability to alleviate fatigue and distress,
water with sesame seeds should be offered, accompanied by the name of the deceased.

Such rites as these must be performed for those whose essence is Śiva, even if they are devoid of the purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi), provided they have been accompanied by the funeral rite (antyeṣṭi). || 125 ||
Every day, libations (tarpaṇa) should be performed by reciting the names of Īśa, Skanda, and the others;
on the first day, three separate libations should be performed for each.
One should increase it by one each day, separately for each [day], up to twelve;
this is the number seventy-five for the libation (tarpaṇa) at every meal.
One should prepare two hundred [offerings], accompanied by the number five times five, for the sake of satisfying the triad beginning with Īśa; or else, there may be only a single meal.
One should give clothing to cover the naked to a consecrated householder;
at the conclusion of the cremation, one should offer [this] on behalf of the deceased, together with garments and rice.
At the conclusion of the libation (tarpaṇa), one should offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) either at a river or elsewhere, or even in the home;
however, for one who is bound by lifelong vows (naiṣṭhika), the daily libation and the oblation are not to be performed.
However, at the end of the cremation, for one day, [one should worship] with Īśa and the other three [deities];
having performed the libation (tarpaṇa) for that purpose, one should worship Śiva for that same purpose.
They should gather together and remove the grief of those men who are attached to worldly things and possess deluded minds, by means of causing them to remember their true nature. 132.
For those who observe the vows of Śiva, the devotees of Śiva, and the friends of Hiraṇyagarbha—those who possess discernment—there is no cause whatsoever for grief. (133)
And thus, if the self were all-pervading and eternal like Śiva, it would always be conscious;
there would be no destruction for it here in this world, and if such [destruction] exists, then it is not [the self].

Due to the absence of the causes for the self's enjoyment, that destruction is metaphorically designated as death, which is the cessation [of the self] through the non-perception of its own qualities. (135)

Even one who is favorable toward a healthy self may act unfavorably [toward others], provided that he possesses no desire for the attainment of his own desired objects upon the removal of what is undesirable. (136)
One who has been initiated by Śiva as described shall become omniscient at the end of the body;
for this [body] is a veil for consciousness, and enjoyment is the means for that enjoyment.
This body and its separation [from it]—that which is the absolute cessation—is said to be the ultimate benefit; for in this sapless plantain trunk of human existence, one seeks only the core essence.
He who acts is utterly deluded regarding that body which resembles a water bubble; though composed of five elements, it has now returned to the state of the five. (139)
What cause for lamentation is there in that regard concerning one's own body produced by one's own actions?
For the earth, the ocean, and even the gods meet with destruction.
How will the world of mortals not go to destruction, resembling as it does a mass of foam, since the deceased, being helpless, must consume the phlegm and tears shed by his kinsmen? (141)
Therefore, one should not weep; rather, the rites should be performed according to one's ability.
On the second day, one may have the cremation of the remaining limbs performed, or one may not.
Accompanied by his sapindas and provided with ghee and milk,
he should perform the collection of the bones from the funeral pyre either on the third day or on the first day.
Then, having taken a clay vessel filled with either milk or curd, and having placed three pieces of wood therein, one should deposit that [mixture] into it. || 144 ||
Alternatively, one may perform the collection of the bones without the formal piling (saṃcayana),
using a new earthen vessel on the first, third, fifth, seventh, or ninth day.
The collection of bones for the Brahmins and others may be done either in sequence or all at once;
one should cast an offering of groats, parched grain, boiled rice, and cakes in the four directions.
This may be an offering to the Piśācas; one should perform it for their satisfaction.
Having withdrawn the limbs with the [respective] limbs, one should cast them away using that very mantra. (147)

Having cast it outside the village for the purpose of throwing it into the Gaṅgā or other waters, on that very day, or at the end of a fortnight, or at the end of a month, or every three months; || 148 ||
One should deposit it after six months, or at the completion of a full year, or even beyond that;
having deposited it there in that sacred ford (tīrtha) and performed a bath along with sesame seeds.
Having performed the libation for the ancestors, one should also offer libations to the gods and others;
one should give gifts according to one's ability and offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) upon that ground.
Those who have a relationship with a single teacher as their disciple, as well as those related to the teacher,
should abandon for three days all ritual acts other than the obligatory ones, such as the recitation of mantras (japa) and so forth.
Others than them, who abide on the path of Śiva— whether they be householders or even those without a home—
shall observe impurity for one day if they are initiated [into the lineage] of a deceased person.
Householders who abide on the path of the world should not transgress worldly conduct;
therefore, those who have been initiated should observe the conventions of the world. 153.
For this one who observes the vow of Śiva, there is neither death nor ritual impurity (sūtaka),
because he is independent of his previous stage of life and because the causes of saṃsāra have ceased.
Even for a householder who remains in his previous stage of life, if he is a man of knowledge who has destroyed the seed of saṃsāra through initiation and is devoted to virtuous actions; || 155 ||
In the case of a Brahmin, impurity lasts for ten days;
in the case of a Kṣatriya, it lasts for twelve days. (156)
For a Vaiśya, purification occurs after ten or five days; for a Śūdra, it is indeed monthly. This applies when four wives have been married by a Brāhmaṇa.
The period of birth-impurity (sūtaka) should be observed in sequence for ten, six, three, and one day;
that same impurity applies to their sons and others on the mother’s side, according to the accepted view.

If one dies after being conceived in a full term, purification occurs through bathing within a moment; however, for the loss of a fetus, the duration for the mother's purification is said to be equal to the number of months of gestation, whether it be male or female.
Before the naming ceremony, before the eruption of teeth, and likewise before the initiation (upanayana),
bathing is prescribed for one day and three days respectively.

And after that, for ten days, it is said that for the relatives in the three [categories], from the age of eight onwards, until marriage, the sequence is as previously described following a haircut. || 161 ||

For brothers, the period of impurity shall last ten days once their names have been given; however, for the parents, it shall always be ten days. O elder brothers, this is the rule for impurity in all cases.

O best of the twice-born, for one who has been given away in marriage, there is impurity lasting for two days (pakṣiṇī) upon the death of her parents or her uterine brothers, and likewise upon the departure of their sons.
A night situated between two days, or a day situated between two nights, is called a "pakṣiṇī" (bird-day); having understood this, one should perform the ritual action.
In the prescribed rule, impurity for sapindas lasts three days, while for those belonging to the group of samānodakas it is ordained to be one day, regardless of where they reside.
After the eruption of teeth, bathing is prescribed for them;
for a Brahmin, until the tying of the girdle, and for a Kṣatriya, until the taking up of the bow. (166)

O best of men, if a Vaiśya dies while holding the goad, or a Śūdra while holding two garments, their period of impurity shall be full; it would be even longer if they have died after [letting go]. 167.
When the tonsure ceremony has been performed, a Kṣatriya becomes pure after six days;
a Vaiśya is purified after nine days, and a Śūdra after twelve days. (168)
O best of sages, all this has been prescribed for kinsmen;
however, when a teacher dies, the period of impurity shall last for three nights.
For that son and his wife, it is traditionally taught that [the impurity lasts] day and night;
however, when birth-impurity (sūtaka) occurs while post-mortem impurity (śāvāśauca) has already arisen, [the following applies]. || 170 ||
Birth-impurity is purified by death-impurity, but birth-impurity does not purify death-impurity;
for even if there should be another birth-impurity during a birth-impurity, O best of the twice-born. (171)

Purification shall occur by the very remainder of the prior period; likewise, a death-impurity [overcomes] a death-impurity, and if a death-impurity occurs during a birth-impurity, [it overcomes] that birth-impurity as well. || 172 ||
In that case, purification occurs through the excess [days], but one is not pure by means of fewer days.
However, when the ten-day period has elapsed, one shall remain impure for three nights.
If a birth occurs after one day has passed, the ritual bath should indeed take place after a year; this applies when the deceased has already performed his daily fire-rituals prior to cremation.
The period of impurity for one who has not maintained the sacred fires is proclaimed to last until the death [is reported];
and likewise for those Śūdras who are devotees of Maheśvara and wear ashes and rudrākṣa beads. (175)
For them, purification occurs on the fifteenth day, whether in the case of birth or death;
likewise, this is the consensus even regarding the five types of teachers and the daughters of Rudra.
In that case, it is stated that even sapinda relatives shall not touch the cremator of those who follow the inferior path (hīnānulomins), as well as those who wear ashes and rudrākṣa beads. 177.
Impurity due to death is twice that of birth; impurity due to menstruation is twice that of death;
and impurity due to childbirth is twice that of menstruation, as is the case for the cremation of a corpse.
Those carriers who have been touched by a *preta* outside the village must remain there until the appearance of the stars,
or even until the appearance of the sun.
Having touched [the object], they should at the end drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or indeed clarified butter;
this is proclaimed as the general rule for mortals. || 180 ||
And likewise for those known as Māheśvara Śūdras and others, as well as for those who know the songs of Śiva and those who dwell in the hermitages of Śiva. (181)
Purification for a temple servant woman is proclaimed to occur after twenty days; however, the period of impurity for male and female slaves shall be as prescribed by the family of their master.
O best of the twice-born, impurity is not prescribed in the case of inverse unions;
however, the lineage of Rudra-maidens is declared to be that of their mother. (183)

In the same way, for temple-prostitutes (devadāsīs), the maternal lineage is declared [to be affected]; and for kings and domestic priests, there is no impurity (āśauca) regarding death or birth. 184.

For one established in the *samaya*, there is never any impurity regarding the daily rites (*nityakarman*), whether he be a householder or a renunciant, provided he is fully committed to his vows. (185)

For those who are engaged in the initiation of Nirvāṇa, whose minds are fixed on spiritual practice, and who have established [the deity] within their hearts, there is no impurity— neither in regard to daily rites nor in regard to occasional ones.

Since impurity regarding optional rites (kāmyakarman) ceases upon bathing, and since bathing is not prescribed separately for one observing a vow, provided he eats from a separate meal-preparation. 187.
This rule has been declared for one's own sake or for the sake of others; however, one may abandon it for the sake of others or for the purpose of concealing [one's conduct) from the world. || 188 ||
Relatives other than brothers, sons, and fathers are known as *jñātis*.
When female *jñātis* have given birth, no period of impurity (*āśauca*) is prescribed. (189)
In the case of those men whose children have died at birth, the impurity must be observed for seven generations;
even in that case, the period of impurity lasts for three days beyond the fifth generation.
Beyond that, if the kinsman is known, a period of three days (pakṣiṇī) should be observed; likewise for a Brahmin married according to the rules to the three [lower] castes beginning with the Raktā.
For those born from Brahmins and the other castes who have been produced through improper unions, purification occurs by a reduction of one, two, three, or four days, respectively. || 192 ||
There is no period of impurity for those born in the inverse order of castes, since they are eternally impure;
likewise, women who belong to common [access] are never purified at all.
Kings who are always purified by means of consecration, as well as great ministers, are likewise [liberated] if they are devoted to Maheśvara. (194)
But those Śūdras who are devoted to auspicious rites and are smeared with ashes and other [purificatory substances] become pure in twenty days, while others do so in twenty-five.
Whatever constant loss is caused by the birth or death of a *preta*, its purification lasts for as many days as those [of the impurity]. (196)
The expiation for that purpose consists of eating only barley at night, preceded by bathing three times a day, worship, fire-rituals, recitation, and burnt offerings. || 197 ||
When there is conjunction without loss, at its end there is a period of three nights;
when there is loss without conjunction, there too at the end there are three days.
Whether it be devotion, knowledge, or detachment—whichever one of these a person possesses correctly, that initiate (samayin) should perform the worship. (199)
Even for one in whom these three are extremely weak or even weaker,
the internal sacrifice (antaryāga) must still be performed at the end for two days.

For one day, subsisting on barley or eating sacrificial porridge, one should recite the Aghora mantra a thousand times at the conclusion of the bath, or perform a fire-oblation (homa) consisting of one-tenth that number.

O twice-born ones, this very same rule is declared for one who has not undergone the cutting of the top-knot (*śikhā*) and for one who serves at the feet [of a teacher], provided he remains established in the sacred observance (*samaya*). 202.
