Even for one who has been initiated into Nirvāṇa and whose topknot has been cut, there is eligibility for all rites—whether daily, occasional, or optional. (203)
One who has not undergone the tonsure of the top-knot (śikhā) is unfit for the daily rites;
likewise, all of these [who have not received initiation] are also unfit to enter temples and similar sacred structures. (204)
However, [if performed] outside the main pavilion (agramaṇḍapa), it does not result in any fault. || 2041/2 ||
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, the Ritual for the Final Rites, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
In the twenty-eighth chapter: the Ritual for the Ancestral Sacrifice (Pitṛyajña).
O best of sages, listen as I describe the ritual for the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña),
which is essential for householders who follow the path of the world.
One should lead [the deity] to the ancestral hall in the courtyard, the outer area, or the temple;
there, one should prepare a pedestal according to the prescribed method for pedestals, complete with its three girdles.
The Guru should then dig a new pit in front of that, measuring one cubit,
smear it with cow-dung and water, and place [the deity] in the center of the pedestal.
The broom (kūrca) should be one span in length, made of five or seven [blades of grass],
or measured respectively by the number of Rudras (eleven) or Antakas (eight), for the Brahmins and the other castes in order.
Having offered a seat with the syllable Om using *darbha* grass or excellent *kuśa* grass arranged with their tips pointing toward the south, one should then invoke the form [of the deity].

Having uttered "svadhā," one should cast [the offering] into the form of Devadatta and others, who are endowed with their respective lineages and so forth, together with the subtle soul (ātman) characterized by those qualities.
One should place the Praṇava, endowed with its lineage and other attributes, as the Self;
and [place] the collection of water for the feet and so forth, along with clothing, perfumes, flowers, and sesame seeds.
Incense, lamps, and food offerings fashioned from māḍhaka-measures or even half of that, as well as whatever else may be pleasing to him; || 8 ||
It was prepared with pieces of sugar-cane and ghee, along with side dishes,
served indeed in new earthen vessels by those free from ritual impurity.
One should always offer betel-leaf (tāmbūla) twice daily;
it should be performed at both times, or else once at a single time.
All of this should be offered under that [deity's] name, accompanied by the *svadhā* mantra and the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).
Alternatively, one may offer the *arghya* and *bali*; otherwise, one should prepare the food elsewhere.
Alternatively, three funeral cakes (piṇḍas) should be offered, or only a single pit;
having prepared it, one should place either a brick, a stone, or a shallow bowl within it.
Having placed the *kūrca* as previously described, one should perform this rite there for seven days, nine days, or ten days. || 13 ||
At the end of that [day] or in the afternoon, one should worship according to the previously mentioned rite;
then, having removed the clay from that place, one should take the lump together with the flowers.
Having taken up that brush along with the bricks, or the stone pedestal, and having joined it with incense, lamps, and so forth upon the pedestal and other such items; || 15 ||
Or else, one should cast it together with musical instruments into the middle of a sacred ford (tīrtha);
or one may lead all of this to a meritorious place such as a river and so forth.
The general rule for Brahmins and the others has been stated; now the specific rule is being declared:
ten piṇḍas are prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa, while twelve are recorded for a Kṣatriya. (17)
Fifteen days of impurity are prescribed for a Vaiśya, and thirty are proclaimed for a Śūdra;
as long as this period of impurity lasts, the rites of offering rice-balls (piṇḍa) and water (udaka) must be performed.
On the fifth day, one should offer a single ball of rice; on the second [day], four;
and on the third, five. This is considered the rule for the beginning of the three-day period.
When ten days have passed and the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite has been performed, then a single *piṇḍa* should be offered; there is no impurity (*āśauca*) due to its non-offering.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, the Ritual for the Ancestral Sacrifice (Pitṛyajñavidhi), in the Great Tantra named Uttarakāmika;
in the twenty-ninth chapter, the Ritual for the Śaiva Śrāddha.
Thereafter, the procedure for the *śrāddha* rite is briefly described for those whose souls are initiated:
the daily (*nitya*), the occasional (*naimittika*), the optional (*kāmya*), the prosperity-rite (*vṛddhi*), and the *pārvaṇa*. (1)
Having understood that the śrāddha is declared to be fivefold, one should perform the rite accordingly:
the daily (nitya) should be offered day after day, and the occasional (naimittika) on the anniversary of death.
That which is prescribed for the sake of desire is called *kāmya*; where is the *pārvaṇa* desired?
The *vṛddhi-śrāddha* occurs at marriages and so forth; thus, there are five types of rites. (3)
For that purpose, food given with faith is called *śrāddha*;
its purification is performed according to the distinctions of days, months, years, and so forth.
The Ekoddiṣṭa Śrāddha, once performed, should be repeated every year; after one year has passed, it should be performed especially on the anniversary of the deceased's death.
The first *navaśrāddha* occurs initially;
thereafter, there are sixteen [funeral rites] on the fourth and fifth days, as well as on the ninth and eleventh days.
The gift made with reference to the clay is known as the *nava-śrāddha*;
however, the *nava-śrāddha* is without mantras and is devoid of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water libations.
O best of the twice-born, at the end of the period of impurity, the ekoddiṣṭa rite should be performed without water, without incense, and devoid of perfumes and garlands.
On the eleventh day, after three fortnights, likewise at the end of each month,
and at the half-year mark— the rites performed on these occasions are joined with the annual ceremony.
It is said that there are sixteen śrāddhas; whatever gift is given among these is known as the sixteen-fold śrāddha, and this is remembered as the ekoddiṣṭa.
If these nine and sixteen śrāddhas are not performed for someone,
he remains a piśāca for a long time, even though hundreds of śrāddhas have been offered for him.
At the gate, on a heap of ashes, and in the sky— in this sequence—
the deceased remains as a preta for three days, three days, and one day respectively.
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, he goes to the world of Śiva;
[this applies] from the day of death until the end of the year, performed every single day. (13)
One should offer food and a water-pot to the preceptor himself,
having first performed the nine-fold śrāddha accompanied by the ekoddiṣṭa rite.
Thereafter, the sapindikarana rite, accompanied by the water-pot (sodakumbha),
should be performed with diligence when the [lunar days] are equal, without abandoning celibacy.
At the end of six months, at the end of three months, or at the end of one month, one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite on the second day; thereafter, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is to be performed.
For one whose sapindikarana takes place before the completion of a year,
his preceptor should provide food along with a water-pot for as long as the year has not passed.
One should first perform the *nava-śrāddha* together with the *ekoddiṣṭa*, followed by the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the feeding [of Brahmins], and the annual anniversary rite (*ekavardhana*).
That [remnant] should indeed be gathered together; specifically, it should be offered to the Guru himself, or to Śiva, or else to one who has been initiated.
At the conclusion of the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, however, the *pakṣa-śrāddha* is prescribed for Vaiśyas;
likewise, the fortnightly (*pākṣika*) and monthly (*māsika*) *śrāddhas* shall be performed by Śūdras. (20)
Everything else would be the same for the three castes as it is for the Brāhmaṇas, especially when the sun has entered the sign of Aquarius during the dark fortnight. || 21 ||
The fourth, the seventh, the ninth, the thirteenth, the new moon day,
and the Maghā constellation— on these one should designate the fortnight of the ancestors (pitṛpakṣa).

On the eighth day, on the remaining festival days, and during the Vyatīpāta yoga, at the solstices, or even upon the appearance of Rāhu (an eclipse), one should perform the rite for the group of Mothers.

One should perform [the rite] even for those who died by poison, during the Gajacchāyā, at the Saṃkrānti, and so forth, as well as for those who died by the method of weapons, fire, falling from a cliff, or entering water. (24)
One should perform the Śrāddha for these on the fourteenth day for their complete satisfaction;
or it may be performed at other times as well, provided that the wealth and the worthy recipient are available.
A Śrāddha for a Rākṣasa should be performed at night, as well as during both twilights;
it may also be performed at night if there is an eclipse of the moon (Rāhudarśana).
A householder who has sons should not perform a Śrāddha on the thirteenth lunar day;
for one performing a Śrāddha under the Maghā asterism, the eldest son perishes.
If one performs the *navaśrāddha* on the fourteenth day of the month of Nandā, or during the three [specific] births, it will cause the destruction of the lineage. (28)
If one performs a śrāddha on the days of Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, or the Moon, it portends the death of the performer.
The asterisms of Pauṣṇa, Āditya, Aindrāgna, Rohiṇī, the three Uttarās, one's own three births, and likewise the twenty-fourth asterism; || 30 ||
Indeed, that month which lacks the new-moon day (amāvāsyā) is impure and a source of sin;
it is censured by the ancestors and the gods, and one should avoid it in all ritual acts.
One should diligently perform the obligatory and occasional rites during the intercalary month (malimluca),
as well as on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha and the third day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika.
The ninth lunar day of the dark fortnight in the month of Nabhasya shall be the new moon;
likewise, the thirteenth lunar day in Māgha is considered the fifteenth (the full moon).
On the three Aṣṭakā days, during the solstices, and also during eclipses of the sun and moon—
at these times, one should offer water mixed with sesame seeds.
That śrāddha indeed becomes equal to a thousand years; of this there is no doubt.
When the sun has entered the sign of Virgo, the ancestors indeed go toward their sons.
Then, upon encountering the scorpion, the ancestors departed in despair;
thereafter, having uttered a most terrible curse, they returned to their own abode. (37)
One who does not perform that ancestral rite (śrāddha) sinks like a cow in the mud;
those who have received [the lineage] maintain a noble succession, like birds on a peepal tree.
"With honey, meat, cooked foods, milk, and milk-rice, he will offer us the śrāddha during the rainy season under the Maghā asterism. (39)
The Śrāddha for the gods is performed in the forenoon, while that for the ancestors is in the afternoon;
the Ekoddiṣṭa is at midday, and that occasioned by prosperity (Vṛddhi) is in the morning.
O best of the twice-born, the *ām-śrāddha* should be performed in the forenoon during the bright fortnight, but in the afternoon during the dark fortnight. (41)

In the event of a fire, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), during an eclipse of the moon or sun, or when one is incapable, the *āmaśrāddha* (offering of raw food) may be performed; indeed, it should always be performed by Śūdras and others.

All those beginning with the best of the twice-born (dvijottama) are commended for the perfection of a śrāddha; they should be accepted according to the excellence of their own caste, or else those born within their respective castes.
The characteristics of a teacher have been declared; one should not, however, disparage those who possess such characteristics.
A knower of dharma does not examine a Brahmin for a rite dedicated to the gods.
When a rite for the ancestors has arrived, one should examine [the recipient] with great care;
for that which is given to one who is devoid of benefit is indeed *sāttvika*. (45)

O twice-born ones, that which is given with a joyful heart and a pure disposition to a learned man who possesses great knowledge for the sake of attaining the wisdom of Śiva is considered *sāttvika*. (46)

Whatever is given to one who is devoid of the Śiva scriptures, even if he has previously rendered assistance, and whatever is given to one who is merely prosperous— all that is considered to be of the nature of passion (rājasa).
O you of excellent vows, that gift which is given to a relative who does not abide by his vows,
and that which is given at night by those seeking rewards— that gift is considered to be of the nature of passion (rājasa).
That gift which is given even to a thief— one who is devoid of the worship of Śiva and so forth, and who steals the knowledge of Śiva— is remembered as tāmasa.
That gift which is given with anger, with the sacred thread not worn over the right shoulder (apasavya), with contempt,
or to a servant, is declared to be tāmasa.
Thus has the primary rule (kalpa) been fully explained; now the secondary rule (anukalpa) is being described:
the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the sister’s son, the father-in-law, and the teacher. (51)
A daughter's son, the husband of a harlot, a kinsman, an officiating priest, or even a low-caste man are considered [eligible];
one should diligently feed a daughter's son at a śrāddha, even if he is observing a vow.
But in the absence of monks, one should feed a celibate student (brahmacārin). Having performed a śrāddha, he who, being deluded, eats at another's śrāddha [commits an offense]. (53)

His ancestors fall away, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and water; likewise, [the ancestors of one who engages in] eating a second time, traveling on a journey, carrying a burden, Vedic study, or sexual intercourse [fall]. (54)
One should avoid giving gifts, accepting them, performing fire-sacrifices, or eating at a *śrāddha* for eight days after having partaken of such a meal.
As for that man who, having made a formal invitation for the sake of a *śrāddha*, does not provide it; || 55 ||

He who, having been invited to a Śrāddha according to the ritual manual, does not eat during the performance of the Śrāddha rite, shall go to the Raurava hell at the request of that [inviter]. || 56 ||
Such a person undoubtedly falls into the Kumbhīpāka hell;
in this regard, they praise three qualities: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.
In a Śrāddha ceremony, there are three purifiers: excellent Kuśa grass, a Kutapa blanket, and sesame seeds;
likewise, rock salt and that which originates from Lake Mānasa.
For these two are indeed the supreme purifiers, even perceptibly and eternally; likewise, asafoetida is recommended, as are non-dried condiments. (59)
Whatever is cooked in the house, whether it be food for chewing or food for swallowing,
one must never eat it without first offering it, nor ever consume it for the sake of the funeral oblation (*piṇḍa*).
Kodrava, all types of salt, as well as jambu fruits, pumpkin, bottle-gourd, eggplant, and even buffalo milk; || 61 ||
One should avoid the citron fruit, mung beans, black pepper, long pepper, all types of prepared salt, and the tips of bamboo shoots.
One should avoid all red substances, with the exception of saffron alone; likewise, one should avoid resinous exudates that are reddish in color and all types of visible salts.
That which stands on the bank, that which has been touched by the feet, that which is white, and that which has stood overnight;
likewise oil-cakes, churned curds, and that which is excessively salty.
But those oils, salt, and condiments which are given with the hand do not reach the giver; rather, the eater consumes the sin. (65)
A śrāddha performed without the thumb, an oblation offered with the knees outside [the thighs],
and food eaten with the knees outside— all such acts belong entirely to the asuras.
Giving, receiving, burnt offerings, eating, and even the offering of oblations—these must be performed with the thumb; otherwise, they become demonic.

One should especially perform the sipping of water (ācamana) with the hands between the knees; likewise, in the forenoon, one should use *darbha* grass as a purifier and all kinds of sacrificial food (*haviṣya*).
But those who have been invited to a Śrāddha or a rite for the gods, if one should serve them meat, he falls into hell for as many years as there are hairs on the body of that animal. (69)
He who eats with his head wrapped, he who eats facing south, and he who eats wearing shoes— it is indeed the Rākṣasas who eat that food.
If one causes the ancestors to be fed at a śrāddha from earthen vessels,
both the giver of the food provided by the officiant and the eater shall go to hell.
Sprinkling with water that has been in contact with a corpse is especially recommended;
however, one engaged in ritual action should avoid touching anything below the navel.
From irreproachable faith, there shall arise long life, sons, wealth, wisdom, incomparable good fortune, fame, friends, health, and prosperity. (73)
Constant loss, mental anguish, the destruction of friends, the depletion of prosperity, quarrels, and exile shall result from performing a Śrāddha at a censured place. (74)
The *bhautika* and the *brahmacārī* are the most excellent for the performance of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*);
having obtained the *santānika* [water] from Śiva, it grants the desired fruits for the sake of the ancestors and the gods. (75)
What man would ever despair after obtaining as a guest one who is devoted to his lifelong vows, especially a high-souled Brāhmaṇa who knows the meaning of the four Vedas? (76)
When the teacher has eaten, it is as if ten million have been fed;
when the practitioner has eaten, it is as if one hundred thousand; and when the initiate has eaten, it is as if ten thousand.
One thousand [should be fed] for one established in the *samaya*; one hundred for a man devoted to Maheśvara;
two practitioners for the sake of the deity; and three preceptors for the sake of the ancestors. (78)
In the case of a *saṃbhava-śrāddha*, it is said that all [deities] are present everywhere as those who favor the left;
however, in the *śiva-śrāddha*, Īśa, Sadāśiva, Śānta, and Śiva are proclaimed [as the presiding deities].
O twice-born ones, Rudra and Ananta are declared to be the Viśvedevas;
these are said to belong to those who have received initiation, and now the portions of Rudra are being described.
Skanda, Caṇḍa, and Gaṇeśa—these three are declared for the sake of the ancestors (pitṛs).
Among them, the two attendants Nandin and Mahākāla are stationed in the pair [of the first two]. (81)
When they are satisfied, everything on earth, up to Śiva himself, becomes satisfied. When the fivefold absence [of duality] occurs therein, then that conception of duality ceases.
The triad of conceptualizations should be located at the base of the arms and the head;
for two [deities], one should be placed on one side and the other on the other, with the two shoulders serving as their respective locations.
Alternatively, one may fashion five [deities] together with a pair of arms on a single [pedestal];
for householders, it should have six deities, but for those bearing sectarian marks (liṅgin), three deities.
Having thus resolved, one should perform the śrāddha rite;
on the preceding day, one should diligently invite the guests according to their seniority.
Having touched the two calves of the elders, the hands of his equals,
and having comforted those younger than him with kind words for a moment, he [did this] to them.
The excellent preceptor who performs the śrāddha, accompanied by the offering of betel-leaf,
shall dwell that night while they remember the Supreme Lord.
Having restrained the collection of his senses and having shown favor and compassion toward the subjects,
on the following day he performed the rites of bathing, worship, and so forth for them.
In the afternoon, however, having performed the rites of bathing and so forth,
he should address those who have arrived with a welcome, including rising from his seat and offering a seat.
Having honored him, one should prepare circles for the washing of his feet on the level courtyard of the house, well-smeared with cow-dung and water.
In a location filled on all sides with lines of the arena,
there are two squares in the east and two well-rounded circles in the west.
Situated to the south and north, at a distance of one cubit between them,
there should be a circular altar (pratimaṇḍala) in front of the pit, measuring twelve finger-breadths.
In the Śrāddha for the mother and the Śrāddha for the father, one should prepare either a mandala or a pit for the sake of the ancestors,
and offer the Arghya water into five vessels.

With perfumes, flowers, kusha grass, and water, accompanied by the limbs of the Vidyā and joined with the Brahma-mantra—one uses water mixed with barley for the sake of the gods, and water mixed with sesame seeds for the sake of the ancestors. || 94 ||
Having sprinkled [the garments] with water for the *arghya* offering, one should consecrate them with the mantras of the limbs of the Vidyā;
likewise, the cloths with the Puruṣa mantra and the perfume with the Hṛdaya mantra. (95)
One should offer flowers with the *brahmaśiras* mantra and incense and lamps with the *śikhā* mantra; any other unmentioned limb of the *śrāddha* rite should be consecrated with the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Having thus purified the substances, one should then perform the ritual action:
having scattered barley grains upon the two upright [posts] and sesame seeds upon the two well-rounded ones.
Having laid down kusha grass across the middle, one should place the ball of rice for the deceased on the south;
one should worship the mandala situated on the south, along with its hermitage, using the weapon-mantra which is a limb of knowledge.

With fragrant white flowers and the like, using the heart-mantra of the limbs of the Vidyā, preceded by the Praṇava and joined with their respective names, [one should worship] that which abides in the gentle [direction]. (99)
In the western mandala, one should worship with the back of the hand using the sacrificial thread placed over the left shoulder (apasavya), ending with "svāhā" and concluding with "svadhā. || 100 ||
Having taken the arghya water separately for each vessel, he should give it to the feet in succession;
then, having offered the arghya and taken earth, he should wash the feet.
Having thus given these two the water for sipping (ācamana) from the gentle mandalas with very cool water, and after they have sipped it, he should then lead them inside.
On a smeared and pure spot to the south, provided with the syllable Om,
he should have them sit upon well-washed seats once they have been identified.
Then he should request them, saying, "I shall perform the śrāddha";
being thus authorized with the words "Do so," he should offer a seat of darbha grass to two [of the ancestors].
But it must not be placed directly into the hands for the ancestors or the Viśvedevas;
rather, having placed the upper garment over the left shoulder, one should offer it with its tip pointing northward upon an uncut [blade of grass].
He should say, "I invoke," when told by them, "Invoke.
Being thus authorized with the words "Invoke," he should do so using his own name preceded by the syllable *praṇava* (Om).

Having performed the three [rites] beginning with *sthāpanā*, the knower of mantras, taking barley for the sake of protection, should then scatter it all around while reciting the *vāmadeva* [mantra].
Then, during the circumambulation itself, one should offer the *arghya* water at the two corners of the cloth;
for the sake of the presence of the two [deities], one should offer it once for each.
Having accepted that arghya and placed it upon a vessel on the ground,
one should kneel upon the earth and worship with barley using the Aghora mantra.
Starting from the feet and proceeding step by step across all his limbs with reverence,
he anointed his entire body with fragrant unguents and adorned him with garlands of flowers.
The wise one should offer incense with the Vāmadeva mantra in its embodied form,
offer the lamp with that same mantra, and offer the sacred thread (pavitraka) with the Īśāna mantra.
One should respectfully offer clothing along with a shawl and a finger-ring; then one should offer another limb [of the body] according to the sequence of the sacred thread (upavīta).

Then, having performed the *apasavya* (leftward) circumambulation for the ancestors—which is anticlockwise—and having offered double-folded *kuśa* grass with the *sadyojāta* mantra, [he should proceed]. || 113 ||
Having been authorized by the ancestors, he should invoke them while recollecting their respective mantras;
having performed the three rites beginning with installation, he should proceed counter-clockwise using only the left hand.
Then the Lord should offer protection with sesame seeds and again offer water for the arghya;
for the purpose of bringing the three [deities] into proximity, he should separately offer [water] into his joined palms with the Aghora mantra.
Having accepted the object as before, he should place it held in his joined palms; with his knee resting on the ground, he should [anoint] starting from the head in due order by means of the Lord.

One should worship with sesame seeds while recollecting the Vāmadeva mantra; thereafter, one should cause perfumes and so forth, as well as incense and lamps, to be offered by means of the Rūpin mantra.
With the *īśāna* mantra, beginning with the purification and ending with *svadhā*, one should perform the rite in the counter-clockwise direction (*apasavya*).
"May it be full" should be said by [the performer], and "May it be full" should also be said by them.
Then, having placed those remnants in their vessel according to the prescribed rule, one should set the vessel face down with the words, "Thou art the station of the ancestors. (119)
Taking a pure vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or leaf, one should provide it for the meal.
Having given water for washing the hands, one should cleanse them again;
and to eliminate the defect of the row, one should perform the *tuṣopahāraka* rites.
"O twice-born ones, for the sake of purifying all [the cooked offerings], preceded by oblations into the auspicious fire, I shall perform the homa in the Śiva-fire; thus he should ask. (122)
Permitted with the words "Do so," he should then perform the oblation (homa) in the fire, [reciting]:
"To Soma accompanied by the ancestors (pitṛmat), svadhā, obeisance (namaḥ)," ending in the dative case.
Then, having uttered "To Yama," and having said "To Aṅgiras, svadhā, obeisance," and then "To Agni Kavyavāhana, svadhā, obeisance. (124)
One should offer the remnants of the oblation while remembering Nara during the meals;
however, for the sake of the ancestors and for the sake of the rice-balls (piṇḍas), one should not offer them to the Viśvedevas.
A man, free from anger, should give desired food and sacrificial oblations;
he should indeed give sweet food soaked in ghee.
Having touched it with the Aghora mantra, one should consecrate that vessel for the purpose of purification; then, [placing] the left hand face-downward, || 127 ||
Having grasped its thumb with one's own hand and inserted it at the end,
one should mutter either the secret mantra or the Mṛtyujit mantra.
For the sake of immortality, one should circulate water all around with the hand;
for the purpose of *āpośana*, one should first offer it into the lotus of the hand.
When it is said, "Eat what is pure," they too should eat while remaining restrained in speech.
One should feed the guest according to one's ability; one should not deliberate over whether it is the right time or not.
The gods, the goddesses, Guha, Viṣṇu, and Dharma himself in embodied form wander about in the guise of guests; therefore, one should not scrutinize them.

Facing north, he should remain reciting [the mantra] dedicated to Īśāna until satisfied; when the food has been offered, he should say, "Are you satisfied? and when it is replied, "We are fully satisfied," [he should respond]. 132.
One should place that food on the ground together with water once;
near the remains of the meal, one should prepare a mandala using cow dung alone.
Having spread out kusa grass with its tips pointing toward the south, as well as sesame seeds with their husks intact,
he should place on his left [hand] rice mixed with sesame and accompanied by all [the other offerings].
Facing the south, standing on the ground with his right knee touching the earth, he should offer three funeral cakes (piṇḍas) mixed with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.
One should place darbha grasses upon it, starting from the northeast (Īśāna) and proceeding in order with the [mantras] beginning with Śambara,
while pouring a stream of water and reciting the Vāmadeva mantra.
For the purpose of clothing, one should offer linen or cotton thread as an ointment;
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should prostrate and ask for forgiveness.
Saying "Forgive me," the knower of mantras should withdraw [the visualization], perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana),
and then first offer the preliminary ācamana to the three [ancestors] and subsequently to the two [living relatives].
One should give betel-leaf for the purification of the mouth to those with clean hands, as well as camphor, fine garments, and household utensils. (139)
For their satisfaction, he should give cows, land, servants, and so forth as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
The performer of the śrāddha, facing south, should offer a vessel filled with water known as the *vardhanī*.
Having held [the vessel], one should recite the syllable *svadhā* and say, "Let it be spoken.
Thereafter, one should utter the triad beginning with Īśa, ending in the dative case.
After the performer of the Śrāddha has uttered "svadhā" at the end, all those beginning with Īśāna should say, "May it be svadhā. Then he should pour water upon the ground.
In this manner, it should be performed three times; thereafter, they should recite, and he himself should recite: "May the gods and the Rudras be satisfied."
"May our donors prosper, as well as the lineage of Śiva.
When these words were spoken by them, O best of the twice-born, he replied with this speech: || 144 ||
Furthermore, the performer should say "Civam," and then the one who performs the śrāddha should say:
"May our faith not fail, and may we have much to give. (145)
Having spoken these affectionate words, he should prostrate and ask for forgiveness;
into that vessel in which the remnants of the offerings were previously placed, [he should pour the water].
Having turned that vessel for the ancestors face upwards, he should then dismiss them;
with the Sadyojāta mantra, he should follow after the ancestors first.
When the performer of the śrāddha asks, "What should be done with the remnants of the food?", those who grant desired boons should say, "It should be eaten together with those you hold dear. (148)
One should give portions of the rice-balls to cows, to Brahmins, or cast them into fire or water;
or the wife of the family head may eat the middle rice-ball.
Then, from her, a son is born who is a portion of Rudra, endowed with auspicious marks,
steadfast, illustrious, renowned, and one who has reached the further shore of learning and its lineage.

In the sixteen purificatory rites beginning with conception (garbhādhāna), as well as in the Nāndīmukha rite for prosperity, a learned man should not offer libations to the ancestors in the śrāddha ceremony. || 151 ||
Likewise, at the Nāndīmukha rite and at other ceremonies for all auspicious occasions,
one should perform the ritual acts by offering rice-balls mixed with curd and jujube fruits made from barley.
One should not perform the *apasavya* rite, nor should one circumambulate counter-clockwise;
in *vṛddhi-śrāddhas*, one should always offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) while facing the east.
And one should offer the rice-ball (piṇḍa) upon darbha grass with its tips pointing forward during rites for prosperity (vṛddhi).
Without having performed the ancestral rite (śrāddha), one should not perform any other ritual act. 154.
The daily *śrāddha* should be without a deity, and likewise the *ekoddiṣṭa*.
The *ekoddiṣṭa* is devoid of deities, having only one *arghya* offering and a single *pavitraka*.
The rite is performed without the invocation (āvāhana) and the fire-offering (agnikaraṇa), with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya);
at the place where the "imperishable" (akṣayya) offering is normally made, they are dismissed with the words, "May you rise. || 156 ||
One should say, "May you enjoy yourselves," and they should reply, "We have enjoyed ourselves.
Or else, a single man who is an expert in omens may be appointed as the leader. (157)
All rites may be performed under one's own name as before; however, [the merit] shall be great, consisting of cows, land, gold, fine houses, vehicles, clothing, and so forth. (158)
Garments, bronze vessels, various kinds of grain, a seat, a palm-leaf fan, an umbrella, and a pair of sandals; 159.
One should give his bed provided with pillows and whatever else belongs to him,
accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and separately offer ten thousand water-pots.
On the day at the end of the period of impurity, however, this Ekoddiṣṭa rite becomes "great";
it includes the mantra for the Navaśrāddha, but is devoid of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) and the water libations.
Without water, without incense, and devoid of perfumes and garlands—
this is declared to be the *piṇḍodaka* (water for the funeral cake) for one who has placed the funeral cake in the alms-bowl.
O twice-born ones, it is not desired that the rice-ball be rotated above while held in a stream of water;
likewise, one should not perform a prostration or utter the word "svadhā. (163)
That offering into the fire is not performed in response to the question regarding the best of Brahmins;
however, the formula "I shall offer into the fire" (agnau kariṣye) is prescribed even in the case of an Ekoddiṣṭa rite.
With food fit for oblation they remain satisfied for a month, but with milk-rice (pāyasa) for a year;
thus the ancestors, bestowing blessings upon those who are disciplined, offer their praise.
The ancestors are satisfied for a month by the offering of red śāli rice and other grains served with various side dishes; of this there is no doubt. (166)
A śrāddha performed at Gayā is said to bestow infinite merit in its entirety.
One should prepare four vessels filled with scented water and sesame seeds.
For the sake of the *arghya* offering, one should pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors, using their names preceded by "aghora" and ending with "bhava. (168)
Saying "Oṃ" and "Thus indeed, O Father," one should perform the remaining rites as previously described.
However, three vessels for the ancestors are considered intended for the specific purpose [of the rite]. (169)
This sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite for a woman, however, should be performed as an ekoddiṣṭa;
it serves the purpose of all rites, just as previously described.
All rites prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be performed using one's own name;
thereafter, one should perform all rituals using the names of Īśa and the other [deities]. (171)
If one should join the *piṇḍa* that has already been consolidated with a separate *piṇḍa*, the performer will certainly become a slayer of his father and a slayer of his mother. (172)
One desiring long life shall obtain long life; one desiring wealth shall obtain riches;
one desiring knowledge shall obtain stainless knowledge; and one desiring pleasure shall obtain excellent women.
Sons, good fortune, health, fame, valor, prosperity, and happiness—the giver of the śrāddha obtains these constantly and does not come to grief. (174)
The Śrāddha for a deceased father should indeed be performed by his sons who are initiated, as well as by kinsmen, relatives, friends, disciples, servants, and teachers who are initiated. (175)
In the absence of a son, however, the wife shall perform the rite; in the absence of a wife, the uterine brother;
for even one who is uninitiated and has not received the sacred thread is indeed qualified for the Śrāddha ceremony.
One whose tonsure ceremony has been performed should indeed offer water and funeral cakes;
he should employ the utterance of "svadhā," but he should not be made to recite mantras. || 177 ||

One should not eat with only one garment on, nor should one perform the worship of the deities; likewise, one should not give gifts, perform ritual sipping (ācamana), offer oblations (homa), eat, or worship the deities in such a state. 178.
One should perform the private recitation of the Vedas and the libations to the ancestors with the foot placed upon a stool,
or likewise with the foot resting upon the knees or the shanks.
But he who performs the offering for his ancestors on land belonging to another, that Śrāddha rite is enjoyed by the ancestors of the owner of that land. (180)
Wildernesses, uncultivated forests, and riverbanks—all these are indeed without owners; one should perform the *śrāddha* and other rites in them. (181)
A Caṇḍāla, a boar, a cock, likewise a woman in her menses, and a eunuch—these must not look upon twice-born men while they are eating. 182.
If they even look on while the house is being given away or at a meal,
then the offerings for the gods and the ancestors go astray.
The Vṛddha-śrāvakas, Nirgranthas, Śākyas, and likewise the Jīvantikas—those who do not follow the Dharma are considered to be the Nagnas and others. || 184 ||

If these [unworthy persons] should indeed behold the food intended for the offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya), the primary portion must be discarded; furthermore, it is prescribed that purification should be performed in such a calamity.
The eighth part of the day, when the sun has grown dim, is called *kutapa*; one should perform rites for the ancestors during that time. (186)
Alternatively, the *kutapa* is described here in another way:
the word of Śiva, purity, and freedom from anger; those devoted to these, along with worthy recipients and the sacred fire, constitute it. (187)
Sesame, Darbha grass, and the proper time—these nine are remembered as Kutapas;
likewise, the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather [are so designated]. (188)

The other group is common to all; one's own father and so forth are not considered [in that category]. Likewise, the lineage of Īśa and others, as well as that of the maternal grandfather and others, have been declared [to be common]. (189)
The mother eats the śrāddha food, which is like nectar, together with her own husband;
likewise the paternal grandmother, and likewise the great-grandmother with her own husband.
Three funeral cakes (piṇḍas) should be offered; by performing it in this manner, one does not become deluded.
The Śrāddha for the mother should be performed on an even-numbered day, and always facing eastward. 191.
The śrāddha for the mother should come first, and that for the fathers immediately after;
however, if she has died childless, the husband shall perform the sapindīkaraṇa rite.
The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite must be performed until the *sapiṇḍana* of the parents is completed;
after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, one should discontinue the *ekoddiṣṭa*.
From that point onward, the offering of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) is not prescribed separately for those who have died childless, whether they be women or men. (194)
For them as well, only the ekoddiṣṭa rite should be performed, not the pārvaṇa;
the twice-born invited for the meal should be those chosen for the wives of the three ancestors beginning with the father. (195)
Or rather, O best of the twice-born, one should give [the offerings] in the mother’s śrāddha only to women;
for a woman falls from her own gotra at the seventh step of the marriage ceremony.
The offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) and water for her must be performed by [the husband] using his own lineage name,
together with meat, marrow, and so forth, while reciting the mantras of the fourth oblation.
She attained oneness with her husband; therefore, she shares his lineage.
The mantras recited at the taking of the hand cause the relinquishment of the father's lineage. (198)
In the case of marriages such as the Āsura and others, a certain distinction is prescribed:
one should offer the oblation using the lineage (gotra) of whichever husband the women have taken. || 199 ||
But if she is of unblemished womb and has remained steadfast in another [husband's] family, then the funeral cake, the śrāddha, and likewise the water-offering must be given by her own lineage. (200)
When the mother has passed away, however, the sapindikarana and subsequent rites shall follow the paternal lineage;
thereafter, the deity is the father.
Having relinquished the paternal lineage, one should not perform [the rite] according to the maternal lineage.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Śaiva Śrāddha," in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
In the thirtieth chapter is the ritual for expiation (prāyaścitta).
I shall declare the rules for expiation; listen, O best of the twice-born!
Injunction is considered to be of two kinds: namely, positive precept and prohibition. (1)
If that [work] is carried out, there will be a proper compendium of Dharma;
but in the opposite case, there would be Adharma, and by that, great sin would arise.
Therefore, when downward movement would otherwise occur,
that which leads the agent to the supreme state above is declared here in the scripture to be the expiation (prāyaścitta).
Because it is equal to that which is most excellent, the fault is generally proclaimed;
however, in the scripture, the conscious self (cidātman) is described as "crossing over" (taraṇa) by means of the letter *ta*.
O Brahmins, because the crossing of the self when it falls downward is accompanied by fault, therefore, O those who have taken refuge in Śiva, expiation (prāyaścitta) has been proclaimed.
There is no action, whether enjoined or prohibited, which, when performed, results in neither merit nor sin; such is the certain conclusion of the meaning of the scriptures. (6)
When the necessary rite has been performed, the counter-rite must be carried out facing east;
it may also be done facing west or from a corner direction.
O elder brothers, it is not possible to state the expiation for each specific distinction,
because the actions are infinite and due to the fault of excessive prolixity in the text.
Thereafter, the eternal atonement is briefly described:
bathing, recitation, meditation on Śiva, breath control, and circumambulation. (9)
The vision of the *liṅga*, of those free from passion and the like, of one's own guru and the spiritual teacher, and of those devoted to the knowledge of Śiva—that is "beholding" (*nirīkṣaṇa*). (10)

For those whose souls have been initiated, their practice consists of beginning with salutations, serving in the abode of Śiva, worshipping the fire of Śiva and the Guru, and taking their meals [only after these rites]. (11)
Then follows bathing in meritorious holy waters (tīrtha), consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
the water of Śiva’s weapon-mantra, initiation (dīkṣā), and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) at a sacred site.
The fast, the consumption of the sacrificial porridge, and eating what remains in the vessel;
the rite of pacification, the pacificatory oblation, that which is called the offering to the directions, and the oblation of the *saṃhitā*—[these constitute the daily duties]. (13)

The fire-offering for the image, the various rites such as bathing with ghee, honey, and milk, festivals lasting one day or more, the cold-water jar, and special worship—[these are the forms of service]. 14.
Thus has the eternal expiation been set forth;
having distinguished their characteristics, that of some is now described here. (15)
Born of a family of auspicious twice-borns who subsisted on the five types of pure food,
he wore a turban, an upper garment, and was clad in new clothes.
Adorned with the five-fold ornaments, the preceptor should perform the expiation;
whether it be an extraordinary penance or for the sake of pacification, he should immediately perform the rite with sesame seeds.
In this case, the examination of the day, fortnight, asterism, ascendant, and so forth, is not approved;
it is proclaimed that if the expiation is performed immediately, it is most excellent.
That which occurs within seven days is middling; that which occurs after a fortnight is inferior. That which concludes after a month is designated as the lowest. || 19 ||
If one should perform [the rites] with pacification (śānti), one must not do so after more than a month has passed;
for the construction of the liṅga, pedestal, temple, and so forth, one should apply the appropriate expiations and other rites.
O best of the twice-born, whether at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end, when a penance has arisen for the sake of reconnection, either the performer or the preceptor [should act]. (21)
Or when the local officials should remain indifferent toward the performance of the rite due to lack of funds, mental agitation, or causes such as attachment and aversion; || 22 ||
"O King, because of their assault through evil deeds, these men who hate me have been born as causes of national upheaval for the sake of your defeat. (23)
And those mortals who seize the property of the gods, who likewise deserve such punishment, should be admonished by my devotees—those ascetics who are free from passion. (24)
"Those best of men who are mine—those who act for the king's benefit, whose deeds are meritorious, and who nourish the kingdom—should perform atonement with faith. (25)
"Knowing that these [transgressions] cause the ruin of the village and are the causes for the decrease of one's own worship and prosperity, one should diligently perform expiation. (26)
Then one should perform the recitation of the mantra and the bath with the prescribed ashes;
facing north for the mantra-body, or facing east, one should hold a rosary of akṣa seeds.
Or the Śivānu, or the Aghora, or the excellent Pāśupata; or the Aghorāstra, or the Śivāstra, or again the Brahmāstras and the ancillary mantras (aṅgas).

One should recite the *melā-mantra*, or another [mantra], starting from one hundred up to a *parārdha*, in accordance with that; meanwhile, one should eat measured portions of sacrificial food (*haviṣya*).
Then he may be without food, or subsisting on alms, eating sacrificial porridge, or drinking milk;
or he may consume vegetables, barley-gruel, oil-cakes, tubers, roots, and fruits.
Recalling that form of the deity and muttering the mantra, one should offer it to Him; this is declared to be *japa*. Now, circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*) is described.
That has been described as being of various kinds according to the distinction between internal and external;
among the liṅgas and temples, it is proclaimed as superior or inferior.
Within the inner circle, the hall, and so forth, the interior is proclaimed to be the best;
it is not possible to perform circumambulation within the womb (the inner sanctum), as it would cause many defects.
The shadow of the liṅga within the inner sanctum, the mixing of offerings (nirmālya), the base of the *somasūtra*, or even the immediate vicinity of the deity [are forbidden]. (34)
If everything is performed after having avoided [the prohibited areas], it brings all fruits;
even within the region of the inner circle (antarmaṇḍala), the Soma-line exists.
It may be half the size of the temple or equal in size to the temple; there may even be a mixture of discarded offerings (nirmālya), and the shadow of the building is also present. || 36 ||
Having avoided all of that, one should then perform circumambulation;
the circumambulation should be performed by way of both the left and the right paths.
The left side is the region of Caṇḍa, while the other is from the line of Soma;
one should perform [the rite] with a gentle gait by way of the left and right paths.
In this manner, one should proceed to the left or to the right even during an internal perpetual festival;
likewise, one must avoid stepping over the shadow of the Abode or during a festival for the God of Gods. (39)
For one who has performed service at that time, it shall not be a source of fault;
nor is there even the slightest entry of fault outside of that. (40)
Even with great effort, there may be many external steps;
yet at every step, the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices shall accrue. || 41 ||
Furthermore, O Brahmins, there is the circumambulation limb by limb from sunrise until sunset;
it is impossible to describe the greatness of the merit of these two.
However, due to the greatness of this sacred field (kṣetra), these same [acts] shall yield infinite fruit.
Thus is the circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa) proclaimed; therein the water of Śiva (śivāmbhas) is now described.
Either in a water-pot or a jar placed upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), provided with thread, cloth, gold, water, a tuft of grass (kūrca), and sandalwood; || 44 ||

Having worshipped it with the limbs [of Śiva] and the Brahma-mantras, that water which remains therein is designated as "Śivāmbhas" (the Water of Śiva); and by reciting the Astra-mantra, it becomes the Astra-water.
Then the Mṛcchra and others are declared, followed by another known as Taptakṛcchra;
then the two, Atikṛcchra and Parāka, and after that the procedure for Cāndrāyaṇa.
One should eat a single meal for three nights and then observe a fast for three days;
thus is the *kṛcchra* penance described, which is known as the *prājāpatya*.

One should drink warm water for three days, eat food with milk for three days, consume warm clarified butter for three days, and when [the fever] is alone, one should remain on [warm water] for three days. (48)
That which is known as *taptakṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* is now described:
[one should consume] twenty-one *nakṣatras* (measures) of milk, three *palas* in total, for one's meal. || 49 ||
The *atikṛcchra* has been fully described; now the *parāka* is explained here.
Abstaining from food for twelve days is traditionally remembered as the *parāka*.
For half a month there should be an increase of morsels in the bright fortnight, and one should decrease them in the dark fortnight;
this is declared to be the procedure for Cāndrāyaṇa, which is essentially composed of water.
One who intends to travel should avoid the four meals— the evening meal at the beginning and end of the day, and the morning and evening meals during the middle of the day— by observing a fast.
Alternatively, a fast is declared to consist of two middle [meals], or half of that, or even a gift alone; in this context, it is called "pacification" (śānti).
One should construct the pavilion in an auspicious direction, or in the southeast or east according to the prescribed method;
then, having prepared a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in its center measuring one cubit.
Then, having dismissed the artisan, one should perform the sprinkling with "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) mantras;
having purified the deity according to the rule, one should conduct the ritual bathing every day.
Having worshipped with abundant perfumes and other offerings, one should commence the rite of pacification;
having consecrated the sacrificial pit and the fire, one should satisfy Śiva along with his limbs (attendants).
Or else, he should employ the Aghora weapon, or the Śaiva weapon, or the Pāśupata;
or another well-mastered Aghora weapon by means of the self of the preceptor.

Having worshipped [the deity] in the pericarp (karṇikā), one should then satisfy [him] along with his limbs (aṅgas), offering sacrificial fuel (samit), clarified butter (ājya) from a cow, and the three sweets (madhuratra) combined together. 58.
One should offer pure food or milk-rice (pāyasa) combined with sesame seeds, dūrvā grass, and unbroken rice (akṣata),
either a thousand times, half of that, or one hundred and eight times.
Every day, one should offer oblations while first reciting these mantras;
at the end of "svāhā," one should then say: "O Blessed One, the state that destroys all obstacles. (60)
One should perform the *kurukuru* rite joined with each mantra at intervals of ten,
or even at intervals of fifty, or at intervals of a hundred mantras.
Having thus completed the recitation and the fire-oblation (homa), one should perform the final rite (pūrṇāhuti) at the end;
and having offered betel-leaf accompanied by mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa).

The Śiva-knowledge, beginning with the Kāmika, is established in five directions; those who have reached the further shore of the scriptures should recite it as it arises from the face of each respective direction.
There, the initiated ones should recite the terrible Tatpuruṣa in the east, Vāma in the south, Jāta in the west, and Īśāna in the north.
Four who have mastered the Vedas should perform the recitation of the *Ṛgveda* and the other [Vedas];
many chanters, or even one, should recite the collection of hymns (*stotra-saṃhati*).
Those who are refined by the initiation of Śiva (śivadīkṣā) and endowed with the cultivation of that goal—
all this must be performed by those who have bathed and are engaged in the fire sacrifice (homa).
Having secured the protection of the sacrificial fire and having offered the *arghya* while facing away,
one should restrain the Lord of Gods there and present the internal and external offerings (*bali*).
Having sipped water for purification and performed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa), he should enter the presence of the deity;
having offered the rite of fire-oblation (homa) to Him, he should pray for the destruction of his sins.
Thus peace has been enjoined; it is declared to be ninefold, [attained] by means of one, three, five, seven, nine, and fourteen days. (69)

For one who has not performed the preliminary rite for the deity Agni, the dismissal [of the fire] into the sacrificial pit is not prescribed; rather, it should be done continuously from that point with three, seven, or twenty-seven constellations.
However, the dismissal (visarjana) of the deity of the fire should not be performed at all;
thus, peace (śānti) alone is proclaimed, and the peace-oblation (śāntihoma) is prescribed. || 71 ||
And that [initiation] is declared to be of two kinds; first, the superior one is described:
in an auspicious quarter, or in the southeast, within a well-decorated pavilion.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) there, one should place a water-pot in its center,
provided with a cord, water, a tuft of grass (kūrca), a cloth, gold, and a lotus.
With his limbs smeared with white sandalwood paste and provided with fruits and sprouts,
[one should place] eight jars all around, equipped with cloths, brushes, and so forth.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) in the central pitcher, one should worship the deity named Pāśupata,
who is mounted upon the seat of the Praṇava, invincible, and possessed of great power.
Five-faced and ten-eared, with three eyes in every countenance,
possessing terrifying fangs and emitting a loud roar, he was exceedingly fierce and very difficult to conquer.
Adorned with a garland of skulls, having the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, squinting-eyed, and licking his great necklace of serpents as ornaments. (77)
He possesses the radiance of ten million times ten thousand suns, crushes the multitudes of obstacles,
and is endowed with ten extremely fierce arms equipped with terrifying weapons.
In her right hands, she holds a sword, a bow, a great trident, a noose, and the gesture of fearlessness;
in her left hands, she holds a shield, an arrow, a skull-cup, the gesture of granting boons, and a spear. (79)
Having thus meditated upon [the deity] endowed with tawny beard and hair of that same kind, one should begin the worship after invoking [the deity] while reciting the mantra. (80)
"Oṃ ślīṅkāra-saṃyuktaṃ paṃ śuṃ huṃ phaṭ namaḥ.
One should worship the Praṇava in the southeastern direction and the syllable ślīṅ in the northeast.

The syllable *paṃ* is in the northeastern quarter, and the syllable *śaṃ* is in the region of the wind (*vāyugocara*). The phonemes beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *phaṭ* correspond to the locations of the heart and the other limbs.
All [the mantras], beginning with the *hṛdaya* and others of the Pāśupata [tradition],
accompanied by the *praṇava* and ending with *phaṭ*, such as the *vajra* and so forth, [should be placed] in those jars.
Having worshipped the deity with perfumes and other offerings up to the final food offering (naivedya),
one should perform the rite before him in a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit, or even on a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila).
In the consecrated fire, as before, having invoked the Lord Pāśupata together with his retinue using the five ritual acts (*saṃskāra*), one should worship and satisfy him.
Then, [he should offer] sacrificial fuel (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), sesame seeds (tila), milk, white dūrvā grass, and cooked rice (caru)—
either one thousand, or half of that, or one hundred and eight times.
One should offer oblations individually while reciting the mantra; the instructor should specify the ritual action, saying: "O Blessed One, pacify all faults! Kurukuru! (87)
Having offered ten oblations for the limbs and ten for the weapons, one should satisfy them;
then, while recollecting the Pāśupata weapon, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having offered the expiatory oblation while recollecting the Pāśupata mantra,
he should again offer the full oblation, betel, and the water of honor (arghya) with his face turned away.
Having performed the dissolution-limb (layāṅga) up to the end of the ritual action, one should protect it;
or, having produced that [deity] every day, one should satisfy the one whose form is the weapon (astra).

Having offered the internal and external oblations and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the preceptor, assuming a subtle form, should pray for his desired object to the Deity whose rites have been dedicated.
Then, having released the deity from the pitcher, one should unite it with the *dvādaśānta*;
thereafter, one should sprinkle the surrounding area with the water from that pitcher.
Or, a person may perform this propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma) using fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked food, without the ritual installation of the water-pot (kumbha),
for a number of days as prescribed for the propitiation.
Next, I shall describe the oblation for the quarters; it is said to be of two kinds:
one is for the purpose of expiation, and the other becomes a constituent part of the ritual bathing and so forth. (94)
Whether in a *liṅga*, or in an image, or on a pedestal, or in a temple itself;
or in a pavilion, or in a garland-stand and the like, or even at the very root of a tree.
For the purpose for which the expiation (prāyaścitta) is performed,
one should construct four towers or water-stations (prapā) in the four directions, as well as four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa).
Having prepared a sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) that is either four-cornered or perfectly circular, measuring one cubit in size, one should sprinkle it with water empowered by the Astra-mantra.
Or, for the sake of all purposes, one should perform that [ritual] around the palace in the four directions;
or, having constructed a single peak (kūṭa), one should perform everything there.
In the middle [of the area], one should provide a platform for the installation of the water-pot;
then, one should complete all the rites within this sacrificial hall.
Then, O best of sages, another pit should be prepared in the northeast for the purpose of offering libations to Maheśvara, together with the limbs of Brahmā.
Having worshipped Śiva according to the rules in a liṅga, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or elsewhere,
the most excellent preceptor should offer sacrifice to the weapon known as Śiva in front of it.
Four-faced, with blazing hair and a radiance like a mass of lightning, his head adorned with a crescent moon and possessing four sprout-like hands. 102.
Accompanied by the sound of thunder, unbearable and of terrible prowess, it possessed twelve eyes and was endowed with a spear, a trident, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons. 103.
Having meditated thus, one should worship Śivāstra with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using its own mantra;
having worshipped Aghora on the right, one should subsequently sacrifice to Pāśupata.
On the Saumya day, Pratyaṅgirā is to be worshipped; her meditation mantra is stated as follows:
"Oṃ Hrīṃ, then the word 'Kṛṣṇavāsase'. (105)
Then, [one should utter] "siṃhavadane," "mahāvadane," and "mahābhairavivarṇe," followed by the word "sarvaśatru. (106)
Then, one should extract the supreme mantra-word "karmavidhvaṃsinī," followed by "cchedanī" and also "sarvabhūtadamanī. (107)
Then one should utter the word "bandha bandha" for all beings;
and the word "sarvavighnān," followed by the word "chindhi chindhi. (108)
One should utter the word "nikṛnta nikṛnta" (cut away, cut away), which destroys all diseases;
thereafter, one should extract the words "bhakṣa bhakṣa" (devour, devour) for all wicked beings.
The word *jvālājihve*, the word *karāle*, then the word *daṃṣṭre*, followed by the word *pratyaṅgire*, and finally the phrase *hrīṃ namostu*. (110)
One should extract [the mantra] with "svāhā"; this mantra consists of the Pratyāṅgirā.
From the Praṇava, there are seven syllables for the Heart, and fifteen syllables for the Head. || 111 ||

The *śikhā* consists of ten syllables; therefore, the *kavaca* has seven syllables. Likewise, from that, the *netra* consists of thirty-four syllables, and the *astra* consists of thirty-four syllables. (112)

The Gāyatrī consists of thirteen syllables, while the Sāvitrī consists of seven syllables; these are joined with the heart-mantra and others, namely: *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *hūṃ*, and *phaṭ*. (113)
She has a lion’s face with fierce fangs and is endowed with an upward-pointing crest of flame possessing the brilliance of fire;
she resembles black collyrium and is possessed of three round, red eyes. || 114 ||
She carries a trident and a hand-drum in her two left hands,
while in her two right hands she carries a severed head and, as for the remaining [hand], a sprout.
Wearing black garments, with a face wet with tears, she was intent on dancing;
she was adorned with pearl ornaments that decorated every limb. || 116 ||
Having thus meditated upon the Supreme Goddess as being endowed with a loud laugh and clad in a black antelope skin,
one should worship her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Alternatively, one should prepare five jars provided with threads and wrapped in cloth,
their interiors filled with scented water, and containing bundles of kuśa grass, gold, and lotuses.
Having placed separate pedestals made of sacrificial grass, provided with lids and sprouts, with their bodies smeared with sandalwood paste, along with a water-pot; || 119 ||
In that manner, one should place Śiva and Ambikā in the center, joined with [the aforementioned mantras];
then, all around, the weapons as previously described, and then also Pratyaṅgirā.
Having performed the sacrifice and made the request for the sake of the oblation, they should enter the fire-sanctuary;
having consecrated their own sacrificial pit and the fire as before.

Having invoked their respective deities along with their limbs (aṅgas), the image-protectors, together with the preceptor, should offer libations according to the rule, using perfumes and other offerings.

And they should perform the study of the scriptures, the recitation of mantras, hymns of praise, and other such recitations, as before, being composed in mind and properly stationed in their respective directions. (123)
The Plakṣa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa are declared to be the fuel for the secondary fire; the Palāśa should be used for the primary fire, or it may be considered suitable for all purposes.

Sesame seeds, clarified butter, dūrvā grass, and fuel-sticks of arka wood anointed with milk, as well as sacrificial porridge (caru), are the materials for the fire-oblation; one hundred or fifty [of each] should be offered.
Each of them, intent on meditating upon their own deity, should offer an individual oblation for atonement,
consisting of a full oblation accompanied by an oblation of betel leaf.
The gift of protection, the offering of cessation, and the complete restraint within the limbs of dissolution;
thereafter, having performed the inner and outer oblations, one who has sipped water becomes the embodiment of the mantra.
Having requested the deity for the manifestation of the ritual action, one should, by the grace of that deity,
perform the offering of ashes to the agent and all other rites in their proper sequence.
The preceptor, having bathed the deity with water contained in jars, should worship it;
and if this has been performed in the temple of the deity, then [he should do so] with the water from the jars.
With a view toward expiation, one should sprinkle that [offering];
this is declared to be the Diśāhoma, which wards off all misfortunes.
This second [rite], the offering to the directions (diśāhoma), is specifically described therein;
however, the worship of Pratyāṅgirā and the weapons (astras) is not prescribed here.
The oblation (homa) is performed with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, sesame seeds, and white rice;
and the oblation is prescribed in the various directions by means of the Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Jyeṣṭha mantras.
This [rite] is approved for use during ablutions and so forth, as well as in the homa performed in the four directions.
I shall now describe the saṃhitā-homa, which cuts away all defects.

Alternatively, when there is a pure intention, one should perform [the rite] in a perpetual fire, in a sacrificial pavilion, in the midst of a fire during a festival or similar occasion, or upon a consecrated mound (sthaṇḍila). || 134 ||
In the scripture, Śiva, together with Brahmā and the limbs [of the mantra], is designated as the *saṃhitā*.
The Guru, consecrated by those mantras, is worshipped with perfumes and other offerings in the fire.
One hundred oblations of palāśa wood, clarified butter, and cooked rice are offered with the Śiva-mantra;
from one-tenth of that number, oblations are likewise made for the limbs (aṅgas) and for the Brahmans.
Then, having performed twenty-five oblations with the Aghora-mantra for the sake of expiation,
one should perform the final full oblation according to the prescribed rule.
This shall be the *saṃhitā-homa*; the *mūrti-homa* is now prescribed.
Whether on the roof of a palace or elsewhere, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) marked with a mandala, [the rite proceeds]. || 138 ||
One should place the Śiva-pitcher in the center and the Vardhanī pitcher to its right;
furthermore, one should place eight pitchers in the eight directions, equipped with the weapons such as the thunderbolt and others.
[The jars] should be provided with their threads, their lids, their cloths, and their gold;
their interiors should be filled with scented water, and they should be illuminated by perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and bright lights. || 140 ||
One should worship Śiva in the central jar and Aghorāstra in the water-pot (karaka);
or else, one may worship the King of Aghorāstras in the central jar, omitting Śiva.
Having set aside even the *vardhanī* vessel, the preceptor should worship the Guru together with his limbs.
Then, having offered a seat, he should say "Huṃ Phaṭ" for the seat of the weapon, concluding with "Namaḥ. (142)
Having offered the weapon-mantra "Huṃ Phaṭ" to the Form, and that Form as well,
one should meditate upon [the deity] who shines like a thousand suns and possesses the roar of the clouds at the time of universal dissolution.
His cave-like mouth was illuminated by the tips of his blazing fangs;
he had three eyes, and his tongue like a flash of lightning, his eyebrows, whiskers, beard, and hair were set ablaze.
He has all the sacred threads, holds a trident, a sword, a spear, and a mallet;
he is four-armed and four-faced, with the crescent moon shimmering upon his crest. 145.
He was dancing, possessed of a massive body and adorned with serpent ornaments, the crusher of the arrogant gods, dānavas, and daityas. || 146 ||
One should worship the weapons, beginning with the vajra and ending with the trident, on all sides;
likewise, one should worship the lotus and the discus in the northeast and the southwest respectively.
The preceptor, having established the fire either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) one cubit in size, fashioned at its center, and circular in shape, or upon a consecrated altar (sthaṇḍila); || 148 ||
Having consecrated it with the five purificatory rites according to the path prescribed for the fire-ritual,
one should invoke and worship Aghora-Astra along with its limbs in the Śiva-fire.
One should offer fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sesame seeds, milk, white dūrvā grass, honey, and the three sweets;
or sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) one thousand times, or half of that, or even a hundred times. || 150 ||
One should offer oblations individually with these [mantras] into the fire of Śiva using the Aghora-weapon mantra;
one should satisfy [the deities] with the limbs and weapons mantras, conjoined with the specific ritual instructions.
Then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* and completed the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*), he again offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, presented betel, and having offered praise and salutation; || 152 ||
Having been requested by his desired disciple, the preceptor should perform the protection rite for the fire-oblation;
for his own sake and for the sake of the patron, he should offer the arghya water with his face turned away.
Having worshipped the limb of dissolution (layāṅga) at the end, one should perform the Śiva-vyāhṛti;
there itself, one should constantly provide protection until the completion of the ritual.
Or else, he should perform the rite of oblation daily upon a sacrificial mound;
having offered the inner and outer bali offerings and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he whose body is composed of subtle atoms [should proceed].
Having gone near the water-pot and informed the Lord, who is present in the form of the weapon, one should then bathe the Supreme Lord with the water from that pot. 156.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, meat, and so forth, ending with food offerings;
having requested the desired boon from the deity and received permission for that which arises from grace. (157)
In the rite of oblation, even the ashes should be given to the patron;
here too, one should perform the study and the recitation of mantras according to the procedure for pacification.
The Mūrtihoma has been fully described; it is declared for the purpose of expiation (prāyaścitta).
Furthermore, another specific detail regarding the Mūrtihoma is stated here. (159)
One should worship Śiva and Ambikā between the Kumbha and the Astra-vardhanī;
one should worship the Mūrtis and the eight Mūrtīśas in the external pitchers.

And one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) in the eight directions with the mantras beginning with Śarva, either upon sacrificial altars (sthaṇḍila) or in the eight fire-pits (kuṇḍa) provided with platforms (vedikā). || 161 ||
One should offer one hundred and eight, or fifty, or half of that number, of fuel sticks, clarified butter, sesame seeds, milk, and barley grains, each separately.
Palāśa, udumbara, aśvattha, and vaṭa are for the cardinal directions, while śamī, parṇa, śrīvṛkṣa, and plakṣa are prescribed as sacrificial fuel for the intermediate directions. (163)
O Indra of the milk-crop, [the ritual] may be performed with five or eight jars, or with five or eight sacrificial pits;
the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) is oriented toward the east.

Having performed everything with mantras, the Guru should perform the fire-oblation (homa) there; or, O Lord, he should offer the oblation according to the Saṃhitā into the eastern or the Īśa fire-pit (kuṇḍa). || 165 ||
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should bathe Śiva with water from the jar;
having worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should pray for the attainment of one's desired goal. 166.
Thus, according to the threefold division beginning with the "excellent" (śreṣṭha), the Mūrtihoma is prescribed;
this Mūrtihoma is to be performed together with the worship and oblation of the presiding deities of the forms (mūrtīśas).
This [rite] is not prescribed for the purpose of expiation during consecration, installation, and so forth;
one should perform it according to the number of days specified for the rite of pacification (śānti).

The "Form-offering" (mūrtihoma), beginning with the bath of clarified butter and so forth, was previously described by me; since it has already been fully instructed, it is not being told again now. (169)

In the case of neglecting the daily worship through the omission of the single twilight ritual and so forth, or in the omission of the worship of the lords of the gates, or in the omission of the five purifications; 170.

In the case of omission, there is no repetition of the preparation and ritual treatment of the seat, nor of the four items beginning with water for the feet, nor even of the oil massage and dry powdering. (171)

Or [if the rite is performed] in Śiva who is devoid of immersion, or joined with oil and the like, or worshipped in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), or even when the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) are omitted; || 172 ||

If incense is not offered, or if it is offered in too small a quantity; or if flowers are offered in the reverse manner; or if the lamp and the arati are omitted, as well as the incense and the arati; (173)

O best of the twice-born, [the rite] may be performed with the lamp used for the *nīrājana* ceremony, whether it is one situated in a row of lamps or brought from elsewhere; or with a lamp [lit by] mice and such, or even with fire.
But when the phallic image, the pedestal, the scriptures, and so forth have been touched by or defiled by other castes;
or when the cloth covering the phallic image and the like has been burnt, as has the temple itself; (175)
Whether it be in the lamp, or in the protective lamp, or in that which consists of sacrificial food and mantras;
or when the curtain is deficient, or in the case of perfumes, flowers, food offerings, and so forth—176.
Upon seeing worms, insects, human bones, nails, hair, and the like;
or upon seeing nails, hair, and the like among the materials offered to the deity. (177)
When Śiva has been worshipped with substances such as phlegm, tears, blood, and the like, or even with impurities produced by ordinary living beings; || 178 ||

When the time for bringing the food offering has come, when it is spoiled by the sprinkling of water, or when that [offering] is stepped upon, or when the sound of a conch shell is heard, or when it is discarded; || 179 ||
How much more so when the substance has already been determined as insufficient for its enlargement, or when the previously prepared linga, image, or other object has a vacant head? 180.

When the garland and other offerings have become withered while the linga and other objects remain worshipped; or when the daily offering has been forcibly taken away, or during the regular fire-ritual (agnikarman); || 181 ||
Or, if a rite for specific desires is performed without having first completed the consecration of the sacrificial pit and fire,
or if a homa is offered in a non-Śaiva fire, or if Vedic and other such rituals are performed [in such a manner], [the following applies].

O best of the twice-born, [this occurs] when the fire has been extinguished while still containing the Śiva-mantra, or when the materials for the *homa* are deficient, or when the daily festival is omitted. (183)

Or, having abandoned the temple, when that [shrine] has been destroyed by flowers, lingas, and the like, or even by falling rain and so forth, or due to causes such as disturbances in the kingdom; || 184 ||

When that inner sanctum has been constructed, at that time, if there is the extinguishing of lamps, the playing of musical instruments, the performance of dance, or the removal of the canopy; || 185 ||
At the time of offering the bali-oblation, if there is the loss of musical instruments or lamps;
if the worship of the sandals is omitted; or if their procession is interrupted; || 186 ||
Or when the Lord of the Astra-mantra has not been invoked in the *pāśupata* liṅga;
or when the prescribed circumambulation is omitted, or when it is performed in the reverse direction. || 187 ||

When enmity and the like have arisen, or when food, a mark, a vessel, or sandals [have been offered] to the body of the preceptor, or when he has been abandoned by the five classes of teachers; || 188 ||

O best of the twice-born, [this occurs] when the verses of praise for happiness are omitted, or during the fall of a courtesan, or when the lamp is extinguished, or when the singing is deficient. (189)

In the event of a deficiency in instrumental music or dance, or the omission of the lustration rite (nīrājana), or likewise if the protective ash-bath (rakṣā) is not administered to its [the deity's] limbs; || 190 ||

When the mirror, umbrella, chowries, and so forth have not been taken away from the Lord, and the worship in the inner sanctum has been performed with flowers and other offerings that have become stale; 191.
Or else, O Brahmins, when Īśa is worshipped with materials containing discarded flower offerings (nirmālya),
those afflicted by diseases such as consumption and leprosy arise from the contamination of such discarded offerings.
By those who are deaf, afflicted by evil diseases, possessed of epilepsy and the like, endowed with wicked characteristics, or having deficient or redundant limbs. (193)

When the deity has been worshipped by the Viśikhas, when the time for the twilight rites has passed, and when Śiva has been worshipped by those born outside the Kula who are other than the Śaivas; (194)
When Śivā has been worshipped by those lacking the requisite authority or by the gods themselves,
this sequence for the expiation of such a daily rite has thus been declared.
The eternal expiation is declared according to the proper sequence:
when one fails to perform the worship of a single twilight, provided that the supreme worship has been performed [at other times]. (196)
There shall be the cessation of the station and the king; at that time, one should perform the oblation for the directions.
With the central [deity] there should be the oblation for the form, and with the inferior [deity], the oblation for peace.
