Having performed the threefold or twofold worship according to his capacity,
the Guru should then prescribe the prescribed expiation for any deficiency in the twilight worship.
Then, for the purpose of removing the fault incurred by the omission of the two twilight rites,
one should bathe the deity with nine jars immediately thereafter.
Then the best of preceptors should perform the expiation previously mentioned;
however, in the case of omitting the worship at the three junctions of the day, there should be twenty-five ablutions.

If the worship at the four junctions of the day is deficient, one must perform the expiation consisting of fifty ablutions and other rites; however, if it is omitted for a single day, [the following applies].
The hundred and eight rites, beginning with the ritual bath, which were previously described, should be performed;
however, if two days are omitted, one should perform this for two days.

If there is an omission of the twilight worship even therein, the expiation prescribed for that is considered necessary; likewise for those days which have been omitted from the worship known as the "daily" (nitya) rite.
One should perform the previously mentioned expiation for that number of days;
up until the limit of one month, one should apply sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) instead.
O best of the twice-born, the presence of the God of gods does not occur otherwise;
O most excellent of the twice-born, when the worship of the gatekeepers is neglected, there is the affliction of obstacles.
For that purpose, having completed the *saṃhitā-homa*, one should worship the door-keepers;
for any worship devoid of the five purifications (*pañcaśuddhi*) is as if it were not performed at all. (206)
If the pedestal and the pillar are deficient, instability arises on the ground;
if the consecration of Śiva is lacking, men will become evil-doers. (207)
Furthermore, in the event of a deficiency in ritual service, men are afflicted by hunger, thirst, and the like; moreover, upon the breaking of the proper sequence, confusion arises on earth. (208)
Upon the breaking of the veil of ignorance, the Guru should observe the distressed condition of the messengers;
having then performed the propitiatory fire-oblation (śānti-homa), he should perform everything else according to the rules.
In the world, if the daily, occasional, or optional rites are deficient in materials such as water for the feet,
or if even a subsidiary part of them is so, there will be the destruction of those respective materials.
If the water for washing the feet or its constituent parts are deficient, there will be a disease of the feet;
likewise, if the water for sipping (ācamana) or its constituent parts are deficient, a disease of the mouth will arise. || 211 ||
If the *arghya* on the head or its constituent parts is deficient, illness will certainly arise;
if it is deficient in *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), that same result will certainly follow for those respective parts. (212)

If the anointing and other rites are omitted, men will become afflicted with disease; likewise, if the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are omitted, or if the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) applied to the limbs are omitted.

In this world, there is no doubt that the destruction of those respective substances occurs when there is a deficiency in the limbs during the taking of the fragrance, or in the taking of the flower and its parts. (214)
O lords of sages, indeed, the destruction of various substances occurs in the world;
if incense is not offered, or if it is deficient in its constituent parts, there shall be terrible disease.
If the striking of the bell is deficient, [the inhabitants] are tormented by piśācas, rākṣasas, and the like; moreover, those who dwell there become afflicted with calamities. || 216 ||
If the offering of a lamp is deficient, or if there is an omission of a limb [of the ritual], one suffers from visible disease;
likewise if there is an omission of the invocation, the oblation, or its constituent parts. (217)
If the food offering (naivedya) for that limb [of the ritual] is not presented, there will be the destruction of crops;
if betel leaves are absent or if a limb is omitted, there will be disease of the mouth.
Then, realizing that if the curtain (kāṇḍapaṭa) were removed, the presence of the deities would perish,
the preceptor should perform an expiation.
Having fully worshipped the deity, O Śivā, one should cause that material to be given as a double amount;
thereafter, the preceptor should perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma) or conduct a ritual bathing (snapana).
O Śivā, if the respective materials are lacking, one should cause double the amount to be given;
or else, a *saṃhitā-homa* should be performed, or the recitation (*japa*) of the Aghora mantra one hundred times.
And when half, a quarter, or half of that [quarter] of these very substances has been offered with the Aghora mantra, [the results follow] in sequence as two, four, and six hundred [times].
Having recited [the mantra], one should then cause that substance to be given to the deity in double the amount.
If these substances are offered to Śaṅkara without the mantra, [the result is as follows].
The preceptor, having worshipped the deity, should give back that very same substance which was taken without permission;
at the conclusion, he should offer it with his own mantra, either doubled in amount or equal to the original.
One should perform the prescribed ritual bathing, or the hundredfold recitation of the Ghoramantra,
in the case of the daily, occasional, or optional rites, as well as when there is an omission of the triad beginning with water for the feet (pādya).
The preceptor, having rotated [the vessel] one hundred times, should give it to the born lords of men;
he should give twice as much of the materials beginning with *yā* (such as *yava*, etc.), or that substance alone.
If the durvā grass, flowers, or unhusked rice grains are deficient, one must then perform a hundred recitations of the Hṛdaya-mantra while the oil massage,
powdering, bathing, and other rites are being carried out.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred times with devotion for an inferior person, one should then cause them to pay double;
when the ritual is concluded, after the anointing with oil and other rites, there is an oblation accompanied by the Saṃhitā-mantra.
In the case of daily, occasional, or optional rites performed with previously prepared sacrificial vessels,
if they are lost, one should perform the *saṃhitā-homa* and then carry out the rite twice over.
By this procedure, one should perform the expiation with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
if the previously consecrated fragrance is lost, one should immediately recite [the mantra] a hundred times.
Or one should offer that same substance in double the quantity or in equal measure,
if the flowers are deficient, lacking, or offered in the reverse order.
One should recite [the mantra] for the Lord one hundred times; thereafter, one should offer twice that amount.
Having recited the Ghoramantra during the incense offering and the rite of lights (ārātrika), one should then recite it twice as much at the conclusion.
At the time of offering incense and the nightly lamp-rite (nīrājana),
one should offer a row of lamps, whether they are already set out or brought by mice and other such creatures.
If the linga, the image, the scriptures, and so forth, are touched by fire—whether by a small or even a great fire—the king will fall ill. (234)
Having purified the Lord with fire and cleansed away all impurities,
one should bathe the Supreme Lord with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) combined with coconut water.
Having fully worshipped the Lord of the gods of gods, one should perform the *mūrtihoma* (image-oblation).
If the fire should become as small as an atom, one should perform a rite of pacification (*śānti*).
If the garments placed upon the linga, the image, and so forth are consumed by fire,
then one should perform rites such as sprinkling with consecrated water.
If [the house] is burnt only in one part, then one should perform a rite for pacification;
in the case of a total conflagration of the dwelling, one should perform a consecratory sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) of the house.
One should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) for the deity when the occurrence of "breaking the abode" (dhāmaccheda) or other such defects arises;
one should perform the expiation prescribed therein, accompanied by the re-consecration (sandhāna) and other rites. || 239 ||
If another color appears on a linga, image, or similar object due to fire,
that which is human-made should be abandoned, while that which is self-manifested (svāyaṃbhū) and so forth should be accepted.
By means of the statement regarding the remedial rite and subsequent action, it should be performed accompanied by a thorough sprinkling;
if a manuscript is even slightly burnt, one should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti).
One should perform the great ablution of Śiva, whether in its entirety or in part;
and with incense made from animal parts, one should recite the fifth [mantra] one hundred times.
If there is a deficiency of lamps, one should recite the Aghora mantra three hundred times;
thereafter, O God of gods, one should cause twice as many lamps to be offered.
Even if the lamp is extinguished, the protection rite should likewise be performed with double the recitation of mantras;
then, having offered sacrificial food (haviṣya) to the deity and performed the ritual bathing (snapana), [one should proceed].
Thereafter, one should cause double the fee to be given for both the invitation and the sacrificial oblation (havis).
Now, if the curtain (kāṇḍapaṭa) is deficient, one should mutter the Kavaca mantra two hundred times.
The same applies even to substances such as perfumes, flowers, and food offerings;
likewise, it occurs upon seeing worms, insects, human bones, nails, hair, and so forth. (246)
If that substance is very small, one should discard it; however, if it is large, one should not abandon it.
Regarding substances offered to Śiva, if nails, hair, or the like are seen [among them], [one should act accordingly].
Having bathed [the image] thoroughly with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should mutter the Aghora mantra three hundred times;
for if Śiva is worshipped with substances such as phlegm, tears, and blood, [the result is as follows].
One should perform the ceremonial bath for the God of gods according to the desire of the performer;
likewise, one should act in the same manner when it is performed with ordinary water or with water mixed with clay.
When bringing the food offering, one should sprinkle water from the cooking place;
if a deficiency or a transgression occurs therein, it will result in evil.

Then, having sprinkled the food offering with the *arghya* water of manifold forms, one should recite [the mantra] a hundred times for the sake of purification, or even when the sound of a conch is absent. (251)
In a place provided with musical instruments, one should recite [the mantra] a hundred times;
however, if it is already determined that the ritual materials are lacking, that act will produce a defect.
Then, O Śivā, having recited the root mantra one hundred times, one should cause twice that amount to be given;
this is the "increase of wealth" (dhanavardhana), which increases the wealth of whatever material has been previously determined.
This expiation is prescribed for the daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites;
likewise, if the linga, the image (bera), and so forth, have their heads missing, they become sources of defect.
Then, having recited the Aghora mantra a hundred times, one should worship with flowers and other offerings;
this should be done while standing with the same faded flowers and other items that were used for the morning twilight worship.
If the worshiped lingas, images, and so forth cause harm to men,
one should recite the Aghora mantra a hundred times and then perform the worship again.
If all the deities become averse to that place because it is devoid of the offering of bali, one should bring double [the amount] for the sake of their satisfaction. (257)
If [the rite] is deficient after ten days have passed, even by a single atom, there must be a hundred oblations;
likewise when the fire-ritual has not been performed for the daily, occasional, or optional [rites].
O best of the twice-born, if an obstacle should arise there, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śānti-homa) and then repeat that [rite] three times or at least once.
If one should perform the teacher’s duties at the two twilights and other times, whatever sacrificial rites have been omitted by the teachers [must be performed]. (260)
With those respective substances, all combined, according to the increase of the days,
that pit (kuṇḍa) or sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), though lacking the [standard] measurement, bestows an increase of water.
Then, having performed the pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) according to the rules, one should perform [the rite] again;
for if the consecration of the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) is lacking, the Śiva-fire will certainly not be perfected.
When such a homa has been performed, whether in a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
or when the Śiva-fire has not yet been fully established, one should perform the consecration (saṃskāra) of those two [the fire and the site] preceded by the proper rites.
Furthermore, O Lord, the fire-sacrifice (homa) must be performed [in the proper manner]; otherwise, there will be no attainment of the deity.
A fire-sacrifice performed in a non-Śaiva fire becomes a source of disease for the Śaiva practitioner.
In a Śaiva temple, there should be only the Śiva-fire (śivāgni) and no other fire;
however, Vedic fire-rituals are not desired in a Śiva temple. (265)
If it is asked how the "declaration of an auspicious day" (puṇyāhavācana) and so forth are described, it has been stated that this is taught in the Śaiva [tradition];
herein, nothing is composed based on one's own independent intellect.
"That it should be performed in a temple of Śiva," and so forth, is enjoined by the Vedas; and this is indeed a Vedic rite, according to the path of established doctrine. (267)

Whether it be established according to the divisions of the Kāmika and other tantras, or even if it is worshipped, neither that which is Vedic nor that enjoined by the Purāṇas and Smṛtis is mentioned here. (268)
O twice-born ones, how much more so is there no entry for the Pāśupatas and others?
For if the fire, once consecrated, is extinguished, it brings about the destruction of the sacrificer. (269)
Then, with the Aghora mantra, one should perform a thousand recitations and libations;
likewise, even for the Nirvāṇa-Śiva, one should offer ten thousand oblations with the Ghora mantra.
One should perform the recitation (japa) joined with that same number for the sake of expiation;
if the materials for the fire-oblation (homa) are lacking, the recitation should be twice as many as those materials.
If the perpetual festival is lacking, it causes all manner of faults for men;
therefore, one should worship the Lord and offer oblations a hundred times with the Aghora mantra alone.
If all three joints are lost, one should perform a propitiatory fire sacrifice (śānti-homa);
if the day and night are lost, one should cause the ritual bathing (snapana) to be performed for Śiva.
Within five days, that same rite should be performed accompanied by one hundred oblations to Aghora;
on the tenth day, one should perform a ritual bath combined with a propitiatory homa.
If its wings or joints are severed, there shall be pacification through a ritual bath;
if it is deficient by one month's interval, there must be a bath and a hundred oblations (or oblations in the ten directions).
O best of Brahmins, thereafter there should be a rite of pacification for three days;
however, if it occurs after that, even beyond a fortnight, the expiation is the Ṛkṣaka.
One should increase the number by pairs until the end of each fortnight;
and a daily festival must be performed by those who provide the instructions for the expiation.
When that perpetual festival was being concluded by means of the image, and once the image had been set aside and the rite was performed using lingas made of flowers and other materials; || 278 ||
Then the practitioner of mantras should recite the Aghora mantra three hundred or two hundred times,
whether due to falling rain or other such causes, or for the sake of averting national calamities and the like.
If the inner sanctum (garbhageha) has been constructed, even during a perpetual festival, the recitation (japa) yields only half its merit;
if the lamp is extinguished at that time, the kingdom shall fall into blinding darkness.
Then, having recited the Aghora mantra a hundred times, one should perform double the number of lamp offerings;
this should be done if there is anything causing a defect in the instrumental music or the dance.
Having performed the *saṃhitā-homa* or the recitation (*japa*) of the Aghora mantra twice a thousand times, one should thereafter engage in dance and instrumental music.
Then, in the event of a deficiency in the canopy, one should recite the third [mantra] three hundred times;
likewise, this should be done in the case of the offering of bali, or the loss of musical instruments, lamps, and so forth. (283)
If the sandals are neglected in worship, or if one resorts to an inferior vehicle, or if a disease of the feet occurs,
one should perform a combined fire-oblation (saṃhitā-homa) or recite the mantra a thousand times while facing south.

If the *liṅga* called Pāśupata has not been consecrated or lacks a presiding deity, there will be obstruction by impediments; one should then mutter the *Ghora* mantra or perform an oblation according to the *Saṃhitā*.
In the case of a festival, it should be done in this manner; however, the opposite applies regarding circumambulation.
When circumambulation is omitted as prescribed, a *saṃhitā-homa* is desired.
When a vehicle falls on a bed or similar object, one should perform the expiation as prescribed for the year;
likewise, one should perform the same expiation when food, a linga, or similar items fall.
If the staff falls, one should perform the expiation prescribed for the food-offering (anna-liṅga);
if the sandals fall, there will be strife in the kingdom, which one should seek to avert.
Having established the water-pot in the center according to the ritual for the consecration of the banner,
and having worshipped the sandals, one should perform the propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma) prior to that.

O best of the twice-born, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the water-pot and having completed it, one should perform the bath; through the recitation of the subsequent rites beginning with the [ritual] piercing, there shall be expiation.
If he does not perceive that happiness has been achieved, then that world remains in a state of distress;
at that time, he should perform a ritual ablution with twenty-five jars.
Alternatively, one may perform a bathing with nine jars or even a bathing with products of the cow;
whatever pleasures are deficient, one should lead those pleasures to become twofold.
If there is an omission for many days, it shall be called the "fifty-fold bath" (pañcāśat-snāna);
or, if the limb of happiness is missing, one should then apply double that amount.
If the five teachers do not perform their respective duties,
then the mortals dwelling here will no longer abide in their own proper occupations.
One should recite the mantras of Īśāna, Aghora, Vāma, and Jyeṣṭha one hundred times each;
even if all [the materials] are absent, one should perform the propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma) over many days.
If one is deprived of happiness and fame, that happiness shall become unattained;
having recited the Aghora mantra a hundred times, one should then double that number.
But during a time of prosperity, if a courtesan falls [from her status], the kingdom falls into distress;
at that very moment, one should perform the propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma) as prescribed.
Or one should perform the *snapana* rite with the *aghora* mantra, or simply recite it a thousand times;
if the lamp of bliss is extinguished, one should recite the *ghora* mantra one hundred times.
In the absence of singing, there will be fear for that kingdom and its happiness will be as previously described;
therefore, an expiation must then be performed to eliminate that fear.
In the event of a deficiency in instrumental music or dance, a continuous oblation (saṃhitāhoma) is prescribed;
or one should mutter the Ghoramantra a thousand times, and thereafter cause double that amount to be given as a gift.
If the Nīrājana rite or its constituent parts are deficient, one should predict danger from fire;
therefore, the Guru, having bathed the deity with products of the cow (gavya) and having worshipped him with devotion, [should perform the rite]. (301)
Thereafter, one should lead forward twice as many [bricks] as those that were deficient;
or else, a pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) or a ritual oblation to the deities (mūrtihoma) is prescribed.
If the protection by ashes has not been granted, one should recite the Aghora mantra a hundred times;
if the mirror, parasol, fly-whisk, and so forth have not been granted, then one should lead [the disciple] away.
If the worship with flowers and other offerings has been performed, yet one performs a thousand or five hundred repetitions of the Aghora mantra, there will be turmoil in the kingdom.
Having performed the ceremonial bath for the God of gods, one should maintain peace for three days;
as long as the remains of previous offerings (nirmālya) remain in the inner sanctum, the deities do not abide there.
Then, having performed the purification of the site and having worshipped the deity with diligence,
one should recite the mantra known as Aghora one thousand times for the pacification of defects.
If one worships Īśa with substances mixed with the remains of offerings (nirmālya),
then the mortals living in that kingdom are afflicted by enemies.

By those afflicted with diseases such as consumption and leprosy, by the deaf, by those suffering from malignant diseases, by those seized by epilepsy and the like, and by those marked with evil characteristics; || 308 ||

If a sacrifice is performed by those with deficient or extra limbs, or by those who are arrow-wounded, that worship leads to the agitation of the kingdom; it is said to be a source of atonement [for such misfortune]. (309)
When the worship has been performed once, the Guru should lead [the disciple] through one hundred repetitions of the *ghora* mantra;
beyond that, he should lead the recitation according to the divisions of time, increasing by a hundred each time.
Above a fortnight, there is the Saṃhitā-homa; above a month, the Śānti-homa;
above six months, there should be the Śānti; and above a year, the Mūrti-homa.

Sacrifices performed only in one's own country and at the proper time bestow the desired fruits; however, when performed in another country or at another time, those very same acts become causes of misfortune.
If one transgresses the time for the twilight worship (saṃdhyā), one should perform a thousand-fold recitation of the terrible mantra;
and that [worship] is declared in the scripture to be fivefold, according to the divisions beginning with Bāla.

The "very young" (atibālā), the "young" (yuvati), and the "very old" (ativṛddhā) are considered most excellent; together with the "exceedingly young" (atibālā) and the "extremely old" (ativṛddhā), these are reckoned as the ghaṭikās. (314)
From the half-ascension of Mārtāṇḍa until the middle [point], she moves toward the east;
she is Atibālā and Bālā, and in all three [of these stages], there is nothing to be grasped.
The Sandhyās are said to follow after them, beginning with the Youthful (Yuvati) and so forth;
one should always commence the worship during those very [Sandhyās] in the forenoon and other periods.
Among those [women], the *uttamā* (excellent) is considered superior; the *madhyamā* (middling) is regarded as being on her sides.
Furthermore, those who are too young or too old are censured for undertaking any enterprise. (317)
If the worship of those two has already begun, the previously mentioned expiation is prescribed;
however, at the commencement of the twilight rite or elsewhere, one should perform the *saṃhitā-homa*.

O one born of the Kula of the primordial Śaivas, if the worship of Śiva is performed by those outside [this tradition], it leads to fault; yet if the twilight worship (sandhyārcana) is performed even once for the sake of another, it is not so. || 319 ||
One should perform the *saṃhitā-homa* during the increase [of the lunar day] such as its waxing;
it is said that after a fortnight there is a *śānti*, and after a month there is a *śānti-homaka*.
O twice-born ones, in two months there should be an image-oblation (mūrtihoma); in four months, an offering to the quarters (diśāhuti);
and after six months, the ritual sprinkling (karmasaṃprokṣaṇa) must be performed.
Since, after six months, there exists a further entitlement for one called a *devalaka*—provided that it is not for the sake of a livelihood—therefore [this applies]. (322)
If he is born in the Middle Country (Madhyadeśa), he has authority therein;
however, for the consecration of a mobile liṅga and for initiation, those from all countries are qualified.
It is prescribed for kings to the south of the Vindhya mountains and for those born as Vaiśyas to the north; it is for one seeking progeny everywhere, but it is never proclaimed for a Śūdra.
But that which is performed by one devoid of authority becomes as if unperformed;
O best of gurus, this applies when the installation and other rites are performed by one called a *devalaka*. (325)
Having performed the re-establishment again, one should carry out the worship according to the prescribed rule;
one who lacks authority should perform it in that same manner.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, the expiation for the daily rite has been declared;
now the sequence of atonement for the loosening of the eight bonds and so forth is being stated.

O twice-born ones, when the eightfold bond is loosened, or when the *liṅga*, an image, or the like is separated, or when it is seized by an enemy, or when the Goddess alone [is seized], [the following occurs].
Either the God has abandoned the Goddess, or he alone has been seized by the enemy;
even in that case, within the abode, there is a distinction between the great and the small due to the differentiation of states. || 329 ||
In the event of the breaking off of parts such as the stūpa, or when water flows beneath the ground,
or when that part has fallen onto the ground, or even when the entire structure [has collapsed], [one should perform the rite].
There is an obstacle when the pedestal (piṇḍikā) falls, or when the surrounding enclosure is destroyed;
likewise when the sacrificial altar (balipīṭha) is missing, or when it has decayed, or even when it cracks. (331)
And likewise, when that enclosure wall or gate-tower has been burnt, collapsed, or otherwise decayed, fallen, or even cracked open; 332.
Or by monkeys, cocks, and the like; by pigeons, pigs, and dogs; by owls, vultures, and crows; and by those who approach their wives out of season, thieves, and donkeys. (333)
Nor by those who have fallen from their caste, nor by ghosts, nor by those who have committed mortal sins, nor by those in a state of birth-impurity;
nor by those born in secret, nor by those afflicted with sinful diseases, nor by Vratyas, nor by those born of inverse unions.
By twice-born men who have committed treachery against their gurus and others and are devoid of initiation, or by quadrupeds, or by other birds, or by reptiles; || 335 ||
Or by others of low birth, or by men who have undergone other initiations, or even by artisans, cobbler-candālas, washermen, and the like. (336)
When the pedestal or the liṅga has been touched, or when the image and so forth have entered the inner sanctum, or previously in the pavilion called the Pratimā-maṇḍapa; || 337 ||
O twice-born ones, [the rite should be performed] in the attendants' quarters, or within the second inner pavilion, or when one has entered the kitchen,
or at the offering altars.

When a *liṅga* has been installed for the sake of others by Śūdras and the like—who are devoid of initiation into *nirvāṇa* but abide by the rules—if it is touched or if the consecrated core (*garbha*) is entered [by such persons], [the rite must be performed]. || 339 ||

In the inner circular hall (antarmaṇḍala) and so forth, in the garland-hall (mālika) and so forth, or in the pavilion (maṇṭapa), or if one has dwelt for a long time in the center, or if there is the casting of impurities; || 340 ||
In the womb, in the half-pavilion, in the image-pavilion, or in an outdoor area; or upon being sprinkled with excrement, urine, vomit, phlegm, liquor, and the like—(341)
When those of the three castes and others who are impure enter within the inner circle, or into the temple, the sanctum sanctorum, half [the area], the image, the pavilion, and so forth; 342.
In a *sāla* tree or one joined with a *mālikā*, in a plain cow-pen, on an image,
a pedestal, a bull, or the like, or in its temple upon a sacrificial altar (*bilapīṭhaka*).
In the servants' quarters, in a well, or in the kitchen itself;
in an assembly hall, or in another part of the royal palace, or in a house. || 344 ||
Whether in the assembly hall or in the pavilion, when Vālmīki has arrived, or when there is the possibility of laxity, or when the "cage of honey" occurs; || 345 ||
Large ants, small ants, red ants, women, and small creatures—should any of these appear at the door or in the bedchamber; || 346 ||
In place of the offerings of oil, clarified butter, and oblations, one should offer them at the door-pillar, in the abode of the wind (the northwest),
or in the location of goats, cows, buffaloes, and so forth, or in the middle of the village.
Whether in a wooden image or one made of stone and so forth, on a path or at a sacred tree (caitya), in a monastery, a water-shed, or even in a grove and the like; || 348 ||
Or, when an anthill or similar growth has arisen at the base of their *liṅgas*, or when the ritual of bathing—whether daily, occasional, or for a specific desire—has been omitted; (349)
Or when there is a deficiency in that limb, or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) for that particular limb;
or when there is an omission of the jars and so forth, or when the jar and other vessels are devoid of the measured proportions. || 350 ||

O best of the twice-born, when the Śiva-pitcher, or the karaka-vessel, or even the kalaśa has been set down— whether it be provided with its various parts and so forth, or offered, or even questioned.
When the bathing is performed upon the image using vessels made of conch, gold, and so forth, or produced from the leaves of the Brahmavṛkṣa tree, it should be done without the wrapping of threads.
If a vessel such as a water-pot is wrapped with even a very small amount of thread, or if the ritual *kūrca* grass is omitted, or if the *utkūrca* and *krama* are omitted; (353)

And in the case of the loss of jewels, gold, garments, and so forth, or of jars and the like, or upon the loss of substances such as cow-products, or when an auspicious day has been omitted; || 354 ||
In the five months beginning with Āṣāḍha and ending with Kṛttikā, when there is no worship of the jar (kumbha) and no application of mantras (mantranyāsa), [the following applies].

If the offering of the sacred grass (pavitrārohaṇa) is omitted, or likewise the offering of the *damanaka* flower, or if the lamp in the Kṛttikā constellation is extinguished due to causes such as disturbances within the kingdom; || 356 ||

On land, at the beginning of the rainy season, or in water, or in a well-protected cave, [one should worship] a stone linga that is devoid of flowers on its head and has been drenched by the falling rain and so forth. || 357 ||
Or when the linga stands with its foundation broken, or is infested by beasts, birds, and reptiles, or is afflicted by other deities; || 358 ||
In such matters as these, an expiation is prescribed.
However, when the eight-fold bond is loosened, one should declare that the kingdom is falling into decay. || 359 ||

Having performed eight or three bindings, one should conclude with a ritual bath at the end; discarding the old [state], one should proceed while reciting the weapon-mantra according to the scripture.
One should perform a hundred oblations with the Aghora mantra using sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and boiled rice;
this applies if the linga or an image has been seized by an enemy.
Then that kingdom will perish and the king will be tormented by enemies;
therefore, with every effort, one must retrieve it and establish it in that very place.

If the primary *liṅga* has been obtained, having installed it in a secret place, one should perform [the rite] with a formidable mantra for the sake of pacifying the fault arising from the uprooting of the *liṅga*. || 363 ||
One should offer a thousand oblations with *jāti* and sesame seeds,
one hundred with *caru* mixed with the three sweets, and a thousand oblations of *dūrvā* grass.
Having performed these at the end, one should establish [the deity] on the eastern ground according to the instructions for installation;
this includes the removal of defects, the opening of the eyes, and the immersion in water.
Those who perceive the ultimate reality should set aside what has been done and perform something else;
when the primary linga, image, or other such object has not been obtained, one should install another new one.
If [the death occurs] after one month and up to three months, then from that point forward,
a daily peace-offering (śāntihoma) must be performed until the conclusion of the installation ceremony.
The installation of the *bāla-liṅga* and so forth above that [level] has not been taught here;
therefore, with every effort, [it should be performed] within the middle three months. (368)
Having installed the young Liṅga and others according to the procedure for the installation of a youth, [he asked:
"By whom was it taken? Where are the thieves and the rest? Where is the Liṅga, and of what nature is it? (369)
Whether it be an image, a face-liṅga, or a bāṇaliṅga and so forth, one should search for it every day; if it is certainly not present elsewhere, [one should seek it there].
Then, having conquered it either by battle or by respectfully offering wealth,
one should bring forth the primary linga, beram, and other images and firmly install them in their own proper place.
O lords of sages, that which has been acquired with great effort within three years, yet remains unacquired after three years have passed— || 372 ||

Having established the primary liṅga and other icons at the root site (mūlasthāna) with the same materials and in the same proportions as before, one should worship them according to the prescribed method of worship.
If the measurement was previously unknown, it should be determined by the most excellent architects according to the proportions of the temple and in accordance with the status of the patron. (374)
Having prepared the *liṅga* according to the prescribed rite, one should install it by the stated method;
or else, for the sake of attaining all perfections (*siddhi*), one should install a *bāṇaliṅga* there.
One should construct the pedestal and the pond first according to this rule;
whether it be the male deity alone, or the female deity alone, excluding the other. || 376 ||
If she has been taken by enemies, he should act in accordance with her status while remaining stationary;
having accomplished the other [necessary tasks] for her and having completed her establishment, [he should proceed]. || 377 ||
At the conclusion, the supreme preceptor should perform the auspicious rite according to the prescribed method;
however, if the primary image has been brought [to the site], it should be placed near that spot at the end of the installation ceremony.
Having installed it in its place according to the prescribed rite, one should worship it daily with devotion;
if the pedestal is lost, one should join another [pedestal] to the liṅga.
If the palace cracks in the east, there will be fear for the king;
if in the southeast, there will be a fire; if in the south, there will be strife. (380)
In the southwest there will be loss of wealth; in the west, the loss of servants;
in the northwest, an increase in enemies; and in the north, the loss of sons. (381)
In the northeast, according to the sequence of the King who Shares in Suffering, the fruit is considered to be as follows:
having performed the previously mentioned pacification (śānti) according to the distinctions of superior and so forth. || 382 ||
At the conclusion, one should perform the reconnection of the abode accompanied by a peace-offering (śānti-homa),
or one should have the temple constructed according to the rules as described in the subsequent ritual procedure.
If there is even a slight discrepancy or defect, one should perform a propitiatory *homa* sacrifice.
This should be done when the temple is half-finished, three-quarters finished, one-quarter finished, or even when it is partially collapsed.
Then, one should perform the reconnection of the abode arising from six, five, four, and three [units];
those of purified soul should carry out the expiation as previously described. (385)
Even when a part such as the dome (stūpī) has been severed, one should observe this same one-day rite;
likewise, if water flows out from beneath the ground or if water falls below [the vessel].
If a limb of it is broken, a fault arises on the ground;
one should then perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma). If it falls into water, [one should perform it] for three days.
Or, having placed the Lord of Gods within a water-pot, one should perform the rites for the dry ground;
or one should sprinkle him with water from the *vastra* vessel at every twilight for the purpose of bathing. (388)
On a site prepared by artisans and accompanied by the sprinkling for an auspicious day,
he should then perform the final consecration at the conclusion of the work on the site.

O best of sages, if the pedestal (piṇḍikā) falls down from its proper place, there will be suffering caused by enemies; however, if the water-pot (kumbha) and the pouring-vessel (vardhanī) remain so, it is auspicious for both Śiva and Śivā.
Having invoked the Lord of the Vidyās, one should lead the Piṇḍī to its place;
one should lead it for three days while performing the pacification (śānti) preceded by the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa).

Therefore, one should perform a thorough sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) if there has been contact with craftsmen and the like; otherwise, if it is devoid of its retinue, there will be the destruction of the group of servants.
Having assembled the retinue, one should then cause the installation to be performed;
for if it is devoid of the offering pedestal (balipīṭha), it will bring about all manner of defects. || 393 ||
Having conceived the pedestal as before, one should then proceed with its installation;
O twice-born ones, this should be done when it has become worn out, cracked, burnt, or fallen, and so forth. (394)
Then, having performed the *śānti*-oblation, one should carry out the ritual sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*).
This applies when the enclosure wall or the gatehouse is decayed, collapsed, cracked, or otherwise damaged. (395)
Then, one should perform the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) declared to cause fear for the king;
thereafter, one should perform the sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) and the rejoining (sandhāna) in cases such as a fracture.
Having sprinkled it with cow-products, one should perform a rite of pacification for one day [if it has been defiled] by monkeys,
cocks, and the like, or by pigeons, pigs, or dogs.
Nor by owls, vultures, crows, those who steal women during their fertile seasons, donkeys, outcasts, ghosts, sinners, or those in a state of ritual impurity. (398)
[It should not be performed] by those born in secret, by those afflicted with sinful diseases, by *vrātyas*, or by those born in the inverse order;
nor by twice-born men and others who have committed treachery against their gurus and the like, or who lack initiation. (399)
Nor by quadrupeds, nor by other birds or reptiles, nor by those of low birth, nor by other men who are situated within the state of initiation (dīkṣā). || 400 ||
If the pedestal, the liṅga, or the image and so forth are touched by artisans, or even by Pāṇas, Caṇḍālas, washermen, and others, then those residing there [must perform purification]. (401)
In the kingdom, all mortals are oppressed by enemy people;
one should discard earthen vessels that have been touched by them, as well as those that are near them.
Having performed the smearing with cow-dung and the rite for a meritorious day (*puṇyāha*), the most excellent Guru,
having performed the bathing with products of the cow (*gavya*), should then carry out the ritual sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*).
When one is touched by those who have committed the offenses of violating the seasons, having intercourse with women, or causing impurity—
even by washermen— the previously mentioned rites such as the propitiatory oblation (śānti-homa) must be performed.
If Caṇḍālas, Pāṇakas, or others should enter, one should perform rites for pacification and so forth;
but if they have entered the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), a ceremonial bath accompanied by a pacificatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma) must be performed.

If one has entered the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) due to seasonal impurity, sexual intercourse with a woman, or other such sins, one should perform a sprinkling purification using monkeys, roosters, and the like.
Then one should perform the sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) exactly as previously instructed;
however, if [the site] has been defiled by Caṇḍālas, washermen, or others, it should be accompanied by a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
The ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) should be performed; thus it is considered to be of three kinds according to the sequence.
Following the direction for rites of pacification (śāntika), one should apply the sprinkling in due order after the fire-oblation (homa).
Regarding the entry into the half-pavilion (ardhamaṇḍapa) by means of three successive stages:
that which is prescribed for the Caṇḍālas occurs in both the first and the second [stages]. (409)
Let an expiation be prescribed for women during their menses upon touching [the image] and so forth;
likewise, for the entry into the pavilion of the image, it shall be performed in three ways according to the sequence.
One should perform the Śāntihoma, the Mūrtihoma, and the Diśāhoma in their proper sequence,
excluding those twice-born who have not received initiation, as well as those between initiations.
Even when entering the residence of one's attendants, this very same [rule] is proclaimed;
the entry of pigeons, crows, snakes, and the like does not entail any fault here. (412)
If Caṇḍālas, washermen, or others should enter the inner precinct, a Mūrtihoma must be performed; in the second case, a Śāntihoma is required.
The application of cow-dung and other such rites are the same for all activities; the expiation prescribed for the surrounding hall applies also to the kitchen.
The expiation for those on the sacrificial pedestals (balipīṭha) should be known as equal to that for a kitchen;
those of the Śūdra class and others who abide by the rules (samaya), though lacking initiation into Nirvāṇa, [are likewise purified]. 415.

If they touch a stable *liṅga* that has been established for the sake of others, an ablution (*snapana*), a propitiatory fire-oblation (*śāntihoma*), and the rite of entry into the womb (*garbhapraveśana*) must be performed. (416)

No fault is found in entering half of the pavilion and so forth, nor within the inner enclosure (antarmaṇḍala), the hall (sāla), and so on, or in the pavilion for the garland-bearers (mālika). || 417 ||
If it has been inhabited by mortals for a long time, or if it has been used as a receptacle for impurities,
one should thoroughly clean the ground and wash it with cow dung and other such substances.

In accordance with the specific consecration (upadhāna), one should perform the auspicious day rite (puṇyāha) and the peace rite (śānti) respectively in the womb-chamber (garbha), the half-pavilion (ardhamaṇḍapa), and the image-pavilion (beramaṇḍapa) on the outside.
In the case of sprinkling with excrement, urine, vomit, phlegm, feces, and so forth,
one should perform the *saṃprokṣaṇa* (sprinkling), the *diśāhoma* (offering to the directions), the *mūrtyākhya* (offering to the forms), and the *śāntihomaka* (peace-offering).
O twice-born ones, one should perform the purification with cow-dung and other rites as previously described;
[this applies to] the entry of the three castes who are in a state of ritual impurity into the inner maṇḍala.
O lords of sages, this shall not lead to any fault for those who have been initiated;
however, upon the entry of others, one should sprinkle them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Therefore, their entry into the outer [temple precinct] does not result in any fault, whether they bear my insignia or are Śūdras born of the natural order (anuloma). || 423 ||
Whether initiated or uninitiated, those who are equal to the three castes are considered to be like Rudra-maidens;
even if initiated but devoid of mantras, they are regarded as equal to Rudra-maidens.

If the five preceptors have been initiated by those such as Brahmins who are themselves initiated, then [the rites for] the temple, the inner sanctum, half [of it], the image, the pavilion, and so forth [should be performed]. (425)

On a *sāla* tree, or on a *mālikā* (flowering vine), or on a solitary gateway (*gopura*), or in a courtyard (*aṅgaṇa*), or on the image (*bera*), or on the pedestal (*pīṭha*), or on the bull (*vṛṣa*) and so forth, or in that temple, or on the sacrificial altar (*balipīṭhaka*).
In the attendants' quarters, in a well, or in the kitchen itself; in an assembly hall, or in another part of the royal palace, or in a private house. (427)
Whether in the assembly hall or in the pavilion, when Vālmīki has arrived, or when Śithilī has appeared, or when Madhupañjara has appeared. (428)
If large ants, small red ants, women, and small creatures arise from the ground and other such places, it brings all manner of misfortune to men. (429)
O twice-born ones, listen now to the results of these [asterisms] in sequence, beginning from the east:
illness, fear, fire-burns, loss of kin, and the arrival of wealth. (430)
The loss of a son, the acquisition of a friend, grain, and the destruction of wealth—these are the results when an anthill is seen from the center up to the northeast. (431)
If [the breath] becomes slack in the middle, pleasure arises;
beyond that, there would be the destruction of living beings, and in the portion of Indra, there would be fear. || 432 ||
O best of the twice-born, at first there will be the arrival of a friend in the fire [quarter];
thereafter, there will be royal agitation; and in the Yama [quarter], there will be the gain of wealth. (433)
And if the death of the wife should occur immediately after that, it would be for the master;
there is prosperity at the limit of Nirṛti, but beyond that, there will be misfortune. (434)
In the western quarter (Vāruṇī), there will first be the gain of wealth, but then fear of thieves;
in the northwest (Vāyudik) there is a maiden, and in the north (Soma) there is fear from enemies.
Beyond that, there will be gain of grain; in the northeast (Īśāna), there will be great fear;
in the northwest (Vāyu), there will be the destruction of the house; and in the place of rest (Śayana), there will be death. || 436 ||
In the place of the offerings of oil, clarified butter, and sacrificial oblations, there shall be the destruction of quadrupeds;
at the door-pipe (dvaranala), there shall be the death of a wife and the loss of servants.
If they are situated in the place of sesame seeds or reside in the abodes of cows, goats, buffaloes, and so forth,
there will be eye disease in the middle of the village or in temples and similar places.

If there is fear for the kingdom which is a constituent part of that [kingdom], it pertains to the king; [this is indicated] by [the appearance of such signs] at the temple, in the assembly hall, at a sacred tree, on a great road, or even in a monastery. || 439 ||
If [cracks] appear at a well, a garden, or the like, there will be distress for the kingdom;
however, if they occur at the base of a linga, one should predict danger for the king. (440)
In the case of the emergence of a honeycomb, the result shall be exactly like this;
likewise, even upon seeing an anthill at the gateway or other such places, the result is declared to be the same. (441)
Having first dug a pit suitable for burial and filled it with salt and other substances, along with fragments of pure clay, so that there may be no further rebirth; 442.
Having performed the sprinkling for an auspicious day, one should sprinkle with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having installed the deity with water-pots (kalaśas), one should perform the fire-oblation (mūrtihoma) for the forms.
One should perform this practice for seven days at a linga possessing the marks of a child, or on a pedestal, or in a temple, or in the inner sanctum, or at the doorway.
One should spend three days in the Jāti-dharmamaṇḍapa and the Beramaṇḍapa; elsewhere, one should perform the rite called Mūrti-śāntihoma for a single day.
In the royal capital, one should perform the Diśāhoma sacrifice for fourteen days;
however, if there is a honeycomb located therein, one should remove that honeycomb.
Having purified [the area] with cow-dung water and sprinkled it with water from a rosary-string,
and having performed the ceremonial bath (snapana) for the Lord of Gods, one should then proceed with the oblation to the quarters (diśāhoma).
According to the number of days previously prescribed by Valmīka, if the daily, occasional, or optional bathing rites have been omitted, [the following should be performed].
If a great illness should befall the performer, he should then perform a propitiatory *homa*;
furthermore, he should perform the ceremonial bath at the prescribed time as previously described.
Or, in the event of the deficiency of any such limb, the kingdom will become devoted to evil;
having recited the Aghora mantra three hundred times, one should perform the complete ceremonial bath.
If the site is devoid of its constituent parts or if instability arises on the ground,
one should offer a thousand oblations of the Aghora mantra and then prepare the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) according to the prescribed rules.

If the Kumbha and other [astrological periods] are deficient, or even if they are established by authoritative means, a quarrel arises in the kingdom; [this is remedied] by reciting the Aghora mantra a thousand times.
Furthermore, one should perform the ablution with the water-pot, the weapon, the hand, and the banner;
thus, with those very same items, combined with double the quantity of substances.
When the jars have been abandoned by the mind, there are three hundred previous Aghoras;
two hundred in the *kumbha*, one hundred in the *vardhanī*, and [one hundred] in the *kalaśas*.
The preceptor, acting as the mantra-master, should recite [the mantras] for them in succession so that their honor may be established;
either the Śiva-kumbha or the Vardhanī vessel has been installed. (455)
If it occurs while accompanied by discord and the like, or without having been granted permission, then it will bring about fault for the king, the queen, and the ritual officiants. || 456 ||
Then the minister should recite five hundred times, and two hundred and one hundred times respectively;
he should always recite the Aghora mantra twice that amount.
Taking another vessel, such as a water-pot (kumbha) or the like, filled with the respective substances,
one should place it in a shallow bowl, a conch, a golden vessel, or one made from the wood of the Brahma-tree (Ficus religiosa).
Having established [the deity], one should bathe the Lord while reciting the Śataghora mantra a hundred times;
if the jars, beginning with the principal one, are encircled with threads, it increases the enemy's power.
Thereafter, the recitation (japa) should be performed one hundred times with the Aghora mantra;
likewise, it is considered an expiation when [the thread] is wrapped with a very fine thread.
If the covering is omitted, the preceptor should recite [the mantra] one hundred times with a terrible [penance];
if the *kūrca* is lacking, the presence of the deities is not found here.
If the ritual vessel (utkūrca) and so forth are inverted, the result is considered to be exactly like that;
at that time, the practitioner of mantras should recite [the mantra] two hundred or three hundred times with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
In the absence of jewels, gold, and so forth, the architect shall be without wealth;
likewise, in the event of a loss of cloth, he should recite the Hṛdaya-mantra one thousand times.
Furthermore, one should perform the ritual bathing with the aforementioned gems as prescribed;
however, if the substances such as the products of the cow (gavya) are omitted, one should predict conflict within the kingdom.
Then, having recited the Aghora mantra a hundred times, one should unite that substance with Śiva;
if it was devoid of the Puṇyāha and the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa), one should again recite the Aghora mantra a hundred times.
If the worship was not performed at the water-jar (kumbha) and the ritual bathing remains unperformed, then one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma);
likewise, if the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) has not been done.

The practitioner of mantra should recite the hundred-fold *ghora* mantra for the purpose of bringing the deity into proximity during the five months beginning with Āṣāḍha and ending with Kṛttikā. (467)
Whatever rites are performed in a temple or a house when the Pavitrārohaṇa is omitted, all of them are indeed fruitless.
Having worshipped the deity according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the oblation to the quarters;
thereafter, in the desired month, one should perform the supreme rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa).
O elder brothers, the procedure for ascending the *damanaka* plant is likewise proclaimed;
if the festival of lights (*dīpāvali*) is omitted, men are tormented by their enemies. (470)

Having then performed the *mūrtihoma*, one should lead her [the image] to the place where she was obtained during a month of disturbances in the kingdom caused by enemies, thieves, and the like, or through mutual conflict. (471)
If there is fear of obstacles from spirits and the like, one should protect [the ritual] in a cave, in water, or on the ground; having performed this rite therein, one should proceed. (472)
Having worshipped the image with perfumes and other offerings, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before it,
upon which a water-pot (kumbha) joined with a vardhanī vessel— either surrounded by smaller jars or not— is placed.
Having placed the Sūtras and other texts together, and having invoked Maheśvara as Soma accompanied by the Vidyeśvaras, one should worship him with their respective mantras. || 474 ||

To the east of that, having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should [offer] a hundred or fifty oblations with the Śiva-mantra, with the Manonmanī mantra, and with the Brahma-mantras accompanied by their ancillaries (aṅgas). || 475 ||
Accompanied by the lords of knowledge (vidyeśvaras), and joined with a hundred oblations for each,
combined with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and cooked rice, one should finally perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One should install the mantra in a water-pot, a small jar, or a pedestal fashioned from clay and other materials, or in a pedestal or a linga constructed of bricks. || 477 ||
The Guru should bathe the pedestal and so forth with the very water contained in that jar;
he should place the Goddess either on the ground in front of the pedestal or upon the pedestal-base (piṇḍikā).
For that purpose, one should perform worship daily upon a *liṅga* or a pedestal (*pīṭha*).
This procedure for the images (*bera*) serves as the cause for their presence.
In whose kingdom a phallic image (liṅga) stands with its head devoid of flowers, that kingdom will constantly suffer ruin from rain, wind, heat, and other such calamities. || 480 ||

A linga that has been served [inappropriately], one situated in a ruined dwelling, one frequented by wild animals, birds, and reptiles, one harassed by cattle, or one defiled by other deities; || 481 ||
It constantly harms the performer and harms even those who are powerful;
therefore, O King, one should have this rite of sprinkling and other such acts performed without delay.
From that time forward, O twice-born ones, one should cause worship to be performed for one's own prosperity— whether it be of the highest, middling, low, or even the lowest kind.
Whether performed once, twice, or thrice a day, it should be joined with recitation;
provided with perfume and incense, it is considered especially distinguished and supreme. (484)

If it remains thereafter with a lamp, then likewise with the food offering (naivedya), then with betel (tāmbūla)—this is considered the most excellent; it is held to be praiseworthy when accompanied by the ritual oblation (bali).

Then the fire-ritual (agnikārya) is to be honored; thereafter, the sacrifice with its festival is excellent; and after that, the [resulting] happiness is supreme. Knowing this, one should conduct [the rites] every day.
One should offer water, flowers, or leaves every day;
however, if the Liṅga is damaged by rain or other such causes, one should construct a temple for it.
If the abode is broken or even if it is harassed by wild animals and the like, one should renovate it and perform its protection by means of door-panels, bolts, and so forth. (488)
If a linga or other image already established in its former place is superseded by a newly installed image of Brahmā or another deity, the wise man should relocate that [original] image elsewhere.
O best of the twice-born, in a sacred field of Śiva, a grove of Śiva, or a village of Śiva,
whether it be Viṣṇu, Viriñci, Śakra, Buddha, or even an Arhat— (490)
O best of the twice-born, those deities such as Anyadeva who are independent [deities] should not be installed; even if they have already been installed, one should relocate them to a distant place.
By that, there shall be peace for the king, as well as for the kingdom and the people;
one should establish a Vaiṣṇava or other shrine outside of the sacred field (śivakṣetra).
"Therefore, this place is indeed suitable for Śiva, the God of gods, who possesses immeasurable splendor, since Śiva is the sovereign lord of all. (493)
Whether it be Vaiṣṇava, Vairiñca, Bauddha, or likewise Mārhataka;
or Saura, Śākra, or even the station of Vahni or Yama.
Or of Nirṛti, or of Varuṇa, or of Vāyu, or of Vaikhānasa;
or of Pārvatī, or of Durgā, or of Kṣetrapa who has the form of the Moon. || 495 ||
And [the worship] of Jyeṣṭhā, Śrī, Bhūmi, and Smara; of Gaṇapa, Skanda, Nandīśa, the Vasus, and the Lord of the Nāgas. || 496 ||
O best of the twice-born, the place ordained for the sages, humans, and asuras is indeed worthy of the Lord; of this there is no doubt. (497)
Those who proclaim that the wielder of the Pināka bow is superior to all, yet remember him as being common [to all], go to the ocean of hell. (498)
"Brahmā, the Lord Viṣṇu, and Rudra are equal," so they say;
yet those of wicked intellect are said to wander about for a very long time indeed. (499)
In the Raurava and other hells, liberation is not considered possible for them in any way whatsoever;
however, I am to be worshipped by those who have me as their sole refuge, and not by others. (500)
Those over eighty years of age, or children under sixteen, as well as women or those afflicted by disease, deserve only half of the prescribed penance. (501)
And even in that case, having recognized the exhaustion [involved], one should apply half of half [the effort];
for it is extremely difficult to perform oneself, whereas with double the effort, it can be done by another.

Having carefully considered the place, the time, the age, the capacity, the caste, the devotion, and the sequence of the ritual, [the gift] should be bestowed; however, fasting is not to be prescribed for one afflicted by illness.

If one is incapable of performing the expiation, it must be undertaken by kinsmen such as the father or brothers after dividing the cost; however, by other people, it must be performed at double the expense.
If they are devotees of Sadāśiva, a penance must be granted for those who have stepped upon children, women, the bound, or the sick. (505)
For one who is less than eleven years of age but more than five, the brother, the father, or some other friend shall perform the penance. (506)
Therefore, for this foolish man, there is neither offense nor sin;
there is no royal punishment, nor does any expiation exist. (507)
That by which a location is indicated is called "diśika";
furthermore, many locations are taught in the scripture, among which the supreme place of liberation is considered the highest. (508)

The locus of enjoyment for the body, as well as the other locations, should be understood in sequence as the heart, the throat, the palate, the center of the eyebrows, and the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). || 509 ||
The region of the navel is said here to be the location of the root of the penis;
however, if the twilight ritual (saṃdhyā) is omitted even once, one should recite the Sadyojāta mantra a hundred times.
If a meditator fails to perform the twilight rites at each junction of the day, he must perform a hundred meditations; however, if the failure is unintentional, it is one meditation per junction.
But when the worship of the deity is omitted intentionally, there must be a fast as well.
Whether one worships at one time or at two times and so forth,
the recitation of the Aghora mantra ten thousand times in a single day shall result in knowledge.

Fasting should also be understood as being required when, despite performing worship for a long time, one fails to do so out of desire, or when there is an omission of the two daily sessions and so forth.
One should perform the expiation according to the very loss of the count;
however, in the case of a lapse of two days or more, it should be performed with a thousandfold [repetition] of various forms.
If the fortnightly worship is omitted, there shall be three hundred [recitations] every day;
for its monthly omission, there shall be ten thousand recitations of the Aghora mantra, with the number increasing accordingly.
After a year, or even beyond that, purification through initiation is prescribed when one's own chosen liṅga has fallen, been burnt by fire, or has been stolen.
If it is touched by humans, monkeys, crows, and the like, then by reciting the Aghora mantra and re-installing another liṅga, it becomes pure; of this there is no doubt. (517)
When the *liṅga* falls from the hand or other parts, there is an increase of two [units] starting from the finger-breadth;
from one thousand onwards, the increase for the *aghora* [mantra] shall be by thousands in sequence.
If the *liṅga* falls upon its support, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times for each *tāla*;
however, if it falls without support, the best of gurus should prescribe double that amount.
If the fall occurs from one cubit up to two cubits, it is declared as follows:
having recited ten thousand [mantras] and so forth, [one should purify] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the nectar (amṛta), and other substances. || 520 ||
Having bathed him, the wise man should worship the deity and especially honor him;
O best of the twice-born, that [rite] is prescribed for the sake of bodily integrity in the case of the Liṅga and other such objects.

If the fall is from a height of two cubits or more, yet the image remains unimpaired, purification occurs through one hundred thousand recitations; or in this case, consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is considered the proper rite.
If an embrace or a clasp of the hands is broken unintentionally, one should perform twice the previously mentioned penance; however, there is no atonement for doing so intentionally.

If [the water] has been touched by Brāhmaṇas and others who have not undergone the Śiva-consecration (śivasaṃskāra), the best of men should recite the Aghora mantra, increasing it by one hundred [repetitions] in successive order. 524.
If the linga is touched by the foot or stepped upon, one should recite [the mantra] twenty thousand times;
if it is touched by dust clinging to the foot, one should recite it one hundred and ten thousand times.

When the symptoms are affected by phlegm and so forth, the best of men should perform thirty thousand, twenty thousand, or many forms [of recitation] with water and other substances appropriate for each. 526.
If [the body] is touched by urine or water, one should recite [the mantra] twenty-five thousand times;
if it is defiled by blood, urine, menstrual blood, or semen, one should recite fifty thousand times.
By touching water associated with that [impurity], one should recite this [mantra] minus a quarter;
however, upon touching feces, it shall be one hundred thousand (lakṣa) minus a quarter by means of that water.
In the same way, one should declare purification upon falling into a pit for discarded offerings;
however, if one falls into a pit containing excrement and the like, one should recite the mantra one hundred and fifty thousand times.
If one is touched by those born in the natural order (anuloma), one should perform the rite appropriate for one's family;
if touched by those born in the inverse order (pratiloma) and so forth, one becomes pure by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
If the linga is touched by those following the left-hand (vāmamārga) or right-hand (dakṣamārga) paths, one should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times;
if it is touched by outcasts (caṇḍāla), dog-cookers (pāṇaka), and the like, purification occurs through re-consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
One should indeed establish that very [fire] with a value of one hundred thousand [offerings] for stability;
furthermore, in the case of a lapse in the daily *homa*, the expiation is performed as if it were a daily rite.
On the eighth or fourteenth lunar day, on a festival day, at the solstices, or during eclipses of the sun or moon,
one should perform a fourfold [penance] in the event of a regular omission.
On other auspicious days, one should perform this fourfold;
one should carry out that previously mentioned expiation for the creation of the fire-altar.
And having taken [the materials], one should perform one hundred and eight oblations for Śiva;
[this applies] in the event of the omission of the vow, other rites, or the observances.
One attains purification by reciting the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times;
however, this does not apply if the *pavitra* has not been prepared during the five months beginning with Āṣāḍha.
Having recited the Aghora mantra three hundred thousand times, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
this is considered the expiation for omitting the Pavitrārohaṇa rite.
When that other month has been completed, the recitation of this mantra is prescribed;
even a hundred thousand recitations is considered equivalent to a Cāndrāyaṇa fast.
Purification occurs through two hundred recitations once the arghya vessel has been discarded;
however, in the event of its destruction, it is achieved by a thousand, and if it is overturned, by half of that.
Or, in the case of a *sphoṭa* [tear] in the *Akṣasūtra*, purification is performed according to the section specified by the *liṅga*.
If there is a break in the nine-strand thread, one should perform a thousand recitations (*japa*).
It is likewise held that a hundred repetitions are required for a worn-out thread due to its falling from the hand;
one should touch with scented water a rosary that has slipped from the hand.
Even one who has performed a hundred recitations of the Gāyatrī becomes pure through that same [rite] previously mentioned for the aforementioned action;
however, in the case of a defect in the bell, one becomes pure by one-eighth of what is prescribed for the Liṅga.

When articles of worship, such as a seat and the like, are touched by the feet, one should recite the Aghora mantra two hundred times; however, if done intentionally, one should recite it ten thousand times.
Upon offering incense made from animal parts, one should recite the fifth [mantra] one hundred times;
likewise upon seeing defiled food offerings containing hair, insects, bones, and the like. (544)
One should recite the Aghora mantra ten thousand times out of desire, or one hundred times if done unintentionally;
this applies whether there is a daily offering of food (naivedya) or a reduction in it, or even for occasional rites.
Having recited ten thousand repetitions of the formidable mantra, one attains purification for having unintentionally stepped upon the Guru, the Deity, or the Śiva-āgama. || 546 ||
One should recite the terrible mantra twenty-four thousand times according to one's desire;
however, for violating the command of the Great Lord, the Guru, or Caṇḍa, one is purified by a hundred thousand recitations.
From consuming substances acquired for this purpose, one incurs a penance reduced by one quarter;
however, for consuming the remains of an offering (nirmālya), one should mutter [the mantra] ten thousand times as a severe expiation for negligence.
The gift [of the substance] should be equal to its consumption; half of that [is required] for neglecting it.
Alternatively, if one consumes it unintentionally, one should recite the five Brahmans.
One who is purified by initiation may, at will, [consume] up to fifteen hundred [offerings];
however, having stepped over the remains of an offering (nirmālya), one should recite the mantra ten thousand times while giving half of that as a sacrificial fee.

In leaping over it, in touching it, and in selling or eating it—[one incurs sin regarding] the property of the gods, the materials belonging to the deities, and the food offerings (naivedya) that have been presented. (551)
Caṇḍadravya and nirmālya are recorded as being of six kinds; the property of the village lord, the property of the deity, and the deity's belongings such as cloth and so forth [are included]. (552)
The food offering prepared for him is presented as the remains of the deity's meal;
that which is given is the substance of Caṇḍa, while the floral remains (nirmālya) are cast outside.
Even if the deity has been dismissed, that which remains on the pedestal is not to be treated as discarded floral offerings (nirmālya);
by giving it away, one is born as a flesh-eater, and by consuming it, one becomes an outcaste (mātaṅga).
By jumping over it, there is a loss of spiritual power; by selling it, one becomes a Śabara;
and by touching it, one is born as a woman—of this there is no doubt regarding the *nirmālya*. (555)
Whatever is touched by the discarded floral offerings (nirmālya) of the deity, or by the arm of a man, or by a person—
therein the previously mentioned [penance] is reduced by one-quarter due to touching, stepping over, or consuming it.
Consumption is said to be of two kinds: that which is unoffered and its opposite.
Of these, the former consists of what originates from the village of the gods and so forth, intended for the God of Gods.
Whosoever, being utterly deluded, takes up rice or any other such thing by whatever means and consumes it, is considered a thief of my wealth. (558)
Whether it be rice or cooked food prepared for my sake, whoever gives it away or eats it is also called a thief. (559)
Those very same [faults] that were previously considered harmful even when consumed by me, are likewise [harmful] in all four ways; thus, my eating [of them] bestows extreme merit.
Having prepared an offering for Śiva, he presents it above that;
then, having offered the remainder to me, he eats it every day with devotion.
This very person is said to be like me who would likewise eat the sacrificial pap (caru);
for a man who, out of greed, eats what has been eaten by me or what has been eaten by Caṇḍa.
That wicked and evil-minded man who eats what is praised as pure out of devotion is said to be no different from the two previously mentioned. (563)
The sin of a pure-souled Brāhmaṇa perishes quickly;
even a man of impure soul becomes purified by eating what has been offered to me out of greed. || 564 ||
O twice-born ones, just as the consumer of flavor meets with destruction upon eating it,
so too shall those who bear my body in this world— the teachers devoted to me— meet their end.
Among those who have me as their sole refuge, no other [offering] is appropriate;
therefore, having consumed my *nirmālya*, one should perform atonement.
O best of the twice-born, listen as I declare the expiation for all those belonging to the four castes, beginning with the preceptors. (567)

Observing silence, bathing at the three junctions of the day, worshipping Śiva, the fire, and the Guru, and performing ten thousand recitations of the Aghora mantra upon a mandala smeared with cow dung. (568)
One should partake of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), sacrificial porridge (caru), and a tooth-stick in succession;
one should observe this vow every night for the purification of sin. (569)
Or even without the fire-ritual, let the mere recitation of mantras be performed;
this vow is declared to be the "Manu-vow," which increases tenfold.
From that [Upa-vrata], the Daśavṛddha-vrata arises, and likewise the Mahāvrata;
in this scripture, the Mahāvrata is declared for those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin).
The penance prescribed for the secondary sins (anupātaka) is said to follow that of the primary ones.
These [primary sins] are: killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, theft, and violating the teacher's bed. (572)
In this context, there are the great sins (mahāpātaka), and the fifth is association with such persons;
thus has desire been described, and it is held to be half the measure of ignorance.

For killing a Brahmin, however, one must observe a quarter of the vow; for killing a Kṣatriya, half of that is prescribed; for the Vaiśya caste, half of that again; and for a Śūdra, half of that is required. (574)
In all cases of offspring born in the natural order (anuloma), one should observe the rules prescribed for the mother;
in those born in secret, half [of that]; and in those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), half of that again.
For all those who have been initiated, the penance is declared to be double;
for the killing of one who has been consecrated, the vow prescribed for an initiate is considered appropriate.
The liquors derived from the jackfruit, the grape, the madhūka, the date, the coconut, the sugarcane, honey, molasses, the mṛdvīkā, maireya, and that produced from the coconut; 577.
One should understand that there are eleven types of intoxicants in general;
the twelfth is *surā* made from flour, which is considered the lowest of them all. (578)
Having drunk liquor made from flour, a Brahmin must then perform a great vow;
for drinking eleven measures of liquor, he should perform a tenth part of the vow.
O best of the twice-born, having once drunk liquor made from flour through negligence,
a Brahmin becomes pure after ten nights by subsisting on cow’s urine and barley.
The increase of days through the practice of two sessions and so forth is highly commended;
for all classes, beginning with the Kṣatriyas, the previously stated rule is declared to apply.
For the theft of gold exceeding one hundred [units], death is prescribed for Kṣatriyas and the other castes; however, for a Brāhmaṇa, there is never death under any circumstances. (582)
For stealing one *niṣka*, ten thousand recitations are prescribed; for five *niṣkas*, it is said to be one hundred thousand;
for ten *lakṣas*, it is up to ten million; and beyond that, the number increases tenfold.

For stealing gold, it is declared that for a Brāhmaṇa the penance lasts up to one hundred lakhs [of repetitions], while for Kṣatriyas and the other castes, it is said to be reduced by half and half again respectively.
For the theft of silver, the fine is considered double that of grain;
for gold, silver, and grain, it is one hundred and eleven [paṇas]. 585.

Indeed, for a poor man, it is only double or more than that [the standard fine] in proportion; however, there is no sin at all in sexual union with another woman, provided it is not with the wife of one's guru. 586.

If one performs officiating at sacrifices, forming a matrimonial alliance, studying together, or eating in the company of those who have committed mortal sins, he too is considered equal to them. (587)
If one should perform a quarter of that penance within the end of a year,
it is declared to be an "anuvrata" for the sake of purification from a minor offense (anupātaka).
O Brahmins, sexual intercourse with a maternal aunt, a sister, one's own daughter, or a paternal aunt is declared to be an *anupātaka* (a minor offense). || 589 ||
Sexual intercourse with the wife of a Brahmin, killing a kinsman, drinking from the hand of a Caṇḍāla, and consuming the leavings of a washerman constitute secondary sins (anupātaka). || 590 ||
O best of the twice-born, having uprooted a linga, a pedestal, or an image and the like out of hatred, one becomes guilty of a sin greater than any other transgression. (591)

It has been said that one should double [the amount] in cases such as fear of kings or thieves; that which was extracted is for the purpose of avoiding defects such as being situated in an inauspicious place or being submerged. 592.
By duly performing the Aghora rite and reciting it one hundred thousand times, one becomes purified.
[This applies even to] the seizure of a deity’s field or the taking of offerings intended for a deity. (593)
The theft of Śiva’s scriptures, the removal of a Śiva-liṅga, and the determination of punishment for the four classes beginning with the Śaivas; 594.
A minor vow has been declared for the sake of purification from secondary sins (upapātaka):
[approaching] the wife of a paternal uncle, a friend, or a pupil, as well as a daughter-in-law and those who have sought refuge. || 595 ||

A queen, a female renunciant, a nurse, a virtuous woman, one of the highest caste, a woman of the same lineage (sagotrā), a maternal aunt, and one who shares the same ancestral lineages (samānapravarā). || 596 ||
The sexual union with these women is declared to be a minor offense (upapātaka),
