as is the act of marrying before an elder brother (parivitti) and the one so married (parivettā), as well as officiating at their sacrifice.
The giving away of a daughter, the disparagement of Śiva, Agni, and the Vedas, hostility toward one's guru, and likewise the misappropriation of what has been entrusted [to one]. (598)

Abandoning one's father, mother, or teacher; giving false testimony or bringing a false accusation; being a mere talker; and being an outcast—these constitute the loss of that [wealth], or alternatively, its acquisition. (599)
The seizing of houses, pleasure-pools, jewels, and groves is a minor sin; likewise, the theft of ponds, wells, tanks, and the like constitutes a secondary offense (upapātaka). 600.
Upon the killing of an elephant, horse, man, woman, camel, buffalo, donkey, or ox, one should perform the *upavrata* penance; in the case of stealing them, it shall be half of that.
Half [of that penance] shall apply to eating its flesh; half of that to eating what has been touched by its excrement;
a quarter of that to touching its urine or the like; in such cases, one should perform a ritual bath.
If one eats food from which a leper has taken a morsel, or is released [from contact] after touching his excrement, one should perform half the penance;
if one touches his hair, bones, or the like, bathing alone is prescribed.
A cow-killer should perform double the penance prescribed for a minor vow (upavrata), while one who steals a cow or eats its meat should perform half of that.
One who steals it or eats its meat should practice a penance equal to that [of the killer].
Dwelling in a cow-pen and following the cows, one is purified by the gift of a cow;
in the absence of a cow, its full value must likewise be given.
Having caused a pregnant cow, a tawny cow, a milch cow,
or a sacrificial cow of good disposition to suffer through confinement or other such means, one should perform double the penance.
One should perform one quarter of the penance for obstructing, two quarters for binding,
three-quarters for officiating as a priest [in such an act], and the full penance for actually causing the fall [of the victim].
Medicine, salt, oil, and oil-cake as food—these should not be given in excess; rather, one should cause them to be given in small quantities at the proper time.
One should not tether [the cow] with a coconut-fiber rope nor with one made of muñja grass;
otherwise, due to a lack of strength, the cow might somehow suffer harm while grazing. (509)
Whether submerged in water or a pond, struck by lightning from a cloud, fallen suddenly into a chasm, or even devoured by a corpse-eating dog; (610)
If she has been struck by cold winds, or even died from being bound, or [died] in an empty house, in the forest, or from falling from a tree during a house fire; || 611 ||
With equanimity and the other [brahmavihāras], one considers their residence, eating, and so forth as supreme;
likewise, the violation of virgins, and the selling of another's wife or oneself. (612)
Atheism, performing malevolent magic, officiating at the sacrifice of one unworthy to sacrifice,
and eating the food of those with low body hair or of outcastes and leavings— these constitute minor offenses (upapātaka).
O Brahmins, if one drinks or otherwise consumes a substance that was contained in a liquor vessel or has been touched by liquor, one should perform this same penance for double the duration.
If a Brāhmaṇa eats during the period of impurity of a Śūdra, he incurs half the penance of fasting;
if he eats during the impurity of a Vaiśya, the Brāhmaṇa incurs half that [penance]; and if he eats during the impurity of a Kṣatriya, he incurs half of that again.
If a Brahmin has eaten during the period of impurity of a king, a Śūdra, or a Viḍa, he should perform half of the penance;
if a Kṣatriya has eaten in the house of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, he should perform half of the penance prescribed for him.
The procedure for eating during one's own period of impurity has been declared only in relation to the funeral rites (antyeṣṭi);
however, by eating food from one who is more impure than oneself, or by eating food from one's own household while in a state of impurity, [the penance is greater]. || 617 ||
One should perform [the penance] reduced by one-quarter, one-half, and three-quarters respectively;
a Śūdra should do so in this manner, and if those other than him should perform it, they should do so according to this rule.
A Brahmin who consumes feces or urine,
or likewise tastes the mouth of a menstruating woman or a woman of the Caṇḍāla caste, shall perform this penance.
Having committed slander against washermen and others, one should likewise observe that same vow;
this vow is prescribed here for the sake of purifying the sin of a Brahmin.
In the case of sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍāla woman, a Pāṇa woman, or a washerwoman, double the penance is prescribed;
however, for the sake of purification, a Brāhmaṇa should perform merely the vow of fasting in water.
In the case of sexual intercourse with the wife of a Brahmin, one should indeed perform the Upavratam penance;
however, the triad beginning with the Kṣatriya (Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra) should perform it reduced by one-quarter for each successive class.
If a Brāhmaṇī woman, having offspring, has fallen by uniting with a Śūdra,
she shall perform half of the vow prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa upon a single act of such approach.
The *upavrata* occurs after one month, the *anuvrata* after six months, and the *mahāvrata* after a full year; beyond three years, she is indeed fallen (*patitā*).
If it is a queen, half of this [penance] is prescribed; if it is a Vaiśya woman, half of that;
and if it is a Śūdra woman through union with a Śūdra, one should perform half of that again. || 625 ||
A Śūdra likewise should perform penance for the sake of purification;
O twice-born ones, in the case of sexual intercourse with a maiden, he should perform twice the penance previously mentioned.

If it is with a Vaiśya, he receives half; therefore, if it is with a Kṣatriya, he receives half of that; and for a twice-born man in sexual union with women beginning with a Brāhmaṇa woman, it is declared that he receives half of that. 627.
Those born in the natural order (anuloma) should perform the penance prescribed for their own mother's caste for the sake of their purification;
however, for those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), the vow is that which is prescribed for a Śūdra, doubled.
A man who has discharged semen into non-human females, into women of lower castes, or into improper apertures,
or even into water, shall observe a vow for one year.
For approaching a river-dancer, a female actor, or one who lives by bamboo-work, the penance is that prescribed for adultery;
and having approached the wife of an outcaste, one should perform half the penance of a Caṇḍāla.
If a woman should become pregnant, the atonement is impossible;
once the fetus has been expelled, she should perform twice the penance previously described. || 631 ||
She should not move about within the house, nor prepare food and other provisions;
she should not sleep with her husband, nor eat together with her relatives.
One should observe this vow after bathing, eating, and approaching a woman during the day, and by binding the penis with iron or similar materials. (633)
O twice-born ones, having eaten the leavings of those of inverse caste (pratiloma), one should perform a vow;
however, having eaten the leavings of those of equal caste, one becomes pure by fasting.
For eating the leavings of one's own caste, the recitation of mantras shall be one thousand for a middling offense and ten thousand for a low one,
along with fasting for two or three nights.
Through contact with the leavings of one of the lowest caste, the sin becomes a hundredfold;
there should be an increase in the number of recitations and fasts, starting from a single night and proceeding in sequence.
Censuring Śiva or a Brāhmaṇa, consorting with a woman who drinks liquor, living by means of women, violence, or medicine, usury, and working for wages; || 637 ||
To have authority over all affairs, to operate great machines, and the abandonment of Vedic study, the sacred fire, and one's sons—these are sins. (638)
Of sesame, rice, kuluttha, śāli rice, mung beans, black gram, niṣpāva, peas, mustard seeds, and barley; 639.
O best of the twice-born, for the theft of saffron, priyaṅgu, nīvāra, kodrava, and other such grains— whether with their husks or without them— one must perform half of the prescribed vow.
And when there is the theft of vehicles, beds, and seats made of bell-metal, brass, stone, iron, tin, lead, copper, and so forth, as well as the theft of clothing; || 641 ||
The mere vow has been prescribed for the release of monkeys, dogs, deer, and for those who eat excrement or are boars; [the penance] is threefold for the release of these.

Whether for the sake of the welfare of wild animals, whether they are vicious or non-vicious, or for the purpose of killing them—such as a hare, a porpoise, a conch, or a crocodile—[one may act]. 643.
And for the purification of that sin, one should observe a vow regarding the killing of an owl,
a heron, a vulture, a crow, or a water-fowl.
Of the cock, hawk, and vulture, as well as the swan and peacock;
of those with eyes like tawny gems, and of the lizard and the hundred-leaved plant. || 645 ||
Of the pigeon, the crane, the ṭiṭṭibha bird, the jarāṅgin, the piṅgalī, the ruddy goose, the owl, and the parrot. || 646 ||
The frog, the cow, the iguana, the chameleon, the mouse, the snake, the muskrat, the fish, the tortoise, and the one called the crab. (647)
The scorpion, the snail, the locust, the fly, as well as the ant, the earthworm, the spider, and others which have been mentioned; || 648 ||
Whether they be terrestrial, aquatic, or others dwelling in the intermediate space,
having committed the killing of any of these, a Brahmin shall observe one quarter of the penance.
Regarding these boneless beings, the recitation of the Śatāghora mantra is prescribed;
furthermore, an expiation for this is here stated by another method as well.
Having killed [a cow] out of desire, a twice-born man should then recite [the mantra] immediately in a cow-pen;
having drunk liquor unintentionally, he should then recite it in the temple of Śiva.
Having committed theft, one should mutter [the mantra] intensely in a cemetery;
for sexual intercourse with the wife of a guru, however, one should mutter it in the forest even without desire.
Having performed the yogic posture with all [the limbs], one should mutter the fifth [mantra] at the mountain peak;
by revolving that which was performed out of desire in public, one becomes purified.

O twice-born ones, purification for an act committed unintentionally or in secret is desired after one thousand repetitions; however, for an act committed intentionally and not in secret, one should recite it ten thousand times.

If it occurs unintentionally in public, there too the purification consists of twenty thousand [repetitions]; even for intentional acts, purification may be attained here, provided there is no betrayal of the Guru.
Therefore, the preceptor must first perform an arduous penance for him;
otherwise, the sacrifice must be performed again, for there is no purification for him in any other way.
The combination of the three sins is common to all, beginning with the Brahmins;
however, when it comes to the drinking of liquor, if it is done by an uninitiated Śūdra, it becomes a minor offense.
Because there is no prohibition regarding that, no fault arises therein;
however, due to the restrictive rule, one must perform three hundred recitations of the *ghora* mantra.
Committing adultery with the teacher’s wife is equal to the four [mahāpātakas]; treachery toward the teacher and treachery toward Śiva—therefore, that becomes a sin. (659)
O twice-born ones, regarding the theft of earthy substances such as wood when no fiery substance is involved,
purification through the recitation of the Sadyojāta mantra is here declared for unintentional acts.
If [this occurs] unintentionally, a recitation (japa) of twenty-five [verses] should be performed, or one hundred [recitations];
likewise, having consumed clarified butter, or salt, sugar, and so forth, [the same penance applies].
Whether intentionally or unintentionally, one should first recite the Vāmadeva mantra while taking hold of a metallic object such as brass, copper, bronze, or the like.

Or, for stealing a cow full of ghee, purification is as before, depending on whether it was done intentionally or unintentionally; likewise for stealing flowers, perfumes, and so forth, or a man or even a woman.
Having offered an ox, elephants, horses, and other such objects, as well as milk, water, or weapons, as before, one should offer them to Īśa and perform the recitation as previously described.
If one has consumed forbidden food, one should recite the Guhyaka mantra a hundred times;
if unintentionally, thirty times; and if intentionally, one should recite it while avoiding liquor and other such substances.
If a wise man, out of delusion, eats the food of a woman in her courses, he should mutter the Gṛhya-mantra ten thousand times;
having muttered it one thousand and five hundred times, he becomes pure by means of bathing.
Beyond that, fasting at night is prescribed for five up to a hundred [repetitions];
beyond that, it is a fast for three nights starting from ten thousand [repetitions].
Having touched one initiated into his own caste, he becomes pure by sipping water;
having sipped water after touching even one not initiated, he should mutter the mantra of his own clan-lord a hundred times.
However, from touching one who has been initiated or one who is being initiated, the expiation is as before;
if that uninitiated person is touched, one should bathe and recite [the mantra] two hundred times.
This same [penance applies] from internal contact for one who has been initiated;
however, for another, one should recite three hundred [mantras] after contact; by fasting, he shall become pure.
That same [penance] would apply to a consecrated person (dīkṣita) upon being touched by a Śūdra;
and for one who has been touched by a consecrated person, there is a fast for five hundred [days].
Others, however, for the sake of their own purification, should perform penance reduced by one quarter;
but upon touching an outcaste, they must observe three nights, whereas for touching a dog, they must observe ten thousand [verses].
In that case, one should recite the fifth mantra without hesitation;
however, due to contact with a Caṇḍāla, a severe and formidable recitation of ten thousand (ayuta) repetitions must be performed.

If a house or similar place is entered by a fallen person (pātakin), one becomes pure by abandoning the vessels, plastering [the area], and performing the Kṛcchra penance; if one has eaten [there], one should perform the Taptakṛcchra.
Having learned of it, he should eat while standing on one foot; then he shall become equal [to the sinless].
For one who enters the house of a washerman or similar person without knowing, the penance is half of ten thousand [repetitions of a mantra].
In the case of contact with many temple-priests (devalakas), one becomes pure through the Kṛcchra or Cāndrāyaṇa penances;
for vessels made of gold, silver, and so forth, purification by water is prescribed.
The purification of conch shells and similar objects may be achieved with cow dung or by scrubbing;
the purification of bell-metal is accomplished with ash, while copper is purified with sour gruel.
This purification for vessels smeared with food remnants has been proclaimed:
a vessel touched by food remnants becomes pure without doubt simply by being sprinkled with water.
The purification of vessels made of gourds and the like, as well as those made of bamboo, is achieved by scrubbing them with cow-hair and water;
for those made of wood or metal, they are purified even more effectively by water alone.
The purification of hides, ropes, and garments shall be by means of alkaline water;
and the purification of water-vessels consists of being carried around a fire.
Whatever grass or other such things there may be, or wood, becomes pure when sprinkled;
likewise, the purification of the ground occurs through scraping and by rubbing it with cow dung. (681)
A vessel made of bamboo or clay that has come into contact with feces and the like must be discarded;
likewise, a woman who has been touched by the remains of offerings (nirmālya) is purified by her menses.
The purification of the remainder is as previously stated; the purification of cloth is by means of water.
And for bowls, leaves, containers, and so forth used for eating, [the same applies]. (683)
In this context, the renunciation of those things employed [for sense-gratification] is prescribed as purification;
however, the true purification of the mind and the senses is achieved through self-restraint (yama) and the other [Yogic limbs]. 684.

O tigers among sages, the pacification of pride is seen for the sake of purification through non-investigation; even the pacification of the intellect is proclaimed to result from the abandonment of attachment.
The vital breaths are always purified through the power of breath control (prāṇāyāma) performed according to the rules;
the purification of the primary principle (pradhāna), whose nature consists of the qualities (guṇas), is declared to result from meditation (dhyāna).
For the self is purified through discernment; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
One should perform a ritual bath after licking the remains of food left by dogs, cats, crows, and the like.
One is purified by seven applications of clay, either above or below the navel;
having bathed according to the rule for the head, one should perform the five ancillaries of knowledge.
The practitioner of mantra should perform one hundred recitations, or double that amount;
if he is touched by one who has not received initiation, he should perform the purificatory bath associated with fire.
If one has mixed discarded flower offerings (nirmālya) out of desire, Caṇḍanāyaka must be worshipped;
then one hundred recitations of that very God of gods, along with his ancillaries, must be performed. (690)
If contact occurs unintentionally with a single [impure object], there shall be a hundred [purifications];
however, for objects made of stone, it is by means of water churned with buttermilk.
The purification of all water-born items, as well as those made of bamboo,
and of oily vessels, is proclaimed to be by means of drying them with water.
Even for impure things, purification may occur through mere sprinkling alone;
likewise, honey and sugarcane juice are purified by boiling.
Fruits are purified by washing, and curd by inspection;
milk is purified by boiling, as are cooked foods by sprinkling.
Now, the purification of this Śaiva preceptor is performed by means of speech:
having caused suffering to others through the actions of speech, mind, and body. (695)

Having recognized [the transgression] through negligence, purification is always achieved by the recitation of the Śakti mantra; indeed, when there is negligence regarding the *samayas*, the recitation of the Śakti mantra is highly recommended. (696)
For stealing clothing, bedding, seats, and so forth, one should recite the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred times;
likewise for offering what is contemptible during rites for the Guru, the gods, or the sacred fire. (697)
O best of sages, when a mendicant is being led away unjustly, he is purified by giving even a small amount of medicine to those who are emaciated or afflicted by disease. (698)
It should always be accepted from everyone; for there is no fault in this teaching.
Just as salt is completely purified by being boiled again with water. (699)
But he who, having acquired wealth by unjust means, seeks to justify it through justice, and for whose sake one would even give up one's life—he is proclaimed a slayer of a Brahmin. (700)
Whether for the sake of the gods, for the sake of his guru or father, or even for his own sake,
he who gives up his life for such a purpose is proclaimed to be a slayer of a Brahmin.
The arsonist, the poisoner, the one with a weapon in hand, the robber of wealth, and the one who seizes land or a wife— these six are known as *ātatāyin* (aggressors).
One may slay even an assailant approaching in battle with weapons drawn, seeking to kill;
by doing so, one does not become a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahan).
Whether they be youths, children, or the elderly, or even a Brahmin of great learning—if an assassin approaches, one should certainly kill him without hesitation. (704)
Those worlds called "Sunless," shrouded in blinding darkness—those do they reach after death who, knowing [the truth], commit suicide. (705)
And one should not abandon the body out of desire when suffering arises, whether one has become weary of the world or has already attained worldly enjoyments. (706)
Through the water of meditative concentration and retention, one should abandon the mind that is dissolved in Śiva;
however, upon hearing censure of the triad beginning with Śiva, one should abandon one's own body.
One may kill him without any fault being incurred, and one shall attain the state of Śiva.
[This applies to those who follow] the Śaiva, Pāśupata, Kālāmukha, or Kāpāladhārin [sects]. (708)
Even if he were to destroy the entire world, that evil-souled one would be slain;
for both the slayer of a Brahmin and the ungrateful person remain so even through the purification of their actions.
The killer of one who has sought refuge and the murderer of a woman are both sinners;
likewise, one who subverts the sacred scriptures shall be equal to a thief of gold.
The theft of a precious horse, a human being, a woman, land, or a cow, as well as the misappropriation of a deposit—all these are indeed equal to the theft of gold. (711)
Deceiving a god or a Brahmin, giving false testimony, killing a friend, and likewise bringing a curse upon a high-souled person—these are specified here as such. (712)
For one who provides medicine, oil, or food for the sake of sustaining the lives of living beings, as well as for a bondsman, no fault is found therein. (713)
Having determined the lunar month and the specific lunar day (tithi) for each year, as well as the asterism (nakṣatra) of the sacred ford (tīrtha),
they first observe the festival during those same days as in former times.
Accompanied by the beating of drums and other instruments for nine days and so forth,
[the rite should be performed] either on a day three times that number, or twice that number, or on that very day.
If that [image] is treated otherwise, it will bring harm to the kingdom and the king;
therefore, a propitiatory rite (śānti) should first be performed, and one should carry out the festival as previously described.

However, it may take place within another month, or during that very month, or on the double of that day; then one should perform the image-oblation (mūrtihoma) and the directional oblations (diśāhuti).
Having performed the festival in due order according to its prescribed rules,
preceded by the hoisting of the flag, it should be celebrated for three times the number of days.
This procedure has been declared; it should be inferred in the same way even for a twofold [liṅga].
If the liṅga is of self-originated (svāyambhuva) nature, this very procedure is prescribed.

Whether in a human-made liṅga made of bamboo or the like, or in a divine one, or even in a stone one, one should again adjust the month, the asterism of the sacred site (tīrtha), or otherwise [the timing]. 720.
The increase of a festival that has been shortened by days yields fruit;
[this applies] during disturbances in the kingdom, famine, and in times of fear from kings, thieves, and the like. (721)
If, due to lack of wealth or other causes, it should prove impossible to perform [the rite] as previously described,
then even in that case, one should first bring about peace.
Alternatively, one may perform the festival even if it lacks the full number of days, following the traditional method;
for a festival constructed with fewer days is more praiseworthy than one where everything is omitted.
If a total omission occurs, a great fault arises for him;
at that time, one should perform the rite of pacification, the pacificatory fire-offering, and the fire-offering to the deity's form.

By this method, whatever [rite] is commenced from the very beginning of all occasional ceremonies that is devoid of the propitiation of obstacles and other [deities], it becomes a cause for the destruction of the kingdom.

Then one should perform a pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) and carry out the festival once more, if the preliminary consecration of the bull (vṛṣādhivāsana) was omitted or if the banner (dhvaja) has already been hoisted. || 726 ||
If cows perish, one should perform the pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) as prescribed;
there, one should perform the bull-sacrifice (vṛṣayāga) at the base of the flagstaff (dhvajadaṇḍa).
However, one should perform the mental placement of mantras and other rites upon the flagstaff that stands above;
if the hoisting of the flag is omitted, one should predict the downfall of the king.
Having performed the rite of pacification (śānti), the officiant should then cause the banner to be raised again;
for if the circumambulation of the banner is omitted, it brings misfortune to the village and its inhabitants.
Then one should perform a propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma) for the removal of all defects;
for an altar that is deficient or lacks the proper characteristics bestows inauspiciousness.
Then, having performed the pacifying oblation (śāntihoma), one should construct an altar (vedī) possessing the proper characteristics;
for if the staff (daṇḍa) lacks the required characteristics, it brings inauspiciousness to the principal deity.
At that time, one should perform either a *mūrtihoma* or a *śāntihoma*;
for if [the deity] is devoid of its own characteristics, it becomes a source of fear like a raised staff.
Upon the destruction of the pride of the aggregates (skandha), one should then perform a pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) when there occurs the breaking,
shattering, or similar damage to the staff, the secondary staff, the shoulder-bearer, and so forth.
At that time, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma); if it is broken, one should lead another propitiation.
If the banner is devoid of its proper characteristics, it brings fear to this kingdom.

The wise one should bring another banner possessing the proper characteristics for the purpose of raising it; he should perform the rite of pacification (śāntikarma) for the raising of the characteristic banner.
In this very manner, one should perform expiation upon the bull for the removal of faults;
if it is devoid of the upward bamboo pole, one should recite the mantra of the Lord of the Banner (Dhvajeśa) one hundred times.
If it is devoid of the lower cord, it does not lead to any fault;
however, if the cord is severed, there will be affliction by enemies, and one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma). || 737 ||
If clothing or other items are bitten by rats, one should then perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma). If a banner falls to the ground, it portends misfortune for the kingdom.
Then, having performed a pacification oblation (śāntihoma) according to the rule, one should raise the banner.
If the banner is joined with cracks or other defects, one should then perform a rite of pacification (śāntikarma). || 739 ||
O twice-born ones, one should raise another banner within seven days;
O twice-born ones, each preceding one would be more auspicious, provided there is only a slight loss.
At that time, one should perform either a *mūrtihoma* or a *śāntihoma*,
especially when this comet is rising and by means of the suppression of the staff and other such [omens].
If the fringe is hanging down, one should perform a propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma) for the pacification of defects;
if it is devoid of the garland of *darbha* grass, then one should likewise perform the propitiatory oblation.
Then, one should wrap the staff, which possesses the proper characteristics, with a garland of *darbha* grass;
alternatively, a rope or a *darbha* garland may be used, according to the rule of circumambulation from left to right.

If she has been joined to the staff, he should recite the Aghora mantra a thousand times and lead her forward by way of circumambulation, starting from the front with a garland of darbha grass and other items.
If the staff is broken or the beard [of the image] is disheveled, one should mutter the Ghoramantra three hundred times;
likewise, if it lacks the banner and bell, there should be no presence of the bull.
Then the preceptor should rotate [the bell] three hundred times with the Aghora mantra;
if the bell falls to the ground, he should mutter the Dakṣiṇa mantra three hundred times.
Having ascended, one should not desire to be bound, just as Śiva was when he was the lord of punishment;
however, at the time of hoisting the banner, if the ritual installation of the water-pot (kumbhanyāsa) has not been performed.
Having performed the ascent of Ketu due to causes such as the piercing of Taurus or Aquarius,
and having concluded with a propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma), one should install the water-pot (kumbha) as before.
Then one should perform the ritual placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa) mentally within the lotus of the heart;
provided that the consecration with the water from the jar of the surrounding enclosure has not been performed.
Once that banner has been raised and suspended from the ring, one should perform a recitation of one hundred repetitions for each [deity] using their respective mantras. (750)
A delay of one, two, three, or four mātrās does not constitute a fault;
however, beyond that, one should mutter three hundred times the terrible mantra ending with the *ravimātrā*.

Once the banner has been lowered below that [pole] and the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) has been performed, he should thereafter raise the flagstaff accompanied by the worship of the bull (Vṛṣabha). || 752 ||
If the drum-beating is deficient, the world becomes mute;
therefore, having performed a peace-offering (śāntihoma), one should then beat the drum.
Prior to the commencement of the festival, there must be the invocation of the deities;
for if the invocation of the deities is omitted, the gods and others will not be present.
One should perform the peace-offering (śāntihoma) as before and carry out the invocation of the deities:
Īśa, Ambā, Skanda, Vighneśa, Bhānu, Caṇḍeśvara, and the others.
In that case, there is no fault in not inviting them; nor is there any fault in not inviting others during a time of distress.
One may either invite the gods accompanied by the hoisting of banners, or one may not.
One should perform the ritual for striking the drum in exactly that same manner;
however, if there is damage to the drum's hide or other parts, or if a crack occurs at the corner or elsewhere, [the procedure must be repeated]. (757)
Having recited the Aghora mantra three hundred times, one should then bring another drum;
likewise, having taken another corner, one should perform the rite as before.
If [the drum] falls on a corner or upon the ground, one should recite the Aghora mantra three hundred times;
likewise at that time or during the offering of bali, if the drum falls to the earth.
At that time, one should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) for the sake of removing the misfortunes of the kingdom;
if a kettle-drum falls to the ground, there will be great danger for the king.
Then, having performed the pacifying oblation (śāntihoma), one should worship the drum with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya),
even if the sacrificial hall has been burnt by fire or is deficient in its characteristic features.
A celestial chariot or a sacrificial altar-pedestal may bring about the ruin of the kingdom;
therefore, one should perform all of that correctly, provided it is during a festival for a festival.
Every day, a peace-offering (śānti-homa) should be performed until the day of the pilgrimage site arrives;
and having recognized that the sacrificial hall is distinct at the conclusion of the festival— 763.
One should perform a rite of pacification for one day to eliminate that defect;
this procedure is common to both the consecration and the expiation.

During the ritual bathing, sprinkling, monthly worship, and other such rites; during the laying of the foundation line; as part of a festival; or in any other instance involving the restoration of what is decayed or the ritual use of bricks—765.
Let it be employed elsewhere in obligatory, occasional, or optional rites, as well as in the accessories of sacrifice; however, this is not the case at the conclusion of the sacrifice. (766)
A pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) should be performed even during a festival lasting for a single day,
as well as in the event of the omission of primary, inferior, or intermediate ritual acts.

One should recite two hundred or three hundred times the non-terrible (aghora) mantras for the peace-offering (śāntihoma). If the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or the ritual limbs (aṅga) are deficient, one should then perform the peace-offering.
As before, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) for the prevention of crop destruction,
using either the Śiva-pitchers, the Vardhanī vessel, or other jars.

Furthermore, if during the other auxiliary rites of the festival there should occur a breakage, a crack, or a deformity in the ritual jars, one should proceed according to the sequence [of the prescribed remedies].
To eliminate defects, one should perform a peace-offering (śānti-homa) and the recitation (japa) of the Aghora mantra five hundred, four hundred, three hundred, or even one hundred times.
Having brought the nine [vessels] beginning with the *kumbha*, one should perform their installation as before;
either the *vardhanī* or the *kumbha* are the lords of the Vidyeśvaras.
If they are devoid of golden lotuses, or provided with only a small amount of gold,
they will cause poverty for the maker after he has recited the Aghora mantra a thousand times.
Furthermore, one should provide what is prescribed by the scriptures for the removal of those defects;
if the jars and other vessels are devoid of cloth, men will suffer from wind-related diseases.
Having recited the Aghora mantra a thousand times, the Guru should again present a garment;
even in the absence of the five jewels and other such items, one should perform the rite in this very same manner.
Even in the absence of the thread-bundle, the covering-cloth, and so forth, one should act in this manner;
however, if the binding of the *kautuka* is deficient, it should be performed on that limb previously mentioned.
That sacrifice is declared to be fruitless; therefore, to eliminate that defect, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) and thereafter bind the protective amulet (kautuka).
One should mutter the Ghoramantra three hundred times when there is a loss of its ancillaries;
likewise, when that daily rite has been omitted, one should perform the consecration immediately.
The tying of the auspicious thread (kautukabandhana) is prescribed when the deity is situated in its former place,
or when it has been brought to the pavilion and so forth, after reciting the Aghora mantra fifty times.
But in the absence of the bali, tāla, and other offerings, one should recite the mantra a thousand times toward the south;
in the event of the lamp going out, one should recite it three hundred times and provide a double lamp.
If a festival is devoid of a procession, it brings all manner of faults upon men;
therefore, one should perform a ritual bath, a peace-offering (śānti-homa), and a return procession.
During the rainy season, in high winds, during a national upheaval, or in times of great fear, circumambulating the village is not desired; rather, circumambulating the temple is desired.
O best of the twice-born, at that time the ceremonial bathing and the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) should be performed,
O lords of brahmins, while the festival of Śiva continues within a single sacred precinct.
If a different festival is celebrated there, it causes confusion for the village;
to eliminate that fault, one should perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śāntihoma).
In the same way, one should perform the expiation for the pacification of the Mothers; furthermore, the offering to Aṅgāraka as prescribed in the Yāmala does not cause any fault. || 785 ||
If the Bali offering is made by a Vāmabhairava-siddha, there will be the destruction of the village.
If the Bali is offered through negligence, one should perform a propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma).
In the same way, one should perform the expiation for the pacification of the Mothers when a great sacrificial offering (baliyajña) has been prepared in a deserted village.
Then one should know that the destruction of the kingdom has occurred; if it has been performed, one should practice pacification.
[This applies] in the residence, in a great sacrifice, or during the enclosure of that temple.

O best of the twice-born, it is especially recommended for one who has taken up residence on another's land, as well as for one whose dwelling is nearby, even when situated far away from others. (789)
Provided it is endowed with various trees and equipped with many dwellings, it would be more praiseworthy than the other; conversely, if the opposite is the case, it brings about calamity.
The dwelling of the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas is declared to be the most excellent;
however, for those who are incapable, there is a secondary rule (anukalpa), and they may perform the rite elsewhere.
Whether it be the favorable dwelling (anulomādhivāsa) or that of the Śūdra, these two are considered middling;
a site consecrated without those is called inferior. || 792 ||
If the interior wind is superior, the circulation of the offering (bali) occurs externally;
when the offering is greater in one place, it is declared to be excellent. (793)
For those who are incapable, there is indeed a secondary option (anukalpa); in such cases, one should perform [the rite] elsewhere.
For those engaged in the secondary option, there shall be either a propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma) or the recitation of mantras (japa).
In a small pavilion, one should perform the recitation (japa) a hundred times;
even in a place devoid of a banner, the recitation here should likewise be by the count of a hundred.
O best of the twice-born, there is no fault if the banner is missing at night;
however, if the materials for the bali offering are missing, men will suffer from the affliction of hunger. (796)
One should recite the mantra of the presiding deity of that day two hundred times;
then, accompanied by offering materials for the bali, one should cause it to be given at the junction of another [period].
If the offering of the *bali* is omitted, hunger-affliction arises for men;
therefore, having performed the *mūrtihoma*, one should carry the *bali* at the end of the procession. (798)
When the bali offering is omitted in a temple, one should mutter the Aghora mantra a hundred times;
in whichever direction the bali was omitted, such as toward a village or similar place, one should perform an oblation according to the Saṃhitā.
Having performed the mantra of the respective lord of the direction one hundred times,
one should offer a bali at the time of departure or at the end of the wind.
If, however, a linga made of cooked rice is not provided, a famine arises on earth;
therefore, having performed a peace-offering (śāntihoma), one should present an offering of cooked rice to the linga.
One should likewise predict the result for cutting, breaking, falling, and so forth;
having made that sign very firm, one should worship the weapon residing therein.
Having immediately performed the *saṃhitā-homa* in that place,
one should then lead [the deity] clockwise starting from the spot where that *liṅga* fell.
One should discard food that has fallen [on the ground], and having prepared the food, one should partake of it;
having finished, as before, one should perform the journey and carry out the *saṃhitā-homa* sacrifice.
If [the offering] falls into the vessels for the *bali*, one should recite the *Aghora* mantra a hundred times;
in the event of a breakage or similar incident, one should take another vessel and deposit the *bali* substances therein.
If the ten weapons, having manifested on the ground,
should fall down extinguished, one should then perform a fire sacrifice for peace (śāntihoma) and bring about tranquility.
Whether they are made of wood or other materials, having been fashioned through cutting, splitting, and so forth, or whether they have arisen from other sources; || 807 ||
Having consecrated [the materials] with their respective mantras, one should complete the rite with a remainder;
then, having brought the metal-made items according to the procedure prescribed for the subsequent rite, one should lead them to the final installation.
When the Śūla weapon has fallen upon the king, fear arises there;
in that case, one should perform the Diśā-homa at the temple or other locations, accompanied by the worship of the weapon.

O twice-born ones, when cutting, breaking, or other such [injuries] have occurred, one should perform the rite of restoration (āpādya) as in the case of subsequent rites; then, as before, one should perform a festival, or else with another weapon.
Having completed the festive rites and performed the concluding rituals accordingly,
one should then perform the consecration by sprinkling [the deity] with the empowerment of the King of Weapons (Astrarāja).
Whether at the time of transport or at any other time, if the image or other [object] falls, the king meets with death; one should immediately perform the remedial rite. (812)
If the image is unimpaired, it should be placed on a pedestal; or, if it has fallen from below the hand, from two hands, or even from three hands, one should gradually lead it upward from that point.

One should perform the *saṃhitā-homa* and the *śānti-homa*, as well as the *śānti*, the offerings to the *mūrtis* and the directions, and the ceremonial bath; furthermore, one should recite the *ghora-mantra* one hundred thousand times.
One should also perform the general offering of food (naivedya),

the concluding rites of the festival, and, in the event of a deficiency in the ritual limbs, the expiation beginning with the reconnection (sandhāna) as prescribed by the rules for subsequent performance.
The preceptor should perform the rite of formal acceptance (adhivāsa) and so forth immediately,
disregarding considerations of the month, lunar mansion, lunar day, weekday, and other such factors.
Furthermore, having tied the sacred thread (kautuka), one should perform the festival and other rites;
even in the case of [an image] lacking a head or other limbs, one should proceed according to the instructions for remedial rites (anukarma).
There too, the wise preceptor should perform the festival, including the concluding rite of rejoining with another image, every day accompanied by peaceful fire-offerings.
Or else, O best of the twice-born, it should be performed by one who has entered another abode,
provided he possesses the desired measurements for the womb-door and so forth, and not otherwise.

Then, having prepared the image and performed the subsequent rites according to the instructions, one should indeed perform its consecration at the conclusion, preceded by the offering of ritual sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa). || 820 ||
O Śivadīkṣitas, one should cause a festival to be held for the deity during festivals lasting nine days and so forth; this is likewise the same rule regarding the Liṅga, O dear ones.

During a festival held outside the village where protective cords have been tied, if the image (bera) is excessively reviled, it brings misfortune to the king; therefore, for his peace, [the following should be done]. 822.
Then one should perform either a *śānti*-oblation or a *saṃhitā*-oblation;
however, if while performing the rite the preceptor should fall upon the ground, then—

One should know that there is no fixed rule regarding the village; for that purpose, the mantra-practitioner should recite the five-hundred-fold mantra of the multiformed one, and it is exactly the same even when [the disciple] has fallen. 824.
If the one offering the oblation should fall at that time, he should mutter that [mantra] a hundred times;
likewise if the weapon, the missile, the food, the emblem, the Lord, or the vehicle should fall upon the ground.
The Guru should mutter the Ghora mantra one hundred times for the omission of worship, and twice that amount for the omission of the Sandhyā and other such rites. (826)

And in the case of the removal of water for the feet and so forth, of fragrance, of flowers, of incense and lamps, or of a lamp that has not been extinguished, as well as in the case of the removal of food offerings and the like; 827.
O most excellent gurus, one should perform the expiation according to the previously mentioned rule, whether the fire-ritual has been omitted or the materials for the oblation have been lost. 828.
Whether the fire of Nirvāṇa is auspicious or inauspicious, as previously stated, if the mounting of the chariot is lacking, men on earth shall become base. (829)
Then, having performed a peace-offering (śāntihoma), one should proceed with the mounting of the chariot;
for at the time of departure, if the chariot or other parts should break, there will be the destruction of the earth.
Having performed the reconnection (sandhāna) that is appropriate for reconnection, one should perform the rite of pacification (śānti).
One should perform it either in that same place or at the temple (dhāman), for the sake of pacifying defects in the vehicle and other such matters. 831.
If he is unfit for the task of rejoining [the funeral pyre], one should then bring another chariot;
or, having brought a palanquin or similar vehicle, one should place Maheśvara upon it.
As before, one should install the Lord of the Gods in his own abode;
however, if a great quarrel should arise at the time of viewing the diversion, [one should act as follows]. || 833 ||
Then one should perform a peace-offering (śānti-homa) and recite the Aghora mantra ten thousand times;
if there is a deficiency in the observation of the ritual, one should perform the Saṃhitā-homa.
If the rite of lustration (nīrājana) is omitted, the expiation is as previously stated;
likewise if the bathing at the end of the procession is omitted, or if the propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma) is neglected.

The absence of divine presence (sannidhi) results in deficiency; the remedy is the ritual of invocation (mūrti), fire-offering (homa), ceremonial bathing (snapana), and the pacificatory fire-rite (śāntihoma). One should perform these for the sake of attaining the presence of the deity.

Or, if the region is presided over by inferior beings or if the path of the gods has been obstructed, one should perform abundant ablutions and a very extensive pacifying fire-offering (śāntihoma). || 837 ||
If the oil massage is omitted, men here will suffer from diseases of the head;
therefore, having performed a pacifying fire-offering (śāntihoma), one should perform the oil massage.
If the festival of the dancing form, previously planned, is deficient, all men become sinners; therefore, one should perform a rite of pacification for that purpose. (839)
Thereafter, one should perform the circumambulation of Naṭeśa at the prescribed time;
if there is an interruption in the giving of offerings during the procession, that procession shall become fruitless. (840)
Then, having performed a pacifying oblation (śāntihoma), one should carry out the ritual gift as before;
however, if there is a deficiency in the hunt, the king will suffer defeat. (841)
Having then performed the *śānti*-oblation, one should lead [the image] during a favorable lunar mansion (*iṣṭabha*);
even at an inferior auspicious site (*kautukatīrtha*), it should not be in the immediate vicinity of the Gaṅgā or other such rivers.
Similarly, after sunrise, once the rites for the sacred sites have been performed,
there shall be atonement through a gradual performance of a peace-offering (śānti-homa) or an oblation according to the Saṃhitā.
This [rite] should take place at the Kautuka-tīrtha once the hoisting of the banner has been performed;
otherwise, one should either perform the Kautuka-bath elsewhere or avoid it altogether.
If there is a deficiency in the powder-offering festival (cūrṇotsava) or in its constituent parts, there will be affliction by disease;
a pacificatory oblation (śāntihoma) should be performed for the whole, and an oblation with the Saṃhitā-mantras for the parts.
Whether the sacred abode has been desecrated, or if there is a lapse in bathing at the holy ford (tīrtha),
or if the festival of powder (cūrṇotsava) is omitted, one should perform the Saṃhitā-homa.
O twice-born ones, that sacrifice which has been interrupted at a great sacred site (tīrtha) becomes fruitless;
having performed a rite of peace for that purpose, one should then proceed with the work of the sacred site.

If that [site], such as a riverbank and so forth, which was previously present, becomes otherwise, one should then perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) for the sake of pacifying the fault thereof. || 848 ||
If there is an omission of the constituent parts of the *tīrtha*, a *saṃhitā-homa* should be performed, which bestows the desired result.
If a human being is born or dies within the temple, there will be great fear for the king. (849)
Then, having cast away the corpse and other such things outside that designated area, one should sprinkle it with cow-dung water in the direction by which they departed.
Then, in that place, one should indeed perform the auspicious-day rite (*puṇyāha*) and the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*);
at that time, one should dig the ground where a death or birth occurred until it is fit for excavation.
Having discarded impure earth, one should fill [the area] with pure earth;
having washed the nearby walls and so forth, one should apply a coating of cow dung on the ground.
One should perform the auspicious day rite (*puṇyāha*) there, followed by sprinkling with products of the cow (*gavya*) in due order;
at the end, one should perform a communal feast for the devotees of Śiva (*śaiva-sambhojana*) and the sprinkling with water (*jala-samprokṣaṇa*).
If the ritual bathing (snapana) and the peace-offering oblation (śāntihoma) are to take place in the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), one should perform them there;
however, if they are to take place in the half-pavilion (ardhamaṇḍapaka), one should perform them excluding the peace-offering oblation.
If the Śāntihoma and the ceremonial bathing are not performed in the image pavilion,
then one should perform the sprinkling with water inside the inner hall.
The bathing of the deities residing within the inner hall should be performed like the *śānti-homa* ritual;
one should also sprinkle those seats located therein with products of the cow (*gavya*) for the sake of purification. (856)
One should discard earthen vessels and wash wooden ones with water;
if [defilement] is outside the inner hall, there is an oblation to the quarters by means of bathing.
In places such as a kitchen or when death occurs,
having first effected purification, one should lead [the victim] around the fire.
Then one should perform either a *śānti*-oblation or a *mūrti*-oblation;
if [the site] is outside the two enclosures, one should perform the *śānti*-oblation.
If a mortal dies within the precinct of a temple that measures twelve daṇḍas, he must abandon that very place and perform his obligatory and occasional rites elsewhere. (860)
If [these] have occurred, there will be the destruction of the village; for that purpose, one should perform the ritual bathing.
Furthermore, if a charioteer dies in the dwelling, or if birds, domestic animals, or wild beasts die, [the same applies].
Or a serpent may be born [there], and the people of the kingdom fall into a state of misery;
in that case, one should apply cow-dung plaster and sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If the ceremonial bathing is to take place in the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), one should perform the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) as well;
however, if it is to be performed solely in the half-maṇḍapa, one should arrange for the bathing alone.
Having sprinkled the deities situated in the pavilion of the gods with the products of the cow (gavya),
and having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should perform the propitiatory fire-oblation (śānti-homa).
All of this, however, is common both during festivals and non-festivals:
the turban, the upper garment, the lower cloth, and the sacred thread. (865)
O you of excellent vows, the head of the preceptor may be consumed by fire, or there may be affliction by fever in the village; and for the pacification of that fault— || 866 ||
The preceptor, having bathed and become pure, should perform the *śānti* oblation;
O lords of sages, it should be exactly the same for the performer, the priest, and the others.

When burning, cutting, or similar damage occurs to clothing, bedding, seats, and so forth, or when they are bitten by mice and other such creatures, the results are stated here in their respective order. (868)
In the corner, there will be an increase in enjoyments; at the edge, misfortune is proclaimed. The birth of a son and fame occur in the center between the tenth and the ninth houses.
It is declared that there will be an extreme calamity, such as disease or death from another cause;
or, having folded a garment three times, [one should offer it] to Brahmā, Indra, Yama, and Agni.
This fault is declared to be a great fault; it is not spoken of in any other context.
In this very manner, for men as well, one should then perform the ritual bath.
Having recited the Aghora mantra one thousand times, one should cause the bitten garments to be given to Śiva,
or to men who are devotees of Śiva, or to those who have received initiation.
If clothing and such items are of divine origin, one should purify them by sprinkling with cow-products;
then one should have a *saṃhitā-homa* performed, or otherwise recite the *ghora-mantra*.
If uninitiated persons, such as Śūdras and others, have entered the sacrificial pavilion,
one should sprinkle it with water empowered by the Astra-mantra and recite the mantra ten times over that formidable [water].
But when a water-pot or similar vessel has been defiled by that [impurity], one should place another in its stead;
likewise, in the event of dogs or other such animals entering, one should first perform the *saṃhitā-homa* sacrifice.

If [the site] has been smeared with cow dung and accompanied by the sprinkling of auspicious water, and provided with the sprinkling of products from a cow, yet [the work is done] by outcastes who follow the inverse order; 876.

One should abandon the water-jars and other items belonging to those [deceased] who have undergone birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (preta), as well as those contained within them; having smeared them with cow-dung, one should perform the rite of circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa).
Having performed the *mūrtihoma* at the conclusion, one should install the water-pot (*kumbha*) and other items as before;
this is proclaimed to be the expiation even for touching [the image] with dogs and the like. (878)
If [the deity] has been entered by Caṇḍālas or others, having performed this [rite], one should cause Śambhu to be bathed in their presence and have the homa of the directions performed.
If images and the like are touched by them, one should perform expiation as previously described;
if the sacrificial hall is consumed by fire, there will be danger in the royal palace.
Having removed the previous pitchers and other items, and having worshipped the Bull-bannered Lord (Śiva),
and having performed the *mūrtihoma* at the end, [one should prepare] the sacrificial pavilion as before.
Having performed the immediate consecration (adhivāsa), one should perform everything as before in the sacrificial pavilion that has been prepared with the installation of the water-pot (kumbha).
Or, if the kitchen, the pavilion, the gateway, or other such structures have been burnt,
one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) and proceed as before.
If the water-shed is burnt by fire, one should perform the Saṃhitā-homa;
likewise if the inner sanctum, the half-pavilion, or the image and so forth are burnt. (884)
In the inner hall and in the outer hall, there should be, respectively, the ritual bathing, the oblation to the quarters, and likewise the oblation to the Mūrtis. || 885 ||
The Śānti rite, the Śānti-homa, and the Saṃhitā-homa—
when a defect occurs in the Liṅga, the image, or other such objects, one should perform the expiation prescribed therein.
One should perform the protective rite (*parivālaya*) for the image in a pavilion as previously described;
this ritual is considered common practice both during festivals and when no festival is being held. (887)
In the event of a fire breaking out in a house within a village or similar place, one should perform the *samhitā-homa*;
when a great conflagration occurs in a village, one should perform the *śānti-homa*.
If a counter-gift is not given, then the garment and upper cloth, along with the turban, the teacher’s property, and the fivefold golden ornaments [must be returned]. (889)
Or, having recited the Aghora mantra one hundred times, he should respectfully offer those items— be they merely a finger-ring or whatever else is desired— to the Guru.
Furthermore, the confusion of teachers destroys the kingdom and the king;
therefore, one should act with a single teacher, established within a single temple. (891)
If one were to reap the fruit of karma performed by another, there would be a confusion of teachers.
The sages said: "Fetching water and such, and the preparation of perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth. (892)
The dedication of lamps and food offerings, the daily worship of the deity, whatever complete adoration there may be, and the worship of the retinue and so forth—[all this is performed]. (893)
The perpetual festival consists of singing and so forth, the preparation of the ritual components such as the ceremonial bathing,
or the arrangement of the preliminary parts of the festival, beginning with the invocation of the deity.
At that time, how can one person alone perform the worship of the root-linga and so forth, as well as the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma), which must be accomplished by many men? Alas! [895]
Śiva said:

O virtuous ones, you are highly wise; I shall now explain samādhi—that state which resides as the sole abode of all action, whether it be obligatory, occasional, or performed for specific desires. (896)
"What you have said—that it must be performed by a single preceptor—is well spoken;
for he is either the son or the grandson of this teacher, or his kinsman. (897)
Those men who have been initiated by him, who are possessed by his command, and who are born into the lineage of Ādiśiva—whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas—[are his followers]. (898)

Or those who are *śūdras* born in the natural order (*anuloma*), such as *gandharvas*, dancers, and so forth, as well as the daughters of Rudra, shall be foot-servants if they are keepers of his command. (899)
The ritual performed by them as well would be considered performed by the preceptor himself,
just as when [a task] is carried out by vassal lords and others appointed by the king.
Whatever royal business has been performed, if it is likewise approved,
yet should it turn out otherwise than what ought to have been done, one should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti) therein.
In that regard, even the fault of confusion results in fruit, and such is the expiation;
whatever ritual action was previously established by the scriptures is to be performed again and again. (902)
Every action must be performed in accordance with what is established by the scriptures; one should not abandon that which is ordained.
Otherwise, if a duty remains unfulfilled, the ruin of the king is proclaimed.
For that purpose, a propitiatory rite (śānti) must be performed to eliminate those defects;
since this was established by the scriptures from the very beginning, prosperity and happiness will follow from it. (904)
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform even more than before. || 905 ||
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, the ritual for expiation, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
Seated upon the throne of the Praṇava, he was invincible and possessed of great strength;
he had five faces and ten ears, with three eyes on each face,
his fangs were formidable, he was exceedingly fierce, and having let out a roar, he was truly difficult to conquer.
Adorned with a garland of skulls, having the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, squint-eyed,
wearing a great garland and serpent ornaments, licking [his lips],
possessing the splendor of ten million billion suns, and the crusher of the hosts of obstacles.
Endowed with ten exceedingly fierce arms and equipped with terrible weapons.
In the right hands, he holds a sword, a bow, a great trident, a noose, and a shield;
and in the left hands, an arrow, a skull-cup, a boon-granting gesture, and a spear.
Having thus meditated upon [the deity] as possessing reddish-brown ash, beard, and eyebrows, and likewise hair on the head,
one should begin the worship after invoking [the deity] while reciting the mantra.
[He saw her] with a lion’s face, fierce fangs, and a luster like fire, possessing an upward-pointing crest,
resembling black collyrium, and endowed with three round, red eyes.
Carrying a trident and a hand-drum with her two left hands,
and carrying a severed head and a sprout with her two right hands.
Wearing black garments, holding a weapon, with a beautiful face, and delighting in dance;
she is adorned with pearl ornaments and every limb is decorated.
Accompanied by the sound of a loud laugh and provided with a black antelope skin.
One should meditate upon Aghorāstra, the subduer of enemies, who possesses the splendor of a thousand suns,
whose tips of the teeth are blazing, and whose cavernous mouth is radiant.
Three-eyed, with a tongue like a flash of lightning, his eyebrows, beard, and hair blazing;
wearing a sacred thread made of all [the serpents], he holds a trident, a sword, a spear, and a mallet.
Four-armed and four-faced, with a shimmering crescent moon as his crest-jewel,
he is dancing, possessing a great form, and adorned with serpent ornaments.
The crusher of the arrogant gods, dānavas, and daityas.

31. In the thirty-first chapter, the ritual for the pacification of portents shall be taught; indeed, I shall teach the pacification of portents which wards off all calamities. If the sun is seen at night, there will be fear of an enemy king.
There, one should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti) accompanied by a feast for Brahmins;
on the new moon day or when the moon has risen, he will become a supreme king.
One should perform the pacification rite as before, using either the medium or the inferior [mantra];
however, if it occurs [at the wrong time], the earth may tremble and the king's downfall will certainly occur.
One should perform a bath with honey, milk, and ghee, using quantities measuring one thousand *prasthas*,
or half of that, or half of that again, or even a hundred *prasthas*.
One should perform the bath prescribed for Śiva for twenty-one days, fourteen days,
or seven days, using ghee and honey, according to the excellent method.
One should likewise perform this rite during the circumambulation of the Prasāda, the Maṇḍapa, and other such structures;
however, if there is agitation caused by rivers, tanks, wells, and the like, a famine will occur.
Having constructed a pavilion on its bank, one should worship Śiva along with Ambā upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in its center,
and in the water-pot (kumbha), the vardhanī vessel, and the eight surrounding jars.

He should worship the seven sacred sites within the golden cloths of the thread [mandala] along with the maiden using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and he should perform the directional fire-oblation (diśā-homa).
One should pour the water from the jars into those [fires], and one should perform this practice for five days.
In the event of the weeping or sweating of the image, one should predict the death of the king.
One should immediately perform a remedial rite to prevent the destruction of all living beings;
having performed the purification of the image, one should then carry out the most excellent propitiatory rite (śānti).
O lords of sages, one should daily perform the peace-offering (śānti-homa) and feed the Brahmins; at its conclusion, one should hold a festival according to one's wealth.
When a rain of blood occurs, there shall be destruction for all;
one should purify palaces, pavilions, and other such structures that have been smeared with blood.
Having performed the smearing with cow dung, one should carry out the circumambulation with fire;
then, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day, one should proceed with the ceremonial bathing using honey and other substances.
One should perform the peace-offering (śāntihoma) according to the method described for earthquakes;
one should do so for seven days, or for two, three, or even seven weeks.
If there is rain of honey, milk, and so forth at the beginning [of the season], one should predict agitation in the kingdom;
likewise indeed if there is rain of earth, oil, stone, blood, and so forth. (15)
One should perform the bathing of that substance according to the path taught for the ground,
having especially worshipped Śiva with abundant food offerings (naivedya).
One should feed the Śaivas afterwards; in this manner one should perform the rite for seven days.
If there is rain of mud and so forth in the world, [the rite] should be accompanied by a bath with milk.
When a linga arises from trees and the like, or blood and the like,
one should worship it with scents and other offerings and wrap it in a pair of garments.
One should perform the *diśāhoma* (offering to the quarters) among them and then feed the devotees of Śiva; for fear of an enemy's army is to be expected, and [this is done] to avert that fear.
One should purify the linga, the image, the tree, and the other components with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra).
Afterwards, one should worship the Vastu deity and then bathe Śiva at its conclusion.
One should perform this according to the constellations prescribed for pacificatory rites (śāntikarma),
if the temple has suddenly collapsed from its base up to its pinnacle.

O King, there will be a defeat because of that; therefore, one should have the *mūrti-homa* performed, as well as the ritual bathing (*snapana*) for Śiva, and one should perform a dance according to one's means.

One should perform this according to the number of days prescribed for pacification or subjugation; following the procedure stated for the Prāsāda-mantra rite, one should proceed with the laying of the first brick and so forth.

If a third, a half, a quarter, or even a half-quarter of the temple is broken, one should perform the rejoining (sandhāna) of the structure; [the measurement for this] is seven, six, five, or four [parts].
The previously mentioned expiation should be performed by those of purified soul;
even if a limb such as the thumb is severed, one should observe this for one day.
In the event of a deficiency in the limbs such as the *nāḍikā* and so forth, one should properly perform the reconnection (*sandhāna*).
In the case of a sudden breach of the abode and so on, the result depends on the direction, such as that of Indra and the others.
The expiation was previously declared; therefore, one should perform it in that same manner when damage occurs to the deities residing within the sanctum. (27)
Then the preceptor should perform the rites as prescribed by the rules for subsequent actions;
and in the event of the collapse of the pavilion or other structures, he should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti) for one day.
If a deity, such as a liṅga or other form, has been moved to another location, the best of foreigners should declare the downfall of the king because of that act. (29)
Having worshipped the deity with perfumes and other offerings, one should perform the most excellent rite of pacification (śānti),
accompanied by a communal feast for the devotees of Śiva and a meal for the Brahmins.
Having established another linga so that it is level with the previous measurement, or likewise a bāṇaliṅga and the like, together with its temple (prāsāda). || 31 ||
Alternatively, if the former linga is accompanied by its temple,
one should relocate it to its original site according to the prescribed ritual procedure.
A small palace should be constructed for the inferior [deity]; one should perform the rites in the former location.
Once the liṅga has moved from its place, one should install it in the east, previously facing north. || 33 ||
In that place, a temple or a ritual act should be performed according to the path prescribed for subsequent rites;
if the tree moves to another location, there will be the destruction of the crops.
One should perform the ritual oblation of the image using fuel-sticks produced from that species of tree for two weeks, while partaking of a Śaiva diet.
When the supreme self-manifested (svayambhū) and other lingas are situated nearby,
one should perform their daily ablution with abundant sacrificial offerings.
One should place another tree of the same species in the eastern direction,
provided it has different flowers and bears different fruits.
If [the tree] produces flowers or fruit within three years, one should perform a rite of pacification for seven days, nine days, or five days. (38)
At its root, the Guru should perform a peace-offering (śānti-homa) every day,
whether upon a Śiva-liṅga, an image (bera), or a pedestal (pīṭha), when heat or other such afflictions arise.
All beings such as those afflicted by fever and other ailments will certainly perish for men,
when fragrant waters from coconut trees and other sources are offered according to the prescribed rite of bathing.
One should bathe the Supreme Lord with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta);
or else, one should bathe Śiva with a prastha each of milk, honey, and clarified butter.
[The offering] consists of four types of vessels, beginning with the *sahasra* and ending with the *āḍhaka*,
filled with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, *uśīra* root, and saffron.
Having applied a great amount of fragrant paste, one should worship with abundant flowers and other offerings;
then one should perform the ritual of the directions (diśāhoma) until the heat has subsided.
At that time, men desiring peace should also prepare a "cool pitcher" (śītakuṃbha).
Whether they be humans, deer, horses, cattle, birds, or reptiles—[all should do so]. (44)
If there were agitation on earth, they would produce another of their own kind, endowed with many heads, hands, feet, noses, bodies, and so forth. (45)

O twice-born ones, horses and other animals are born with their own color or a different color, joined with such things as the contraction of the eyebrows, or lacking distinct colors, depending on the karma produced in their previous births.
Having abandoned such things as they are, one should immediately perform a remedial rite;
having worshipped Śiva according to the rules, one should perform the oblation of the quarters (diśāhoma).
Having duly honored the Śaivas, one should perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma);
one should feed the devotees of Śiva or lead the deity [in procession] for seven or five days.
When there is the expiation for cattle, elephants, and horses within their dwelling,
one should daily perform the ritual offering for the site (vāstubali), the propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma), and worship with sacrifices to the lords of the field (kṣetreśvara).

Or, if during a battle there should arise fear of war for the king from mountains and such, he should worship Śiva according to the rules and cause the oblation (homa) of the directions to be performed. || 50 ||
One should bathe the Supreme Lord; one should perform this for nine or seven days.
If the sweating [rite] is performed on the *liṅga*, the image (*bera*), or the pedestal (*pīṭha*), there will be danger to the kingdom.
Having washed [the image] with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra and performed worship, one should perform the rite of pacification (śānti) for seven days,
whether at the Linga, the icon (bera), the temple (vimāna), the pavilion (maṇḍapa), or the gate-towers (gopura), and so forth.
In the hall of the retinue, in the śāla tree, and in the pavilion of the assembly of the Lord of Gods.
When lightning strikes the assembly hall, one should predict disease for the king;
one should perform pacification rites in sequence along the path of the nine walls.
In that regard, this procedure should be performed for the *liṅga*, the pedestal (*piṭha*), or the image (*bera*).
Then, having performed the directional oblation (*diśāhoma*) together with the great ablution (*mahā-snapana*), [the following should be done].
The bath consists of one hundred and eight [substances], combined with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
accompanied by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), as well as honey, milk, and clarified butter.
Having bathed Maheśvara with four vessels of one thousand [pala] or similar measures up to a *prastha*, one should worship him, feed the Brahmins, and perform a peace-offering (*śānti-homa*).
When this has been performed for seven days, one should hold a festival at the conclusion; O lords of sages, even when the temple is entirely broken, it should be done as previously described.

If the sacred site (dhāman) should collapse unexpectedly, one should perform whatever was prescribed for that; likewise, O elder brothers of Śiva, the expiation (prāyaścitta) should be performed for this [collapse] at the pavilion and other such locations.
One should daily feed Śaivas who are experts in the Śiva scriptures;
for them, that atonement which was proclaimed in the royal palace is declared to have been granted.
If a tree that is cool, or an aśvattha tree, or any other tree that embodies a deity is struck down,
a great pacification (mahāśānti) must be performed for seven days.
Having performed a daily peace-offering (śāntihoma), one should plant another tree of the same species either to the east of that tree or right there in its vicinity.
If [the planet] is in a planet-house (graha), a well, a pond, or a river, there shall be peace for one day;
however, if it is a female elephant in rut, there will be the destruction of mounts.
Peace should be performed for seven days, and likewise a peace-offering (śānti-homa) should be conducted in that house;
otherwise, when there is a great agitation of the winds, there will be turmoil in the kingdom.
One should perform a rite for peace for five days, three days, or even a single day;
however, if smoke arises from the fire, it brings fear to the master.
One should sprinkle that place with a stream of cow-products (gavya), then dig the ground;
having filled it with pure earth, one should then smear it with the five kinds of clay (pañcamṛd).
There, the sprinkling for an auspicious day (puṇyāha-prokṣaṇa) should be performed, as well as the feeding of Brāhmaṇas there;
and there, a rite of pacification (śānti) should be carried out, which dispels the nine types of obstacles.
If smoke arises from the seat of the *liṅga* while it is defiled, one should perform this rite:
one should bathe Śiva with a thousand *prasthas* of milk, or half that amount if [the defilement] is caused by wind.
Half of that, or even half of that again, is the cool pitcher (śītakumbha) placed near it;
this applies when the color of the linga, the image (bera), the pedestal (pīṭha), and so forth, has changed.
One should recognize the king's illness and likewise cleanse him until he is stainless,
using ground clay, bilva, darbha grass, turmeric, and water mixed with dirt.
The pacification ritual should be performed in this manner by one who is senior, middling, or otherwise distinguished,
using sandalwood, ushira root, camphor, saffron, and agallochum combined together.
Having produced an abundant fragrance, one should anoint [the image] with that scent with devotion;
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should pray for the destruction of misfortunes.
One should always feed the Śaivas as well as ordinary Brāhmaṇas;
when the sound of kettledrums and other instruments is made oneself, a great pestilence breaks out.
Having sprinkled the drum and other instruments with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra, and having worshipped them with perfumes and flowers,
one should perform the desired propitiatory rite for the Lord of the Gods.
Or even at sunrise, or upon the appearance of the moon, another king shall arise in that kingdom where this occurs. (741.2)
One should perform the desired pacification for a period ranging from nine days down to a single night.
O Indra, if a rainbow is seen at night, there will be fear from the enemy's army.
If Venus and the other planets abandon their houses during the day or when stars are visible, there will certainly be drought in the world; likewise, if the lunar mansions fall from their houses.
To prevent the destruction of vehicles, one should perform a rite of pacification for that purpose. || 77 ||
For nine days up to a single night, according to one's means,
one should recite the Ghoramantra three hundred times during the conjunction of the fire-asterism (Kṛttikā) and the lunar eclipse.
If a thunderbolt falls every day for more than six days, a fault would arise on the part of the king; therefore, one should perform the oblation to the quarters (diśāhuti).
Or for seven days, or five days, for as many days as its fall [lasts]. || 791/2 ||
For the sake of removing the king's faults,
one should perform a ritual bathing with milk and other substances, provided that a lightning strike has occurred within seven days.
If a halo encircles the orbs of the moon and sun for more than five days, the king who presides over that orb will be overcome by his enemies. (811/2)
One should especially perform rites of pacification (śānti) that distinguish between the superior, middling, and other grades;
for when the burning of fire occurs in the directions, famine arises upon the earth.
Then, one should proceed with the milk-consecration for the deity according to the instructions for bathing;
at the conclusion of that, one should indeed perform the peace-offering (śāntihoma) for five days.
If a Liṅga or other object is worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, but with a different color [than prescribed],
