one should predict the disease of *masūrikā* for all castes alike.
Having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rules, one should perform the oblation for the quarters (diśāhoma);
one should offer abundant sacrificial food for five days or even three days.
If a tree known as a Bodhi tree, which is a caitya, should suddenly fall with its roots,
one should predict illness for the king and indicate it as a sign of death.

Having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rites, one should perform the most excellent propitiatory rite (śānti); for wherever a tree falls, one should perform a propitiatory rite for that region.
One should plant a tree of that same species there or in its vicinity;
for if its shoots fall down, a great upheaval of the kingdom will surely occur.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) in the direction of the middle of the best [branch] for the sake of peace;
however, if that single branch falls, strife arises on the earth.
One should perform the pacification (śānti) as superior, middling, or inferior; thus it is considered to be of three kinds according to the sequence:
for two weeks, seven days, or nine days, and likewise with seven, five, or three fires.
Or else, O eldest brother, one should perform the rite of pacification during three fortnights;
in this very same manner, one should perform it for other principal trees.
When locusts and the like arise, a famine occurs on earth;
one who desires prosperity should perform the Śaiva image-homa for three weeks.
Whether they be men, wild animals, domestic cattle, birds, or reptiles,
if they become insane, one should perform the Diśāhoma for seven days or for three days.
Or one should perform [the rite] for three days when death occurs among elephants or horses;
when excessive rain arises, one should declare famine upon the earth.
With thousands of *prastha* measures of roasted barley flour (*saktu*), along with powders of *rātri* and other such [medicines],
or with half that amount, or half of that again, or even with a hundred *prastha* measures, or half of that.
Or one may bathe the deity with half [the amount], according to the procedure prescribed for bathing;
afterwards, having stirred together turmeric mixed with camphor.
One should wrap the liṅga, the pedestal, or the image with six pieces of cloth as a mere covering;
likewise, one should offer numerous lamps made of agallochum and camphor wicks.
One should then heat the mudga-rice and perform the śānti-homa;
one should do this for seven days, five days, or three days.
If the king’s chief queen, his principal horse, or his elephant, or else his preceptor or domestic priest should die, there will be danger for the king. (991.2)
Having worshipped the God, the Lord of Gods, one should perform a rite for peace for seven days;
or, in the event of the death of an elephant or a horse, one should perform it for five days or three days.
Reciting the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra eight thousand times along with one hundred and eight oblations,
he should sprinkle water upon the head of the king while remembering that mantra.
One should give the remainder for the purpose of bathing and drinking for the sake of achieving longevity;
and every day, O God of gods, one should offer protection born of Your grace through the fire-oblation (homa).
Even the ashes should not be taken by the teachers who have mastered the Śaiva Siddhānta;
within seven days, the wise king should choose her.
Furthermore, O limb of the king of kings, one may likewise seize the preceptor, the domestic priest, the queen, an elephant, or even a horse. 1041.2
In a palace, or in a pavilion and so forth, or on a wall, or at a gate-tower, or above the quarters of the attendants, or atop the king’s residence. (1051.2)
If the barking of a dog occurs upon the planets, on a garland, or similar objects, or if the crying of cats and other such animals takes place; 1061.2.
Then mortals would suffer the loss of their positions;
to prevent that, one should slay it, and having abandoned it, one should then cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
One should bring about the desired peace there even during the crying of a lizard or a frog;
or else, in the case of a cat's cry, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) for peace or the recitation (japa) of a formidable mantra.
One should especially perform a rite of pacification for one day when there is the howling of jackals;
if fire should arise in a stable for horses, one should perform a rite of pacification for seven days.
When a firefly-like light ascends upon a *liṅga*, a skull, a pedestal, or the like,
it indicates either a queen or her consort, or some other man.
One should recognize their fault as being one that brings misfortune even to the gods and the king;
having slain him and bathed those [images], one should perform a propitiatory fire-sacrifice (śānti-homa).
One should perform the ritual bath (snapana) for Śiva for one day or three days;
or, for the sake of a king or other men, one should mutter the mantra intensely upon their bodies.
Whether at the base of the *liṅga*, on the pedestal (*pīṭha*), on the image (*bera*), within the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*),
or among the retinue (*parivāra*), living beings or flies may be born.
If [the earth] is abundant, there will be an agitation of the ground; to pacify that defect, one should purify that site and then bind it with the eightfold bonds and so forth.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), one should perform the rite of pacification (śānti) at the conclusion according to the proper method;
likewise, one should personally perform it during the opening of the door-panel or its closing.
When a disturbance has arisen in the kingdom, one should perform rites for pacification for seven days;
for comets of various forms move everywhere throughout the sky. (1161.2)
When that sun has set, or even before its rising,
white, red, and other colors are seen resembling stars.
If a dog with a long tail appears contrary to what is prescribed, there will be a very great upheaval in the kingdom;
then, O best of men, one should perform propitiatory rites through the superior, middling, or inferior methods.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, the Procedure for the Miracle-Quelling Rite, in the Great Tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
Chapter thirty-two: The Procedure for Subsequent Rituals.
I shall now describe the eternal procedure for remedial rites (anukarma-vidhi) applicable to all cases:
when a temple has collapsed, is cracked, its face is decayed, it is dilapidated, or when there is confusion regarding the cardinal directions.
In inferior [cases], such as birth and so forth, one should employ measures and weights that are inferior;
however, in superior cases, one should likewise apply them with excellent substances and appropriate measurements.

Whatever object is associated with measurement, all that should be brought forward as before; likewise, whatever limb such as the *adhiṣṭhāna* is produced in reverse order, it too is associated with measurement.

That [liṅga] is also without defining characteristics, and its transformation is likewise accepted; in the case of the *svāyambhuva* and other types of liṅgas, one should apply the same reasoning as before.
Or else, it should be understood as prescribed in the scriptures; in that case, no fault is found.
Alternatively, it may be made of stone on the exterior, while on the interior it may be made of bricks.
In the human abode, five-peaked pentads should be arranged;
they should be placed where there is no fixed location, yet especially so in their own proper places.
One should fashion a Nāgara [temple] in the Nāgara style, a Vesara in the Vesara style;
likewise, it should be made in the Drāviḍa style, and the same is considered appropriate for the Varāṭa and other styles.
In a dense cloud-like celestial mansion (vimāna), a residence is likewise desired;
however, if one perceives the residence as dilapidated, one should cause another to be constructed in that very direction.
The wise man should construct it in the eastern or northern corner;
the entrance should be as desired, either facing east or facing west.
If the embryo is lost, one should restore it, and likewise the first brick;
if the nose or other limbs are deficient, one should perform the rite again in that same manner.
If it is not possible to establish it otherwise according to the prescribed measurements,
one should not move the Śivaliṅga, whether it be well-established or poorly established.
That which is joined with defects such as decay, yet endowed with worship, is well-situated (susthita);
whereas that which is free from defects such as decay, yet devoid of worship, is ill-situated (dusthita). || 12 ||
When the restoration of a dilapidated [shrine] is performed, the primary fruit is desired for the doer;
that which was formerly worshipped destroys [evil], while if it remains unworshipped, it utterly destroys [the merit]. (13)
Therefore, one should extract the essential [teaching] according to the scripture for the sake of happiness:
that which is worn out, burnt, emaciated, or bulky, as well as deficient or excessive in measure. (14)
A linga that is broken, scarred, uneven, devoid of auspicious marks, struck by lightning, cracked at the joints, or split asunder [should be abandoned]. || 15 ||
That which is used for malevolent rites, that which is full of internal cavities, and that which has missing limbs— these sixteen types of lingas are to be avoided in every respect.
A pedestal, a stone slab, or a bull that is worn out by age and the like should be abandoned;
likewise, one that is excessively high or low, situated in a confused direction, located in the center [of an impure area], or standing on uneven ground.
A linga that has moved, been shaken, fallen, or caused to fall, as well as one installed by an ignorant person, or one for which no mantric rites have been performed; || 18 ||
Even if the application of the stone has been abandoned, it should not be considered as not established;
for in that very same way, these [other materials] are indeed to be established, provided they are free from defects.
Established by Asuras, sages, and gods who know the reality,
one should not cause it to be moved— even by ritual procedure— if it is decayed or broken.
One may wear it for reasons other than fear of kings, thieves, or fire;
however, if it is carried away by water or stolen by such [a person], whatever [merit] had been gained thereby is lost. (21)
There is no contradiction regarding the gender; one becomes pure by reciting half of a hundred thousand [mantras].
Their installation should be performed either in those [spots] or elsewhere, with the face oriented as previously described.

One should install the liṅga with due reverence within a distance of one hundred daṇḍas, provided it is not subject to water damage; or alternatively, one may install it within a distance of one thousand bows (krośas).
This same [procedure] would apply even in the case of an image; however, if it is defective, one should employ another.
Whether the image be made of stone, clay, baked earth, wood, or precious gems—|| 24 ||
One should avoid, however, one who lacks eyelashes, eyebrows, facial lines, and so forth;
one who is deficient in limbs must be abandoned—of this there is no doubt. (25)
In an image made of iron or clay, one should firmly fashion the hands, nose, feet, ornaments, ears, teeth, and other features using their respective materials. || 26 ||
In the case of one deprived of the head, one should set aside the other [limbs] and employ a new one;
or, for one deprived of feet or arms, one should perform either the abandonment or the reattachment.
The secondary limb (upāṅga), the limb (aṅga), and the minor limb (pratyaṅga) are known as the three types of bodily limbs.
The limb is the primary piercing point (pradhāna-śūla), and it is called the Brahmadaṇḍa.
The chest, the staff-like torso, the waist, the arms, the elbows, and the forearms;
the thighs, the knees, and the shanks—these are declared to be the secondary limbs (upāṅgas).
The wise one should understand the remaining parts from the staff;
however, when the Brahmadaṇḍa is absent, one should begin the installation of the Śūla.
If a single part or all parts are deficient, one should perform the re-consecration;
provided that the previously installed Brahma-staff is endowed with the proper characteristics.
One should re-establish that very [deity] there without a formal re-consecration;
however, when breakage or other such incidents occur, one should perform a re-installation.
One should cast a stone, earthen, or baked [image] into deep water;
those made of gems should either be discarded or taken up for the purpose of crafting.
Having cast the wooden [image] into the Śiva-fire, or having immersed it in earth, fire, a pit, or water,
one should employ molten metal therein for the work of casting the image.
One should join that radiance or the pedestal there or elsewhere;
if the deity is unestablished, one should join it to that pedestal and so forth.
For the sake of its equipment, it may be joined even with another deity;
likewise, if the pedestal (pīṭhī) possesses the proper characteristics, so too should the Brahma-stone and the bull.
O bulls among sages, those [mantras] should be employed everywhere, yet they must be abandoned here;

If these are unavailable, one should likewise properly construct a pedestal using bricks;
thereafter, the stone [image] should be joined so that its form becomes as it was before.
In a square [temple], it may be circular; or in a circular one, it may be square.
This applies likewise to the pavilion (maṇḍapa), the surrounding area (parivāra), and the residence for the attendants (parivārālaya).
Then, one should arrange the ritual procedure for the subsequent rite according to the previous rule;
one should delineate the inner circle of the pavilion and so forth as before.
Therefore, the increase or decrease of the site causes misfortune for the king;
[the site] should be constructed with its proper dimensions, according to the scriptures, and endowed with ornaments.
If it were otherwise in the case of the immeasurable [directions], no fault would be found there;
however, an increase toward the east or north is auspicious, while a decrease toward the west indicates enemies. (42)
Death occurs for the performer [of the rite] in the south; therefore, an increase [in height] is not desired there.
However, an increase all around that site—whether equal or unequal—is permissible. (43)
In the case of a city gate as well, one should perform the subsequent rite exactly as prescribed for the temple;
this applies especially to villages and the like, houses and the like, and halls.
O lords of sages, that which is deficient by being either too short or too long is not desired;
therefore, one should make it equal, or even make it greater.
One should extend the ground either according to the rules of logic or even all around, increasing it toward the east and north;
one should determine the area for the house and the row of buildings by means of numerical measurement.
In every respect, one should perform what is improper and inferior according to the stated sequence;
yet, even among all those things thus mentioned, some distinction is intended. (47)
One should make [the image] inferior or equal to the excellent materials, as previously described;
even when the covering is worn out, it should be equal to the primary abode, the seat, and so forth.
However, having performed the ritual placement of mantras upon the sword-blade, one should bring another [image];
and one should worship daily in a linga or the like, in a full jar, or on a pedestal.
Alternatively, one should install another [image] following the ritual of dismissal (visarjana);
[one should consider] what its form is, what its measure is, of what it is composed, and what has not been extracted from it.
The method for the extraction of all these [mantras] is now declared:
one should construct a pavilion (maṇḍapa) in front of that, specifically in the southeast corner.
It was provided with an eastern gate, joined with a single archway,
endowed with all ornaments, and furnished with inner garlands and the like.
There too, having performed the worship of the doors and so forth, as well as the worship of Śiva upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
one should perform the satiation of the mantra in the fire prepared in the pit (kuṇḍa) and other such vessels.
Having sipped water, the supreme preceptor should offer the bali-oblation toward the various directions, accompanied by fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and the sacrificial oblation.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should feed those who bear the Śiva-liṅga;
then one should inform the Lord that this [act] brings about the dawn of faults.
"Your words are that peace shall prevail once its extraction is performed;
therefore, O Sadāśiva, remain present here for the sake of its extraction. (56)

Thus, having spoken regarding the removal of karma, one should perform a pacificatory oblation (śāntihoma) with milk, clarified butter, honey, and dūrvā grass, reciting the mantra of Śiva eight thousand times.
Having approached nearby, the minister, having bathed [the deity] with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra), should worship;
he should employ the word "Vyāpakeśvara" ending in the dative case. || 58 ||
This is declared to be the root mantra (mūlamantra), beginning with the syllable Om and ending with the word "namas.
Then follows the term "Vyāpakeśvara," and thereafter the words for the heart and other limbs.
The five limbs, beginning with the heart, should be employed ending in the dative case, preceded by the *praṇava* (Om) and joined with the word "namas" at the end.
One should not join a seed-syllable (*bīja*) with them; rather, the *liṅga* [mantra] should be placed upon the seat of the *praṇava*.

The practitioner of mantras should worship the one stationed upon the sacrificial mound with perfumes, flowers, meat, and other offerings; then, uttering the Astra mantra, he should cause the being residing therein to hear [the command].
"Whatever being dwells here depending upon this [place], let it abandon its mark and go wherever it pleases by the commands of Śiva. (621.2)
"Śambhu shall be present here, joined by the Vidyās and the lords of the Vidyās.
Having spoken thus, he offered the *arghya* with the Great Weapon (*mahāstra*) while facing away.
Therefore, having invoked the deity, the Guru should install him in the pitcher,
which is joined with a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) placed in front and provided with gold and cloth.
The Guru should install Ambikā in a vardhanī vessel that is provided with a water-strainer (kūrca), a lid, sacred threads, and sprouts, and prepared in that manner.
Having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should place it in a secure location;
and daily worship should be performed, accompanied by peace-offerings (śānti-homa).
Then, having offered a thousand oblations for each portion with the Pāśupata weapon,
and having sprinkled [the site] with ashes for the sake of pacification, the Guru should touch it with kuśa grass and perform the silent recitation (japa).
Having offered [the oblation] from the end of the reverse order up to the Ārghya, one should dismiss the deities of the tattvas;
at the conclusion of that, [one should dismiss] the Mūrtis and Mūrtīśas established in the liṅga, piṇḍikā, and so forth.
Or, having caused it to be moved by a bull with a rope made of gold thread,
the Guru, reciting "May there be auspiciousness," should cast it into the water while the people look on.
Furthermore, for the sake of nourishment, one should offer a hundred oblations each to the Kṛkādika deities and the lords, as well as for the purification of the site of the palace.
One should protect the temple there with the Mahāpāśupatāstra;
furthermore, the best of preceptors should install another [image] of that same measurement here.
[This applies] to self-manifested lingas, whether they be divine (daivika) or those of the sages (ārṣika),
as well as those made of metal (gāṇava) or stone (lohaja), and those found in rivers, springs, and the like.
In those cases where such signs have been indicated, the rite of the jar (ghaṭasthiti) must not be performed;
however, for human lingas, that which is called the rite of the jar is prescribed.
If the jar remains for up to seven days, a fortnight, or a month, it is auspicious;
however, if the Lord of Gods remains in the jar beyond that, he causes all manner of evils.
Therefore, with every effort, at the end of a month or even before,
having installed a child-liṅga or similar object, one should place the mantra within its center.
Then, during the days between that [period] starting from one month up to twelve years, having taken the Lord of Devas from there, one should install him in the root-liṅga. || 761.2 ||
If the primary liṅga has not been obtained due to constraints of place and time,
one should install it with the primary liṅga by the end of thirty-six years.
On the day and lunar fortnight specified for the installation of a *bāla-liṅga*, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*);
for that [installation], it should be performed twice or thrice over a period of twenty-four years.
If it has been performed, the best of preceptors should perform a double homa;
for that deity remains in its root station for thirty-six years or more.
Having abandoned the marks of a child and so forth situated there, one should install [the deity] down to the very root;
even in the case of the Sakala [form], it should be exactly thus, though some specific distinction is desired.
Within twelve years, one must certainly re-install [the deity] at its original site;
otherwise, the original image (mūlabera) must specifically be re-established in that very place.
O twice-born ones devoted to Śiva, this very same procedure is prescribed for temples and other structures;
however, in the case of a stainless sword, one should first perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantras and then begin the other rites.
The Guru should thus place the vessels for the retinue deities; whatever object, such as a Śiva-liṅga or the like, has been installed by an ignorant person— 831/2.
The Guru should again perform the consecration for him, as previously described, by means of astrologers or other experts who have not been excluded from the Śiva-initiation.

Those other than those established on the path of the Śiva-siddhānta, such as the Pāśupatas and others—even by them, that installed liṅga should be worshipped again after performing the consecration (saṃskāra). || 851/2 ||
First, the Pāśupatas are proclaimed; next, the Somasiddhāntakas;
and others are to be known as the Lākulās—each of these is remembered as being threefold.
There are nine divisions based on the distinction between the left-hand (vāma) and right-hand (dakṣiṇa) Siddhāntas;
furthermore, there are four other types of Śaivas established in Mantra and Tantra.
Garuḍa, Abhairava, and Vāma are established in the Bhūtatantra;
each is further divided into three, arranged as before.
One who follows the Mādi-Śaiva tradition should also worship the liṅga installed by them;
that should be known as the supreme Yāmala state, and it is here called "mixed" (miśra).
It is considered to be threefold through the division of the Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, and Siddhānta systems:
the Vāma is worthy of Pārameśvara, and the Dakṣiṇa is worthy of Bhairava.
The wise know all the Siddhāntas and Yāmalas to belong to the Ādiśaiva [tradition];
however, everything distinct from the Siddhāntas is declared to be Raudra.
It is divided into many varieties through the distinctions of left, right, and mixed, and so forth;
it includes the worldly, the Vedic, and others, as well as that which follows the path of the supreme self-knowledge.
Likewise, O Soma, there are the Pāśupata, the Siddhānta, the Calākulam, the Gāruḍa, the Bhairava, the Vāma, the Bhūtatantra, and the Yāmala. || 931/2 ||
The Kāpāla, the Pāñcarātra, the Buddhist, and likewise the Jaina doctrine;
the system of Bṛhaspati, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and likewise Vaikhānasa.
The Vedānta, the Mīmāṃsā, the Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstra, the Vāstuśāstra, the Sūtra, the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga), and the Itihāsa. || 951/2 ||
Likewise, regarding the four Vedas that were questioned therein:

Once Śambara residing within the liṅga is known, the withdrawal of the mantra is performed as previously described.
If that mantra is unknown, the Guru should join it with the *praṇava*;

Having unified the mantras residing in those respective signs by means of the lamp, one should,
while recollecting them, extract the lamp together with the atoms (mantras) that possess those signs.
Having withdrawn [the deity] with the previous mantra, the Guru should withdraw it by means of the mudrā;
then, having purified that liṅga again with the previous substances and with the arrow (śara), [he should proceed].

One should perform the mental ritual, beginning with the plowing and ending with the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), accompanied by its respective mantras and provided with its respective fire-oblations (homa). || 115 ||
The Guru should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) according to the procedure prescribed for the installation of a liṅga;
however, the extraction of the characteristic marks (lakṣaṇoddhāraṇa) and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) in water are not required here.
Having set aside the act of reclining and the act of installation, one should perform all other rites;
these may be performed either in the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) or in the pavilion (maṇḍapa). || 117 ||
There, in front of the deity, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a consecrated mound (sthaṇḍila);
this applies when the deity is Svayambhū, Bāṇa, a Ṛṣi, or Gāṇādhipa.
When [the thread] is cut, torn, or broken, pacification (śānti) is prescribed there;

One should perform the consecration with milk using one hundred and eight *prasthas*;
then, having performed the propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*), one should subsequently cause the ceremonial bath (*snapana*) to be performed.
Thereafter, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas, and then feed the devotees of Śiva;
having given them abundant sacrificial food (havis), one should then cause betel-leaf to be offered.
At midnight, one should offer the bali-oblation either in a village or in a house;
it should consist of mung-bean rice, milk-rice (pāyasa), cow's milk, and combined with plantain fruit.
This should be performed for seven days for the removal of all defects;
thereafter, one should constantly honor the preceptor with gold, garments, and other offerings.
At the conclusion of that, one should perform the ceremonial bath and offer abundant sacrificial oblations;
having restored the deity who was shattered by all its limbs, one should re-establish it as new once again.

this is proclaimed to extend from villages, hamlets, and cities up to the end of the daṇḍas.
In the case of pillars, it should be up to the measure of a hand; for the measurement of the *liṅga*, up to a barleycorn (*yava*);
for images, up to four barleycorns; and for the arrangement of the pedestal, up to a *mātrā*.
From the door and other structural members up to the *mātrā* [unit], the measurement is like the tip of a hair at the *brahmasūtra*;
even that should not be performed [as a separate act] at the front of the *liṅga*, for such is the declared measurement to be observed. 129.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, the Procedure for Subsequent Rites, in the great tantra named the Uttarakāmika.
In the thirty-third chapter, the Procedure for the Performance of Optional Yoga:
I shall now explain the performance of optional yoga in brief.
The accomplishment of desired objects shall come through mantras, and many mantras are considered [to exist]. || 1 ||
All mantras shall be efficacious and all shall bestow the desired fruits;
among them, the Aghora-atom (mantra) is the destroyer of extreme defects and possesses a dark-blue color.
With his matted locks bound by a serpent, adorned with a garland of skulls, his eyes were intensely tawny like those of a lion, and he was endowed with exceedingly white fangs. || 3 ||
He has the moon as his crest, a broad face, and wears a serpent as a sacred thread;
he possesses a massive body, great tusks, and is adorned with the sound of tinkling bells.
He is the destroyer of the great asuras impaled on the tips of great spears;
he holds a sword, a shield, a bow, arrows, a severed head, and the power of Time (Kāla-śakti).
Holding in his hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, a skull, a noose, a spear, and a mace;
with two fangs protruding from his terrifying, white face.
He is the eternal protector of his own army, the one who strikes fear into the enemy host, the destroyer of actions employed by foes, and the warder-off of all diseases. || 7 ||
He who is compassionate toward his devotees is capable of destroying all defects;
he is eternally surrounded by [the attendants] such as Asitāṅga and others, or he may be unenclosed.
Āsitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmattabhairava, Kapālī, Bhiṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra is remembered as the eighth. || 9 ||
They have four arms and three eyes, are dark-complexioned, and possess great strength;
they hold tridents and severed heads and are joined in the *añjali* gesture at their hearts. || 10 ||
With formidable fangs and terrifying faces, they are endowed with the movements of their master;
"Oṃ Juṃ Saḥ" is this mantra, and the deity is named Mṛtyuñjaya.

This very one is Amṛteśa; at the beginning, it may or may not be joined with the *kūṭa* (the peak syllable), and it is endowed with the seven syllables of the seven metals, beginning with mercury and ending with white [silver].
With the syllable *ha*, one should recite "the body," beginning with "rasa" and so forth;
and at the end, one should recite the word "protect, protect" (*rakṣa rakṣa*) in the repetitive form.
First, one should extract the word "Devadeveśa," and then apply the root mantra of Devadatta's vital breath (prāṇa). || 14 ||

The seat (pīṭha) should be fashioned with the syllable *juṃ*, and the form (mūrti) should be *oṃ juṃ sat*. One should place the peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) or the ninefold temple-mantra (*prāsāda*) in the center. || 15 ||
One should assign the limbs to Brahmā, beginning with the letters *va*, *ha*, and *ka* (the gutturals), and *oṣṭhya* (the labials).
O twice-born ones, there is no mantra equal to this Mṛtyuñjaya.
Seated within a jar of nectar and resting upon a white lotus throne,
he has four arms and three eyes, and his matted hair is adorned with a crescent moon.
Clad in a tiger skin and adorned with the tusks of a lordly elephant,
he holds a trident and a mace above, and a jar of nectar between the two.
If he has six arms, he holds a trident and a rosary,
a skull-cup and a water-pot in his left hands, and the gesture of yoga (yogamudrā) with both hands.
There is no mantra equal to this for protecting life and so forth;
there has been none, nor will there ever be—this which has been declared is the truth. (20)
One should also consume food that has been transformed into nectar by means of the three-syllable mantra;
through that, it quickly becomes nectar, and when tasted, it shall become the conqueror of death.
Having carefully collected water with the Lord Amṛteśa, one should drink that water over which the mantra has been recited a hundred times; one certainly becomes immortal.
One who offers unbroken stalks of dūrvā grass mixed with milk into a fire kindled with fuel from the brahmavṛkṣa tree shall not suffer death.
For one who constantly worships the Lord whose nature is the conqueror of death (Mṛtyuñjaya),
death shall not occur for him for a long time.
It is said that by [this practice] for one month, a hundred years [of merit] are attained; by two months and so forth, it becomes two hundred years.
O you of excellent vows, by practicing this every month, [the result is achieved] within a single year.
Having circumambulated, praised, and honored the practitioner, Kāla departs from this place; of this there is no doubt. O Brahmins, what I have spoken is the truth. (26)
He purifies by his glance, his speech, his conduct, and his touch;
rivers, provinces, gardens, cities, and so forth—of him there is no doubt. (27)

O twice-born ones, why then should I not speak of the Aghora weapon, which consists of a garland of seed-syllables, [and which protects] a frightened living being, as well as one's own self and one's own refuge? (28)
The god wears red garments, possesses a luster like that of crushed collyrium,
is endowed with eight arms, has hair standing erect, and bears prominent fangs.
With prominent fangs and a lower lip, with eyes like a blazing fire,
he was radiant with a garland of small bells and joined by anklets on his feet.
Equipped with the seven weapons, adorned with all ornaments, wearing a white sacred thread, and beautified with red flowers. || 31 ||
Adorned with ascetic scorpions as neck-ornaments, and [scorpions] upon his waistband, belly, neck, ears, heart, and forearms; || 32 ||
He is radiant with fourteen serpents upon his feet and hands,
seated in the center of a lotus throne, three-eyed, and of fierce form.
He holds a trident-base, a vetāla, a sword, and an auspicious hand-drum with his right hands, and a middle trident with his left hands.
Having meditated upon [the deity] who holds a bell, a shield, and a skull-bowl, facing the destruction of enemies, with his left foot placed forward, one should worship the Aghora weapon.
Furthermore, O twice-born ones, listen as I describe meditation according to the truth:
one should meditate upon the subduer of enemies, who possesses the brilliance of a thousand suns and wields the non-terrible weapon. (36)
With the tips of his teeth ablaze, his cave-like mouth radiant, possessing three eyes, with a tongue like a flash of lightning, and with glowing eyebrows, beard, and hair; (37)
He has four arms and four faces, wears a serpent as his sacred thread, and holds a trident, a sword, a spear, and a mallet; he is crowned with the shimmering crescent moon. (38)
He was dancing, possessed of a massive body and adorned with serpent ornaments, the crusher of the arrogant gods, dānavas, and daityas. || 39 ||
"Prasphura sphura"—thus is the heart proclaimed;
"ghoraghoratara"—this is proclaimed as its head. (40)
Then, "tanurūpā" is proclaimed as the Śikhā-mantra; and the word "caṭa-pracaṭa" repeated [twice] constitutes the Kavaca. (41)
Then, having uttered "kaha kaha," one should remember "vama mandaya";
having twice pronounced "ghātaya," the fifth limb is proclaimed.

At the end [of each limb], one should place "ūṃ phaṭ"; likewise, the heart and other limbs should be in the dative case, joined with "namaḥ" at the beginning and preceded by the syllable Om (praṇava). 43.

One should contemplate [this] during an invasion by a hostile army, at the onset of a great disease, and for rites of pacification (śāntika), nourishment (pauṣṭika), subjugation (vaśya), and expiation (prāyaścitta). || 44 ||
What is the use of this extensive discourse? Even when a time of fear has arrived, fevers, planetary afflictions, poisons, and the like are destroyed by this mantra. (45)
Whatever rites of malevolent magic and the like others perform using mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth—even mantras joined with yogic power—[are consumed] like moths in a fire. (46)
In this same manner, the preceptor should meditate upon and worship the Pāśupata weapon, the Śiva weapon, and the Kṣurikā weapon. || 47 ||
Having worshipped Aghora, one should then worship the Astra-mantra in front of him;
to the right of the god Aghora, one should worship the god Sadāśiva in the center.
One should especially worship the deity Aghora in the southern face;
in the four directions, one should worship the four weapons, beginning with Śiva.
Having thus worshipped within the inner circle the Pāśupata weapon preceded by Aghora and the Kṣurikā weapon, one should worship those belonging to that same class all around.
Having abandoned the Śivāstra, one should worship the supreme Pratyaṅgirā right there;
or else, for victory in battle, one should worship her in the middle of the station of the Kṣurikā.
O twice-born ones, he who worships you in this manner is considered by me to be equal to myself; for him, there is nothing unattainable in this world or in the three worlds.
This which has been declared is true; it must be guarded with great effort.
The sovereign of practitioners (sādhaka) must always be protected with special care. 53.
The extraction of the Dakṣiṇāmūrti mantra is now declared here;
by means of that mantra, mastery over speech is attained, and it is praised for the production of victory.
Indeed, all other fruits arise through his grace;
one should employ the word "Bhagavat" followed by "Namaḥ" and ending with the term for the Perfectly Awakened One (Saṃbuddha). (55)
One should likewise apply the word "Dakṣiṇāmūrti" and recite "medhāṃ prayaccha svāhā"; this is declared to be the root mantra. || 56 ||
The extraction of the heart-mantra and the others from the vowels has been fully described;
one should append "namaḥ," "svāhā," "vaṣaṭ," "huṃ," and "phaṭ" at the end [of each]. (57)
Resembling pure crystal, endowed with a serene countenance,
accompanied by the Gaṅgā and the moon, and with his hair coiled into a topknot.
Clad in a tiger skin and endowed with four arms,
he holds a rosary of pure crystal and the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā) in his right hands.
In his left [hands], he holds a lotus and fire, or else the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; or alternatively, he holds a book, and possesses three eyes.
Having thus meditated upon the God, the Lord of Gods, who is yoked to a great bull and surrounded by hosts of attendants, one shall accomplish all undertakings.
The letter *ha* mounted upon *ya*, endowed with the sixth vowel, joined with the fourteenth vowel, and adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*. || 62 ||
Alternatively, in another way, [one may visualize] Bhairava with a distorted face;
this is the supreme seed-syllable (bīja) of Bhairava, joined with an upward-pointing *repha* (the letter *r*). 63.
This mantra is proclaimed by the name Saṃgrāmavijaya;
by the power of this mantra, one shall become a conqueror of the three worlds. (64)
Whatever action is performed by anyone whatsoever in the three worlds, if it is devoid of the King of Mantras, the practitioner will not achieve success. || 65 ||
One should meditate upon the Sun-god, who is seated upon a lotus, accompanied by his Śakti, born from the heart-lotus,
endowed with four faces, and of supreme ruddy hue.
Śiva, who pervades the quarters with his four powers, who has mounted the body of his beloved as half of his own form, and who grants fearlessness and boons while holding a rosary and a skull-cup;
For the sake of prosperity, I bow to the hand holding the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), which is adorned with the noose and goad and measured by the host of planets.
One should duly extract the Brahma-mantras and the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga) in their proper sequence; one should worship the four groups of four, beginning with Vistāra, upon the four faces.
Thereafter, one should worship the limbs of enjoyment (bhogāṅga) beginning with ghee in the southeast corner;
the eye is said to be in the southern direction within the inner enclosure (garbhāvaraṇa). || 68 ||

The powers (śaktis) such as Dīptā and others are on the outside, the planets are further out from them, and beyond those are the world-protectors (lokapālas); the Guru should worship them in this sequence.
Or even one who delights in the realm of desire (kāmāvacara) should always meditate upon the Sun;
O best of the twice-born, I shall now explain the extraction of the Praty-aṅgiras mantra in brief.
It bestows all devotion, is the supreme destroyer of all diseases,
the eradicator of fevers, epilepsy, and pestilences, and the annihilator of consumption.
It destroys the hosts of diseases produced by the magical rites of enemies;
endowed with a fourfold army, it is supreme in bringing about the destruction of foes.
One who is constantly protected by his own army and capable in all undertakings—having extracted the syllable *oṃ hrīṃ*, [one should add] "to the one clad in black" (*kṛṣṇavāsase*) at its end. (73)
And then [he recited] "siṃhavadane," "mahāvadane," as well as "mahābhairavivarṇe" and "sarvaśatrupade. (74)
Then, one should extract the supreme mantra-word "Karmavidhvaṃsinī," followed by "Chedinī," and also "Sarvabhūtadamany. (75)
Then, one should utter the word "bandha bandha" (bind, bind) for all beings;
the word "sarva vighnān" (all obstacles), and the word "chindhi chindhi" (cut, cut).
The phrase "cut through all diseases, cut them through" is that which [is taught]. || 761/2 ||
The word "jvālājihve" (O flame-tongued one), the word "karāle" (O terrible one), and again the word "daṃṣṭre" (O fanged one).
The word *pratyaṅgire*, then *hrīṃ*, followed by the word *namo astu*,
and then *te svāhā*— one should extract this mantra which consists of the *Pratyaṅgirā*.
This is the renowned *Pratyaṅgirā*, consisting of one hundred syllables in its essential form.
The first seven syllables constitute the heart (*hṛdaya*), and the [next] fifteen syllables are the head (*śiras*). (791ab)
From that [the *śiras*] consists of ten syllables; from that, the *kavaca* has seven letters;
likewise from that, the *netra-mantra* has four syllables, and the *astra* consists of thirty-four.
The [mantras] beginning with the heart, consisting of thirteen syllables, are formed from the Gāyatrī Sāvitrī of seven syllables, joined with *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *vauṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, and *phaṭ*.
She has a lion’s face with fierce fangs and is endowed with a lustrous upward-pointing crest;
she resembles black collyrium and possesses three round, red eyes.
Carrying a trident and a hand-drum in her two right hands,
and carrying a severed head and a sprout in her two left hands.
Roaring and rejoicing with sounds such as "aṭṭahāsa," she wears black garments, has a mouth full of blood and flesh, and is intent on dancing.
Adorned on all her limbs with ornaments worthy of pearls,
she was named Kṛṣṇājinaghaṭā and was worshipped by the gods as Bhairavī.
Meditating upon the Goddess with a one-pointed mind, one shall destroy all enemies, eliminate all diseases, and ward off the mantras of others. || 861/2 ||
To attain the state of a Vidyadhara, the most excellent practitioner should offer oblations of black agarwood, or else the filaments from his own navel.
Through oblations of kadamba buds and other offerings, one certainly attains success with Yakṣiṇīs;
a wise person should diligently offer priyaṅgu and plantain flowers.
The flowers of the *karavīra*, ghee combined with honey, and sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *khadira* wood and others quickly bring about satisfaction. (891/2)
When combined with *siddhārtha*, pearl, and *aśvagandhā* (horse-herb),
along with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with milk, it will become momentary at that very instant.
Combined with *dhūrtūra* flowers and joined with the resin of *khadira*,
black and blue ghee indeed paralyzes [the effects] of malevolent sorcery.
A red lotus flower and red sandalwood of equal measure, combined with the ghee of a tawny cow and the milk of a tawny cow. || 921/2 ||
One should perform ten thousand oblations; one certainly performs them swiftly.
[The materials are] the urine of a buffalo, the urine of a goat, the urine of a donkey, and milk. (931.2)
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of that flower from the Girika tree together with the bones of Aṅgiras; this will bring about the destruction of that family.
Saffron, yellow pigment (rocanā), cotton-seed, guggulu resin, and bamboo-pith—[the application of] these will certainly cause instantaneous piercing; of this there is no doubt.
One should likewise offer oblations of *nimbapuṣpa* and *vrīhi* rice combined with *nimba* oil and mixed with the milk of the *arka* plant until the rite is completed.
For the pacification of diseases such as consumption (rājayakṣmā) and others,
the preceptor should perform oblations with sesame seeds smeared with ghee and with dūrvā grass sprinkled with ghee.

One should offer fine *dukūla* cloth and beautiful parched grains (*lāja*) combined with the three sweets; for the purification of abdominal diseases, [one should use] *śuddhī*, *pathyā*, and black pepper.
For the sake of accomplishing the fire-rite, one should perform oblations preceded by the seed-syllable of fire,
using milk and ghee for diseases such as eye ailments and others.
The knower of mantras should offer everything with honey using the Netra mantra;
for the destruction of intermittent fever (viṣamajvara), one should offer mango leaves.
Just as one who has conquered death by bathing in ghee while it is still fresh, so too,
O Rudra, destroy all calamities through peace and the recitation of the Khila hymns and others.

For the sake of pacifying ailments such as those caused by clothing and the like, for the pacification of mustard-seed and phlegm disorders, and for the pacification of bile disorders, one should perform oblations with very cooling substances such as sandalwood.
Or a thousand, or ten thousand, or a hundred thousand, or even three times that amount. || 103 ||
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, the procedure for the rules on the yoga of optional rites, in the great tantra known as the *Uttarakāmika*.
The god wears red garments, possesses a luster like that of crushed collyrium,
is endowed with eight arms, has hair standing erect, and bears prominent fangs.
With prominent fangs and a full lower lip, with eyes like a blazing fire,
he shone with a garland of small bells and was adorned with anklets on his feet.
Equipped with the seven weapons, adorned with all ornaments,
wearing a white sacred thread, and beautified by red flowers.
Adorned with neck-ornaments joined with held-up scorpions,
and blazing with fourteen serpents upon his waist, belly, neck, ears, heart, hands, arms, feet, and hands.
Seated in the midst of a lotus throne, three-eyed and of fierce form,
he holds in his right hands a trident-base, a vetāla, a sword, and a beautiful mace, and in his left hands the middle of the trident.
Having visualized [the deity] facing the enemy with the bell, shield, and skull-bowl held before him, and with his left foot extended forward, one should worship the Aghora-weapon.
Among them, Aghorāṇu is the destroyer of extreme defects;
he possesses a dark complexion, his crest-jatā is bound by a serpent, and he is adorned with fragments of skulls.
With eyes exceedingly tawny like honey, endowed with white fangs,
moon-crested, large-mouthed, and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread.
He has a massive body and large tusks, is endowed with the sound of tinkling bells,
and is the destroyer of great asuras impaled upon the tip of his great trident.

He holds a sword, a shield, a bow, and arrows; he bears a severed head and a black spear; his hands carry the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, a skull-cup, a serpent, a noose, a javelin, and a mace.
Two fangs, terrifying and black, protrude like stakes from the tip of his mouth.
He has four faces and flaming hair, with a luster like a mass of lightning;
his head is adorned with a crescent moon, and he possesses four sprout-like hands.
Accompanied by the sound of thunderbolts, unbearable and of terrifying prowess,
it was endowed with twelve eyes, great power, and the boon of being born from a trident.
Having meditated thus, one should worship Śivāstra with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using its own mantra.
Seated in the center of a nectar jar, resting upon a white lotus throne,
he has four arms and three eyes, and his matted locks are adorned with the crescent moon.
Clad in a tiger skin, adorned with the crescent moon as his ornament,
he holds a trident and the gesture of fearlessness (or a *ḍamaru* drum) in the upper [hands], and a nectar jar between the two middle [hands].
If he has six arms, he holds a trident and a rosary;
in his left hands, a skull-cup and a water-pot, while his two hands form the gesture of yoga (yogamudrā).

There is no mantra equal to this for the protection of the vital breaths and so forth. One should meditate on the Sun-god, who has ascended a lotus, possesses a spear, is born from the heart-lotus, holds a lotus in his hand, is endowed with four faces, and whose quarters are pervaded by four supreme, ruddy Śaktis.
I bow for the sake of prosperity to Śiva, who has mounted half the body [of his consort], who bestows fearlessness and boons, who holds a rosary and a skull-cup,
and whose hand grasps a noose and a goad while leaning upon a khaṭvāṅga staff.
34. In the thirty-fourth chapter is the procedure for consecration by sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa).
I shall explain the procedure for consecration by sprinkling, which cuts away all defects:
namely, the clockwise turn (āvarta), the counter-clockwise turn (anāvarta), and likewise the repeated turning (punarāvartana).
Then, sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is said to be of four kinds;
that which is performed at the root, the tip, and the middle, as well as the placement [of the vessel] in its proper place, is considered [the fourth]. (2)

That is declared to be an "āvarta" (whirlpool); it is called "anāvarta" (non-whirlpool) when it is touched by fallen persons, by those who have committed mortal sins, or likewise by Caṇḍālas and other low-born castes. || 3 ||
When the worship has been neglected for more than a month, when the ritual of the site has fallen apart,
and when the *liṅga* and its pedestal have become unstable, it is traditionally known as *anāvarta*.

Having taken [the deity] from the root-mouth and placed it again in the child-abode (bālālaya), the re-establishment from that [abode] into the root [abode] is known as "returning" (punarāvartana). || 5 ||

And in the case of images that are mixed with other materials, or whose powers are diminished by weapons and the like, or which are colorless, or which are devoid of primary and secondary limbs; || 6 ||
When the leather [covering] is torn, when it is lacking, when the ornaments and so forth are missing, when the lotus seat is absent, and when the rites pertaining to the pedestal are omitted; || 7 ||
When the pedestal-bond (*pīṭhabandha*) is separated, that which is situated between them is called *mucyate*.
Others say there should be two repetitions for the journey-offering (*yātrāhoma*), while others maintain it should be devoid of that.
One should cause all the twice-born to recite [the mantras] for the month, fortnight, lunar mansion,
and so forth, and should perform [the rite] according to the very path prescribed for the installation of the Liṅga.

O you of excellent vows, one should perform the remaining rites without regard for time—neither the lunar day, nor the asterism, nor the day of the week, nor the divisions of the zodiac and so forth. (10)
One should perform the removal of the marks, the ritual immersion in water, and likewise the laying on the bed, excluding the "whirlpool" and "face-whirlpool" [mantras] from these.
It should be known as "anāvarta" (non-returning), for here there is no returning again; one should perform everything like a *āvarta*, but it must be provided with two roots.
Therefore, O Brahmins, I shall briefly describe the *antaritaka* rite:
the depositing of jewels, the opening of the eyes, and the consecration (*adhivāsana*) in water. (13)
O Brahmins, except for the consecration of an image, one should perform the bedding-rite;
having wrapped all the limbs of the image with a new cloth, [one should proceed].

One should perform the ritual placement of the jar (*kumbhanyāsa*) and the fire sacrifice (*homa*) according to the previously mentioned procedure; at the conclusion, one should perform the ceremonial bath (*snapana*), and all other matters are the same as before.
In this way, the mortal who causes [this] to be made shall attain a meritorious state.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, the procedure for sprinkling, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
35. In the thirty-fifth chapter, I shall describe the ritual procedure for the consecration of the pedestal (pīṭha) and the installation of the pedestal, preceded by its defining characteristics.
A pedestal whose length and width correspond to those of the *liṅga* is the means for accomplishing all goals.
It should be as high as one-eighth part of Viṣṇu’s portion, free from defects in its shadow, and provided with a pedestal that emerges from the edge of the rising portion for worship. || 2 ||
Having prepared such a pedestal, what man would not attain perfection?
It should be equal to the length of the *liṅga*, or even half the length of the *liṅga*. (3)
The measurements are twenty-seven units, with each part being twenty-six units;
the height of the mouth of the liṅga should be three times or five times that [measurement].
In that interval, for a devotee of such [devotion], the width of the pedestal (pīṭha) is proclaimed to be twenty-seven units,
according to the measurement of the liṅga.
Beginning from fifteen finger-breadths and increasing by one finger-breadth at a time,
up to sixteen finger-breadths, it extends to a limit of twenty finger-breadths.
O twice-born ones, the width of the pedestal for liṅgas should range from one cubit up to nine cubits; a width of the pedestal greater than that of the liṅgas is not desired.
Its top should be equal to its base, or it may be smaller; however, a base that is deficient is not desired.
Having made the width of the base [gradually decrease] from one-sixth to one-sixteenth [of the total height], [the top should be equal to the base].

The pedestal (pīṭha) is proclaimed to have a width equal to one part, or it may be described as having a height of one Viṣṇu-part; for a pedestal with a height of two Viṣṇu-parts, the Brahmā-part is [one part].
The height of the pedestal (pīṭha) should be one-fourth [of the total height] or increased by one-third;
the measurement for the ninth part between those two, when divided into eight parts, has been declared.
O best of the twice-born, the *nandhāvarta* stone should be avoided even in small quantities;
likewise, the measurement of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) applies to human-made ones as well as to those that are self-manifested (*svayaṃbhūta*) and so forth.
Even for a mobile linga, some general rule is stated:
the pedestal (pīṭha) is measured to be equal to, half of, or double the size of the linga.
O best of the twice-born, the measurement for the width and the middle part is indeed seventeen; this is declared to be the root measure that should be adopted. 13.
O twice-born ones, its height should be equal to half its width, or equal, or even greater;
when each of these is divided into seven parts, there are seventeen measurements.

In the case of the *liṅgas* of Svāyaṃbhuva and others, there may be an elaboration regarding the dimensions of the *liṅga* and so forth; however, there shall be no fault regarding the pedestal (*pīṭha*). Having understood this, one should perform the rite for the pedestal accordingly.
The Vedāśrama is considered to be circular, or else it takes the form of a pedestal (pīṭha);
this is likewise prescribed for a liṅga made of metal, a liṅga of jewels, or even a Bāṇaliṅga.
One should fashion the width of the pedestal as one-third, one-fourth, or even one-sixteenth of that [measurement], in the case of the middle [type]. (17)
The pedestal (māna) is said to be seventeen [aṅgulas] in measure, either square or oblong;
its middle part is made double in length, and it is considered to be as previously described.
The length of the pedestal (pīṭha) has been fully described; now its height is being stated:
the height is equal to its width, or half of it at the end.
O best of the twice-born, the modified portion should be seventeen units in measure;
one should likewise determine its height to be one-quarter greater than its width.
In the center of the area occupied by the base, it is traditionally known as the "nine-fold measurement.
The height of the lotus is considered to be one-fourth of the height of the dome (biṃba). || 21 ||
One-eighth of the breadth is proclaimed as the other [measure]; having divided the middle part into eight parts, one should determine the ninth measurement by means of those divisions. (22)
Starting from the width of the base (sthānaka), the width of the tip of the lotus increases by one finger-breadth (aṅgula) at a time, up to a maximum of twelve fingers.
The expansion of the lotus on the seat measures twenty-three mātrās;
its size begins at half a finger-breadth and extends up to a maximum of thirty-six fingers.
The best [measurement] is said to have a base width one-third greater than its height;
the middling is when it is reduced by a twelfth part after being divided into sixteen parts. || 25 ||
The width is proclaimed to be of ten kinds, joined with seven [units].
However, in the middle [type], the length is equal to the width or twice as much. (26)
The length of the ground is proclaimed to be divided into nine parts;
when its height is divided, it should extend from one-third up to eleven parts. (27)
The upper lotus should consist of one, two, three, four, or five parts;
the lower lotus should be made with the remaining parts, or it may be smaller than the upper petals.
A pedestal (pīṭha) is said to be provided with four or eight petals, or perhaps sixteen petals; it should be spacious, elevated, and well-proportioned in its placement.
One should fashion it upon the pedestal with an extra height added;
its length and width should extend from one-third [of the base] up to eleven parts (rudrabhāga).
Having divided [the width] into one, two, or three parts on each side, one should then establish the *bhadra* in the middle using the remaining portions. || 31 ||
One should have a seat (pīṭha) constructed everywhere, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious;
if there are many [deities], one may provide a single seat for them all, provided it is done for the sake of aesthetic beauty.
Whether it be circular, elongated, or even in the shape of a half-moon, a lotus-shape should be fashioned; and for one seated there, a half-moon [design] should be made.
I shall now describe the ornamentation for the height of the pedestal (pīṭha) of the liṅgas.
According to the measurement of sixteen parts, the base (pādukā) is proclaimed [to be one part]. (34)
The *jagatī* is said to consist of four parts (*vedāṃśa*), while the *kumuda* consists of three parts (*guṇāṃśa*).
The lotus consists of eight parts (*vasvaṃśa*) plus one, and the *karṇa* is said to consist of five parts (*vahnyaṃśa*).
In a height of sixteen parts, the pedestal (pādukā) shall consist of two parts;
the measurement of the lotus (padma) shall be five parts, and it is said that the circular part (vṛtta) shall be two parts.
The fillet (paṭṭikā) is one-fourth of the height of the upper lotus;
it should be adorned with ghee and water, and this is considered the lotus-pedestal (padmapīṭha). || 37 ||
In the twenty-first part, the pedestal (pāduka) is formed by the fire-parts (three parts);
above that, the lotus is formed by five parts; the fillet (kampa) is one part, and above that, [the neck] is from three parts.
Karna, however, should have one tremor; the upper lotus [is formed] by the elemental portions (bhūtāṃśa);
two rows should be above, and one part [is for] the bearer of ghee (Agni).
In a height of sixteen parts, the *pādukā* (pedestal) occupies one and a half parts;
the *jagatī* (plinth) band occupies one part, and the height of the lotus (*padma*) is three and a half parts.
In a height of sixteen parts, the *pādukā* (pedestal) occupies one and a half parts;
the *jagatī-bandha* (moulding base) occupies one part, and the height of the lotus (*padma*) is three and a half parts.
The upper portion, measuring one part of the sky (vyomāṃśa), is called Kumuda;
above that, there is a circular band (paṭṭikā) measuring one part.
The *karṇa* (corner) should be two parts, the *stupada* half a part, the *paṭṭikā* one part, and the *ghṛtavārī* the remainder; this is declared to be the *śrīkara* pedestal.
In twenty-five parts, the space-portion shall be the pedestal;
in one part, the lotus; and the space-portion shall be the pedestal. || 44 ||

The *jagatī* should consist of four parts; the lotus-bud (*padmatuṇḍa*) from three parts; the neck (*gala*) from half [of that], the lotus from one-third, and the circular part (*vṛttaka*) from two parts.
The *kumuda* is one part, the *vājana* is one part, and the sky (*vyoma*) is one part; the *karṇa* is said to be two parts, and the *vājana* is indeed one part. (46)
The *mahāvājana* is declared to consist of one part and two parts;
the *kaṃpa* is said to be one part, and the *ghṛtavāri* half a part. (47)
The pedestal (pīṭha) is declared to be of the Śāmbhava type; otherwise, another is prescribed.
Having divided the height of the pedestal into twenty-one parts, [one should proceed as follows]. (48)
One should know that the *pāduka* is made with one part, the *jagatī* with one part;
the *karṇa* is made with one part, and the *padma* with three parts.
The *kumuda* and the lotus (*padma*) are each one part of the *vājana*; the *karṇa* is two parts, and the lotus of the *vājana* is one part. (50)
Two parts for the great fillet (mahāpaṭṭī), and by a portion of a quarter-part [for the lotus];
the *kaṃpa* above should be filled with ghee and water—this is considered the one named Vijaya.
In the eighteen-fold division, the sky-portion (vyomāṃśa) shall be the pedestal (pādukā);
it is said that the lotus (padma) shall be one and a half parts, and the fillet (kaṃpa) shall be one part.
By means of a portion equal to that of the *jagatī-veda*, the *kumuda* should consist of three parts;
there should be one part for the *kaṃpa* of the *karṇa*, and on one side, the *kaṃpa* should be two parts.
The great fillet (mahāpaṭṭī) consists of two parts, the molding (vājana) one part, and half of that is the base (mūmāpīṭha) joined with ghee and water; this is the prescribed measure.
In the portion for the modifications and its elevation, the *pādukā* measures one part;
the lotus (*padma*) is bound with this same measure, and the *jagatī* shall consist of one part. (55)
From the lotus, the neck should be made with two parts; there is no lotus above the half-and-half [division].
There should be a *kumuda* (water-lily) with two parts, and a lotus (*padma*) with half and then half again.
Kaṃpaṃkarṇa, however, is half [of the width]; Kaṃpañcavārija is half; the Mahāpaṭṭī is half a part; and on the top of the Aṃśena it is one and a half parts.
That which is known as "Ghṛtavāri" is declared here to bring about prosperity;
when it is high in the portion of Rudra, the sky-portion (vyomāṃśa) becomes a "pāduka."
One part for the Guṇāṃśa, one part for the Jagatī, and two parts for the Karṇa;
one part is declared for the Vājana, and two parts for the Mahāpaṭṭī.
The Nandikāvṛtta is said to consist of one part of *ghṛtavārī*;
one should divide the height into fifteen parts, and half of that shall be the height of the pedestal (*pādukā*).
With half [of that measure] there should be a trembling lotus; from the half [measure], the neck is one-third [of it].
A lotus is made with one part, a water-lily (kumuda) with two parts, and a lotus with one part.
Half [of the height] is for the neck, one-third for the lotus, and one and a half parts for the fillet;
joined with ghee and water in half a part, this is declared to be the Svastika [type].
In the eighth part of the height, there should be a two-footed pedestal;
the lotus should be made with one-third [of that], and the fillet (paṭṭikā) fashioned with one part.
The *karṇa* is said to be six parts, and the *vājana* one part;
the *abja* is declared to be two parts, and the *vājana* is desired to be two parts [of that]. (64)
With one part of ghee-water, this becomes the full moon;
one should divide the height into sixteen parts, and with one part [of that], the pedestal (pādukā) is formed.
Then, by two [parts] there is a lotus; by one, the neck at six parts;
by one part there should be a fillet (kaṃpa), and by two parts from the two parts [there is the base].
The great portion (mahāpaṭyaṃśa) should be one unit; from there, the wind (vāyu) should extend upwards.
Thus the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and the pedestal (pīṭha) are formed; now another [method] is stated here.
In this height consisting of three sixths, the pedestal (pādukā) shall be two parts;
a space of one part is called the fillet (kaṃpa), and the lotus (padma) is said to be two parts.
It is said that the *kaṃpa* is one part; the remainder is exactly as before.
However, when there are nineteen parts, the *pādukā* shall consist of two parts. (69)
Again, the *kaṃpa* should be made with one part, and the second *kaṃpa* with two parts;
the *padma* should be made with one part, and the remainder is declared to be as previously described.
O best of the elder brothers, those which are the seats (adhiṣṭhānas) proclaimed by Svāyaṃbhuva, those secondary seats (upapīṭhas) should also be applied here.
Above that, one should provide ghee-water; with one part and a half, or with two parts, it should be prepared with devotion for the attainment of desired goals.
One should emerge from the great boundary (mahāpaṭṭi) together with the others;
it should be provided with ghee or water, and its shape should be either circular or square.
Or one may conceive of it as endowed with a single foundation;
having taken the measurement of the ear, one should apply it to the base and other parts. || 74 ||
One should apply the increase and decrease of that measurement from one barley grain up to eight finger-breadths (aṅgula). || 75 ||
In all parts of the pedestals— whether they are with parts (sakala) or without parts (niṣkala),
mobile or immobile, made of metal or born of gems, or in the form of a Bāṇaliṅga— [the procedure applies].
Whether it be made of stone, wood, clay, or even metal, the measurement for a flawless [image] shall be as follows; its dimensions are now described.
The width of the base (pīṭha) should be three parts, and the width of the root of the water-channel (praṇāla) should be equal to that;
the width at its tip should be half of that—this is suitable for all liṅgas. || 78 ||

O best of the twice-born, the measurement for the middle [part] in the sixteen-fold division is known as seventeen parts; the length of the stalk is either half the measure of the pedestal or one-quarter.
In the middle [section], one should likewise take a measurement of exactly seventeen [units], divided either equally, or with one-quarter added, or with three-quarters added.

At the base of the water-channel, the neck [of the spout] should be measured according to that [same unit] as three-quarters, one-half, or one-quarter less than five, three, or twenty-three [parts]. (81)
In the seventh part, one should arrange the portion consisting of five, four, and three [units] at the front;
or it is said that the water-channel may be twice as wide as the depth of the channel for speech.
The lotus above that [pedestal] is to be shaken at its base on both sides;
above that, it is to be shaken by one, two, and three space-units respectively.
The measurement for the water-channel (praṇāla) is now stated;
its measure is half the width of the ear (karṇa), and having divided the height of the pedestal (pīṭha), [the channel's height] is determined.
The three-fold seventh part is the portion of the Vedas, increased by one part;
it ends with ten parts, which is indeed the thickness of the pedestal's stalk (pīṭhanāla).
A linga born from the same source is best; in its absence, one born from a different source may be used.
However, a linga with a single, undivided base is not desired here by those who seek worldly enjoyment.
Other desirable and excellent [images] may be made of gems, such as crystal and the like;
an image from a single solid rock is preferred, but in its absence, one that is carved from separate pieces is acceptable.

The section ending with the limbs (aṅgas) should be divided; above that, the section born from the undivided (akhaṇḍaja) should be joined with the channel (praṇāla), and it is likewise desired even when there is a division below that.

The sections (khaṇḍas) ending with the objects beginning with "without defects" (nadoṣa) and "abundant" (āḍhya) are proclaimed as the pedestals (pīṭhas). For those who possess all [attributes], there should be no stalk; otherwise, the pedestal should have a stalk. || 89 ||
Whether devoid of ghee and water or provided with them,
it is fashioned for the Bāṇaliṅga and other types of liṅgas as being either square or triangular.
Having fashioned that, one should then construct a pedestal above it;
one should make the radiance attached to the pedestal, or separate from it, or joined with something else.
It was joined with various pedestals for the sacrificial vessels, fashioned with strings of pearl garlands,
strung with various rows of flowers, and endowed with various flames of fire.
Adorned with all ornaments, pleasing to him, and provided with a dense [canopy],
it may be equipped with an archway, circular, or elongated according to the prescribed measurements.
Endowed with the eightfold measurements fashioned according to the specific gender [of the image], these characteristics have thus been declared; now the installation is being described.
On the pedestal (piṇḍikā) is the goddess Umā, and on the liṅga is Sadāśiva;
the union that is performed between these two is called Pratiṣṭhā.
Yoga should be known to be of two kinds: that which is prior and that which is subsequent.
The former has already been described in the ritual for the installation of the *liṅga*.
O Brahmins, the second [case] is described: when her action was performed previously in one way, she should perform it exactly the same way again; otherwise, it would cause harm. (97)
In the Mānava [Tantra], the covering of the pedestal (pīṭha-saṃkalpa-pidhāna) is proclaimed;
it may be square, circular, or even endowed with another form. 98.
In the case of divine, Ṛṣi-made, Bāṇa-made, or Svāyambhuva liṅgas,
the procedure should be performed everywhere, either according to the established tradition or endowed with the original form.

One should perform [the rite] with the previous substance, or else one should proceed with a superior one; one should carry out the entire ritual for the installation of the *liṅga* according to the path prescribed [in the scriptures]. (100)
O Brahmins, it is said that one should have [the rites] performed; let the remainder be understood as follows:
one should carry out the rite of sowing the sprouts according to the procedure previously described. (101)

On the top floor of the palace, in an auspicious location toward the northeast, one should construct a sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa). The dimensions for this pavilion are proclaimed according to the procedure previously described.
In the center of that, one should construct an altar according to the procedure for the installation of a liṅga;
one should construct sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) around it in the numbers nine, five, or one.
The sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be shaped like a vulva (yoni) and provided with three tiers (mekhalās).
To the east of that, or in the northern direction, there should be a bathing pavilion for the purpose of ritual ablution.
Having thus accomplished everything, one should thereafter commence the ritual action;
having performed the special worship, one should praise and bow down again and again. (105)
Having informed Śiva and obtained his permission, he should commence this ritual action.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of the Liṅga, [he should place] the Śiva-vessel and the Vardhanī.
Having placed [the central jar] in the middle, one should arrange eight jars all around,
provided with threads, lids, kūrca-grass, cloths, and sprouts.

Immediately thereafter, one should worship it with perfumes, garlands of blood, incense, and other offerings; then, having had the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited, one should [install] the image together with its pedestal.
Having invoked the Liṅga, one should place it within the Śiva-kumbha of the Liṅga;
having invoked the Goddess from the pedestal, one should place her in the Vardhanī at the center.

Having placed you around the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), one should worship them with perfumes and other offerings, ending with the food offering (naivedya); and prior to that, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).

One should offer a thousand oblations with the root mantra using sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, parched grain, and sesame seeds; or alternatively, one hundred oblations for each of these individually.
One should perform the expiation by offering oblations one hundred times with the Aghora mantra;
having prepared a sacrificial mound elsewhere, one should then install those [deities] there.
Daily worship should be performed constantly upon the *liṅga* and the water-pot (*kumbha*).
Having cut the pedestal with a chisel made of gold while uttering the *astra-mantra*, [one should proceed]. (113)
Having cast that [substance], along with the nectar (sudhā) and other items produced from it, into deep water,
a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) should be performed daily, or at least one hundred times.

Then one should perform its consecration; the procedure for that is stated here: having performed the rubbing with emery and [cleansing] with the five earths and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), || 115 ||
With decoctions, water, cow urine, and cow dung,
one should bathe the Supreme Lord in the midst of the water while reciting the Praṇava and the Astra-mantra.
Having worshipped in the center of the pavilion with garments, sandalwood, flowers, and other offerings,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and then place the pedestal (piṇḍikā) upon it.
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should mark the sign of the vulva (bhaga);
then, while reciting the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, one should satisfy it with honey and clarified butter.
In a vessel made of copper or bell-metal, filled with honey and clarified butter,
the wise man should present it along with gold while recollecting the Netra-mantra.
The best of preceptors, having covered [the items] with a concealed cloth, should show them— namely a heap of grain, a cow with its calf, and a maiden— while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having bathed the Goddess as before, one should worship her with garments, perfumes, and other offerings;
then, having led her in circumambulation of the village, one should settle her on the bank of a body of water.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound there, one should place the pedestal upon it;
one should then set out eight water-pots for the lords of the world-protectors in their proper order.
Having worshipped the goddess and the water-jars, which are provided with hanging tufts of grass, covered with new cloth, and placed upon a wooden plank within the water; 123.
One should place eight water-pots around it, joined by cords,
covered with cloths and gold, and presided over by the Śaktis.
Afterwards, having reached the pavilion provided with four archways, adorned with canopies and banners, and decorated with garlands made of darbha grass, pearls, and flowers; 125.
It was blazing everywhere, surrounded by flaming fires,
endowed with all auspicious marks, and well-attended by Takṣaka.
Having fed the Brahmins, one should smear [the ground] with cow dung;
then, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), one should perform the Vāstu-homa sacrifice. || 127 ||
Having consecrated the doors with the weapon-mantra (astra), one should worship the doors and the door-keepers;
then, entering by the eastern door, with a gentle countenance and remaining in an upright posture, [one should proceed].
Having meditated upon the auspicious mantra-body within the heart, the navel, and the bindu, he should hold a sword in his hand, endowed with worshiped self-awareness. || 129 ||
Having performed the prostration with five limbs (pañcāṅga-praṇāma), having worshipped the Lord of the Kumbha weapon,
and having completed the consecration of the fire in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), [he should worship] Maheśvarī because of her dwelling in the waters.
Having brought [the deity], one should perform the bathing known as *snapana* in the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*) as prescribed,
using clay, decoctions, the products of the cow, flowers, leaves, fruits, and water.
One should bathe Śivā with kuśa grass, fragrant water, and the five nectars (pañcāmṛta);
having clothed her in a pair of garments, one should worship her with perfumes.
Having performed the tying of the auspicious thread either on its stalk or on its neck,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with śāli rice amounting to four droṇas.
Having strewn it around with *darbha* grass and flowers, one should arrange half that amount of rice, half of that in sesame and parched grain, and then, in sequence, skins and other materials.
Then, having prepared the bed, or in its absence, one should represent it with garments;
having prepared a seat there, one should install the pedestal (piṇḍikā) while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Having covered it with a pair of garments, one should place a water-pot (karaka) in that spot,
wrapped in thread and cloth, and endowed with the nine gems.
One should worship the lotus of the Sahama, along with its filaments, fruit, sprouts, and cloth;
in its center, one should worship the Goddess seated upon her throne with perfumes and other offerings.
Eight vardhanīs, numbering eight, together with kūrca-grass, cloth, and thread, adorned with gold, provided with sprouts, covered with lids, and bearing fruit. || 138 ||
One should place [the deities] presiding over Vāmā and the others externally, arranged all around;
then, having worshipped the pedestal (piṇḍikā) and the vessel for increase (vardhanī) with perfumes and other offerings.
One should install the embodied form of Mūrtīśvarī conjoined with the Mistress of the Principles (Tattveśī).
One should install the triad of principles below the ear, on the throat, and above the ear.
Action, Knowledge, and likewise Will—these are proclaimed as the lords of the three principles (tattvas). They are Dhārikā, Dīptimatī, Ugrā, Jyotsnā, Cetā, and Balotkaṭā. || 141 ||
The forms Dhātrī and Vibhvī are to be contemplated in sequence from the [other] forms;
or else, in the fivefold system, whatever may be unmentioned here should be taken [as included]. 142.
One should perform everything according to the procedure prescribed for the installation of the *liṅga*;
having worshipped it with sandalwood paste and other offerings, one should commence the rite of *homa*.
With sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, sesame, mustard seeds, and barley;
and with wood from the Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, Nyagrodha, and Plakṣa trees, [one should perform the rites] starting from the eastern direction.
The śamī, khadira, māyūra, and śrīvṛkṣa trees are for the southeast corner;
