however, the palāśa should be the primary one, or indeed the palāśa alone is considered suitable for all [corners]. (145)
One should offer oblations with the root mantra of the Goddess one thousand times, or half of that, or one hundred and eight; and with her ancillary mantras, one-tenth of that amount.
One should begin with the sprinkling for pacification and the touching with *darbha* grass;
then, one should perform oblations (*homa*) in each individual fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) using the principles (*tattva*), their presiding deities (*tatveśvara*), and so forth.
One should perform the expiation by offering oblations with the Aghora mantra recited one hundred times;
then, having performed protection with ashes, *darbha* grass, and sesame seeds, one should offer the *tattva-bali*.
The preceptor should offer the inner oblation (antarbali) and the oblation to the lords of the fields (kṣetreśabali).
Then, at the clear dawn, the pure preceptor, together with those possessing physical forms, [should proceed].
Having performed the daily rites and offered the general *arghya*, the Guru,
having worshipped the doors and their presiding deities, should then raise up the Great Goddess.
Then, having worshipped both the pedestal and the *vardhanī* vessel with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings, ending with betel leaves.
Having gratified [the deity] with fire-oblations and performed the expiatory rite,
one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the root mantra, which cuts through all defects.
Having performed the circumambulation of the temple accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments and joined with dance and song, one should place [the deity] within the inner sanctum.
One should install it according to the procedure prescribed for the consecration of the *liṅga*;
however, if the installation of a pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) for a *bāṇaliṅga* takes place, [the following applies].
In front of that, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) within the pavilion or similar structure, one should place that liṅga,
covered with nine cloths, such that its head faces the auspicious directions.
Having removed the nectar and other substances from the pedestal,
one should place the pedestal back in that very same spot and install the liṅga there.
Having placed the jewels in the pit of every pedestal, the true Guru, or having deposited gold, should perform everything else as previously described. (157)
Immediately thereafter, one should perform the eight-fold binding or the three-fold binding,
followed by the consecration with the "Auspicious Day" (Puṇyāha) water and the sprinkling with the water from the Peace-pitcher (Śāntikumbha).

Having performed the rite for the seat according to the previously stated method, the Guru should then place the [seed-syllable] called Kriyā upon the pedestal, following the path described before. (159)
One should also place the Śiva-pitcher and the Vardhanī vessel upon the tip of the Liṅga;
the Vāmā and other [vessels], joined with the Vardhanī, are situated within the interior of the altar.
Having placed [the vessel] before the deity, one should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) by means of the "placement of life" (jīvanyāsa);
or, having established the *vardhanī* vessel, it should be joined with the eight *vardhanīs*.
Having placed the altar (vedikā) in the center, one should begin for the purpose of the deposition of the vital breath (jīva-nyāsa).
Then, the deposition of the vital breath should be performed in three locations or upon the seat.

When the jar has been established upon the *liṅga* and other supports, one should especially perform the ritual bathing at the time of the *nyāsa*, or alternatively, the rite of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) at the conclusion.
Or one may worship properly with water alone, or with perfumes and other offerings,
for as long as the moon and the sun endure, and for as long as the earth stands.
Therefore, O Goddess, always maintain your presence here.
The installation of the Liṅga has been described; one should cause the southern half to be given as a sacrificial fee.
For four days, or three, or two, or even one day continuously,
a special worship (viśeṣapūjā) accompanied by fire-oblations (homa) must be performed.
One should perform the oblation with the previously mentioned potent grains mixed with milk-rice;
or else, on the fourth or the first day, the Caṇḍakalpa rite should be performed.
Furthermore, that [result] would not be desired in the case of arrows and the like;
or rather, let it be considered that the fruit of establishing a pedestal is the same as that of the consecration of a liṅga. (168)
Since it has been stated that the foundation is the same in both cases.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, the procedure for the consecration of the sacred seat (*pīṭha-pratiṣṭhā-vidhi*), in the great tantra known as the *Uttarakāmika*.
Now I shall describe the ornaments for the pedestals (pīṭha) of the liṅgas.
According to the measurement of sixteen parts, the plinth (pādukā) is proclaimed;
the base (jagatī) is said to be four parts, and the kumuda should be three parts.
One part is said to be the *vasvaśra* (octagonal) lotus; one part is called the *karṇa* (corner); the *paṭṭikā* (fillet) is known by one part, and the *mahāpaṭṭī* (great fillet) by two parts.
This *bhadrapīṭha* (auspicious pedestal) is considered to have a height of one part for the *ghṛtavārī* (water-receptacle).
In that height of sixteen parts, the pedestal (pādukā) shall consist of two parts;
the measurement of the lotus (padma) shall be five parts, and the circular base (vṛtta) is said to be two parts.
The portion of the Vedas (four parts) shall be the upper lotus; the fillet (paṭṭikā) shall be by the portion of Aśvinī (two parts).
This lotus-pedestal is considered to have a height equal to the clarified butter (ghṛta, four parts).
Even in the case of twenty-one divisions, the pedestal (pāduka) above consists of [one] part.
The lotus [pedestal] consists of five parts, while the tremor (the capital) is one part, extending three-quarters of the way upward.
With one [part], there should be a tremor at the ear; with the elemental parts (bhūtāṃśa), there is an upward lotus.
With two [parts], there would be a row above, held by water from a single portion.
In the sixteen-fold division of its height, the *pādukā* occupies one and a half parts;
the *jagatī* and *bandha* occupy one part each, and the height of the lotus (*padma*) is three and a half parts.
The sky-portion (vyomāṃśa) with an upward projection is called the *kumuda* by means of two [parts]. Above that is a circular form, and the fillet (*paṭṭikā*) is measured at one part.
The corner (*karṇa*) is made of two [parts], the lotus (*padma*) of one, and the fillet (*paṭṭikā*) of half a part.
With the remainder, however, the seat that bestows prosperity is said to consist of ghee and water.
The sky-portion (one part) out of twenty-five shall be the pedestal;

above that, the lotus is made with one part, and the bowl (vājana) is made from the sky-portion (one part). The base (jagatī) shall consist of four parts, and the tip of the lotus (padmatuṇḍa) from three parts.
The neck (galamarda) should be three parts; the lotus (padma) three parts; the circular part (vṛttaka) one part;

the kumuda and the lotus (padma) one part each; the base-ring (vājana) from two parts of space (vyomabhāga); the ear-ornament (karṇa) is said to be two parts; and the base-ring (vājana) indeed one part.
The *kañca* is said to consist of one part, the *mahāvājana* of two parts,
the *kampa* of one part, and the *ghṛtavāri* of half a part; this is declared to be the *śāmbhava-pīṭha*, while otherwise it is prescribed differently.
Having divided the height of the pedestal (pīṭha) into twenty-one parts, one part is considered for the base (pādukā), four parts for the jagatī,
one part for the fillet (karṇa), and one part for the lotus (padma); [the remaining] three parts [are for the rest].
The *kumuda* is one part, the *vājana* one part;
the *karṇa* is two parts, and the *vājana* is one part; the *padma* is one part, while the *mahāpaṭṭī* is two parts; the *padma* is one part, and [the next] is one part.
There may be a *kampa* (projection) of one part above the *ghṛta* and *vāri*; this is considered to be called *vijaya*.
In the division of eighteen parts, however, the *pādukā* (pedestal) occurs in the portion of space (*vyomāṃśa*).
It is said that the lotus (*padma*) is one and a half [parts], while the *kampa* occurs from a single part.
In the Jagatī Veda portion, Kumuda should consist of three parts;
Kampa should be one part, and Karṇa two parts on one side, with Kampa again being one part.
The large border (mahāpaṭṭī) consists of two parts, the frame (vājana) one part, and it is joined with ghee and water for half [a part]; this is considered the Umā-pīṭha.
In the modified portion and its elevation, the *pāduka* (pedestal) shall measure one part;
the lotus (*padma*) shall be measured by one part, and the *jagatī* (platform) shall be formed by the portion of the bond (*bandha*).
The lotus-base and the neck [should be made] with two parts; the upper lotus with half of a half [of those].
The *kumuda* should be with two parts, and the *padma* with half of that. The *kaipa* and the ear should be with half [a part], and the *kampa* and the water-lily (*vārija*) with half [a part] each.
The great fillet (mahāpaṭṭī) is said to be half a part, and the water-band (ghṛtavāri) on the top is declared to be one and a half parts; this is taught here as bringing prosperity.
On the Rudra portion, however, at Tuttaṅga, the sandal (pādukā) shall be one fathom in measure.
The width of the *guṇāṃśa* is one part, while Karṇa is two parts.
The *vājana* is said to be one part, and the great band (*mahāpaṭṭī*) is two parts;
the *nandikā* surrounding it is declared to be one part of ghee and water.

One should divide the lunar portion (tithyaṃśa) for the *tuṅga*; one and a half parts shall be the *pādukā*. With half [of that] there shall be a *kampa*, and with three parts the *gala*; with half [of that] there shall be a *kampa*, and with three parts the *padma*; with half [of that] there shall be a *kampa*, and with three parts the *gala*.
The lotus is one part; the lily and the lotus are each two parts;
the neck is half [of that]; the lotus is three parts; the fillet is one and a half parts;
and the half-part is joined with ghee and water—this is declared to be the *svastika* [pattern].
Of the eighteen parts of the height, two parts shall be for the pedestal (pādukā),
three parts for the lotus (paṅkaja), and one part fashioned for the fillet (paṭṭikā).
The ear is said to be six parts, and the fillet (vājana) one part;
the lotus (abja) is declared to be two parts, and the fillet is desired at two parts.
With one part of excellent ghee, this becomes the Full Moon [mandala].
One should divide the height into parts: the sky (the dome) by one part, the pedestal by one part, the lotus by two parts, the *kampa* (fillet) by one part, and the neck by six parts.
The lotus should be one part, and from two parts [each], the stalk;
the height of the vessel containing ghee and water should be according to the measure of one-sixteenth part.
The sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) is thus the seat (pīṭha); furthermore, another [method] is stated here.
In that height divided into eighteen parts, two parts shall be the pedestal (pādukā);
one part is said to be the fillet (kampa), and two parts are called the lotus (padma).
It is said that the *kampa* is by one part; from six parts, the neck (*gala*) is formed.
By one part there is a *kampa*, and the lotus (*padma*) shall consist of two parts each.
The great cloth (mahāpaṭṭī) should extend upwards from the shoulder-measure by the amount of a cubit.
In the nineteen-fold division, the pedestal (pādukā) shall consist of two parts;
the fillet (kampa) by one part, and again the fillet by two parts.
There may be a slight tremor in the lotus; the rest has been described as before.
This is declared to be the Svāyaṃbhuvakalpa, along with those which are the presiding seats.
O best of the foremost, those secondary seats (*upapīṭha*) should be joined here.
In the thirty-sixth chapter, the procedure for the installation of the *bāṇaliṅga*:
I shall describe the installation of the *bāṇaliṅga* in brief and in due order.
The asura named Bāṇa was mentioned; and for the sake of his spiritual accomplishment, he [was instructed] with devotion.
He requested various types of lingas for the purpose of worship;
Maheśvara granted fourteen crores of lingas.
Having worshipped them, at the end of time he deposited them in these locations:
in Liṅgādrau, in Kālikāgarta, on Śrīnaga, and in Kanyakāśrama.
At Kanyātīrtha in Nepal, at Mahendra and Cāmareśvara, and elsewhere in the midst of rivers and especially on mountains. || 4 ||
The measurement of these [liṅgas] is declared to range from the size of a māṣa bean up to the length of a hand;
alternatively, one may adopt a measurement increased by a quarter-aṅgula according to one's preference.
However, a Bāṇaliṅga that exceeds the proper measurement of width is not desired;
it should be free from lines, dots, stains, and the like, or at least free from such defects.
Among all types of lingas, the Bāṇaliṅga is preeminent;
it excels in bathing, worship, incense, and the offering of perfumes, flowers, and food.
O best of Brahmins, in other rites such as those pertaining to Svāyambhuva and others,
no restriction regarding the construction of temples, pedestals, and so forth is prescribed.
The best of those skilled in ritual procedures should construct a temple for the Bāṇaliṅga outside of all villages and settlements, or even within them.
The pedestal (pīṭhikā) may be made of stone, clay, metal, excellent wood, gems, and so forth;
the pedestal should be of a single color for the sake of accomplishing all desires and aims. (10)
O twice-born ones, one-third of the height of the liṅga, or two-fifths,
or even half of the liṅga, should be made for the depth of the pit (ānanta).
Or, according to one's preference, the measurement of the cavity (khāmāna) has been described;
and when it exists in a continuous flow, it has the form of a Bāṇaliṅga.
Whatever other auspicious sign there may be that brings all happiness, such as a mountain and so forth, it is declared to be exactly like that [liṅga]. (13)
The face should be known as elevated, whether in its thick or thin portion;
it may be thick or thin, yet its form should be radiant and directed upwards. (14)
The linga is declared to be made of precious gems, and likewise considered to be made of metal;
whether it be natural or carved, when properly joined, it is excellent.
The same is prescribed for images made of jewels and even of iron; likewise, it is considered so for those made of earth.
And for all of these, the primary consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is now being described.
The most excellent time is prescribed for the installation of a stone linga;
for the installation of a mobile linga, an image, and the like, it is considered middling.

For one desiring liberation, all months, solstices, lunar mansions, days of the week, and so forth, would indeed be of low quality; therefore, no such rule regarding them is prescribed for those [liberation-seeking acts]. (18)
In the same manner for a Bāṇaliṅga, however,
having first performed the Vajrabandha and other rites, one should then begin the installation.
One should perform the rite of depositing the sprouts according to the procedure previously described;
thereafter, one should carry out the placement of jewels—nine, five, or one jewel.
One should place a golden [image] in the middle of the pedestal cavity;
the removal of [external] marks is not desired, for its own form shall be the mark. || 21 ||
Having performed the purification of the liṅga with clay and water using the Astra-mantra of Śiva,
one should perform the preliminary immersion (adhivāsana) of the water in nine, five, or one sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
One should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) together with an altar (vedikā) for the purpose of consecrating the liṅga;
however, for rites concerning the planets and the like, it is considered acceptable that the sthaṇḍila be without an altar.

The dismissal of the artisans, the declaration of an auspicious day, the feeding of Brahmins, the smearing [of the site], the examination of the ground, the worship of Vāstu, the fire-ritual, and the libation should be performed. (24)
One should perform his worship upon a sacrificial post (sthāṇu) as previously described;
then, having brought him from the midst of the water, one should lead him through purification with the products of the cow (gavya) and other substances.
Having worshipped and wrapped the auspicious [liṅga] with a cloth and applied the *pratisara* cord,
one should then place it upon a bed in the center, along with the Śiva-pitcher and the *vardhanī* vessel.
O Lord of Knowledge, [the vessel] should be joined with a water-pot (kumbha), provided with a cord,
a lid, gold, and cloth, and filled with scented water.
Having established them, one should perform the sacrifice for all [deities] conjoined with their respective Lords of Principles (tatveśas);
having thus offered the Mūrtis and the Mūrtīśvaras into the Śiva-fire, one should proceed.
One should offer oblations consisting of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, and sesame seeds,
reciting the root mantra one hundred and eight times as prescribed.
O best of the twice-born, one should perform the oblation for Manonmanī with half [the amount] and for the limbs with a tenth part;
then one should perform the oblation for the principles (tattvas), the lords of the principles (tattveśvaras), and so forth, as previously described.
Having covered the linga with a cloth, one should present the food offering;
then, having bathed in the morning and worshipped the presiding deities of the pavilion.
One should offer oblations into the fire for the Liṅga with the Maghora mantra forty times;
then, having received the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), being satisfied, and having obtained the ornaments for the five limbs, [the rite is complete].
When the auspicious moment has arrived, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa).
O Preceptor, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall consist of nine coins, beginning with one.

Having performed the ritual visualization (saṃkalpa), one should place the seat, the image, and the root-mantra upon Śiva; with those waters, one should establish the God and the Goddess, who is the very form of the pedestal.
At the conclusion, one should cause the ceremonial bath (snapana) to be performed and offer the food offering (naivedya) with devotion.
Whatever has not been mentioned here should be carried out according to the procedure for the installation of a Linga.
The fourth oblation and the worship of Caṇḍeśa are not prescribed for him;
he should worship the God every day according to the procedure stated for the ritual of worship, bowing with the Vidyā.
There is no way to move an image of a cultured person (śiṣṭaliṅga); one should not, even by means of ritual, shift an ordinary image that has become worn out or is defiled by defects, in an instant.
Having made [the image] very firm with gold plates and so forth, one should perform the rite of pacification (śānti) either in a water-pot,
on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), in a mandala, or upon a pedestal and the like.
Having worshipped the Lord of the gods in a location determined by the eastern direction, and having worshipped Manonmanī in the northern part of the prepared pavilion and so forth, (verse 39).
Accompanied by the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) and worshipped with offerings such as perfumes and the like,
he— adorned with the five-fold ornaments— remains until the ritual task is completed.
One should perform the dismissal at the end and carry out the peace-offering (śānti-homa);
or one may perform the oblation at the beginning and the end, or indeed perform the oblation every day.
In that case, sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) is not desired; rather, half of that [rite] or even just the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed.
One should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) there in front of the Liṅga and place the water-pot (kumbha) upon it.

Therefore, O twice-born ones, one should perform the invocation into the pitcher and apply the pitcher-mantras; however, the ritual bathing is not desired except in the procedure for the restoration of a dilapidated temple.
Even with those jars, one should perform either a full bath or merely a sprinkling;
at the conclusion of the rite, one should perform the ceremonial bath and worship Śiva with special care.
This very procedure is prescribed for the rite of severing bonds;
it applies to the rite of severing on dry land when the rite of "white elixir" (sudhā) has not been performed.

If it perishes in a mere moment, there can be no worship here of the ritual act; even offerings such as the fire-oblation (homa) would not be desired to be performed. One should instead worship the Liṅga. || 46 ||

One should bring about peace through offerings of fragrance and other non-material substances, or by means of a fire oblation (homa). One should perform the oblation to the forms (mūrtihoma) and the oblation to the directions (diśāhoma), according to the relative gravity or lightness of the rite.
If the pedestal and the platform are being prepared, there should be a ritual bathing of both the deity and the pedestal,
due to the possibility of either becoming loose or firm within their interior structure.

O best of the twice-born, having performed purification with cloth and other means, just as one cleanses faded floral offerings (nirmālya), one should sprinkle it there with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra for the purpose of bathing.
If there is a break [in the ritual], a bath lasting many days, a great ceremonial bathing,
and likewise a great oblation are prescribed for the pacification of the king and the kingdom.
And for the people residing in the village and those living in that place, as well as for the builder, the one who causes it to be built, and especially for the preceptor (deśika). || 51 ||
When the temple has fallen or been destroyed, this [rite] is prescribed for the deity;
this is stated to be the general rule for all lingas, beginning with those of the Self-born (Svāyambhuva).
This rite should be performed with reference to the artisan, accompanied by ritual sprinkling;
all else shall be the same, as it possesses the common characteristics of the ritual action.
Let there be no confusion of Manvantaras regarding the Liṅgas of Svāyambhuva and the others;
by this very method, the installation of those made of jewels is prescribed.
Just as with iron and other metals, it is proclaimed that [the image] is produced from gold and so forth; and its installation is declared to be either mobile or immobile. (55)
Movement is said to be of two kinds: primary and secondary.
For the purpose of worshipping paintings, statues, and so forth, [the movement] is performed at their respective front. (56)
It is said that you are the worshipped limb (aṅga), while the other is considered the primary subject (prādhānika);
and the worship of the possessor of the limbs (aṅgin) is performed at the time prescribed by the scriptures. (57)
Likewise, his ritual activity shall be accompanied by perpetual festivals and the like;
elsewhere, there shall likewise be pure dance and similar perpetual festivals.
Having abandoned the other [options], that which was previously indicated for one's own sake is distinguished. || 581/2 ||
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, the ritual for the installation of the Bāṇaliṅga, in the great tantra known as the Uttarāmāmikā.
37. In the thirty-seventh chapter: The Ritual for the Installation of the Kāmyaliṅga.
I shall now describe the installation of the Kāmyaliṅga, preceded by its defining characteristics.
The desired objects are to be known as *siddhis* (accomplishments), and these *siddhis* are recorded as being of many kinds.
It is of four kinds—lesser, middling, and superior—and each of these is said to be threefold, according to the distinctions of "excellent" and so forth. || 2 ||
The fruit is twofold, being both seen and unseen; it is further divided into superior and inferior.
The inferior consists of sovereignty over hundreds of kings, while the middling consists of the attainment of power.
O Lord, supreme mastery over the sky and the highest equality with the gods—each of these is further divided into many types, such as the state of a Vidyeśvara and so forth. || 4 ||
The state of being a Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa), the state of Rudra, the state of Brahmā, and the station of Viṣṇu—
such divinity as this and other like states are called "supreme" by the wise.

The supernatural powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and others, as well as the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin)—these and other such excellent accomplishments (siddhis), O best of sages, [are attained]. (6)

The middling [level] consists of pills, gold, the underworld, swords, mallets, and so forth; the inferior is considered to be for the sake of overcoming untimely death, heightening status, subjugation, and the like. (7)
If it were something perceived, then that which is experienced by this very body,
or by another body, would be seen as a product of illusion, both here and elsewhere.

The bliss that exists in the state of Rudra, such as that of Amareśa and others, which is the effect of Māyā, should be known as the lower (apara); the higher (para) is the station of Ananta and the rest, which is the state of the Pata.
There is neither spiritual perfection nor liberation without taking refuge in the *liṅga*.
Those who desire perfection and liberation while disregarding the *Śivaliṅga* [attain neither]. (10)
Have these dull-witted ones crossed the formidable ocean of existence?
Have they attained the fruit desired in worldly life, and are they considered gods perfected in their accomplishments? || 11 ||
Fools who mutter prayers to a jewel-liṅga are deluded; what logic is there for one whose mind is confused?
Therefore, for the sake of attaining perfection through reliance on a liṅga, one should properly take refuge in a [true] liṅga.
Viṣṇu and the others, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the sages of great luster,
having worshipped the Liṅga according to the prescribed rites, attained their most desired fruit.
It was established by Svāyaṃbhuva, or by sages, gods, hosts of attendants, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others; it was never established by mortals.
Or, having himself established [the image] endowed with all the characteristics, after having examined it according to the scripture, according to the time, and according to the place. || 15 ||
Therein, the preceptor or even the practitioner should accomplish the siddhi;
and for the benefit of kings who are themselves unable to perform it.
The supreme guide shall accomplish success for the sake of the four classes, or for the benefit of himself or another; he is the benefactor who acts for the welfare of the agent. 17.
For the sake of the *liṅga*, one should go to a source of materials according to one's own task;
having taken stone or other substances, one should bring them in accordance with the requirements of the rite.
Those substances are said to be of eight kinds—stone, clay, metal, and wood—as well as gems and ephemeral objects; they are described here in their entirety. (19)
White, red, yellow, and black—thus it is of four kinds;
the stone of all four castes is considered to be the Dhātrī.
These four are prescribed for a Brahmin, three for kings, two for Vaiśyas, and one for a Śūdra; by rule, these are declared to be stones and pieces of land. (21)
The various types of clay produced from those respective elements are prescribed for the purpose of the *liṅga*;
the fruit resulting from stone *liṅgas* is declared to correspond to their specific forms.
The fruit of all four types of clay should be known as lordship over the earth; for one desiring prosperity, it should be made of gold, and for one desiring a kingdom, of silver.
An iron image is for the purpose of killing; one made of bronze is for driving away [enemies];
one made of brass is to be known as for causing ruin; and one made of tin is for the increase of sons.
A liṅga made of copper is for one desiring prosperity, while one made of lead destroys disease;
this is declared to be the iron liṅga. Now, the jewel liṅga is described.
A Vajra-liṅga, when established on the earth, bestows sovereignty; a pearl liṅga shall grant health;
and from a sapphire liṅga, one attains all desires.
From a great liṅga made of sapphire, one shall attain the station of Viṣṇu;
from lapis lazuli, there shall be the destruction of disease; and from topaz, good fortune.
From a liṅga made of emerald one attains health, from one of coral one gains power over others,
and from one made of rājāvarta stone one enjoys great prosperity.
Nīla is for the enjoyment of the lords of serpents; Śaṅkha bestows good fortune;
Maṇija and Pulaka likewise lead to the destruction of enemies. (29)
Sasyaka is for the production of crops; that born from the sun-gem (sūryakānta) is for the sake of the sun;
candrakānta is for the conquest of death; and that born from the ruby (padmarāga) bestows prosperity.
Crystal is for the sake of all accomplishments; that born of the earth (iron) is for divine accomplishment;
vaikrānta is beneficial for great success, as is that which is red and produced from the *yathaskānda* [mineral].
The class of mantras associated with minor accomplishments (kṣudrasiddhi) is refined by the purificatory rites;
it is said that from these qualities, eight fruits arise in the case of the superior classes of gems.
Thus has that made of jewels been described; now that made of wood is told:
one made from a tree possessing heartwood leads to prosperity, while one made from a milky sap tree leads to long life. (33)
The sandalwood from the *raktāhvaya*, *candana*, *aśoka*, *śiṃśupā*, *aśoka*, and *bilva* trees is excellent, possesses fragrance and virtue, and bestows knowledge, good fortune, and fame. (34)
Even in the absence of all suffering and the like, for the destruction of diseases born of malevolent spirits (piśāca),
or else, according to the astrological sign (nakṣatra) of the practitioner, the liṅga may indeed be made of wood.
Then the kāraskara, āmalaka, udumbara, and jambuka;
the khadira, kṛṣṇa, and kakubha; and thereafter the śirīṣa and aśvattha.
The Punnāga, the Nyagrodha, the Palāśa, and likewise the Plakṣaka;
the Ambaṣṭha, Bilva, Arjuna, Kāśa, Śālmalī, and likewise the Vakula. (37)
The piṇḍī, the sarja tree, the vañjula, and likewise the panasa; the āmra and the arka, the kadamba, as well as the agni and the nimba. || 38 ||
The Madhūka tree belongs to the Aśvinī constellation; these trees correspond to the preceding constellations.
When these stars are occupied by these trees, rites such as those for peace (śāntika) and so forth should be performed.
Having fashioned a liṅga, one should perform rites such as killing (māraṇa) during the asterism of the victim;
for those seeking victory, a liṅga made from the root of the white Arka plant should be used for the sake of triumph. (40)
Sandalwood brings all things under one's control, while red sandalwood bestows prosperity; Sarala wood fulfills all desired objects, and Khadira wood destroys disease.
The wood of the Saptaparṇa, the Sāla, and the Rājādana tree is especially effective for all castes in accomplishing all desired objects. (42)

A liṅga made of udumbara wood leads to nourishment and peace; one originating from nyagrodha leads to subjugation; and one made of aśvattha wood leads to health, while a liṅga made of khadira wood brings about well-being.
O best of the twice-born, a liṅga made of vibhītaka wood is for the purpose of exorcising enemies;
a liṅga made of wood is declared to be a temporary liṅga.
Cow dung is a conventional means for the sake of liberation and prosperity; it destroys disease.
Food is for one who desires food, and flour-based food bestows nourishment. (45)
An image made of molasses is said to bring delight for the sake of accomplishing desired goals;
an image fashioned from clarified butter brings joy even to those who are suffering. (46)
Fresh butter, rich in qualities, produces delight; a clay linga is likewise beneficial.
A linga made especially from ashes wards off all diseases.
A Liṅga made of flowers, according to one's respective caste, bestows nourishment;
that which is made from Bilva leaves and other such materials, O son, increases progeny.
A linga produced from that seed is a cause of special satisfaction;
a linga made from grain or rice bestows the fruits of those respective substances. (49)
A linga made of bulbous roots is the cause of the realization of Brahman;
likewise, a linga fashioned from flour or parched grain removes disease.
A linga fashioned from water brings peace and nourishment to living beings;
a linga that is painted yields manifold fruits immediately.
The linga that is smeared with camphor, sandalwood, and other such substances is age-defying;
thus the materials have been described, and now the characteristics are prescribed.

The linga, according to its divisions such as the "eldest" (jyeṣṭha) and so forth, is prescribed by the measurement of the interior of the temple for the primary purpose of attaining supernatural powers (siddhi), while liberation (mukti) follows as a secondary result.
Those measurements of the linga starting from one cubit (hasta) lead to liberation;
furthermore, through the application of the prescribed rules, they also result in enjoyment along with its six ancillaries.
The lower [type] is known to be half of the *garbha*; the superior [type] should be five parts and three parts.
Within that interval, at the eighth division, there are indeed nine *liṅgas*.
Below each of those, there are indeed three;
O best of the twice-born, the measure of the womb is declared to be thirty-six [units]. (56)
Alternatively, in a palace, one should [construct] a fire-altar divided according to the Vedas;
specifically, having set aside two parts for the doors, the altar-base (pīṭha) should be included.
And as before, the measurements for the marks have been prescribed,
beginning from one finger-breadth and increasing by one finger-breadth at a time.
Up to one hundred and eight [fingers], it is measured by three types of finger-breadths;
beginning from one cubit, it increases by six finger-breadths.
One should determine the measurement up to a maximum of nine cubits according to the standard of the cubit;
however, stone [structures] situated below one cubit are not recommended for temples.

O best of the twice-born, a wooden liṅga is considered to be one-quarter [the size] of that [stone one], while a metal one is half its size; a jewel-liṅga, moreover, should measure from one finger-breadth up to a span.
One should employ that which is joined with auspicious [planets] such as Ārdrā according to the nature of the rite;
having applied a stone held in the hand, one should use it for rites such as *uccāṭana* (driving away). 62.
In one part of the length of the liṅga, the width should be one-fourth;
one should divide all siddhi-liṅgas into three equal sections.
One should place [the image] upon the seat of Indra, which is square, or eight-sided, with a tuft of hair, bearing a rounded head, and joined with a crescent-shaped head.
In the eastern direction, for the sake of accomplishing one's desired aims, the Vajraśiras Liṅga is established;
having applied it for vajra-activities such as the rite of immobilization (stambhana) and so forth, it is thus proclaimed.
Above the *liṅga*, in the portion belonging to Rudra, one should fashion a square with five parts;
an octagon as before; and within the circle, a heptagon, excluding its own direction.
On the Āgneya-pīṭha, that Liṅga should be installed for the sake of attaining mastery over the eastern quarter;
the Liṅga, endowed with Śakti and the Śiras, should be placed upon a pedestal consisting of the limbs of Śakti.
O twice-born ones, a Liṅga of the nature of fire brings about peace as well as fierce splendor, the destruction of enemies, the affliction of foes, and the burning of the enemy. 68.

In the ninth part, the two sides—eastern and western—are marked with five [lines], and the southern side of the two principal arms is encircled with three; this is the sequence for the fire-emanation (agnicyuti).
To achieve mastery over the southern direction, one should install [the deity] upon a southern pedestal;
one should install the Liṅga, joined with the head of a staff, according to the prescribed rite.
In the southern direction, there is heavy punishment, yet an increase in lifespan and personal prowess;
situated in the region of the enemy, there is destruction, and then, in the south of the city.
It brings about pestilence, dissension, and disease; of this there is no doubt.
However, if the length is divided into twenty-two parts, a square is formed by four-fifths of that measure.

O twice-born ones, one should establish an eight-sided figure, as before, together with a circle and a ten-sided figure upon the Rākṣasa pedestal for the sake of accomplishing the means of one's own direction.
One should place the skull-topped staff (khaḍvāṅga) upon the pedestal with its blade facing upward;
through the piercing of the stake, it effects the destruction of enemies, incites hatred, and causes delusion.
When combined with mantras according to the prescribed ritual, it brings about the destruction of that army, madness, and the outbreak of a plague of Rākṣasas; of this there is no doubt. (75)

In the height, the portion belonging to Manu (the seventh) is a four-cornered square; the portion belonging to Brahmā (the first) is likewise a square, an octagon, a circle, and a crescent moon at the top.
Having established it in the western quarter, one attains the lordship of that direction;
that [image] should be joined with a noose at its head according to the ritual rules for the Body of the Noose (Pāśakāya). || 77 ||
Having established supreme peace, nourishment, prosperity, increase, and happiness, one shall obtain the destruction of disease and good fortune; of this there is no doubt. (78)
In the Gāyatrī portion, there is sovereignty; in the extensive [portion], it is sevenfold. When divided by nine and then by three, in the middle, there is an increase of six and six [units].
Above that, however, there should be a circular head-piece made of tin in the portion of Rudra;
having installed it in the northwest, one attains mastery over the quarter of Vāyu.
The Guru, the knower of mantras, should install the liṅga, joined with the top of a banner, upon a base marked by a banner; by means of that liṅga, he [effects] expulsion, agitation, and confusion.
One will undoubtedly cause severe emaciation and separation from one's enemies;
the previously mentioned Vāruṇa Liṅga is accompanied by the Yakṣa Liṅga, which has its head turned upward. 82.
Having installed [the linga] in the direction known as Yakṣa, one obtains lordship over the Yakṣas;
likewise, the preceptor, having installed a mace-headed linga in the Gadā-marked quarter, [attains the same].
It is considered to bestow Jāmbūnada gold, happiness, and exceedingly great strength;
as well as victory, fortitude, the attainment of sovereignty, and even lordship. (84)
There is no doubt that he attains the presence [of the deity] through mantras;
having made half the length like that of Rudra, one should fashion the lotus-born [deity] with six limbs.
One-tenth part is the Viṣṇu-lineage, increased by the Rāmas on the sides;
it is octagonal and circular, fierce, with three elevations in the middle of the sides. (86)
Having placed a liṅga with a cock's egg attached to its head upon the Īśāna pedestal,
one should ensure the liṅga is aligned with its own directions and possesses a trident at its head.
By performing the rite known as Śūlā, one shall attain the status of a lord of the earth;
it bestows the state of a master of yoga for the sake of knowledge, realization, and liberation. (88)

Likewise, that which bestows auspiciousness and happiness, as well as the attainment of imperial sovereignty, [is formed] when the height is divided by nine; it is a four-cornered [shape] with a fifth part [of the side]. || 89 ||
Having installed a linga with a square base, its form as before, and topped with a parasol,
in the northeast (Īśāna) direction, one shall attain the status of the lord of one's own quarter.
That very lotus on the head of Abja becomes established upon the body marked with a lotus;
it attains the state of a sky-farer (khacarī) and is the means for achieving the fruit of universal sovereignty.
In the portion of the *gāyatrī* (twenty-four degrees), when the sign is its exaltation, a square is formed by five degrees;
as before, in the middle circle, the head is like a gourd.
Having established it upon a Garuḍa-pīṭha, there shall be mastery over that direction;
the preceptor, moreover, should be joined with the head of the discus on a site marked by a discus.
Having pierced through, one shall attain the power of Pātāla and the elixir of immortality (rasāyana).
In the ninth part of the length of the liṅga, the portion of Brahmā consists of three parts.
Likewise, Viṣṇu and Hara are also present there in their full extent;
this is the most excellent Siddhiliṅga, with a pedestal fashioned from the *vicchāyā* stone.

In the case of divine lingas made of water and other elements, or those worshipped by the world-protectors (Lokapālas), a thousand-linga rite should be performed; that should be conducted as previously described.
This bestows all desires; it is the defining characteristic of Vāgīśī.
In the portion of the altar belonging to the Veda, when divided by the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), [it is] not [to be taken] in the ninth part.
One should fashion the one hundred and eight liṅgas using threads joined to the sense-objects;
the liṅgas beginning with Āḍhya should be made with equal segments according to their respective heights.
O twice-born ones, the heads [of the liṅgas] indeed resemble an umbrella, a cock, a crescent moon, or a gourd; likewise, there are the dhārā-liṅga and those with one, two, three, or more corners.
The accomplishment of goals, the birth of a son, the attainment of a city, the fulfillment of desires, death, eradication, the pacification of defects, nourishment, and subjugation. || 100 ||
Attraction, health, passion, emaciation, wealth, happiness, delusion, darkness, splendor, and destruction—these are the [powers] belonging to the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas of the Piśāca class. || 101 ||
The power of the Asuras and of men, as well as the state of Īśānabhairava;
the status of a god and the sovereignty of the king of gods, and whatever fruit of all desires there may be—102.

The state of Rudra and the fruits [attained] from these liṅgas, such as the one-edged (ekāśraka) and others, are likewise; indeed, the seats (pīṭhas) should also be conceived according to their various distinctions.
The characteristics of the lingas have been declared; now they are analyzed according to the channels (śiras).
When the eight parts are divided into four, there is an increase by one part for each division.
The varieties of fruits include the *puṇḍarīka* and others;
they bring about the splendor of the *puṇḍarīka* and so forth, and bestow vast fortune upon one who possesses broad [shoulders]. (105)
One obtains everything from the Śrīvatsa, victory from the Śatrumardana,
and by increasing its height by one-fourth, it becomes the Kukkuṭāṇḍa-śiras.
Since Prajāpati obtained offspring through that which increases progeny, one-third of that [revenue] should be used for the maintenance of the head [of the state] and other such purposes. 107.

The form of the cucumber (trapuṣa) bestows lordship over the seven worlds, as well as fortune, longevity, and the attainment of perfections; it is the cause of prosperity through the increase of one's sixth part [of the harvest]. 108.
Since the Sādhyas, the Ṛṣis, and the gods attained supreme prosperity by worshipping these [deities] according to the common ritual, so too do the best of men [attain it]. (109)

At the end of those [words], the indeclinable *pada* which has attained its own intended meaning is declared to be "visible from afar" (*viśīrṣa*) like an umbrella, as in the case of *vajra* and other such terms. (110)
The Śakti is fashioned in the arcāṃśa portion, the Veda portion, and the Vajra portion;
through this threefold division, it is fashioned in the arcāṃśa when divided by Rudra (eleven).

When divided according to the directions, three daṇḍas with a half-portion [of the total] constitute the sword-hilt (khaḍgamastaka); it is said that this occurs when increased by a half-portion in an eightfold division.
The top of the mace is one-quarter of the height of the banner-staff;
on the portion of the crocodile, the top of the trident is three units high, measuring one and a half parts.

In the Vasunandāṃśaka, following the division of the parts within the lotus of the wheel (cakrapaṅkaja), the characteristics of the head have been declared; now the extraction of those characteristics is being stated.
When the portion for the image (arcāṃśa) is divided into nine parts, one should mark the decorative marks (lakṣma) at the third part;
from the midpoint of the mark, two side-lines (pakṣarekhā) extend, and at their tips are the "elephant-eye" (gajacakṣus) features.
One should place the marks of the vajra and so forth upon the head for the sake of achieving the equilibrium of the directions:
the vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, and likewise the banner. (116)
O best of the twice-born, if one desires the station of the gods such as Brahmā and Viṣṇu, these ten weapons—the mace, trident, discus, and lotus—[should be worshipped]. (117)
Then, the pedestal is marked with those weapons; and because it bears the marks of those weapons, the area of the liṅga is divided into nine parts, with marks made upon each ninth part.
If [the weapon] is placed in the region of the enemy, it brings destruction to both oneself and him;
from piercing the eyes of the second [target], there arises eye disease and so forth, ending in death. (119)
From the third thread of the mouth, lameness and certain death result;
from the fourth thread of the neck, there is the destruction of enemies and bondage.
From piercing the fifth bhūta, there shall be defeat for the king;
likewise, from piercing the sixth part, it causes the destruction of sons and wife.
In the region of the heart, there arises a spear-like pain born of the heart; in the region of the belly, there is distress and pain in the abdomen;
but in the region of the navel, there shall be a total fear of enemies.
The results of the measurement lines for the image have indeed been described in sequence according to the ninth part;
nevertheless, here [they are stated] according to the third part, which consists of six parts.
One should gradually decrease or increase by a fourth part of a barleycorn for the sake of removing defects in the piercing; in this manner, one should fashion the characteristic marks.
In the Gāyatrī portion, when the linga is elevated, the width of the marks is one part;
the fashioning of the head is such that its characteristic crest (śikhā) comes into being.

Then, for the Aindra [weapon], there is the form of a thunderbolt (vajra), with a sharp point, a middle like a blade of kusha grass, known as a spear (śakti), joined with a crossbar (viṣkambha), and having a raised head. || 126 ||
In the southern [direction] is the form of the tip of Yama’s staff, honored by the tips of nooses and chisels;
in the north-western [direction], it has the tip of a tongue; and in the northern [direction], it has the edge of a mace.
The Śūlāśramīśvara Liṅga has its top shaped like a banner in the north-west;
among common types, it possesses its own characteristic form which accomplishes one's specific purpose.

Alternatively, O twice-born ones, one should fashion the weapons such as the vajra in the middle of the *lakṣma*; however, in rites such as *staṃbhana* (paralysis), that which is honored by the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) should be performed.
In the case of an image, the construction of the altar should take place in the ninth or seventh part;
however, one must not use gems, pearls, or corals that possess impure radiance.
The same applies to the *bāṇaliṅga* made of iron, which is characterized by its own brilliance; even if it lacks the [standard] marks, it is defined by its width, height, and circumference. (131)
O best of Brahmins, if the *liṅga* possesses auspicious marks, it grants the accomplishment of all goals; I shall now describe the characteristics of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and the base (*piṇḍikā*).
The pedestal (pīṭha) should be equal in length to the liṅga, joined with an elevation representing a portion of Viṣṇu;
[the directions] are then Aindra, Āgneya, Yāmya, Rākṣasa, and Vāruṇa.
The Vāyavya, Yākṣa, Aiśānya, Brāhma, and Gāruḍa types are declared to be the measures of the pedestal (pīṭha); the piṇḍikās are considered to be three-quarters [of that measure]. || 134 ||
These shall have the names beginning with Aindrī; thereafter, I shall describe the forms of the seats (pīṭhas):
the four-cornered, the womb-shaped, the half-moon, the triangle, the circle, and the hexagon.
One should construct the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) according to its characteristics as either eight-cornered or circular;
however, in the case of a four-cornered pit, one should proceed by omitting a portion from each side out of eighteen parts.
I shall describe to you the auspicious Gāruḍa pedestal, which has a double projection on all sides and a width equal to half the area of the field, serving as their ornament. || 137 ||
The *aindra* [mandala] is exclusively a four-sided figure, devoid of feet, necks, and so forth;
if there is a *yoni*, it should be placed one by one in sequence within the portion of the *rasa*.
The *pājjagatī* is the pericarp; from the emergence at the neck, there are two bands (*paṭṭikā*).
This is declared to be the *āgneyaka* pedestal (*pīṭha*), while the *piṇḍikā* consists of sixteen parts.
In its height, which is divided into nine parts, the *pājjatī* consists of one part, the *karṇikā* of three parts, and the neck (*kaṇṭha*) of four parts; above that are two fillets (*paṭṭikā*).
Thus the southern [direction] has been fully described; above that is the southern pedestal (piṇḍikā).
In the southwestern (rākṣasa) direction, it is described as being divided into one, two, and three parts respectively.
In the Rākṣasa [style], there is a *pājjagatī*, a *karṇikā*, a neck, and two bands (*paṭṭikā*);
above that is the *rākṣasī* pedestal (*piṇḍī*) in the Vāruṇa [style] divided by Rudra [eleven].

With three [units] having the form of a pair of moons, there is the jagatī and the balance-beam (dhaṭa); the pericarp and the neck should likewise be formed, with two fillets (paṭṭikā) extending from the projection.
Above that is the Vāruṇī Piṇḍī in the north-western direction, Viśvabhājita;
it consists of the digits of the Moon corresponding to the forms of Indu-tejas, Aṅghri, Rūpa, Akṣi, and Rūpayugma. (144)
The *pājjagatī* consists of a pitcher (*kuṃbha*), a lotus-bud (*vetrāsya*), and a neck (*kaṇṭha*), each measuring one unit in width;
the *paṭṭikā* protrudes from it, and above that, the *vāyavī* is prescribed.
Including the Āpya ornament, there are sixteen petals on the ankle and twelve on the calf, respectively; from the throat upwards, they are in reverse order.
One should lead the pedestal (piṇḍikā) above that, provided with eight petals;
having made it the portion of Rudra in the northeast, by means of the numbers one, three, and three.
The neck and the pericarp (karṇikā) should be made of moonstone fragments;
above that, the pedestal (piṇḍikā) should likewise be made of either Brahma-stone or Garuḍa-stone.
Or, according to the forms of its configuration and arrangement, it is considered to be Rākṣasa;
above that are two planks (paṭṭikā), and above that is the pedestal (piṇḍī) of Īśa.
In the fifth part, the form [is made] with one eye and one quality; the base, the pitcher, and the pericarp are formed with one part each;
the neck with one part, and then the fillet with two parts, due to its projection.
Above that, O twice-born ones, I shall describe the characteristics of the Vaiṣṇavī pedestal (piṇḍikā).
The Āgneyī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Aindrī pedestals each have two girdles (mekhalā).
The southern [girdle] belongs to the Rākṣasīs, the northern to the Yakṣīs; the Brāhmī girdle has three bands, the Vāyavyā has six bands, and the Vāruṇī has five bands. (152)
The portion belonging to Viṣṇu is sixteen units in height, equal to the width of the pedestal (pīṭha) of the lotus (puṇḍikā);
the remainder shall be the height of the pedestal, while the girdle (mekhalā) is outside the excavation.
The *vajra* should be the pedestal marked with a *vajra*, and the *vajrī* the pedestal-base marked with a *vajra*.
The pedestal for a thousand *liṅgas* is provided with ornaments and joined with two *yugas*.
In the case of a stone [liṅga], the *piṇḍī* should likewise be made of stone;
in the case of an earthen one, it should be earthen; in the case of one made of wood, the *piṇḍī* should be made of wood; and in the case of one made of metal, it should be produced from metal.
The best [liṅga] should be made of jewels, or it may be made of the finest metals;
the height of mobile liṅgas should be twice the portion allocated for worship. || 156 ||
The pedestal (piṇḍī) should be equal in length to the liṅga, and the liṅga should be positioned all around it;
one should increase the thickness of Rudra in the case of slender liṅgas and decrease it in the case of thick liṅgas.
O twice-born ones, one should indeed decrease or increase the portion of Acyuta, for there is no falling away from him;
one should decrease or increase it so as to be equal to the pedestal (piṇḍikā).
In the case of movable liṅgas, this should be done using materials made of gems;
the pedestal (piṇḍikā) should be beautiful, measuring the size of a mung bean or a finger-joint.
The height of the pedestal together with its elevation should be equal to the circumference of the liṅga;
for in its subtlety, it possesses a single quality by which it is most powerful and overcomes all defects.

The brilliance of all varieties of gems is the cause of their presence; whether their weight, measurement, and size should be taken into account by the wise or not [depends on the specific context]. || 161 ||

One should fashion [the image] from wood, gemstone, clay, or metal, or else it may be made of fragrant substances and the like; however, realgar (manaḥśilā) is not used for the sake of accomplishment.

That linga which is beneficial for liberation, as well as the Bāṇa-linga which grants the accomplishment of all goals, or any other linga originating from a river or a spring, [is likewise auspicious]. || 163 ||
Just as the form of the *liṅga* becomes a bestower of boons when established with mantras, so too,
in the fierce [deities], it is divided into two by the "lump" (*piṇḍī*) located below the hand.
In fierce rites, the portion of barley should be greater than the pedestal;
that which has a smaller measure than the pedestal leads to the destruction of enemies, while that which is larger than it increases them.

In rites such as eradication (uccāṭana), one should employ a woman with missing limbs; for the provocation of disease, one who lacks auspicious marks; and for the destruction of women, one who is deficient in characteristics—each to be fashioned according to the specific rite.
The Unmanifest has thus been described; now the Manifest-Unmanifest is being explained.
It should be made with equal proportions, consisting of four, eight, and circular parts.
One should fashion one, two, three, or four faces on the previously mentioned front face,
and five faces in the four directions and in the center.
One should perform [the rite] with one, three, or four faces according to the previously stated rule;
having arranged two faces as before in the east, one should then arrange them in the west.
And above the four faces, one should fashion a fifth;
on each face there is a mass of matted hair, with the crescent moon serving as its crest-ornament.
O best of the twice-born, for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation, [the deity] has three eyes in each face and two pairs of arms and shoulders, arranged as is beautiful.
Having divided the auspicious pedestal into two parts, one should employ iron that is very firm;
this is known as the manifest-unmanifest (vyaktāvyakta), and now the manifest symbol (vyaktaliṅga) is described.
Seated in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana), resembling pure crystal, having five faces and ten arms, with three eyes in each face. || 173 ||
Facing the mouth, with a mass of matted hair and the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, he is joined by five bodies and endowed with two final [limbs]. (174)
One should fashion its eastern face, O fair-browed one, with beautiful cheeks and a smiling lower lip,
resembling Jāmbūnada gold, and provide it with two arms.
In his right hand he holds a rosary, and in his left a citron;
his right [face] is like collyrium, terrifying, and with its mouth wide open. 176.
His matted locks were bound with a serpent, he was adorned with a garland of skulls, his high-pointed beard was thick, and he held a trident and a staff in his two hands. (177)
The northern face is on the left, with the luster of a pomegranate flower;
it is adorned with many ornaments and possesses a complexion like that of a young woman.
The western [face] is rich with hands arisen from the right, has the luster of silver, is endowed with the appearance of a youth, and possesses eyes resembling lotuses. (179)

The fifth [face] is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, appearing as if absorbed in meditation; it resembles crystal, is profoundly peaceful, and possesses a smiling countenance.
The face of Īśāna shall be upward-facing, with hands adorned with bracelets;
thus endowed with such a face, the face is to be colored and anointed.
Clad in garments of the Kali age, adorned with divine ornaments, bestowing all desires, peaceful, and endowed with the thirty-two marks of perfection. || 182 ||
One should fashion the body and the instruments of Īśāna, provided with doors, in accordance with the ritual procedure for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (183)
One should fashion the proportions, colors, divine weapons, gates, and so forth; one should construct the body of Īśāna according to the excellent measurement of ten tālas.
The preceptor should fashion the bodies of the deities, beginning with the Puruṣa, measuring half the height of the Lord's body; he should make the upper parts of the bodies, not the lower parts.
One should fashion the god Sadāśiva, endowed with the five bodies possessing the previously mentioned characteristics and measurements, in a manner that is appropriate and auspicious.
Or one should meditate upon Sadāśiva in this form, whose nature is knowledge;
one should visualize him with an upward-facing gentle countenance, ten arms, and three eyes.
He is endowed with a crown of matted locks, with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament;
he has a serpent for a sacred thread and is clothed in a tiger skin.
The god who is dancing with a beautiful smile, the bestower of all desired things, is thus known as Śrīkaṇṭha; he is also called by other names. (189)
Three-eyed and endowed with sixteen arms and two feet,
he is joined with a crown of matted locks and bears a dhattūra flower upon his head.
Adorned with garments of various colors and decorated with braided hair and other ornaments,
he stands upon his right foot and is equipped with divine weapons.
He is endowed with a slightly broken face and a left foot,
and he holds a bull, a banner, a shield, a severed head, fire, and a jharjharī drum.
A peacock feather and an elephant trunk are held in the left [hands]; thus they are remembered as having eight arms.
Also [held are] a trident, a snake-hand, an axe, and a noose. (193)
He holds a mace and a lamp, with a hand-drum and the gesture of fearlessness;
he is adorned with serpent ornaments and embellished by two earrings. (194)
Endowed with all auspicious marks and wearing anklets upon her feet,
Gaurī stands holding Skanda at her left side.
Thus he is described as dancing with his head upward, or otherwise; he may also be endowed with various weapons and possess twenty arms. (196)
Or else, with two new hands equipped with various kinds of weapons, the right [hand] should extend down to the left shank, while the left foot is raised up. (197)
Either the left hand is contracted or the right is extended;
the other [hand] should be in the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya-hasta), while the two others are endowed with the axe (ṭaṅka) and fire (anala). 198.
Having abandoned his axe or trident, or holding a ḍamaru drum in his other hand,
or having cast aside his fire like a deer, this Rudra is known as Kāla.
Three-eyed, four-armed, and fierce, holding a khaṭvāṅga staff and a skull-cup, and endowed with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness—this is Rudra, known as Vāma. (200)
This very one, when devoid of the khaṭvāṅga and joined with the trident (śūla), is named Aghora Rudra; he is Bhīma, the destroyer of worldly existence. || 201 ||
Three-eyed, four-armed, endowed with a face possessing ten thousand tusks, and pure;
yet another [form] joined with a crocodile and adorned with a crown of matted locks. (202)
Equipped with a bow and arrows, and provided with a deer and a chisel;
he has his left foot placed upon the head of a ghost, resting on its petal-like surface. || 203 ||
Alternatively, [one may worship] the two lotus-footprints upon the crests of devotees;
or [the Lord] joined with Gaurī on his left, having the crescent moon as his crest-ornament. (204)
This is Rudra, the Lord of Serpents, the bestower of the fruits of all desires;
he has three eyes and two arms, is peaceful, and is adorned with matted locks and a crescent moon. (205)
On his left side, accompanied by Pārvatī, he is either seated or standing, personally intent upon bestowing boons. (206)
The Goddess may be situated upon his left thigh, or her form may be raised up on his left arm;
or else, O Lord, her right arm may rest upon his shoulder.
On the slope of that mountain, this god who grants all desires resides;
Gaurī and Gaurīśvara are present there, endowed with four arms. (208)
Equipped with a skull and a trident, and endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; they may have three eyes or two eyes, and possess dangling feet. || 209 ||
The two Bhairavas at the feet of the one who has three eyes are of a prostrate luster;
or there may be four-faced, five-faced, or [many] Bhairavas. (210)
Or they may be devoid even of the Bhairavas, or seated upon a lotus,
joined with Kālāntaka and the others, or situated above the devotees.
This one is celebrated as Rudra, the trident-bearer who grants all perfections;
he is the glorious one, whose beloved is united with half his body, and whose vehicle is the bull.
With two hands or four hands, joined in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
or else, joined with a deer and an axe, he has beautiful eyes upon his forehead.
Or if he were Vilocana, or Umā’s body situated on his right side, or Ardhanārīśvara by name, or half of Hari joined with Hari; (214)

He has four arms, four faces, and three eyes; he bears the crescent moon upon his crest, and is either equipped with a trident and a lotus, or endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Equipped with a skull-topped staff and a trident, and seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana),
he is known as Nīlarudra by name, [also called] Vyāgrogra’ṣṭika.
Four-armed and three-eyed, endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and holding a peacock feather and a chowrie, he is proclaimed as Bhīmarudra. || 217 ||
With deer-like eyes, he may be accompanied by a rosary, or holding a fruit and the gesture of fearlessness;
or with hands granting boons and fearlessness, he possesses a peaceful form and a smiling face. || 218 ||
Adorned with a crown of matted locks and endowed with the standing posture and other attributes, this Rudra is the Lord of All (Sarvaśarva), the bestower of desired fruits. || 219 ||
Śarva-Rudra, the three-eyed one, is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
he holds a skull and a trident and stands in the bound lotus posture (baddha-padmāsana). || 220 ||
He is endowed with the deer-impelling trident (mṛgaṃśūla) and possesses four arms;
he may also hold a noose and a severed head, or alternatively, hold a ṭaṅka-axe and a noose.
Bestowing boons, he stands upon a lotus seat;
he is known as Bhavarudra, the destroyer of the cycle of existence for all. || 222 ||
The eleven Rudras are remembered as holding skull-bowls and tridents in their hands;
they are endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, possess prominent fangs, and have fierce gazes.

Alternatively, they may be white in form, standing upon bulls or seated upon lotuses, and endowed with the boon-granting and fear-dispelling gestures, like the gods [of the directions] at Mṛgaṭaṅkā. || 224 ||
The Rudras, beginning with Kapālīśa, possess the forms of their respective directional guardians;
they are fierce, equipped with various weapons, and are the protectors of those respective directional guardians.
Or else, they are endowed with their respective guardians of the quarters, or possess the forms described by Rudra;
for what is the use of saying much more here—whatever gods there are, they possess the form of Rudra.
Those Rudras who are endowed with a peaceful disposition are there declared to be Maheśvaras;
thus their characteristic has been described, and now their installation is being told.
This name and so forth, joined with the phoneme together with the bindu and nāda,
conjoined with the [letter] at the end of the thirteenth, and linked with the designation ending in the dative case (caturthyanta).
One should extract the root mantra according to the sequence of the limbs beginning with Brahmā;
for the Rudras and the forms of Rudra, the mantra is that of Īśvara, which brings peace. (229)
Alternatively, the time for the sowing of seeds, the placement of jewels, and the opening of the eyes are also proclaimed here according to the procedure previously stated by them. (230)
Purification, circumambulation, the preliminary consecration with water, and the construction of the pavilion;
therein, the arrangement of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) numbering nine, five, or one. || 231 ||
O Brahmin, [one should perform] the carving of the seat, the meal, the rite for the site (vāstu), and the fire-oblation (homa);
then the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), the vāstu-homa, and immediately thereafter the purification of the image (beraśuddhi). || 232 ||

The auspicious rite, the preparation of the sacrificial ground, as well as the placement of her bed, the worship of the jars and other vessels, and the offering of food oblations and the like. || 233 ||
The placement of the forms of the Tattvas and so forth, accompanied by their respective lords,
as well as the fire-oblation (homa) performed with leaves of the Palāśa, Bilva, Vaṭa, Udumbara, and Pippala trees.
With *apāmārga*, *aśvattha*, and *khadira* wood, starting from the eastern direction;
but for the principal [oblation], with *palāśa* wood, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and sesame seeds.
Then, on the second day, the full offering of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) according to rule, the ceremonial bathing, and an abundant meal [are performed].

If the installation of a *liṅga* is to be performed, the festival for the worthy deities should be conducted as described in the general procedure for installation; indeed, every ritual act must be performed. (237)
O Brahmins, every rite for the Mukhaliṅga must also be performed according to the method taught in that chapter; the specific details therein are now being told.

Having placed either a single atom or even a minute particle of that which is desired by men into the ritual emblem (liṅga), one should begin the rite according to one's own chosen lunar mansion (nakṣatra). || 239 ||

"Having ever relied upon a *liṅga* such as that of Svāyaṃbhuva, rites such as *abhicāra* (malevolent magic) should not be performed; if they were, it would happen to oneself. Thus ends the rite for the installation of a *kāmya-liṅga* in the great tantra, the *Uttarakāmikāgama*.
The thirty-seventh chapter.
In one part of the length of the *liṅga*,
the width should be one-fourth; one should divide all *siddhi-liṅgas* equally into three sections, [shaping them] as square, octagonal, and bearing a head like a tuft of grass (*kūrca*).

One should place a half-moon joined with a head upon the seat of Indra (the eastern throne) for the sake of achieving one's desired goals in the eastern direction; having joined it with a vajra-body, the linga is proclaimed as being like a vajra-head for purposes such as immobilization (stambhana) and so forth.

Above the *liṅga*, in the portion belonging to Rudra, one should fashion a square with five parts; an octagon as before within the circle, and an equilateral figure toward its own direction, except for the southeast.
That *liṅga* is placed on the Āgneya pedestal to ensure mastery over the southeastern quarter.
O twice-born ones, having installed the Liṅga together with Śakti and the head upon the pedestal which is a limb of Śakti,
it is peaceful yet fierce; its splendor brings about the destruction of enemies and the like,
and it causes heat and burning for the foe— such is the fiery Liṅga.
In the ninth part, with five [units] one should mark the two sides, front and back; with three [units], the two principal arms; and the southern circle is the junction of fire.
One should place it on the southern pedestal in due order for the sake of attaining the goal of one's own mother in the southern direction.
One should install the Linga, joined with the head of the staff (daṇḍaśiras), according to the prescribed rite.

The Guru-daṇḍa is situated in the southern direction; it brings about an increase in lifespan and manliness. When situated in the region of the enemy, it causes destruction from the city in the south.
It brings about pestilence, dissension, and disease; of this there is no doubt.
O twice-born ones, when the length is divided into twenty-two parts, one should fashion a square with five parts, an octagon as before, a circle, and a decagon.
One should place [the deity] upon a Rākṣasa seat for the sake of accomplishing the practice of one's own direction;
moreover, one should place the head of a sword upon the pedestal,
which effects the destruction of enmity, hatred, and delusion through the piercing of the stake.
It causes the destruction of that army, madness, and the outbreak of the Mārī demon;
there is no doubt about this when it is combined with mantras according to the rules.
In the *utsedha* portion, which consists of one human part, the *brahma-bhāga* is four-cornered.
Having established a square, an octagon, a circle, or one topped with a crescent moon in the western direction, one shall attain the status of the lord of that quarter; likewise,
one equipped with a noose at its top is for the deity Pāśaka according to the ritual injunctions.
Having established [the deity], one shall attain supreme peace, prosperity, increase of fortune, excellence, the destruction of disease, and good luck; of this there is no doubt.
[One should install] the previously mentioned Vāruṇa Liṅga and the Yākṣa Liṅga, which is endowed with an upward-facing head.
Having installed [the Linga] in the direction known as Yakṣa, one obtains mastery over the Yakṣas;
the preceptor should install a mace-headed Linga on the body of the mace,
which is considered to bestow the attainment of Jāmbūnada gold and happiness, as well as great strength.
One obtains victory, fortitude, as well as the acquisition of a kingdom and sovereignty;
there is no doubt in this matter when [the deity] has become present through mantras.
In the elevation of the planetary portion, however, it is four-cornered and five-part.
Having established a circular linga, adorned with a parasol on its top and clothed in garments as before,
upon the Brāhmī [mudrā], one shall attain lordship over the directions beginning with the east;
its length should be one part of the Gāyatrī and its width seven parts.

When nine parts are divided by three in the middle for the increase of the six flavors, above that there should be a circle; in the portion of Rudra (eleven parts), the head should be made of tin. Having established it in the northwest, one obtains mastery over the direction of Vāyu.

The Guru, the knower of mantras, should install the *liṅga*— equipped with a banner and a crest— upon a base marked by a banner. By means of that *liṅga*, he shall undoubtedly cause the enemy's eradication, agitation, confusion, intense exhaustion, and separation from his remaining kin.
Having made half the length as in the Raudra [temple], one should fashion the Padmasambhava [temple] with six parts (rasa) for its limbs;
the Viṣṇu portion is an eleventh part, increased by three parts on the sides. The Raudra [temple] is octagonal and circular, with three elevations in the middle of the sides.
Having established a linga with a cock's head upon the Āiśa-pīṭha,
one attains mastery over food; and having established a linga with a trident-head upon the pīṭha called Śūla, one attains the status of a lord of the earth.
Knowledge and discernment lead to liberation, bestow the state of a lord of yogis,
grant auspiciousness and happiness, and likewise bestow the perfection of sovereignty;
that very lotus on the head of the Lotus-Born One is established upon her whose body is marked by a lotus.
One attains the state of Khecarī, which is the means for achieving the fruit of universal sovereignty.
In the Gāyatrī portion, however, when the Liṅga is prominent, a square is formed with five parts (pañcāṃśa);
as before, in the middle circle, the head is shaped like a trapuṣa fruit.
Having established [the deity] upon a Garuḍa pedestal, there will be the fruit of mastery over that direction;
the preceptor, moreover, should have the wheel joined at the head and marked with the wheel-sign.
Three-eyed and four-armed, fierce, bearing a khaḍvāṅga and a skull-cup, and endowed with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness— this is Rudra, known as Vāma.
This very one, when devoid of the khaṭvāṅga and joined with the trident, is named Aghora-rudra; he is formidable and the destroyer of fear.
Śarvarudra, however, has three eyes and is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
he is equipped with a skull and a trident and stands in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana).
He is joined with the Mṛgaśūla weapon, endowed with four arms,
and may also hold a noose and a severed head, or alternatively, hold an axe and a noose.
Endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, standing upon a lotus seat,
he is known as Bhavarudra, the destroyer of existence for all.
Three-eyed, four-armed, endowed with a face possessing ten thousand fangs, and pure; yet another form joined with a crocodile, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
equipped with a bow and arrows, and provided with a deer's horn.
With the sole of his left foot placed upon the head of Bhūta,
joined on his left by Gaurī, and adorned with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament—
this Rudra, the Lord of Serpents, bestows the fruit of all desires.
Thus the Unmanifest has been explained; now the Manifest-Unmanifest is described.
In the case of the Equal-Liṅga, it should be made square, octagonal, and circular.
One should fashion one, two, three, or four faces as previously described,
and a fifth face in the center, facing the four directions.
Above the four faces, one should fashion a fifth;
on each face there is a mass of matted hair with a topknot, adorned with the crescent moon as its crest-ornament.
Each face has three eyes, and [the deity possesses] arms, shoulders, and so forth.
In the thirty-eighth chapter, the procedure for the *ārṣa-liṅga-prāsāda* is taught;
indeed, the procedure for the temples of the *ārṣa-liṅgas* is now declared.
It was established by all the Ṛṣis, the seers, beginning with Kauśika. || 1 ||
Whether thick at the base, thick in the middle, or thin, whether it has a triangular, circular, or fruit-like shape, it should be devoid of any central core-line (mānasūtra). || 2 ||
That which was described as "other than human" is the *ārṣa* [style]; now it is being stated:
the pedestal (*pīṭha*) should be twice the size of the portion for worship, and the inner sanctum (*garbhageha*) should be three times that.
The measurement of the wall should be half of that, or equal to it, or even one-third;
and that [height] should be twice the width, or perhaps two-thirds more.
The pedestal (pīṭha) is said to be three times the measurement of the width of the liṅga, plus either half of it or even one-seventh more.
Then, its inner sanctum (garbhageha) shall be provided with walls occupying two-thirds [of the space]; its height shall rise as previously described, or it is also stated otherwise.
The width of the *liṅga* is [calculated] from the ear-line; it is joined with half of the double distance to the end.
The width of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is increased by one and a half or two and a half times its own measurement.
The width of the pedestal is said to be up to one and a half times [the height];
or it may be twice, thrice, or even four times that.

The hall for the lute (nālīgṛha) should be spacious; it may consist of two parts, or three-quarters [of the total width], while the thickness of the wall should be one and a half parts, two parts, or equal to one part.
The *udaya* (height) shall be as previously stated, and it is described otherwise [in another way]:
the width of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is said to be equal to the circumference of the *liṅga*. (10)
The inner sanctum (garbhageha) should be threefold, or three parts out of five, or one part out of two; having determined this, one should begin the construction of the wall's width.
The width of the ear-base (karṇapīṭha) shall be two parts of the pūjāṃśa;
the tube-house (nālīgeha) shall be four times that, and its height shall be six parts of it.
The width of one part is described otherwise;
the width of the ear-base (karṇapīṭha) is twice the width of the liṅga.
The *nālī* house should be three parts [in length], while its width is three, four, or five parts;
one part is its [inner] breadth, though it is stated otherwise as well. (14)
In the portion of the circumference that is the modification, there are fourteen karṇakas;
the piṇḍikā is broad, and the nālī is said to be four times that.
The width of the wall shall be one-third of that [measurement], or one-eighth;
the corner (karṇa) shall be double the width, diminished by one-tenth of its own measure.
