The pedestal (pīṭha) is the Tāra [unit], and from that, the fivefold [measurement] constitutes the tube-house (nālīgṛha).
One should begin the half-thickness of the wall with one part out of seven of those five. || 17 ||
In the inferior and intermediate [types], there are eight parts in the pedestal and likewise in the tube-house;
these are highly esteemed, so let that which is desired be taken by the excellent [disciples]. (18)
This has been declared in the Svāyambhuva Liṅga; let that also be accepted.
Thus it has been explained for the single-storeyed [temples], as well as for the two-storeyed and other types of abodes.
Whether it be with a foundation or without a foundation, the portico and the wall itself—
having established the temple according to the previously stated rule— one should lead it up to two stories from the asterism.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Temple of the Ārṣa-liṅga," in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
39. In the thirty-ninth chapter, the procedure for the temple of the *pauruṣaliṅga*. Now, the procedure for the temple of the *pauruṣaliṅga* is described:
the *pauruṣa* [liṅga] is that which has been installed by human beings endowed with devotion. || 1 ||
If that [liṅga] was previously installed in an unknown ancient temple,
one should construct a temple here according to the measurement of the liṅga.
The width of the pedestal (pīṭha) should be three times the measurement of the breadth of the liṅga;
it should be one-third of the height of the house, or according to a division into three or four parts.
The width of the wall has been specified; its height should be as previously stated.
From one and a half times the diagonal of the linga's diameter, it may be increased by half [the diameter]. || 4 ||
One should take the width of the pedestal to be one and a half times [the height] at most;
or it may be fourfold, fivefold, or even threefold that [height].
The hall for the lute (nālīgṛha) should be spacious according to the measurement of the width of the pedestal;
it may be equal to, double, or one and a half times the width of the pedestal.
The *udaya* (the height) should first be as prescribed by the deity, though it may also be stated otherwise;
the pedestal (*pīṭha*) should be twice the portion of the worship, while the *udaya* is measured by its width.
A tube four or five times [the width] is prescribed here for the house;
all that remains beyond that should be arranged as before. || 8 ||

From the *liṅga* comes the pedestal (*pīṭha*), from that the womb (*garbha*), and from the womb the determination of the wall (*bhitti*). [The dimensions range] from one to seven barley-corns (*yava*) starting from the measure (*mātra*), increasing by one at each step.
One should conceive of its increase and decrease up to three measures;
the pedestal (pīṭha) should indeed be within the womb (garbha), and it should be according to the width of the temple (prāsāda).
Half of that or three-quarters is declared to be the distance between the walls;
or one should take an eighth part of that interval, or even a quarter of it.
The sunrise is declared as before in the *Svāyambhuva* and other [Purāṇas];
likewise, that too is the measure for that village in the *Paurāṇa-pauruṣa*.
The base (adhiṣṭhāna) is proclaimed as having a fillet (paṭṭikā) member;
the plinth (upāna), the jagatī, the neck (kaṇṭha), and the fillets (paṭṭikā) are found in the kumuda and other parts. 13.

In this manner, one should determine the extent of the dry land within the ancient, divine abode of Puruṣa; in a human abode, it extends to the edge of the plinth, and the water-channel extends to the edge of the enclosure wall.

The width of the terrace (pīṭha) should be divided by the height of the mansion (harmya), and the resulting quotient should be even; likewise, if the outer portion is also made even, it is prescribed as such.
If it is a pair, it must be exactly a pair; a mixture among them is not desired.
A Liṅga made of three metals is prescribed, or one made of human bone (pauruṣa). || 16 ||
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, the procedure for the temple of the Pauruṣaliṅga, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.

40. In the fortieth chapter, the procedure for the temple (prāsāda) according to the [nature of the] liṅga. Now, the temple is specifically described according to the liṅga: "The self-manifested (svāyaṃ), the Bāṇaliṅga, the divine (daivīka), and the sages' (ārṣaka). (1)
A wise man should construct a temple for those [liṅgas] which were established by high-souled beings such as the Siddhas and Vidyādharas, using the remains of their liṅgas. || 2 ||
One should design the temple according to the measurements of these [elements], whether by their portions, their proportions, their width, or even their height,
as well as by the measurements of their corners.
One should take twice that amount, or even threefold, fourfold, or multiplied five- or sixfold; let the first [measurement] be doubled and so forth.
O you of excellent vows, there are eight divine measures or nine measures;
each subsequent one should be half of the preceding, and thus thirty-two are said [to exist].
O best of the twice-born, the measurement of each individual pedestal has thus been described;
the size of the pedestal may be double, triple, or quadruple [the measurement of the image].
The width of the womb-body may also be five or six times [the height];
one should calculate the intermediate measurements as before.
In a spacious inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), having divided the space from one part out of two parts up to six times the interval, [one should proceed] by means of one part.
The width [of the projections] should increase by one part up to twice the [original] measure; the measurement for the interval between the walls should be determined as before.
From the *liṅga* comes the pedestal (*pīṭha*), from that the womb-chamber (*garbha*), and from the womb-chamber the wall (*bhitti*)—this is the determination.
From one [unit] up to seven barley-corns, there is an increase of one *mātrā* at each step.
Thus it should be in the interior of the pedestal (pīṭha), and likewise in the extent of the temple (prāsāda);
for the sake of completing the measurement of fingers and cubits, one should carry out [the construction] up to seven measures (mātra).
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Temple according to the [Type of] Liṅga," in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
In the forty-first chapter: "The Procedure for the Temple and Liṅga for All Regions."
The proper installation of a universal *liṅga* and so forth is now correctly described;
this applies to the temple, or the *liṅga*, or the pedestal, or even the stone itself.
The procedure known as the universal (sārvadeśika) is approved everywhere;
one may perform it in a sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic region. || 2 ||
Especially in a royal region, it is the cause of victory for kings;
for the sake of accomplishing virtue, desire, and wealth, it is called the fulfiller of all desires.
All others always grant liberation to both the one who performs the rite and the one who causes it to be performed.
The Nāgara style is for the Kṛta Yuga, while the Draviḍa is prescribed for the Tretā Yuga.
In the Dvāpara age, the vesara coin was to be used for transactions throughout all regions; in the Kali age, however, the varāṭa and the sāliṅga are approved everywhere.
O lords of sages, the variety known as varāṭa— derived from Nāgara, Drāviḍa, Kāliṅga, and even Vesarā— is superior and suitable for all regions.
It is said that its fruit is universal; it excels [all others], such as the self-born (svāyaṃbhuvam), the arrow-like (bāṇam), the divine (daivikam), and likewise the sage-composed (ārṣakam).
Just as it has been declared by the best of Brahmins, O lords of sages, so too in the human realm, excellence of fruit is desired in the case of the linga and other such objects. || 8 ||
Therefore, those seeking the highest good should perform that which is known as "universal" (sārvadeśika);
for in that case, there is neither the fault of mixing tantras nor even the mixing of mantras.
Whether it be the confusion of teachers, or the confusion of countries, the fault of the confusion of time, or even the confusion of the ages; ||| 10 ||
Since there is no distinction made for others due to possible confusion,
the measurement of height and breadth is prescribed specifically for the temple of the Universal Lord.
Starting from three or four cubits and increasing by two cubits at a time,
the measurement up to fifty cubits shall be the standard for all regions.
Regarding the elevations for pacification (śāntika) and other rites at the primary sanctuaries and so forth of all regions:
in a division by two, there are seven types beginning with three parts and ending with seven, corresponding to the pacificatory and other rites.
The best of teachers should accept [the measurements] starting from one and a half cubits up to three times that;
it may be less or more than the measurement joined with one, two, or three cubits.
O twice-born ones, it is not desired that the entire [structure] be measured by the length first, according to the rule;
rather, it should be measured either by the width and the height, or by the width and the height [alternately]. 15.
One should examine [the site] by its width, length, or diameter;
and in this context, other matters such as the *āyā* and so forth are also mentioned briefly.
One should multiply the desired measure by nine, nine, and seven respectively;
having divided by eleven, one should declare the remainder as the *āya*.
One should multiply [the year] by eight, nine, ten, eleven, six, eight, and seven respectively;
having also subtracted [the sum], one should designate the remainder as the expenditure (vyaya). || 18 ||
O King, one should spend the day with the stars increased by the flavors (six) and the channels (sixty), starting from the day of the patron and ending on the day of the deity such as the Liṅga. 19.
One should multiply the obtained [number] by the asterism; birth and the others follow in due order:
Tuṣṭi, Sampat, Vipat, Kṣema, Pratyara, Sādhaka, and Vadha. (20)
Maitra and Paramamaitra belong to the first sequence;
in the second, Saṃpad and the others are proclaimed as before.
One should avoid the auspicious third birth-constellation, as well as the eighth house of death and the destructive [constellation], or else [perform it] in the third [year] or its opposite.
The remainder should be known as auspicious; having understood this, one should employ it.
One should avoid inauspicious conjunctions such as separation, as well as the Asura and Mānuṣa gaṇas. (23)

One who desires success (siddhi) should avoid it, but one who desires liberation may do as he wishes. That which is diminished by seven, six, five, four, three, two, and nine [units]— 24. One who desires success should avoid it, but one who desires liberation may act according to his desire.
That which has been diminished by seven, six, five, four, three, two, and nine; || 24 ||
The first portion [of the calculation] should be known as that of the thieves (taskara); their result occurs according to their names.
The Guru should increase it by the Rudras, the cavities (randhra), and the qualities (guṇa), and decrease it by the sources (yoni). || 25 ||
The eight sources beginning with Dhvaja, the seven sources beginning with Ṣaḍja, the five elements beginning with Earth, or the three fires beginning with Dakṣiṇa. || 26 ||
The [musical] banners and so forth are to be understood as being of four kinds, as considered previously;
namely, Ṣaḍja, Vṛṣabha, Gāndhāra, Pañcama, and likewise Madhyama. (27)
Niṣāda and Dhaivata—these seven are the sources; among them, Ṣaḍja and Vṛṣabha are praised. Among the elements, Earth and Water are in the middle. || 28 ||
Likewise, among the fires, the Gārhapatya and Āhavanīya are praised;
as are the five well-known fires beginning with Dakṣiṇa, starting from the Earth and so forth. || 29 ||
One should divide the increased [number] by eight and seven;
however, Sunday, Saturday, and Tuesday are censured, while in an auspicious conjunction they bestow good fortune. (30)
O Brahmins, one should fashion the primordial Māyā within the palace, the pavilion, the enclosure wall, the gate tower, as well as upon the Liṅga, the image, and other such objects.
However, one must not look at the *liṅga*, the *bera* (image), or the *tuṅga* (pedestal).
[The temple] should be three parts, four and three parts, five and three parts, or two parts [of the total height]. || 32 ||
One should determine the inner sanctum (garbhageha) as four parts out of six, or five parts out of seven, or alternatively, three parts out of four. || 33 ||
In an eight-part division, the inner sanctum (garbha) is desired to be three, four, five, or six parts;
in a nine-part division, the pillar-base (nālikā) is made of three, four, five, six, or seven parts.
Or one may construct a mixed wall in the even and odd bays;
it should be one-third of five parts, or two-fifths, or indeed three-fifths.
In a six-part [division], it should be four parts; or in a seven-part [division], exactly three parts;
or four parts in the middle, or five parts in a six-part [division]. (36)
When the width is divided into eight parts, one should arrange the *bhadra* in the middle with nine parts, five parts, or four parts. (37)
One should make it one-quarter, half, or three-quarters [of the width], while the projection (nirgama) should be two parts;
or, for the Bhadra, it may be situated on both sides like the form of Rudra and so forth.
Or, the best of teachers may likewise imagine it in this manner;
now the universal liṅgas are described according to the measurement of the womb (the inner sanctum).
When the Prasāda is measured at fifty [units], it is excellent with three [parts];
at nine parts, it is middling with five; and with half [of that], it is inferior. (40)
Furthermore, through its internal subdivisions, there are another six;
by measuring the intervals between each of these, the total measure is thirty-three.
When the interior has been divided into twenty parts, one-tenth would be inferior;
with eleven parts it would be middling, and with twelve parts it would be excellent. (42)
Alternatively, in the middle desired division, there may be nine [units] for the linga and so forth;
or, having divided the womb (garbha) into nine parts, the height of the linga may be nine [units].
The lowest [measure] is one-quarter of the womb, while the highest is three-quarters;
in the middle [measure], there are eight divisions according to their respective internal distinctions.
The measurements for the liṅgas have been declared as thirty-three;
alternatively, one-third of the interior of the temple shall be the minimum measurement.
Half of the *garbha* should be known as the middle [measurement], while five parts of three [the *garbha*] are considered the best.
Having made the middle [measurement] as before, it should be thirty-three units in measure. (46)
In the length of the *liṅga* and its modified portion, it is beneficial [to calculate] by means of the essences of the four elements;
beginning from one cubit and increasing by one finger-breadth at a time. (47)
The measurement for the height of the liṅga should extend up to nine cubits;
this is determined when the interior of the sanctum (garbhagṛha) has been divided into twenty-one parts.
A thirteenth part is excellent, while a tenth part would be inferior;
having made it thirty-three units in measure as before, it is considered middling.

In the length of the liṅga, the portions for the modifications are beneficial when measured by the essences of the four elements; the widths of the liṅga are proclaimed to be five parts (arrows) plus one-third. || 50 ||
When the height of the liṅga is one-fifth of the gāyatrī measure, the width is five parts;
or else, when the height of the liṅga is one-eighth or one-tenth of that measure, the width is five parts.
Alternatively, the width of the liṅga is proclaimed to be one-fourth [of the base];
its length, having been divided into twenty-one parts, is [measured] by portions of six, five, and four.

O eminent sages, the detailed dimensions of the liṅgas have been declared in the scripture; let the measurement [of the temple] be integrated with the liṅga, including the doors, pillars, and other features. (53)
Alternatively, one should divide those lingas into parts by means of finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
or else, for the sake of achieving auspiciousness in length and other dimensions, one should divide them according to fractional parts (aṃśas). || 54 ||
Beginning from the sixteenth part and adding twenty-four,
the Guru should divide that by one hundred and then add one part.
Or, by means of those [measures], the Guru should examine the liṅga, the image (bera), and so forth;
whether it is symmetrical, increasing, dominated by Śiva, or follows the three-part rule.
O twice-born ones, the Svastika, the Sahasrākhyam, and the Dhārāliṅga—this enumeration is set forth according to their number and in sequential order. || 57 ||
Having divided the height of the liṅga into three parts, one should make three sections in sequence;
this [liṅga] whose width is equal to those parts and which consists of even segments is called the Samakhaṇḍa.
O lords of sages, this [mantra] may be joined with the previously mentioned Tāra (Om), or it may consist of equal parts;
when the twenty-first part of a fortnight is remembered as a single portion within the Gāyatrī portion, it becomes Śiva-like.
In the portion of Brahmā, four, five, six, and seven parts are prescribed;
from each of those [subsequent portions], there is an increase of one part for Hari and Īśa respectively. (60)
There are four types of *vardhamāna* [pots] for the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes in successive order;
or else, the *vardhamāna* is prescribed in another manner.
In a single cubit, there is indeed one finger-breadth; in two or three cubits, it is three mātrās;
in four or five cubits, it is five; and in six or seven, it is seven.
The distance between the two liṅgas and the two apertures should be known as nine finger-breadths;
one should provide [the measurement] in the sequence of one, two, and three, when increased according to the seasons.
In the portions of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, however, there is also the rule for the elephant (hāstika);
[the measurements are] seven, seven, and eight parts, five, five, and six parts respectively.
The portion for fire (Agni) is four times four parts, and for fire again it is four times two parts;
thus, the Liṅga exceeds Śiva [in height] in the sequence beginning with Brahmā and the others. 65.
Having divided the height of the liṅga into nine parts, Brahmā and the other two [deities] occupy three parts each;
for Nāha and the others, starting with Rudra, they occupy six, seven, and eight parts respectively.
This threefold measurement of the linga is recommended for Śūdras;
according to the ninefold measurement of the linga, goats and other animals are assigned three and four [units] respectively.
The Svastika-liṅga has been described, and it is also explained otherwise:
in a length of thirty parts for Śiva, [it is formed] from nine directions and nine Rudra-parts.
Alternatively, for those [deities] beginning with Brahmā, their respective portions and so forth should be assigned in sequence;
when thirty-three [deities] are established in the liṅga, the svastika type is suitable for a Śūdra.

The [mantra] known as Sahasra and the one known as Dhārā should also be understood here according to what was previously stated; and the Mukhaliṅga is also to be contemplated here according to the previously mentioned rule. (70)
One should apply the head-ointment for these [deities] according to the previously mentioned procedure;
one should give a greater portion of the head-ointment to the Liṅgas. || 71 ||

Alternatively, one should fashion the characteristic [of the pedestal] as a whole or as three parts, with an additional portion for the molding, according to the procedure prescribed for the installation of a Śiva-liṅga.
The width of the pedestal should be equal to the width of the liṅga,
or its width may be three times the measurement of the liṅga’s diameter.
The width may be four or five times [the height], or even double;
or it may be twice, thrice, or four times the portion for worship.
The width of the pedestal (pīṭha) is prescribed as being equal to the respective measurement of the ear [of the image], or similar to its girth (nāha),
or twice the measure of its girth.
The measurements for the intervals between those sanctuaries (pīṭhas) have also been stated:
they should be one-third or one-fourth of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha). || 76 ||
O best of sages, the width of the pedestal (pīṭha) should be half that of the womb (garbha),
and its height should be equal to one part of Viṣṇu, or else it may be joined with half the height of the base (pāda).
Having divided the Brahma-portion into eight parts, one should increase the space by one part;
that [height] is five parts above the base, or its pinnacle may be higher than the height of the Viṣṇu-portion.
One should perform its ornamentation according to the very same method used for establishing the pedestal;
it should be twice or even thrice the measurement of the linga's width.
One should fashion the tortoise and the mountain with four and five qualities respectively; one should then divide the measurements of their respective intervals into nine parts.
One should fashion the Brahma-mountain (the pedestal) so that its height is equal to the length of the linga, or equal to its circumference, or similar to the width of the pedestal. || 81 ||
One should fashion the height of the Brahma-mountain as being equal to its width, or three-quarters, or half, or even one-quarter of that.

Likewise, having divided the middle portion into four, one should join it with the height of the stone; the measurement of the linga's width (viṣkaṃbha) should be equal to one part of the modification.
One should construct the Brahmaśailāvaṭa in front of the city, increasing by one part from the beginning and ending at four parts, both in height and in width.
One should arrange [the measurements] up to two finger-breadths by increasing them one by one;
there is a certain distinction in this matter regarding the length of the portion for worship. (85)
O twice-born ones, if the pedestal (pīṭhikā) is fashioned so as to be connected with the exit [of the base],
then no defect of shadow will occur between the Liṅga and the pedestal.

This ritual brings about the highest accomplishment for the country, the lord of the country, the one who performs [the rite], and likewise the one who causes it to be performed; this procedure applies to all lingas. (87)

In the same way, if the portion for the pedestal (pīṭha) is made half the size of the portion for the worship (pūjā), or if the pedestal is larger than the portion for the image (arcā), or even smaller on its sides, [the defect is as previously described]. || 88 ||
Or, a pedestal fashioned in this manner, or a pedestal-liṅga (pīṭhaliṅga), bestows liberation;
however, for the sake of supernatural powers (siddhi), that [latter] is censured, whereas both are equally granters of success if they are identical.

In the construction of a temple, the rites beginning with *śāntika* and those beginning with *ucchraya* have been declared; following that, the calculation by means of *rodha* is not described here from beginning to end.
Even in the collection of those [mantras], there would be no great fault if they were universal;
this is especially true for the Svayambhū, Daivika, Bāṇa, Gāṇa, and Mauna [mantras]. (91)

Their characteristics are not intended to be described in detail by way of width or height, nor according to the divisions of Brahmā and others, due to the distinctions in the characteristics of the head. (92)
And because its own form is characterized by the *brahmanandi* stones, it is joined with three parts, beginning with *brahma*, or with two, or with one. (93)
Whatever specific form it possesses, that indeed is its very nature; likewise, the temple, the pedestal, and whatever constitutes their interior dimensions and so forth [are determined by that]. 94.
It is desired that [the procedure] be universal, since they are universal;
when the decay and so forth of temples, pedestals, and the like have occurred. (95)
One should construct the pedestal and the temple according to the rite for restoration (*jīrṇoddhāra*).
When the application of stone has been abandoned, the application of stone is now described. (96)
If one reveals the portion situated below the visible part of the *liṅgas* such as Svāyambhuva and others by means of digging and so forth, it brings suffering to men, O thief. (97)
The visible portion should be known as consisting of the portions of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara;
one should examine the linga situated below that by means of its base alone.
If purification is performed out of ignorance, death certainly awaits the performer; there is no doubt.
Thus has the characteristic of liṅgas from all regions been described. 99.
The ritual procedure for consecration is that which is described according to the previously stated method.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, the procedure for the temple of the universal Liṅga, in the great Tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
42. In the forty-second chapter: The Ritual for the Installation of the Aṅgaliṅga.
I shall now explain, in brief, the installation of the Aṅgaliṅga.
The liṅga is said to be twofold: namely, the primary (pradhāna) and the subsidiary (aṅga).
That linga for which there exist pavilions, attendants, enclosures, gate-towers, and so forth,
is remembered as the primary one.
That which consists of fivefold enclosure within the middle [mandala], being devoid of its retinue, is renowned as an "auxiliary" (aṅga) when it does not conflict with the primary [mandala]. (3)
Established in an auspicious direction for the sake of enjoyment and liberation in all directions,
the western, northern, and eastern quarters are proclaimed to be the auspicious directions.
One should construct for them a celestial mansion (vimāna) and other structures, including the primary sanctum (mūladhāma) and the measurement hall;
there, one should install either a liṅga or an image, or both.
If the deities are proclaimed to be outside the three enclosures,
one should perform their retinues and so forth there, or according to the abbreviated method.
In that place, constant festivals and the like do not lead to contradiction;
one should have the temple, the linga, and so forth constructed according to the pure Śaiva path.
Neither by a Pāśupata, nor by one observing the Great Vows (Mahāvratin), nor by any Buddhist, Ārhataka, Kāpālika, Pāñcarātra, or others. (8)
It must not be performed by others who abide in different philosophical systems;
yet, if it is performed by those who have been granted [the authority] through negligence, it shall instantly accomplish that Śaiva [result].
The measurement of the *liṅga* of the body should range from one cubit to three cubits;
it must not be made larger than that, for if it is so made, it brings all misfortune.
One should never cause a temple to be built taller than fifteen cubits;
rather, one should construct it according to the measurement of the interior of one's own residence, or by means of finger-breadths.
The temple and the linga alone are intended to be universal;
the plowing and other rites for these may or may not be performed separately.
One should first perform the rites beginning with the laying of the foundation bricks;
having thus constructed the linga, the vimāna, and so forth, the wise man should consecrate it. (13)
Since it was ordained from the very beginning, it is therefore called *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration);
this includes rites such as the laying of the foundation stone (*mūrdheṣṭakā*) and so forth, as well as the restoration of what is dilapidated (*jīrṇoddhāra*) and the like.
Everything that has been enjoined should be performed according to the previously stated procedure,
even when the rites such as the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) for the root-mantra are being carried out.
At that time, O best of the twice-born, the Pavitrārohaṇa rite for the Aṅga, Liṅga, and other components may or may not be performed; it should be done separately, according to the scriptures.
In this way, the man who causes the installation of an image or a liṅga shall obtain long life, prosperity, fame, good fortune, health, enjoyments, and many offspring. (17)
Having attained his desire, at the end of the body he rejoices together with Śiva;
[this occurs] by increasing one by one, beginning from one and ending with the number of Rudras.
Or one hundred and eight, or half of that, or half of that again;
or one hundred, or half of that, or half of that again, or even more than a hundred is excellent. (19)
Thus, whoever causes this to be done is none other than I; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, the ritual for the consecration of the *aṅga-liṅga*, in the *Uttarakāmika-mahātantra*.
43. In the forty-third chapter, the procedure for the installation of Sadāśiva and the installation of his attendant deities shall be described, preceded by their defining characteristics.
One should construct him with materials such as stone and others previously mentioned, according to the specific rules.
He is seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), white in color, and possesses five faces;
he has a tawny luster, a crest of matted hair, and is adorned with ten mighty arms.

He carries in his sprout-like hands, positioned on the right side, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), serenity (*prasāda*), as well as power (*śakti*), a trident (*triśūlaka*), and a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*).
He holds a serpent, a rosary, a hand-drum, a blue lotus,
and a citron in his left hands, appearing most serene.
Or rather, it is endowed with internal meditation perfected through the chapter on worship, and its eyes are fashioned from the triad of powers: will, knowledge, and action.
Joined with the digit of the moon of knowledge and characterized by the shower of digits,
the Brahma-sūtra and so forth should be performed, as proclaimed by Sukheśa.
Thus, Sadāśiva is to be fashioned together with Manonmanī;
in this way the characteristics have been declared, and now the procedure for installation (pratiṣṭhā) is described.

The commencement on the appropriate day and so forth, as previously described, should be understood; then follows the offering of the sprouts, at the conclusion of which comes the placement of jewels and the opening of the eyes.

Then one should perform the purification of the city and other structures by circumambulating them clockwise; thereafter, one should bring the pavilion for the preliminary water-consecration (jalādhivāsana) as previously described.
In the pavilion, one should arrange the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) according to the number nine, eight, or one;
those pits may be circular or have sides corresponding to the cardinal directions.
Thereafter, he performed the ritual for the artisans' release, as well as the feeding of the twice-born,
the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), the fire-offering for the site (vāstuhoma), and the formal acquisition of the ground.
Upon the altar above the Vedyūrdhva, one should perform the preparation of the bed as before;
having performed the purification of the image, one should then bind the *kautuka* (protective thread).
One should lay the deity upon the bed with his head toward the east and his face turned upward;
one should place the Sadāśiva-pitcher in the region of the deity’s head.
One should worship Sadāśiva, endowed with all auspicious marks, in the *kumbha* (vessel);
having placed the *vardhanī* (overflowing vessel) to the north, one should worship Manonmanī within it.
Having placed eight jars all around, one should worship the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) within them;
then, having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the principles (tattvas), the forms (mūrtis), and so forth, one should carry out the fire-oblation (homa).

Having consecrated the sacrificial pit and the fire, and having offered fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, sesame seeds, barley, parched rice, and finally white mustard seeds along with milk; || 16 ||
The Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Vaṭa trees should be placed in the directions starting from the east;
and the Śamī, Aravinda, Māyūra, and Bilva trees should be in the south-eastern corner.
The Palāśa wood should be used for the principal [oblation], or it is considered acceptable everywhere;
having offered as before for each [deity], the preceptor, being pure, [proceeds] in the second [part].
Having raised the image and performed the sacrifice for the jars and the fire as before,
and having fully honored the preceptor and others, one should then cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given.
Then, when the auspicious moment has arrived, one should place the seed-syllable before the pitcher;
having taken the seed-syllable from the pitcher, one should install it in the heart along with its location.
Having taken the seed-syllable with the *vardhanī* vessel, one should place it upon its pedestal;
if that goddess is the Sahajā, one should place it in her heart.
Having taken seeds from others, one should place them around the pedestal;
and with the waters of those respective jars, one should perform the consecration in those respective locations.
One should begin the bathing, the abundant food offering, the worship, and the festival;
having performed the bathing of the Goddess, one should then have the auspicious rites conducted. (23)
Whatever has not been mentioned here should be performed as stated in the section on general installation;
one should carry out all rites, such as the daily worship and so forth, exactly as before.
Indeed, that man who performs the installation of Sadāśiva in this manner shall enjoy his desired pleasures in this very world and, at the end, go to supreme Śiva.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, the procedure for the installation of Sadāśiva, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
44. In the forty-fourth chapter, the procedure for the installation of the Goddess:
I shall describe the installation of the Goddess, preceded by her defining characteristics.
Having procured materials such as stone and so forth, one should then fashion the image from them.
The installation of Gaurī should be performed in a village or similar place, within a temple of Śiva, in the eight directions and the intermediate quarters, or in a desired and delightful location.
Its temple should be constructed with a width ranging from three cubits up to fifty-one cubits; its height and other dimensions, however, should be as previously described.
It should be shaped like a roof-ridge (valabhī) or joined with suitable [ornaments].
If it is desired to be in the shape of a roof-ridge, one should divide that [area] into four parts.
The length, however, increases by one part at a time; thus, with six parts, it becomes the womb (garbha).
One part is prescribed for the wall, or one may divide that thickness into three parts.
The inner sanctum (garbha) should be two parts, and the wall on all sides one part;
or, when the width is divided into four parts, the length may be six parts.
The *garbha* is known by eight syllables, or it is described otherwise;
when the *tāra* is divided fivefold, the length [of the *garbha*] is six [syllables].
Or with seven, or eight, or nine, or likewise ten.
In the sixth part, one should determine the length of the inner sanctum (garbha) and its wall by increasing from one part up to double the measure, as previously described.
Thus, when the width has been determined up to twenty parts,
one should determine the length to be double that respective measure.
On the second floor and so forth, one should construct verandas and walls in great numbers,
extending on all sides by one-quarter, one-half, or three-quarters [of the width].
One should then arrange it with two parts and a half, including one-third;
or, excluding the outer veranda, the entire area is desired as the solid mass.
One should visualize the group of six, beginning with the foundation, as before: in the form of a hall, in the form of an assembly hall, and likewise in the form of a palace. (13)
The number of stūpas on the head is eleven, beginning with one;
these are proclaimed as the different forms of the Goddess among the deities of the directions.
The deities of Śiva’s abode, Gaṇeśa, or even the six-faced one (Kārttikeya),
as well as lions or bulls, are proclaimed to be his vehicles.
Or the śūkas may be in the corner; otherwise, one should proceed as previously described. It is taught that [the temple] should face east, west, or south. (16)
Or rather, one should make it face north; that is the ground of all prosperity.
If it is constructed according to the measurement of the womb (garbha), its width is especially distinguished.
Alternatively, they may be measured according to the specifications stated for images;
the deities of the directions should be installed in their sanctum, possessing forms identical to those goddesses.
Or else, Rudra, Skanda, and Īśa [should be placed] at the ends of the twelve [fingers];
one should fashion a bull or a lion in the corners of the palace.
O Lord, for all the deities residing within the walls of the temple,
their consecration is proclaimed to be identical with the consecration of the temple itself.
In the playful incarnations of Rudra, no formal installation (pratiṣṭhā) is prescribed;
one should nevertheless fashion the enclosures, the surrounding structures, the pavilions, and so forth.
Or else, the Śaktis beginning with Vāmā are established in the retinue;
likewise Śrī, Durgā, Kṣmā, Śaśinī, Gāyatrī, and Uṣā.
Or, O best of sages, these may be established: Sandhyā, Sarasvatī, Prajñā, Medhā, Śruti, Smṛti, Svāhā, and Vaṣaṭ.
Dhṛti and Mati are proclaimed as goddesses in the order starting from the east;
alternatively, these seven are declared to be the Mothers accompanied by Jyeṣṭhā.
The goddesses are considered to be Dehalī, Peṣaṇī, Culkī, Khaṇḍanī, Ulūkhalī, Musalī, Mudgarī, and Vardhamānī. || 25 ||
They are considered desirable when having four or two hands, or alternatively, they are thought to have lotuses in their hands.
[The deities are] Vṛṣa, Gaṇādhipa, Skanda, Mahāśāstā, and Dhaneśvara. || 26 ||
One should install Vīra, Kṣetrapāla, and Bhāskara in the eastern direction; and one should likewise fashion Vighneśa in the south-west or the south-east.

Or one may visualize Indra and the other deities as those weapons in the eastern direction; and in the region of Īśa (the northeast), one should place the goddess Aśani, the bearer of the remains of offerings.
The best of teachers should visualize the previously mentioned retinue;
especially on the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha), all the apsarases are stationed. (29)
The height of the Goddess is said to be threefold, in accordance with the Śiva-liṅga;
or it may be equal to the sacrificial pedestal (pūjāśa), or twice or even thrice that size.
The height of the pedestal (ucchraya) may be four or five times the width, or it may be one and a half or two-thirds of that; or, within those proportions, the desired measurement may be nine parts.
Having divided the height of the worship image into one hundred and twenty-four parts,
[one should mark] the ends of the eyebrows, eyes, nose, mouth, and ears, as well as the ends of the arms, armpits, and breasts.
The measurement of the Goddess in the form known as Niṣkala is according to the measurement of the Liṅga; her measurement according to the measurement of the Pratimā has thus been properly described.
In the case of a domestic image, one should determine the measurement either by finger-breadths (mātrāṅgula) or by barley-corns (yava);
thereafter, this Goddess should be fashioned according to the stated proportions.
The goddess has four arms and three eyes, with one face that is exceedingly serene;
she is clothed in fine silk garments and adorned with a crown containing a casket.
She is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, holds a noose and a goad in her hands, possesses two arms or two eyes, and has her arms hanging down. || 36 ||
That goddess Kanakaprabhā is exceedingly peaceful, holding a lotus in her hand;
she may also hold a white lotus, or she may hold a trident and a noose.
Alternatively, she may have six arms with hands holding a conch and a discus as desired;
her face is terrifying with protruding fangs, she has five faces, and she is endowed with ten arms.
Or she may be terrified by weapons spoken by the gods, or intent on embracing the gods; or she may be seated upon the thighs of the gods, or joined in the standing or sitting postures.
With her left foot extended, or with her other foot hanging down, she is proclaimed as being either accompanied by the God or alone. (40)
She may be dark, white, or red, according to the desire of the practitioner;
she may possess a straight form or be endowed with two bends.
One should hang a thread from the tip of the nose down to the sole of the right foot;
the thread situated between the ankles is known as the Śiva-thread (śivasūtra).
From that sūtra, the middle of the breast situated on the left side is one finger-breadth (guṇāṅgula);
that sūtra reaching the middle of the navel is recorded as being one finger-breadth [below it]. || 43 ||
The distance between two sutras is called a *veda*;
O twice-born ones, the distance between the *jānu-sūtra* [knee-line] is declared to be one *guṇāṅgula*. (44)
The distance between the two thumbs is considered to be one and a half viśva-angulas;
the space between the two heels is recorded as being one-third of that measure.
O twice-born ones, the height of the tip of the girdle should be equal to that of the nipple;
the wrist should be one and a half Viśva (thirteen) finger-breadths from the navel.
The distance between the middle of the side and the middle of the upper arm is one mountain-digit (parvatāṅgula).
From the tip of the hanging hand, the top of the thigh is six digits away.
The middle [measurement] from the wrist to the knee is four finger-breadths;
the middle [measurement] between the side of the body and the middle of the upper arm is six finger-breadths. || 49 ||
This may be merely an illustration, for there is no fixed rule in the Sūtra;
in the independent [Tantra], two kinds of measurement for the Goddess are taught in the scripture. (50)
O best of the twice-born, the measurement of the Mūladevī has already been stated; the measurement for the deities who are members of the procession and so forth is the same as that of the Mūlabera.

The measurement has been declared according to the dimensions of the *liṅga* as well as according to the principal deity; the measurement for the limbs should be taken as equal to the knees or the thighs.
In this manner, the Goddess is to be fashioned; her designation is considered to be twofold:
as Manonmanī and as Gaurī. However, there is no difference in the characteristics of these two. (53)
O best of Brahmins, wherever the form of Sādāśiva is conceived, there let it be conceived; at that time, it receives the name Manonmanī.
She assumes the names Gaurī and others according to the various differences in her dancing forms and so forth;
having fashioned the Goddess with all her characteristic marks, one should then consecrate her with mantras.
The Great Māyā (M) with the internal letter Ra (R), endowed with the Bindu and Nāda;
this is the mantra of Manonmanī, wherein the pair ending in Kha (Kha-Kha) is placed in the position of Ha (Ha).
This is declared to be the Gaurī-mantra; or it is considered to be "sa-vi-ra-gau. Alternatively, the mantra is joined with the great Māyā (Hrīṃ) and the two portions of Viṣṇu (Klīṃ). || 57 ||
The third letter of the eighth group, joined with the fourth vowel,
and marked with the bindu and nāda, ending in the crest (śikhā)— this indeed is the seed-syllable (bīja) of the Goddess.

The syllable *aiṃ* joined with *klīṃ*, followed by *sauḥ* conjoined with the *bindu* and *nāda*, and then combined with *haṃsa*, constitutes this mantra; or it may become a mantra consisting of the *śrībīja*. (59)
Thus, the fourfold mantra of the Goddess is known as the eternal;
thus the root-mantra is proclaimed, and within it is the arrangement of the Brahma-aṅgas.
The two heart-cavities are rooted in the [two] birth-syllables; these are known as the Mūrti-vidyā-mantras.
Alternatively, the Ādi-śakti-mantra is also known as the Mūla-mantra. (61)
Thus the mantra has been prescribed; next, the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is described.
The time should be taken as before, as well as the offering of the ritual sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa).
Having first established [the image] facing east upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) within the pavilion, one should place it;
on that central pedestal, a golden [image], and to the east, a sapphire (indranīla).
Vaiḍūrya, coral, pearl, and likewise diamond;
topaz, gomedaka, and similarly emerald, O twice-born ones. (64)
With the heart-mantra and the mantras beginning with *vāmā*, a golden [image] is prescribed for all cases;
however, one should perform the opening of the eyes by applying golden nails.

The libation with offerings beginning with honey, the veiling of the face with a cloth, the beholding of cows and Brahmins, and likewise the honoring of grains and mortals, are performed as before. (66)
One should perform worship of the preceptor and the artisans, purify the image with clay and other materials,
circumambulate the village, and then perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) in the water.
One should place water-pots all around him, presided over by [the goddesses] beginning with Vāmā;
furthermore, there are pavilions in the four directions of the Prasāda, as well as in the southeast and northeast.

One should properly construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) numbering five or one according to the count of Ṛks for the womb-shaped (yoni) altar; and to its north, one should likewise duly prepare a bathing platform as before.
The expulsion of Takṣaka, the feeding of Brahmins, the smearing with cow-dung, the sprinkling of auspicious water, and the worship of the deities of the site (Vāstudevatās). || 70 ||
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and altar (vedi) as before, and lead the Goddess to her bed as previously described.
Having brought that Goddess from the water, one should perform her ritual bathing (snapana) as before.

Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should bind the protective thread (kautuka) with the heart-mantra; then one should lay the Goddess upon the bed with her head toward the east.
Having wrapped it with a red cloth, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
then, one should place the principal jar upon the region of the goddess’s head.
Having meditated upon that [deity] whose form is described by its characteristics, one should worship it with incense and other offerings;
then, having placed eight jars around [the deity], they should be presided over by Vāmā and the other [Śaktis].
All the esteemed jars, filled with garments, gold, and other such items, [should be placed] up to the knees, the neck, and the head, [representing] the Self, Knowledge, and Śiva respectively. 75.
The Guru should place Māyā, which pervades up to the limit of Sadāśiva-śakti;
she is considered the sovereign of the three principles (tattvas): Action, Knowledge, and Will. (76)
One should then install the forms: Dhārikā, Dīptimatī, Ugrā, Jyotsnā, Cetā, Balotkaṭā, Dhātrī, Vibhvatī, Mūrtīśvarī, and Yuktā. (77)

In the ritual placement (nyāsa) consisting of the five forms (pañcamūrti), Vāmā and the others are considered the guardians of the forms; one should subsequently worship them in sequence with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, ending with food offerings (naivedya).
The preceptor, together with those bearing the forms [of the deities], should place the Mūrti-mantra, the Brahmāṅgas, the Mūla-mantra, and the Devī-mantra, and then commence the rite of Homa.

One endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics, born into a Śaiva lineage, should perform the recitation of the Vedas in the four directions and the muttering of mantras in the corners. (80)
Having consecrated the sacrificial pit and the fire, one should offer libations with fuel-sticks and other materials,
as well as with parched grain, ghee, rice, fried grain, sesame, mustard, and barley.
The Palāśa, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Vaṭa trees are in the directions starting from the east;
and the Śamī, Khadira, Māyūra, and Śrīvṛkṣa trees are in the southeast corner.
The *palāśa* [leaf] is considered suitable for the primary [rite], and it may also be used everywhere;
[the number of leaves] should be a thousand, or half of that, or one hundred and eight.
The preceptor should perform oblations with the root mantra, equal in number to that [total], or half of it;
this is prescribed as the offering for the Mūrtipas, while offerings with the Brahmāṅgas are made in the eight directions.
The Guru should offer libations to Mūrti and Mūrtīśvara in their respective kuṇḍas;
he should offer libations to the Preceptor (Guru) in the principal kuṇḍa, accompanied by all the deities.
One should begin the sprinkling with the water of pacification (śāntyaṃbhaḥ) and the recitation of the respective mantras;
one should likewise perform the touching with darbha grass for each individual portion.
Then, at dawn, the preceptor, having purified himself along with the image-makers,
shall raise the Goddess and the jars, and as before, he shall gratify the fire.
After offering the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should then enter the temple;
having performed the consecration as before, whether in a human or a divine [image], one should install it.

Having first placed a stone slab, filled with gems, gold, and other precious materials, and having led the Goddess Īśvarī to her abode as before, one should install it while reciting the root mantra. (89)
At an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction of stars, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa).
If [the deity] is mobile, one should perform the placement of mantras upon the bathing altar.
Having placed the jars (ghaṭas) in front of the Goddess, one should place the seed-syllable from the main jar (kumbha) in her heart;
then, from the secondary jars (anukumbhas), one should assign the mantras around the pedestal (pīṭha).
Then, one should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the Tattvamūrti and so forth as before;
subsequently, one should consecrate [the deity] in each respective location with the waters from their corresponding pitchers.
At the conclusion, the preceptor should cause the ceremonial bathing (snapana) to be performed, offer the food oblation (naivedya), and conduct the festival;
then, having praised [the deity] with various hymns, he should recite this verse.
"As long as the moon and the sun endure, and as long as the earth remains, so long must you, O Goddess, remain here in this temple. (94)
Having fully honored the preceptor and the others, he should then cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given,
according to the distinctions of "excellent" and so forth as prescribed for the installation of the Liṅga.
Then, for this goddess who is the primary and innate [deity], one should avoid the fourth ritual action among her auspicious rites.
O Brahmins, thus has the establishment of the marriage rite been described;
the mortal who performs it in this manner shall attain a meritorious state. || 97 ||
Thus, that mortal who, endowed with meditative devotion, should cause such an installation to be performed,
shall enjoy his desired pleasures here in this world and, at the end, go to the state of Śiva.
Having established his parents and twenty-one generations of his lineage in heaven, listen now, O best of Brahmins, to the daily worship and other rites of the Goddess. 99.
Having performed purification, sipping water, bathing, the twilight worship, and the libation according to the previously stated rules, one should enter the temple.
Having washed his feet and hands and sipped water according to the prescribed rite,
and having consecrated his body with the *sakalīkaraṇa* ritual, he should prepare the common *arghya* offering.
Having sprinkled that door with water, one should worship the female guardians of the door (dvāranāyikās),
as well as the conch-treasure (śaṅkhanidhi) and the lotus-treasure (padmanidhi) on both sides of the door.
The two gatekeepers should be depicted holding swords and shields in their hands, adorned with crested crowns, dark as jewels, and terrifying in appearance. (103)
Endowed with all ornaments and adorned with every kind of jewel,
they worshipped the Goddess Vāṇī situated in the middle of an udumbara tree, with branches extending upward on both sides.
Having worshipped Gaṅgā and Yamunā, one should worship the Weapon-deity (Astradevatā) situated at the threshold;
otherwise, one should worship Viśālākṣī, Jaṭilā, and Mūrdhagā.
One should worship Samṛddhi and Dhṛti on the right branch,
and Sarasvatī and Gaṅgā, who are considered to be white in color, on the left branch.
And all the others were dark-complexioned, adorned with every ornament, holding swords and shields, and having either two or four arms. || 107 ||
Having worshipped the door-keepers mentioned by the deity— namely Vimala and Subāhu— at the two door-panels on the right and left, one should enter.
Having worshipped Vāstoṣpati while seated on one's own seat facing north,
and having conjoined oneself with one's own Śakti, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) as before.
One should perform the immersion in nectar (sudhāsaṃplāvana) and the invocation of the self (ātmāvāhana) until death;
then, with those same mantras, one should perform the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) and the ritual placement on the body (dehanyāsa).
One should perform the placement of the thirty-eight kalās, conjoined with the Praṇava,
for the worship of the Goddess who has five heads and two faces.
One should perform the placement of the thirty-one *kalās* upon the single face;
these are said to be the *kalās* beginning with Śaśinī, considered as solitary units.
Alternatively, having transformed the body into a Śaiva form by means of the Śiva-mantras,
one should worship the Goddess, Skanda, Gaṇeśa, and all the others.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon his body, he should perform the internal sacrifice (antaryāga).
He should carry out the procedure of worship in the heart, and he should arrange for the fire-oblation (homa) on the navel.
One should meditate on the Goddess Īśvarī, the bestower of boons who faces in all directions, upon the forehead;
then, having performed the purification of the site, one should prepare the special arghya offering.

Having purified that collection of substances— consisting of perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains— with the heart-mantra, and having worshipped himself, he should perform the purification of the mantra.
Then one should perform purification, even for worship that has been stale;
[we] know Gaṇāmbikā, we meditate upon Mahātapā. || 117 ||
Having first uttered "ity uktvā," and at the end [of the mantra] "tanno devī pracodayāt," one should recite this mantra, perform worship, and then offer [the oblation]. || 118 ||

The best of worshippers, reciting the mantra of the Goddess’s weapon and having performed the purification of the image, should either discard the remains of the offering (nirmālya) for the Goddess who wears them, or [retain them]. || 119 ||
If it is made of wood or iron, one should perform a bath on every festival day;
however, if it is made of plaster, paintings, and so forth, purification is desired through ritual worship.
Alternatively, by means of the wind produced from a palm-leaf fan empowered with the weapon-mantra,
the garland shall remain unfading right there, like a lamp that does not go out.
Daily worship is not desired; rather, it is considered appropriate in this manner once a year.
Alternatively, if there is a stone image, its washing is prescribed therein.
One should visualize a seat in the center consisting of Śakti in the form of the support (ādhāra),
and in the directions beginning with the east, one should visualize Ananta, Dharma, and the others, joined with Ananta and the rest.
In the upper and lower coverings, upon the pericarp of the lotus, is the Śakti-maṇḍala;
and the series of maṇḍalas beginning with Vāma are formed by the powers of Kriyā, Icchā, and Jñāna.

Then, one should worship in due order with the mantra "to the seat of the Goddess"; having fashioned the image with those Brahma-mantras, one should perform the ritual of its digits (kalās) as previously described.
Having prepared the body of knowledge (vidyādeha), which is the very form of the worshipable image (pūjābera),
the Mistress of Gods should manifest herself there through her grace by means of the Praṇava.
Having filled [the vessel] with flowers while following the heart-mantra (hṛdayamantra), one should invoke and establish the Goddess with the root-mantra (mūlamantra) and the heart-mantra.
Having performed the veiling with the heart-mantra by means of the cessation of proximity,
and having performed the placement (nyāsa) starting from the heart, one should display the Great Mudrā.
Having lifted up the vessel for the *arghya*, one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) at the feet with the *hṛdaya* mantra;
one should give water for sipping (*ācamana*) to the mouth, and the *arghya* to the head with the *Īśāna* mantra. || 129 ||
Alternatively, one may offer the water for the feet and other items separately as before;
then, accompanied by fragrance and flowers, one should offer incense with the mantra of Hṛt.
One should perform the bath either with the five nectars and other substances combined or without them;
having wiped oneself dry with a cloth, one should subsequently wrap oneself in a garment.
One should offer the secret rinsing of the mouth (ācamana), along with scents, flowers, and incense;
having offered the lamp with the root mantra, one should present the food offering (naivedya). || 132 ||
O best of the twice-born, one should worship the Āvṛtti mantra, either accompanied by the oblation (havis) alone or by itself;
thereafter, one should worship the Heart mantra within the sphere of the fire.
One should worship the head at the northeast (Śārva), the crest-lock in the direction of the Rākṣasas (southwest), and its covering in the northwest;
then, having worshipped the weapon in all directions, one should worship Vāmā and the others starting from the east.
One should worship the Gaṇas, the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyās), the World-Protectors (Lokapālas), and their weapons all around;
one should honor her with one, two, three, or four such enclosures (āvaraṇas). || 135 ||
Furthermore, having offered incense, lamps, mantras, flowers, and the like, as well as food offerings, ritual oblations, and burnt offerings, one should conduct the daily festival.
For that purpose, the Goddess should indeed be fashioned with one face and four arms;
her hands should display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, while another pair holds a conch and a discus.
Seated upon a lotus posture, one should worship the goddess Manonmanī therein;
one should worship Medhā, Prajñā, and Uṣā with flowers, food, and unbroken grains (akṣata) upon the lingas.
Having performed the circumambulation of the temple according to the previously mentioned rite,
or else having performed the worship of the sandals, one should enter the sanctuary.
If many images have been prepared for perpetual festivals,
one should designate among them whichever image is most excellent for that purpose, according to one's desire.
One should always worship Śivā once, twice, or three, four, five, six, seven, or eight times a day. (141)
The eternal festival has been ordained, which bestows all desired fruits;
it consists of the festival itself, the ceremonial bathing, and the rite of ascending with the *damanaka* plant. (142)
The Pavitrārohaṇa, the Kṛttikādīpa, the Saṃvatsarādi-khelā, and that festival known as Vasantotsava; 143.
Likewise, there is a monthly festival and a monthly food offering;
furthermore, O best of the twice-born, the rite of fulfillment is specifically a means of atonement. (144)
One should arrange for the removal of the worn-out [images] as previously described;
however, on the festival banner (dhvaja), one should depict either a lion or a bull.
Especially during the Pūrva-phalgunī constellation, one should perform rites at sacred fords (tīrtha);
likewise, on the festival of Śiva, the festival of the Goddess is considered to take place every day.
Setting aside the flag-offering and the bali-oblation,
take up either the discus-weapon or the trident alone, or else the weapon of the Goddess.
An image for the festival should be fashioned, characterized by the previously mentioned marks;
once the auspicious thread-tying (kautuka) has been performed for the Goddess, there shall be no exit from that village.
Wherever there may be an offering or a gift, there must certainly be a vehicle; or else, a vehicle elsewhere, or even in the temple—indeed, all these are considered acceptable. (149)
If it is joined with one or more *sāla* trees on the outside, it is proclaimed as excellent;
O elder brothers, this rule is common to all deities. (150)

One should perform the installation of the *dhāma-mūrdha* bricks and the stūpa as before, joined with the deities of the directions and their forms, and accompanied by the central pitcher (*kumbha*) in the center. || 151 ||
One should perform the establishment of the abode (dhāmasaṃsthāpana) together with the previously mentioned procedure;
its installation is everywhere accompanied by the stationing of the Child (Bāla), or not.
Through the grace of the Goddess, universal sovereignty shall accrue to the king;
therefore, one should perform the royal consecration in the presence of the Goddess. 153.
Thus has the ritual of installation and so forth been correctly explained by the Goddess.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, the ritual for the installation of the Goddess, in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
She may have two arms or two eyes, with her hands hanging down;
she holds a lotus in her hand, is exceedingly peaceful, and possesses a golden luster.
Alternatively, she may have four arms and three eyes, with a single face that is most serene.
The goddess was clothed in fine linen and adorned with a crown of karṇikāra flowers.
She is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and holds a trident and a noose in her hands.
The goddess has four arms and three eyes, with one face that is exceedingly serene;
she is clothed in fine silk garments and adorned with a crown of karṇṭa flowers.
She is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and holds a noose and a goad in her hands.
The Goddess has four arms and three eyes, with one face that is exceedingly serene;
she is clothed in fine silk garments and adorned with a crown of karṇikāra flowers.
Bestowing boons, she is joined with a noose and a goad held in her hands.
The goddess has four arms and three eyes, with one face that is exceedingly serene;
she is clothed in fine silk and adorned with a crown of karṇikāra flowers.
She is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and holds a trident and a noose in her hands.
The goddess has four arms and three eyes, with one face that is exceedingly serene;
she is clothed in fine silk garments and adorned with a crown of karṇikāra flowers.
She is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and her hands also hold a trident and a noose.
The goddess is clothed in fine linen, adorned with a crown and a casket,
joined in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and holding a noose and a goad in her hands.
Alternatively, she may have six arms, holding a conch and a discus in her hands as desired.
Goddess Dukkūlavasanā is adorned with a crown and a casket;
she exhibits the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and her other two hands hold a parrot and a blue lotus.
Alternatively, she may have six arms, holding a conch and a discus in her hands as desired.
45. In the forty-fifth chapter, the procedure for the installation of Vighneśa:
I shall describe the location of Vighneśa, preceded by its characteristics and so forth. His abode should be within the city, in one of the eight directions, or in the intermediate space.
In the abode of Śiva, in the eight directions, in that region, in pavilions and the like,
in places such as sacred trees (caityavṛkṣa), or at their roots, or in every temple— [there he is] desired.
Whether in a marketplace, on a street, in a house, or wherever else,
it is taught that the face of Vighnesha may indeed be directed toward any desired direction.
Now, [the temple] is endowed with a width ranging from one to thirty-three cubits,
and is provided with floor levels ranging from one to nine stories.
Specifically, it may be mounted on the back of an elephant, or otherwise endowed with another form;
accompanied by Vighneśvara in the cardinal directions, and joined by a mouse in the corners.
Or, a group [of deities] rich in the form of Skanda is declared to be the lowest abode;
it is provided with a virtuous interior as before and joined with the first brick.
It may be joined with the forms of the deities of the quarters and the central jar, or not;
it may also be joined with the installation of the *dhāman* according to the previously described method.
It is provided with walls and pavilions, and adorned with pavilions and the like;
its pavilion may be shaped like a cow's tail or even like a peaked roof.
He was addressed by his attendants on all sides; and that [account] is told here as a digression:
he possessed a universal form, wide eyes, was imperishable, and was intoxicated with pride.
One should [worship] his eight forms— Unmatta, Lalita, Bhīma, and Tīkṣṇadaṃṣṭra— in their proper order, along with the eight seats presided over by the lords beginning with Nidrā.
One should properly fashion a mouse at the front of the eastern door;
and at the gateway, one should fashion the two gatekeepers, Vikaṭa and Bhīma.
Likewise, one should install Kumbhodara, the bearer of the remains of offerings (nirmālya), in the northeast;
as well as Āmoda, Pramoda, Sumukha, and Durmukha.
Avighna, Vighnarāja, Bhakṣyāśī, and Pañcahastaka—these are known as the guardians of the eight forms; otherwise, they are described differently. (13)
He has the face of an elephant, protruding lips, and is the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśa) and the Master of the Gaṇas (Gaṇādhipa).
He is Vināyaka, the Single-Tusked One (Ekadanta), the lover of food (Bhakṣyapriya), and he has a serpent as his girdle (Ahimekhala). || 14 ||
These are like Vighneśvara; they are the eight guardians of the forms of Vighneśa.
The two door-keepers stationed at the entrance should be made in the form of spirits (bhūta), each with two arms.
Adorned with hāla-pallava in their hands, they hold staffs in their right hands;
endowed with fierce fangs, they stand on a single foot upon the necks of lions. 16.
The two gatekeepers are fierce with distorted faces, resembling the color of blood;
likewise, there is a rat of smoky color with red eyes and prominent fangs.
He has a sharp tail, four feet, and is adorned with garlands of tinkling bells;
he has a pot-like belly, four arms, and holds a chisel, a trident, a sword, and a staff.
Red in color and greatly radiant, he stands upon a noble throne;
they are white in color, large-bodied, fierce, and clad in ancient garments.
Their arms are joined with their own teeth and smeared with nooses, goads, and thighs;
known as the retinue (parivāra), they stand facing Gaṇeśa.
In another tradition, all the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālas) are proclaimed as the retinue;
one should arrange the offering pedestal (balipīṭha) and the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha) as previously described. || 21 ||
The eight forms beginning with Āmoda are said to be on the eight petals of the pedestal;
Bhūteśa is in the pericarp, and the world-protectors and their weapons are outside.
O best of brahmins, listen briefly to its characteristics:
one should construct it with materials such as stone according to the supreme measurement of five tālas.
When the *garha* is divided by fifty, starting from five parts and increasing by one up to thirty parts, the measurement of the womb (*garbha*) is thus declared. (24)

In this manner, the measurement should also be determined here based on the height of the pillar and the door, or else according to the measurement prescribed for the characteristics of an image, or that pertaining to the *liṅga* and other such objects. (25)
One should divide [the height] from the hair down to the feet into sixty-four parts:
the *uṣṇīṣa* is one part, and the hair is two *aṅgulas*.
The face should be twelve finger-breadths (arkāṅgula) and the neck is said here to be two;
from there down to the heart, it is traditionally remembered as eleven finger-breadths (rudrāṅgula).
From the navel to the end of the penis, it is twelve *aṅgulas*;
likewise, from there to the knees, the length of the knee is fifteen *aṅgulas*. || 28 ||
The shanks should be known to be equal to the thighs; the height of the soles is two mātrās.
From the hairline to the eye-line, a measurement of four aṅgulas is prescribed. [Thus it is] released. 29.
The length of the elephant's trunk extends from the root of the tusks to the knees;
its circumference at the base is four mātras, the same as the length of the tusks.
One should fashion a single tooth either on the right or on the left;
the width of the pitcher at the top, however, shall be three finger-breadths for each.
The eye is said to extend four finger-breadths from the root of the ear;
the two ears should be ten mātrās in length, and their width should be six mātrās.
The space between the armpits was previously stated to be fifteen finger-breadths;
from the armpit up to the end of the upper arm, it is remembered as being six finger-breadths. || 33 ||
The width of the middle part of the body is declared to be twelve finger-breadths (manvaṅgula);
from the heart to the boundary of the navel, it is said here to be ten finger-breadths.
From the navel down to the genitals is said to be eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
the two thighs are eight finger-breadths, and the two knees are three finger-breadths each.
The two shanks, ending at the soles, are fashioned with eight finger-breadths;
Jagavaktra, Gaṇādhīśa, Bhūtarūpa, and Mahodara [are the names of these parts]. || 36 ||
With a serpent as his sacred thread, his thighs and knees were like lumps of gold;
he shone with the luster of a blue lotus and was adorned with four staff-like arms.
With his left hand turned inward like an elephant’s trunk, seated in the lotus posture,
he should hold his own tusk and an axe in his two right hands.
In his left hand he holds a sweetmeat ball (laḍḍuka), a rosary, and a blue lotus;
he wears red garments, and his complexion is either dark-blue or golden. 39.
He was covered by a yellow garment, radiant with a crown and diadem, wearing a white sacred thread, and adorned with all manner of ornaments. (40)
One should then have Gaṇeśa fashioned, holding a goad and a tusk in his right hands, and a noose and a sweetmeat (laḍḍuka) in his left hands, either in a standing or a seated posture. 41.
O twice-born ones, he is adorned with three eyes, or else with two;
he may be seated upon a lotus, or upon a throne, or even upon a mouse.
Seated upon his desired throne, adorned with a halo and other ornaments, Vighnarāja may thus be represented either alone or accompanied by Śakti.
If the deity Gaṇeśa is joined by Bhāratī and Śrī on his left and right, or otherwise joined by a single Śakti, that characteristic is now described. (44)
Seated upon a throne, adorned with a jeweled crown and other ornaments, dark-complexioned, holding a spear, and clad in the directions as his garment (naked). || 45 ||
The goddess, adorned with all ornaments, naked, fair-faced, and endowed with two arms, was placed upon his lap. || 46 ||
She is renowned as Vighneśvarī, beautiful in all her limbs,
holding a noose in her hand and likewise a secret object in her right hand.
One should likewise contemplate the Lord of Mantras, even as he touches the deity—himself four-armed, three-eyed, and holding a noose and a goad. (48)
O twice-born ones, the goddess Guhyakā holds a piece of sugarcane with her left hand,
and she touches a piece of sugarcane even with her lotus-like foot.
O twice-born ones, having performed these preparations, he should begin the consecration with those mantras;
[the seed-syllable] which is the third of the second [varga], conjoined with the first vowel. (50)
One should likewise contemplate the seed-syllable of Vighneśvara as joined with the Bindu and Nāda,
or else as endowed with the thirteen vowels.
O twice-born ones, the third letter of the ka-series, conjoined with fire (ra) and Māyā (ī), and enclosed by the Hṛllekhā (hrīṃ), constitutes the three-syllabled seed-mantra.
Alternatively, one should conceive it as conjoined with the venerable seed-syllable of speech;
or else, one should perform the five Brahmans and the six limbs according to the power of the root mantra.
One should extract the six-syllable mantra with the syllables *huṃ* for Vakratuṇḍa;
the heart and other [limbs] are formed by *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, and *vauṣaṭ*. || 54 ||
O best of sages, they are said to be joined with the syllable *phaṭ*.
The third letter of the second [varga] and the final letter of the sixth varga [are also included]. (55)
The third of the seventh [group], joined with the fourth of that same group;
its second, its first, and the fourteenth letter. (56)
This ten-syllable seed-mantra is joined with the Bindu and Nāda;
one should then extract the third letter of the second [varga], as well as the Brahmāṇya limbs.
Having uttered the word "viri" three times, and then again "gaṇapati," one should utter "varada" and then speak the pair of "varada."
Then the word "bring all the worlds under control" (sarvalokavaśam ānaya), followed by the word "svāhā"—this is the desired mantra for one endowed with power. (59)
The heart-mantra and others are proclaimed by means of mantras beginning with the syllable *oṃ*.
Furthermore, the mantra is enclosed within *hṛllekhā* and is joined with both cause and effect.
This mantra, beginning with the word "Gaṇeśa," belongs to Pradhāna.
Then there is the ocean of sugarcane juice, followed by the ocean of curd, then Suvarṇadvīpa, and then the Kalpavṛkṣa tree.
The lion-throne and the mantras should be on the seat of Śakti and Vighneśvara;
one should then place the root of the right hand upon the nose and at the top of the head.
One should curve the tip of this [middle finger]; this is the Gaṇeśvarī mudrā. Another is called the Mūla-mudrā; one should extend the middle finger. (63)
Then, having bent the ring finger and brought the index finger [to it],
and having formed the thumb like a horn— this is the mudrā known as the Root (mūla).
With this mudrā, the supreme guru should perform all the rites;
thereafter, the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) should be performed, preceded by the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa).
At the previously mentioned time, one should place the jewels upon the pedestal, or not at all;
or else, five [jewels] made of gold, along with a golden needle.
Recalling Indra and the other deities according to the previously mentioned method,
and having formed a cluster of lotuses, one should perform the opening of the eyes.
With honey and clarified butter together with gold placed in vessels, reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, [he should worship] along with golden nails, heaps of grain, covered cloths, and so forth.
If the obstacle is accompanied by the Goddess, one should perform it separately for her;
then, having performed the purification of the image (beraśuddhi), one should circumambulate the village and other such places.
One should consecrate the deity in water using the *hṛdaya* mantra, provided with a long beard [of grass].
One should then place eight jars around it, presided over by the lords of the directions beginning with Āśā (East).
For the sake of the sacrifice, one should construct a pavilion in front of the temple or on its two sides;
it should be adorned with sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) and other features shaped like a lotus, or resembling the directions of Yama, Varuṇa, and the Moon.
O lords of sages, the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are said to be nine, five, and one in number; they are circular, triangular, and ten-cornered respectively.
The primary sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is everywhere proclaimed to be circular;
having thus prepared the pavilion (maṇḍapa) according to the method previously described, [one should proceed].
After dismissing the artisan, he should then feed the twice-born;
having performed the sprinkling for the auspicious day (puṇyāha), he should then cause the Vāstu-homa sacrifice to be performed.
Or one should perform the ritual enclosure of the ground according to the previously mentioned procedure; having brought Vighneśa from the water, one should install him upon the bathing altar.
In the pavilion situated to the north, one should perform the ritual bathing as before;
finally, having tied the protective thread (kautuka), one should recite the all-pervading mantra (sarvātmaka).
Having prepared a bed upon the altar above the sacrificial mound with five eggs and so forth,
or with five clean cloths, he should lay the deity upon it while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Having enveloped it with two red garments,
one should perform the placement of the jar (kumbha-nyāsa) at the region of Vināyaka’s head, provided with a thread and a tuft of grass (sūtra-kūrca).
A water-pot accompanied by fine cloth, an *apanasa* fruit, and leaves of the mango and *aśvattha* trees;
or else with water containing the five gems, or even water containing a *māṣa* of gold. (79)
One should place eight jars filled with citron fruits and other offerings all around;
provided with cloth, gold, and so forth, one should worship them with perfumes and flowers.

Having worshipped the *kumbha* (vessel) with incense, flowers, and the like, while it is presided over by the *gaṇeśa* together with the *sāsana* and *sadeha*, one should employ the previously mentioned meditation.

In the same manner, the most excellent gurus should place the elephant-faced [Gaṇeśa] and the others in the surrounding jars, or even those headed by Āmoda, ending with the food offerings (naivedya). 82.
If there are two vardhanīs on both sides accompanied by two goddesses,
or if there is one, having placed it in the north, one should worship it there again.

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the principles of Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman, along with those residing within the Sadeśānta, and having worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings, one should worship their respective lords in due order.
