Having uttered the name of the Lord of the Tattva whose essence is Gaṇeśa, ending in the dative case and followed by "namaḥ," one should install the Lords of Śiva-vidyā by that same path.
The embodied forms and the lords of the embodied forms are considered to be the "forms" (mūrtis) as previously stated;
Indra and the others, the elephant-faced one (Gaṇeśa) and the others, and Āmoda and the others are indeed the presiding deities (adhipas). || 86 ||

In the five-fold system, however, the lords of the forms (mūrtīśas) are considered to be five, and from the first among the eight [mantras], the form-mantra (mūrti), the Brahma-mantra, the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), the body of knowledge (vidyādeha), and the root-mantra (mūlaka). || 87 ||
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) and worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa);
[the officiant] should be born from a family of Śiva-devotees or Brahmins and be endowed with the previously mentioned ornaments.
One should perform the rite of fire-oblation (homa) together with those who bear the form of the Guru;
the recitation of the Vedas should take place in the four cardinal directions, while the muttering of the root-mantra (mūlajapa) should be performed in the corners.
Having consecrated the fire and the sacrificial pit according to the path prescribed for fire-rites,
he should place Tatpuruṣa and the other [faces] in the cardinal directions and the Hṛdaya and other mantras in the corners.
Having invoked Īśa, who is joined with Pradhāna and all the embodied and unembodied lords,
and having worshipped him with perfumes and other substances, one should satisfy him with these offerings.

One should perform the homa for the Tattvas and their Lords with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, sesame seeds, cakes, molasses, and barley; and one should carry out the homa for the Mūrtis and their Lords.
One should perform the sprinkling with water of pacification and the recitation of the respective mantras, as well as the touching with *darbha* grass, thus for each individual portion. (93)
Then, at dawn, the preceptor, having become pure along with the image-makers,
should raise up Vighnarāja and satisfy the pitchers and the fire.
As the occasion for expiation, however, one should offer a hundred terrible oblations;
having then given the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the Guru should enter the temple.
Whether it be for a human or a divine [temple], having consecrated it as before,
one should install the foundation stone (kaśilā), filled with gems, medicinal herbs, and other substances, using the primary mantra.
Then, one should install Gaṇādhipa together with the Brahma-stone,
having first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Gaṇeśāna as before while reciting the root mantra.
At an auspicious moment and under a favorable lagna, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa).
O twice-born ones, if the image is mobile, the placement of mantras should take place upon the bathing altar.
Having placed two water-pots on either side, one should place the seed-syllable in the heart of the central jar; then, from the other jars, one should assign the mantras around the pedestal.
One should consecrate [the deity] in each respective location with the waters from each respective jar;
thereafter, one should perform the placement (vinyāsa) of the principles (tattva), the forms (mūrti), and so forth, as previously described. || 100 ||
At the conclusion, one should perform the ceremonial bath (snapana), present the food offering (naivedya), and conduct the festival;
O lords of sages, this is especially so if Gaṇeśa is accompanied by Bhāratī and Śrī.
The most excellent gurus should perform the consecration of those two according to what has been stated;
indeed, if she is accompanied by Vighneśvarī, one should install her under that name.
One should place the water-jars situated at the sides of the main pitcher while reciting the supreme mantra;
then, one should perform the installation specifically upon their hearts.
If a wise person should thus perform the installation of Vighneśa, he who desires long life shall obtain it, and he who seeks wealth shall obtain riches. (104)
One desiring knowledge shall obtain pure knowledge; one desiring pleasure, an excellent woman;
and [others shall obtain] sons, good fortune, health, fame, valor, and auspicious prosperity. (105)
By the installation of Vighneśa, one shall indeed obtain liberation in the hereafter;
O best of sages, listen now to the brief procedure for his worship.
Having risen in the morning and completed the necessary purification and bathing,
one should perform the salutation of the Sandhyā and the libation with mantras, exactly as before.

Having performed this, the Guru— whose two hands and limbs have been washed, who has sipped water (ācānta), and who has performed the sakalīkaraṇa rite— should enter the abode while holding the general arghya vessel.
Having sprinkled that door with water, one should worship Vikaṭa and Bhīma;
or, as prescribed by the gods, one should worship Subāhu and Vimala at the two thresholds.
Having entered, placing the *heti* on the threshold with his right foot,
and having worshipped the Lord of the Site (*vāstvīśa*), he remains seated on his own seat facing north.
Having joined the self with the power (śakti), one should protect it, having destroyed its [limited] state;
endowed with a body made moist by the nectar (amṛta) arising from that. || 111 ||

Having purified the hands with the Astra-mantra and anointed them with sandalwood paste, [he should place the mantras] of Īśāna, Aghora, Vāma, and Sadyojāta upon the fingernails and palms, and those of the [five] eyes upon the palms. 112.

One should place the Root-mantra and [the mantras of] the Heart, Head, Crest, Armor, and Weapon in sequence upon the fingers beginning with the thumb; then one should again contemplate the Root-mantra on the tips of the hands.
One should perform the deposition of the body (dehanyāsa) with those mantras, or else with the root-mantras accompanied by the Brahma-mantras;
one should likewise arrange the deposition of the thirty-one kalās as if for a deity.
Having thus assumed a subtle body, either accompanied by the placement of the letters (lipinyāsa) or not,
the practitioner, having meditated upon himself as being like Gaṇeśa, should proceed to the internal sacrifice.
Alternatively, having made one's own body Śaiva by means of the Śiva-mantras,
and having worshipped and offered oblations to Gaṇeśāna, one should meditate upon him in the heart, the navel, and the bindu.
Then, having performed the purification of the site (sthānaśuddhi), one should prepare the special arghya offering,
provided with fragrance, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (akṣata), either together with the previously mentioned substances or without them.

In the same manner, one should offer water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the arghya offering— either individually or all together— having sprinkled each of these substances with the arghya water itself.
Having consecrated oneself with the heart-mantra and worshipped one's own self while remembering it as the essence of all,
one should then perform the purification of the mantra and subsequently proceed to the purification of the image.
Having performed the worship that has remained overnight, one should recite: "We know Vakratuṇḍa," and then the words "we meditate upon the elephant-faced one. (120)
"May he impel us toward that state of the Tathāgata (dantipada), having spoken the subsequent word.
Reciting this, one should then worship with either the specific *arghya* offering or the general *arghya*.
Having removed it from the heart, one should place it outside for the bearer of the *nirmālya*;
or else, one should discard it and perform the purification of the image with a mind focused on the prescribed procedure.

O twice-born ones, if that image is made of metal, there should be a bath on every festival day; however, if it is a painted image or the like, purification is considered to occur through the purification of the ritual worship.

Having thus performed the purification of the self, the ritual substances, the mantras, and the image by means of a gentle breeze arising from a palm-leaf fan obtained through the power of the weapon-mantra (astra), || 124 ||
One should fashion a seat in the center with the Praṇava, facing toward Dharma;
below and above it, one should place Adharma and the others, with a lotus between the two covers.
Having produced [the lotus] in the water of the Praṇava, joined with a yellow pericarp,
one who is endowed with Śakti should perform its ritual seating according to the stated method.
Then, one should worship [the deity] in due order with the mantra "gaṇāsanāya";
having invoked the form as before and having conceptualized the body by means of the mantras.
There, by means of the *praṇava*, one should manifest Vighneśa through his grace;
with hands filled with flowers, [one should do so] while following the heart-mantra.

Having first performed the *niṣṭhurā* [mudrā] with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), one should perform the *avakuṇṭhana* (concealment). Then, with the subtle mantras beginning with the heart and ending with the weapon (*astra*), one should display the *mahāmudrā*.

Having offered water for the feet with the heart-mantra at the feet, one should offer water for sipping with the face-mantra at the mouth; then, while recollecting the Lord, one should offer the respectful oblation (arghya), along with fragrance, flowers, and incense.
Or, having bathed [the image] with water enriched by the five nectars while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra, and having wiped it with a cloth, one should subsequently clothe it with a garment. || 131 ||
Having offered water for sipping with his mouth, he should grind sandalwood, agallochum,
and kuṣṭha together with camphor, or simply sandalwood alone.
Having offered [the oblation], one should offer incense combined with black agallochum while reciting the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra),
or else incense made from the resin of white sandalwood and camphor.
One should cause fragrant and variegated flowers, which blossom in all seasons and bloom at that very moment, to be offered as before.
One should cause lamps lit with oil and ghee to be offered while reciting the heart-mantra;
thereafter, one should cause an offering of food (naivedya) to be presented, either consisting of mung-bean rice and other items, or otherwise.
The quantities of the perfumes and other offerings are as stated in the section on worship facing west;
thereafter, one should worship the surrounding deities (āvṛti) until the conclusion with the offering of incense.
And in the fire [quarter], as well as in the directions of the Rakṣas, Vāyu, and Īśa, one should place the seed-syllables beginning with the Heart;
then outside of that, the [deities] beginning with Gajavaktra and those headed by Ānanda.
One should properly worship Indra and the others, as well as their weapons, on the exterior of that [mandala];
or one may worship the host with one, two, or three layers of enclosures.

Furthermore, one should perform the offering of incense, lamps, and the chanting of mantras, as well as the presentation of food offerings, ritual oblations, and fire sacrifices, according to the previously established procedure.
The preceptor [should offer] fuel-sticks of *palāśa*, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, and flattened rice,
in a number of one hundred and fifty or ten, while reciting the root mantra.
One should perform the fire oblation (homa) with those ancillary rites numbering one-tenth of the root mantra;
thereafter, one should conduct the daily festival according to the procedure for the Gaṇa-liṅga.
One should worship the Gaṇa in that [liṅga] with the previously mentioned measure;
one should worship the Gaṇa-weapon in the flowers, food, and unbroken rice-grains (akṣata) upon the liṅgas with the Heti-mantra.
This perpetual festival should be performed, whether accompanied by a physical image (bera) or not;
having performed the circumambulation of the temple according to the previously mentioned rule. (143)
Or, equipped with the worship of the sandals, he may enter the temple once, twice, three, four, or five times a day. (144)
One should worship the Gaṇa either for six, seven, eight, or nine days, or at all times;
having understood this, one should constantly worship Gaṇeśvara with the constituent elements of worship.
Thus, the daily worship (nityejyā) has been prescribed as bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
for the attainment of desired goals, one should perform a special sacrifice on the fourth lunar day.

Provided with various kinds of food offerings and accompanied by the ritual bathing and other rites, the bathing ceremony is performed as before; however, one should place Gaṇeśvara in the central pitcher.
In the system of four directions, there are [the deities] beginning with Āmoda; in the conception of five, there are eight; and in the number nine, there are twenty-five. (148)

The world-protectors, Viśvarūpa and the others, reside in the cardinal directions and the intermediate spaces; these eight world-protectors, beginning with Vasu, are established as the Vāstu deity. (149)
From the first three [groups], three [deities] are to be worshipped in the three sets of eight in successive order;
these are considered the deities for the forty-nine pitchers. (150)
In the [list] of one hundred and eight, there are those beginning with the hundred mentioned in the *Ganasahasranāma*;
however, in the [list] of one thousand and eight, all the gods are proclaimed. (151)
Now, O eminent sages, is Vighneśa to be worshipped everywhere?
If Gaṇeśa is accompanied by Vāk and Śrī, one should install a pair of vardhanīs.
If he is joined with only a single *śakti*, he should place the *vardhanī* vessel to the north;
as for anything not mentioned regarding the ritual bathing (*snapana*), one should perform it exactly as previously described.
The festival of Damanāroha, the rite of Pavitrārohaṇa, the Dīpāvali, the spring sacrifice (Vasantejyā), or indeed the monthly festival; 154.
The offering of fresh oblations is also specifically a form of expiation; furthermore, one should perform the restoration of dilapidated structures and other rites as previously prescribed. (155)
However, one should paint a rat upon his banner;
or else, there should always be a festival for Śiva, or indeed a festival for Vighneśa.
Setting aside the flag-offerings and the bali-oblations, as well as the vehicle alone, take up either the discus-weapon, the trident-weapon, or the weapon of Vighneśa. (157)
An image for the festival should be fashioned, characterized by the previously mentioned features;
furthermore, whatever materials for offerings and substances for oblations are required for the festival [should be prepared]. (158)
All those [rites] not mentioned here are declared to be like those spoken for Śiva:
subjugation (vaśya), eradication (uccāṭana), causing dissension (vidveṣa), killing (māraṇa), and nourishment (pauṣṭika).
One should perform rites for pacification, immobilization, and so forth with this mantra;
when any disease arises, one should pacify it with this mantra. (160)
Its foundation is everywhere either provided with the station of the Child (Bālasthāna) or not;
one should first install Vighneśa because of the preparation of the abode of Śiva.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, the procedure for the installation of Vighneśa, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.

He has the face of an elephant, is the lord of the Gaṇas, possesses a terrestrial form, and has a large belly; he wears a garland of skulls as his sacred thread, and his thighs and knees are like massive, solid masses of clouds; he has the luster of a blue lotus and is adorned with four powerful arms.
His trunk is curved and not bent, and he is seated upon a lotus throne.
One should represent Gaṇeśa as holding an axe in his own two right hands,
a sweetmeat ball (laḍḍuka) and a rosary in his left hand, and an utpala lotus in the other [left] hand;
he may then be fashioned either in a standing or a seated posture.
Or else, he may be wearing red garments, or have a dark-blue luster, or a golden radiance;
he is covered in a yellow tunic and is resplendent with a diadem and crown.
He wears a white sacred thread and is adorned with all ornaments;
he holds his own horn and a goad in his right hands, and a noose and a sweetmeat in his left.
With his trunk curved in a clockwise circle and seated upon a lotus throne,
one should then fashion Gaṇeśa, whether in a standing or a seated posture.
[He saw] the goddess, dark-complexioned, holding a spear, naked, resting on his lap, adorned with all ornaments,
naked, fair-faced, and endowed with two arms.
One should meditate upon her known as Vighneśvarī, beautiful in all her limbs,
holding a noose in her hand, and likewise touching the Lord— the leader of mantras— with her right hand. One should contemplate her in this manner.

O twice-born ones, [one should meditate upon] the Lord Guhyaka, who has four arms and three eyes, who holds a noose and a goad, and who is endowed with a piece of sugarcane; O Goddess, he touches with his left hand a piece of sugarcane held by Puṣkara.

He has the face of an elephant, is the lord of the Gaṇas, possesses a ghost-like form, and has a large belly; he wears a serpent as a sacred thread, and his thighs and knees are as massive as dense clouds; he has the luster of a blue lotus and is adorned with four powerful arms.

One should then have Gaṇeśa fashioned, either standing or seated, with a trunk that is neither curved to the left nor to the right; holding his own tusk and a goad in his right hands, and a noose and a sweetmeat (laḍḍuka) in his left hands.
Or else, Gaṇeśa is joined by Bhāratī and Śrī on his left and right;
he is seated upon a throne and adorned with a jeweled crown and other ornaments.
46. In the forty-sixth chapter: the procedure for the installation of the Dancing Form (Nṛttamūrti).
I shall now describe the installation of the Dancing Form (Nṛttamūrti), endowed with its specific characteristics:
it has four arms, three eyes, and is possessed of matted locks that are spread out. || 1 ||
He is endowed with a crown of matted hair and covered by the hoods of crooked serpents;
those [hoods] situated on his back and sides should increase by one starting from five.
There should be thirty matted locks at the end, with spaces between them,
adorned with the flowers of *dhuttūra*, *āragvadha*, *arka*, and other such plants, and tinged with a reddish-brown hue.
Having joined his palms in reverence, he is accompanied by the Ganges situated on his right side and by the crescent moon positioned on his left flank.
Adorned with garlands of *vakula* flowers, liberated from snakes and other such creatures, clothed in a tiger skin, radiant, and embellished with all ornaments. || 5 ||
He has a tiger-skin garment draped over the root of his left arm;
he may be clothed in divine raiment, or even accompanied by a deer-skin.
He was adorned with a wooden skull-cup of Brahmā decorated with various flowers,
and he held the tip of a boar’s tusk, tiger claws, and tortoises.
Adorned on his chest with a necklace strung with conch shells and jewels,
he stands with his right foot planted and his left raised above it.
With his foot curled and whirling, his hand gracefully extended, and his eyes acting as bees upon the lotus-like bimba-fruit of Ambikā’s face; || 9 ||
Adorned with bound tinkling bells and likewise beautified by anklets,
he is enriched with leaf-shaped earrings on his left and right ears, as well as crocodile-shaped earrings.
With a serpent with its hood raised held in his right hand that grants fearlessness, and with fire held in his other left hand; || 11 ||
Equipped with a small drum (ḍiṇḍima) and provided with a sacred thread (upavīta),
he resembles the whiteness of cow’s milk and is adorned with a ring the size of the sun.
Accompanied by various serpents, Apasmāra (the seizure demon) also remained there,
situated on the head, on the forehead, on the right side, and within the right nostril.

One should extend a string from the right side of the navel to the ankle; this is proclaimed as the "middle string. From the middle string of the forehead, it is likewise measured at two units (dvimātra). || 14 ||
Between the two *hikkā* lines, that which measures three *mātras* is proclaimed;
that line is accepted here as being in contact with the left thigh at the hip. (15)
The distance between the two lines and the two ankles is recorded as one finger-breadth;
from the line to the end of the bent knee, it is exactly twelve digits.
From that line to the end of the left shoulder-blade is eleven fingers and seven units;
from that same line to the left knee is forty-one fingers. || 17 ||
From the [central] thread, the right flank is declared to be eight aṅgulas; from the thread, the left flank is declared to be twelve aṅgulas. || 18 ||
That line from the right thigh is eleven fingers and seven units long;
on the left side of that line, it is declared to be nine units.
From the thread, the left maṇṭha is declared to be five finger-breadths;
from the thread, the right side is designated as the neck (kaṇṭha) portion. || 20 ||
According to the Sūtra, however, [the measurement] ends at the left arm and is joined with a reduction of three finger-breadths;
or else, the laying down of the thread is described by another method.

From the edge of the pupil to the end of the head, from the tip of the nostril to the navel, and from the right side of the waist to the middle of the ankle of the standing foot—[these are the measurements]. (22)
Having touched [the center], the thread that is cast down is declared the middle thread (madhyasūtra).
Five units (mātras) to the left of the thread is the face; the throat is three units.
At the ends of the arms it should be fifteen digits (tithi), at the armpits nine digits;
in the middle of the belly it should be eight digits, and the hips by fourteen fingers (viśva).
The hip should be forty-eight finger-breadths; elsewhere it should be sixty units.
That thigh should be nine units, and its height up to the heel should be four units.
The neck should be seven finger-breadths wide at the mouth and one rasa (six) units elsewhere; at the end of the arms it should be three mātras, and at the end of the armpits, eleven mātras.
The abdomen should be eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas) wide; the hips should be the measure of a yuga (four aṅgulas);
the waist should be the measure of the Vedas (four aṅgulas), and the knee should be eight aṅgulas. || 27 ||
The height [of the pedestal] should be equal to the tip of the foot or just the face; having understood this, one should act accordingly.
One should know that the height for a standing [image] is equal to the knees, while for a seated image with curled feet, the height is as described. || 28 ||
The distance between the two heels and the two knees is proclaimed as *dvimukha*;
the height of the hips is considered the measure for raising the left knee. (29)

The distance between the middle of the thighs and the navel is nine units; the distance from the knees to the wrist of the outstretched hand, up to the mani-bandha (the base of the palm), is one mantra-unit (twelve units).
Therefore, the wrist of the hand of fearlessness (abhayahasta) measures six finger-breadths;
from the base of its thumb to the end of the "breast-eye" (stanākṣa), the distance is two [finger-breadths]. || 31 ||

That [measurement] should be equal to the defect and equal to the height; furthermore, one should know that the elbow of the staff-handed [deity] from the middle of the arms is seventeen finger-breadths.
The height of the fire-altar (agni) should reach the end of the arms, and that fire-altar is five finger-breadths in elevation;
its width is one kola, and it is endowed with three flames.
The hand holding the *ḍamaruka* should be raised to the ear and exceed [the length of] five fingers;
the height of the *ḍamaruka* should be that of the *dhātu*, while its width at the mouth should be equal to the [height of the] *bhūtas*. || 34 ||
The throat is of medium width, bound all around by the mechanism of the vocal cords; it is endowed with a single tongue and possesses a deep resonance. || 35 ||
From the wrists to the ends of the forearms, the other [measurement] is thirty-four;
the height of the elbows is twelve, eleven, nine, and eight units respectively. (36)
The measurement for epilepsy (apasmāra) should be according to the measurement of the god's face,
beginning from two faces and ending at five faces.
O best of the twice-born, the measurement of the seventh [deity] is declared to be half the measure of the face; Apasmāra should be made with four tālas.
One should divide the space from the uṣṇīṣa to the soles of the feet into sixty-six parts;
that which extends from the uṣṇīṣa to the hairline is proclaimed as the *kolaka*. (39)
From the hairline to the end of the bow [the forehead] is recorded as being eight parts;
the throat is said to be half a finger-breadth, and the ear is stated to be one and a half [finger-breadths]. (40)
It is declared that [the space] from the heart to the end of the hiccups is six finger-breadths;
likewise, it is traditionally taught that from there to the navel is six finger-breadths.
Therefore, the length from the root of the genitals to the end is said to be one *kauśikāṅgula*;
the height of the thigh is seven parts, and the elevation of the knee is two measures.
The height of the shank shall be seven parts, and the height of the foot two mātras;
it has two arms and two eyes, with its upper body facing downwards.
Indeed, a serpent is on his left hand, while his head is on the right;
he possesses a graceful, adorned, and undulating form, with his head joined to his left side.
The length of the Jahnavī is said to be equal to that of the god's mouth;
she has two arms, three eyes, and is adorned with a crown of baskets.
Adorned with all ornaments and with palms joined in reverence,
she should cause [the water] to flow from the upper part down to the lower part in the form of a stream.
Whether joined with or separated from this Goddess Gaṅgā, the extent of its radiance and space is one hundred and ten finger-breadths. || 47 ||
The staff of that [standard] measures three hundred and thirty-seven cubits in length, and its width is one part;
it may be either less or more by measures ranging from one up to ten.
From two finger-breadths down to half a finger-breadth, the crescent moon is of seven kinds;
according to that [measurement], one should fashion the goddess situated at the side according to the prescribed rule.
One may perform either the *bhṛṅgiraṭi* or the *bhadrakālī*;
then follows the *bhujaṅgatrāsa*, and after that the *bhujaṅgalalita*.
Indeed, there is a certain distinction [in this mudrā] like that of one terrified by a serpent;
having raised the palm, one should gradually place it above the knees while standing. (51)
Whether it consists of two morae, three morae, or even four morae,
that which is known as *bhujaṅgalalita* is here called *bhairava*.
Everything is like the fear of a serpent; however, a specific distinction regarding that is stated:
one should lift the right foot and lead it toward the left foot.
With feet, situated in the middle of the body and joined with the soles of upturned feet,
he has either four arms or eight hands, adorned with various divine weapons.
Having obtained materials such as stone, one should thus fashion Naṭeśvara.
Thus the characteristics have been declared; now the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is described.
The time [for the rite] is declared as before, and likewise the planting of the sprouts; one should duly perform the placement of the jewels and the opening of the eyes as previously described. (56)
Then one should perform the purification of the image and circumambulate the city and other sites;
thereafter, the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsana) should be performed, and one should lead the image to the pavilion as previously described.
Subsequently, one should lead out blunt [lines] on all sides, numbering nine, five, and one; these may be square, circular, or have corners according to the cardinal directions.
In the pavilion, he should feed the Brahmins, numbering ten more than a thousand;
then, for the purification of the pavilion, he should have the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited five times.
One should perform the Vāstuhoma according to the prescribed rules at the Samarīcipada;
or, even without the Vāstuhoma, one may carry out the ritual demarcation of the ground (bhūparigraha).
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited, one should lead [the image] to a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) above the altar;
thereafter, one should prepare a bed and purify the image.
Having performed the tying of the protective thread (kautukabandha), one should cause [the deity] to lie upon a bed;
one should place the balance-scale (dhaṭa) with the face of Śivā toward the head-region of the deity.
Having placed the *vardhanī* vessel to the north, one should install Gaurī within it;
having meditated upon her form as described in the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), one should worship her with perfumes and other offerings.
One should meditate upon the Goddess, who has three eyes and a face resembling the moon,
holding the Vedas in her [upper] hands; in her left [lower] hand a lotus, in another the gesture of granting boons, and in the other a rosary.
Her body adorned with divine ornaments, worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods, she is Manonmanī herself, the auspicious bestower of desire and wealth every single day.

The most excellent Guru should bring eight jars from all sides, presided over by the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), and worship them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, ending with the presentation of food (naivedya).

The Preceptor should also install the principles (tattvas) along with their respective lords (īśvaras), as well as the forms (mūrtis) and the lords of the forms (mūrteśas); then, at the proper time, he should commence the fire-oblation (homa) together with the guardians of the forms (mūrtipas).
Having performed the consecration of the sacrificial pit and the fire, one should carry out the fire-ritual as prescribed:
[offering] fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, mustard seeds, barley, and sesame seeds.
The preceptor should offer oblations of *priyaṅgu*, *śāli* rice, and *mudga* beans in sequence;
and [offerings of] *udumbara*, *vaṭa*, *aśvattha*, and *plakṣa* trees should be placed in the directions starting from the east.
Śamī, Apāmārga, Bilva, and Khādira are for the southeast corner;
the Palāśa is for the principal [fire], and thus the sacrificial fuel sticks (samidh) are described.
One should perform the study of the Ṛgveda and other scriptures and the recitation of mantras according to the rules;
and having dispelled [obstacles] with hymns accompanied by song and dance, and with the resonant chanting of the Vedas. (69)
Then, having remembered the peaceful Sadāśiva at the end of the night and at dawn,
the Guru, together with the image-makers, bathed and became one whose body was purified by mantras.
Having first lifted the image facing east with his whole being, and having removed the cloth, the broom, and other such items, the Guru should worship it with perfumes and flowers.
The most excellent of gurus should satisfy the jars and the fires within the sacrificial pits;
then he should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra "Śiva" ending in "Vauṣaṭ."
Then one should worship the preceptor with garments, gold, rings, and so forth;
the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is prescribed as before, and thereafter one should begin the installation.
Then, having lifted the linga from the altar, the Guru should place it in the bathing pit;
he should install a movable one in the middle of the temple, while an immovable one [is installed elsewhere].
Then, having lifted the jars and accompanied by the sound of all musical instruments,
the wise man should circumambulate the palace and lead them before the image.
Taking the seed from the pitcher (kuṃbha), one should place it in the heart of the Great Lord;
taking the seed from the vardhanī vessel, one should deposit it upon the lotus of His pedestal.

The Guru should consecrate the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) upon the lotuses of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) in their respective locations, and he should install the Goddess according to the path prescribed for the sacrifice of the Goddess.
At the conclusion of that, the wise preceptor should also cause an auspicious rite to be performed; thereafter, he should conduct a festival according to his means.

Whatever has not been mentioned here should be performed according to the general rules established [in other sources]. The mortal who performs the consecration in this manner, endowed with meditative visualization (bhāvanā), [attains success]. || 79 ||
Having enjoyed pleasures even in this very world, he shall go to the station of Īśāna.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, the procedure for the installation of the Dancing Form, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
He has four arms and three eyes, his matted hair is disheveled and abundant,
he is adorned with a crown of matted locks, and his head is encircled by the hoods of crooked serpents.
With palms joined in reverence, accompanied by the Ganges on his right side and the crescent moon situated on his left,
he is radiant, clothed in a tiger skin and adorned with all ornaments.
He wears a tiger-skin garment draped over the root of his left arm;
he stands on his right foot with his left foot placed above it, its toes curled and turned inward, while that hand is well extended.
Adorned with bound tinkling bells and likewise beautified by anklets,
he possesses leaf-shaped and crocodile-shaped earrings on his left and right ears; and on his right hand,
which is held in the gesture of granting fearlessness, there is fire, but not on the left.
Equipped with a drum and endowed with a sacred thread,
resembling white cow's milk and marked by the digit of the sun,
he stands upon the person afflicted by epilepsy, accompanied by various serpents.

47. In the forty-seventh chapter, the procedure for the installation of Somāskanda: I shall explain the supreme installation of Somāskanda, the Lord of Bliss, endowed with its defining characteristics; that is now being proclaimed.
He has four arms and three eyes, adorned with a crown of matted hair;
he is endowed with all ornaments, and his hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
He holds a black axe in his right hand raised upward,
while his left ear is adorned with a lotus leaf and a crocodile-shaped earring.
Wearing the sacred thread, with a serene mind, his left leg extended while reclining,
and joined by Gaurī on his left side with her right leg resting upon him.
Endowed with all the auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament,
[he is to be visualized] at the forehead, the nose, the navel, the center of the big toe, and the middle of the foot.
The thread established touching the hip is known as the middle thread (madhyasūtra).
From the end of the mouth, from the root of the pippalī, and likewise from the side of the neck—(6).
From the center of the nipple, it is considered to extend to the waist and the sides;
from the crown of the head, it goes to the hump, the spine, the throat, and the middle of the buttocks.
That which is called the back-thread (pṛṣṭhasūtra) is stated to be one and a half mātrās from the side;
having left that space on both sides, therefrom comes the length of the thighs.
The knee [measurement] is one-and-a-quarter finger-breadths on the left; for the hanging [part], it is three finger-breadths.
From the thread up to the end of the left knee, the measurement of the upper body is half [of the total].
O best of the twice-born, from the base of the thighs to the end of the navel is six mātrās;
from the tip of the sole to the middle of the thigh, the distance between the two is three fingers (guṇāṅgula).
From the sūtra, the distance from the hanging foot to the heel shall be one and a half viśva-angulas;
from the bracelet to the lower part of the wrist, it reaches the boundary of the front of the waist.
The distance from the navel to the wrist is said to be sixteen finger-breadths;
if it is the "bestower of boons" (varada) [mudrā], however, it is desired that it be equal from the back of the hand to the navel.
When joined with the Vāmadevya [Sāman] through the mastery of its specific chapter, he becomes Soma himself together with Soma; such would be the procedure for Somāskanda.
The preceptor should fashion Skanda in the center of that [mandala], occupying one part out of ten parts as prescribed by the gods, or two parts, or three parts.
Having two eyes and two arms, he is adorned with a crown and a casket; there are crocodile-shaped ornaments on his ears, and he is decorated with all types of jewelry.
With a lotus in the hand on the right side and the other hand extended,
or else with two hands holding lotuses, or again, endowed with a circular form.
Whether seated upon the lap of the Goddess, or holding a lotus free from mud, or whether sitting or standing—Skanda is thus described. (17)
This very [deity], when devoid of Skanda and Umā, shall likewise be in a comfortable posture; such is the characteristic held for Soma, Somāskanda, and Sukheśa.
Their foundation should be established at an auspicious time, preceded by the ritual of the sprouts;
thereafter, one should perform the deposition of jewels for the God, the Goddess, and Guha.
One should place a golden lotus or a golden peacock upon the Goddess or upon Skanda,
accompanied by the specific mantras prescribed in the chapter on consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
The Guru should place his gaze very affectionately upon those very lotuses of the sacred seats (pīṭhas),
and having performed the unsealing with his vision, he should carry out the purification of the image by circumambulation.

The preliminary consecration of the water (jalādhivāsana) should be performed as before; one should construct a pavilion (maṇḍapa), having caused it to be brought [to measure] eight directions, circular, or having four corners.
Outside the paved floor, there should be sacrificial pits numbering nine, five, or one;
then, having dismissed the artisan, one should thereafter feed the Brahmins.
One should perform the Puṇyāha rite, the sprinkling, the Vāstuhoma, and the preparation of the sacrificial mound;
one should arrange a bed in the center and then have the ceremonial bathing performed.
Then, having tied the three auspicious knots, one should lay those [three] down;
thereafter, having wrapped them separately with cloths, one should install the jars.
Having placed the Śiva-pitcher at the head of the couch and the Vardhanī pitcher to its north,
one should place the Soma-skanda pitcher on the right side.

Having placed [the deity] presiding over the aggregates (skandhas) and worshipped it with perfumes and other offerings, the Guru, whose intellect is authorized by meditating upon the form described in the defining characteristics, [proceeds]. (27)
Having placed eight jars all around, presided over by the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas),
one should lead forth the forms of the Tattvas and so forth according to the procedure of their respective chapters.
Having performed the consecration of the sacrificial pit and the fire with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, and parched grain,
one should duly carry out the fire-oblation (homa) with sesame seeds, grains, indramudga beans, and mung beans according to the prescribed rite.
Palāśa, udumbara, aśvattha, vaṭa, and so forth are prescribed for the cardinal directions and intermediate points; those originating from śamī, khadira, māyūra, and śrīvṛkṣa are likewise recommended.
Even in the case of the primary [deity], the first [rite] is prescribed; one should cause the ritual to be performed until its completion.
Furthermore, the Guru should offer libations to the Six-faced One and the Goddess at the primary [stage].
If these [deities] have separate pedestals, one should construct a separate pavilion for each;
on the second day, one should satisfy the deity, the water-pot, and the fire according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having received a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of ten niṣkas and more from the image-makers and others,
the Guru was respectfully honored with garments, gold, rings, and other offerings.
O Great Lord, one should place the seed-syllable from the pitcher into the heart;
then, having extracted it from the *vardhanī* vessel, one should deposit it upon its pedestal.
If that goddess is Sahajā, one should place [the seed-syllable] in her heart;
from the jar of Guha, one should take that syllable of Guha and place it in the heart of Guha.
Having placed them on a pedestal all around others, one should consecrate them;
if these [deities] belong to different pedestals, one should construct separate pavilions for each.
One should perform auspicious rites according to the rules,
especially those not mentioned here, as prescribed for the general installation.
Thus, that best of men who should establish these [images] shall attain oneness with Viṣṇu and shall obtain perfection in this world. (38)
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, the procedure for the installation of Soma and Skanda, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
Four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with a crown of matted hair,
he is endowed with all ornaments, his hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
His right hand is raised, holding a black axe, while his left hand rests upon his left ear; he wears earrings shaped like a lotus leaf and a crocodile.
With the sacred thread placed over the left shoulder, with a tranquil mind, lying on his left side with his right leg slightly extended,
he shall thus find a comfortable posture.
He has four arms and three eyes, adorned with a crown of matted hair;
he is endowed with all ornaments, his hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
and his upper right hand is joined with a black axe.
With lotus and crocodile earrings resting upon his right and left ears,
wearing a sacred thread, serene in soul, he lies with his right foot extended.
With his right foot resting upon a sal tree, he is joined by Gaurī on his left;
he is endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament.
Joined on the left by the Goddess who is well-known through that very chapter, he is Soma;
he indeed becomes Soma, and this shall be the ritual procedure for Somāskanda.
He has four arms and three eyes, adorned with a crown of matted hair;
he is endowed with all ornaments, his hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
and his upper right hand is joined with a black axe.
With lotus and crocodile earrings resting on his right and left ears,
wearing a sacred thread, serene in soul, he lies with his left foot placed upon [the other].

The preceptor should fashion Skanda in the center of that [mandala], standing with his right foot on a *sāla* tree and joined by Gaurī on the left; he should be made with one part out of ten parts of the deity’s height, or with two parts, or with three-fourths of those parts.
Having two eyes and six arms, he is adorned with a crown of *karaṇṭa* flowers;
he has crocodile-shaped ornaments on his ears and is decorated with all kinds of jewelry.
Or he may be seated upon the thighs of the Goddess, or holding a lotus in his hand.
He has four arms and three eyes, adorned with a crown of matted hair,
endowed with all ornaments, and his hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
his upper right hand holds a black axe.
With lotus-fiber earrings on his left and right ears,
wearing a sacred thread, and with a serene soul, he lies upon his left palm,
his right leg slightly raised, joined by Gaurī on his left side.

Endowed with all the primary marks and adorned with every ornament, joined on his left by the Goddess, he should be like the moon itself through the perfection of that meditation; thus the rite of Somāskanda shall be accomplished.
The preceptor should fashion Skanda in the center of that [mandala], occupying one-tenth, two-tenths, or three-tenths of the divine portion;
he has two eyes, six arms, and is adorned with a crown and a basket-shaped head-ornament (karaṇḍa).
Alternatively, he may have two hands with a lotus, or be endowed with a dancing form;
or he may have four arms and three eyes, adorned with a crown of matted hair,
equipped with all ornaments, and holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
His right hand is raised, holding a black axe, while his left hand rests upon his left ear; he wears earrings shaped like crocodiles and holds a lotus leaf.
Wearing the sacred thread, with a serene soul, he lies with his left foot on the ground, while his right foot is supported;
he is joined by Gaurī on his left side.
The preceptor should fashion Skanda in the center of that [mandala], using one-tenth of the divine portion, or two portions, or three-fourths of a portion;
he has two eyes, six arms, and is adorned with a basket-shaped crown.
With two crocodile-shaped ornaments on his ears and adorned with all kinds of jewelry,
he may also be seated upon the thigh of the Goddess, or holding a lotus free from mud in his hand.
Four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
endowed with all ornaments, and having hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
His right hand is raised, holding a black axe, while his left hand rests upon his left ear; he wears earrings shaped like crocodiles and holds a lotus leaf.
With his sacred thread (upavīta) and a serene mind, he lies with his left foot resting on the ground,
while his right foot is supported, and he is joined by Gaurī on his left side.
Endowed with all the auspicious marks and adorned with all ornaments,
[the image] should be made with one-tenth of the height of a god, or else with two-tenths.
Or the preceptor should fashion Skanda in the center of that [mandala] using one-third of the dimensions;
he has two eyes and six arms, and is adorned with a basket-shaped crown.
He holds two balls of rice for the two ancestors, is adorned with all ornaments,
has a lotus in his right hand, and his other hand is extended.
48. In the forty-eighth chapter, the procedure for the installation of Candraśekhara:
I shall now describe the consecration of Indumauli (the Moon-crested Lord), preceded by its defining characteristics.
Having procured stone and other materials, the Guru should fashion the image from them.
Four-armed and three-eyed, he stands in the *samapāda* posture; his two frontal hands display the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*). || 2 ||
The left hand should display the gesture of granting boons (varada), and the right hand the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya).
If that [right hand] is made to grant boons instead, then the other [left hand] becomes the lion-ear (siṃhakarṇaka) gesture.
Alternatively, the hands may be placed touching the thighs or the hips;
the other two hands, like antelopes' horns, are positioned at the ends of the arms.
The two deer-horns (mṛgaṭaṅgau) are at the ends of the ears; the scissors (kartarī) is situated on the left.
When the two deer-horns face away from each other and then toward each other, they are so described. || 5 ||
The *kartarī* [measure] of the arms is proclaimed as being middling;
for the *hikkā*, the middling *kartarī* is thirty-one finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
The distance between the wrists and the middle of the arms is twelve finger-breadths;
the distance from the end of the hips to the elbows, measured forward from the two hands, is the same.
The distance from the nipples to the edge of the breasts may be one arrow-length (four fingers), or one *kauśika* (eight fingers), or even half a finger less;
the height of the *puṣkara* (the navel) is above the navel, reaching up to the edge of the breasts.
From the navel to the tip of the hand of fearlessness (abhaya-hasta) is recorded as being nine finger-breadths (guṇāṅgula);
from the tips of the breasts to the tip of the hand of fearlessness is desired to be twelve finger-breadths.
The region below the girdle should be level with the root of the penis;
at the base of the thighs, it should either touch the edge of the girdle or have a different quality.
Then, one should fashion the distance from the thighs to the middle of the body, and likewise the distance between the two knees, by means of two and a half parts or simply two parts, respectively.
One should fashion it with one, one and a half, or three [units];
alternatively, it is traditionally taught that from the middle of the knee, it should be one and a half finger-breadths.
The base, middle, and tip of the two shanks are respectively four, five, and six finger-breadths;
the middle of the two big toes is declared to be five finger-breadths.
The portion between the heels is said to be [the base]; from there, one should hang the lines.
On both sides of that, three lines should be drawn extending to the mouth, the ears, and the arms.
One should suspend those nine [strings] in the front, at the back, and in the middle;
having placed a long plank above them, one should cause them to hang down.
The thread should be positioned in front of the forehead, nose, heart, navel, genitals, and the middle of the two feet, so that it touches the nostrils and the belly.
[One should touch] the interior of the mouth, the pippalī joint, the root of the ear, and the nipple;
as well as the exterior of the ear, throat, and breast, and that which touches the hip. (17)
Having led [the cord] from the mouth to the interior of the base, another [cord] is considered to be touched by the arm;
in this manner, the best of teachers should suspend three cords along the sides.
At the center of the nape of the neck, the back of the head, the ears, the buttocks, and the heels, it should be suspended from the head so that it reaches as far as the back and the hump. 19.
O best of sages, the central thread should be situated within the body;
one should especially fashion the crown ornament (uṣṇīṣa) with three finger-breadths.
On both sides, in front, and behind, it is provided with four enclosures;
in the center there should be a crocodile-shaped pinnacle (makarakūṭa) joined with seven hollows (koṭara).

On the two sides there should be a leaf-ornament (patrakūṭa), and on the back there should be a jewel-ornament (ratnakūṭaka). Its front part should be ten finger-breadths long, while at its base is the width of the mouth.
I am not, however, that which consists of the three qualities; on my left is a half-moon, and on my left is a great serpent adorned with all ornaments.
One should form a knot with five matted locks specifically using three strands; one strand is wound once, while the remaining ones hang down at the sides.
This is indeed the crown of matted hair (jaṭāmakuṭa), declared to be the ornament for all;
it may be adorned with a leaf of jewels or even a leaf of conch-shell.
The left ear is adorned with a lotus leaf,
while the right is joined with earrings shaped like a crocodile and a lion.
The hair hanging down to the ears when asked about it, and the hanging of the tips of the matted locks from the sides down to the base of the arms. || 27 ||
The chest should be fashioned as joined with a pair of necklaces and likewise provided with a central medallion; the arms should be equipped with armlets. (28)
Adorned with beautiful leaf-shaped bracelets and embellished with every kind of gem, they were draped with hanging strings of pearls; and before them was a jeweled ornament.
The tips of his hands were adorned with bracelets, and his fingers were provided with rings; he was equipped with a secret hero’s upper garment, a sacred thread, and a waistband.
Adorned with all kinds of jeweled anklets and artificial faces,
it was joined with a waist-band and provided with a web-like network at the end of the feet.
Is Candraśekhara thus accompanied by the Goddess or not? Is she seated on the same throne or a separate throne, or is she embraced by the Lord? (32)
The deity may be embraced by her, or she may be embraced by him in turn;
the mantra may be joined with an embrace, or it may be without any break.
Thus the characteristics have been declared; now the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and so forth are being described.
The time is also indicated as before, and the offering of the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) is likewise.
One should perform the placement of jewels, the vision [of the deity], the liberation, the purification of the image, and the circumambulation;
thereafter, one should conduct the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsana) and lead the pavilion (maṇḍapa) as previously described.
One should construct sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) around [the central area] numbering nine, five, or one;
these pits should be circular, shaped according to the directions, or polygonal.
Afterwards, one should feed the Brahmins and then have them pronounce the "Puṇyāha" (auspicious day).
O best of the twice-born, the Vāstu-homa sacrifice should be performed at the spot where the pepper was placed.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should proceed to the preparation of the bed;
one should perform the ritual bathing, the tying of the protective thread (*kautuka*), and the mounting of the bed separately.
Then, one should worship the pitcher at the head-region and the *vardhanī* vessel to its north, while recollecting their forms as described in the technical manuals (*lakṣaṇa*). || 39 ||
Having placed eight jars all around, one should place them presided over by the Vidyeśvaras;
having likewise placed the principles (tattvas), the forms (mūrtis), and so forth, as before, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa).

Having prepared the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) and performed the consecration with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, sesame seeds, parched grain, and grains of indraka, as well as those known as vaṭa and udumbara; 41.
The Aśvattha and Palāśa trees are likewise considered suitable for fuel-sticks in the cardinal directions; the Śamī, Apāmārga, Śrīvṛkṣa, and Māyūra [trees] are for the southeast corner.

Having offered oblations for each [deity] as before, at the conclusion of the full oblation, the supreme preceptor, the Guru, should respectfully worship the deity, the water-pot, and the fires at dawn. (43)
Accompanied by the image-keepers with garments, gold, rings, and other offerings,
and having received the ritual fee (dakṣiṇā), he should perform the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) as previously described.
Having placed the jars in front of the image, one should deposit the seed-syllable from the *kumbha* into the heart of the deity; on its pedestal, one should deposit the mantra of the *vardhanī*.
If she is the Sahajā Devī, one should place her in his heart;
then, one should place the seed-syllables of the other [deities] all around the seat (pīṭha). || 46 ||
If the Goddess belongs to different seats (pīṭhas), one should perform separate pavilions;
at the conclusion, one should likewise cause the auspicious bathing ceremony and the raising of the image to be performed.
The preceptor should cause an abundant offering of food (naivedya) to be prepared and have it presented anew;
furthermore, whatever has not been mentioned here should be adopted from what is prescribed for the general installation rite.
Indeed, that man who performs the installation of Candramauli in this manner shall attain all his desires in this world and, at the end, obtain liberation. || 49 ||
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, the procedure for the installation of Candraśekhara, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
Four-armed and three-eyed, standing in the *samapada* posture,
he is endowed with the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), while his two frontal hands hold lotus buds.
Either the thighs and back are formed, or the waist is fashioned;
the other two hands, like deer-hooves, are positioned at the ends of the arms.
The *mṛgaṭaṅka* consists of the two hands positioned at the ends of the ears with the scissors-gesture (*kartarī*) applied;
the *mṛgaṭaṅka* is described as being either turned away from each other or facing toward each other.
But for each of those three lines, there should be a half-moon on the left or the right,
either with a jewel-pattern or a conch-shell pattern.
The chest should be fashioned as joined with a pair of necklaces and likewise bordered by a jeweled band (*karṇikā*); the arms should be fashioned reaching to the edge of that jeweled band,
and the arms should be equipped with armlets (*keyūra*).
Adorned with beautiful leaf-shaped bracelets, embellished with all kinds of jewels,
he wears a lower garment, an upper robe, a sacred thread, and a waistband.
Four-armed and three-eyed, he stands in the *samapāda* posture;
his two frontal hands are joined in the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*).
The left hand displays the boon-granting gesture (varada) and the right hand the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya);
the other two hands hold a deer and an axe, positioned at the ends of the arms.
When the two hands are positioned like a pair of scissors at the ends of the ears,
whether facing away from each other or facing toward each other, they are described as *mṛgaṭaṅkau*.
But for each of those three lines, one should draw a half-moon on the left or the right,
either with a jewel-patterned line or even with a conch-patterned line.
The chest should be fashioned as adorned with a pair of necklaces and likewise provided with a central medallion;
the arms should be equipped with armlets.
Adorned with beautiful leaf-patterned bracelets and embellished with all kinds of jewels,
he wears a lower garment, an upper robe, a sacred thread, and a waistband.
Would Candraśekhara be thus, together with the Goddess, or not?

Four-armed and three-eyed, standing with feet even in the *sthānaka* posture, his two front hands display the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*); the other two hands, holding a deer and an axe, are positioned at the ends of his arms.

When the two *mṛgaṭaṅka* [hand gestures] are positioned at the ends of the ears, either turned away from each other or facing one another, they are called *kartarī*. When the same [two] *mṛgaṭaṅkas* are tripled in size on the left and the right, they are known as the *ardhacandraka*.

The chest should be fashioned with either a jewel-patterned band or a conch-patterned band, joined by a pair of necklaces and likewise provided with a central medallion; the arms should be equipped with armlets.
Adorned with beautiful leaf-shaped bracelets, embellished with all kinds of jewels,
and bound at the waist with upper garments and sacred threads worn as coverings for the chest—
whether she sits upon a separate seat or is embraced by the Lord, she is present here.
49. In the forty-ninth chapter, the procedure for the installation of Purāri:
I shall now describe the installation of Purāri, as well as his characteristics.
He has four arms and three eyes, and is endowed with a crown of matted hair (jaṭāmakuṭa).
He was perfectly endowed with symmetrical proportions and possessed by a steady composure;
he was adorned with a makara-shaped earring resting upon his left ear.
He is joined with a black axe in one pair of hands,
and endowed with a bow and arrow in his other pair of hands.
The distance from the end of the hairline to the tip of the penis is nineteen finger-breadths (mātras), measured from the navel down to the wrist. || 4 ||
The middle part between the side and the upper arm is five finger-breadths (śarāṅgula);
from the base of the arm to the end of the hand, it is said to be sixteen finger-breadths.
Or else, the destroyer of Tripura has two hands, with his left hand abandoned by another;
his gaze is directed toward the head, to the right of the black orb.
One should suspend the measuring cord from the left nostril while standing on the right foot, O bull among sages, facing forward.

The distance between the heart, the navel, the genitals, the left foot, and the knees, measured along the plumb line, should be equal; the deity is situated in the left fire-sector (south-east), while the firm bowing occurs at the point of equality.
One should make the distance between the big toe and the heel ten parts;
or else, one should place Pārvatī on the left side, endowed with her characteristic marks.

Having performed this, one should then cause the installation (pratiṣṭhā) of the enemy of Tripura (Śiva) to be carried out at an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction, after having performed the rite of the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa).

One should perform the placement of jewels, the liberation of the eyes, the purification of the image, and the circumambulation; thereafter, one should lead [the deity] through the water-consecration, the ceremonial bath, and the tying of the auspicious thread.

Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the pavilion, one should construct sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) numbering nine, five, or one; these may be either angular or circular, or they may have as many corners as there are directions.
Having thus prepared the bed and placed Maheśvara upon it,
one should place the Śiva-pitcher and the Vardhanī vessel at the head of the Lord of Devas.
Having meditated upon the sacrificial oblation (caru) as described by its characteristics, one should worship it right there;
one should worship the eight jars and the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) surrounding that.

The Guru, having been meditated upon with offerings beginning with perfumes and ending with the food offering (naivedya), and having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the principles (tattva), the forms (mūrti), and so forth, should perform the fire sacrifice (homa). || 15 ||
Having consecrated the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the fire with fuel-sticks (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), cooked rice (anna), and sesame seeds;
[he should place branches] of the Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa trees in the directions starting from the east.
Śamī, Apāmārga, Śrīvṛkṣa, and Māyūra are [placed] starting from the southeast corner; and that of the principal tree, the Palāśa, is likewise on the left side in all cases. (17)
Having offered oblations for each [deity] as before, up to and including the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
then, on the second day, there is the satiation of the divine jar and the fire.
Having been honored together with the presiding deity (mūrtipāḥ) and having received the previously mentioned sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
one should then perform the ritual placement of mantras (manunyāsa) when an auspicious moment (sumuhūrta) arrives.
Having taken the seed-syllable from the pitcher, the Guru should place it in the heart of Śiva;
having taken the seed-syllable from the *vardhanī* vessel, he should place it upon that pedestal.
If the Goddess shares the same seat, one should place her within his heart;
if she has a separate pedestal, one should perform a separate pavilion for her.
The preceptor should subsequently perform auspicious rites and lead the ritual bathing at its conclusion;
he may then conduct a festival with abundant offerings, or he may not.
Whatever has not been stated here should be understood as being the same as what was said regarding the establishment of the general [mandala].
Thus, the installation of the Enemy of Pura (Śiva) has been fully described as the bestower of desired fruits. 23.
He who has thus caused this consecration to be performed with devotion shall enjoy manifold pleasures here in this world and, at the end, go to the state of Śiva.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, the procedure for the installation of the Enemy of Pura (Śiva), in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
He has four arms and three eyes, is endowed with a crown of matted hair, possesses a symmetrical posture, and is perfectly situated in the prescribed stance.
He is endowed with a crocodile-shaped earring situated upon his left ear,
and his two other hands are joined with a dark axe.
He is endowed with a bow and arrow held in his right hand;
the goddess is on his left side, while the enemy's hand is high and the arrows are at the limit of his private parts.
Or one should fashion Pārvatī on the left side with her characteristic marks;
having thus fashioned the enemy of Pura, one should then perform the consecration.
50. In the fiftieth chapter, the procedure for the manifestation of the Liṅga: The installation and other rites of the deity manifested as the Liṅga are now declared.
One should properly fashion the Liṅga according to the measurement of the womb (garbha), as previously described.
When the height of the *liṅga* is divided by five, four, six, or seven, one should discard the portion below the *śama*;
having discarded that same amount or half of it, [the measurement] above that interval is used.
One should properly fashion the form of Candraśekhara as before;
it should extend from the base of the *liṅga* up to the knees, and its dimensions should not exceed the range of the sense organs.
In the upper and lower regions of the *liṅga*, one should fashion the *haṃsa* and the *sūkara*;
one should respectfully construct the *haṃsa* according to the measurement of the face of the image.
One should draw a boar with its snout pulled toward the ground, facing away from the *bimba*; one should lead [the proportions] by parts of that *liṅga* using one, two, three, four, or five units.
Brahmā and Viṣṇu stood at his two sides, bowing and acting in accordance with him;
their feet were turned sideways, and they were beautiful in all their limbs.
He is renowned as Liṅgodbhūta, honored by Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
or he may be devoid of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, yet joined with Haṃsa and Sūkara.
Thus the characteristics have been taught; now the ritual for consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is described.
The time should be taken as before, and likewise the offering of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa).
Afterwards, having constructed a pavilion,
one should arrange therein sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) numbering nine, five, or one, surrounding it on all sides.
Indeed, there is no other way for the placement of jewels;
first the opening of the eyes, and immediately thereafter the purification of the image.
The circumambulation of the city and other sites, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) in the water, the decoration of the pavilion, and thereafter the Vāstu-homa sacrifice.
Or, at the outset, the wise man should have the demarcation of the ground performed as previously described;
then, having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) upon the altar (vedi), he should thereafter arrange a bed.
Then, having lifted the deity from the water, one should purify the image;
having performed the tying of the *kautuka* thread, one should lay it upon a bed.
One should fashion Brahmā and Viṣṇu beginning with the opening of their eyes;
one should place Brahmā on the right and Viṣṇu on the left.
Then, having wrapped it with cloths and worshipped it with perfumes and other offerings, one should place the principal pitcher at the head portion of those [images]. || 15 ||
The wise one should place the *vardhanī* vessel to the north of the *śivakumbha*,
and all around it, he should place eight jars representing the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*).
The preceptor should meditate upon the form as it has arisen from its characteristics;
having worshipped it according to the ritual with its forms, postures, and dispositions. (17)
One should assign the principles (tattvas), forms (mūrtis), and so forth of the god Brahmā-Viṣṇu as before; for the god Kavi-Viṣṇu, however, they are to be assigned as previously described.
Then the preceptor, together with the image-guardians (mūrtipas), should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) using sacrificial wood (samit),
rice, clarified butter (ājya), parched grain (lāja), sesame, mustard seeds, and bamboo shoots.
Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Plakṣa trees are in the directions starting from the east; Śamī, Apāmārga, Śrīvṛkṣa, and Māyūra are in the intermediate corners starting from the southeast.
The Palāśa wood is for the Pradhāna, and that too is always on the left;
having offered oblations with these substances in sequence to Brahmā and Viṣṇu as well, [one should proceed].
The Guru should perform the libation with sacrificial fuel and other offerings in the principal fire-pit;
then, having passed the remainder of the night, at the clear dawn, he should proceed.
The preceptor, whose self is perfectly pure and who knows the reality, together with the image-makers,
having extracted the images and worshipped them, [prepares] the fires in the sacrificial pits.
Having fully worshipped the preceptor and others, he should then cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given.
Prior to the auspicious moment (muhūrta) and the passing of the nāḍikās, he should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa).
Having lifted the jars from the altar, he should place them upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) situated in front of it.
Having taken the seed-syllable from the pitcher (kumbha), one should place it in the heart of the deity;
having taken the seed-syllable from the vardhanī vessel, one should consecrate the region of the feet.
Then, having performed the nyāsa of those [mantras] from the lords of knowledge (vidyeśas) upon him, one should bathe the Lord with their respective waters;
likewise, having performed the nyāsa of the seed-syllables of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, one should consecrate him.
One should perform the ceremonial bathing and worship, concluding with a festival;
afterwards, the preceptor should install the images to the south of Brahmānanda.
The preceptor should install Viṣṇu on the left side of the deity; whatever is not mentioned here should be performed according to the general rules for the installation of images.
Indeed, whatever man should thus perform the installation of the Liṅgodbhava,
he shall become wealthy and wise in this very world, and at the end, he shall attain union with the Divine.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, the procedure for the installation of the Liṅga, in the great Tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
One should properly determine the *liṅga* according to the measurement of the womb (*garbha*), as previously described.
If the *liṅga* is taller than that, one should subtract one-sixteenth from it, divided by five, four, six, or seven parts.
One should properly fashion the form of Candraśekhara as before;
below the liṅga, it should extend down to Śarva’s knees, remaining beyond the range of the senses.
One should fashion the Haṃsa and the Sūkara in the upper and lower regions of the Liṅga; one should respectfully construct the Haṃsa according to the measurement of the face of the Bimba.
The Boar has its face drawn down by the measurement of two *bimba*s;
Brahmā and Viṣṇu stand on its two sides, bowed and favorable toward it.
51. In the fifty-first chapter, the procedure for the installation of Dakṣiṇāmūrti:
O best of Brahmins, listen to the installation of the Lord of the South, which pertains to the threefold yoga consisting of exposition, song, and practice.
From the Vyākhyāyuk-jñānamudrā, Geyī is produced, endowed with a lute;
when deprived of two [hands], he is the Yogī, distinguished by various forms. (2)
He is four-armed and three-eyed, with a radiance as white as jasmine or the moon;
he is proclaimed to have a complexion like white coral, gold, or dark blue.
Either clad in a tiger skin or wearing divine garments,
he should be provided with an upper cloth and a white sacred thread.
Either with disheveled hair, or wearing a crown of matted locks,
or bound with a cloth band, he is endowed with a fine skull-cup.
Adorned with *dhūrtūra*, *āragvadha*, *nāgapatra*, and *candra*,
it is endowed with the five seals (*pañcamudrā*) and joined with the *gaṅgā* and *kiṅkiṇī*.
Again, he is seated upon a rock below the banyan tree,
or else he stands upon a tiger skin in the vīrāsana posture.
One should let the right leg hang down, resting upon that knee,
and form the stalk of the left foot with the *tumburu-mudrā* of the right hand.
Endowed with the gesture of showing (sandarśa), holding a book in her left hand, that book should have a length of thirty-two dance-measures (nṛttamātrā). || 9 ||
Alternatively, when the left hand is extended with the *nāga* [mudrā] joined,
one should recognize it as the *varada* [mudrā], with the wrist resting upon the knee.
When he holds the staff with his hand placed upon the forearm and the knee,
it resembles a blooming lotus, with the fingers extended downward.
In both his outer hands, he should be visualized as holding a rosary accompanied by flames, or else a lotus, a blue water-lily, or even a serpent. || 12 ||
The two arms should be fashioned as bracelets, with the eyes clear and even; the gaze should be fixed on the tip of the nose, or the left hand may hold a beautiful book.
One should draw a line with a slight curve from the left side through the middle of the body;
the thread [should extend] from the heart on the left, and then successively from the navel to the penis.
Having abandoned the measure, the time, and the portion, it stands in the middle;
with its feet hanging down, it is situated at a distance of half a finger-breadth from the central thread.

Increasing by half a finger-width (ardhārdhāṅgula) at each step until it reaches one and a half barley-corns (sārddhayava), the height from the base of the thumb to the tip of the breast shall indeed be [that measure]. || 16 ||

One should know that the distance between the eyes is one *madhyama* finger-breadth; from there, the distance from the thumb to the breast, and from the navel to the wrist, is declared to be *dhṛti* finger-breadths. (17)
The space above the hand holding a book, from the navel to the wrist, consists of nineteen units. (18)
From the middle of the chest and from the middle of the side, the distance between the two [shoulders] should be six fingers;
from the other wrist and from the middle of the arm, it should be nine fingers.
The distance between the two [shoulders] should be ten units from the base of the arm to the middle finger;
the height of the collarbone (hikkā) from the sūtra-line should then be two units, as should the elevation of the tip of the bracelet (kaṭaka).
From the very crown of matted hair, they have nipples reaching to their throats;
they are endowed with all the arts and wear white sacred threads.
Clad in white garments and the like, and adorned with sacred ash and rudrākṣa beads,
Kauśika is dark-complexioned, while Kāśyapa is yellow-hued.
Bharadvāja is red in color, and the two Gautamas have a smoky luster;
one should place one, two, or all three of these on the two sides.
Thus he should be the embodiment of exposition; thereafter, he is considered the embodiment of song (geyamūrti).
Both his right and left hands have bracelets at the middle of the upper arms.
The lute should first be placed like the right [hand];
then, while she is seated, he should place it upon her right thigh, which rests on the right hip.
Outside the thighs is the *kolaka*; its root is above the *kaṭaka*.
The left part is equal to that, while the four-faced part exceeds it by one part.
Its width is one kalā, while its circumference is as before; the width of its curved opening is six aṅgulas, or perhaps its length is also six aṅgulas.
That [measurement] should be doubled, and half of that should be the other; having understood this, one should proceed accordingly.
From the wrist to the end of the hand, starting from the *hikkā-sūtra*, it should be done in sequence. (28)
It has been stated that [the length] from the wrist is thirty finger-breadths;
the stalk (nāla) extends from there down to the navel, while everything else remains as previously described.
Thus, accompanied by an exposition,
he remained seated with his gaze fixed upon that [object], his eyes constantly contracted with speed.
The left hand should be extended; this is considered the Yogamūrti [form].
Then, with the left foot contracted, its heel placed upon the pair of hips— || 31 ||
Its knees are raised high, the staff-like arms are joined with beautiful elbows, the gaze is directed forward, and there is a slight bending as before. (32)
It was crowded with various wild animals and filled with diverse beasts of prey,
and it was frequented by various groups of sages as well as by Siddhas and Vidyādharas.
One should fashion that mountain adorned with spirits, kinnaras, and other flower-bearing trees; at its side, there should be a banyan tree on a grassy meadow.
Abounding with fruits, branches, and twigs, and frequented by various birds,
at its base on the right side, he sat in the shade, filled with compassion.
Seated with due respect upon a throne adorned with jewels and covered with an upper layer of tiger skin, together with the sages Kauśika and others.
They were the progenitors of the Śiva-dvija families, standing all around with minds imbued by the Āgamas, having been initiated by the Supreme Lord.
Thus have the different forms of Dakṣiṇāmūrti been illustrated:
that accompanied by exposition is declared to lead to knowledge, while that accompanied by song leads to enjoyment through the fire-sacrifice.
"Knowing that yoga is to be understood as the giver of liberation, one should practice it—whether sitting or standing, and whether surrounded by sages or not. (39)
Whether devoid of the banyan tree, or surrounded by spirits and the like,
or situated on a ground inhabited by spirits, it is declared to be Dakṣiṇeśa.
Thus the characteristics have been taught; now the procedure for consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is described.
The selection of the day and so forth should be undertaken as before, as well as the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa).
One should construct the pavilion as before, with nine, five,
or one sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) arranged around it, either facing the cardinal directions or having their corners aligned with those directions.

The placement of jewels, the two eyes, and liberation; likewise, the purification of the image, the circumambulation of the village, and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) in the water. || 43 ||
Then follows the sprinkling for the auspicious day (*puṇyāha-prokṣaṇa*), and afterwards the feeding of Brahmins;
or else the *puṇyāha* rite, the fire-oblation for the site (*vāstu-homa*), and the formal acquisition of the ground (*bhū-parigraha*). || 44 ||
Having performed the rites for the God of gods and for the sages as was appropriate, and having prepared a raised altar on the sacrificial ground, he should arrange separate beds.
On the bathing altar, O Śivā, one should have the ritual bathing performed by the sages;
then one should lay the Lord upon the bed along with the sages, such as Kauśika and others.
On the right side, however, one should also lay down Bharadvāja and the others on the right;
having adorned them individually with cloth, kūrca-grass mats, and so forth, one should cause them to lie there separately.
