This has been stated as the general rule for the Vyākhyāna, Geya, and Yoga [tantras].
One should place one's own jars, adorned with cloths and other ornaments, in the region of the head. (48)
The wise one should place the *vardhanī* vessel to the north of the *śivakumbha*;
he should then place the *vasu* jars on all sides, presided over by the *vidyeśas*.

Having worshipped according to the sequence with the forms, shapes, and substances, and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Reality, the Embodiment, and so forth, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa).

Having offered the *tattva*s and so forth as previously described, and having likewise performed the rites for the sages as prescribed, he should perform the consecration of the fire-pit and generate the Śiva-fire.

One should offer oblations of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, sesame, mustard seeds, and bamboo shoots; however, for the great rites and the principal offering, one should use the *palāśa* wood.

The oblations of *bailva* wood should be offered in the corners; one should satisfy the principal sages by offering these substances in sequence, concluding with the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Having thus dispelled the remainder of the night, at the clear dawn,
the Guru, having bathed along with the attendants of the deity's form, performed the consecration of the mantra-body.

Having worshipped and lifted up the images and the pitchers, and having worshipped the fires in the sacrificial pits as well as the preceptor and others, one should cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given individually.
Within a muhūrta, or at the end of the first hour (āḍikā), one should commence the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa).
Having placed the jars upon the pedestal (biṃbapura) on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) prepared as before, [one should proceed].
Taking the seed-syllable from the pitcher (kuṃbha), one should place it in the heart of Śiva;
taking the seed-syllable from the vardhanī vessel, one should place it upon its pedestal.
One should place the seed-syllables (bījas) of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) upon the pedestal, starting from Indra;
and with the waters of their respective pitchers, one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) of those respective regions.
One should also place the seed-syllables (bījas) of the sages within their hearts,
and then perform their ritual bathing with the waters from their respective pitchers.
The supreme guru should place the entire corpus of the Āgamas, beginning with the Kāmika and including its sub-divisions, into the books held in the hands of Śrīkaṇṭhamuni.
Thereafter, one should install the Lord of Gods, and the sages to his right and left;
then one should cause an extensive ceremonial bath, a festival, and abundant food offerings to be performed.
One should perform the installation of the unspoken general [form] as described for the spoken one;
the man who thus performs the installation of Dakṣiṇāmūrti [attains the goal]. || 62 ||
Having enjoyed all the pleasures here that his own soul desires,
he shall, at the end of the body, undoubtedly go to the Supreme Lord as his creator.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, the ritual for the installation of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, in the great tantra *Uttarakāmika*.
When accompanied by the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyāna*) and joined with the posture of teaching (*samāsya*),
with the eyes always slightly contracted through the application of the gaze (*akṣipātayoga*), and the left hand extended, this is considered the form of Yoga (*yogamūrti*).

Then, with his left foot slightly contracted and the heel placed upon the hip, the tips of his knees raised, and his arms beautiful with staff-like forearms; his gaze and the bending of his body are as described before.
He has four arms and three eyes, and his splendor is white like a kunda flower;
he is proclaimed to have the luster of white coral, gold, or a dark blue-black hue.
He may wear a tiger-skin garment or be clad in divine raiment.
He is endowed with an upper garment and a white sacred thread;
his hair may be disheveled, or he may wear matted locks in a crown, or he may have his hair bound with a cloth-band, or he may be joined with a fine skull-bowl.
Adorned with *dhuttūra*, *āragvadha*, and *nāgapatra* flowers, and decorated with the moon;
endowed with the five seals (*pañcamudrā*) and joined by the *gaṅgā* and *kiṅkiṇī*;
and furthermore, situated above a mountain at the base of a banyan tree.
Standing upon a tiger skin in the *vīrāsana* posture,
with the right leg hanging down and the left knee placed upon it,
one should position the left foot like a lotus stalk and the right hand in the *mudrā*.
He is endowed with the gesture of showing [the way], holding a book in his left hand;
alternatively, his left hand is described as joined with a serpent. In the other two hands, he holds a rosary and is provided with a net.

Thus should be the form of Vyākhyāna (the Teacher); thereafter, the form of Geya (the Singer) is considered as follows: the hands are raised with both bracelets on the right and left, and the vīṇā is held at the tip of the right forefinger, resting upon the bracelet.
One should place the ring on the right side of the thigh of the woman who is seated;
the pin, however, is on the outer side of the thigh, its base being above the ring.
52. In the fifty-second chapter: The Ritual for Alms-gathering and Consecration.
I shall here describe the characteristics of the alms-gathering and of the Skeleton [deity] as well.
O best of the twice-born, listen to the ritual for consecration, O most excellent of the twice-born! (1)
With one foot joined to the pedestal, endowed with four arms, wearing the sacrificial thread, peaceful, and the Lord ready for departure. || 2 ||
One should fashion that beautiful figure as adorned with ornaments, wearing a girdle of swords, gentle, radiant with a crown of matted hair, clad in white silken garments.
He holds a conch and a lotus leaf in his left hands, while his right ear is adorned with a crocodile-shaped earring;
his right foot is bent, and his left foot is firmly planted.
Alternatively, his own body may be endowed with symmetrical proportions and possessed of luster;
he holds a mace in his right hand and a drum (ḍhakkā) in his left, as described previously.
The tip of the middle finger of the right hand should touch the tip of the tongue of Kṛṣṇa;
likewise, on the other left hand, one should hold the staff, the staff of Time (Kāladaṇḍa).
The root of both these staffs is situated above the root of the trunk;
it is joined by various groups and crowded with various beings.
On the left, he is accompanied by a skull-bowl containing the sacrificial offering (bali) placed upon the head of a corpse, and is surrounded by many spirits (bhūtas) assuming various forms. || 8 ||
Amidst the sounds of drums, trumpets, and other instruments, and the clamor of singing and dancing,
women of faultless limbs were utterly enchanted by my performance.
With their ornaments and garments disarrayed, they were intent on offering oblations;
some were accompanied by blessings, while others were eager for embraces. (10)
Having led the thread from the crown of the head to the center of the forehead,
one should lead it for one finger-breadth (aṅgula) from the tip of the left nostril to the base of the big toe of the standing foot.
Leaving eight barley-corns to the right from the heart, three [units] to the right of the navel,
and seven finger-breadths to the left of the penis, there shall be the [central] portion.
The space between the two big toes is declared to be the measure of a *smṛti*;
that between the two heels is the measure of a *muni*; and the distance from the knees to the mouth is likewise [a *muni*]. (13)
Alternatively, the distance between those two is desired to be one and a half finger-breadths;
the curved section at the hand-stroke is the joint ending at the navel-limit.
That which extends from the navel to the wrist is called a "part" (bhāga);
it is the middle portion between the sides and the exterior, consisting of the mere elements (bhūtamātraka). || 15 ||
The hand reaching to the mouth of a doe should be equal in length to the middle of her thighs;
from the middle of her thighs to its tip, it should measure twenty-one mātrās.
With his face turned downward, he should maintain mindfulness of the ankle-joint, joined with the tip [of the tongue];
the middle and outer parts of the side [of the tongue] should be at the level of the middle, reaching only as far as the nether world (pātāla). || 17 ||
Holding a skeleton and a corpse in his hands, he should be as tall as the armpit;
the distance from the end of the arm to the wrist should be sixteen finger-breadths.
The peacock feather (piñcha) is said to be the size of the sun's orb, while the handle (daṇḍa) is one cubit long;
the length of the feathers should be equal to that, reaching as far as the tip of the nose of the deity. || 19 ||

O lords of sages, the wise man should fashion a skeleton staff for the Lord, reaching from below down to the throat; indeed, O masters of sages, he should cause a skeleton to be placed at the tip of the staff.
O God, women may become celestial maidens whose boundaries are defined by their breasts and navels;
likewise, all elemental forms may be created at will by the Three-faced One.
This very one is another god, naked and devoid of a skeleton; his matted locks are scattered and rest upon both shoulders, serving as his ornament.
It should be placed at the region of the waist and encircled with a serpent-thread;
one should likewise fashion the left hand holding a skull-cup and granting boons.
One should depict his other left hand holding a divine drum (ḍhakkā),
and his other right hand holding a peacock feather.
A serpent should be depicted standing at the side, with its head facing east and its mouth directed toward the left;
or one may arrange it so that it is joined with the left corner. || 25 ||
One should fashion the back of the hand with the skull reaching down to the navel;
from the navel to the wrist, it is said to be sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in length. || 26 ||
The ḍamaru should extend as far as the ear from the wrist of that hand;
it should reach the ear in sixteen mātrās, and the remainder should be like the skeleton.
Hara is said to be the one who wanders for alms, either joined with Viṣṇu separately or not;
O best of sages, I shall now briefly describe his installation.
The time is indicated as before, and likewise the ritual of the "sprout" (aṅkura) has been described;
then, having performed the placement of jewels (ratnanyāsa) upon the deity and the spirits in due order.
The wife sits on a separate seat, and the supreme guru sits with her in one place;
or else, he should perform the placement of jewels for Kṛṣṇa and the others.
Having performed the opening of the eyes and subsequently the purification of the image,
one should carry out the preliminary ritual of the immersion in water (jalādhivāsana) followed by the circumambulation of the village.
Having approached the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa), one should arrange it as before:
nine, five, or one fire-pit (kuṇḍa) shaped like a circle, with corners facing those directions.
Having dismissed the artisan, the wise man should feed him for the sake of his purification;
he should perform the Puṇyāha rite and the Vāstu-homa, and prepare separate altars and beds.
Having set aside their ritual bathing and the protective thread (kautuka) separately, one should purify them;
the deity is in the center, his consort to his right, and the elemental beings (bhūtas) to his left.
One should have everyone depicted according to their actual appearance, adorned individually with garments and other ornaments;
however, if there is a separate skeleton-staff, it should be laid down at the region of the head.
One should place the water-pot (kumbha) and the prosperity-pot (vardhanī) between Śakra and Śaṅkara;
and for the others, one should place the pot upon the head and the excellent vardhanī.

Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa), the Guru should worship [the deities] with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, joined with their respective mantras; he should worship Vīreśa in the Bhūta-kumbha with the mantra "Salutation to Vīreśa."
One should worship [the deity] with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), saying "Salutation to Nandanā," in the vardhanī vessel;
then, having placed Kaṅkāla in the Kaṅkālakumbha, one should install the principles (tattvas) and the rest.
The principles (tattva) and so forth [are assigned] to Śiva as before; however, they are stated again for Vīreśa.
The forms (mūrti) should be as before, as well as Pramukha and Durmukha. (39)
Pramoda, Tatāmoda, and Vighnarāja are the presiding deities of the forms;
as stated by Viṣṇu, one should likewise perform the fire-oblation during the Kaṅkāla period.

Having performed the consecration of the sacrificial fire-pit (kuṇḍa), one should perform the oblation (homa) with fuel-sticks (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), cooked rice (anna), parched grain (lājaka),
sesame seeds (tila), and indraka-grains, together with unbroken rice (akṣata).
The Palāśa, Khadira, Aśvattha, and Udumbara are prescribed for the cardinal directions;
the Śamī, Vaṭa, Śrīvṛkṣa, and Māyūra are for the intermediate corners starting from the southeast.
Even in the case of the principal [deity], there is the same [procedure] for the *palāśa* leaf; and that [leaf] is always on the left.
However, the preeminent teacher, having invoked the deities in the principal [spot], should offer libations.
Then, on the second day, the libation was offered to the gods, Kumbha, and Agni;
they were worshipped with garments, gold, and other offerings by the image-keepers, who received their sacrificial fees.

Then one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa); having placed the water-pots before the image, one should take the mantra from the pitcher and place it in the heart of the deity.
Having taken [the seed-syllable] from the Vardhanī vessel, one should place it upon its lotus-throne;
having taken the seed-syllables from the others, one should deposit them in their hearts.

At the conclusion of the installation, the preeminent teacher should cause the deity to be bathed with the respective waters from the jars, perform the great festival of bathing, and present the food offering.
The general rule for what is to be included when not specifically mentioned is as stated in the section on installation;
the mortal who acts in this manner shall attain a meritorious state.
The placement of all the limbs, including the central line and the other lines, should be at intervals of two finger-breadths each.
The number of hands, as well as the garments, ornaments, and seals (mudrās), the colors such as white and others, and the postures of the deities are established [as follows]. 50.
O twice-born ones, this rule regarding the teacher, the artisan, and the patron—according to their desire for beauty—is indeed common to all deities. (51)
The foundation for these [practices] everywhere is whether or not one possesses the state of a child;
and regarding the wandering for alms, the foundation is likewise said to be the [meditation on] skeletons. (52)
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, the ritual procedure for the alms-round and consecration, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.

The Lord was equipped with sandals on his feet, endowed with four arms, wearing a sacrificial thread, peaceful, and intent on departing; he was gentle, with a bound sword, and radiant with a crown of matted hair.
Or else, she has symmetrical limbs, her own body endowed with beauty,
joined by various gaṇas, surrounded by various beings,
and is joined on her right side by a skull-bowl situated above the head of a corpse.
This very Supreme Deity should be depicted as naked and devoid of a skeleton, adorned with matted locks hanging down on both sides,
and his waist region encircled by a serpent-string.
One should fashion the left hand as granting boons (varada) and holding a skull-cup;
the other hand situated on the left side should be joined with a divine drum (divyaḍhakkā),
and the other hand situated on the right side should be made to hold a peacock feather.
He should be depicted resting on the side of a serpent, positioned in the eastern-left corner facing the deer-faced [deity],
joined with the left corner; alternatively, one may conceive him as being provided with sandals upon his feet and endowed with four arms.

One should depict that beautiful and adorned Lord as performing a sacrifice, peaceful, and intent on departing; he is gentle, wearing a bound sword, radiant with a crown of matted hair, and clothed in silken garments.
In her left hand she holds a conch and a leafy branch, and in her right a crocodile-shaped earring;
her right foot is bent and her left foot is firmly planted on the ground.
She carries a mace in her right hand and a drum (ḍhakkā) in her left, while the two front hands hold [the previous objects].
The tip of the middle finger of the left hand should touch the tip of Kṛṣṇa’s tongue;
in the other left hand is a peacock-feather fan and a staff of death (kāladaṇḍa),
the bases of both staffs resting upon the upper part of his shoulder.
Accompanied by various groups and crowded with various spirits,
he should hold an oblation vessel (*balipātra*) containing non-left-hand (right-hand) spirits upon its rim;
holding a skeleton and a peacock feather in his hands, his height should be equal to that of an armpit.
53. In the fifty-third chapter, the ritual for the installation of the Lord Bali: I shall now describe the installation of the Lord Bali and its characteristics.
Regarding the daily festival, it has been stated that the [measuring] cord and other elements should be as white as the moon.
Or else, for the sake of expiation and so forth, or for the accomplishment of all desires,
one should perform the daily festival (nityotsava) with those [same] mantras, especially with the excellent ones.
O lords of sages, I shall briefly describe the consecration:
the time, the sprout-rite, the ritual with jewels, and the liberation through the vision.
Purification, circumambulation of villages and other places, and remaining in water have already been explained; therefore, one should perform all such acts accordingly.
One should have a pavilion constructed there, containing nine, five, or one sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). The pits may be circular, angular, or have as many corners as there are directions.
O twice-born ones, among the three alternatives, the circular pit (kuṇḍa) is indeed the most excellent;
thereafter, having dismissed the artisan, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas there.
Having performed the *puṇyāha* sprinkling, one should cause the *vāstu-homa* sacrifice to be performed;
then, having brought the image out of the water, one should lead it to a bath with clay and other substances.
Then, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should bind the protective thread (kautuka).
Afterward, one should prepare a bed; first, a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) should be made upon it.
One should cause the Lord to lie upon the bed, adorned with red garments and other ornaments;
as before, one should place the jars around the Śiva-jar.
One should worship the deity named Pāśupata with weapons in the Śiva-pitcher, which is richly adorned with fine cloth at its top; all [the deities] are adorned with garments and other ornaments.
Then, having meditated upon the form described by the characteristics of the Tārā, [one should worship her] with perfumes and other offerings,
using the mantra "huṃ phaṭ" followed by the name in the dative case.
With the mantra "Dīpaṃ ślīṃ paśu-pūrvaṃ ca huṃ ca phaṭ namaḥ," one should worship the complete deity known as Pāśupata.
The vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *au* are considered to be the *sadyojāta* and other [faces];
the mantras beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *phaṭ* are the *hṛdaya* (heart) and other [limbs]. || 13 ||
The mantras, beginning with *oṃ* and starting with the *hṛdaya*, are properly divided according to rule;
they are accompanied by the *hṛdaya* and other limbs, ending with *huṃ phaṭ* or *namaḥ*.
And by means of the form born from the cavity of the heart, or even by the subtle body of knowledge (vidyādeha),
which is fashioned from the syllable *huṃ* and filled with the [essence of the] lake.

The Guru should worship the eight weapons, beginning with the vajra, all around; then, having offered to the principles (tattvas) and the lords of the principles (tattveśvaras), he should install the forms (mūrtis) as before.
The wise and supreme preceptor should install the lords of the forms, such as Vajra and the others;
having performed the consecration of the sacrificial pits and prepared the fire of Śiva.

One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the previously mentioned root-mantra and the limbs of Brahmā, using clarified butter, cooked rice, grains, sesame seeds, parched grain flour, and the aforementioned number of offerings.
The best of gurus should perform [the rite] together with the mantras of the True Form (Tattvamūrti) and others;
and in the directions starting from Indra (the east), there should be Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa trees.
The *śamī*, *khadira*, *śrīvṛkṣa*, and *pippala* trees [should be placed] from the southeast corner;
even for the principal [fire], there should be a *palāśa* tree, and on the second day one should perform [the rite].
Having fully worshipped the preceptor and the others, one should then bestow sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Then, placing other jars in front of the image, one should recite the mantra from that [central] jar into one's heart.

One should install the lotus-seat of that [deity] and install its retinue; one should perform the ceremonial bathing, the festival, and offer abundant food offerings, or else cause them to be performed.
One should perform the installation as previously described for the general case where it has not been specifically mentioned;
thus should one who performs the installation of the weapon-deity (astramūrti) act. (23)
And he indeed attains happiness, both in this world and in the next, as well as liberation. || 231/2 ||
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, the ritual for the installation of Balibhartṛ, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
54. In the fifty-fourth chapter, the ritual procedure for the consecration of Śarabheśvara:
I shall now describe the consecration of Śarabheśvara, preceded by its defining characteristics.
[The image] should be shaped like a bird, golden-hued, and endowed with two wings.
It was endowed with upraised wings, possessed two red eyes,
and was equipped with four feet in the form of lion-paws.
Equipped with very sharp claws, standing upon the feet of the Vedas,
endowed with a divine tail, and possessed of well-spread matted locks.
Above the neck, it has a human form, endowed with divine ornaments;
it has the face of a lion, fearsome tusks, and is possessed of terrifying prowess.
He saw Narasiṃha, who was destroying the world with his fierce impulse for destruction,
yet whose massive body remained motionless as he stood with palms joined in reverence.
Viṣṇu, whose body was bent low and whose face was turned upward, had eyes like lotus petals;
he stood with two feet in the sky and two within his belly.
One should have the god Śarabheśvara fashioned facing the sky;
having thus described his characteristics, his mantra is now told.
The first seed-syllable of the eight groups [of consonants], adorned with the fourteenth [vowel], endowed with the sixth vowel, and accompanied by the bindu and nāda. || 8 ||
Śārambha is said to be the seed-syllable (bīja), and Śarabheśvara as well;
thereafter, Hariharas is likewise [the name], with these two words ending in the dative case.
At the beginning, one should employ [the mantra] joined with the Praṇava and ending with a salutation for the sake of Śarabheśa, for the attainment of desired success in worship and other rites.
The preceptor should fashion the Brahma-mantras and the limbs with the first syllable;
the first becomes Vajradeha, the consumer, and the disjoiner.
Māraṇa, Udīrghahasta, Tīkṣṇadaṃṣṭra, and Jaṭādhara— these eight, who are fond of offerings, are stationed starting from the eastern direction.
In worship, consecration, and other rites, these [mantras] are situated in order around [the deity];
the extraction of these mantras occurs by means of the first syllable of their respective names. (13)
One should fashion Śarabheśvara from materials such as stone and the like,
and then perform the consecration on a day when an auspicious lunar mansion is rising.
One should have the rite of offering the sprouts performed according to its specific injunctions;
one should also perform the unbinding of the eyes, the offering of jewels, and the ritual placement (nyāsa).
The purification of the clay and other materials, the circumambulation starting from the village,
and the preliminary ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsana) should be performed separately for Viṣṇu and Śiva, as previously described.
Having constructed a pavilion as before, with nine square sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas),
provided with either five fire-altars or a single fire-altar.
One should perform the removal of the architect (the image), the sprinkling of auspicious water,
the feeding of Brahmins, the removal of their remnants, and then the final cleansing once more.
The declaration of an auspicious day, the worship of the site (vāstupūjā), the fire-rite (agnikārya), the preparation of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍilakalpana),
the bed, the ceremonial bath, and the binding of the marriage-thread (kautuka) are to be performed as previously described.
One should lead the two [deities] separately onto their respective beds; as previously stated, the foot should be placed according to the deity, with the head toward the eastern direction.
O Lord, having placed Hari upon a broken seat with his left side facing down,
and having wrapped him in a red cloth, one should begin the installation of the water-pot.

One should place the Śiva-pitcher and one should place the Viṣṇu-pitcher; together with their threads and covers, and provided with cloths and other items, they should be positioned near the head [of the deity].
Having offered water-pots filled with gold, garments, and other such items,
accompanied by sacred threads and water, and empowered by Vajradeha and the other [deities], || 23 ||
The Guru, knowing the previously described nature of the individual soul (aṇu), should worship it with perfumes and other offerings;
having invoked it from the heart-center into the manifested form and performed the ritual of integration (sakalīkaraṇa).
Having performed the ritual with the heart-mantra and having invoked that mantra with the root-mantra,
one should worship Viṣṇu as previously described, after having consecrated him with the Śarabheśa-mantra.
O God, one should first cause the installation of the forms (mūrti) and their lords (mūrtīśa);
for it is traditionally taught that the forms are Vajradeha and the others, while their lords are known as [the respective deities]. (26)
Then, having performed the consecration of the sacrificial pit and the fire,
one should perform the oblation with fuel-sticks of the *pālāśa* tree, as well as with clarified butter and sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
Having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with sesame seeds, parched grain, and the best of crops, together with the mantras of the presiding deities of the forms,
on the second day there shall be the worship of the fire, the water-pot, and the gods.

Having received the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), being satisfied and honored along with the guardians of the deities (mūrtipās), the Guru should duly commence the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa). || 29 ||
Having consecrated other jars in front of the Lord of Devas,
the Guru, having taken the seed-syllable from the jar, should place it in the heart of Śarabheśa upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Taking the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu, one should place it in the heart of Narasiṃha;
taking the seed-syllables from the others, one should place them around the lotus of the pedestal.
One should bathe the Supreme Lord with the waters from each of those pitchers;
having performed the ritual bathing, one should present the food offering and conduct the festival.
Having thus installed the deity, one should worship it every day;
the mode of worship shall be as before, but the mantras used should be those of Śarabha.
One should perform the ritual for the bathing festival and its preliminary rites according to the prescribed rules;
and the Preceptor, by means of mantras, should destroy those belonging to the faction of his enemies.
Upon the arising of all diseases, one should destroy them with this mantra;
by means of this ritual, one should bring about subjugation, attraction, and enmity. || 35 ||

One should perform the installation in this manner for the Lord of the Śarabha-mantra, just as the general procedure for installation was stated for those [mantras] not specifically mentioned here. || 36 ||
O twice-born ones, I consider that by means of devotion and meditative cultivation, such is the extent of his mass of merit after he has enjoyed its fruits in this very birth. (37)
He shall obtain those desired things even in the next world, as well as the state of lordship.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, the ritual procedure for the installation of Śarabheśvara, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
Having the form of a bird, golden-hued, and endowed with two wings;
joined with upward-pointing wings and possessed of three red eyes.
One should visualize [the deity] with lion-like feet, endowed with four arms,
and possessing the four Vedas as its feet standing upright, joined with nine very sharp [lines].
Endowed with a divine tail, beautifully spread out and possessed of matted locks,
its upper neck is human in form and joined with a divine crown.
He had the face of a lion, possessed terrifying fangs, and was endowed with formidable prowess;
he was a Man-Lion who was intent upon the destruction of the world.
Viṣṇu, whose eyes were like lotus petals, stood with palms joined in reverence, his great body motionless, his form bowed down, and his face turned upward.
With his two feet placed upon the sky and his belly resting against it,
one should represent the god Śarabheśvara as facing toward the heavens.
55. In the fifty-fifth chapter: The Ritual for Bestowing Grace upon Caṇḍeśa and Others.
Now, O Lord, I shall fully describe the installation of Caṇḍeśa Nandīśa, who effects the grace of Viṣṇu, preceded by its defining characteristics.
Then, the most excellent of teachers should have an image of the Moon-crested Lord (Candraśekhara) together with Umā fashioned, either on the left or on the right.
Thus, [one should meditate on Him] extending from the knees to the navel, up to the breasts, chest, throat, and face;
whether He is seated comfortably or standing, accompanied by joined palms in the añjali gesture.
One should fashion Caṇḍanāyaka, my devotee, who is endowed with a divine gaze,
beautiful in all his limbs, and measured at ten *tāla*s in height.
O bestower of boons upon the gods, with the other [hand],
he should encircle the tip of the garland around the head of Caṇḍa, O God.
However, a certain distinction is desired for the temple of Nandīśvara:
[the deity should be] two-eyed, two-armed, peaceful, and with palms joined in reverence. (6)
One should fashion him with matted locks well-spread, adorned with a crown of matted hair,
accompanied by a slight bend [of the body], and intent upon hearing the sacred tradition (āgama).
One should cause Nandīśvara to be propitiated first according to the prescribed measure;
for the grace of Nandīśvara is thus obtained, and likewise, it brings about the favor of Viṣṇu.
Having left Ānandīśvara, he beheld Viṣṇu there, endowed with his characteristic marks,
holding a discus in one hand joined in añjali-mudrā, and a conch and a lotus in the other two hands.
O King, one should certainly cause this discus of the Viṣṇu-form to be fashioned;
likewise, one should cause Śiva to be fashioned as being inclined toward bestowing grace upon others.
Thus the characteristics have been taught; now the procedure for consecration is described, including the sowing of seeds on the appropriate day and the arrangement of jewels in both locations.
The opening of the eyes, as well as the purification and circumambulation of the city and other sites,
the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the thread, and the preparation of the sacrificial pavilion.

O twice-born ones, the construction of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas)— whether circular, square, or having eight corners— numbering nine, five, or one, is to be performed according to the characteristics previously described.
O Brahmin, [there should be] the expulsion of Takṣaka, the offering of food, the sprinkling of merit,
the Vāstu-homa on the altar, and separately the sacrificial mound and the bed.
The ceremonial bath (snapana) and the tying of the protective thread (kautuka) for the deities should be performed separately as before;
then, having caused [the deity] to ascend the bed, one should lead [the deity] to lie down upon it.
If the gods, desiring to bestow grace, are seated upon a broken seat,
O Lord of Gods, one should lead them to a bed at the feet of the deity.
On the shoulder-region of the Supreme God (Viṣṇu) are Śiva’s water-pot and the *vardhanī* vessel;
these are considered the eight forms intended for the grace of the gods.

O best of sages, having grasped the specific perfection of each respective chapter and performed the consecration of the sacrificial pit and fire, one should commence the oblation with the ritual materials.
With sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, sesame, and unbroken rice, one should proceed in order;
first, there should be palāśa, vaṭa, plakṣa, and udumbara wood.
The Śamī, Khadira, and Śrīvṛkṣa trees, as well as the Aśvattha, should be placed in the southeast corner;
the Palāśa tree should be for the principal deity, and it should be situated to the left of all [the others].
The Guru should satisfy Caṇḍanandīśa and Viṣṇu in the primary [offering];
then, for the expiation, he should perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) separately, accompanied by the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Then, in the second [rite], the guru who knows the reality, being purified by the guardians of the forms (mūrtipas),
having worshipped and raised up the deities, [places] the fires from the jars into the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
When eight muhūrtas have passed, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with concentration;
having been worshipped by the image-bearers (mūrtipas) and others with garments, oblations, rings, and so forth.
Having received a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of ten niṣkas or more, the teacher, with a satisfied mind,
having prepared the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), should place water-pots (ghaṭas) in front of the image along with streams of water.
Having taken the mantra from the pitcher (kumbha), one should place it upon the heart of Śiva;
having taken the mantra from the vardhanī vessel, one should place it upon its pedestal (pīṭha). || 25 ||
If [the practitioner] desires the Goddess to be on the same seat, he should place the mantra in her heart;
having taken the seed-syllable from the others, he should place it around the perimeter of the pedestal.
One should place the respective mantras upon the pitchers for the deities beginning with Caṇḍeśa;
one should also consecrate each respective deity with the water from its respective pitcher. || 27 ||
One should cause the ceremonial bathing, the festival, and abundant food offerings to be performed anew;
if the Goddess is seated upon separate pedestals, the Guru should cause the rite of auspiciousness (kalyāṇa) to be performed.
And if a mortal acts in this way, he shall attain liberation at the end.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, the procedure for the grace-bestowal of Caṇḍeśa and others, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
Then, the best of preceptors should cause the form of Candraśekhara, accompanied by Umā, to be fashioned either on the left or on the right.
Thus, [the deity] is situated in the knees, thighs, navel, heart, breasts, throat, and mouth;
whether seated comfortably or standing, he is endowed with palms joined in the añjali gesture.
Having abandoned Nandīśvara in that [mandala], one should fashion Viṣṇu, endowed with his characteristic marks,
holding a discus and a lotus in two hands and a conch and a lotus in the other two hands;
for this form of Viṣṇu, the Discus-armed Lord, one should have [an image] made.
Then, the most excellent of teachers should have [the image] made with Umā accompanying him, in the form of Candraśekhara, either on the left or on the right.
Thus, [the deity] is situated within the knees, thighs, navel, breasts, chest, throat, and mouth;
whether seated comfortably or standing, he is accompanied by joined palms in the *añjali* gesture.
One should fashion my devotee Caṇḍanāyaka, endowed with a divine gaze,
beautiful in all his limbs, according to the measurement of ten *tālas* for the smallest size.
O bestower of boons upon the gods, with the tip of the garland and the other end as a bracelet,
the god should encircle the head of Caṇḍa with the garland.
However, regarding the temple of Nandīśvara, a certain distinction is prescribed:
[the deity] has two eyes and two arms, is peaceful, and has his hands joined in the gesture of reverence (añjalipuṭa).
One should depict him with matted hair well-spread, adorned with a crown of matted locks, possessing graceful curves, and intent upon hearing the sacred scriptures.
One should first cause that gracious Nandīśvara to be propitiated with prostrations.
56. In the fifty-sixth chapter: The Ritual for the Installation of the Deity Who Bestows Grace upon Devotees.
O best of the twice-born, listen as I shall fully explain the installation of the deity who bestows grace upon devotees, preceded by its defining characteristics. 1.
The deities beginning with Sadāśiva have already been explained;
they alone are intent on bestowing grace, desiring to favor their devotees. (2)
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, sages, and human races; from ants to elephants and all others—whatever is moving and whatever is stationary. || 3 ||

O twice-born ones, they are declared in the scripture to be worthy of favor; for favor is considered manifold, consisting of initiation, exposition, touch, sight, speech, and [the gift from] the mouth.
That man whose body is presided over by Śiva, even if he meets death,
shall become Śiva himself, freed from all sins.
Therefore, he who, at the time of departure, touches his own chosen *liṅga* and effects the release of the vital breath (*prāṇamokṣa*), becomes Śiva himself; of this there is no doubt.

Having clearly articulated her lineage and other details, and having fashioned a physical form endowed with beautiful features—whether seated, standing, or even reclining—one who possesses auspicious marks; || 6 ||
Having fashioned an image with hands joined in the añjali mudrā using materials such as iron and others, the wise man should install it, beginning with Sadāśiva.
Then the wise preceptor should fashion that seat and the form of that deity;
such is declared to be the characteristic of the Lord for the purpose of bestowing grace upon devotees. (9)
Now I shall describe the consecration; listen, O best of the twice-born!
The time is prescribed as before, and likewise the ritual of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa).

Likewise, the placement of jewels, the opening of the eyes, the purification of the image, the circumambulation of the village, and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) take place in the middle [night]. || 11 ||
One should perform the rite known as the Pratiṣṭhā-maṇḍapa according to the previously stated procedure;
there, one should have sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) constructed, numbering nine, five, or one.
The [structures] should be made square, or the principal one should be circular;
then follows the ritual dismissal of Takṣaka, the enjoyment by Brahmins, and the sprinkling of meritorious water.
The preparation of the sacrificial mound, the bed, the bath, and likewise the tying of the auspicious thread;
the mounting of the bed and the installation of the water-pot should be conducted as before. (14)
The pitcher for the devotee at his feet, endowed with the respective meditations, accompanied by the self-mantra, and joined with the pitchers of the Vidyeśvaras; || 15 ||
In the same manner, one should perform the placement of the forms and so forth according to the previously stated procedure;
having performed the consecration of the fire-pit and other elements, one should carry out the fire-oblation (homa).
O twice-born ones, with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, sesame seeds, bamboo, and barley—
using [branches from] the Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Nyagrodha trees starting from the eastern direction [and proceeding clockwise].
The Śamī, Apāmārga, Śrīvṛkṣa, and Plakṣa trees belong to the domain of Agni; however, the Palāśa is the primary one, for its very nature is that of fire itself.
Then, on the second day, having performed the worship of the Kumbha and the fire,
and being honored with garments, gold, and other offerings, they were accompanied by the image-bearers and those who had offered water for the feet.
Having received a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of ten niṣkas or more, the preceptor, with a satisfied mind,
should then perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), having first placed the water-pots before the image.
Having taken the mantra from the pitcher, the preceptor should place it upon the heart of the deity;
if the deity is joined with the goddess, then the preceptor [should place] the goddess-mantra.
One should place [the mantra] upon the heart of the Goddess, or otherwise upon the pedestal;
thereafter, one should always bathe those two with water from the pitcher.
Then one should place the seed-syllable of Bhaktakumbha within the heart of Bhakta;
having taken the seed-syllables from others, one should place them around the pedestal (pīṭha).
One should reverently bathe the pedestal even with the water remaining in the pitcher;
at the conclusion, one should perform the ceremonial bath and then offer the food oblation (naivedya).
There should be a festival at the conclusion of that; this has been declared as the general rule.
The specific details, such as those concerning the destroyer of Tripura (Śiva), are prescribed in the ritual manuals for installation (pratiṣṭhā). || 25 ||
Likewise, those who are endowed with devotion and the ritual procedure prescribed for installation—whatever mortal acts in this manner shall attain a meritorious state. || 26 ||
One seeking a son obtains sons; one seeking wealth shall obtain wealth;
one seeking a deity attains a deity; and one seeking liberation shall attain liberation. || 27 ||
Whatever enjoyments a man desires, he shall obtain them all, provided that his son or even his grandson performs [the rite] on behalf of the deceased. (28)
Or else, while still living, one should make oneself known by the name of Śiva.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Installation of the Deity for Bestowing Grace upon Devotees," in the great tantra known as the *Uttarakāmika*.
Having properly articulated the lineage and other details, and having fashioned a physical form with distinct features,
one should visualize her as seated, standing, or even reclining, endowed with auspicious marks.
Having fashioned an image of Sadāśiva and the other deities out of materials such as iron, the wise man, with palms joined in reverence, should install it.
57. In the fifty-seventh chapter, the ritual for the installation of Kālāri-Kāmaghna: I shall describe the installation of Kālāri, the destroyer of desire, endowed with the proper characteristics.
He has four arms and three eyes, and is adorned with a crown of matted hair.
With his left foot tucked up, clad in a tiger-skin garment,
he then raised his right foot, possessing sharp fangs and a formidable nose.
A trident is held in the right hand and a needle in the left;
alternatively, an axe is held in the right hand and a serpent-noose in the left.
The trident of the god Kaṭākṣadṛṣṭi is situated in Kāladeva; it is said to be facing downwards, or else it is located within the Kālakuṇḍa.
The distance from the tip of the needle-seal (sūcimudrā) to the navel is the limit;
from the wrist of that hand to the middle of the side is one kalāngula.
From the wrist-joint of that hand to the tip of the spear held at the ear, the distance to the tip of the ear should be two tālas;
this is equal to the length of the other hand.
The interval from the tip of the ear to the wrist is proclaimed to be one *yava*;
likewise, the head, the right hand, and the left nostril and so forth [are measured] constantly.
The thread should lie in front, from the right side of the navel to the tip of the left foot;
from that thread, the root of the genitals on the left side is considered to be the interior.
The thread is said to be drawn on the left side at the distance of the standing knees;
indeed, it should be level with the height of the knee of the raised foot and the front of the waist.
From the middle of the shank to the tip of the sole is known as the *samocchraya*;
the heel-tip of the right foot should be at the fifteenth [mark] on the southern thread.
The two bracelets on the hands of another, and likewise that which is held in the hand of one with a spear;
that thread should be known by the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśvara) as being the measure of a barley grain (*yava*) by means of the right [hand]. (11)
From the sūtra, the knees should be joined, and the [length of the] leg should be seven guṇas;
the top of the raised sole should be equal in measure to the shank.
One should depict Kāla as having fallen down, with eyes rolling and fainting,
vomiting blood, wearing red garments, and likewise having reddish hair.
Holding a trident and a noose, with outstretched feet, a face made terrible by fangs, and blood-red eyebrows and eyes. || 14 ||
One should have [the image] made nine tālas in height with the pride of being a divine abode;
or else, one should respectfully have it made with hands joined in the añjali gesture at the proper time.
Alternatively, one should lead away that which has fallen from the Liṅga after it has been removed;
or, according to the measurement of the Kālānta-liṅga, one should lead it away as previously described for the emergence of the Liṅga.
Another stands with three bends, facing [the deity], his body smeared with ashes;
Mārkaṇḍeya stands at his side, excellent, with his hands joined in a flower-offering gesture.
One who is afraid of time should act; one should be content with whatever is granted by Hara, whether it be joined with long life like that of Mārkaṇḍeya, or even devoid of it.
Whether accompanied by the foot or not, when situated within the body of Apasmāra,
he is thus called Kālāgni and is said to be the destroyer of Manmatha.
One should cause Manmatha to fall instantly by the mere casting of a glance upon Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who is established in yoga.
Having divided [the height] into ten parts, one part at the beginning and seven parts for the rest, the height of Manmatha is prescribed; it is adorned with gold.
Resembling pure Jāmbūnada gold, he was joined with the five-arrowed flower;
likewise, the fish-bannered god was joined with the form of a sugarcane bow.
The one called Devabhāgavasantā is beautiful even when joined with Mitra;
likewise are Lambhinī, Tāpinī, Vedinī, and Drāviṇī. (23)
They say that Māriṇī is named Śara; the bow is on the left, and the arrows are on the other side.
Manmatha, joined with Mitra, or alone, is [represented] by a single arrow.
Thus the characteristics have been declared; now the procedure for consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is described.
One should prepare the day, the sprouts, and the sacrificial pavilion as previously [stated]. (25)
O twice-born ones, one should construct sacrificial pits in the pavilion according to the number nine, eight, or one, shaped as triangles, circles, or squares, aligned with the cardinal directions.

Immediately after the placement of the jewels and the opening of the eyes, the Guru should perform the purification of the image, the circumambulation of the village, and the preliminary consecration in the water as before. (27)
One should perform the rites for the deity and for the time separately; likewise, the bed, the sacrificial altar, the ground, and the bathing should each be performed separately.

At the time of the god’s desire for sleep, the bed should be prepared at the place of the deity's feet; one should perform the tying of the marriage-thread (kautuka) and the mounting of the bed separately, as previously described. || 29 ||
One should place the Īśa-pitcher in the region of the head and the Vardhanī pitcher to its north;
then, while recollecting its mantra, one should place the Kāla-pitcher in the region above that head.
If Kāma is present, one should place a jar richly adorned with cloth and other ornaments in the region of his head;
if he is accompanied by Mitra and Abhaya, two jars should be placed for those two as well.
The Guru [approached] two friends named Devabhāga and Vasanta, who were lying on beds arranged at the sides of Kāma and were joined together.
One should place [the vessel] enriched with cloth and gold, surrounding it with cloths as before;
then, one should worship those [vessels], which consist of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), with perfumes and other offerings.
Having performed the placement (vinyāsa) of Tatveśvara and the others, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
O God, the principles (tattvas) and so forth are as previously stated for Kāmatas, according to what has been taught.
One should also place the presiding deities (mūrtīśas) of Kāla, who possesses five forms; the pervasion (vyāpti) of the principles (tattvas) known as Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva is thus intended.
From Sound (Śabda) up to Time (Kāla), and likewise up to Īśāna, the forms are designated as before; [the seasons] known as Spring and Summer [are assigned]. (36)
The lords of the forms (mūrtīśvaras) are considered to be the rainy season, autumn, and winter;
having performed the consecration of the sacrificial pit and the fire with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, and sesame seeds— 37.
One should offer unbroken rice, parched grain, fried paddy, and mustard seeds in sequence;
and branches of the Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa trees in the directions starting from the east.
The *śamī*, *khadira*, *māyūra*, and *śrīvṛkṣa* trees should be placed in the southeast corner;
the *palāśa* tree should be at the principal [entrance], and it should be on the left side in all cases. (39)
The wise preceptor should then determine the time for the principal [rite];
having thus passed the remainder of the night, at the clear dawn, he should proceed.

The most excellent Guru, his own self perfectly purified, having worshipped and extracted the *biṃba*, [performs] the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) upon the jars and the fire situated in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). (41)

Honored with garments, gold, rings, and other offerings by the image-makers and others, and having received the ritual fee (dakṣiṇā), he [the preceptor] should then proceed at an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction of stars.
Having placed the jars in front of the *biṃba*, while recollecting the *śivakuṃbha*,
and having respectfully placed that of Śiva upon its pedestal, one should place the *karaka* upon it.
One should place the seed-syllables of Vaidya, Īśa, and Kumbha all around that pedestal;
having taken the mantras from others, one should place them in the hearts of those respective [deities].
One should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana), abundant food offerings (naivedya), and a festival; or one may perform them anew.
Whatever has not been mentioned here should be carried out according to the general rules prescribed for installation (sthāpana).
Thus, the mortal who performs this, having enjoyed his desired pleasures, attains the Lord again at the end of the body; of this there is no doubt. || 46 ||
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, the ritual procedure for the consecration of Kālāri-Kāmāntaka, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
He has four arms and three eyes, is adorned with a crown of matted hair,
stands with his right leg slightly bent, and is clothed in a tiger skin.
Then [he appeared], holding the foot of Dakṣa in his teeth, with sharp fangs and a formidable nose;
a trident was in his right hand, or else a needle was in his left hand.
The axe is held in the right hand, and the serpent-noose is in the left;
the side-glance of the God is fixed upon Kāla.
The trident (śūla) is said to be facing downwards, situated at the throat of Kāla;
it is joined with the needle-gesture (sūcīmudrā), its tip reaching up to the hands and its base reaching as far as the navel.
From the tip of the raised sole up to the shank, one should visualize it as mere memory;
however, one should make that fallen portion have closed eyes and be unconscious.
One should have [the image] made at a height of nine tālas according to the pride of the deity;
or else, one should respectfully have it made at the appropriate time with palms joined in reverence.
Alternatively, one should lead the [image] that has fallen after emerging from the *harāliṅga* to the first *kālāntaliṅga*,
in the manner prescribed for those born from a *liṅga*.
The excellent Mārkaṇḍeya stood at his side with his hands joined in a hollowed gesture of reverence.
One who is afraid of time should act with contentment and humility;
whether engaged in inference or free from it, one should follow the path of Mārkaṇḍeya.
58. In the fifty-eighth chapter, the ritual for the consecration of Kalyāṇamūrti:
I shall describe the consecration of Kalyāṇamūrti, endowed with its defining characteristics.
He is joined with matted hair and a crown, with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament.
The God is described as having three eyes and four arms, proud of his fresh youth, standing in a frontal posture with his body held straight. (2)
With his left foot drawn in and his right foot standing [on the ground],
he possesses the luster of the hand of the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva) and is endowed with two hands of another.
One who possesses excellent left hands suitable for holding water,
or whose right hand is taken up by one's own [wife], is possessed of a tranquil mind.
One should hang the cord from the tip of the nose down to the middle of the breasts on the right;
then from the middle of the navel to the left, and likewise to the outside on the right.
Having reduced each finger by one unit, it should be equal to the line of the navel; the height of the back of the excellent hand is the circumference between the wrists.
Likewise, from the middle of the arm to the end of the side, there should be an interval of nineteen [units];
O best of sages, the interval to the end of the flank should be six units.
The perpendicular distance from the root of the penis to the hip of this [image] is said to be eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas),
extending from the navel to the wrist.
It is traditionally taught that from the middle of the arms to the ends of the sides is the measure of five finger-breadths (śarāṅgula);
likewise, the distance between the two big toes is equal to the distance between the two heels of the face.
The space between the two knees is declared to be one kalā;
the distance between the two hands is considered to be like a half-moon or a lotus petal.
O best of Brahmins, the measurement of the goddess has been described here as before:
the distance from the goddess's eye to her chin, and from her armpit to her nipple. (11)
To the left side of that goddess stands the goddess Śrī, endowed with all auspicious marks,
her two hands joined as they touch the hips of the goddess.
O Śrīdevī, the navel and the space between the arms are likewise [measured] by twelve parts of the sun (twelve finger-breadths);
the distance between the two big toes shall be eighteen finger-breadths.
Thus, the Śrīdevī is proclaimed to be at a distance of one rasa-aṅgula from the two heels;
she extends from one-tenth of the height of the deity up to eleven parts.
Ten million times that portion was Śyāma, endowed with a crown and diadem,
holding a conch and a discus, and grasping them with both hands.
Equipped with a water-pot and a staff, he is declared to be Viṣṇu;
one should cause his gaze to rest from the tip of the nose down to the end of the big toe.
The center of the navel from that thread is recorded as being one *veda* [four finger-breadths] in measure;
the height and width of the water-pot (*kuṇḍikā*) are considered to be one *tāla* and one *aṅgula* respectively.
The height and width of its neck are one *kalā* and one *kolaka*;
the mouth is said to be five *aṅgulas*, and the height of the nose is one *kolaka*.
Its root should be at the tip of the kalā, and its shape should be like a mouth;
the height of that lotus is one aṅgula, and from its root to its tip it measures three [aṅgulas]. || 19 ||
With five [fingers], one should place the right hand of Hari upon the sprout-like left palm;
above that, one should position the right hand for the falling of the stream.
The water-pot (kuṇḍikā) should reach the height of the root of the hand, and the navel-line should be level;
from the navel to the wrist, it is traditionally taught that this constitutes the measure of a single element (dhātu).

From the wrist-joint on the other [right] hand, however, up to the edge of the water-pot (culuka) by way of seven [units], there should be the Varada mudrā and two bracelets on both the left and right hands. 22.
According to the measurement prescribed by Hari, one should also have Brahmā fashioned,
four-faced and four-armed, adorned with matted hair and a crown.
Facing the fire, with a serene countenance, resembling the powder of saffron,
he was girt with a belt of muñja grass and provided with the sacred thread as an upper garment.
The two hands other than the left, raised upwards, hold a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) and a book (vakṣa);
the two hands other than the right, located at the front, display the gestures of granting boons (vara) and fearlessness (abhaya). || 25 ||
The two wild [lines], ending at the wrist and the mouth [of the hand], are accompanied by the action of the *sruva* ladle;
the thread [is drawn] across the forehead, the tip of the nose, the middle [of the face], and between the navel and the ankles. (26)
From the navel to the end of the thighs is ten parts;
from the navel to the base of the big toes is ten fingers' breadth.
The *abhaya* [mudrā] extends from the tips of the nipples to the navel; the *maṇibandha* [mudrā] extends to the middle of that.
In between those, the *viśvamātṛ* [mudrā] extends to the ends of the sides of the arms, [measured] by the six [rasas]. 28.
The space between the knees and the upper body is proclaimed as the form of Brahmā; likewise, it is situated in the lotus posture (padmāsana). || 29 ||
The diameter of the fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa), which is provided with three circumferential ridges (mekhalā), shall be twenty-two finger-breadths according to the measurement of the deity's fingers.
O best of sages, it is said that each girdle (mekhalā) shall be one finger-breadth [in width];
its breadth shall be twelve finger-breadths, and its length shall be seven tongues [of fire]. (31)
This fire, possessing five tongues and ten thousand flames, stands in the middle of the sacrificial pit;
it is the measure for the hand-threads starting from Śiva, which differ by two [units].
The raising of the hands and feet, as well as other limbs, is described here;
likewise, their bending, contraction, or even extension. (33)
This is the established method for the collection of treatises on the bow, arrows, and so forth;
likewise, the regulation of weapons is enjoined by all the scriptures. (34)
Having seen only the end of all that which is set forth in the scriptures, [one understands] all ornaments according to the distinction between the left and the right. || 35 ||
O best of the twice-born, the viewing of all images should be performed in this very same manner for all goddesses, and especially for those such as Nara and others. (36)
Thus the characteristics have been explained; now the procedure for consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is described.
Having determined the time as before, and having performed the rite of offering sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) as previously done, || 37 ||
The best of teachers should install Brahmā to the left of the deity, Viṣṇu to the north, and Lakṣmī with Gaurī to the south. (38)
Afterwards, one should place the nine gems upon the Lord of Gods, Hara;
and for the remaining ones—Brahmā, Gaurī, and the Goddess Śrī—one should place gold.
Then, having performed the liberation of vision (*dṛkmokṣa*) according to the method taught in that chapter,
one should perform the circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*) of the sanctified image, the city, the village, and so forth.
One should cause the Lord to dwell within the center between the right and left [hands];
one should place Brahmā and Viṣṇu on the two sides, and Ambikā and Śrī on the flanks of Brahmā.
Having reached the sacrificial pavilion prepared as before,
[one should perform the rites] in the eastern, southern, and northern directions, provided with three bathing altars.
To the east of this, in the place of Āpyendu, there was a well-constructed maṇṭapa, provided with nine, five, or one sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) shaped like a womb (yoni). || 43 ||
The bathing of the Goddess, accompanied by her three brothers, is declared as before;
and likewise, in the pavilion of the God, there are nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in number.

The best of those skilled in ritual design should fashion [the mandalas] as having five or one [units] in number, resembling squares, or with corners corresponding to the directions, or else circular.
After dismissing the artisan, one should then feed the Brahmins;
likewise, there should be the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), the Vāstu-homa sacrifice, the preparation of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), and the ritual bed.
The ceremonial bathing of Keśagaurī and the various auspicious rites for the goddesses Śrī and Devī should be performed separately;
one should then cause the deity to lie upon the bed on the left and the right sides.
Then the Guru should have Kṛṣṇa lie down upon a separate bed;
and in the pavilion of the Goddess, he should place the Goddess Śrī on the right side.
One should place the fire to the north, having separately prepared a bed;
one should cover the God with a red cloth and the Goddess with a yellow one, as should Keśava.
The preceptors should be gathered in each excellent pavilion by Kṛṣṇa with a white lotus and by the Grandfather (Brahmā) with one of that same color.
The preceptors, those bulls among sages, should be honored for each respective deity;
and upon the head of the supreme deity, one should place the Śiva-pitcher (śivakumbha) and the vardhanī vessel.
One should place two jars at the head-regions of Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
one should place other jars all around, presided over by the Vidyeśvaras.
O Goddess, one should place three jars at the head-region of the fires of Śrī Pāvaka,
and eight jars presided over by Vāmā and the others should be placed all around.

One should worship each of the deities individually with offerings beginning with perfumes and ending with food oblations, [visualizing them] as having the forms arising from their respective marks and as being endowed with meditative concentration and autonomy.
O Lord, one should cause the placement of the principles (tattvas), the forms (mūrtis), and so forth for the [deity] to be performed as before;
for others, one should place the principles and so forth as described in their respective chapters.
Then the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed after having prepared the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the fire;
[it is offered] with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, sesame, mustard seeds, and mudga beans.
The *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *vaṭa* trees are in the directions starting from the east; the *śamī*, *apāmārga*, *śrīvṛkṣa*, and *māyūra* are in the southeast corner. (57)

But at the principal [offering], because it is made of *palāśa* wood, [he should offer] on the left side in every case; having offered daily as before, the best of teachers, at the conclusion of the full oblation— || 58 ||
One should sleep either in one's own house or in that place for the sake of pacifying exhaustion;
then, having performed the daily rites at dawn, the practitioner should worship the Guru.
Accompanied by garments, gold, rings, and other items, along with the image and the water for the feet;
at the conclusion of that, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of five niṣkas or more.
Having placed the jars before the image, one should deposit the seed-syllable;
then, taking the seed-syllable from the *vardhanī* vessel, one should place it in the center of the Heart-mantra of the Goddess.
If Umādevī is innate (sahajā), she is divided within the center of the seat (pīṭha); or else, the goddess is divided across the seats, and one should place the mantra pertaining to her [there]. 62.
Having taken seeds from others, one should place them around the pedestal;
having worshipped them, one should perform the ceremonial bath and worship as prescribed for the ritual of adoration.
Having offered the food offering (naivedya) with this mantra, one should perform the festival of consecration (pratiṣṭhotsava).
O best of the twice-born, listen to what special feature there is in this regard.
Just as she is considered the Goddess of the gods beginning with Sadāśiva, so too should that Goddess be worshipped in the *Svatantra* [Tantra], O Lord Padmanābha. 65.
When [the images] are installed outside of palaces, pavilions,
and so forth, their placement of hands and other limbs is according to their respective directions, starting from the east.
Or rather, they should be made so that they obtain beauty and possess strength;
their goddesses should be placed at their side, or else not turned away.
In all the tantras, in no way whatsoever are deities such as those mounted on bulls, nor goddesses such as Dakṣiṇeśā and others, ever approved [as primary objects of worship]. (68)
Just as the deities on the walls of a palace obtain distinct songs through their installation, so too a mortal who acts in this manner shall attain his desired fruit. (69)
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, the ritual for the consecration of the Auspicious Form, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
Adorned with a crown of matted locks, having the crescent moon as his crest-jewel,
possessing three eyes and four arms, he is proud of his fresh youth.
The posture known as Sthānaka is proclaimed to be characterized by equal bending;
in it, the left foot is contracted while the other foot remains standing.
With hands resembling those of the Moon-crested Lord, he is endowed with two excellent hands;
his left hand is particularly suited for holding water.
Or, with a serene mind, the right hand may be held by one's own right [hand] as previously described; O best of Brahmins, the measurements for the Goddess here are:
the eye, the mouth, the chin, the armpit, and the navel.
Then, on the other side of that goddess, stands the goddess Śrī, endowed with all auspicious marks;
her navel is like the center of the sun,
and from one-tenth of the height of the goddess, she extends for eleven units.
Dark-complexioned, adorned with a crown and diadem,
holding a conch and a discus in his two hands, and further endowed with a water-pot, he is declared to be Viṣṇu himself.
According to the measurement of Hari, one should also have Brahmā fashioned;
four-faced and four-armed, adorned with a crown of matted locks, facing the fire-oblation, serene, and resembling the powder of saffron.
He should be endowed with a girdle of muñja grass and a single lock of hair, wearing a sacred thread and an upper garment;
his two right hands should be raised, holding a water-pot and a rosary,
while his two left hands should display the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness.

O best of the twice-born, the casting of the *sruva* ladle, the performance of the rites, and the fashioning of the *kaṭaka* and *āmukha* ornaments for all [images], as well as the arrangement of all ornaments according to the distinction between left and right, must be observed for all idols.
59. In the fifty-ninth chapter, I shall explain the ritual procedure for auspicious rites (*kalyāṇa-karma*). This auspicious rite is also [performed] among all the eternal deities;
it should be performed at the auspicious moment previously mentioned, either on that very day or on the following day.
On the third or fourth day, during the daytime or at midnight,
[he should perform the rite] at a water-booth, in a pavilion, or in a chosen location smeared with cow dung.
Having prepared an altar there, covered with a white cloth,
one should install the Lord of Gods upon it, adorned with ornaments worthy of his majesty.

Accompanied by the five great sounds of musical instruments, with parasols, fly-whisks, and mirrors, and with various incenses and lamps, he was brought forth on palanquins and other vehicles. || 4 ||

One should place the fire, personified as the deity's form, upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) made of sand and other materials situated in front and facing east, between the deity and the sacrificial mound.
To his left is Aja, with a gentle face and a face turned toward the south;
and on his right side is Viṣṇu, adorned with garments and ornaments.
The preceptor should offer water for the feet, water for sipping, a pair of fine garments,
and an upper cloth for the purpose of a covering to the Lord’s heart.
Having placed the fire upon the sacrificial ground, one should perform the five purificatory rites (saṃskāras);
having worshipped Śiva together with his six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), along with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and grains.
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) accompanied by all the ornaments,
the preceptor should establish Gaurī and Īśvara within his heart on the left side.
One should offer water for the feet, water for rinsing the mouth, and the respectful offering (arghya) with that same mantra;
one should then offer an auspicious thread to the Goddess with the heart-mantra.
One should cause a pair of garments to be given for the purpose of an upper covering;
then, one should place Lakṣmī, beautiful in all her limbs, at the side of the Goddess.

O Lord, the Guru—born of a twice-born family, having thoroughly studied the Śiva-āgamas, and being devoted to Śiva—should bind the *kautuka* (sacred thread) upon the God and the Goddess with his whole being. (12)
Wearing a turban and an upper garment, and adorned with the five-fold ornaments, another preceptor of serene intellect was pointed out by this preceptor. (13)
Wearing two garments and a ring, and having meditated upon his own body as being like that of Viṣṇu,
he should offer water with both hands and a water-pot while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
In the other hand, which belongs to Śiva, he should afterwards apply ashes to both [hands];
then he should cause the declaration of "an auspicious day" (puṇyāha) to be recited, as well as the hymns (sūkta) by those who have the Vedas as their wealth.
One should satisfy the fire with sixteen fuel-sticks using the Śiva-mantra and its limbs;
then, one should offer the Madhuparka mixed with jaggery, milk, and ghee to the Lord with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
One should offer water for sipping (ācamana) with the mouth [mantra], and again,
having offered sixteen oblations of clarified butter (ājya) with the heart mantra, one should then offer another sixteen with clarified butter.
Having offered the food oblation and side dishes, and having performed the rite of peace with the heart-mantra,
one should also offer betel-leaf with that same mantra, having praised the Supreme Cause.
Having made it thirty *darbha* blades in length, tied with a knot and measuring two *tāla*s,
and having meditated upon it as the "Hand of Śiva," one should place it on Gaurī’s heart with the *hṛdaya*-mantra.
Therefore, the Guru should mutter the principal seed-syllable into the right ear;
then, having placed a stone upon a mound of rice on the sacrificial ground, [he should do the same] in the left ear.
Having grasped the goddess’s right ankle with the previously mentioned Śiva-hand,
the Guru should place it upon that very stone while reciting the Heart-mantra.
Then, by the command of the Lord, one should satisfy Viṣṇu with the Uṣṇīṣa and other mantras;
having first prepared four hands of darbha grass as before.
One should visualize two hands of Śiva and two hands of the Goddess;
then, having kindled the fire of Śiva, one should cast [the offerings] with those respective hands. || 23 ||
With his hand, adorned with rings, he likewise [offered] exceedingly white, pure parched grains (lāja) purified by the Astra-mantra to the Preceptor and the others.
He should offer [the oblation] into that fire with the *hṛdaya-mantra* while reciting the *Śivānuṣṭubh*;
then, having circumambulated the fire clockwise, the Guru should touch a stone.

Having given the gift of parched grain and performed a circumambulation following the rightward path, and having likewise completed this other [rite], one should then offer the oblation with the *vyāhṛtis*.
Having performed one hundred and eight [recitations] and having offered the final oblation at the end with Śiva,
he should dismiss that Śiva, together with his limbs (retinue), who resides in the fire, as before.
Then, having extinguished the Śiva-fire, one should discard that ash after worshipping it with abundant perfumes, flowers, garlands, and other offerings.
Then, on the fourth day, one should have the fourth rite performed;
either on that very day or on another, during the daytime or at midnight.
When the fire has been consecrated with the five purificatory rites (saṃskāras) by means of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and grains,
one should offer one hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra alone, and ten oblations for each of the [other] Śārṅga-mantras.
Having offered one hundred oblations with the Adhōrāstra mantra, he should offer the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Śiva-mantra.
He should provide a bed made of skins and other materials, or he should cause five garments to be brought.
Having purified that [image] with the armor-mantra (varman) and placed it upon a new wooden stool,
one should install the couple there and gratify them with cakes and other offerings.
One should have the ceremonial bathing (snapana) performed, or at its conclusion, the festival of Śiva;
whether the deity is mobile or immobile, one should install it upon its throne.
The learned one should lead the god Dvīśrīya as the bearer of oblations (vahni) before him;
to the left of the fire, or to the left of the goat, he should place Aja, Hari, or the reverse.
In this very way, O twice-born ones, one should perform the marriage rite for other deities, as well as for Ambikās of different seats and for the primary Liṅga.

However, in the case of the Śrī Haribera, where the Brahmabera has been abandoned, one should perform the worship by honoring those [deities] upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with perfumes and other offerings. || 36 ||
Having brought forth the primary liṅga from the inner sanctum to the pavilion and having installed the Goddess upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should perform the marriage rite.
He who performs the consecration rite for one of such auspicious form should do so with all these groups of his own kinsmen, remaining unwearied. (38)
Endowed with long life, prosperity, and fame, and accompanied by sons, grandsons, and others, he shall obtain happiness in this world that is difficult even for kings to attain. (39)
O best of the twice-born, my devotees who have been consumed by fire do not return; they go to the unsurpassed state of Śiva at the very end of their bodies' feet.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, the procedure for auspicious rites, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
60. In the sixtieth chapter: The procedure for the installation of Viṣṇu-mūrti.
I shall now describe the installation of the image of Viṣṇu-mūrti, endowed with its specific characteristics;
one should especially fashion the image from materials such as stone and the like.
O Dakṣa, O elder brother, [he] has Umā as half [of his body] and is marked by the crescent moon.
The left hand holds a skull-cup together with matted hair,
and on the right side of the forehead, it is joined by half an eye.
The ear-ornament (patra) should be on the left ear, joined even with a small ball (vālīka); it should be made together with a conch-shell earring (kuṇḍala), or otherwise without that [ball].

One should meditate upon the Goddess as holding a ṭaṅka and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) in her right hands, and a blue lotus in her left hand; she is radiant with weapons or has her eyes fixed upon a mirror.
The mirror should be circular in shape like a face; its handle should be half that size.
Its tail-end should be shaped like a bud, and it should be resplendent with ornaments on its base.
The left half [of the body] is depicted as breastless, adorned with variegated garments, clad in a tiger skin, and with the left foot drawn up. || 7 ||
The left foot is well-placed and adorned with an anklet; it is accompanied by a graceful bend, and there is a downward inclination toward the knee and the toes. (8)
The left [hand] should have the luster of emerald, and the right should resemble a gem;
[these are located] at the navel, heart, and private region, on the left, the right, and the left [respectively].
Having set aside the portions on the moon (the left side), one should lead the thread from the front foot to the middle of the chest;
thereafter, the thread for the height of the hand of the lotus (the navel) and for the nipples.
It is said to be twelve finger-breadths, or even all-finger-breadths (viśvāṅgula);
the middle part of the two arms, however, is six finger-breadths in the middle.
The middle of the heel to the big toe should be fifteen finger-breadths;
O lords of sages, the remainder should indeed be made according to the words of Candraśekhara.
Thus, O twice-born one, [the rite for] Ardhanārīśvara is completed; now hear that for Haryardha.
Having performed the half for Maheśa as before, one should perform the other half for Viṣṇu.
He possesses two arms and holds a conch; a bracelet is considered appropriate there.
He is endowed with yellow garments and adorned with all ornaments. (14)
O Moon-crested One, the remaining work, such as the laying of the thread and so forth, should be performed;
one should likewise carry out the division of Hari’s half and the portions of Brahmā and the others.
Having thus brought it to completion, one should then perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
