O best of Brahmins, listen now to that consecration in brief. || 16 ||
The time was previously ordained; likewise is the offering of the sprouts, the placement of jewels, the opening of the eyes, and the purification of the image with clay and other materials. (17)

One should perform the circumambulation of the city and other sites, as well as the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) in the water; this is declared to be the general procedure for installation, which one should carry out according to the prescribed path.

However, O Devāṇu, the preceptor should cause half a share to be joined with the Kāraṭas; for the offerings of mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa) and the planets, one should prepare a single sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
One should fashion a single quadrangular pit (kuṇḍa) toward the east and south;
then, having dismissed the artisan, one should thereafter feed the Brahmins.
Having performed the sprinkling of merit (puṇyodasecana), one should then lead [the image] to the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Upon that, one should prepare a bed, along with the ritual bath and the protective amulet (kautuka) separately.
The wise one should bind the cord on both front hands;
having performed the act of ascending the bed, he should reverently lay the deity to rest.
The preceptor should place the Śiva-kumbha upon the head-region of the deity,
and he should place the Vardhanī upon the head-region of Umā.
If it is Viṣṇu, the preceptor should place the Viṣṇu-pitcher upon the region of its head; having meditated there upon that respective half-portion of the body, he should perform the worship.
Having placed water-pots filled with parched grain and presided over by the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas),
the supreme preceptor should lead [the procession] with offerings such as perfumes, garlands, incense, and food oblations.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the principles (tattva) and their respective lords (īśvara), one should contemplate their pervasive presence (vyāpti).
Having placed the eight forms of the earth (kṣmāmūrtyaṣṭaka), one should also place the lords of those forms (mūrtīśa).
However, a certain distinction is prescribed regarding the placement of the lords of the forms:
Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra, Citta, and Balotkaṭa. (27)
One should install Dhātrī and Vibhvī, and then Indra and the others, as well as the directions (kāṣṭhā) and so forth, in their proper sequence;
for the installation of Viṣṇu’s half [image], one should install Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, and Rudra.
Puruṣṭuta, Viṣṇu, Govinda, and Vittanāthaka—
these are the forms in the Nyāsa consisting of the five mūrtis, according to the previous method.
The knower should place Brahmā and Keśava from the west, but Gaurī and Īśāna in the northern half; furthermore, he should place Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
Then, one should duly install Janārdana and Puruṣṭuta; furthermore, on the right side of Viṣṇu, one should also install the lords of the five forms.
One should place the Śiva-mantra on the portion belonging to Śiva, and that mantra elsewhere; one should then assign the Saṃhitā mantras, beginning with Īśāna, to the other half of the deity.
In that very place, one should apply other deities, as well as the seed-syllables (aṇu) and mantras spoken by the gods;
likewise, having understood them through proper reasoning, one should deposit other mantras as well.
Having consecrated the sacrificial pit, he should then generate the fire therein;
having invoked the forms and the lords of the forms situated in their respective directions.

The preceptor should perform the fire-oblation with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, sesame seeds, bamboo, and barley, using all the mantras as before for the principal deity.
The Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa trees are in the directions starting from the east;
the Śamī, Apāmārga, Śrīvṛkṣa, and Āyūrā are in the southeast corner.
Even though the *palāśa* may be used for the primary [deity], some distinction is desired:
on the half-month of Viṣṇu, the *tulasī* is for the secondary [deity] and the *palāśa* for the primary one. (37)
Then, on the second day, one should worship the gods, the water-jars, and the fires with perfumes and other offerings, as well as with garments, gold, and finger-rings.
Having worshipped the Guru with offerings such as an image and water for his feet, one should then cause him to receive a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
When an auspicious moment has arrived, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa).
One should sequentially place the mantras of the pitcher (kumbha) and the vardhanī on the portion belonging to Śiva and Umā;
however, in the half-portion belonging to Viṣṇu, one should place the mantra of the vardhanī upon the pedestal (pīṭha).
One should place the seed-syllable of Kṛṣṇa from the jar of Kṛṣṇa within the heart of Kṛṣṇa;
having taken the seed-syllables from the others, one should place them all around that pedestal.
One should cause a festival to be held, along with an abundant ceremonial bath and food offerings;
whatever has not been mentioned here should be adopted from what was declared regarding the installation of the deity.
The installation of Viṣṇu and Māriṣa is said to lead to both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, the procedure for the installation of Viṣṇu and Umā, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
The left half is Umā, while the right body is that of Hara;
the former has matted hair and a crown, and is marked by the crescent moon on its forehead,
whereas the latter has a karṇikāra-flower crown and is adorned with a garland of skulls.
On the right side of the forehead, there should be a petal joined with half an eye;
on the left ear, there should be a petal joined even with the hairline.
One should fashion it with a conch-shaped earring on the right, or otherwise without it.
He holds a ṭaṅka and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) in his [right] hands, while an utpala lotus is in his left hand;
he is a portion of Umā, endowed with breasts, adorned with variegated garments,
clothed in a tiger skin, and his right foot is intended to be bent.

The left foot should be well-placed and adorned with an anklet; it should possess a graceful bend and be inclined toward the *kolaka* and *aṅgulaka* positions. O lords of sages, the remainder should indeed be performed like that of Candraśekhara.
Having performed [the rites] as before, one should place half of Mahendra and half of Viṣṇu on the other side;
the conch accompanied by two arms is considered to be the bracelet there.
Endowed with yellow garments and adorned with all ornaments,
the remainder— beginning with the laying of the ritual lines (sūtrapāta)— should be like that of Candraśekhara.
61. In the sixty-first chapter: The Ritual for the Installation of the Threefold Form (Trimūrti).
I shall describe the installation of the Threefold Form, preceded by its defining characteristics:
[The deity] is red in color, has three eyes, and his hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Dark-complexioned and equipped with an axe, adorned with a crown of matted locks,
he likewise approached straight on, standing upon only one foot.
On both sides, the southern and the northern,
above the region of the hips, he is endowed with the half-bodies of Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
One should fashion the pride (māna) of Brahmā and Viṣṇu as being equal to that of the woman;
they are considered to have their palms joined in reverence and to stand upon one foot.
Alternatively, those two [deities] may be placed on either side of the Śiva-liṅga with their heads bowed;
or they may be installed separately, seated upon a single pedestal.
Alternatively, the Liṅga may be situated in a separate shrine in the center;
Brahmā and Viṣṇu are likewise considered to be on its right and left sides respectively.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva are considered to be the three forms [of the Divine], whether they abide in separate abodes, or in a single abode, or are joined together in a unified abode.
Whether facing east or facing west, accompanied by their retinues and so forth,
they may be situated in various distinct types of enclosures or located within a single enclosure.
Or else, deities such as Nṛttamūrti and others should be installed in the center;
thus has the characteristic been taught, and now the procedure for installation is being described.
O best of sages, the installation of the Śiva-liṅga, as well as that of Brahmā and Keśava, should be performed according to the specific chapters dedicated to each.
Now, the procedure for the installation of Ekapāda is stated.
As previously mentioned, the time is the same; at that very time, the planting of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) is performed.
One should perform the placement of the jewels (ratnanyāsa), the inspection of the site (dṛṅmīkṣa), and the purification of the image separately;
then one should first prepare the pavilion (maṇḍapa) as a dwelling for the water [consecration].
One should have sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) constructed there, numbering nine, five, or one;
they may be octagonal, circular, or square.
The expulsion of Takṣaka, the enjoyment by the Brahmins, the sprinkling of holy water, the sacrificial mound, the bed, the bath, and the binding of the protective amulets. || 14 ||
One should first perform the mounting upon the bed and the installation of the pitcher separately for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara on their respective right hands.
Having placed three jars at the head-region of the deity Brahmā-Viṣṇu,
one should place the Vardhanī jar to the north of the Śiva-jar.
Having meditated upon each respective form right there, one should worship it with perfumes and other offerings;
one should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the principles (tattva), the forms (mūrti), and so forth, for them as prescribed.
Having performed the consecration of the fire-pit and other rites, one should indeed cause the oblation (homa) to be offered with sesame,
mustard, mung beans, black gram, and peas, using bamboo vessels.
The *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *nyagrodha* trees are located starting from the eastern direction;
the *śamī*, *māma*, *śrīvṛkṣa*, and *plakṣa* trees are in the south-eastern corner.
But in the primary [rite], it is made of *palāśa* wood, or it is considered acceptable everywhere;
then, on the second day, there is the propitiation of the divine pitcher and the fire.

Honored with garments, gold, and other offerings, accompanied by the ritual water for the feet (pādya), and having received a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of ten niṣkas and more, the preceptor was satisfied in mind.
Then one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), having first placed the vessels before the image;
taking the mantra from the jars, one should deposit it into the heart of the deity.
Having taken the seed from the *vardhanī* vessel, one should place it upon its pedestal;
one should then place the seed from the Brahmā-Viṣṇu jar into its heart.
Having taken seeds from others, one should place them around the pedestal;
and with the waters of their respective pitchers, one should perform the consecration in those respective locations. || 24 ||
One should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) and a festival, as well as an abundant offering of food (naivedya);
whatever mantras have not been mentioned here should be taken from those prescribed for that specific deity.

One who establishes this [temple] with a fourth part of the wealth [acquired] by a man through the three forms [of the Lord], having attained happiness in this world, goes in the end to supreme Śiva. || 26 ||
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Three Forms," in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
Red in color and three-eyed, with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
he is joined with a black battle-axe and adorned with a crown of matted locks.
He stands upright, endowed with evenness in both his feet; likewise, he is symmetrical on both sides, the right and the left;
and from the region of the hips upwards, his body is possessed of the proportions of Brahmā.
One should conceive of the pride of Satī and Mānava as belonging to Brahmā and Viṣṇu respectively;
they have their palms joined in *añjali*, stand on one foot, and are positioned to the left.
62. In this sixty-second chapter, the rite for the consecration of the bull-mounted [deity]:
I shall now describe the consecration of the bull-mounted [deity] endowed with its specific characteristics.
He has four arms, three eyes, and is adorned with a crown of matted hair.
An axe should be in the right hand, and a deer in the left hand;
the right front hand, however, should hold a curved staff with a bracelet.
One should place his left forearm upon the head of the bull;
that hand may have the swan-wing gesture (haṃsapakṣa) or it may have the banner (patākā) turned downwards.
From the middle of that, the navel-line should be equal [to the distance] to the tip of the thumb.
From the tip of that [thumb] to the end of the navel-line is eleven finger-breadths (pañcādhikadaśāṅgula).
From the wrist-jewel-binding (maṇibandha), two finger-breadths (aṅgulas) to the side [should be measured];
from the base of the forearm to the middle of the heart, it should be five finger-breadths. || 5 ||
From the wrist of the hand down to the root of the penis, it should be nineteen mātras; from the side, it should be at the level of the wrist.
The distance between the middle of the flanks and the middle of the arms shall be seven finger-breadths;
the deity is endowed with an even bend and is also joined with the standing posture (sthānaka).
The thread situated from the middle of the forehead and the nose to the middle of the ankle of the right foot is known as the Śiva-sūtra.
The thread passing through the center of the heart is declared to be three finger-breadths (guṇāṅgula) in length;
the thread from the interior of the navel to the root of the penis is four finger-breadths (mātra).
The distance between the right knees is five finger-breadths (guṇāṅgula);
the space between the two heels of the right foot is five finger-breadths (śarāṅgula), and there is curvature in the feet.
The remainder, however, should be two finger-breadths, like that of Candraśekhara;
to his very right, one should have the Goddess fashioned, endowed with all her characteristic marks.
Then, either joined by the Goddess on his own right side, or in consideration of the [specific] form,
he should be depicted with his own limbs other than the weapons, arranged in a reversed manner.
Or, joined with him, he may be mounted upon a bull; in this way, he becomes the bestower of liberation.
The bull stands behind him, with its knees, thighs, and hump raised as high as those of a deity.
The boundary for the penis is the navel; the rest is entirely as before.
Having thus completed the deity, one should proceed with the installation using stone or other materials.
At the proper time, one should perform the planting of the sprouts, the depositing of jewels, and the ritual sprinkling;
then follow the untying of the bull's eyes, the purification, and the circumambulation of the village.
Having performed the ritual consecration of the water (jalādhivāsana), one should construct a pavilion as before;
there, one should have sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) made in the number of nine, five, or one.
They may be square, circular, or have sides facing the cardinal directions;
after dismissing the artisan, one should feed the Brahmins there.
Having performed the sprinkling with the *puṇyāha* rite, one should place the sacrificial mound and the bed;
then one should perform the ceremonial bath and the tying of the auspicious thread, even for the bull, as prescribed.
Having placed [the deity] upon the bed, he should thereafter establish the jars:
the Śiva-jar and the Vardhanī jar at the head of the Śiva[-bed]. (19)
If the bull is distinct, one should cause it to lie down at the feet of the deity,
having separately prepared a bed with its head directed toward the south.
One should place a bull-pitcher upon the head of the bull;
having placed eight pitchers around it, one should worship the Vidyeśvaras there.

The wise and most excellent guru, having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the principles (tattva), the forms (mūrti), and so forth, upon the deity and also upon the bull (vṛṣa), using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings ending with the food offering (naivedya).
Having performed the consecration of the fire-pit and other rites,
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sacrificial fuel sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and black gram.

The Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa trees are indeed located in the directions starting from the east; and the Śamī, Apāmārga, Śrīvṛkṣa, and Māyūra trees likewise exist [in the subsequent directions].
Even at the primary [offering], one should indeed satisfy the bull there with *palāśa* leaves;
then, on the second day, having satisfied the gods, the water-pots, and the fires.

The Guru, having been properly honored with garments, gold, and other offerings, and having received the ritual fee (dakṣiṇā), should thereafter perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa). || 26 ||
Having placed the jar before the deity upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), the preceptor should then take the seed-syllable from the jar and install it in the heart of the deity in due order.
Taking the *mantra* of the *vardhanī* vessel, one should place it upon its pedestal;
if that goddess is Sahajā, one should place it in her heart.
Having recollected the mantra, one should place the seed-syllables of Taurus and Aquarius upon the heart of the bull;
then, taking the seed-syllables from the others, one should place them around the pedestal.
If the Goddess is seated on a separate pedestal, the preceptor should perform the installation separately;
thereafter, he should cause the consecration (kalyāṇa) to be performed according to the prescribed rite.

One should cause a festival to be held, along with an extensive ritual bathing and abundant food offerings; furthermore, whatever has not been specifically mentioned here should be adopted as prescribed for general installations.
Thus has been described this installation of the form whose vehicle is the bull;
whether the bull be solid or even insubstantial, it is approved.
Those who have performed the installation with devotion and accompanied by meditative visualization attain that state of Śiva, having enjoyed pleasures according to their desire.
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, the ritual procedure for the consecration of the Bull-mount, in the great tantra named Uttarakāmika.
Mounted upon a bull, four-armed and three-eyed, adorned with a crown of matted hair;
an axe is in his right hand, and a deer is in his left hand.
The right hand, however, is at the waist with a curved staff;
one should place the left forearm upon the head of the bull,
with either a hand, a swan-wing, or a downward-facing banner.
The line from the navel to the tip of his middle finger shall be equal;
endowed with an even bend, he is joined by the divine standing posture (*sthānaka*).
To his right, one should have the Goddess fashioned, possessed of all auspicious characteristics.
Then, either joined by the Goddess on his own right side according to the perspective of the [deity] form, or joined by his own limbs— excluding the weapons— in their reverse positions,
he, mounted upon the bull, shall thus bestow worldly enjoyment.

A bull should be fashioned standing upon the back, with its knees and thighs elevated as high as the [upper] arms of the deity; it extends from the organ to the limit of the navel, while everything else remains as before.
63. In the sixty-third chapter: The Ritual for the Installation of Gaṅgādhara.
I shall now describe the installation of Gaṅgādhara, endowed with his characteristic features:
he has four arms and three eyes, and is adorned with a crown of matted hair.
Although his right hand was held in the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*), the other [hand] was positioned like a bracelet;
with that hand, he grasped a single matted lock of hair together with the Gaṅgā.
Standing with a serene mind, joined by the black axe (kṛṣṇāparaśu), his matted hair should reach up to the level of Karna’s [ear] above. || 3 ||
In that interval, however, there is the two-faced [deity] endowed with the *mābhaṅga* [gesture];
the *sthānaka* is its *uṣṇīṣa*, located between the nose and the right [side].
The thread [should be placed] on the left side from the heart, and indeed on the right from the navel and the private parts;
the *hikkā* is four *mātrās* from the thread, and three finger-breadths from the left knee.
The distance between the two big toes is fifteen finger-breadths, and that between the two heels is five;
the opening of the left foot is three finger-breadths to the left of the thread.
O best of sages, the remaining task to be performed for the Lord of the Crescent Moon is this:
one should fashion the Goddess, endowed with all her characteristic marks, on the left side of the God.

One should fashion Bhagīratha, reaching up to the limit of the breasts within the navel of the deity; he should extend to the throat with a span of eight tālas, be depicted in a relaxed posture, and be endowed with matted locks.
Clad in bark garments, with palms joined at his heart and head,
having two eyes and two arms— one should likewise become Gaṅgādadhara.
At the proper time, there is the offering of the sprouts, the placement of jewels, and indeed the opening of the eyes;
however, for the Gaṅgā, the placement of jewels is not to be performed, nor is the opening of the eyes.
Likewise, for Bhagīratha as well, there was the depositing of jewels by five [persons], the purification of the images, and the circumambulation of the village, the city, and so forth. (11)
The pavilion worthy of sacrifice for the preliminary consecration with water is according to the previous method;
the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are square, numbering nine, five, or one.
Having performed the dismissal of the artisans, one should provide a meal for the Brahmins;
having sprinkled [the site] with water from the Puṇyāha rite, one should then proceed with the Vāstuhoma sacrifice.
The preceptor should lead [the deity] to the sacrificial mound, the bed, the image, the ritual bath, and the protective thread, as was done for Bhagīratha’s Gaṅgā and for the Lord himself.
If Bhagīratha should be seated on a broken seat while lying down, one should arrange his bed in the place where the feet of the Lord [would otherwise be]. || 15 ||
Beside the head of the Lord of Gods, one should place the Śiva-pitcher and the *vardhanī* vessel;
near the region of Bhagīratha’s head, a jar adorned with cloth and other ornaments.
Or one should perform [the rite] with a row of golden jars belonging to the Gaṅgā;
having placed eight jars around [the deity], one should have them presided over by the Vidyeśvaras.
The most excellent guru, engaged in meditation upon the previously described forms and configurations,
should worship all the deities in sequence with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
O Lord, one should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the forms and so forth for Him as before,
together with the five lords of forms (mūrtīśas) of Bhagīratha.
The wise one should assign the five forms according to the previously mentioned method;
the lords of these forms arise from the syllable *bhakāra* and consist of the atomic mantras beginning with Sadyojāta.
One should join the fourteenth [letter] with the *bindu* and *nāda*, ending in the fourth case, at the end of one's own name; this indeed is the root-atom (*mūlāṇu*).
The extraction of the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) and the others should be performed using the very syllables of Bhagīratha;
one should carry out the rite for Gaṅgā according to the path prescribed by that same rule.
Having performed the consecration of the sacrificial pit and the fire with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain,
and sesame seeds, one should subsequently offer oblations with garments, gold, and finger-rings.
One should cause them to give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and then perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa).
Having placed the respective pitchers (kumbhas) before each of those deities, the most excellent Guru [should proceed].
Having understood the mantra of the Śiva-pitcher (kumbha), one should place it within the heart of Śiva;
taking the mantra of the Vardhanī vessel, one should place it upon its pedestal.
Having taken the seed-syllable of Anya, one should place it around the lotus of the seat (pīṭha);
having taken the seed-syllable of Gaṅgā, one should place it in her heart.
Having recollected the seed-syllable from the jar of Bhagīratha, one should place it in his heart;
then, one should bathe that very spot with the water from each respective pitcher.
If the Goddess is on the same seat as the *vardhanī* vessel, one should place it upon her heart;
if the Goddess is on a separate pedestal, one should perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) separately.
At the conclusion, one should have the auspicious bath performed and then hold a festival;
furthermore, one should provide an offering of land according to the donor's desire.
What has not been stated here should be understood as being included, according to what was said regarding the establishment of the general [definition]:
"Is this Maheśvara joined with Bhagīrathī, or is he disjoined? (30)
The man who, with devotion, performs the installation of the Lord of the Jāhnavī, attains happiness in this world, joined by his own kinsmen and people. (31)
One should go as far as the soles of one's own feet; indeed, the Śaiva bath is difficult to obtain! || 311/2 ||
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Installation of Gaṅgādhara," in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
64. In the sixty-fourth chapter: The Ritual for the Installation of the Guha.
I shall describe the installation of the Guha, preceded by its characteristics.
[It should be performed] in the center of the city, or in the southeast, or in the south, or in the center between those two.
It may be in the southwest, in the west, in the northwest, or in the north; or it may be in the intermediate space between them, or likewise in the abode of Śiva.
Likewise, it may be performed in the temple of another deity, or on a mountain, or near a mountain, or by a river, in a garden, or in a similar place. || 3 ||
Or else, in a royal capital and so forth, or in a field of merit, or in houses,
or in the locations of palaces, pavilions, and the like, or near sacred trees.
The abode of Kumāra, being the residence of the beloved one, is characterized by specific architectural marks;
it should have a width ranging from one to thirty-three cubits.
O twice-born ones, a width exceeding thirty-three cubits is not desired for that temple; it may be adorned with the form of Skanda placed in the cardinal directions, or it may be entirely alone.
Rudra is rich in the form of Vighnarāja (Gaṇeśa), or he may be joined with Haṃsaka;
or he may have Gaṇaka and Koṇa, or he may be alone as the abode of Guha.
It is desired to have from one to seven stories on the lower levels, provided with the appropriate floors;
it is endowed with the sanctum and other features as prescribed by the path taught by Śiva.
Likewise, it is joined with the crown-brick (mūrdheṣṭakā) and the pinnacle (sthūpī),
as well as with the installation of the deities assigned to the directions and the central pitcher (madhyakuṃbha).
Richly endowed with the establishment of the divine abode according to the previously mentioned procedure,
it is adorned with the aforementioned pavilions and the like, as well as with enclosures and the like.
Facing east, facing west, or facing south or north, accompanied by the deities of his retinue—these are described here in passing. (11)
The lord of the yakṣas, the lord of the rākṣasas, the lord of the piśācas, and the king of the bhūtas;
the gandharva, the kinnara, the leader of the daityas, and the sovereign of the dānavas. || 12 ||
These, situated in order from the east to the northeast, have four arms;
they are endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and are equipped with a sword and a shield.
Equipped with a sword and a shield, they have two arms and possess a luster like that of collyrium;
they are considered to be either of terrifying form or perfectly peaceful, with their hair tied up.
Śakunī, Pūtanā, Revatī, Ardhapūtanā, Vaktramaṇḍī, Śakārī, Niśāntā, and Meṣadevatā. (15)
Then there is Kārttikeya, also known as Guha; he has six faces, holds a spear in his hand, is borne by a peacock, and is the commander of the army with a spear in his hand. (16)
Or these guardians of the image (mūrtipās) of that [deity], all with palms joined in reverence, holding vajras and lotuses, and endowed with the syllables spoken by Skanda. || 17 ||
They may have four arms or two, and six faces or one face;
these should be installed around [the central deity] in order, starting from the east and so forth, according to the yoga.
One should designate Indra and the others as the eight seats (pīṭhas), or the peacock for the first-born [Brahmā], or the elephant;
one should likewise designate Vighneśa, Kṣetrapa, and Bhānu as the great seats (mahāpīṭhas).
One should also place the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) and the attendants as spoken by Śarva;
on the petals of the sacrificial pedestal, starting from the east, one should place Indra and the other lords of the planets in the center.
One should fashion the two door-keepers at the entrance, resembling dark-blue gems,
positioned respectively on the right and left of the door, having either two or four arms.
Holding swords and shields, they display the needle-gesture (sūcimudrā) and are filled with wonder;
they are dark-blue or red in color, or white and black, and are terrifying.
One should place the two gatekeepers named Jayākhya and Vijayākhya, who have deformed faces,
and the excellent Skanda Caṇḍa, who holds the Vedas in his hand, in the northeast.
He may have two arms, displaying the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and the boon-granting gesture (*varada*) upon a vajra-lotus;
he is known by the name Śākalya, or else there is a sacred seat (*pīṭha*) for that purpose.
O best of brahmins, listen briefly to its characteristics:
one should fashion [the image] out of materials such as stone, according to the specifications prescribed for the iconographic features of an image.

O twice-born ones, the characteristics of the image of Guha have been declared according to universal proportions; it should be constructed together with the womb-chamber, the door, the pillars, and so forth. (26)
He has two arms and two eyes, is most beautiful with a sublime Brahmanic luster;
he holds a lotus in his right hand, while his other excellent hand hangs down.
He should be installed in the form of a child for the very prosperity of the village;
he is two cubits in height, adorned with a sacred thread, possessing a *śikhā*, and equipped with three girdles.
Holding a loincloth and a staff, with his left hand resting on his hip—this Skanda, the bestower of knowledge, should be installed on mountains, in forests, and other such places. (29)
He may have four arms and three eyes, with clusters of lotus petals on his ears, or he may be adorned with crocodile-shaped earrings and hold a rosary and a spear in his two hands.
He may be endowed with both the Varada and Abhaya gestures, or accompanied by two Śaktis, or he may be joined with only one Śakti; the characteristics of these are now stated. (31)
She has two eyes and two arms, is peaceful, and holds a lotus and a water-lily in her two hands;
she appears dark and red in hue, situated on the right and left sides respectively.
O fair-faced one, one should fashion Gaurī endowed with all auspicious marks;
she is most beautiful and is known by the names Gajā and Gajavallī.
Thus, endowed with these characteristics, he should be installed either in a town or even in a city;
he has six faces and six arms, the sun in his ears, and is possessed of the moments (kṣaṇas).
He may have six necks or a single neck, and is endowed with six heads; he holds a spear, the gesture of fearlessness, a sword, a rosary, and a cock.
This [image], accompanied by a mongoose and endowed with red garments, possessing a luster like that of the crescent moon, should be installed for the prosperity of the royal capital. (36)
Adorned with a crown and a basket-shaped ornament, endowed with three eyes,
he carries a spear, a pestle, a sword, a discus, a noose, and the gestures of granting fearlessness.
In his right hands, he carries a thunderbolt,
a bow, a shield, a banner with a peacock, a goad, and displays the gesture of granting boons.

Wearing the sacred thread (*upavīta*), seated upon a peacock, and joined by the two [deities] Śakti and Tatpuruṣa—this [form of Śiva] should be installed in villages and other such places, as well as in temples, for the sake of success. (39)
Thus, the fivefold division of the Skanda Purāṇa is according to the distinction of its locations;
it is held that there are nine versions in the Dvāpara age, while others consider them all to exist everywhere.

Having prepared it in this manner with those mantras, one should then begin the consecration (pratiṣṭhā). [The seed-syllable] is the third letter of the letter Śa, conjoined with the sixth vowel. (41)
Endowed with the fourteen vowels, adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*, it consists of the name of Subrahmaṇya in the dative case, ending in *namaḥ*, and preceded by the *praṇava*. (42)

That which is known as the root-seed (mūlabīja) is the basis for the conceptualization of the limbs of Brahmā; it is [accompanied] by syllables ending in the long and short vowels up to the letter 'śa', or ending with the [five] classes of consonants, or ending with the word "namaḥ". (43)
One should extract the limbs of Brahmā using the words beginning with "Īśāna" and so forth;
[the heart mantra] is joined with the word "mahāsenāya" and the word "vidmahe. (44)
Then, one should join the word "dhīmahi" with "ṣaḍānanāya"; thereafter, it is joined with the word "skanda" followed by "tannaḥ," and at the end, it is joined with "pracodayāt. (45)
This should be the seed-syllable (bīja) of the Gāyatrī; one should employ it preceded by the letter 'D' (Dīpaka).
It is remembered as the root-mantra (mūlāṇu) born from the cavity of the heart, and as the mantra of the Mūrti-vidyā.
The mantras for Gajā and Gajavallī are fashioned according to their respective names;
thereafter, the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) should be performed as before, having first performed the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa).
At the auspicious time previously mentioned, one should place five jewels with the Heart mantra of the two goddesses, or else five golden lotuses.
Having formed a cluster of lotuses, one should perform the opening of the eyes;
one should prepare [the offering] with honey and clarified butter, together with gold, placed within a vessel.
With his heart, the Guru should perform the placement of the golden nails and the offering of grain; he should gaze upon the Brahmin while remaining concealed by a cloth, with his whole being.
If Skanda is accompanied by the Goddess, one should have him installed separately from her;
having performed his purification as previously described, he should perform a circumambulation of the village and other sites.
One should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) of Skanda, who is provided with a long beard, in water while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra;
the mantra-knower should then place jars around him, presided over by Indra and the other deities.
In the four directions of the temple, from the southeast to the northeast, one should arrange a pavilion and construct sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) numbering nine, five, or one, resembling lotuses.
O Brahmin, it should be provided with a bathing platform arranged in the northeast,
the ritual dismissal of Takṣaka, the consumption [of offerings], and the smearing with cow dung.
O God, there should be a sprinkling with meritorious water for the libation of the sacrificial fire;
the sacrificial mound and the bed are as before, covered with skins, woolen cloths, and other garments.
Having brought that Skanda from the water, one should perform the ritual bathing as before;
having worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should bind the protective thread (kautuka) upon his heart while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Having placed Skanda upon the bed, one should lay him down with his head toward the east;
having wrapped him in cloths and worshipped him, he should be joined with the image together with its seat.
One should [worship] Guha with perfumes and other offerings, together with the root mantra and its limbs, along with the body;
and one should place a jar, provided with a cloth and other items, enriched with thread, upon the region of the head.
Having placed [the deity] in that image just as [in the previous one], one should worship Skanda;
if he is accompanied by the Goddess, having installed her as well, one should worship the *vardhanī* vessel there.
Having placed eight jars around [the central one], one should worship the Guhas and the Vidyeshvaras;
all the jars are considered to be provided with threads, cloth, gold, and other such materials. (60)

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the three principles (tattva) along with their presiding deities, starting from the knees up to the neck and head— namely Ātmavidyā, that which is called Śiva, and Mūrti— one should then place the lords of the forms (mūrtīśvara).
The elements, beginning with earth, are considered the forms (mūrtis), and the world-protectors (lokapālas) are considered the lords of the forms (mūrtīśvaras);
or else, those previously mentioned are their lords—one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for them.

The Guru, born of a family of twice-born brahmins, shall be adorned with the five previously mentioned ornaments, wearing an upper garment, a turban, and fine raiment, and having bathed, he shall be as Śiva himself.
Accompanied by such image-bearers (mūrtipas), having performed the consecration of the sacrificial pit and the fire,
he should invoke Skanda as the principal deity, together with Brahmā, the limbs, and Locana.
One should offer libations to the Three Realities (tattvatraya), which are well-protected and accompanied by the Embodiments (mūrti) and the Lords of the Embodiments (mūrtīśvara),
as well as to Gaja and Gajavallī, when these two are available.
A thousand, or half of that, or a hundred, should be the number of root-mantra oblations for the Guru;
for the limbs of Brahmā, it should be one-tenth; and the offering for the image-bearers (mūrtipas) should be half of the root-mantra's portion.

The guardian of the image (mūrtipā) should offer oblations in the cardinal directions with the mantras beginning with Īśa-hṛdaya according to the rules; he should also [worship] the deities of the respective directions and their presiding forms, along with the vessel for peace (śāntighaṭa).
Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, grain, sesame, parched rice, and rice grains for Indra;
then the Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa trees in the cardinal and intermediate directions. (68)
The Śamī, Apāmārga, and Śrīvṛkṣa are to be used for the oblation, with the Pippala as the last;
the Palāśa may also be used for the primary rite, or it may be employed in all cases.

The recitation of the Vedas should take place in the four directions, and here the chanting (japa) should be performed in the corners; one should perform the sprinkling with water for pacification and the ritual of chanting the respective mantras.
In this manner, one should perform the touching with darbha grass for each respective portion;
then, at dawn, the preceptor, having become completely purified, [should proceed] together with the image-makers (mūrtipās).
Having extracted that six-faced [mantra], one should well-satisfy the Kumbha and Agni;
however, for the purpose of expiation, one should offer a hundred oblations with the Dakṣiṇa [mantra].
Having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the preceptor should enter the abode,
whether it be human or divine, provided it has been consecrated as before.
Having placed a stone slab filled with gems, grain, and other such substances within its heart,
one should install the Six-faced Lord (Kārttikeya) upon it while reciting the root mantra.
At an auspicious moment when the ascendant is favorable,
one should then install the six-faced deity (Kārttikeya) facing the entrance, accompanied by the Brahma-stone.
Having placed the jars before the deity, one should perform the ritual placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa).
Taking a seed-syllable from the jar, one should place it upon the heart of the Six-faced One (Kārttikeya).
If the Goddess Satī should place the mantra upon that *vardhanī* vessel,
one should place the other mantras around the pedestal and upon the other jars.
One should sprinkle the Six-faced One with the waters contained within those respective jars;
thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the principles (tattva), the forms (mūrti), and so forth, as previously described.
At the conclusion, one should cause the ceremonial bathing (snapana) to be performed, as well as the offering of food (naivedya) and the festival (utsava),
while honoring the preceptor (guru) and the image-keepers (mūrtipās) with garments and other gifts accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
Having performed the sacrifice with [offerings] for Hemāṅgulī and as prescribed for the installation of images,
one should perform whatever has not been mentioned regarding the eternal installation (sanātana-pratiṣṭhā).
O best of the twice-born, the man who thus performs the installation of Ṣaṇmukha obtains long life and also attains liberation in the hereafter. (81)
Having obtained good fortune, great prosperity, health, fame, happiness,
and auspiciousness, a man attains liberation even in the hereafter.
O best of Brahmins, listen briefly to his worship:
then, having performed the necessary purification and bath in the morning, he should become self-controlled. (83)
One should perform the ritual attendance at the twilight (sandhyopasthāpana) and the satiation of the mantras as before;
then, having gone to the abode and entered within, one should have both feet and both hands washed.

Having sipped water and consecrated himself with the mantras of Skanda, Īśāna, Hṛdaya, and the others, he should prepare the eternal *arghya* offering using those waters while reciting the *astra* mantra.
Having sprinkled water upon the door and worshipped Jaya and Vijaya,
as well as the weapon (hetī) named after his own name on the *dumbura* tree, he should enter within and perform worship.
The Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha), facing north, seated upon his own throne and possessing a subtle form,
having established himself within his own power, remains in a state of destruction for the sake of protection.
Having purified his great body with a flood of nectar arising from the *śakti*,
and having properly cleansed the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), he offered excellent sandalwood paste with his hands.
Having placed Īśāna on the head and Aghora on the left big toe and so forth,
with the two palms joined at the eyes, one should unite them with the seed-syllable (aṇu) of the body-base.

Having placed the subtle mantras of the heart, head, crest, and so forth upon the little finger and the other fingers, one should again perform the placement (nyāsa) on the palms, accompanied by the supreme root mantra.

One should perform the placement of the body (*dehanyāsa*) with those mantras, either accompanied by the *brahma-mantras* or not; likewise, one may or may not perform the placement of the thirty-one energy-syllables (*kalā-mantra*) as previously described.
Having thus assumed a subtle body and contemplating it as being like that of Guha, the practitioner of mantra,
having performed worship and offered oblations, should meditate internally upon the cave within the heart, the navel, and the bindu.
Then, having produced a Śaiva body by means of the Śiva-atomic mantras (śivāṇus), one should worship Guha;
the purification of the site is performed by means of the enclosures, the binding of the directions, and the ramparts.
Having prepared the special *arghya* with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains using the *hṛdaya-mantra*,
or else with those [substances] prescribed for the limbs of worship, one should likewise offer water for the feet (*pādya*) and water for sipping (*ācamana*).
Or, having sprinkled the collection of ritual substances with that [water] alone as the *arghya*,
he should consecrate himself by reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra* while performing the ritual worship, uttering the purificatory mantras for the sake of purification.

Having performed the worship and offered the eternal arghya with the Gāyatrī, one should place that [remnant] upon the head; and having offered it, one should give the remains of the offering (nirmālya) to the wearer.
Or one should abandon it, or purify that image according to the previously mentioned method;
if that image is made of metal, its bathing should take place on every festival day (parvan).
O twice-born ones, if the rite arises from a painting and so forth, the worship is purified through purification;
thus is the purification of the self, the stream, the substance, the mantra, and the image. (98)
Having thus prepared the seat for Guha with the Praṇava and other mantras,
one should then place the Praṇava in the center and arrange Dharma, Adharma, and the rest.

Then, having conceived a seat upon the pericarp of the lotus at the end of the lower and upper coverings— a secret throne— and having invoked the form [of the deity] into this seat, one should [place] the heart-mantra and the other seed-syllables therein.
One should assign the garland-mantras beginning with Īśāna, or all the syllables of the Brahma-mantras;
then, having conceptualized the body of knowledge (vidyādeha), one should [visualize] the six-faced one upon it with the root mantra.

With the [mantra] following from the heart, having offered a respectful salutation with a full handful of flowers, one should invoke the Lord into the image, bring Him there, and establish Him with the heart-mantra. 102.
Having first performed the *niṣṭhurā* [mudrā] with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), one should perform the *avakuṇṭhana*.
The placement of the mantras from the heart up to the eyes is called *avakuṇṭhana*. (103)
One should perform the transformation into nectar with the root mantra for the Mahāmudrā;
then, in sequence, the water for the feet at the feet, the water for sipping at the heart, the water for the face at the mouth, and the arghya offering at the head.
With the mantra ending in "jāti"—namely, *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *vauṣaṭ*—one should offer fragrance, flowers, and incense to Guha, as well as the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth. (105)
One should bathe the deity in the *vibhūti* [shrine] with ground *āmalaka* fruit and other ingredients;
then, having wiped it with a cloth and offered water for sipping (*ācamana*) to Guha, one should recite the mantra. 106.

Having ground sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and kuṣṭha in the previously specified proportions, one should smear Skanda with them while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, or simply with sandalwood alone. (107)
One should offer incense made from black agalloch wood with the heart mantra,
or [incense] consisting of the resin of white sandalwood, or that produced from ashes, to the family priest.
One should cause fragrant and variegated flowers, blossoming in all seasons and awakened at that very moment, to be offered as before. || 109 ||

One should offer the preparation of oil and other substances with the heart-mantra as before; one may offer the oblation with the invocation using the heart-mantra according to the previously stated rule, or otherwise.
The measure of the perfumes and other offerings is as stated in the worship of the western face;
thereafter, one should worship the enclosure (āvṛti) with the offering of incense until the conclusion.
One should place the seed-syllables of the Heart and the other limbs in the directions of Fire (SE), Lord of Wealth (NE), Rakṣas (SW), and Wind (NW), as well as in the intermediate directions;
outside of that, the eight forms of the Lord (Aṣṭamūrtis), and further out, the deities beginning with Indra.
Then one should worship the god Guha with three weapons, or with three coverings; or again, with two or even with one, one should offer incense and lamps.
Having performed the recitation of mantras and the like, he should sing; having offered the *japa*, he should present it.
Having given the food offering (*naivedya*) and the sacrificial oblation (*bali*), he [should worship] Guha in the Śiva-kuṇḍa and the fire.
Having invoked the deity along with his limbs, one should offer oblations of *caru* mixed with *palāśa* fuel-sticks and clarified butter,
reciting the root mantra five hundred, one hundred and fifty, or twenty-five times.
One should perform the oblation with that same proportion and carry out the six-limbed (ṣaḍaṅga) offering;
after giving the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should then perform the daily festival (nityotsava).
At the conclusion of that, one should perform the *tāṇḍava* dance according to the previously mentioned rule;
one should conduct the annual festival for a period from one day up to nine days.
One should draw a peacock upon the banner and perform the hoisting of the banner on that day,
or on a day three times or twice as long as that day.
A wise person should cause the festival to be performed preceded by the offering of the sprouts, or preceded by the beating of the drum, or preceded by the hoisting of the banner. 119.
Śakunī, Revatī, Pūtanā, Maṇḍapūtanā, Vaktramaṇḍī, and then Niśāntā, whose deity is Meṣa, are proclaimed. (120)
O twice-born ones, these six of excellent vows are to be known as the Śakārīs of the Subrahmaṇya; they are to be understood as the six Kumāras, and their names are as follows.
Senāpati, Sureśa, Harasūnu, Surāgraja,
Subrahmaṇya, and Kumāra are proclaimed as the six Kumāras.
A hexagonal pit is desired in the northeast or in the southeast;
the weapon-mantra should take the form of a vajra, and one should worship with flowers or rice grains.
Two-eyed and two-armed, fierce, with the tip of his crest blazing intensely, he holds a sharp vajra in his right hand and a painting in his left hand. 124.
Śukunī and the others, ending with Kumārī, are considered the presiding deities of the days.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Installation of Guha," in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
He has two arms and two eyes, is most auspiciously Brahman-like, and is exceedingly beautiful;
he holds a lotus in his right hand, while his other excellent hand hangs down.
The deity in the form of a horse-tail should be installed for the very prosperity of the village.
Two cubits in height, adorned with the *yajñopavīta* thread, wearing a top-knot and a sacred girdle,
holding a loincloth and a staff, with his left hand resting on his hip—
this Skanda, the bestower of knowledge, should be installed on mountains, in forests, and other such places.

He has four arms and three eyes, his ears are adorned with leaf-shaped ornaments, and he wears crocodile-shaped earrings; he holds a rosary and a spear in two hands, or else he is endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, or perhaps he possesses two spears.
He has six faces and six arms, endowed with twelve ears and twelve eyes;
he may have six necks or a single neck, and is adorned with six crowns.
This [image] should be installed for the prosperity of the royal capital, equipped with a spear, a shield, a sword, a rosary, a cock, and a mace.
Clad in red garments, possessing a luster like that of the crescent moon,
he is endowed with a crown and a casket, and is possessed of three eyes.
He bears the Śakti, the mace, the sword, the discus, the noose, and the gesture of fearlessness in his right hands; likewise, he holds the thunderbolt, the bow, and the shield in his left hands.
Likewise, [the deity] bears a peacock-banner, a goad, and the gesture of granting boons;
he wears the sacred thread, stands upon a peacock, and is endowed with two spears.
This [image] should be installed in a village and so forth, or in a temple and so forth, for the sake of accomplishment.
65. In the sixty-fifth chapter, the procedure for the installation of Caṇḍeśa:
I shall describe the installation of Caṇḍeśa, preceded by its defining characteristics.
And that [inference] is accepted as being of two kinds, distinguished by the dependence on another (paratantra). || 1 ||
In the beginning or middle of the city, the temple of Caṇḍeśvara should be situated in one of the eight directions;
alternatively, it may be located in the north-east, the north, or between the north and the east.
In the region of the inner mandala, within the inner enclosure (antarhārā) and the surrounding gallery (veṣṭaśālaka),
it should be provided with an extent of one to thirty-three cubits.
He is endowed with this very perfection characterized by the [divine] abodes (dhāman),
and is likewise possessed of the stages of existence (bhūmi) beginning from the first up to the seventh.
It should be joined with the form prescribed for the Dhāman, accompanied by Caṇḍeśvara in the directions;
it may also be accompanied by the chosen deity, or it may be alone, or accompanied by the bull (Vṛṣa). || 5 ||

Combined with the first brick of the womb (garbha) brought forward according to the previously stated rule, joined with the crown brick (mūrdheṣṭakā), and accompanied by the installation of the stūpa; || 6 ||
O lords of sages, if the subsidiary limb (parāṅga) is connected to the southern door,
then for the installation of the independent [deity], one should face the south, east, west, or other directions.
And for the establishment of the dwelling, the wealthy [sacrificer] should perform it with a central pitcher placed in the eight directions, according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Everything previously mentioned regarding the measurement of the womb (garbha) and so forth should be applied here;
it should be provided with a wall and a pavilion, and surrounded by a retinue on all sides.
Rudrabhakta, Rudra, Caṇḍa, and Caṇḍapa,
as well as Mahābala— these, O Brahmins, were the two servants of Aṣṭaṅka and Pāṇīśa.
Born from the wrath of Rudra, these eight forms constitute the retinue;
they are white, of massive body, and joined together with palms in reverential salutation. (11)
They may have their topknots or be devoid of them, seated in the Vīrāsana and other postures; they may be clad in animal skins or assume fierce forms.
Or else, Indra and the other deities for that purpose, or the pedestal (pīṭha), or the bull (vṛṣa) in the east;
or one should arrange everything from the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) to the final pedestal as before.
The two door-keepers, Dvāpara and Dvika, should be depicted holding staffs;
Caṇḍa and his follower Caṇḍamānya are not desired, or else they may be placed before the preceptor.
The offering (bali) should be presented on the sacrificial pedestal according to the prescribed location;
the offering is beneficial when accompanied by the deities mentioned, their retinues, the lords of the field (kṣetrapālas), and the suns. || 15 ||
It should be constructed from materials such as stone and so forth, endowed with the characteristics as previously described,
with a middle measurement of ten tālas or at least nine tālas.
The image is described as being endowed with the prescribed measurements, proportions, and so forth;
it is Caṇḍanātha, seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana), difficult to behold, and terrifying.
Wearing a serpent as a sacred thread, with a great fire vomited from his mouth, resembling terrible soot, matted-haired, and bearing the moon upon his crest; || 18 ||
He has four faces and four arms, holding a rosary and a trident;
he carries an axe and a water-pot in his left hands, and his eyes are like the sun, red as the rising sun.
Alternatively, he has the luster of the color of a conch shell, possesses four arms and three eyes,
is adorned with the crescent moon, is clothed in an elephant hide, and is seated in the heroic posture (vīrāsana).
His two palms are occupied with the Pināka bow and the unfailing arrows,
while he is adorned elsewhere by the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Alternatively, he may have two arms, wear white garments, possess three eyes, and have the luster of collyrium;
or he may be endowed with a crown of matted hair, his locks being made white.
Whether standing, seated, or lying down with the left side downward,
he has his left foot hanging down and his left hand following the arm.
Alternatively, he may have a boar’s hand, or he may be endowed with eight chisels;
or his right hand may be joined with a chisel, or he may have his hands in the añjali gesture.
Endowed with the glance of Śaṅkara, his head bowed down with grief, seated in the utkuṭaka posture, peaceful, wearing matted hair, and holding a staff in his hand. || 25 ||

In this manner, Caṇḍanātha should be fashioned, seated upon his chosen throne; or else, he may be depicted with two hands holding a bell and a thunderbolt, and two others holding a noose and a trident.
Alternatively, he who obeys the command of Śaṅkara should be depicted with four arms;
a certain special feature regarding this is now described specifically for the land of Siṃhala.
In the Kṛta age, [the image] is eight cubits; in the Tretā, it is considered to have six arms;
in the Dvāpara, four arms; and in the Kali age, it is considered to have two hands. || 28 ||
However, in all other regions, this division is not mentioned;
or else, Caṇḍanātha may be accompanied by the Goddess, or not.
That goddess Śyāmalā, adorned with all ornaments on her two hands, is renowned by the name Dharmamati; she is excellent and holds a blue lotus.
Having thus prepared the image, one should lead it to the consecration with the mantra.
The mantra for the seat is "Caṇḍāsana," ending in the dative case and followed by "namaḥ. (31)
The word *caṇḍamūrti*, preceded by *dīpa* and ending with *namaḥ*, in the dative case—this is designated as the *mūrti-mantra*. (32)
The root mantra is prescribed as "Oṃ Caṇḍeśvarāya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," and it should be accompanied by a lamp placed before it.
The Guru should extract the [mantras] beginning with Īśāna from the staff using the *cakora* method;
those beginning with the Heart-mantra (Hṛdaya) and so forth should be preceded by "Oṃ Caṇḍa" and end with "Huṃ Phaṭ Namaḥ. (34)
Therefore, there is another mantra consisting of the names of the forms ending with *hūṃ phaṭ*;
or else, the mantra is fashioned for Caṇḍa in another manner. (35)
This is declared to be the Caṇḍa-mantra, consisting of words of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), mantras endowed with the syllable *hūṃ*, and joined with the word *caṇḍāya*.
Alternatively, Caṇḍanātha is proclaimed as being surrounded by the ancillaries of knowledge (vidyāṅga);
thereafter, the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) should be performed, preceded by the ritual sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa).
The time is as previously stated, and the placement of gems is also as before;
the placement of gems and other items upon a golden image is not described here.
Having formed a cluster of lotuses, one should perform the opening of the eyes;
with honey and ghee mixed with gold, [the image] should be placed in a vessel while reciting the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-āṇu).
Having performed the placement of golden nail-plates and the purification of the image with cloths and other materials,
one should then perform the circumambulation of the temple and the city.
One should consecrate the deity with water while it is surrounded by eight jars dedicated to Indra and the other deities;
for the sake of the sacrifice, one should construct a pavilion in front of the temple and on its two sides.

O twice-born ones, one should construct sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) resembling a half-moon in the southern, western, or eastern directions; they may be nine, five, or one in number, and may be either circular or angular.
Having thus constructed the pavilion according to the previously mentioned procedure,
he should then dismiss the artisan and feed the devotees of Śiva.
Having performed the sprinkling for an auspicious day, one should perform the Vāstu-homa;
then, having brought water, one should perform the ritual bathing of Caṇḍeśa as previously described.
Having tied the protective thread (kautuka) at the end while reciting the mantra of the Universal Self (sarvātman),
one should prepare the bed upon the altar according to the sequence beginning with the "egg-born" (maṇḍaja) elements.
One should cause [the deity] to lie down with five pure garments while reciting the Heart-mantra;
then, having wrapped [the image] with two cloths, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the water-jar (kumbha).
In the region of Caṇḍottamāṅga, one should place [the vessel] provided with a thread, a brush, and a cloth, along with gold, a ṭaṅka, abundant water, and sprouts. (47)
Likewise, one should place eight such jars around the outside;
and if Caṇḍeśa is accompanied by Devī, one should place the Vardhanī vessel to the north.

Having worshipped the water-pot (kumbha) with sandalwood and other offerings, while employing the previously mentioned meditation, it should be empowered by the command of Caṇḍeśa together with his body. (49)
The practitioner of mantra should worship the Heart, Head, Crest, and Armor mantras, along with the weapons, on the jars situated outside all around, starting from Īśāna and ending in the north.

Alternatively, having worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas) or the eight fierce forms (caṇḍamūrti) among them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should install the principles (tattva), the forms (mūrti), and so forth.

One should also install the science of the Self known as Śiva, Brahmā and the other [deities] who are its lords, as well as the world-protectors (lokapālas) who are the embodiments of the earth and its rulers. || 52 ||

Alternatively, one may worship the previously mentioned forms, or else those such as the Rudra-devotees; one should worship Caṇḍa together with his seat, his form, and accompanied by the Brahma-aṅgas.
Together with the preceptor and those bearing the [sacrificial] forms, he should cause them to approach the sacrificial pit for the purpose of the fire-oblation;
having consecrated both the fire and the pit, he should place the mantras beginning with Tatpuruṣa in the various directions.

In the corners, the practitioner should satisfy the deities beginning with Hṛdaya, along with Brahmā and the limbs, as well as Caṇḍapa, using sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, excellent food, and sesame seeds in the principal [fire].

Parched grain flour together with barley, and fuel-sticks of *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *vaṭa*, and *plakṣa* [should be offered] in the various directions; for the principal rite, however, the *palāśa* alone is used.
One should separately offer libations to Śamī, Khadira, Māyūra, and Śrīvṛkṣa in the southeast corner, as well as to the Tattvas, their forms, and their respective lords, in due order.
One should perform the sprinkling with water of pacification and the recitation of the respective mantras for each portion, as well as the touching with *darbha* grass for every part. (58)
Then, at dawn, the pure preceptor, together with the image-makers,
having lifted the image of Caṇḍa, should satisfy the pitchers and the fires.
Having performed the *pārya* and *pūrṇā* rites, the preceptor, together with the image-makers,
was honored with garments, gold, rings, and other gifts, and received his sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
The lowest [fine] shall be two niṣkas; the middle one shall be double that;
and the highest is declared to be triple. For others, it shall be as previously stated.
O best of the twice-born, the installation of the stone slab and other components should be performed;
having installed them in the temple at an auspicious moment, one should then apply the mantras.
The supreme preceptor, standing upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of the gods,
should bathe the fierce form (Caṇḍavigraha) with the waters contained within those respective jars.
If one should perform an extensive offering of food (naivedya) and a mobile festival for the Goddess,
one should also carry out her installation ceremony.
"Is this installation of Caṇḍeśvara accompanied by the stationing of Bāla or not?
For that bull among men who performs the installation of Caṇḍeśa in this manner... (65)
One desiring long life shall obtain long life; one seeking wealth shall obtain riches;
one desiring knowledge shall obtain pure knowledge; and one seeking a son shall obtain a son.
He who desires prosperity should take refuge in Mahālakṣmī; he who desires pleasure, in excellent women;
and he who has taken refuge in Caṇḍeśvara, for him there is no cause for worldly existence.
The installation of Caṇḍeśa is well known, and his worship is now described.
Having performed the bathing and other rites as before, one whose body has been rendered complete through the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa [should proceed]. (68)
First, one should offer the general water-offering (*sāmānyārghya*) to Caṇḍeśāna with the *Hṛdaya-mantra* and the weapon-mantra (*hetimantra*).
Having worshipped the two door-keepers with that [offering] and with perfumes and other articles, one should worship the weapon-mantra in the middle of the door.
Having entered the *ālaya* and performed internal purification,
and having consecrated the body (*sakalīkṛta-deha*), one should perform the worship of Caṇḍa within.

Having performed the purification of the site with the enclosure of missiles (*astraprākāra*) and the binding of the quarters (*digbandha*), and having offered water for the feet (*pādya*) and water for sipping (*ācamana*), one should offer the *arghya* with the heart-mantra and the *saṃhitā* mantras.
Or, having sprinkled the substance with only the *arghya* water, he should touch it with the *hṛdaya-mantra*;
having worshipped each [deity] with its own [mantra], he should recite the mantras with the *hṛdaya-mantra* for the purification of the mantras.
Having performed the previous worship and recited "caṇḍeśānāya vidmahe," one should then utter the phrase "ṭaṅkahastāya dhīmahi. (73)
Then, after uttering the word "Caṇḍa" followed by the word "Padas," and having offered the general *arghya* and removed the *nirmālya*, he should recite "pracodayāt. (74)
Having purified [the site] with the Caṇḍa-weapon mantra and with the water of the general arghya offering,
one should consecrate the seat of Caṇḍa and the form, and then sequentially [invoke] the mantras of Īśa and the others.

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the heart-mantra and the others in their respective locations, and having invoked and established Caṇḍapa with the root-mantra from the point (bindu), one should perform the rites of presence (sannidhi) and firm fixation (rodhana) with the heart-mantra.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the heart and other limbs, as well as the meditation on their non-duality;
then, having offered water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya) with the heart mantra, [one proceeds].
Having worshipped Caṇḍeśvara with massages, ointments, and the like, as well as the nectar of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one who is able should offer clothing, fragrance, and flowers.
One should offer incense and a lamp with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) according to the rules for the limbs of worship;
likewise, one should offer to the [deities] beginning with Hṛdādi, the devotees of Rudra and others, and the lords of the quarters along with their weapons.
Having worshipped those [deities] all around Caṇḍanātha with the offering of water for the feet (arghya),
and having presented the food offering (naivedya) as prescribed by the rules, together with betel-leaf (tāmbūla).
If it is a limb from another [offering] that has been enjoyed by Śiva, one should also offer it;
having performed the recitation (japa) and offered it to Him, one should bring the sacrificial oblation (bali) to the retinue.
When one has the means, one should perform a fire sacrifice with fuel-sticks of *palāśa*, clarified butter, and cooked rice;
one should perform the oblation with the root mantra, its ten-fold portion, and its ancillary mantras. (82)

Then, one should cause another perpetual festival for the image of Caṇḍa to be performed with flowers, cooked rice, and unbroken grains (akṣata), which have been consecrated by the weapon-mantra of Caṇḍeśa.
At dawn, midday, and at night, or else accompanied by the fierce *beras*,
he should enter the temple while engaged in the worship of the sandals (*pādukā*).
One should worship Caṇḍeśa with devotion every day at times chosen for one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, or eight divisions [of the day]. 85.

Now, the specific procedure for the worship of Caṇḍanātha as a subordinate limb is being described. First, one should perform the worship of the residual [deity] on the pedestal and so forth with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra).
Having resolved, "To Caṇḍeśa," the food offerings and other items presented to Śiva at the conclusion of the worship belong to Caṇḍeśa, O best of worshippers. (87)
Having gone to that temple and worshipped with pure water, perfumes, garlands, and other offerings, one should afterwards offer even the remains of Śiva’s worship (śivanirmālya).
This [practice] is declared to be common for one's own sake and for the sake of others;
thus, worship performed as an eternal sacrifice is ordained as bestowing the fruits of both devotion and liberation.
Through the worship of Caṇḍeśa, one indeed constantly obtains longevity, wisdom, good fortune, incomparable prosperity, and other benefits as well. (90)
One should perform a special worship with an ablution for the sake of attaining one's desired goal.
The ablution is to be performed as before; however, in this case, Caṇḍeśvara is placed in the central jar.
If he is accompanied by the Goddess, one should place the Vardhanī vessel there and worship her;
in the ritual arrangement of the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti), five are assigned to the directions starting from the east.
In the consecration with nine jars, there should be the eight [deities] beginning with Rudrabhakta;
outside of that, in the group of twenty-five, there should be Indra and the others, preceded by Vajra.
In the fifty [petals], one should worship only the Caṇḍeśāstra in the outer bath;
but in the hundredth place, outside of that, one should worship only the Hṛdaya.
One should perform the festival of Damanāroha, the Pavitrāroha,
the Dīpāvalī, the Vasantejyā, and the monthly ritual observances.
One may perform the rites of offering fresh food (naivedya), the restoration of a dilapidated temple (jīrṇoddhāra), or the rite of atonement (niṣkṛti);
however, during a festival, one should merely draw the banner (dhvaja), the chisel (ṭaṅka), or the bull (vṛṣa).
Even during the festival of Śiva, the festival of Caṇḍanātha should be performed here;
either by omitting the flag-homa and the bali-offering, or by means of the procession alone.
One should fashion the image with vehemence; therein, the technique of chiseling (ṭaṅkā) should be employed.
O twice-born ones, whatever ritual action is not mentioned regarding the rites of consecration, festivals, and so forth— [98]
All of that should be understood as before, together with the atom of Caṇḍeśa. || 181/2 ||
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, the ritual procedure for the installation of Caṇḍeśa, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
Alternatively, he may have two arms, wear white garments, possess three eyes, and have a golden luster;
or he may be adorned with a crown of matted locks, his hair rendered pure white.
Whether standing, seated, or lying down with the left leg placed upon the right.
With the right foot planted on the ground and the left hand following the arm, [he stands].
Holding a chisel in his right hand, with hands joined in *añjali* gesture following his arms,
endowed with the gaze of Śaṃkara, and with his head bowed low in grief.
Alternatively, he has the luster of the color of a conch shell, possesses four arms and three eyes,
is adorned with the crescent moon, is clothed in an elephant hide, and sits in the heroic posture (vīrāsana).
With his two palms occupied by the Pināka bow and the unerring arrow,
he is further adorned elsewhere by the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Alternatively, he has two arms, wears white garments, and is the lord of the constellation Aśvinī;
he is either endowed with a crown of matted locks or his hair is made white.
Whether standing, seated, or lying down with his left leg upon the right thigh.
With the right foot resting on a support, the left hand follows the arm.
Alternatively, he may have a hand like a boar's, or be endowed with the other eight [marks];
he may possess a squinting gaze, or his head may be bowed down with grief.
Alternatively, he may have two arms, wear white garments, possess three eyes, and have the luster of collyrium; or he may be adorned with a crown of matted hair, his locks rendered pure white.
Whether standing or seated, or lying down with the left foot extended;
or with the left foot supported and the left hand following the arm (or the left hand reaching the knee); or joined with a chisel by the other hand, or else with palms joined in *añjali*.
Possessed of a gaze that is agitated, or else with his head bowed down by grief.
Either wearing a crown of matted hair, or with his hair whitened; standing, or seated upon a throne, or lying down with his right side downward.
Endowed with a gaze of agitation, or with his head bowed down by grief,
or else by two terrifying frowns, or by a pair consisting of a noose and a trident.
Or he may be depicted with four arms as an observer of Śaṅkara’s command;
Caṇḍanātha is seated in the lotus posture, difficult to behold and terrifying,
wearing a serpent as a sacred thread, and emitting great flames from his mouth.
He has a terrifying appearance, wears matted hair, and has the moon as his crest-jewel;
he possesses four faces and four arms, and holds a rosary and a trident.
He holds a ṭaṅka and a water-pot in his left hands, and his eyes are like the sun, red as the rising sun.
66. In the sixty-sixth chapter, I shall describe the ritual for the consecration of a devotee of Śiva, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon the devotees of Śiva.
Whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or those born of intermediate castes; || 1 ||
Whether they be women, elders, an anointed king, or those endowed with devotion to Śiva—whether living or deceased. (2)
Having fashioned images of them and consecrated them, one should worship them;
likewise, the Śaivas and Pāśupatas who take refuge in the observance of the Great Vow (mahāvratadhara). || 3 ||
By whichever path Lakula, Bhairava, and the others were initiated, by that very same path let their installation and other rites be performed. (4)

According to the path of the Śiva-siddhānta, the supreme installation (sthāpana) of all [deities] is considered to be of two kinds: that which is self-principal (svapradhāna) and that which is subordinate to another (parāṅga). || 5 ||
Whether in a village or at the bank of a river, or even on the shore of a lotus pond; or in a forest, a grove, or a delightful mountain.
A temple for one's own deity should be constructed in another suitable location, such as within a shrine room or a hall inside a temple; it should be built in a structure designed for that purpose.
Accompanied by its retinue, it is proclaimed as the principal [deity] everywhere—in temples and the like, as well as in garlands, pavilions, and so forth. (8)
That which is fashioned without an entourage is intended as a subsidiary limb;
it begins at three cubits and increases by two cubits at a time.
The width of the vimāna is desired to be twenty-one cubits; likewise, the length, height, the inner sanctum (garbha), and other elements such as the pavilion (maṇḍapa) are to be measured accordingly.
The Sāla and the meritorious Gopura, the inspection of the Āyādi measurements, the procedure for the first laying of bricks, and likewise the installation of the Garbha; || 11 ||
The procedure for the topmost brick has already been explained previously;
for that purpose, there should be either a Śiva-liṅga or an image of Śiva.
One should fashion an image of Skanda, Nandin, or others, or a likeness of the deceased,
joined with gold and other such materials as prescribed.
It may be made of stone, metal, wood, clay, or even of jewels; it may be half-colored, radiant, or fashioned from cloth and other materials.
Whether it be a *liṅga* or an image (*pratimā*), their measurement should be taken according to the method prescribed for *liṅga* and *bera*,
from the temple structure or from the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*).
[The height] should be measured from the door or from the height of the feet, according to the measurement-finger (mānāṅgula),
or by the subdivision beginning with six barley-corns, or by the maker's own measurement-finger (kartṛmātrāṅgula).
When the measurement of the palace and other structures is divided into nine parts, there shall be the categories starting from the best;
the height should increase by three or two finger-breadths (aṅgulas), ending at ninety-six aṅgulas.
This is declared to be the *māna* (measure), endowed with the portions of birth and so forth;
it is multiplied by the half of the qualities of Vasunanda and divided by eight times the solar *nāḍīs*.
The income, the expenditure, and the source; the day multiplied by eight and divided by nine;
and that which is divided by seven and nine respectively. (19)
The portion to be removed has been fully described; let it be made favorable by conforming to the sacrificer and also by conforming to the syllables of the deceased's name. || 20 ||
O best of the twice-born, if it is a liṅga or likewise a pratimā, it should be fashioned according to the specific proportions (tāla) prescribed for each.
One should have an image of the deceased made according to the prescribed measure of eight tālas,
whether it be depicted as seated, bathing, or mounted upon a vehicle.
Whether on a seat or in a standing posture, the wise man should arrange either the lotus posture (padmāsana) or the lion throne (siṃhāsana), or both may be employed according to the rule.
Or it may be joined with a seat as desired, or square according to the sequence; likewise its height, width, length, and ornamentation [should be prepared].
One should proceed according to the manner of the Pratimokṣa and the previously mentioned rule;
whether one has a topknot, or has tied-up hair, or is shaven-headed, or wears matted locks. (25)
If the king has been consecrated, he should be depicted as wearing a crown and diadem,
