equipped with his preferred weapons, or else accompanied by a gesture of salutation.
Endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament,
whether they be singers accompanied by dancers or worshippers, let them act as they desire.
If women are adorned with ornaments suited to themselves, such are the characteristics described; now the installation and other rites are being declared.
In this case as well, the application of beeswax (madhūcchiṣṭa) should be performed according to the method prescribed for the image;
thereafter, one should perform the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) prior to the consecration.
Then, having performed the placement of the jewels (ratnanyāsa), one should perform the opening of the eyes;
having prepared the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) as before, one should place the cloth-painting (paṭa) upon it.
Having conceptualized the Praṇava as the pedestal, one should place the image upon it;
then, with strokes from a golden needle, one should draw a black circle.
Having drawn a circle of light and fixing one's gaze on a hair’s breadth,
one should perform this rite after reciting the mantra of the eyes.
The learned man should satisfy [the ancestors] with honey and clarified butter using golden dūrvā grass;
he should then show him two vessels filled with honey and ghee.
One should touch with a golden nail while reciting the Netra-mantra;
likewise, one should touch grains, a cow with its calf, and a maiden while reciting the Brahma-mantra.
Having displayed the cloth painting and set it aside, one should then perform the purification of the image;
adorned with all ornaments, one should lead it on a procession through the village and other areas. (35)
One should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) of the image together with the jars of the world-protectors (lokapālas).
For the sake of the sacrifice, one should construct a pavilion in front of it and on its two sides.
One should fashion there sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) numbering nine, five, or one;
thereafter, having dismissed the artisan, one should perform the feeding of Brahmins.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice grains upon the altar according to the previous measurement,
and having performed the purification as before, one should then circumambulate the village and other sites clockwise.
The ritual immersion in water, the preparation of the sacrificial pit in the pavilion, the altar of rice and other grains, and the five types of beds made of skins and so forth. (39)
Having conceived the fourfold [elements] beginning with Dharma, along with the one called Ādhāra and Ananta, one should fashion the human seat (pīṭha) with the syllable Om (praṇava). || 40 ||
The Guru should lead the image to the bathing altar; having placed the icon upon a pedestal made even of stone or other materials, according to the previously mentioned procedure. (41)
Having wrapped it in garments and adorned it with perfumes and so forth, as well as garlands and other ornaments, one should place the image— its protective cord (pratisara) tied— upon the bed.
One should place the cushion in the east; there, the image shall be at the head.
To the north of the head, one should place the primary water-pot (kumbha).
On all sides, eight jars adorned with cloth, gold, and thread,
filled with sandalwood water and joined with fruits and sprouts [should be placed].
One should place the mantras in their midst; the procedure for that is stated here:
it should be such that [each syllable] ends with the letter *sa*, is joined with the first vowel (*a*), and is endowed with the nasal dot (*bindu*). (45)
The mantra of the Self is declared to be either the word "haṃsa" or else the letter ending in "sa";
with that very letter, one should fashion the limbs of Brahmā.
Or rather, the ancillaries of knowledge (vidyāṅga) belong to that [mantra] which is properly articulated;
or the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* belongs to the installation of the female [deity], by means of which the arrangement of Brahma’s limbs is performed.
Where the installation is performed together with one's own wife,
one should place a water-pot for the sake of the wife to the north of the primary pot.
If there are two wives, one should place another *vardhanī* even in the southern direction;
if there are many, *karakas* should be taken, several on each of the two sides.
In all matters of establishment, women are proclaimed to be the Vardhanīs;
likewise are the elements beginning with earth, as well as mind, ego, and intellect.
In the surrounding jar, the eight Vasus are considered to be worshipped;
for women, however, the deities are proclaimed to begin from the east. || 51 ||

Having worshipped the Guardians of the World (Lokapālas) in the Puruṣa or in the eight jars starting from the east with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should install the Tattvas and the Lords of the Tattvas (Tattveśvaras).
The three principles have been declared as the knowledge of the Self (ātma-vidyā), which is called Śiva:
namely, the Self (ātman), the inner Self (antarātman), and the supreme Self (paramātman). (53)
One should install them in sequence as the presiding deities over each respective reality (tattva);
for women as well, it should be exactly thus, and the earth and other elements are considered their forms.
In the fivefold system, however, there are eight [deities]: indeed, the five beginning with Earth (Kṣmā), and Indra and the others as the guardians of the forms;
but in the other system, the guardians of the forms are those beginning with Nivṛtti.
Having assigned those respective Brahmas, one should assign their respective forms to the heart;
then, having assigned the letters from 'A' to 'Kṣa' in sequence to the head and other parts of the body.
Having performed the placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa) with one's own mantra, one should place the limbs (aṅganyāsa);
then, having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should cover it with a cloth while reciting the armor-mantra (varma).
Then, having gone to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should commence the rite of fire-oblation (homa);
as before, one should perform the consecration of the pit or the installation of the Śiva-fire.
In the center of that, having invoked the deity along with his limbs (attendants) and worshipped him,
one should offer libations with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, sesame seeds, and other substances, while the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) perform the rite.
The Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa trees are to be placed in order starting from the east;
the Śamī, Khadira, Māyūra, and Śrīvṛkṣa trees are to be placed starting from the southeast corner.

Having offered one hundred, fifty, or twenty-five oblations even with *palāśa* wood in the primary fire, and then having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) directed toward the Lords of the Principles (*tatva-tatveśvara*), [one should proceed].

O twice-born ones, having performed three oblations for each of the embodied and unembodied lords, one should perform a hundred-fold fire-sacrifice with the Ghorā mantra to ensure the rite is free from defects.
Having touched [the disciple] from the crown of the head down to the feet, he should sprinkle him with water for pacification;
then, having offered the internal and external oblations, the Guru, being pure, [should proceed].
Then, having passed the remainder of the night, at dawn, the most excellent Guru, together with the guardians of the images, bathed, completed the twilight rites, and fulfilled his duties.
Possessing the five spheres of perception, with his uṣṇīṣa and upper garment [visible], endowed with the ornaments of the five limbs, his mind was delighted by the right-hand [deity]. || 65 ||
In the same way, he was accompanied by those who bore his image and were well-honored, by those who muttered prayers,
by students, by astrologers, and by artisans who had been gratified.
Having worshipped the doors and the guardians of the doors, and having performed the worship of the ritual jar (kumbha), the Guru,
after honoring the fire situated in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) according to the prescribed sequence.
Having raised the image from its bed and placed it upon a vehicle in a proper manner,
one should then lead the image to a place of worship or lead it to a bathing pit.
One should arrange the placement of the jewels as before during the installation;
having made the seat the Praṇava, one should conceive of the stationary form (sthāṇu) as being established there.
Then, having performed the placement of the *mātṛkā*, one should perform the placement of the vital breath (*jīvanyāsa*),
after having bathed [the deity] with the water from the jars placed all around.
One should worship the devotee of Śiva with garments, perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and likewise with other services.
At the conclusion, one should hold a festival according to the extent of one's wealth;
from that time forward, a person should worship that devotee every day.
Born into a lineage of the original Śaivas, he abides within the five spheres of experience;
likewise, he performs the necessary duties such as purification, ritual bathing, the twilight prayers, and salutation.
Having performed this and entered, the Guru, offering the general *arghya*,
should worship Puruṣa and Prakṛti on both sides of the entrance.
Having entered the inner sanctum and worshipped the immutable Supreme Self in the center of the site, he should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having first performed the mantra-body [visualization] and then carried out the purification of the site,
one should prepare the special *arghya* water combined with flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and water.
A person should sprinkle the collection of ritual substances according to the previously mentioned procedure;
for the purification of the mantras, he should recite the mantras beginning with the syllable Om and ending with Namaḥ.
For the purification of the image, one should bathe the image and so forth with toy-water (astratoya),
having prepared the sixfold seat according to the previously mentioned procedure.
In the center of that, the wise one should fashion the form, worshipped with the form-mantra (mūrti-mantra),
endowed with its respective appearance, using the specific root-syllable (mūla-aṇu) for each.
Then, having performed the placement of the vital breaths (jīvanyāsa), one should place [the mantras] in the heart and other parts as prescribed;
one should offer water for the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), and the respectful offering (arghya) with the Heart-mantra.
Having bathed [the image] with pure water or with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth,
and having wiped it with a cloth, he should offer clothing, perfume, and incense.
One should offer an oblation of food accompanied by a lamp and side dishes,
as well as betel-leaf, during the three junctions of the day, or at least during two of them.

Alternatively, one should worship during a single twilight, either accompanied by offerings and festivals or not; or one may worship until the end of the lamps or until the end of the food offering, according to one's capacity.

During the solstices, the equinoxes, the transits of the sun, eclipses, and other such occasions, the ritual bathing should be performed according to the prescribed rule and in the sequence previously described.
In the central jar, one should place the letters beginning with 'kṣma' (kṣa, ma) in the first enclosure;
outside of that are the sixteen vowels, and outside of that, the letters beginning with 'ka' are prescribed.
Thus, that which possesses both obstructions is called the middling kalpa; however, that which is joined with only a single obstruction is proclaimed as the inferior. (86)
Then, if one has the means, one should perform a festival every month, or on the birthday of the devotee, or even on the birthday of the performer [of the rite]. (87)
An annual festival should be performed, as well as a marriage ceremony for every [newlywed] couple,
lasting for nine days, or seven days, or five days, or even three days.
Alternatively, it may even be performed for a single day, accompanied by the offering of oblations (bali) and fire-sacrifices (homa);
the rites beginning with the hoisting of the flag (dhvajārohaṇa) should be carried out according to the desire of the performer.
On all festive occasions and the like, a bull should be made as the banner for everyone,
accompanied by the eight auspicious symbols (maṅgalāṣṭaka) as prescribed according to their respective castes.
One should beat the drum at night accompanied by the weapon-mantra of devotion,
and offer oblations to Indra and the other gods, together with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
On the first night of the festival, one should perform the consecration for the sacrifice;
having constructed the sacrificial hall according to the rules, it should be provided with an altar.

One should perform the auspicious rite of the sprouts (maṅgalāṅkura), provided with five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) including those in the east and other directions, or even joined with all auspicious elements.
O twice-born ones, for the sake of offerings and festivals, having fashioned an image of the devotee—either small or large—and having installed it according to the prescribed rite; || 94 ||

Having tied a protective thread there according to the ritual injunctions, and having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the center of the altar with rice and other materials, one should place the water-pots.
The supreme preceptor should perform the installation with that wealth and worship those very deities mentioned therein; he should worship the gods every day, both evening and morning.

At the end, one should perform the *hoa* (oblation) accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; the materials for this are also to be given by the Brahmins according to the procedure described for the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
One should offer the bali-oblation in the evening and in the morning, accompanied by small images;
at the conclusion of the bali, one should perform a festival endowed with all ornaments.
One should perform the rite of the circumambulation accompanied by song, dance, and other arts;
at the conclusion, having performed the powder-festival (cūrṇotsava), one should carry out the ritual of the sacred ford (tīrthakarma). || 99 ||
Every day, there should be a special worship of the root-liṅga; at the conclusion, one should perform a pure ablution and lead [the deity] back to the root-liṅga and other [images]. 100.
O lords of sages, if one is incapable, one may perform only the festival itself, even if it is devoid of the raising of the banner or lacks the offerings and burnt oblations.
O best of men, that person who performs the consecration of a devotee of Śiva shall obtain the fruits of long life, health, victory, prosperity, and fame. || 102 ||
Beforehand, one attains union; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, the ritual procedure for the installation of a devotee of Śiva, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
67. In the sixty-seventh chapter, the ritual for the consecration of the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha-pratiṣṭhā-vidhi):
I shall now explain the consecration of the seat of knowledge in brief.
That knowledge is said to be of two kinds: the refined (saṃskṛtā) and the innate (anyātmikā).

One should establish a seat for the Vidyā in a palace or similar structure, in the four cardinal directions, in the intermediate directions, or in the intervening spaces, or even in a place designated by the devotee. || 2 ||
Starting from three finger-breadths and increasing by one finger-breadth at a time, the length of the book may extend up to twenty-five *mātrās*. (3)

The measurement for the width should begin at one finger-breadth of the sky (vyoma) and increase by a quarter-finger-breadth at each step until it reaches twelve fingers (ravimātra); alternatively, it may be provided with five bands (pañcapaṭṭī).
It may be made from birch bark, from *kulaka* leaves,
or from palm leaves, or it may be fashioned from gold and other precious materials.

Or else, one should have it engraved by skilled and auspicious artisans upon stone or wood; or [the image] may be fashioned from ink, or from saffron and other pigments, or from flowers and similar materials.
The preceptor or even the disciple should draw [the mandala] with a brush;
one should begin during an auspicious day, asterism, and conjunction, under a favorable lunar mansion.
One should not diligently cause this Śiva-jñāna to be written by means of an animal;
furthermore, a wise person should not engage in its study in the presence of animals.
One should write it in straight lines with letters produced from various regions that are endowed with beauty; one should not write at the edge of the leaf.
Having worshipped Śiva with perfumes and other offerings, and having honored the Mātṛkā— who is the very form of Śiva—
with garments and other gifts, the preceptor should also worship the leaf-inscription.
On a portion of ground smeared with cow dung and adorned with colored lines, strewn with heaps of flowers and perfumed with incense; || 11 ||
A man, having first become pure, should either write, hear, or read [this] in a place provided with a burning lamp and surrounded by pure Śaivas.
A wise man should not cause an impure version to be written down, according to how it was written by the reciters;
for the knowledge of Śiva has, over time, been lost in its authoritative form. || 13 ||
Of that which was written with deficient or redundant syllables by those who were negligent, and of that whose reading was corrupted or destroyed by those of small intellect; || 14 ||
And [the text] has been edited by teachers possessed of little knowledge, containing useless words and repetitions in meaning. (15)
[That which is] contradictory to what has preceded and followed, opposed to one's own established tenet, excessively corrupted by meter, and devoid of both word and meaning; || 16 ||
A wise teacher who properly performs the purification (*saṃskāra*) in various instances for one who is possessed of such defects as these; || 17 ||
He who knows the true meaning of the Śiva-tattva is a knower of the supreme knowledge of the Lord;
he should gradually teach it to disciples who are devotees of Śiva.
The gift of knowledge is said to be that which is given in accordance with the Śiva-vidyā, using words in Sanskrit, Drāmiḍa, or various regional dialects. (19)
Here, he [teaches] by means of words derived from Prakrit, pure ones, as well as Sanskrit,
and worldly (laukika) words, according to the suitability of the disciple.
And by means of local dialects and other such methods, as well as through scriptures corresponding to those [dialects], he should awaken all people everywhere, even those residing in remote regions.
Just as there is no end to Śiva, the perfect and great-souled one,
so too there is no end to him whose essence is knowledge and whose nature consists of all qualities.
The fruit of the gift of knowledge is sovereignty characterized by qualities culminating in Śiva;
it brings fame in this world, the prosperity of Brahmā, wisdom, beauty, wealth, and happiness. (23)
He who, having studied impurely himself, should teach knowledge to another, goes to a terrible hell; he is a sinner, a destroyer of knowledge. (24)

A wise and highly intelligent person should daily cause this work, which illuminates the knowledge of Śiva, to be written according to their capacity, and worship it with devotion as if it were Śiva himself. (25)
For as many syllables as there are in the book of Śiva-knowledge,
for that many thousands of yugas shall the man who gives it dwell in the city of Śiva.
Having rescued ten generations of ancestors and ten generations of descendants,
as well as his mothers, fathers, and lawful wives, the wise man attains heaven together with them.
Having established all of them in heaven, he himself shall go to the city of Śiva;
so too shall he who recites even a single verse, or half a verse, of the knowledge of Śiva.
One should recite it, or contemplate it, or write it, or cause it to be written;
or one should listen to it with a single-pointed mind and reflect upon its meaning. (29)
The merit of one who causes others to hear this is great;
likewise, for one devoted to the knowledge of Śiva, [the merit is great] through providing food, clothing, and so forth. || 30 ||
One should protect [the manuscript] until its completion and thereby obtain the fruit of the gift of knowledge;
or, by having it made for a price, one enjoys that very same fruit. (31)
O twice-born ones, that king in whose kingdom the exposition of the knowledge of Śiva takes place prospers; he becomes a powerful sovereign of kings.
Whether in the kingdom, in the office of royal preceptor, in the command of the army, in other duties, in the role of domestic priest for all, or in any other observation of state affairs; || 33 ||
One who is a pure Śaiva is fit; he is even more excellent if he belongs to a lineage, provided that his established tenets do not contradict the Veda and the Vedāṅgas.
Likewise, he who determines the meaning of the scriptures— whether they be the Pāśupata, the Gārūḍa, or others in various ways— he knows the Dharma, and no one else.
And he determines the meaning of the scripture according to the Śuddhaśaiva [tradition];
his intellect would be characterized by tamas, and he is excluded from dharma. (36)
Therefore, a king—especially one who follows the Siddhānta Śaiva tradition and delights in the knowledge of pure Śaivism—should understand the rites for pacification and nourishment. || 37 ||
Furthermore, rites such as malevolent magic (abhicāra) and the like must not be performed by anyone else who is devoted to the Dharma and is an excellent member of the spiritual lineage. || 38 ||
Action performed by that very [deity] always yields fruit for human beings;
thus has the power of knowledge been explained, and now its installation will be described. (39)
Beginning from three cubits up to thirty-three cubits,
there may be a school for learning, a large palace, or a pavilion.
According to the distinctions such as the single hall (eka-śālā) and others, the halls may possess the defining characteristics;
the width of the seat of knowledge (vidyā-pīṭha) shall be seven finger-breadths in extent.
By increasing [the measurement] by two finger-breadths (aṅgulas) at each stage, it becomes thirty-one aṅgulas;
by that, the length is declared to extend up to fifty cubits (karas). || 42 ||
It may be square and symmetrical, or it may be rectangular;
otherwise, one should carry out everything according to the procedure prescribed for the rules of the seat.
Then one should know the ritual preparations and sprinkle [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the pavilion, one should place it upon a cloth.
Just as in the Śiva system, the seat and other requisites are joined with the form and the lord of the form,
so too in the Śiva division Śiva is to be worshipped, and in the Rudra division he alone is indeed worshipped.
In the center, one should place the Śiva-kumbha, and on the two sides, the two Vardhanīs;
there should be only a single worship for these two, while the Vidyeśas are surrounded on the outside.

Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) as previously described, provided with sacrificial wood (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), sesame seeds (tila), and accompanied by the oblation (havis). || 47 ||
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of barley, he should perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Once it is completed, the most excellent Guru, having received the sacrificial fee, should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa).
Having placed Śiva in the center, one should place the Goddess upon the fillet.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Ritual of the Seat of Knowledge," in the Great Tantra known as the *Uttarakāmakā*.
68. In the sixty-eighth chapter: The Ritual for the Installation of the Ten Weapons.
I shall now describe the installation of the ten weapons, preceded by their characteristics:
the thunderbolt (vajra), the spear (śakti), the staff (daṇḍa), the sword (khaḍga), the noose (pāśa), and likewise the goad (aṅkuśa).
The ten weapons are the mace, the trident, the lotus, and the discus;
he has one face and two eyes, and is adorned with a crown and a jeweled casket.
One should fashion [the image] with two arms, palms joined in reverence, endowed with all the auspicious marks,
according to the measurements prescribed for the characteristics of an image.
The female [deities] are to be known as Śakti and Gada; the neuter ones are Cakra and Padma;
the remaining [eight] are to be understood as males, fashioned at a height of eight tālas. || 4 ||
Equipped with weapons at the top of their respective [staffs],
starting from one *tāla* for their own [length] and increasing by one-eighth of a *tāla* at each step, they reach a height of four *tālas* at the base.
The wise one should fashion the weapon according to the method described in the section on the group of missiles;
the weapon should be placed upon their head or above the crown.
Either between the two hands, or on the hand other than the left,
one should set aside the goad and instead fashion a banner in its place.
Thereafter, the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) must be performed; its ritual procedure is stated here:
first, one should perform the deposition of jewels (ratnanyāsa), and after that, the ceremony for the opening of the eyes (netramokṣaṇaka).
One should perform the satiation of the eyes, look upon grains, and [apply] honey with clarified butter;
then, having consecrated the cow and adorned the weapon, one should lead it forth.
Having led [the image] around the village in a clockwise direction, one should have it lie down in the midst of water;
having constructed the previously described pavilion, provided with four doors.
The pavilion should be provided with either a single altar or separate altars;
it is said to be ten-fold in number, consisting of a water-shed accompanied by sacrificial pits.
In the former case, it is provided with the configurations of the respective fire-pits (kuṇḍas) according to their own directions;
however, in a single pavilion, there may be fire-pits on all eight sides surrounding it.
Between Indra and Īśāna there is a circle, and between the Pitṛs and Varuṇa there is likewise a circle;
thus, the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) shall number ten.
One should feed the Brahmins for each Vāstuhoma individually;
then, at the conclusion of the Puṇyāha rite and the sprinkling of water, one should prepare an altar (sthaṇḍila) endowed with the proper characteristics.
One should prepare a bed with many cloths or even with just one;
having made the seat the Praṇava, one should spread it over with Darbha grass and flowers.
Having brought it from the water, well-bathed, worshipped, and adorned with auspicious thread-ornaments (kautuka),
one should place the image upon the bed with its head toward the right.
The preceptor should cover all [the vessels] with cloths and install the jars;
or he may install eight jars or water-pots around [the central one], starting from the eastern direction.

One should fashion the root mantra (mūlāṇu), the Brahmā-mantras, and the limbs (aṅgas) with their respective colors; one should worship the root mantra in the central jar and the Brahmā-mantras in the cardinal directions.

Having worshipped the limbs in the intermediate directions, one should remember the Vāpti-mantra within the range of Puruṣa and perform the fire-oblation with one's own mantras, consisting of sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and sesame seeds.
One should perform one's own fire-oblation in one's own fire, equipped with an offering full of oblation-material.
Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, Vaṭa, and other trees [should be placed] in the cardinal and intermediate directions. (20)
The Śamī, Khadira, Māyūra, and Śrīvṛkṣa are proclaimed [as suitable];
the Palāśa is for Brahmā, while the Śrīvṛkṣa is considered the fuel-wood for Viṣṇu. (21)
Having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in the morning, one should begin the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa),
having worshipped [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, together with the food offering (naivedya) as prescribed.
One may or may not perform the ceremonial bathing; indeed, the festival itself is likewise [efficacious].
The mortal who causes this to be performed in such a manner is liberated from all misfortunes.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, the procedure for the consecration of the ten weapons, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
69. In the sixty-ninth chapter, the procedure for the installation of the trident (*triśūla-sthāpana-vidhi*):
I shall describe the installation of the trident, preceded by its defining characteristics.
It may be made of gold, silver, copper, iron, stone, or other materials.
In the inner sanctum, from the ninth part up to the end of the third part of the ninth part,
the measurement for the large tridents is desired to be one part.
Having divided each [dimension] eightfold, and likewise the measurement in many ways, O Lord, let the door-pillars and the deities, or the measurement itself, be duly considered. (3)
Starting from one cubit up to four cubits,
the most excellent of preceptors should determine the portion for the [main] image by following the same procedure as previously described.
One should divide the thirty parts and so forth that have been obtained by one hundred; then, one should employ one light for the sake of achieving auspiciousness and other results.
The sacrificial stake (śūla) is considered to be of two kinds: worldly (laukika) and technical (yaugika).
That which is favorable to the sacrificer, the king, and the village is regarded as worldly.
That trident which is free from defects of birth, age, and parts, endowed with qualities favorable to the rudrākṣa,
and fashioned according to the prescribed finger-measurements, is considered fit for yoga.
A worldly image (laukika) located in another place is considered common;
a regional image (yugika), however, is that which is fashioned according to the specific form of the patron residing in another city.
This should be applied elsewhere as well, or in the case of images exactly in this same way;
having divided the height into ten parts, or [alternatively] by two, three, or four [parts].
The measurement of the middle [leaf] may be one-eighth of that, or the height of the central leaf may be one-quarter of that measure; furthermore, those measurements may be taken individually.
Having divided that [measurement] into thirty parts, the width of the middle petal is formed by two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine of those parts. (11)
One should take up the measurement of the leaf and lead it evenly to form a square; then, having released that leaf-measurement, one should do the same on both sides.
One should fashion the rounded shape there according to the measurement of both [the sides];
just as the span of the middle leaf is, so too is the span of the side leaves.
An increase of one-fourth, one-fifth, or one-sixth is desired for the *tāra* (silver), depending on whether it is based on the middle leaf, the exterior, or the interior. (14)
The side-petals should be fashioned with their roots and tips made slender;
one should increase the root-base by half the strength of the petal-root.
The half-leaf and the tip of the leaf should be thin;
at the tip, by means of the width of the leaf, it should be half of that, O Lord, starting from the base.
Or, O lords of sages, one may fashion that side with the tips of two leaves,
or likewise fashion the middle of the leaf-tip, or whatever remains.
In that same manner, it is taught that [the measurement] extends from the base to the end for both side-petals;
the width of the petal is in four, five, six, seven, or eight parts.
The wealth [of the design] is said to be [determined] by a ninth part, or otherwise on the petals;
beginning with half a barley-corn and increasing by a quarter-barley-corn increment. (19)
Alternatively, there may be wealth in the middle region measured by a finger's breadth;
however, that leaf which is smaller than the middle of the central leaf is a lateral leaf.
One should fashion a bud protruding by one, two, or three *yava*s at the base, the tip, the middle, and both sides of the central petal. (21)
Having divided the width of the petal into five parts, two or three of those parts shall constitute the length of the foot at its base; half of that [length] shall be for the two side-petals.
Its width is said to be half of that, or one-quarter;
the width of the middle foot is twice that of the side feet. (23)
One should make a variegated ornament at the base of the petals;
beneath that, a *pālikā* should be made, measuring half a part in the length of the petals.
The width of the plank should be increased by one part of the Rudra-fraction (eleven), or increased by two parts, or divided into nine parts and increased by one. || 25 ||
O twice-born ones, the wealth [of the area] is considered to be one-fourth or three-fourths, with two lotuses below; the width is held to be one-eighth of the desired portion.
O best of sages, the height of the vessel, shaped like a jar, should be one and a half *pādas*;
its neck should be made half of that, as before.
The mouth [of the vessel] is conceived by others as being one-quarter less than the diameter of the pot, or half of it;
one should divide that measurement of the nāḍikā, which is like a jar, into eight parts.
One should make an interval of one part; the *hīrikā* should be of that same measurement.
O twice-born ones, the staff (*daṇḍa*) should be fashioned beneath the *hīrikā* according to the prescribed rule.
The width of the staff (daṇḍa) should be one-fourth or one-third of the mouth's width;
if it is a metal staff, it should be half of that, or otherwise according to the requirements of beauty.
At the base of the staff, however, there should be a lotus, equal to the middle petal, or half of that,
or else within the eighth part [of the height], the measurement may indeed be divided ninefold.
The width is equal to that [height], or three-quarters, or half, or a quarter; or the intermediate measurement may be used; having divided that height into ten parts— || 32 ||
One should fashion a lotus with three or two bands,
making it circular, square, or a combination of both.
Or else, there should be a band above that [pedestal] with a corded border;
in the center of the middle petal, one should draw the face of that lotus.
Alternatively, at the base of the middle petal is the one whose vehicle is a bull (Śiva);
his height is one, two, three, four, or five parts of the ninth part of the petal's height.

One should search for another deity according to the authoritative scriptures— whether accompanied by the Goddess or not, whether joined with a bull or not, or even another deity among the world-protectors (lokeśas) or their weapons.
Alternatively, O twice-born ones, one should fashion four garlands on the intermediate corners of the *pālikā* like the leaves of the *aśvattha* tree, or it may even be devoid of them.
One should fashion a handle for it joined with the tip of a staff, or alternatively,
one should have the Lord of Bulls (Vṛṣeśvara) fashioned upon the corners above the *pālikā*.
A certain distinction regarding the stone or clay trident is now stated:
it should extend to the middle leaf by three-quarters or even by half [of its total height].
The width of the staff (daṇḍa) may be one-eighth of the measurement from the middle [of the base], or it may be equal to its height, or indeed equal to its width. (40)
Just as wealth consisting of staffs or wealth consisting of leaves has been prescribed,
one should likewise arrange ornaments such as anklets and the like below the leaves.
On a four-cornered stone, one should draw the shape of a trident;
or, on the other side of the trident, one should likewise draw a bull.
Alternatively, one should place a staff upon a man or a matted-haired ascetic (jaṭila) in the eastern part; then, one should fashion a trident above that staff.
One should firmly install the trident either on the head of the bull, or on the back of the bull, or directly upon the sacrificial pedestal; that is declared to be its consecration.
For that purpose, one should procure from a tree those [woods] recommended for the sacrificial stake (śūla);
the sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) should likewise be performed at the prescribed time, lunar mansion, day of the week, and so forth. || 45 ||
The wise man should perform the *saṃghāta* [stroke] with eight bindings and so forth using the staff,
as well as the *padmasaṃghāta* stroke along the path on both the upper and lower sections.
The laying of jewels and likewise the opening of the eyes should not be performed;
however, if there is the installation of a stationary image, one should indeed cause the laying of jewels to be done.
If there is a statue or the like, its sight brings liberation;
having performed purification with clay and other materials, one should circumambulate the city and so forth.
Having performed the ritual residence (vāsana) in water, one should then take refuge in the pavilion (maṇḍapa),
which is of the previously mentioned dimensions and provided with a single *bhūta* and a *graha*-fire pit (*kuṇḍa*).
It was purified by the consumption of food by Brahmins, accompanied by the abandonment of Takṣaka,
joined with the Vāstu-homa, and provided with a sacrificial altar and a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila).
It should also be joined with the bedding and the fivefold [elements] such as the egg-born;
then, having brought the image, one should bathe it according to the previous procedure.
Thereafter, the Guru should tie the *kautuka* (sacred thread) upon three lotus leaves,
and he should also tie the *kautuka* upon the image and the bull.
Afterwards, one should lay [the deceased] upon the bed with the head toward the east and the face turned upward,
covering [the body] with white and red cloths while reciting the weapon mantra (astra-mantra).
At the top of the trident, one should worship the Śivāstra weapon, which is adorned with cloth and a golden lotus, possesses four arms, and is embellished with a crescent moon.
Four-faced, with blazing hair, adorned with three eyes, his own mouth endowed with fangs, and holding a spear, a trident, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons. (55)
Resembling lightning and the five [elements], it was formidable and accompanied by the sound of thunder;
it was endowed with sixteen years [of maturity], possessed a beautiful luster, and was marked with the svastika.
If there is an image of Śarva, a jar for Śiva, and a vardhanī vessel,
and if there is a bull, one should worship those [deities] within those [vessels] in the proper sequence.
And when the eight vases beginning with the vajra are arranged all around,
one should install the principles (tattvas) together with their respective lords, as well as the forms (mūrtis) and their respective lords.

As before, the preeminent gurus should place the principles (tattvas) and their respective lords upon the image, the bull, and the staff— from its middle to its tip and up to the edge of the leaf-patterns.
The forms of Śūla, beginning with Vajra as before, are considered the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās).
Having thus installed the forms and the lords of the forms, the Guru should install the weapon of Śiva (śivāstra).
Then, by virtue of pervading that [lotus], one should install all the gods and Manus;
one should install Rudra on the middle petal and Brahmā on the right-hand petal.
Having invoked Viṣṇu in the left [vessel], Pārvatī in the *pālikā*,
Ṣaṇmukha in the region of the *kumbha*, and Vināyaka at the mouth of the *kumbha*.
At the tip of the staff, one should worship the Teacher (Śāstṛ); at the middle of the staff, the Ādityas;
at its base, Caṇḍarāja; and Lakṣmī at the tip of the eastern petal.
On the south [he should place] the seven Mothers, Jyeṣṭhā on the petal of the western direction;
Durgā indeed in the northern region, as well as the Rudras, the Ādityas, and the Vasus.
At the base of the staff, he should likewise worship the Aśvins and the eighteen Gaṇas;
then, having performed the consecration of the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) and the fire, he should perform the oblation (homa) at its conclusion.
With fuel-sticks, clarified butter, rice, parched grain, sesame, and grains mixed with Indra-seeds, [one should offer oblations];
and the Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa trees are placed in the directions starting from the east.

Alternatively, the wise and most excellent preceptor should offer libations with *palāśa* leaves in other vessels, or he may do so with them in all [the vessels]; he should satisfy Śiva along with his limbs (attendants) in the principal vessel.
In the eastern pool, one should worship Pārvatī; in the southern, Brahmā; in the northern, Viṣṇu;
in the western, the Commander of the Army (Kārttikeya); and in the southeast, the two Sun-gods (Ravī).
One should worship Vighneśa in the southwest, Madana in the northwest, Caṇḍarudra in the northeast, Lakṣmī in the eastern pit, and the Mothers in the southern one. (69)
One should worship Jyeṣṭhā in the western pit and Durgā in the northern direction,
accompanied by their respective directional forms and so forth, according to the previously mentioned number.
The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and the two Aśvins— these eighteen groups as well—
are to be gratified by the offering of one oblation each in the principal sacrificial pit.
The preceptor should offer libations to the deities, such as the one mounted upon the bull, as before;
he should then seat all the deities, including Vajra and the others, within the lotus as previously described.
One should reverently bathe the Trident with the respective waters from the jars;
one should perform an extensive ritual bathing, offer abundant food oblations, and conduct a festival for the mobile [image].
Whatever has not been mentioned here should be understood as being included in what was stated regarding the general installation;
for that best of men who performs the installation of the trident in this manner, [attains the supreme goal]. (74)
Having enjoyed pleasures right here, one shall attain liberation at the end.
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Trident," in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
70. In the seventieth chapter, the ritual for the consecration of the lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*).
O best of the twice-born, listen as I describe the ritual for the lion-throne for gods and others, for kings and others, and for high-souled mortals. (1)
The gods and others, headed by Śiva, are considered to be many;
the first among them is the Cakravartin, and the second is the Adhirāja. || 2 ||
The third would be a lord of men; his characteristic is now described:
he who protects the earth as far as the four oceans. (3)
One who protects seven kingdoms is declared a *cakravartin*;
however, he who protects three kingdoms is declared an *adhirāja*. || 4 ||
Narendra is to be known as one [of these], yet many others are also considered [to be so], such as Pārṇeya and the rest; their seats were also many. || 5 ||
The height of the door should be divided into three parts; the best [height] is one-third, while the lowest is half of that.
Having divided the interval between them into eight parts, nine heights are thus proclaimed.
O King, its height should be equal to the rise of the door, or perhaps nine-tenths less;
it should be like a lordly elephant, reaching as high as the arms, thighs, or the navel.
This measurement of the regions is proclaimed specifically for kings;
it begins from fifteen finger-breadths and increases by two finger-breadths at each step.
The heights are said to extend up to fifty-five parts;
alternatively, they are considered to be equal to the height, or three-quarters, or half.
Having made the width four times the intermediate measurement, it is nine measures;
for the inferior [images] the measurement shall be inferior, while for the superior [images] everything is desired [to be increased].
Let a lion-throne be fashioned as either square or oblong;
for the universal emperors of the gods, it should be square, level, and circular.

Starting from one-eighth [of the total height] and increasing by that same increment, one should make the length of the lion-throne more than double; one should then have it fashioned in finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
Starting from two finger-breadths and increasing by two finger-breadths at each step, it should be made up to double that size; the same rule is prescribed for the length as well.

The measurement for the gods is outside the foot [of the stūpa], while that for the universal monarchs (cakravartins) is within it; for all others as well, the measurement is held to be up to the end of the foot.
The width of the foot is said to be either the whole [unit] or all [units] among them;
beginning with one and a half *aṅgulas*, one should increase it by half a measure (*mātra*). || 15 ||
Up to five finger-breadths from that wall, with a projection of one-fourth or one-fourth of a quarter of the wall's thickness,
the wall should be constructed there according to strength and according to beauty.

O twice-born ones, the divisions according to width are considered to be one, three, and five *muni*s (seven), while those according to length are said to be nine more than the previously mentioned divisions.
Between the legs, there should be legs upon a pedestal;
on the leg, between the legs, or elsewhere, one should have figures of lions made.
One should decorate [the throne] with various wonderful designs of crocodiles and sea-monsters;
it should be at one-third or one-fourth of the height of the lion-throne, or even lower.
The *upapīṭha* (subsidiary pedestal) should be made with one, two, three, or four *mātrās*, exceeding [the base] in width; its form is described here. || 20 ||
It is declared to be of two kinds: stationary and moving; [the stationary being made] of clay, stone, wood, ivory, metal, or even with lime.
A stone image is not desired for men; rather, everything made of ivory, wood, gold, or gems, and adorned with jewels, is suitable among the gods. (22)
The lion-throne (siṃhāsana) is the most excellent for kings; its characteristics are described here.
When it is divided into twenty-seven parts in height, there should be a projection, a lotus, and a plowshare [moulding]. (23)
The *vetra*, the *tala*, the *padma*, the *kumuda*, the *padmapaṭṭikā*, the *vetra*, the *karṇa*, the *vetra*, the *kampa*, the *patra*, and the *kapotaka*. || 24 ||
The *vetra*, *karṇa*, *nidrā*, and the *masūrādhāra-paṭṭikā* [should be] seven, one, half, and half a part, or else the *vyoma* [should be] four parts and half a part. || 25 ||
The Bhadraka [temple] is proclaimed to have nineteen parts by means of half-parts, quarter-parts, eighth-parts, sixteenth-parts, thirty-second-parts, sixty-fourth-parts, and with a half-part added.

In its height, there are thirty parts; [the measurements are] half a Veda (two), a pair (two) with a half (making two and a half), a half of a half-part (one-quarter), half-parts (one-eighth), one and a half (one and a half), and eight parts with a half (eight and a half). || 27 ||
By successive halving of half-parts— namely, by one-half, one-quarter, one-eighth, and one-sixteenth of the sky (the total height)—
one forms the lotus, the fillet, the ear, the fillet, and the molding.
The lotus, the tremor, the ear, the throat, sleep, and the band;
the foot, the upper band, sleep, the lotus, and the dove. (29)
And when [the hands] are positioned at the sides of the embrace, with the palms facing upward,
this is declared to be the *saumya* [mudrā], endowed with twenty-one limbs.
If these very [elements] are placed in the mouth and joined with the son of Subhadrā (Saubhadra),
and the pair of Bhadras is on both sides, it is proclaimed as Śrīvaha.
Of the five types of seats, the Vijaya seat should be prescribed at the back;
it is enriched with the height of Vyāsa’s seat and rests upon a support shaped like a lentil seed (masūra).
O best of the twice-born, it may be constructed with a height and width according to one's desire; in its center, a makara-arch should be fashioned according to a proportional division of that width.
The lotus-consecration should be completed in the middle of the archway;
from the base of the archway, a band of crocodiles projects outward by its own width.
O twice-born ones, it should be adorned with many ornaments such as the fist-bind, the encircled serpent-head, the tremor, the toss, and the pigeon.
One should decorate it with various wonderful figures such as sea-monsters (makaras) and crocodiles;
furthermore, one should fix iron arrows, spikes, and cloth strips.

One should decorate [the structure] made of gold with silk cloths and the like, or with various gems; moreover, one should fashion a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) made of gold upon the back of the archway (toraṇa).
One should fashion a lotus endowed with various jewels and possessed of infinite hoods, or alternatively, one may simply make a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa). || 38 ||
One should place either a canopy, a lattice-work, or simply a seat;
or one should employ a five-limbed pedestal beneath the lotus-seat.
The worship of the twelve limbs should be performed for the four [deities] beginning with Padmaka;
the neck is said to be one-fourth of the ten parts of the upapīṭha.
The small tremor (kṣudrakampa) should be made with a measurement of two parts for its upper and lower sections;
the great tremor (mahākampa) is to be fashioned, and the pedestal (upapīṭhaka) consists of five parts.
In each of the four quarters, when [the planet] is in its exaltation, [the degrees of the ascendant] are respectively two, one, half, half, four, half, half, two, one, and two and a half. (42)
The sandal, the lotus, the cane, the tremor, the throat, and the cane;
the cane-lotus, the fan, the lotus, the tremor, and the cane, in due order. (43)
One should construct this twelve-fold, charming *upapīṭha*;
on a height divided into twenty-eight parts, there shall be the *jagatī*, the lotus, and the neck (*gala*).
Vetra, Gala, Padma, Kumuda, Padma, and Kampa; Vetra, Gala, Vetra, Kampa, Nidrā, and Kapotaka. (45)
In the upper part, between the *āliṅga* and the *prativājana*, there is a *masūraka* support above;
from the base upwards, there is a *paṭṭikā* in sequence.

[The proportions are] one and a half parts, then one part, and then by halves, quarters, eighths, sixteenths, thirty-secondths, sixty-fourthths, one hundred twenty-eighthths, seven parts, and finally by halves, quarters, eighths, and three parts. || 47 ||
It is celebrated as "Śrīkānta" by means of half, half of a half, and one-quarter [units];
this indeed is below the throat, according to the proportions of one eye, half, and a quarter. (48)
One should join the *karṇa*, the *vājana*, the *nidrā*, the *vedikā*, and the *padmakampakam*; it should be circular and beautiful, constructed with thirty-two parts.

In the high [section], at the ninth part, half, one and a half, two and a half, three and a half, four and a half, five and a half, six and a half, seven and a half, eight and a half, nine and a half parts; || 50 ||
The sandal, the lotus, and the eye are lotuses; the lily and the lotus are lotuses.
The vessel, the lotus-staff, and the vessel are lotuses; the vessel and the lily are lotuses. (51)
The *vetravājana* is said to extend from the base for fourteen units (*aṅga*);
the *upapīṭhaka* for the four [deities] beginning with Śrīkāntā shall consist of eight units.
The *pādukā*, the lotus, the staff, the lotus-staff, and the *vājana* are formed with portions equal to one, four, half, half-an-eye, and half [of the eye] respectively. (53)
The *paṭṭikā* and the *vājana* [should be placed] upon that height divided by eleven;
the *upapīṭha* should consist of eight parts, or it is considered that all [elements] may be applied everywhere.
Many characteristics of palaces have been described previously,
including all their foundations as well as their pedestals.
And these [mudrās] should be employed here by teachers without restriction, especially for those such as gods who have their feet supported. (56)
Let a footstool be fashioned, closely attached to the body of the lion-throne,
measuring one-fourth of the height and width of the lion-throne.
The upper portion of the neck is made to tremble with various movements of the lotus-like head, so that,
by the measure of its graceful beauty, it resembles a circle formed by its seven parts.
From the size of a barley grain up to the maximum measure, let the increase or decrease be prescribed;
or else, one may employ all the postures (āsanas) that are auspicious.
One should perform the exit and entry of its limbs— whether one-quarter, three-quarters, or equal in measure—
either according to the strength of the aesthetic beauty (śobhā) or the power of the musical force (bala).
Now the procedure for all types of seats is being stated:
their circumference, length, height, and every other dimension. (61)
One should multiply the four bonds of bondage by the planets in their respective order;
then, the preceptor should divide the results by the numbers seven, five, twenty-seven, and four to obtain the remainders. (62)
Income and expenditure, the lunar mansion, the womb, and especially the day of the week; the Śāka, Sāla, Panasa, Śiṃśupā, and Candana trees [are auspicious] for a seat. (63)
The *tinduka*, *arjuna*, *tāla*, and *nimba*—which is the fragrant tree (*surabhuruha*)—as well as the *likuca*, *sahakāra*, *kuṭaja*, and *kaṭphala*. (64)
The *śrīparṇī*, the *jāti* trees, and the four kinds of milky trees (*kṣīravṛkṣa*), as well as the *jambū*, the *madhūka*, and that which is called *vaikaṅkata*. (65)
And for the sake of the seat, one should collect [the materials] by way of taking the substances;
having thus prepared the lion-throne (siṃhāsana), one should consecrate it immediately thereafter.
The time is declared as before, according to what is favorable for the patron;
then, having dismissed the artisan, after the sprinkling of the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha), [the following occurs].
Having sprinkled [the image] with the five products of the cow while reciting the heart-mantra,
one should wash it with water mixed with eight kinds of earth and with water containing *kuśa* grass.
Having bathed [the deity] with pure water while reciting the fivefold Brahma-mantra,
one should immediately thereafter bathe it again with scented water alone.
Having placed that [image] upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should cover it with cloths and kuśa grass;
then, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and incense while reciting the respective mantra.

Having uttered the word "siṃhāsana" (lion-throne) ending in the dative case along with its illuminator (the seed-syllable), it should be joined with the word "namas" (salutation) and endowed with its own seed-syllable. || 71 ||
Having thus recited the mantra, the most excellent preceptor should perform worship;
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before it, he should offer oblations with fuel-sticks and other materials.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge, together with sesame seeds and parched grain, while reciting that mantra.

Then, having performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the preceptor should sprinkle the lion-throne with the water from the peace-pitcher (śāntikuṃbha) and worship it again with perfumes and other offerings.
He was bathed, wearing white garments, adorned with a crown,
endowed with all ornaments, and accompanied by a parasol and chowries.
At an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction, one should install the king;
such is the consecration for the royal throne, which is even more distinguished when performed for a deity.

The arrangement of the forms and the lords of the forms, conjoined with the principles (tattvas) and their respective lords, that same deity accompanied by the fire-oblation (homa), and endowed with the mantras of the seats (āsanas). || 77 ||
With the [mantras] beginning with Ādhāraśakti and ending with Śivāsana, one should place eight jars in the eight directions; and between Indra and Śarva, in the center, [one jar].
Having established the principal pitcher (pradhānakumbha) provided with gold, cloth, and other offerings,
one should worship the deities of the world-protectors (lokapālas) surrounding the seed-syllable of Śiva’s seat (śivāsanāṇu).

Having thus performed worship at the beginning, the best of preceptors should then commence the fire sacrifice (homa); having satiated the mantras of the seat, he should do so at the conclusion of the full oblation.
Having placed all the mantras of the seats upon the lion-throne, the Guru should install the seed-syllable of Śiva’s seat, located within that [mantra], into the water-pot.

Having established [the deities], the most excellent teacher should place the world-protectors around [the vessel] with water from the jars, having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using those respective mantras.
Having bathed the Lord of the Gods of gods with a special ritual worship,
one should install the Lord of gods at an auspicious moment and a favorable planetary conjunction.
There, one should worship the teacher with garments, gold, and rings;
and one should cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given to the form of the Guru according to one's ability.
The dimensions of other types of seats are now described:
[seats made of] gold, silver, copper, brass, and bell-metal. (85)

[The materials] arising from mixed metals, stone, wood, clay, lime, and gems; those produced from ivory; and [metals] such as tin, lead, iron, and so forth, are for the sake of minor accomplishments (kṣudrasiddhi).
If the material for the pedestal (pīṭha) has been specified in this manner, then by its authority,
starting from two or three finger-breadths (aṅgula) and increasing by one finger-breadth at a time— || 87 ||
The measurement for the width is stated to be fifty *mānas*;
[the height] is one and a quarter, one and a half, one and three-eighths, or three-quarters of a *māna*, and so forth.

The measurement for the length is prescribed as two finger-breadths, or by increasing by half a finger-breadth up to a limit of one hundred finger-breadths; now the measurement of the feet is being stated.
Beginning from a single measure and increasing by a measure at a time up to fifty cubits, the length of the pedestal (pādāyāma) is proclaimed. || 90 ||
Beginning from half a finger-breadth and increasing by one-quarter of a finger-breadth, the width is proclaimed to extend up to twelve fingers, while its length is said to be one-fourth of that.

And those whose feet are straight—characterized by the lion, the serpent, and the bull—are radiant like spirits; they may have hooves like those of a donkey, or they may possess wheels, or perhaps not.
They may have the form of birds, humans, or the appearance of other remaining beings;
and they should be made seated upon lion-thrones placed atop lotus pedestals.
They may be made either as single units or joined with their own heads and feet;
they may have faces on the inside or faces on the outside, and they may or may not be provided with foot-ornaments.
They were adorned with various silk cloths, bamboo strips, bells, and the like, as well as leaves, lotus petals, jewels, and other ornaments.
Then one should join either an *anelikā* or a *phalakā*, provided with its feet joined for cutting and situated high above and below. (96)
Alternatively, a plank above the feet may be joined as desired,
increasing by one barleycorn or half a barleycorn at a time, up to the measure of eleven (rudra).

A seat made of wood is prescribed as appropriate for those such as the goldsmiths, provided it is equipped with side-boards, lotus-petal designs, and decorative carvings such as hīraka and the like. || 98 ||
One should decorate the panels with jeweled bands, lotuses, and various types of cane-work,
or else the panels may be left plain.
Above that, from the base of the globes (gulikā), they are endowed with various tremors,
joined with various dances, and provided with iron pins.
One should fasten it firmly with various silk cloths and flowers, or not at all;
it may be square, perfectly circular, or even oblong.
The seat should be well-constructed, having eight, sixteen, or fifty-three sides, and so forth; its legs should likewise be of that same form.
The first [sections] consisting of three, four, five, and six [syllables] should be joined as desired, so that it becomes like a tortoise provided with four feet, a head, and a tail. (103)
Likewise, one should perform the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana); other [postures] should also be inferred in this manner.
One may or may not cover it on all sides with gold, tiger skins, and so forth.
The characteristics of the *āya* and other dimensions shall be according to the path described in the *Siṃhāsana*;
this measurement shall extend up to the end of the planks for those who have abandoned the work of the upper [parts]. 105.
But for those associated with that [central deity] and those outside of it, the measurement is one-quarter less;
the consecration of these seats has already been described previously.
One should perform the characterization of the Āyas and so forth according to the previously stated rule.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, the procedure for the consecration of the lion throne, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
71. In the seventy-first chapter: The Procedure for the Installation of Chariots and Other Vehicles.
I shall describe the installation of chariots and other vehicles, preceded by their defining characteristics.
The chariot is said to be of many kinds, distinguished by its various wheels.
It may have three wheels, or four, five, six, or seven;
or it may be joined with eight or nine wheels, or even two wheels, being called a cart (śakaṭa). || 2 ||
The widths of the load-bearing sections should be three, four, five, six, seven, or eight spans (vitasti); their length is now described.
O best of the twice-born, the *akṣa* is declared to be the inner space, while the *upadhāna* is known to be like a small boat, filled with the dense *bhārata* syllables. (4)
The width of the Bhāgarabāhya should be half of the Viśālā, increased by one-quarter, or decreased by one-quarter;
its internal measurement should be provided with six [units].
O best of the twice-born, this is the task concerning the axle-load:
wherever there is an axle-load, the conjunction therein is described.
One should bind it with iron bands, nails, and very large nails at its own tips, so that for the sake of its respective protection, it may become more firm. || 7 ||
Below that, for the sake of protecting the letters, one should construct spires on each of their respective middle and side sections;
these spires should be equal in height to their respective towers and half as wide as the towers.
The axle-protectors should be suspended with iron bands and made firm;
they should be provided for each wheel, whether they be symmetrical or asymmetrical.
Having fashioned the crest (śikhā) at the bottom of the site (vāstu) provided with a small cut,
one should bring the supporting base (upādhāna) for the purpose of inserting it above the axle.

For the purpose of providing a cushioning support for the axles, one should reduce the width; however, for the purpose of entry, one should divide the broad portion intended for carrying loads into sixty parts.
One should increase that by an equal or greater number up to sixty as the denominator for the sky (the zero);
the square root of twice that minus one-quarter is declared to be the length. || 12 ||
One should increase the half of the front and rear portions by one-eighth;
one should determine the width at the length to be one and three-quarter parts. || 13 ||
O auspicious lady, when [the two] are to be made near each other, either in front of that or situated beside it,
the measurement for those two is also considered to be according to the rule stated as one-fourth.
Or may there be even greater auspiciousness at the beginning than the auspiciousness at the end, O elder sister of Śiva!
Or may there be only auspiciousness desired at the beginning of the auspicious moments, according to one's devotion. (15)
One should perform either the Brahmāsana posture or practice it without [any specific] seat;
the measurement of the Bhadra and Upabhadrās may be equal or even greater.
Whatever measure of the auspicious chariot (rathabhadra) may be joined together, all that shall constitute the length of the load; one should not construct a joint within the load. || 17 ||
They are endowed with thicknesses of three, four, five, six, and seven parts, and are endowed with widths of two, three, and four parts of the great elements. || 18 ||
The weights, beginning with two and ending with nine, increase by one *akṣa* each;
their widths are three, four, five, six, and seven *ardhanīvrakas*.
One should employ other tested men capable of bearing burdens among these [guards], whether they are stationed at the front, the rear, or in the intervals. (20)
Above the Pratyakṣa, one should join the five-fold binding of the openings,
beginning from the fourth part up to the eighteenth part.
One should make the width extensive for those who are skillful and capable of bearing the burden;
the space between the rim and the hub of the wheel should be increased by one part at a time.
The ten parts are for the control of the rim of the wheel and its thickness;
outside of that is the measurement of the flame, equal to the interval between the rim and the hub.
O best of teachers, all this should be the length of the eyes; O best of teachers, one should make the eyes circular or without corners.
One should perform the fivefold rites involving the five-seized [planets] joined together in their own midst, numbering one million,
as well as the fierce rites against crows and other such beings.
According to one's capacity, the large [weights] and those of similar value are considered;
the measurement of the wheels, however, is regarded as being between one and two bhāras.
The wealth of the wheels is said to be one, two, three, four, five, or six parts, or more than that, up to eight parts beyond two parts. (27)
O twice-born ones, there should be an increase of one, two, or three finger-breadths at the region of the navel;
likewise, there should be spokes between those two [circles] on the outside.
The base and the tip should be joined with tapering proportions, consisting of two or three parts of the void;
from three and eight, there is an increase by eight until reaching sixty-four.
O best of sages, his charioteer should be either Ṣaṇmukha, or Nandīśa,
or Brahmā holding a discus in his hand, or Śakra.
The *upapīṭha* (subsidiary pedestal) should be above the *bhāra*; its measurement is stated here as follows:
starting from one part and ending at two parts, by increasing by one part [at each stage]. (31)
From that, there is an emergence from the *bhārabāhya* by means of the *upāna*;
then, through the expansion of the *bhārabāhya*, they end with the portions of *rasa*. (32)
Or the Guru should divide that exaltation by twenty-nine parts, using [the sequence of] three, one, sixteen, five elements, nine, zero, and three. (33)
One should construct, starting from the base, using one part out of three:
the plinth (upāna), the lotus (padmaka), the fillet (kaṃpa), the corner (karṇa), and the fillet (kapaka).
The lotus, the pedestal, and the base are cited as examples for the purpose of illustration;
[they are formed] by one-quarter, one-half, one-third, and two-thirds [of the total height]. || 35 ||
One should lead [the line] by a third part, or less by a fourth part, or even more;
their entry and exit shall occur according to the requirements of beauty and strength.
The *dhāma* has been declared as the *upapīṭha*; let everything [prescribed] for it be performed here, in the four corners, in the centers, and likewise in the *bhadra* and *upabhadra* sections. (37)
One should decorate the neck with *gulikās* and *nāṭakas*, each measuring one-quarter [of the height];
or the *upabhadraka* should be made with a height equal to that of the *upapīṭha*.
One should construct a firm covering of wooden planks above the auspicious [pedestal];
the planks should have their weight centered, and one should decorate them with feet and other ornaments. || 39 ||
One should join the lotus bud at the middle of the board's end;
its stalk, together with its base, should extend seventy-two finger-breadths upwards.
That which ends in hundreds is declared to be the root; one should know it by its division. It is endowed with wealth ending in eight, or likewise in the circle of eight stages.
Up to six-twelfths (one-half) of its extent, it should be tapered at the top;
there, it is joined with a curvature, combined with a *kuṃbha* and a *maṇḍi*, or joined at two points by a *gaṇḍikā*.
The lotus is joined with a pedestal, and above that is a lotus bud;
this begins from one-fourth [of the base] and increases by a space-equal portion.
The lower part should be joined with the peaceful [upper] part, provided with a broad belly;
it may be three-quarters as wide, or equal in width at its base.
O twice-born ones, the outer instrument (bāhyakaraṇa) may be thin-tipped, circular, octagonal, or have petals like a blooming flower; within this, the inner instrument (antarakaraṇa) is as follows.
Above the *bhāra*, one should construct a *vājana* provided with a small opening;
above that, another *vājana* endowed with abundant space as desired.
O twice-born ones, one should construct the *upapīṭha*, which extends from that [base] up to the neck, using either two pieces of wood or a single piece of wood. (47)
When that connection is to be established,
two bonds— each grasping five [fingers]— should be placed by the wise above the thumb and the index finger.
According to the desired thickness and width, whether in connection with that [base] or elsewhere,
one should likewise bring it to a state of equal division at its base and its tip.
Above the *antarvājana* should be the *upapīṭha*, extending up to the neck;
there, the feet should be placed at the conclusion of the *upapīṭha*.
Two planks are to be fashioned, situated upon its feet;
there, two [boards] are fixed together, extending five units in length.
Likewise, in the case of the two foremost *bhara* measures, it is thus described as being internal;
one should construct the *adhiṣṭhāna* (base) above the *upapīṭha*, and that is what is called [the base].
It should be equal to the *upapīṭha*, or half of that, or one and a half;
in its center, that which is the measure of the six [parts] should be taken as before. (53)
Its height should be equal to twenty-eight parts;
[the measurement] is by means of five, two, one, seven, one, zero, two, one, one, and two eyes [units]. (54)
One should perform the *padma*, *karṇa*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *padma*, *vājana*, *sadanta*, and *galakampa* movements within the great *vājana*. || 55 ||
One should perform this according to the method stated for the *upapīṭha*, adjusting for any deficiency or excess;
one should likewise perform the entry and exit in that same manner. || 56 ||
O best of the twice-born, this should be placed within; it may be either Upabhadra or Bhadra. Above the pedestal (adhiṣṭhāna), the group of four feet (pādavarga) should be constructed.
The foundation (adhiṣṭhāna) should be equal [to the base], or it is declared to be double;
its height within should be nine measures, or else increased by one-eighth of a quarter-measure.
One should decorate every section with pillared bases, with *nāṭaka* motifs, with rows of beasts, and with pillars in the forms of lions, spirits, and elephants. (59)
At its end, one should lead it very firmly with small-footed iron arrows (nārācas).
The measurement of the platform above the group of feet is now declared.
Beginning from three parts and increasing by one part at a time, it culminates in nine parts; this is called the alaṅkāra [type]. || 61 ||
Then, in the remaining sixteenth part, [the measurements are] one, three, four, and seven;
then sky, one, moon, and moon-parts; and finally, the horse. 62.
Sleep, the pigeon, the embrace, the vehicle, the counter-vehicle, entry, and exit—these should be understood according to the principle stated for the abodes (dhāmas). || 63 ||
This is declared to be the first *ātala*, auspicious and characterized by equal emergence;
it may end with a *pāda* or end with a *bhadra*, and is joined with a decrease from the root.
On both sides as well, it may extend from one unit up to the portion of the *rasa* (six), being devoid of any inward recess; in this very manner, the *upabhadra* [is defined]. 65.
The chariot is said to have one story, or it may be provided with two stories and so on up to nine;
from the base level upwards, it may extend from six to thirty parts, being either symmetrical or otherwise.

The height of the *prastara* (the base) should be the measurement for the two *kapota* (dovetail) mouldings, each having a height of two *tala*s; in this very manner, one should construct those with three *tala*s and so forth.
One should cover the upper surface with planks made from the heartwood of trees,
one finger thick, or as desired, ensuring they are very firm.
One should indeed cover both the auspicious and the inauspicious with a cloth;
by this method, one should perform either the entry or the exit.
One should prepare the cords for the lines of the feet and the rafters of the bedstead;
having omitted the points of entry and exit, one should fashion the cord for the door-frame.
If it is joined with many stories and some particular feature is desired,
it should resemble the form of a staircase for the purpose of ascending the chariot.
O eminent sages, the width of the *bhadra* at its front or at both its rear sides should be equal to the depth of the entrance for each story of the *bhadra*.
Or a staircase should be constructed according to its prescribed rules—either devoid of an *upabhadra*, or possessing a *bhadra*, or even ending with a *bhāra*. || 73 ||
Having then abandoned all this, one should construct only the minor pedestal (upapīṭhaka) upon the base; above that is the station of the deity.
Leaving aside the *upapīṭha* in this context, there is only the *vāmasūra*;
its external application is thus described, while its internal [application] is stated hereafter.
Between the feet, small feet should be fashioned by the wise, situated upon tremors and bound to upward tremors.
Above that, one should prepare many *viṣṭaras* (seats) made from grass-blades, each measuring five *grahas* in length and nine in width; one should perform this for each individual spot.
The *tulāmukha* [pediments] should be made following the odd-even rule as desired;
above that, they should extend outwards, and the covering above that is considered the *icchādana*.
Above that, the Vijaya [arch] should be constructed according to one's desire from the height of the *dhana-ṭuṅga*, adorned with various spikes and plaques that grasp at the five [elements]. (79)
One should bind it very firmly with iron bolts, small nails, hooks, pulakas, and crooked bands at the joints. (80)

This is declared to be the *raṅga* (stage/arena), provided it is equipped with nine arches (*toraṇa*). If it is further provided with foot-projections (*pādākūṭa*), its measurement is said to be that of a chariot (*ratha*). || 81 ||
Starting from the *vedatāla* (four beats), one should decrease by half a *tāla* until the length of the foot reaches eight *savas*, beginning with three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and so forth.
It should increase by one-quarter at each step up to a maximum of four finger-breadths;
its width is declared to be one-quarter of its height, according to the proportions of the structure.
Equipped with a top, a base, and a pinnacle, the legs are joined with pot-shaped elements and the like;
they are provided with many ledges and fixed upon wooden planks.
One should fix the base with palm-tree wood wedges,
and likewise with iron bolts, so that the edge is very firm.
One should place the prastara above the pāda, making it suitable for the ascent of the *lupā*;
the procedure for the ascent of the *lupā* is performed according to the method for constructing the *śikhā*.
One should firmly cover another area with bricks made of gold, silver, or copper, along with small trees, and provided with a pinnacle of vital energy (ojas).
Thus, the chariot, as it was commanded, endowed with auspiciousness and other qualities,
is described by the Lord of Mountains in detail, both in its breadth and its length.

Then, one should increase the height of the entire [structure] by both [the base and the neck], or by the neck alone, using two, three, or four [units]; these are multiplied in sequence and then divided.
The seven elements, the constellations, and the netherworlds (pātālas) are assigned as the *āya*, *yoni*, *tāra*, and *vāraka*.
The lunar day (*tithi*) is tripled; this chariot is considered to be thirty cubits in length.
O best of Brahmins, the auspicious and inauspicious [omens] regarding carts, palanquins, and the like have been declared; now the installation of the chariot is being described. (91)
Having dismissed Takṣaka, one should thoroughly wash [the image] with pure water,
as well as with cow urine, cow dung water, kuśa-grass water, and the waters used for that [ritual].
Having sprinkled it with cow-products, one should perform the auspicious day rite (puṇyāha) and the sprinkling of water;
having also sprinkled it with the weapon-mantra, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should tie the *kautuka* (sacred thread) upon the lotus-bud with the *hṛdaya-mantra*,
covering it with a cloth while reciting the *dhāma-mantra*, accompanied by the *tatva-tatveśvara*.
One should sequentially arrange the embodied and formless deities, along with the Moon and the Sun, within the wheels situated in the south and north.
In the Harimakṣa regions, one should worship the deity known as Ādhāra;
having worshipped Vṛṣa in the Upapīṭha, one should propitiate Ananta in Dhāra.
The wise man should sequentially place Dharma and the others upon the feet, Adharma and the others above them, and [the remaining principles] below and above the coverings.
One should meditate upon the plank beneath the seat, and right there, the lotus above it; one should likewise recollect the pericarp, the nine Śaktis, and the throne of Śiva.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara, the lords of the chariot, along with Īśāna, reside upon the summit as the leaders of the stūpa of Śiva. || 99 ||
