Having reached the end of the lotus bud by way of the temple path, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) at its front; upon that, [place] those [images] provided with threads and cloths.
One should place nine jars provided with golden wicks and other [ornaments]; therein, one should install Śiva in the center, Bhānu in the east, and Indu in the southeast.
One should place Śakti in the south, Niṛti in the pitcher, Vṛṣabha in the west, and Ananta in the northwest.
One should place the first [portion] of the ritual substances in the northern jar and the remainder in the northeast direction;
having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should perform the rite of fire-oblation (homa).
Or,
for those who have established the [deities], there should be nine or five fire-pits (kuṇḍas) surrounding the gateway, or one situated to the east.
Having invoked [the deity] and prepared either a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or consecrated fire-pits (kuṇḍas),
one should satisfy Śiva along with his limbs (aṅgas) as the primary object of worship by means of a hundred oblations.

One should satisfy Bhānu and the others, two by two, in their respective directions within the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) according to the two sets of five kalpas; however, in the single kalpa, one should satisfy everyone in the pit belonging to one's own Guru.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, grains, parched rice, and sesame seeds;
the preceptor should perform the homa with the [five] principles (tattvas), their forms (mūrtis), and their presiding deities (īśas). || 107 ||
The Palāśa, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Vaṭa trees are assigned to the directions starting from the east;
the Śamī, Apāmārga, Śrīvṛkṣa, and Pippala trees should be situated in the intermediate directions.
Palāśa wood is proclaimed as the primary fuel for the sacrificial fire;
having offered full oblations and performed the worship of the pitcher and the fire on the second day.
When the auspicious moment has arrived, the architect, the astrologer, and the craftsmen, having received their sacrificial fees, should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa).

One should well sprinkle each respective location with the water contained in its corresponding pitcher; whatever is not mentioned here should be performed according to the general procedure for installation.
Having thus ascended the chariot, the man who performs the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) shall become wealthy and illustrious in this very world and obtain his desired fruit. || 112 ||
Having thus properly prepared the chariot, one should perform the chariot procession (rathayātrā).
It is proclaimed to be of three kinds: Paiṭhī, Śekharī, and Maṇḍī. (113)
Starting from fifteen finger-breadths and increasing by the measure of one *vyoma* (zero) at each step,
the width of the palanquin (*śibikā*) is considered to extend up to ninety-six parts.
Starting from twenty-one finger-breadths, one should increase it by one unit at a time,
determining the length up to one hundred and nineteen.

This measurement of the *īṣikā* is declared to be external, intermediate, and internal; however, for the gods and even for kings, the external measurement of the foot is distinguished as superior. (116)
The middle of the foot is considered common, with its extent defined by its width; likewise, the outer part is the *eṣikā*, while the middle is proclaimed [as the *sāmānya*]. 117.
The internal measurement in pādas that has been proclaimed for all [the systems] results in years by means of three, four, six, seven, or nine elements. (118)

The length is said to be one cubit (hasta) or one span (vitasti); it should be known as either a span or twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula), and it should be beautiful with designs such as the *māyā*. 119.
Alternatively, one may calculate it from the width or from the length;
or one may take the entire measurement and divide it by eight, three, three, or four, and then by twelve and twenty-eight. || 120 ||
O brahmins, that [distance] alone is the limit, being tripled by the Vasus and the stars;
it is considered to extend from the earth up to the sky in succession by thirty sages.
The income, expenditure, source, lunar mansion, lunar day, and day of the week [should be considered];
or else, the income may be according to the width and the expenditure according to the length.
By that very [calculation], the birth asterism (yoninakṣatra) is proclaimed by means of its width;
from the conjunction of breadth and length, the lunar day (tithi), the weekday (vāra), and the exaltation (tuṅga) are determined.
It is said that [the base] consists of three measures and the two single measures up to the end of its own half-span;
the height should be up to one cubit, and now the ornamentation is described.
Starting from three finger-breadths and increasing by one quarter-finger-breadth at each step,
the width of the arrow-shaft (iṣikā) is considered to extend up to eighteen finger-breadths.

O twice-born ones, beginning from the measure of a fathom (*vyāmamātra*) and increasing by the measure of a foot (*pādamātra*) at each step, it is taught that the *iṣikā* [posture] extends up to seven measures, being largely characterized by its abundance.
From one *vyoma* (zero) plus half a quarter (*pādarddha*) up to seven *mātras*, the measurement is well declared to be one *hasta*, whether circular or square. 127.
The form of the hand is proclaimed to be either circular (vṛtta) or square (āyata);
by increasing it by one-eighth part at a time, it extends up to twice that [original] measurement.
The projection of the bricks from the ears of the hands has been fully described;
however, there is this specific rule regarding the hand: it extends up to eight times its own diameter.
The thickness and width of the fillet (paṭṭikā) are prescribed according to suitability, ranging from one quarter-measure (pāda) up to four measures (caturmātra). || 130 ||
By means of tigers, lions, elephants, horses, men, and vidyādharas; by means of pills, footprints, and foot-tracks; and by means of turbans, [foot]prints, and the absence of footprints. (131)
With small bells, creepers, iron arrows, and corner-joists, as well as with decorative elements such as pigeon-holes and lattice windows, [the temple was adorned]. || 132 ||
And with crocodiles, bracelets, small beads, and foot-bindings, made of gold, silver, copper, or other materials, whether produced by artisans or derived from trees. 133.
One should decorate the palanquin according to one's means and for the sake of beauty;
this is declared to be the Paiṭhī, characterized by a crest and a pinnacle. (134)
If it has legs and platforms, and is adorned with the shape of a pavilion, it is a maṇḍī;
[the trees] are śūka, kāla, timira, panasa, niṃba, and arjuna. (135)
A palanquin endowed with the proper characteristics should be constructed from Madhūka, Khadira, or other trees that are described as having heartwood. || 136 ||

And its sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) should be performed according to the procedure for the lion-throne (siṃhāsana). I shall now describe the dimensions of the couch (paryaṅka) and the details of the palanquin (śibikā). || 137 ||

Similarly, that which is joined with expansion, joined with the interval of the three qualities (triguṇa), and joined with four feet and so forth, is said to be the measurement of a foot (pāda). || 138 ||
The length of the feet is declared to begin at three finger-breadths and increase by one finger-breadth up to fifty;
from two finger-breadths, it increases by a quarter-finger-breadth.
O best of the twice-born, at the base of the pillar it should be as wide as a lunar day (tithi),
provided with many moldings and adorned with various diamonds.
O best of the twice-born, one should provide it with many holes for the strings and attach it with iron at the three ends; on its side, one should fashion a wooden peg or a flat board.
There should be an abundance of fruit-bearing branches, arranged according to their beauty and strength, adorned with various silk cloths and various garlands. (142)
It is adorned with various iron arrows and features such as hair-erecting thrills;
it may be made of iron, ivory, wood, or even a combination of these.
When it is joined with the śibikā, yadvada, ādya, and so forth, it becomes a source of prosperity; this is called the paryaṅka, and furthermore, the bālaparyaṅka. 144.
It is described as being like a palanquin, devoid of an exit for the ears, provided with legs like those of a bedstead, and joined with a single strip of cloth. (145)
That which is placed at the base of the foot, equipped with small wheels,
and fashioned from trees such as the neem (nimba) and others, is called a *bālaparyaṅka*.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, the ritual for the installation of chariots and other [objects], in the *Uttarakāmika-mahātantra*.
72. In the seventy-second chapter, the procedure for the characteristics of the sacrificial implements:
I shall describe the characteristics of the implements in brief and in due order.
Fuel sticks made from trees suitable for sacrifice are recommended; they should be twelve finger-breadths in length.
Those blades of grass should be of equal length, free from bends, knots, and the like;
they should be firmly tied together with thirty darbha leaves and reach the length of an arm.
The bundles (veṇikā) or circular mats (viṣṭara), made of darbha grass, should be of that same measurement,
straight, with their tips intact, and produced from the same sacrificial wood as the kuṇḍa.
The enclosing sticks (paridhis) are said to be flawless, cut evenly, and equal in size;
likewise, the four seats (viṣṭaras) are considered to be of the same nature as the enclosing sticks.
Beginning with three *darbha* blades and increasing the number of sky-like *darbhas*,
one should gather *darbha* grass for the purpose of the *kūrca* up to a total of thirty-six blades.
Its length should be equal to that number [of knots], and furthermore, starting from eleven units,
each knot should increase by half a finger-breadth (ardhāṅgula) up to two fingers.
The measurement of the flame that curls clockwise around the book is said to be two mātrās; it increases by one mātrā at each stage, ending at nine mātrās.
Alternatively, other *kūrca*s are considered to be devoid of knots at their tips;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara are considered to reside respectively at the base, the middle, and the tip of the *kūrca*.
This is the method of placing the *utkūrca*; those [syllables] which go downwards in the *adhah-kūrca* are reversed.
The *utkūrca* is said to bestow peace (*śānti*), while the *adhah-kūrca* bestows nourishment (*puṣṭi*).
A tuft of grass (kūrca) should not be made inside [the vessel];
it should be employed in rites of sorcery (abhicāraka), consisting of two, three, or five darbha blades, including both their roots and tips.
It should be purified, strung with a clockwise twist, or otherwise devoid of such a twist;
it must be provided with a hole suitable for being worn on the ring finger. || 11 ||
The previously mentioned knot-peak (granthisikhara), which is pure and exceedingly beautiful,
is presided over by Īśvara as before, both on the right and on both sides.
At the time of performing rites such as the worship of the gods, there may be a need for something to be worn on the hand; for that purpose, a desirable ring made of gold should be provided.
It should be fashioned from twenty-three darbha blades,
measuring thirty-six finger-breadths in length, starting from the size of an arka flower.
The *darbha* garland, joined with an interval as desired and provided with a suspension loop, should be fastened by the little finger.
And it should be fashioned with a cord dyed with *aśvattha* leaves,
beginning at three cubits and increasing by one finger-breadth [at each stage].
Its length should be fifteen cubits, and its width half of that;
or, when the interior is equal, the measurement is proclaimed to be nine parts of eight.
The height of the door is said to be equal to its width or its length;
likewise, the measurement of the two pillars and the pedestal begins from three finger-breadths (trīṅgula).
Increasing the length by one finger-breadth at a time up to thirty units,
one should construct the archway (toraṇa) for the consecration and other rites using sacrificial trees.
One should lead the foundation elsewhere with bricks or with wood;
the excavation should be according to the desired measurement, and the measurement of the pinnacle (śikhā) should likewise be so.
Above the seat, there should be tridents with nine or five prongs;
starting from seven finger-breadths, they increase by the measure of a single void (finger) [up to eleven].
One should fashion the *śūladaṇḍa* (the staff of the trident) with a length equal to one side [of the base];
its width, increasing by one-quarter [at each end], should be two *aṅgulas* at the base and twelve *aṅgulas* at the tip.
One should have their thickness made according to the desired measurement;
thus is the toraṇa described, and now the eight auspicious signs (maṅgalāṣṭaka) are spoken of.
Beginning from nine finger-breadths and increasing by one finger-breadth up to thirty-six *mātrās*, one should determine their length.
Among those, a width of one quarter, a half, or three-quarters is prescribed; however, in the case of the division of the interior as desired, the measurement of nine parts is declared.

One should fashion the eight auspicious objects (maṅgalāṣṭaka) from sacrificial wood or metal, with a thickness starting at one finger-breadth and increasing by a quarter-finger up to seven finger-breadths.
The mirror, the full water-pot, the bull,
the pair of chowries, the śrīvatsa, the svastika, the conch, and the lamp— these are the eight auspicious symbols of Śiva.
For other gods and goddesses as well, during the eight auspicious occasions (aṣṭamaṅgala),
one should set aside the bull and instead employ their respective vehicles for that purpose.
One should perform the Śaiva-aṣṭamaṅgala rite for the gods or for those of the [four] stages of life (varṇins),
either in a village or in one's own home, according to the capacity of the patron.
One should draw [the designs] on mirrors and other such surfaces; their measurement is now stated:
beginning from five finger-breadths (aṅgulas), they increase by one void-finger (vyomāṅgula) each.
One should perform their length up to twenty-five units;
the width should be known according to that proportion, or it may be one-fourth more than a mirror.
Or, with one-quarter of that value, one should provide for it a quarter-measure;
likewise, for the full water-pot (pūrṇakumbha), a measure of one quarter is prescribed.
The face should be turned slightly sideways with a creeper-like curve; outside of that, the measure of the creeper should be the same for the foot, whether it is standing or lying down.
It should be provided with lotus feet and topped with a parasol;
the Śrīvatsa is as previously described, while the Svastika is used for entering a village.
The conch should be known as facing upwards during creation, and reversed in liberation;
one should likewise place the Śrīvatsa, the lotus foot, and the parasol [in their respective positions]. (35)
O twice-born ones, listen: one should place the deities upon the heads of women;
one should worship the Sun in a mirror and the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa) in a full water-pot.
One should worship Mātariśvana in the chowrie, Sarasvatī in the svastika, Vimala in the conch, and Havyavāhana in the lamp.
The preceptor should install Lakṣmī in the *lakṣmī*-padma and the bull in the *ukṣa*-padma with their respective mantras;
he should then place a pair of chowries in the eastern and western sections.
One should place each [image] on the altar, either on the right or the left;
or else, omitting eight *aṅgulas*, one should worship them in that location.
One should cause [the images] to be made with a vajra, a śakti, a staff, a sword, a noose, and likewise a goad; or else a banner, a mace, a lotus, and a wheel. || 40 ||
O best of the twice-born, one should fashion either a banner or a goad, omitting the staff;
these may be made of metals or of sacrificial wood, and if of metal, it should be according to the measurement of the image.

Having formed the gods with both hands joined in the añjali gesture, one should know that Jāyā, Śakti, and Gada possess female characteristics, while the remaining ones possess male characteristics. 42.
Their characteristics are described as being nine tālas in measure;
one should place the vajra and other symbols upon their heads, on the topknot, or in the hand. (43)
Their measurement is prescribed according to the size of their bodies:
thirty-six finger-breadths in length and eight finger-breadths in width.
Beginning from fifteen finger-breadths and increasing by two finger-breadths at each step, the length is said to extend up to forty-nine units.
Whether it be made of metal or produced from wood, one should measure them by the *mātrāṅgula*;
here, their width is stated according to the desired measurement.
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be fashioned according to the prescribed rule; that procedure is now described here.
One should fashion their cavity according to the rule, either on the side or in the middle.
Its length should be thirty-six finger-breadths or even thirty-five; its width at the base is six finger-breadths, and it has a pedestal with a thumb-sized pericarp.
It has three deep [indentations], with four, five, or six circular depressions;
it is seven finger-breadths wide, cut in half, and its opening is folded four times.
With its narrow base and broad upper portion, sloping toward the front with an exit for the clarified butter,
it has a pedestal rising from the vase, a six-fold neck, and a sacrificial altar at the tip of the handle.
The measurement for the pitcher (kalaśa) may be as desired; if there is a pedestal (vedikā), it should be two finger-breadths [in height], adorned with various vessels, canes, and lotus petals.
The ladle (*śruk*) should be auspicious, having the shape of the back of a shallow bowl (*śarāva*);
from its mouth downwards, it should be one unit less than the side of the bowl at the level of the handle.
The *sruk* ladle is joined with a handle made of cane, its width being equal to the span of the little finger;
alternatively, it may be thirty *aṅgulas* in length and eight *aṅgulas* in width.
The half of the rear portion is said to be solid, while the mouth is only the width of a *kauśika*. The mouth should be made triangular in shape and provided with a cavity in its center.
The *karṇa* (ear) should be desired at two *aṅgulas*, and the *vedikā* (pedestal) is considered to be eight *aṅgulas*.
Below that, the *gaṇḍikā* (corner-block) should be made, increasing by half a *mātrā* at each step.
The staff is said to be nine finger-breadths in length;
its circumference should be six finger-breadths, or eight finger-breadths according to the measurement of a fist.
Alternatively, another method for measuring the *sruva* ladle is described here:
it should be thirty-two finger-breadths in length and seven finger-breadths in width.
That solid part, however, is four mātras in height and six aṅgulas in length;
the ear is five aṅgulas in length and three aṅgulas (the measure of an arrow) in width. || 58 ||
The altar (vedī) shall be seven finger-breadths in length, and the lotus (padma) shall be five finger-breadths;
the pedestal (gaṇḍikā) is said to be one finger-breadth, and its circumference (nāha) is four finger-breadths. || 59 ||
The circumference of this staff should be half a finger-breadth less than its length;
at its base, it should have the shape of a vase, measuring two finger-breadths in height and ten finger-breadths in circumference.
The pedestal (pāda) should be at the base of the pitcher (kalaśa), or it is described otherwise:
thirty-six aṅgulas in length and eight aṅgulas in excellent width.
The mouth should be seven finger-breadths wide and possess a thickness equal to half its width;
in both breadth and length, it should resemble the snout of a boar.
The tip should be made with one-third [of the measurement], and having done so, one should discard the remainder;
the length of the corner (karṇa) should be two mātrās, and its width four aṅgulas.
The altar (vedikā) should be eight finger-breadths in length, with a width equal to that;
its middle cavity is said to be three or four finger-breadths [in size]. (64)

The staff should be made six finger-breadths [in width]; in its middle, there should be three nodes (gaṇḍikās). These should be made four finger-breadths [in height], increasing by half a finger-breadth for each successive one. || 65 ||

The staff shall be thirteen finger-breadths long; at its base, there is a pot as described previously. The *sruk* ladle and the *sruva* spoon should have that same source and those same measurements. || 66 ||
One should fashion it as being shorter by one, two, or three finger-breadths in length;
at the base of the handle and at the bowl, its circumference should be six finger-breadths.
The neck should be half that measure and should become gradually thinner;
at its front, the place for the clarified butter (ājyasthāna) should be made in the shape of a city gate (gopura).
On the back [of the vessel] there should be two knobs; this is the lotus-pattern of a *karṣāpaṇa*.
A new one is best, but in its absence, an old one may be used. (69)
O twice-born ones, having given wealth to the guru, one should accept the *purākaraṇa*;
then, by his command, that shall become the means for enjoying it.
Because of the prior recitation of a thousand *aghora* mantras during the seizing of the ancient instruments,
by whatever scripture and in whatever place a ritual was previously performed.
In that regard, O wise ones, the procedure established by those scriptures has been prescribed;
for rites such as festivals where it is not explicitly mentioned, one should adopt the method from other sources.

Whether it be a missile, an image, or the ritual implements of a deity, that which has been perfected within its own proper abode is excellent; however, one situated in another's dwelling should not be accepted.
If the image and so forth are endowed with inauspicious Āyās and the like because they are contrary to the characteristics of that [deity] and so on,
then the image and so forth which has been installed must be made conformable to those characteristics.

O best of sages, he should perform the initial festival rites and so forth for that very [image], and carry it out for the purpose of purifying the fault of its movement from one location to another. (75)
One should perform the *śānti* oblation with fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and cooked rice (*annaka*), numbering one thousand,
accompanied by abundant offerings using the mantra of the small temple (*hrasvaprāsāda*).
The archways should be characterized by the species of milky trees;
their height for the smallest [size] is five, six, or seven cubits.

One should calculate the tips of the fingers of others as being eight and four digits (aṅgulas) long; among those, that which is beyond the hand is known as the *para*, characterized by its own increase.
The distance between the two branches should be equal; otherwise, it would diminish in height. Alternatively, for others, it should be twelve or sixteen finger-breadths.
In the small-scale measurement system, the arch (toraṇa) ranges from one to four cubits;
its height is prescribed as being either equal to its width or half of it.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, the procedure for the characteristics of the instruments, in the great tantra *Uttarakāmikākha*.
73. In the seventy-third chapter, [the topic is] the ritual procedure for the rite of happiness (*saukhya-karma*):

at the beginning and end of the rites of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and festivals, as well as during the daily festival (*nityotsava*), the rite of happiness must be performed; listen, O twice-born ones, according to the rule.
And that pleasure with the daughters of Rudra is considered to be of two kinds;
O Kauśika, Rudra created the Apsarases for the sake of providing delight. (2)
In their ancient lineage, that family of Rudra’s courtesans was born as eternally untouchable by those of the pratiloma castes and others. || 3 ||
O best of the twice-born, those very ones are said by others to be the daughters of Rudra;
formerly, they were created by me in the Devatāru forest for the sake of diversion. || 4 ||
O best of the twice-born, having assumed a beautiful form, I entered there;
seeing me, the wives of the sages standing there were filled with respect and could not contain their joy.
With their hair and garments disheveled, they were born afflicted by passion;
indeed, I have seen them all in such a state with great care.
Merely by my glance, they conceive an inexhaustible womb;
those who are born from such various wombs are considered to be the courtesans of Rudra.
"Having honored them all there, what will be our means of livelihood?
Being asked thus, I spoke as follows: "Listen to that which has been uttered by me. (8)
If that which is the most excellent for my worship is accompanied by happiness,
then that alone is pure dance, according to the characteristics proclaimed by Bharata.
That [image] should be employed in worship day after day for the sake of my pleasure by women born of that lineage, together with the five preceptors.
When this had been spoken in due order, they prostrated themselves upon the surface of the earth;
and by me, being pleased, all of them were indeed initiated with the initiation.
O best of the twice-born, having summoned Nandin and taken the staff held in his hand, he touched their heads with it.
From that time forward, they have existed on earth under the designation "Nandas";
and because their heads were touched by the staff, they are also called "Daṇḍins."
Let pure dance be performed by those renowned for their birth in noble families;
likewise, let there be dancers, drummers, singers, and flute-players. (14)
Likewise, the Mauravika—these are proclaimed as the five teachers;
they are born from the anuloma unions of the four castes and have exerted themselves in the Nāṭya-veda. || 15 ||
Those devoted to me are free from blemish; they are skilled in meditation, proficient in song, dance, and instrumental music, and they possess knowledge of the nine dramatic sentiments.
Among them, the one declared to be the most excellent was a dancer who knew the science of dance;
he was himself capable of dancing and was devoted to the counting of rhythmic measures (mātrā).
Mardaka was well-trained in the science of wrestling; when the pure dance had commenced, he was intent on observing its movements. (18)
The singer, skilled in the science of song and proficient in the seven notes, leads the performance by means of the distinctions of those seven notes. (19)
The flute-player (vāṃśika) should be exactly like that, but he must have undergone training in the flute;
for the sake of pleasure, he should play the flute according to the distinctions of the udātta and other accents.
The Maura-vika is considered to be at the mouth [of the drum] during times of pleasure;
the Nartaka and another, the Mardaka, are situated on the right side.
The singer and the one called the flutist are stationed on the left side;
in front, the drummer and the one named Saumya likewise play the mukha-drum.
Although all of these have already been consecrated previously, if there is to be a rebirth for them, a further initiation (punardīkṣā) must be prescribed; that [initiation] is now described briefly.
On an auspicious day, those women who are more than fifty years of age but less than fifty-five years of age are suitable; others are never suitable under any circumstances.

O twice-born ones, one should have a pavilion constructed for the sake of comfortable dancing, endowed with the proper characteristics; starting from thirty-two cubits, it should be reduced by two cubits at a time.
From the gods down to the trident-bearers (Śūlapāṇi), there are three grades each—superior, middling, and inferior; among these, let that which is desired be chosen. (26)
In this manner, one should take possession of the pairs [of deities] according to the sequence beginning with the gods;
or else, all the pavilions previously constructed are common to all.
Dancing should be performed by means of various gestures such as the *paṅkti-hasta* and others;
furthermore, all the pavilions (*maṇḍapas*) should be constructed as consisting of the digits (*kalās*) beginning with *nivṛtti*.
And in the center of that, one should perform pure dance according to the rules;
then, having worshipped Naṭeśa along with his limbs (attendants) in the pavilion with perfumes and other offerings.

Having summoned the Rudra-prostitutes, one should sprinkle them with water from a conch shell consecrated by the recitation of the five-syllable mantra and others, once they have been smeared again in front of the door.
One should fashion a seat consisting of the Praṇava in the center of that [mandala];
having taken a washed cane by which the preceptor has been struck.
Having placed the staff with its tip pointing either eastward or northward,
the preceptor should worship Nandin there with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Clad in new garments, wearing a garland and a turban,
with an upper robe and beautiful flowers, his limbs smeared with white sandalwood paste, and adorned with finger-rings, he was a true Śaiva.
Having received the five niṣkas and other sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
his disciple, taking them, should place them in order on the head and other parts [of the body].
One should place the entire mantra "śivāya namaḥ" upon the head;
having worshipped it thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings, one should again place the staff as before.
Without uttering the name beginning with "Nanda," so that he may attain awakening,
I shall give him another, more exalted name, Daṇḍin.
"Having thus instructed her, 'For the sake of being favorable toward your dancing at the time of my festival and other occasions,' he should place a cluster of flowers into her hand. (37)
Taking that [flower], he should then offer it to the Guru with palms joined in reverence;
then, taking flowers again, he should present them to Śiva. || 38 ||
Then, one should perform the dance beginning with the "five steps" (pañcapadī) and so forth, as taught by Bharata; it is pleasing to Śiva and brings about happiness in the presence of Śiva. (39)
In this way, the initiation of women is described as being performed among the five types of preceptors;
it may take place either in the house of the teacher or in one's own delightful home.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods in the central portion together with his limbs, one should place a water-pot before him, provided with gold, cloth, and other offerings. (41)
One should consecrate that water by reciting the five-syllable mantra;
then, having performed their ablutions and being provided with white garments and other such items, one should [invite] five preceptors.
Having sprinkled his head with that water, he should touch it with the *kūrca* [grass-bundle];
then, being endowed with the five-syllabled mantra, he attains the authority for ritual action.
The entry of the Rudrakanyās is first described in brief:
prior to the designated day, one should perform the auspicious rite of the sprouts (maṅgalāṅkura).
Having constructed two pavilions facing east on the four sides of the palace,
one should bring the pedestal and the sacrificial altar (balipīṭha) into the pavilion according to the requirements.
Having prepared either a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila) in the center of the pavilion and in front of it,
one should worship the Lord of the Gods on the preceding day.
The Rudra-maidens, numbering as many as the Yugas, having fasted, with cleansed teeth, well-bathed, and adorned in all their limbs, [were present] with perfumes and other offerings. || 47 ||
Endowed with all auspicious signs, there were likewise five such preceptors; having performed obeisance to Śarva, they were tranquil and equipped with bound *pratisara* amulets.
And having accepted [the invitation] on the previous day, he should perform this rite at dawn;
having installed the God of the lords of gods with a thousand jars and other [vessels], [he should proceed]. 49.
Having worshipped [the artisan] with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, together with abundant sacrificial food (havis),
and having properly dismissed the craftsman from the pavilion, one should smear [the ground] with cow dung.
Having performed the sprinkling with meritorious water, one should then feed the Brāhmaṇas;
in the center of the central pedestal, one should worship the god Sadāśiva.
Naṭeśvara, together with the Goddess, his seat, and his Brahman-form—along with his limbs and attendants—is now described in its enclosure. (52)
One should worship Nandin in the eastern direction, Brahmā in the south,
Skanda in the western region, and Viṣṇu in the north.
Outside of that, one should worship the world-protectors and a network of weapons;
having worshipped Rudra in the eastern direction together with the goddess Gaurī.
As before, one should worship Brahmā,
accompanied by his retinue, together with Sarasvatī, and joined by the world-protectors and the rest, in the south.
In the western pavilion, the wise one should worship Skanda together with the world-protectors and others; to the north, he should worship Viṣṇu, surrounded on the outside by the world-protectors.

Having consecrated the fire and the sacrificial pit, and having invoked and worshipped one's own deity within the respective fire with perfumes and other offerings, preceded by the joining of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna); || 57 ||
One should perform the hundred-fold oblation with ten repetitions for each enclosure;
one should carry out the full rite with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, and sesame seeds.

Having fully worshipped the deity on the stage, one should perform pure dance, provided that the best of the twice-born have previously been consecrated according to the procedure mentioned before. (59)
If they are dependent on that [deity], one should perform the consecration and have them dance;
at the commencement of the dance, there should be a special worship of the preceptor.
O twice-born ones, one should provide maintenance for the five preceptors and the maidens with garments, ornaments, and other such items, so that they may feel affection toward them.

At the conclusion of the perpetual festival, happiness should be provided by a Rudra-maiden who has performed her ablutions, is adorned with ornaments, and is arrayed in white garlands and the like. (62)

Having worshipped Raṅgeśa, accompanied by the five preceptors, along with the surrounding enclosure as before, one should then [worship] in front of him that which is endowed with the nine dramatic sentiments (nāṭyarasa).
One should perform pure dance accompanied by the contemplation of the meaning of the verses;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are remembered as the presiding deities of the three junctions of the day.
One should recite three verses in succession at dawn, midday, and evening:
"Accompanied by songs with the sweet sounds of swarms of bees intoxicated by various fragrances scattered among *mandāra* flowers..."
May this handful of flowers, increasing through various ritual gestures, be offered by me to the Lotus-Seated One.

With a dance born of the tradition of dancing, overflowing with aesthetic flavor and accompanied by continuous emotional expression, let there be an offering of handfuls of flowers, resonant with the humming of bees intoxicated by fragrance, for Puruṣottama.
Accompanied by female dancers and others consecrated by Śiva, including the daughters of Rudra; increasing with various kinds of dramatic performances;
and for the prosperity of the king and his kingdom, [it was adorned] with showers of various flowers.
May this handful of flowers be offered by me to the Supreme Lord. || 67 ||
In the rites of installation, sprinkling, expiation, and portents;
in festivals, ritual bathing, monthly worship, and the performance of fire oblations (homa); || 68 ||
It is especially distinguished at the beginning of the ritual for raising the banner, and in rites performed for specific desires.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, the Ritual for the Action of Happiness, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
74. In the seventy-fourth chapter, the procedure for the specific regulations is prescribed:

now the specific [distinctions] among all [practitioners] in all rites are set forth—the preceptor (ācārya), the practitioner (sādhaka), the other [the spiritual son] (putraka), and the initiate (samayin).
These five were created by Maheśvara, each succeeding one superior in qualities to the preceding; this distinction arises from refinement, while their specific status is declared by birth. (2)
The four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, as well as the six anuloma [castes], are indeed superior by virtue of their qualities as before; thus is the distinction of birth declared. (3)
One is distinguished by age, by knowledge, by devotion, or even by dispassion;
likewise, one is distinguished by yoga, by ritual action, or even by conduct.
First the royal preceptor, then the king, then his queen, then his domestic priest, then his sons, and finally the ministers— these are distinguished in this sequence.
The preceptor, the officiating priest, and the astrologer— these are, in their respective order, superior within the abode of Śiva for both the formless (niṣkala) and the other (sakala) aspects.
Afterwards, King Maṭhapatī was appointed by him;
thereafter came my perpetual devotees, who were materialistic and free from wages.
There were attendants and worshippers, devoted and provided with sustenance;
there were independent singers and those intent on the chanting of mantras and the like.
There were five preceptors, my daughters, and deities who served as musicians;
the superiority among them was proclaimed according to their respective duties.

For others not mentioned by name, having understood their specific excellence with due respect according to their respective actions and even according to their status as Brahmins and so forth— || 10 ||
O Lord, one should perform worship during auspicious occasions such as the Pavitrārohaṇa;
for all of these, the principal [rite] is prescribed according to the command of the preceptor.
He by whom it is declared, "I am the guide," is the excellent Guru.
The command of the Guide is my own command; that has been spoken by me in the Śiva-Āgama. (12)
Therefore, at the outset, he should be worshipped by all just as I am;
for it is recognized here that excellence is established through the sequence beginning with the true path.
The Path of the True Being, the Path of the Son, the Path of the Companion, and likewise the other, the Path of the Servant—among these four, superiority is held to exist in successive order. (14)

One who follows the true path, having abandoned worldly impressions, being capable, pure, and endowed with devotion, shall become a follower of the Putramārga, proficient in all the Śaiva Āgamas. || 15 ||
He has adopted a person as his son, and he is a preceptor who performs the rites for progeny. || 16 ||
One who follows the shared path (sahamārgī), one devoted to the worship of Śiva, the fire-sacrifice, recitation, and oblation;
or one who possesses the knowledge of Śiva—whether he be a Praveśaka or an Aupadeśika.
He established the Dāsamārgī, Śivodyāna, Liṅga, Bimba, Ālaya, and other sites; he performed Śaiva dances, prostrations, hymns, and songs, and he was the crusher of the wicked. || 18 ||
Having deliberated in this manner with the Śaivas in many ways, one should specifically designate [the site] as endowed with such qualities. || 19 ||
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, the procedure for the special ordinances, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
75. In the seventy-fifth chapter, the procedure for the rite of destroying diseases:
I shall now describe the method for destroying diseases in brief and in due order, for all mortals, and especially for kings. (1)
For quadrupeds—such as cattle, elephants, horses, goats, and buffaloes—these [rites] are especially effective against fever, malevolent planets, possession, and epilepsy. || 2 ||

It is used for the treatment of consumption, edema, splenic disorders, abdominal tumors, colic, and insanity; and in cases of the aggravation of vāta, pitta, and kapha, as well as burning sensations, delusion, and severe pain in ulcers.
In cases of the arising of large abdominal tumors, urinary stones, cysts, urinary disorders (prameha), and so forth, as well as other great diseases born in the head, eyes, teeth, or ears; (4)

O best of the twice-born, when a disease has arisen from the mouth or other parts of the body, or when it has appeared without being previously mentioned, or when it occurs in elephants and other animals, [the following applies]: || 5 ||
The procedure for consuming ghee is prescribed for the purpose of curing that disease, for the cause of preventing future illness, and for the sake of nourishment and strength. (6)
In a temple, on a riverbank, on a mountain, or even in a forest;
or in some other meritorious place, or in one's own home in that particular spot.
In a place that is secluded, delightful, pure, and smeared with cow dung—
whether upon a linga, a mandala, a water-jar, a sacrificial mound, or on a wooden plank and the like— || 8 ||
Having invoked and worshipped the gods headed by Śiva as before, with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and accompanied by oblations of clarified butter; || 9 ||

Having bathed the supreme deity with the nectar of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances, the wise practitioner, having performed worship, should perform the recitation (japa).
Ten thousand, or half of that, or even half of half of ten thousand;
or a thousand, or half of that, or indeed one hundred and eight.
One should perform the rite of recitation (japa) in accordance with each respective mantra;
having uttered the mantra: "O God, destroy, destroy the disease! (12).
Having recited this, and especially the verse concerning Devadatta,
and having performed the recitation in this manner, one should offer it to the chosen deity.

Having offered praise and prostrated before the Lord of Gods, who is provided with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), and accompanied by kuśa grass and dūrvā leaves, one should take recourse to the place for the fire-oblation (homa).
To the east of that, in the northeastern quarter,
one should duly bring forth the Śiva-fire in either a square or circular pit (kuṇḍa), or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
In the center of that, having invoked one's chosen deity (iṣṭadeva),
one should worship it with perfumes and other offerings, or with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, rice, and sesame seeds as prescribed by the ritual manual.
Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) as one-tenth of the recitation (japa), or one hundred and eight times,
and having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should then discard the ashes from that [fire].
Having approached the divine Kumbha and the Śivāgni, the Guru, having informed him of the homa-rite, praised and prostrated before the deity. || 18 ||
The wise one should sprinkle the afflicted person with water contained in that jar;
he should then apply an anointing of its ashes while joined with the meditation on that mantra.
The preceptor should offer a bali-oblation of curd-rice mixed with ghee to Rudra and the other deities;
or he may offer the bali at the conclusion of the fire-sacrifice (homa), as it is also taught otherwise.
Having fashioned an effigy out of flour in accordance with his form,
one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, up to the offering of the bali oblation.
Rice-milk porridge (pāyasa) combined with various seasonings, or even that made from mung beans; pure cooked rice mixed with clarified butter, or accompanied by curd, cakes, and the like.
Every day, however, at the three junctions of the day, or else at a single time,
one should [perform this] at the foot of a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa), or even on a public road.
Or one should cast it near a mother’s dwelling, or in a cremation ground and the like;
whichever being here exists by depending upon Devadatta. (24)
This very great offering (bali) for him is considered to be a common mantra;
it may last from one day up to ten days, or from a month up to a year.
This offering, accompanied by incense and lamps, is declared to be for one's own self among living beings here, lasting from one year up to a hundred years. || 26 ||
The Patākā, Svādu, Pānīya, Yukta, and Sādhāraṇa are considered [the five types].
Alternatively, another method for the liberation from disease is now described. || 27 ||
Having worshipped the deity in the linga or other forms and having completed the recitation and fire-offerings,
[one should offer] an image made of gold or silver, fashioned from a hundred niṣkas.
Or else, it may be fashioned with half that amount, or with twenty-five;
or this [image] may be fashioned with ten niṣkas, or even with five niṣkas. || 29 ||
The wise man should fashion a representation either half that size or measuring exactly one *niṣka*; he should not practice stinginess regarding his wealth.
Having assumed a form afflicted by disease according to each respective appearance,
he may take on the form of Time (Kāla), or the form of the rim of a wheel (Nemi), or yet another form.
Having worshipped according to the previously mentioned rite, one should cause that to be offered to Śiva;
by this method, the sick person shall become free from disease—of this there is no doubt.
Whether it be merely the offering of oblations, or for the duration of four months,
or up to five or six months, [it results] in the destruction of disease.
Alternatively, the destruction of disease is described in another way:
on the eighth or fourteenth day, or even on the full and new moon festivals of both fortnights. || 34 ||
On the occasion of an eclipse, at the equinoxes, or during either of the two solstices; or on one's own birth-star, or following the birth-star, in a pure and delightful location. (35)
Then, having smeared the sacrificial ground with cow dung, one should sprinkle it with water consecrated by the weapon-mantra;
having prepared the altar there, one should finally arrange nine new jars.
Whether numbering twenty-five, or likewise five,
or even just one among them, there should be a jar in their midst filled with a droṇa [of water].
[He should provide] [pots] together with their threads, together with their lids, together with cloths, joined with gold, endowed with all medicinal herbs, and provided with various seeds. (38)

[He should offer] vessels together with water-strainers, provided with sprouts, joined with sandalwood paste and unbroken rice, filled with fragrant water, and accompanied by their respective mantras. || 39 ||
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and especially with incense and lamps,
[one should offer] those [oblations] obtained by reciting the respective mantras a hundred times, either previously or in all four [directions].
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) specifically either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or even on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
the wise one should offer oblations into the Śiva-fire, combined with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked food.
Therefore, having collected that ash, the Guru should bathe the diseased person while they are seated upon a wooden plank in a place smeared with cow dung.
One should bathe the person afflicted by disease with substances located in those respective northern regions,
having first cleansed them with flour-cakes, barley, and the like, or with products derived from cow dung.

One should bathe [the deity] while recollecting the mantra accompanied by the respective visualization, or else one should sprinkle it with the mantra; thereafter follows the smearing of that sacred ash.
Even one afflicted by disease should then worship the preceptor,
whether for kings, crown-wearers, or high-souled local lords.
The Guru should prepare one hundred jars together with eight additional ones;
he should prepare no fewer than fifty from among them.
In all the jars, however, only one mantra is worshipped;
and especially in the central one, the Guru should bathe them with those [mantras]. (47)
Now, there may be another application for the specific destruction of disease:
beginning at sunrise, one should stand in water and recite the mantra. (48)
One should perform the recitation daily, either ten thousand times, or half of that, or half of that again, or one thousand, or even one hundred and eight times. (49)

One should perform libations everywhere with those [mantras] previously mentioned and those yet to be described; or else, it is considered best to perform them in a number equal to the oblations (homa) or equal to the recitation (japa). || 50 ||
If one is able, one should perform the recitation daily while standing in the midst of water;
by this method as well, [one may do so] on birch bark, tree bark, and so forth.
At an auspicious moment and a favorable planetary conjunction,
one should write the syllables with saffron, corresponding to the patient, preceded by the worship of their presiding deity.
Having performed it together with the preliminary oblation, combined with recitation and libations,
or simply the recitation alone, or indeed accompanied by yellow orpiment (gorocanā).
Having inscribed the syllables with a stylus or with an iron nail, the Guru,
after worshipping them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, should then have them fashioned into pellets.
Having fashioned it from gold, silver, copper, or even tin,
or else with lac, that [amulet] should be worn until liberation from the disease.
One who is weak yet strong and steadfast is honored by all on this earth;
[this mantra] may be worn on the ear, on the neck, on the crest-lock, or even on the hand. (56)
Or, for the sake of the mantra's presence, the mantra which bestows all fruits should be worshipped daily below the region of the waist.
Or, endowed with faith, one should constantly perform the recitation (japa) and worship;
or one should constantly perform worship and fire-offerings (homa), combined with recitation and libations (tarpaṇa). || 58 ||
The mortal who acts in this way is freed from misfortunes;
he shall become powerful, pleasing to behold, and a king preeminent in righteousness.
For all those who are incapable, the capable one is the instructor in action;
or else, when appointed by him, no other is [qualified], especially in royal affairs. (60)
Trust should be placed in him who is devoted to the welfare of others;
he is proclaimed everywhere and in every way as a true follower of Śiva. 61.
Now, the pacification for diseases that afflict elephants and so forth is described here:
[it should be performed] either in the middle of the elephant stable, or in a pleasant spot where a sacrificial stake (śūla) is located. || 62 ||
In the temple of Śiva or Viṣṇu, or that of Durgā or the Sun, or even in the abode of Vighnarāja, the Teacher (Śāstṛ), or the Mothers; || 63 ||
On the bank of a river, by a pond, in a divine garden, or in another location,
one should smear the ground with cow dung and then sprinkle it with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra.

Then, having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) according to the prescribed rite with śāli rice and grains, it should be provided with parched grain and darbha grass and filled with a droṇa measure of water.
He [should offer] a brush together with its cover, accompanied by scented water and provided with cardamom,
saffron, camphor, and the three fruits.
One should properly worship the formidable weapon (Aghorāstra), together with its limbs and its seat, there, accompanied by dūrvā grass blades and smeared with white rice.
Seated in the center of a lotus throne, six-armed and three-eyed, adorned with all ornaments, and possessing a radiance equal to the full moon. || 68 ||
Equipped with a skull-topped spear and provided with a bow and arrow,
with hair standing erect and three distorted eyes, he bears a sword and a shield.
Having meditated thus, O best of the twice-born, upon the form of the Aghora weapon—
endowed with the previously mentioned ritual actions and white in color— 70.
One should present an offering of food accompanied by perfumes and flowers, along with incense and lamps, as well as betel leaves together with various side dishes.
The preceptor should perform the recitation every day one thousand times, or half of that, or one hundred and eight times, using the King of Weapons mantra.

In front of that, in the eastern direction, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the Śiva-fire within either a circular, square, or quadrangular pit, or even upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila). || 73 ||
Accompanied by sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and cooked rice, and combined with sesame seeds and rice grains;
[the ladles] are made from milk-trees, from the bilva tree, and from the brahma-tree. (74)
The sacrificial fuel sticks (samidh) should be highly praised; or it is considered that an oblation of dūrvā grass may be used—one thousand, or half of that, or one hundred and eight.
Then, having performed the expiatory oblation (prāyaścitta), one should perform the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) at the end;
having collected that ash, one should dismiss the deity into the water-pot (kumbha).
Then, by the constant application of ash accompanied by sprinkling, the planetary afflictions and diseases are destroyed, and their nourishment is restored. || 77 ||
There shall be no occurrence of diseases, and they shall indeed possess long life;
wherever this ritual is performed, their lord shall be victorious.
One should offer the bali-oblation to Rudra and the others, ending with Kṣetrapāla,
as well as to the guardians of the world (Lokapālas), upon a maṇḍala prepared with cow-dung.
Whether near the elephant stable or at the site of the fire sacrifice, this very same procedure is prescribed for the protection of horses and other animals. (80)
However, O best of practitioners, the smoke-colored deity should be meditated upon;
[as well as] a herd of elephants, or horses, or cattle, buffaloes, and so forth.
Then, that which was afflicted by the king of weapons should be properly protected;
one should contemplate it all as freed from disease, joyful, and flourishing. (82)
One should perform this in the forenoon, at midday, or at night; it is especially recommended whether performed once, twice, or thrice a day.
The king who causes this to be performed constantly shall become meritorious and victorious;
he should honor the performer so that the latter may be satisfied. (84)
The protection of horses and elephants is described differently:
having first performed the libation with water, immediately thereafter— || 85 ||

Having worshipped Adhōra in a water-pot (kumbha) or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) as prescribed by the scriptures, using eight droṇas or half of that [four droṇas] in measures of khārīs made from droṇas; || 86 ||
Or, O twice-born ones, if he is poor, he may do so with half that amount, or even with half of that again;
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice grains, or with half as many grains of husked rice.

The preceptor, having placed in the center of that [area] a jar filled with one *droṇa* measure [of grain], accompanied by sesame seeds mixed with parched rice, and provided with perfumes and flowers; || 88 ||
It should be provided with a lid, a tuft of hair, a sacred thread, and young sprouts;
it should be joined with the previously mentioned substances and filled with fragrant water. (89)
In the center of that, having invoked Aghora while maintaining the previously mentioned visualization,
one should offer sandalwood paste mixed with camphor, flowers, incense, and a lamp.
Then, having offered as an oblation either pure milk-rice (pāyasa) or other food,
accompanied by betel leaf, one should subsequently complete the fire sacrifice (homa).
Accompanied by sacrificial fuel (samit), clarified butter (ājya), and cooked rice (caru), as well as sesame, mustard seeds, and parched grain (lājaka),
[the offering should be made] with fuel-sticks produced from milk-exuding trees or with dūrvā grass.
Either a thousand, or half of that, or one hundred and eight;
or by the number fifty, or by the number twenty-five.
One should offer oblations for each substance while reciting the Aghora mantra;
facing north, one should likewise offer the Aghora-weapon mantra and its companion mantras, beginning with the word "bhakta."
The oblation may be offered in two fire-pits, or even in a single sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
one should satisfy [the deity] with the principal mantra during the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having offered a separate *pūrṇāhuti*, one should perform the *bali* offering at its conclusion;
one should present the *bali* with rice mixed with ghee in the center and in the eight directions.
The oblation (bali) ending with "svāhā" is declared to be performed with the Aghora-weapon mantra;
one should then perform this oblation in the northeast direction of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The Aghora-weapon, accompanied by great flames and sparks from its crest, has now been worshipped and gratified by him; therefore, it is pleased with his strength.
"Protect, protect the rider of the elephant, and especially his master!
Svāhā! At the end [of this mantra], an offering (bali) is desired, as is especially the libation (tarpaṇa). || 99 ||
One should perform this ritual in the forenoon, at midday, or at night;
however, if it is a great offering (mahābali), one should perform it at midnight.
Food mixed with honey and ghee, combined with curd and parched grain, joined with plantain fruit and accompanied by cakes. || 101 ||
One should always offer a bali-oblation, accompanied by various sounds and joined with Bhairava and the other deities, even in villages and similar places, provided it is not devoid of lamps.
O best of the twice-born, he should especially remain in the royal palace at the place of protection,
equipped with the banner of the Aghora-weapon and observing the vow of silence.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the guardians of the field (kṣetrapāla) and to Rudra and the others according to the prescribed ritual;
at the conclusion of that, one should then sprinkle those afflicted by disease with the water from the ritual jar.
Uttering both the Aghora mantra and that Astra mantra at that time,
one should apply ashes consecrated with those two mantras while recollecting them.
One should give the ashes produced from the fire-oblation; thus the best of the twice-born shall be free from disease.
The performer should satisfy the Guru and the preceptor with food and other offerings. (106)
When the Guru is satisfied, all things, both stationary and moving, are satisfied; having performed the Aghora rite in the temple and other locations, the Preceptor establishes [the deity]. (107)
One should worship Śailāda daily, perform the fire-oblation (homa), and offer the bali;
having first established him within the water-pot (ghaṭa), one should proceed with the placement (nyāsa) and other rites of worship.
Diseases and calamities perish upon this earth through this alone;
or else, by means of libations, worship accompanied by fire-offerings. (109)
One should constantly perform sacrifice, fire-oblation, and the offering of bali;
this is said to be common to all mortals as well. (110)
One should perform the fire-oblation as part of the recitation-rite, practicing it daily at the conclusion of worship;
or one may perform recitation alone for the sake of pacifying all calamities.
The destruction of diseases of elephants is accomplished by another method:
having reached a pure location, one should smear it with cow dung. (112)
Having taken up a jar filled with a *droṇa* measure [of grain], which has a luster like that of a *bimba* fruit,
and having wrapped it with a thread made of *droṇa*-grain, (he should proceed).
On a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) prepared with half that amount of rice, half of that amount of sesame seeds,
and half of that amount of parched grain (lāja), the wise man should perform the ritual bathing.
In the center of that, one should place a *kūrca* made of five blades of *darbha* grass;
and within the middle of the jar, one should place these substances, including sandalwood.
One should add the three fruits together with kuṣṭha and uśīra,
and having powdered them, include cardamom and cloves as well.
Having covered it with a lid, the wise one should fashion the seat, consisting of that which is called the Support (Ādhāra), Ananta, and the four beginning with Dharma. 117.
The fourfold group beginning with Adharma, however, is provided with foundations below and canopies above;
in their midst, one should visualize a lotus, along with its seed-syllable, stalk, and petals.
The Guru should worship the pedestal with its respective mantra;
he should then contemplate the water-pot as having become the [divine] form, endowed with the previously mentioned visualization.
In the center of that, the Guru should worship the god Aghora, facing south, by reciting the Aghora-aṇu mantra and offering water for the feet and other oblations.
One should offer water for the feet (pādya) at the feet, combined with sandalwood and uśīra;
it should be provided together with cardamom, cloves, and the three fruits (phalatraya). || 121 ||
One should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya), followed by the eight-limbed arghya:
water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, rice grains, flowers, and sesame seeds.
The eightfold *arghya* is said to consist of barley together with white mustard seeds, sandalwood, *laghu*, and *kuṣṭha*; these are called the "triple fragrance" and so forth. (123)
Immediately thereafter, one should offer various flowers, leaves, and incense;
then, while reciting the Astra mantra, one should place [the weapon] at the base of the lotus petal on the right.
Having worshipped the Aghora-weapon as before, the Guru, having offered water for the feet and other offerings,
[should worship it] either together with its own enclosure or indeed without an enclosure.
One should worship Bhairavānatha, Sitāṅga, and the others starting from the eastern direction.
[These are] Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, and Unmattabhairava. (126)
Kapālī, Bhīṣaṇa, and Saṃhāra is remembered as the eighth;
having worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas) outside of that, and their weapons further outside of that.
Or, having worshipped the deities of the weapon-enclosure and the world-sustaining Bhairavas with perfumes and other offerings, one should offer a lamp produced from clarified butter.
One should offer to the God an oblation of food accompanied by side dishes and clarified butter;
then one should present water for drinking to Aghora and to his weapon (astra).
Having offered betel-leaf, the preceptor should mutter [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
then, having offered that recitation to Aghora and to his weapon (astra), [he should do so].
In front of that, the wise and learned one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) upon a sand mound;
as before, the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be performed, having been purified by the fivefold consecrations.
Having invoked [the deity] into the fire according to the very sequence prescribed for sacrifice,
one should perform the oblation with fuel-sticks from milk-producing trees, with clarified butter, and again with sacrificial porridge (caru).
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of parched grain mixed with rice and sesame seeds,
and finally, one should offer betel leaf to one's own deity in the form of the Astra-mantra.
Having performed the homa, one should then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) at its conclusion;
then, having collected that ash with the Aghora mantra, one should protect it with the Astra mantra.
Having performed the limb of enjoyment (bhogāṅga) and the limb of dissolution (layāṅga), one should dismiss the fire;
then, having offered the oblation-rite to the one in the form of Aghora residing within the pitcher.
Having received permission, the wise one should then pray for his desired undertaking;
having offered the arghya for the turning away [of the deity], he should withdraw the limbs of enjoyment.
Having performed the limb of dissolution (layāṅga), one should withdraw the Aghora [mantra] whose body has set;
then, within the lotus of the heart, one should likewise withdraw one's own and other Śambaras.

Having drawn water from that [pitcher], one should sprinkle it upon the person afflicted by disease, or alternatively, one should sprinkle them with those waters; one should perform this practice every day.
For the sake of all purposes, one should sprinkle that ground or the courtyards and so forth;
or, setting aside the Aghora and Aghorāstra mantras, one should worship within the center of the pitcher.
For one day, or three days, or even five or seven days; for a fortnight, or a month, or even two or three months. (140)
Or it should be performed daily; this rite beginning with the Pālaka-mantras removes fever.
Wherever this is performed, there is peace, and elephants and other animals are freed from disease.
They shall indeed become nourished; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Likewise, the Lord of the World will certainly become nourished and free from disease.
This very same rite should be performed for the pacification of diseases in horses;
O best of the twice-born, one should likewise cause it to be done for buffaloes, goats, and cows.
Then, one should cause the materials that have been consumed to be given to the preceptor;
every day, one should provide food and other offerings accompanied by clarified butter.
At the conclusion of that, O best of kings, one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's capacity;
in this manner, one should constantly perform the ritual by day or by night. (145)
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, one should offer the *bali* offering; one should perform this daily at night, either in the stable of elephants or horses, or even in the courtyard.
Alternatively, a bali offering combined with food and clarified butter should be made near that [image].
One should smear a clean and pleasant spot with cow dung. (147)
Having sprinkled [the area] with water empowered by the Aghorāstra mantra,
one should establish the protective enclosure of weapons, beginning with the vajra and ending with the discus.
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should present the bali-oblation ending with "svāhā";
one should cast the bali for the Lord of the Field (Kṣetreśa) in the direction between Vāyu and Varuṇa.
Having abandoned the terrible Aghora weapon, one should worship only the Madhyama [weapon], together with the enclosure of weapons, just as the offering (bali) is made to Rudra and the others. 150.
In whatever kingdom this offering is performed daily with devotion, there is no fear of calamities, nor does the affliction of disease exist there. (151)
Diseases that have already arisen will certainly be destroyed; of this there is no doubt—for the performer, the one who causes it to be performed, and especially for the preceptor.
The worship of that Aghora weapon, accompanied by fire-oblations and offerings, proceeds in whichever kingdoms it exists. (153)
O twice-born ones, there shall be an increase in lifespan, prosperity, and freedom from disease;
there is no yoga like this which is the cause for the destruction of sins. (154)
Since there is nothing [superior] in the world, one should therefore practice in this way with diligence.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, the ritual procedure for the destruction of diseases, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
76. In the seventy-sixth chapter, the ritual for the protection of kings:
I shall now explain, in brief, the method for the protection of kings. [One should use] fine ash produced from the *kalpa* fire and consecrated with mantras. (1)
The most excellent preceptor should apply a slight red mark above the navel for the king;
he should then recite the mantra upon the forehead, the face, the heart, the navel, and both armpits.
The wise practitioner, recollecting [the deity] beginning with Īśāna, or using the *iṣṭamantra*, should offer [the oblation];
he should perform it with the three fingers situated in the middle, which represent the deities.

Being pure, one should offer [the oblation] with the thumb and ring finger, identifying them with those respective deities, starting from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa, and proceeding in order from Īśāna onwards.
One should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, starting from the root and proceeding in due order, with their respective appropriate mantras that correspond to each officiant.
All mantras should be appropriate and endowed with the four classes [of syllables]. One should employ for a Brāhmaṇa those beginning with *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.

It is taught that for a Kṣatriya the mantra ends with *svāhā*, for a Vaiśya it is considered to end with *vauṣaṭ*, and for Śūdras it ends with *vaṣaṭ*; O God, this [mantra] should be accompanied by the visualization of the deity.
Or let their protection be performed with the mantras of the lords of their respective classes;
one should then give them a sacred thread consecrated with the mantras of the lords of their respective classes.
Or else, one should offer it after consecrating it with mantras favorable to oneself;
two sacred threads (yajñopavīta) are considered suitable for a king as an upper garment.
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, the Ritual for the Protection of Kings, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
77. In the seventy-seventh chapter, the ritual for the worship of Durgā: I shall describe the ritual for the worship of Durgā, which accomplishes all desires and aims;
first, however, listen to the worldly rites of exorcism, O best of the twice-born.
When the sun has entered Virgo, the eighth lunar day joined with the bright fortnight and conjoined with the Mūla asterism is known as Mahānavamī.

Or, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja when it is conjoined with the Mūla asterism—that is known by the name Mahānavamī, which is extremely rare to encounter in the three worlds. (3)
Having worshipped Ambikā, the Mother of the World, on the eighth and ninth days of the month of Āśvayuja, one becomes free from sorrow and overcomes enemies in this world.
He threatens others who hold swords at his side with roars of "huṃ";
even animals such as buffaloes are employed in his presence.
All those embodied beings who cast off their lives in the courtyard of Bhavānī go to a happy rebirth, for no evil exists there.
Their residence shall be in heaven; those heroes, beloved by the celestial nymphs (apsarases), are to be honored by people as steadfast men in every place and in every city.
In every house, in every village, and in every forest, intent on partaking of food,
the Guru [should perform the rite] in a region sloping toward the east or north with hands measuring eight cubits.
One should have a pavilion constructed, and to the southeast of it, a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit,
provided with three girdles and a yoni shaped like a leaf of the Aśvattha tree.
One should worship all royal insignia and all weapons upon the altar; indeed, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) for them everywhere.
The Guru should worship those [deities] daily with their respective *tanmātras*, perfumes, and other offerings;
likewise, the fire-oblation (*homa*) for Durgā especially should be performed with those very same mantras.
One should perform oblations with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial offerings, and milk-rice;
one should then present the remnants of the oblation to the horses and elephants.
One should constantly parade five elephants and horses adorned with *pratisarā* amulets through the city, preceded by various musical sounds. (13)
Every day, after the king has duly worshipped his respective ancestors and deities,
he should worship the royal insignia with fruits, garlands, and ointments.

At the time of the investiture with the sacred thread, the remnants of the oblation should be given to the elephant, along with offerings ending with the food-oblation (naivedya), accompanied by betel leaves and various cakes.
Victory is proclaimed for the king even in the seizing of that [enemy];
O best of Brahmins, listen as I proclaim the mantras for worship. (16)
"Just as the clouds cover this earth for the sake of Śiva's welfare, so do you cover the king for the increase of his victory and health. (17)
Oṃ chaṃ, obeisance to the umbrella! You are born of the lineage of the Gandharvas; you are once again the ornament of your family, by the truthful word of Brahmā, Soma, and Varuṇa.
Oṃ tuṃ! Homage to the horse;
through the power of the sacrificial fire, may you, O horse, be victorious, as well as by the splendor of the sun and the ascetic heat of the sages. (19)
By means of Rudra’s ascetic celibacy and the power of Pavana,
remember yourself as a prince, remembering also the Kaustubha jewel.

The destination that one who kills a father or a mother would reach, as well as one who speaks falsely for the sake of wealth and a Kṣatriya who turns his back in battle—that same destination he shall attain. (21)
The sun, the moon, and the wind indeed behold the doer of evil;
you shall quickly go to that destination, and this speed shall belong to you.
O horse, if you do not meet your end on the path of battle,
then, having conquered your enemies in combat, may you live happily together with your master.
"Oṃ, salutation to the horse"—
this is the mantra for the horse; O banner of Śakra, you of great heroism, you are the fair-winged one (Suparṇa) abiding in your own form.
The king of birds, Vainateya, as well as the banner of Nārāyaṇa. || 24 ||
Oṃ, salutations to Dhvaja;
he is the descendant of Kaśyapa, the remover of immortality, the enemy of the serpents, and has Viṣṇu as his vehicle.
He is immeasurable, invincible, and indeed the slayer of enemies in battle. (25)
O destroyer of enemies, may Garuḍa, who moves with the speed of the wind and stands ever near you, protect the warriors endowed with horses and righteousness.
Kumuda, Airāvata, Puṣpadanta, Vāmana, Supratīka, Añjana, and Nīla—these eight are the elephants of divine origin. || 27 ||
Āṃ Gaṃ, obeisance to Gaja.
Their sons and grandsons are the eight forest-dwelling regions:
Bhadra, Mandra, Mṛga, and Gajasankīrṇa. (28)
Born in forest after forest, the great elephant whose origin is the forest—may the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts protect you. (29)
"O Lord of Nagas, protect your husband; let the agreement be observed.
May you attain victory in battle; go on your way with our blessings for your well-being. (30)
May he obtain prosperity from Soma, strength from Viṣṇu, splendor from the Sun, speed from the Wind,
steadfastness from Meru, victory from Rudra, and fame from the god Purandara.
In battle, may the Nāgas protect you, along with the quarters and the serpents;
may the Aśvins, together with the Gandharvas, protect you always from every side.
The mantra for the elephant: Oṃ haṃ, obeisance to the elephant!
Agni, the Vasus, Rudra, Vāyu, Soma, and the great ṛṣis.
Nāgas, kinnaras, gandharvas, yakṣas, hosts of bhūtas, and grahas; || 33 ||
The Pramathas along with the Ādityas, Bhūteśa together with the Mātṛs,
Skanda the leader of the Gaṇas, and Varuṇa have all taken refuge in you.
May the king attain victory over all his enemies who destroy the Vraja; may the dogs and the defilements employed by his foes from every side be destroyed. 35.
Let the hosts of enemies fall around you, slain by your splendor,
just as they did at the slaying of Kālanemi and as they did when you destroyed Tripura.
Just as you shone during the battle between the gods and the asuras against Hiraṇyakaśipu, so too do you shine today; remember your vow.
Upon seeing this blue and white [image], may the enemies of the king perish quickly, conquered in battle by various terrible diseases and by weapons. (38)
Wiped away by your descent, they became healthy at once—
those known as Pūtanā, Revatī, and Kālarātri.
Having swiftly destroyed all enemies, you have been taken up by me as a banner.
The mantra for the banner (patākā) is:
Oṃ Paṃ, obeisance to the banner.
The sword is the destroyer, the blade, sharp by nature, and difficult to approach. (40)
Śrīgarbha, Vijaya, and likewise Dharmadhāra—these eight names of yours were spoken by Brahmā himself. (41)
Oṃ Khaṃ! Salutations to Khaḍga;
your asterism is Kṛttikā, and Maheśvara is your presiding deity.
Gold is your body, and Janārdana is your creator-deity. || 42 ||
O Father, O Grandfather, O God, protect me always!
You are the bestower of peace in battle; you are indeed armor against all calamities.
Protect me, protect me! I am worthy of your protection, O Sinless One; salutations to you! Om Vaṃ, salutations to the armor. O Drum, by your sound you cause the hearts of my enemies to tremble.
O King, for you who are preeminent on earth, there shall likewise be a son named Vijayavardhana,
at whose thunder-like roar the elephants of your enemies will tremble with joy.
"By your voice, let there be joy for you that brings us delight, just as by the sound of a rain-cloud, terror indeed arises in women. (46)
And likewise, by your sound, may there be victory for you over Rudra and his enemies in battle:
"Oṃ duṃ! Salutation to the drum, the great measure of all weapons, the destroyer of all weapons! (47)
O bow, protect me always along with your most excellent arrows.
Om Caṃ, salutations to the bow; you are meritorious, the merit of all meritorious things, and the auspiciousness of all auspicious things. 48.
Supported eternally by Viṣṇu, therefore, be the bestower of peace!
Oṃ śaṃ, salutation to the conch; you who resemble the form of the moon, as white as a mass of snow! 49.
O beloved of the immortals and non-immortals, quickly drive away all evil!
Oṃ, salutations to Cāmara;
you were fashioned as the foremost of all weapons by the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Having extracted the tip of the trident weapon and formed a firm, auspicious grip,
this sword has been given to Caṇḍikā, which destroys all that is evil.
You have been expanded by you and presented to the gods;
you have become the limb of all reality and the warder-off of all that is inauspicious.
O Kṣurika, protect me always; grant me peace, homage be to you!
Oṃ kṣuṃ, homage to Kṣurika, for the expulsion of the wicked and for the protection of the virtuous. || 53 ||
"You were created by Brahmā for the sake of establishing worldly affairs;
grant fame, grant happiness, and indeed become a god to the king. (54)
Strike all these enemies; O Hemadaṇḍa, salutations to you!
Om Kaṃ, salutations to Kanakadaṇḍa!
Be victorious; you are a god, the destroyer of enemies, and a bringer of joy. || 55 ||
