The destroyer of suffering, the bestower of Dharma, the peaceful one, and the annihilator of all misfortunes—since these eight powerful lions are present here with you, [you are truly a lion]. (56)
Therefore, O Brahmin, you are eternally praised among the gods upon this lion-throne;
Śiva himself is present in you, as is Śakra, the lord of the gods.
The god Hari resides within you and performs penance for your sake.
Salutations to you, O auspicious one who is beneficial in every way; may there be well-being for the king. 58.
"Victory over the three worlds! O Presence, salutations to you, the Lion Throne!
Om Siṃ, salutations to the Lion Throne;
one should perform this rite for the movement through the worlds preceded by the mantra. (59)
On the eighth day, one should worship the goddess named Durgā, fashioned from gold, with fruit offerings, flowers, incense, lamps, and unguents.
Having fashioned an image—whether made of silver, copper, stone, wood, or clay—and adorning it with paintings according to one's means; || 61 ||
One should perform this rite either in the forenoon or at midday;
the king, having bathed, adorned his limbs, and consecrated his body with the ritual applications (sakalīkṛta).
Having bathed [the image], one should then anoint it with sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron,
along with camphor, and offer many fragrant flowers.
With water-lilies and fragrant flowers, accompanied by incense and lamps, together with food offerings (naivedya) joined with fruits, and along with dance, song, and so forth. || 64 ||
One should worship her, who possesses eight arms and crushes the demon Mahiṣāsura, with bilva leaves combined with *droṇa* flowers. 65.
Upon her chest she bears a skull adorned with a trident;
she is decorated with a trident, equipped with a bow and arrow, and holds a sword and a shield.
Adorned with the conch and the discus, decorated with all ornaments,
holding an excellent rosary and a trident, she stands upon the demon Mahiṣāsura.
Having worshipped her who follows the lion, who has three eyes, who destroys all enemies, and who possesses four arms joined with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; || 68 ||
She stood there in a peaceful form, endowed with the conch and the discus, amidst various kinds of songs and diverse types of dances. (69)
Having thus passed the night with joy, at dawn when the sun rises,
one should have buffaloes and rams with soft necks slaughtered in front [of the deity].
One hundred, or fifty, or twenty-five, or even half of that, according to one's desire;
then, at the time of afternoon on the ninth day, [one should worship her] seated upon a chariot.
The king himself, accompanied by his army, should cause Bhavānī to roam through the kingdom;
or some heroic man sent by him with abundant weapons [should do so]. (72)
The wise man should offer a bali-oblation to the beings consisting of food mixed with clarified butter and soaked in honey;
he should present this bali in the cardinal and intermediate directions while reciting this mantra.
May the gods— the Ādityas, the Vasus,
as well as the Maruts, the two Aśvins, the Rudras, the Suparṇas, the Pannagas, and the Grahas— accept this offering.
Asuras, Yātudhānas, Mātṛs, serpents, Piśācas, Ḍākinīs, Kṣetrapālas, Vetālas, Yoginīs, Pūtanās, and Śivās; || 75 ||
The Jṛmbhakas, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Vīras, Vidyādharas, and men;
the guardians of the quarters, the guardians of the worlds, and those who are the Vighnas and Vināyakas—[all these were present]. (76)
May the great sages, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, perform rites for the peace of the worlds;
may they not create obstacles for me, nor be my adversaries. (77)

"May the bhūtas and pretas be gentle, satisfied, and bringers of happiness. With these words, the king should cause the Goddess, who stands as she is and destroys all obstacles, to be paraded through the kingdom, either on foot or in a vehicle. (78)
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, the ritual procedure for the worship of Durgā, in the Uttarakāmika Mahātantra.

78. In the seventy-eighth chapter, the ritual for the lustration (*nīrājana*) of horses; indeed, I shall fully explain the lustration known as the "Peaceful Lustration" (*śānti-nīrājanā*) for horses. One should perform it in the month of Āśvayuja, and one should perform it every year.
One should perform it on the ninth or the eighth day, or even on the fifteenth or the twelfth; especially during the bright fortnight.
One should construct it to the north-east of the city, or it may be made in another location; the procedure for that is stated here.
The sacrificial shed (āgāra) is declared to be eight ratnis in width, ten cubits in height,
and twenty cubits in length.
One should construct an altar measuring six [units] in length, with four tiers and three central sections;
its pinnacle should be half of that, and this is considered the altar for kings.
One should fashion a deep place for the fire in the center of the altar,
measuring one cubit in size and provided with three girdles.
Having first performed the protective rite (pratisara) combined with small bells and medicinal herbs,
he led the horse, surrounded by virtuous women, near the water.
On the bank where the water flows clockwise, one should lead the altar (vedī) facing east;
above that, a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be constructed for the purpose of the fire-oblation according to the previously mentioned measurements.
Having consecrated the sacrificial pit and the fire, the best of preceptors should perform the oblation;
then, once the fire is awakened, he should offer this oblation to Brahmā.
Then [offerings] to Viṣṇu, Agni, and the Rudras; to Śakra and Varuṇa;
and then to the immovable God (Acala), to Senānī, and to Dhanada.
One should offer these oblations in sequence to the Nāgas, the rivers, and Brahmā and the others, and one should deposit the bali offering upon them.
Whether in a river, or in the ocean, or in tanks, lakes,
and the like, one should bathe [the image] and install it with the groups of medicinal herbs as prescribed.

One should rub these [elephants], which have been freed from their afflictions, cleansed of impurities, and have bathed after drinking [the medicinal liquid] and entered the water, with a paste of sesame and mustard seeds mixed with curd. || 13 ||
Having entered the stable for the mounts, endowed with celibacy,
he should bind potent medicinal herbs upon them for their protection.
The wise one should offer oblations both morning and evening for seven days as before;
having purified the clarified butter with *kuśa* grass, he should present the clarified butter with *kuśa* grass.
When the fire has been kindled with fuel-sticks, one should offer a second oblation;
then, with the sacrificial ladle, one should offer clarified butter as the third, and present the licked horse.
One should also satisfy the fourth [deity] with curd, cakes, and excellent rice;
at the Brāhma-muhūrta at dawn, when the world is resounded by the chanting of the Veda.
Just as the rays of the sun and the moon do not touch the horses [of the chariot], so too should be their movement; bathing in the morning is recommended for them. 18.
At both times, and especially for the principal horse, one should daily cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), accompanied by benedictions and auspicious rites. (19)
When the seven nights had passed, having bathed and stood before them,
on the eighth day he bathed them with white mustard seeds and cow's milk.
At the junction of Uttarāṣāḍhā and Śravaṇa,
on the ninth day of the bright fortnight, he should cause [the king] to dwell outside the city.
In the north-eastern direction, or in a pure place sloping towards the east, where the water flows clockwise, which is pleasant, spacious, and not crowded by trees. || 22 ||
There, having erected an archway ten cubits high, eight ratnis in width, facing east, and adorned with garlands; || 23 ||
Beside that, having fashioned a mound, the king— accompanied by all auspicious rites and surrounded by the citizens— should perform the ritual as before.
One should go joyfully to the house of peace accompanied by conch shells, trumpets, and other instruments;
having entered the house of peace, one should perform this ritual procedure. (25)
Māñjiṣṭhā, candana, kuṣṭha, haritāla, manaḥśilā, vacā, dantī, guḍūcī, and that which is known as priyaṅgu and arjuna. (26)
Haridrā, svarṇapuṣpa, and then vahnimantha; likewise sa-kauśa, girikarṇī, hīyamāṇa, and kaṭambharā.
One should place Sahadevī, Nāgapuṣpa, Kapikacchu,
Śatāvarī, and Somavallī into the jars.
In eight jars, accompanied by garments and other offerings, with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings as well; (29)
Having offered various kinds of oblations such as cakes and the like,
one should perform the fire sacrifice in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) as before, with the previously mentioned substances in their proper order.
Seated upon a tiger skin, the king, accompanied by his preceptor,
together with a knower of the Vedas and a physician, faces the eastern direction.
Having ascertained the auspicious or inauspicious signs from the fire at the conclusion of the final oblation,
he should mount the best of horses and lead it to the vicinity of the archway.
Gradually, with words of consolation and efforts such as singing and instrumental music, [he should be adorned] with white sandalwood paste and garlands, and provided with white garments. (33)
Then, one should offer the remainder of the *homa* as a sacrificial ball (*piṇḍa*) combined with milk, curd,
and plantain fruit to the excellent horse.
If one should eat it quickly, it will lead to victory;
then, with water alone, [one should use] two branches from an udumbara tree.
Then the preceptor should sprinkle the king, the elephant, and subsequently the army with mantras for peace and prosperity. || 36 ||
Then the wise brahmin should pierce the chest of the earthen image with a spear made of black iron,
using mantras for malevolent rites (abhicāra).
Having assigned guards for the horse and mounted it, the king, endowed with auspiciousness, should proceed toward the northeast direction for the sake of achieving victory. (38)
In this very manner, one should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the elephants and other animals;
however, that should be performed during the month of Kṛttikā under the constellation of Aśvinī.
One should perform [the rite] on all the lunar days previously mentioned;
however, regarding the elephant-vehicle, this is the specific rule: it should be square and shaped like a peak (kūṭaka).
The square enclosure is now called the "elephant-ground";
one who is composed should construct this square measuring one hundred cubits.
One should offer fifty, or twenty-five, fuel sticks on all sides! || 42 ||
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, the procedure for the lustration of horses (*vājinīrājana*), in the great tantra known as the *Uttarakāmika*.
79. In the seventy-ninth chapter is the ritual for the royal lustration (*nīrājana*).

On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, at the onset of night during the evening twilight, one should perform it upon a beautiful altar adorned with archways and garlands in the illustrious *Cāturantaka* temple.
Having kindled a new fire and offered oblations with mantras, the most excellent guru [illumined] the sacrificial fire with lamps made from the wood of the *vardhamāna* tree.

Having worshipped with jujube fruits, tufts of grass, leaves, flowers, and unbroken grains, as well as with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should first perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for Bhava.
He likewise [worshipped] Gaurī, who is dear to him; Hari; Lakṣmī; the Four-faced One (Brahmā);
Vighneśa; Caṇḍikā; Sūrya; the Yakṣas; and the hosts of Mothers.
Then one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for Guha, the hosts of ancestors, and all the Nāgas;
one should also perform the lustration of the cows and cause it to be waved before the buffalo and other animals.
Frightening away the web of obstacles with the great sounds of the ringing bell,
the most excellent preceptor should perform the special lustration ceremony for the king.
The supreme Garuḍa [carried] the horses, the elephants, and the royal insignia,
as well as the king seated upon his throne, surrounded by the foremost of his vassals.

One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for the deity, who has been worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, either by noble women or by courtesans endowed with beauty and youth.
O best of the twice-born, in whatever kingdom, city, or village this is performed,
their king attains happiness and likewise there arises an abundance of food.
It is also prescribed for all four castes when disease arises. || 91/2 ||
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, the ritual for the Night-Royal Consecration (*rajanīrājana-vidhi*), in the great tantra named the *Uttarakāmika*.
80. In the eightieth chapter, the ritual for the Puṣya-consecration:
I shall describe the Puṣya-consecration, which is purifying and destroys evil.
For the sake of destroying all calamities, listen, O best of the twice-born! (1)
In a meritorious and delightful place, one should devoutly construct an auspicious altar measuring one *ravidhasta* (twelve cubits) in size, such that it has a central foot.
It was provided with twelve pillars, devoid of a central altar,
resembling the surface of a mirror, and adorned with ornaments.
To its western side and to its southern exterior,
two altars (vedikās) should be constructed, measuring five or six cubits in size.
It should be square and level, with a height of two cubits,
provided with stairs on its sides, and likewise joined together as a pair.
Having thus prepared everything, the king should perform his consecration during the month of Puṣya,
under the Puṣya asterism, at sacred fords and sanctuaries.
In sacred gardens and especially in auspicious places,
in the directions of Kubera, Indra, and the intermediate quarters, the preceptor, endowed with the mantra, [should perform the rite].
On the day preceding that, the noble-minded one should perform an offering (bali) with the astrologer,
consisting of curd, parched grain, and unbroken rice, together with perfumes, flowers, and other such items.
"Let all the gods come here, desiring worship;
as well as the quarters, the nāgas, the twice-born, and whoever else is entitled to a share."
Having thus invoked all [the deities] for one month, the most excellent preceptor should speak as follows,
O Lord of the Earth, after first having performed his own worship and bestowed peace upon the king.
Having spoken thus and offered the oblation, one should examine the dream at night;
if it is auspicious, one should begin the work in the morning, but if it is inauspicious, one should perform a rite of pacification.
Thereafter, one should decorate the pavilion, equipped with doors and archways;
then, one should perform here the auspicious rite of sowing seeds (maṅgalāṅkurakarma) as previously described.
O twice-born ones, one should fashion a bhadrāsana from the wood of a sacrificial tree,
beginning at five or six finger-breadths and extending up to fifty cubits.
The pedestal (māna) is said to be on the auspicious seat (bhadrāsana), whether it be sabhadra or vibhadraka;
it is especially provided with two steps at the front and the back.
To its south, one should prepare a seat provided with a footstool;
it should be made with steps and endowed with the desired measurements.
On the day before, one should perform the *śrāddha* for the occasion of prosperity (*vṛddhi*) according to the prescribed rite;
at night, one should fashion a protective amulet (*pratisara*) adorned with all ornaments.
At dawn, one should perform the sacrifice to the planets according to its prescribed ritual;
beginning with a square of four cubits, increasing it by six finger-breadths [at each step].
Whatever measurement is desired for the maṇḍala, up to the extent of six cubits,
one should divide that into one hundred parts and then proceed in order from the south.
The land of Bhārata-varṣa is considered to be one ninth [of the earth], and its natural color is regarded as [the color of] the castes (varṇa).
Himavat is proclaimed to be two parts [in extent] and white in color. || 19 ||
The region called Kimpuruṣa is proclaimed to consist of nine parts;
it is said to be golden in color, and Hemakūṭa occupies two of those parts.
To the north of Hemakūṭa is Harivarṣa, which is said to be golden in color; it is bounded on both sides by the Niṣadha and Nīla mountains.
Their arrangement extends from west to east;
beginning from the northern ninth-part (navāṃśa), designate the [respective] year.
That [mountain] should be known as golden-colored; by its divisions, it would possess peaks.
It should be known as having the color of a peacock, endowed with a beautiful golden hue. (23)
Gold is indeed proclaimed to have nine parts and the color of fire;
white stone (śvetācala) has two parts and, when combined with gold, becomes white in color.
The Ramyavarṣa is proclaimed to be nine parts with a golden hue;
Nīlācala consists of two parts and is endowed with the luster of lapis lazuli.
The thirty-four parts situated in the middle are occupied;
beginning from the eastern direction, they are joined with thirty-two parts. (26)
The region of Bhadrāśva has been described; it is proclaimed to be white in color. On the western side, Mālyavān is fashioned, endowed with a black color.
Starting from the western direction, there is the region Ketumāla; it consists of thirty-two squares and is black in color. By name, this is Gandhamādana.
One part on all sides shall be Ilāvṛta, the rainy region;
one part shall be white-colored, and the central portion shall be square.
One should rotate the Meru mountain by means of a thirty-second part of these;
then, having stretched a cord across the circle from the northwest to the southeast.
In the same manner, one should extend the diagonal lines from the southwest to the northeast;
the eastern line should be white in color, while the southern line should be golden.
In the west it should be black in color, and in the north red in color; as for all the remaining regions, they are proclaimed to be yellow.
Jambūdvīpa is said to be divided into a hundred parts;
outside of that, the salt ocean is declared to be equal in extent to Jambūdvīpa.
Śākadvīpa is likewise, each being double the size of the preceding;
the islands and the oceans outside are proclaimed to be seven in number.
Jambūdvīpa is declared to be one hundred thousand yojanas in extent;
outside of that, the Salt Ocean (Kṣāroda) is proclaimed to be of the same measure.
From the salt ocean, milk is twice as large; from the milk ocean, curd is twice as large;
from the curd, clarified butter is twice as large; and from that, the ocean of nectar is twice as large.
The liquor should be twice the size of the Rasa ocean, and the Svādūdaka likewise;
beyond Jambūdvīpa is Śākadvīpa, and beyond Śākadvīpa is the one named Kuśa.
From Kuśa, Krauñca is designated; from Krauñca, likewise, Śālmalī arises. From that comes the one named Gobheda, and from Gobheda, again, Puṣkala.
It should be known that outside the Sweet-water [ocean] is what is remembered as Lokāloka;
it is red in color on the inside and is proclaimed to be black on the outside. (39)
Ten times ten million [yojanas] is to be known as the extent for the sporting of the celestial dwellers;
beyond that, O twice-born ones, is to be known the best of mountains called Lokāloka.
The hermitage of the gods is considered to be ten thousand [yojanas] in extent; on the Himālaya there are Piśācas, and their names are indeed as follows: 41.
Dhvaja, Caṇḍa, Kaṃlāsa, Kadalī, Baka, Vaḍavāmukha, Dvipāda, and Kāraka are recorded [as the types of mountains]. || 42 ||
Jvālā, Kumbhapātra, as well as Kumbhī, Pratundika, Pratundika-upavīra, Pravīra, and Lūkhala are recorded [as the names of the mountains]. || 43 ||
Ulūkhalī is Markaṭī; Markaṭa is Cakrī and Ṣaṇḍaka;
Cakraṣaṇḍī is Pāṇipatra; and Pāṇipatrī is Vāsukī. || 44 ||
Vāsuki is considered Pāṃsukṛt, and Nipuṇa is considered Pāṃsumathinī; Nipuṇā is to be known as Balibhuj, and thereafter Uccheṣaṣā is considered [the fifth]. 45.
Praskanda and Skandikā are declared to be thirty-four in number;
one should worship them with meat, food, liquor, Pratisara, and other offerings. (46)
Śveta, Cala, and Ditasuta were the Dānavas who were proclaimed;
Hiraṇyakaśipu by name was the first, and Hiraṇyākṣa was the second.
These two sons of Diti are to be known as Vipracitti and Anantara;
then follow Dvimūrdhan, Śambara, and Śaṅkuśiras. (48)
Yama, Śaṅkukarṇa, Dvipāda immediately after him, Gaveṣṭi, Meṣavaktra, Makhavān, and Kapiloman. || 49 ||
Vāmana, Marīci, and likewise Ikṣupa are proclaimed;
Bhāga and Abhāga are to be known, and they are remembered as the Śālāgrahas.
Dikkṣobha, Sukeśa, Ketuvīrya, Śatahrada, Mantrajit, Aśvajit, Raji, and Udāhrada are thus proclaimed. (51)
Devijit, Ekavaktra, Subāhu, and Vāraka are considered [the sons];
as are Vaiśvānara, Sulobha, Draviṇa, and Mahāśiras. || 52 ||
Svarbhānu, Pūṣapūrva, Dvibhuja, Ghṛtarāṣṭraka, the one known as Candratāpana, Sūkṣma, and Niścandra indeed. (53)
Then Svarṇanābha is proclaimed, followed by Mahāgiri; then Ābhiloka, Sukeśa, Malaya, and likewise Malaka. (54)
Naya, Nagamūrdhan, and Mahodara are proclaimed; as well as Pramoda, Kumuda, Aśvagrīva, and the one named Vaiśravaṇa. || 55 ||
Virūpākṣa, Carūpatha, Hara, Rājā, Hiraṇyayuk, Śatamakha, Śambara, Śarabha, and Maya—[these were the sons]. || 56 ||
Śarabha, Yasa, Sūrya, and Candramas are declared to be his [names];
there are sixty-four such names, and their worship is as previously described. (57)
On Mount Śṛṅgavat, the Pitṛs are declared to be worshipful;
they are considered to be the Subhāsvaras, the Amṛtas, the Agniṣvāttas, and the Upahutas. (58)
Then the Somapās are to be known, and the Vijñeyas who are of good fortune;
the Kravyādas and the Ājyapas are likewise declared to be three distinct groups. || 59 ||
They are considered to be twenty-one in number, divided into seven groups;
first are the Agniṣvāttas, then the Barhiṣads, and after them the Somapās.
The Haviṣmants and Ājyapas should likewise be Sukālikās;
indeed, there are exactly ten [deities] known as Agni, Anagni, Havyavāha, and Havissaumya.
She should be worshipped with offerings of sesame, oil, food, and meats, as well as with protective cords (pratisara) and other such items;
and on Mount Nīla, the sages beginning with Kāśyapa should be fully honored.
Kāśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, Bharadvāja, Gautama, Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, and Marīci are considered to be there. (63)
Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Aṅgiras, Bhṛgu, Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sananda, and Sanātana; || 64 ||
Then Dakṣa, Jaigīṣavya, Dahanaikata, Dvita, Trita, Jābāli, Durvāsas, and Durvanītaka. || 65 ||
Kaṇva Kātyāyana, Mārkaṇḍeya, Dīrghatamas, Śunaśśepha, Vidūratha, Sādhu, and Saṃvarta—these are also considered [to be such]. || 66 ||
Cyavana and Parāśara, then Dvaipāyana;
then Yavakrīta and Devarāta, as well as Devarāja and Aja.
And the forty sages are to be worshipped with perfumes such as Pratisara and others, or with the mantras of the Rig, Yajur, and Sama Vedas, or by their respective names.
On Mount Niṣadha, various [serpents] such as Ananta and others are proclaimed; Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, and Kārkoṭaka are remembered [there]. || 69 ||
Padma, Mahāpadma, and Śaṅkhapāla is remembered as the eighth;
one should worship these eight with mixed perfumes and flowers, along with Gulika.
Having offered white sugar, honey, and ghee, one should present the *pratisara* and other items;
the gods are to be worshipped on Mount Mahāmeru, and they are considered to be thirty-three in number.
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala, Pratyuṣa, and Prabhāsa—these are considered by me to be the eight Vasus. (72)
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Virūpākṣa, and Raivata;
Hara, Bahurūpa, and the Rudra named Tryambaka—[these are the eleven]. (73)
Sāvitra, Jayanta, Pinākin, and Aparājita—these are declared to be the eleven Rudras; as well as Indra, Dhātṛ, Bhaga, and Aryaman.
Tvaṣṭṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Vivasvat are beyond that;
Savitṛ, Pūṣan, and the radiant Viṣṇu are declared to be the twelve Ādityas.
Having worshipped Prajāpati, the Vaṣaṭkāra, and the thirty-three deities with prostrations, incense, and indeed oblations of clarified butter; || 76 ||
One should offer the arghya for the Pratisarā on the mountain named Hemakūṭa;
the Gandharvas and Apsarases, namely Citrasena and Agnisenaka, are to be worshipped.
Suvarṇa, Gaṇapa, and then Dhṛtarāṣṭra; after him, Sūryavarcas, Yugaputra, Suśiras, and Amarānandin. (78)
Dvedhāmatis, Citraratha, and Parjanya are considered [the next];
then Urvīśa, Kali, Parvata, and likewise Nārada. (79)
Sādhana, Sandhi, Kuhara, Karālaka, Kṛtavīrya, Brahmacārī, Suparṇa, and also Mīna. || 80 ||
Hiraṇya and Sucandra are the twenty-seven Gandharvas; then follow the Akṛtis, the Codayantīs, and the Gandhavatīs.
The Ūrjas and the Yuvatis are declared to be the Hetukās;
then follow the Stavās, the Amṛtas, the Mods, and after that, the Suśivas.
Rūpā, Bhīravā, Śauryā, and Satyā—these are the fourteen;
and Menakā, Sahajanyā, Puñjikasthalā, and [Pūrvacitti] preceded them. (83)
Ghṛtasthalā, Ghṛtācī, Viśvācī, Pūrvacittikā, Pramlocantī, Anumlocantī, Mocayantī, and then Anugā. (84)
Rurudrāruṇā, Priyā, Atrasā, Subhagā, Dāsī, Ariṣṭā, Manovartinī, Sukeśā, and Tilottamā. || 85 ||
Agnibhārī, Hemā, Menakā, and Urvaśī—these twenty-four were adorned with fragrant scents and beautiful garlands. || 86 ||
Then, having performed a sacrifice to the *Apratisara* deity on a mountain rich in gold,
he should worship the Yakṣas as well as the great Vaiśravaṇa.
Māṇibhadra, Suśiras, Vibhaṇḍaka with the five [attendants], Vidhṛta, Pūrṇabhadra, and Virūpākṣa, the king of the eight yakṣas. (88)
Having worshipped with offerings of all kinds of unguents, one should bestow the thread and other items;
then, on Mount Nīla, the knower of mantras, the most excellent among those who know mantras, becomes a Siddha. (89)
Then there was Prājña, Haṣarāja, Siddha, Pūjita, Siddhimatparama, Siddha, and likewise Kesarabhadraka. || 90 ||
One should worship these eight perfected ones with offerings of all colors;
one should present the Pratisara and others, together with the nine planets, upon Mount Meru.
O Hero, Vighneśa, together with the constellations and the Mothers, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Mahādeva, and the Viśākhās along with the world-protectors. || 92 ||
One should worship him together with the celestial women and their attendants,
such as the Daityas, along with offerings and the colored powders in their proper sequence.
And one should give them the *pratisara* and so forth; their names are indeed these: Āditya, Soma, Aṅgāraka, and then Budha. (94)
Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Arka (the Sun), Rāhu, and Ketu—these are declared to be the nine planets; after them indeed follow the Kṛttikās. || 95 ||
Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Abhijit, and Śravaṇā are in the west;
likewise Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, and Pūrvābhādrapadā. || 96 ||
Uttarābhādrapadā, Revatī, and Aśvinī are considered [the next];
then Bharaṇī, and thereafter Brāhmī and Māheśvarī in the north.
Vārāhī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Kaumārī are likewise considered [the goddesses], as well as Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍī, Vīrabhadra, and the Lord of the Gaṇas. 98.
Skanda, Viṣṇu, Mahādeva, and Brahmā as Viśākhaka; likewise Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, and Varuṇa. || 99 ||
Vāyu, Dhanada, and Īśāna is considered the eighth;
Śacī, Bhājīvana-skanda, Dhūmrā, and Maṇḍalavartinī. (100)
Pūrṇā, Sinīvālī, Kuhū, Rākā, and Anumati;
Āyatā, Vyayanī, Prajñā, Menā, and Balā followed thereafter. (101)
These are declared to be the fourteen celestial women; the wise man should worship them in order, followed by the two Aśvins, the Nāsatyas, the Dastras. 102.
The most excellent preceptor should then bestow upon all of them a protective amulet, a garment, a banner, an ornament, and likewise a sacred thread.
Then, having offered the five-colored oblation called *sārvarṇika*,
one should [place] jars filled with clarified butter upon the western altar.
[The vessels] should be provided with threads, lids, and cloths, and adorned with sprouts;
there should be twenty-eight, eight, or one hundred and eight [of them].
Having established it firmly, one should place sixteen substances— such as threads, cloth, and so forth— in its four corners, arranging them within those [corners].
First are the three Jyotiṣṭomas, then Abhayā and Aparājitā;
likewise Jīvā, Viśveśvarī, Vārā, Samāṅgā, and Vijayā. (107)
Sahā, Sahadevā, Pūrṇakośā, Śatāvarī, Ariṣṭā, Śivā, and Bhadrā—one should place these in the jars. || 108 ||
Brāhmī, kṣamāyujā, all kinds of seeds, gold, auspicious items as they may be available, and likewise the juices of all medicinal herbs. || 109 ||
Red flowers, all types of fragrances, bilva, and vikaṅkata wood;
medicinal herbs with auspicious names, gold, and other auspicious items. 110.
At the outset, one should spread out a tanned hide that has reached its full lifespan through aging,
possessing auspicious characteristics, with its neck and head pointing toward the east.
Then [he gave] the king's armor, skin, and blood that was unwounded; and a third [skin] from the lion, and after that, from the tiger. (112)
One should spread these four skins upon that altar and worship them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, while reciting the Mṛtyujit mantra.
Above that, O auspicious one, he should place [the image] seated upon a lion-throne (siṃhāsana),
fashioned from gold, silver, copper, or made from the wood of milk-exuding trees.
It should be one and a quarter, one and a half, or one cubit in height;
for a sovereign emperor (sārvabhauma), that is the best, while for a regional monarch (maṇḍalika), it is the smallest.
Or one might imagine that what was composed immediately before is itself the middle;
thus, everything is considered to belong to a single [work] through the distinctions of superior, middling, and so forth. (116)
Above that, one should place a golden flower in its center [the vessel],
[an image of the deity] which has performed its ablutions, whose limbs are anointed, and who is adorned with all ornaments.
He should install the lord of men, who is like Indra, together with his preceptor, astrologer, ministers, and vassals, surrounded by the chief priests and others. (118)
It was accompanied by the sounds of Vedic recitations proclaiming an auspicious day, along with dancing and instrumental music,
and songs of auspicious praise preceded by the installation of the Śiva-liṅga.
Wearing a garment of beaten silk and adorned with ornaments on five limbs, the Guru,
having covered [the disciple] with a woolen blanket, should perform the consecration while facing north.

Clarified butter (ājya) is declared to be of luminous nature; clarified butter is the supreme destroyer of sin. Clarified butter is the food of the gods; in clarified butter all the worlds are established.
Whatever impurity has come upon you—whether terrestrial, atmospheric, or celestial—may it all go to destruction through contact with this clarified butter. 122.
Having removed the woolen blanket and placed it aside, and with the water kept in the jars,
along with various fruits and flowers that are sweet and fragrant— 123.
The preceptor should consecrate the lord of men with this mantra: "May the gods and those who are the ancient Siddhas consecrate you! (124)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; the Maruts, the Sādhyas, and the hosts of Maruts;
the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the two Aśvins, the best of physicians. || 125 ||
Aditi, the mother of the gods, Svāhā, Sandhyā, Sarasvatī, Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Śrī, Sinīvālī, and likewise Kuhū. || 126 ||

The lunar mansions, the auspicious moments (muhūrtas), the fortnights, days and nights, their junctions, the years, the lords of the days, and the divisions of time—kalās, kāṣṭhās, kṣaṇas, and lavas. || 127 ||
May all the auspicious divisions of Time consecrate you,
as well as Aditi, Surasā, Vinatā, and Kadrū.
May the wives of the gods who have been mentioned, as well as the mothers of the gods, and all the auspicious hosts of Apsarases, consecrate you. (129)
The hosts of gods dwelling in celestial mansions, along with the Manus, the oceans, the highly fortunate rivers, the Kinnaras, and likewise the Puruṣas. || 130 ||
The highly fortunate Vaikhānasas, those twice-born Vaihāyasas, the Seven Sages together with their wives, and whatever other abodes of Dhruva there may be— 131.
Marīci, Atri, Pulaha, Pulastya, Kratu, Aṅgiras, Bhṛgu, Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, and then Sanātana. (132)
Sanātana, Dakṣa, Jaigīṣavya, and Jābāli;
Ekata, Dvita, Trita, Jābāli, and the two Kāśyapas. (133)
Durvāsas, Durvinītā, Kaṇva, Kātyāyana, as well as Mārkaṇḍeya, Dīrghatamas, and Śunaḥśepha were far away. (134)
Aurva, Saṃvartaka, Cyavana, Atri, Parāśara, Dvaipāyana, Yavakrīta, and Devarāta with his younger brother. (135)
May these and many others, whose auspicious names proclaim merit, sprinkle you with waters that destroy all calamities. (136)
The Guru [should perform the rite] with these Atharvaṇa mantras, or with the Rudrādhyāya, along with the Mahārauhiṇa, Kūśmāṇḍa, and Kubera-hṛdaya mantras. (137)
Having recited the mantra "hiraṇyavarṇā" and the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and having recited either the Śiva-aghora or the Mṛtyuñjaya [mantra], || 138 ||
One should consecrate the lord of the earth, and having gazed upon him, one should then bathe him;
the sovereign of the Kṣatriyas should be wearing a pair of cotton garments. (139)
Then, accompanied by the sounds of "auspicious day" (puṇyāha) and the resonance of conchs and trumpets,
he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and worship the gods, his own guru, and the Brahmins as well.
Then one should worship the banner, the weapon, and one's own white parasol; and one should worship their respective parts from one another using the previously mentioned mantras. || 141 ||
Having changed into a pair of garments,
adorned with all ornaments and endowed with every decoration, he entered the sacrificial altar.
And having spread there the skins of a bull, a spotted deer, a ruru deer, a pṛṣata deer, and one known as a lion or tiger; 143.

In a fire-pit or even upon a sacrificial mound at the mouth [of the vessel], the most excellent gurus should perform the fire-oblation with sacrificial fuel-sticks and clarified butter, one hundred times each.
The Palāśa fuel-sticks are considered the supreme means for conquering death;
at the conclusion of the fire-oblation, the best of gurus, with palms joined in reverence, should address the God as follows: || 145 ||
May all the hosts of gods depart, taking the worship from the king, after granting abundant success and for the sake of returning once more. (146)
At that time, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor as a cause for his satisfaction;
and the king of men should especially bestow gifts upon the Brāhmaṇas.
Then, having bowed to that God, the Lord of Gods, the king shall release all people from that bondage and offer him villages, gold, and other gifts. (148)
Having given [the gift], with a satisfied mind and adorned with a crest-ornament (kakuṭa) and other decorations,
he should then mount an elephant and enter toward his palace.
For the purpose of destroying all portents, for the cessation of all diseases, for the attainment of universal sovereignty, and for the accomplishment of long life and health. || 150 ||
For the sake of destroying all enemies and for the victory of the king,
one should perform the Puṣyābhiṣeka every year in a sacred place.
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Punyābhiṣeka," in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
81. In the eighty-first chapter, the ritual procedure for the sacrifice to the planets (*graha-yajña-vidhi*).
I shall proclaim the sacrifice to the planets, which brings about the propitiation of the planets;
for from the movements of the planets, all manner of suffering arises for everyone. (1)
When the area for the pavilion or the house has been divided into nine parts,
the preceptor, together with the initiated disciples, should perform worship and then offer oblations.
The Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu—these nine indeed should be worshipped by their respective names. (3)
The Guru should perform the ritual worship in the mandala, beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
That [mandala] may be circular, quadrangular, triangular, or provided with five arrows (*bāṇa*).
The mandalas of the planets are said to be long-quadrangular, five-cornered, resembling the outer corner of an eye, like a winnowing basket, and resembling a banner; now their colors are described.
The Sun and Mars are red; Venus and the Moon are white; and both Mercury and Jupiter are known to be yellow.
One should know that Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and likewise Ketu are black;
having meditated thus, the wise man should worship them in sequence with perfumes and flowers.
For all [deities], incense is made of guggulu with either oil or ghee;
the lamp is thus prescribed, and the food offering is said to consist of rice.
Rice may also be used for the purpose of the oblation; cow's ghee is considered the preferred offering.
One should prepare a place of worship either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a leveled mound (sthaṇḍila).
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sesame seeds combined together;
[using wood from] the Arka, Palāśa, Khadira, and Apāmārga trees respectively.
The Aśvattha, Udumbara, Śamī, Dūrvā, Kuśa, and fuel-sticks (samidh) [should be used];
or else the Palāśa or Khadira, provided that Kuśa grass is available at one's own dwelling.

Alternatively, those two sacrificial ladles, the *sruk* and the *sruva*, produced from a milky tree (*kṣīravṛkṣa*) or made from *palāśa* leaves, are praised when they possess the proper characteristics.
At the conclusion of that, one should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Hotṛ priests for the sake of attaining the fruit [of the rite]. || 13 ||
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, the ritual procedure for the sacrifice to the planets, in the great tantra known as the Kāmika.
82. In the eighty-second chapter, the ritual of the *pratisara*:
I shall explain the *pratisara* for kings in all auspicious rites. On the night preceding the designated day, the tying of the protective thread (*kautuka*) should be performed.
The pure preceptor, having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa,
should prepare a sacrificial mound with rice and place a cooking pot upon it.
A vessel completely filled with white rice, accompanied by the sprinkling of water for the auspicious day (puṇyāha), as well as a sacrificial thread, a bracelet, and a ring. || 3 ||
Having fashioned an auspicious golden flower as a protective amulet (pratisara) made of gold,
one should wash it with the Astra-mantra and water for the guest-offering (arghya), and then place it upon the rice grains.
Having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should consecrate it with the mantras in sequence:
the head with the Īśāna mantra and the sacred thread with the Varma mantra.
The best of preceptors should consecrate the bracelet with the heart-mantra, and likewise the ring;
or else, he may consecrate everything with the *bahurūpa* mantra.
The preceptor should likewise place that amulet and the sacred ash, mixed with sandalwood paste, in the northeast, while meditating upon it with his very heart.
One should arrange the offerings, beginning with flowers and ending with Soma;
or else, one may offer betel while recollecting the mantra known as Puruṣa.
Having placed either a single blade of dūrvā grass or one made of silver in the southeast and southwest, he should consecrate it with the Hṛdaya mantra.
Then, having covered it with cloths, one should cause it to be paraded through the city,
seated upon an elephant and adorned with all ornaments.
When the auspicious moment had arrived, the Guru, accompanied by astrologers and surrounded by Brahmins led by the family priest, was attended by all manner of auspicious rites.
Having performed his purification, with his limbs anointed, wearing a linen upper garment, and endowed with all ornaments and all decorations. (12)
One should seat the king upon the lion-throne and other seats facing the east,
having performed the sprinkling with the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) mantra and offering flowers and other items according to the preceding mantras.
Having given everything to the king while reciting the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra,
he should tie the protective thread (kautuka) on his right hand, facing the northern direction.

Having recited the mantra for the Universal Self (Sarvātman) and applied the sacred ash, the most excellent Guru should then perform the ritual assignment [of the mantras] beginning with Īśāna, according to the prescribed rule.
First, having recited the Bṛhatsāman and chanting it at the outset,
one should offer coconut fruits here together with parched grain, flowers, and other offerings.
Having established [the ritual site] on all sides, the preceptor should perform the *pratisara* rite;
the patron should worship the guide, the astrologer, and the domestic priest. (17)
Then, by this ritual procedure, one should also honor all the brahmins with auspicious recitations for the sake of the trident-bearing God of gods.
This applies also to other deities and to those of the four castes.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for Pratisāra," in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.

83. In the eighty-third chapter, I shall explain the procedure for the sixteen gifts of the "weighing on the scales" (*tulāroha*). These sixteen gifts are taught for the accomplishment of all desired aims, especially for the four classes beginning with the Brahmins and for the lords of the earth.
At times such as eclipses and the like, especially in an auspicious location,
[the site] should be measured at twenty cubits, with one-eighth of that being eight cubits.

One should construct either a peaked pavilion (kūṭa) or a square pavilion (maṇṭapa), and within it, one should prepare an altar (vedikā) measuring nine, six, or seven cubits, or from two cubits down to half a cubit.
It should be twelve cubits in both width and height, provided with twelve pillars;
outside of that, there are nine square sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
It was provided with four gates, adorned with four archways,
furnished with garlands of *darbha* grass, and endowed with banners in every direction.
O twice-born ones, this which is joined with the eight auspicious symbols and adorned with a canopy is declared to be common to the weighing-scale (tulā), the load (bhāra), and other such rites.
The Bilva, Aśvattha, and Palāśa are considered sacrificial trees;
those originating from the Panasa and Āmra, or the Khadira, are also praised.
Sometimes it is desired to be made entirely of wood, and sometimes of mixed materials; the height of the side pillars is considered to be seven, six, or five cubits.
The northern [section] should be above that, measuring six or eight [units] in length;
by decreasing it by three finger-breadths, the measurement is said to be ninefold.
With a broad side-pillar, it is endowed with both width and height;
the height is proclaimed to be one and one-quarter or three-quarters of the base. || 10 ||
The length of the beam of the balance should be either two cubits or three cubits; its width, however, shall be ten finger-breadths. || 11 ||
The width may be either greater or less by one finger-breadth;
likewise, the length or the span should be joined with thirty-six units.
The width is eight finger-breadths plus five barley-corns,
while the circumference of the middle part is prescribed as thirty-six mātras.
One should decorate the top, the base, or the middle with gold bands;
three suspension loops should be fashioned upon the beam of the scale.
It should be made of copper or else of iron;
its opening should be at the top in the middle, and it should have a very beautiful suspension loop.
One should fix a single tongue in the middle of the balance beam at the archway;
furthermore, one should drive a firm iron peg into the center of the northern side.
The Lord’s support consists of a gnomon provided with a hollow and equipped with a ring,
made of copper weighing seven, eight, or six hundred [palas].
Exceeding one finger-breadth in measure, provided with four apertures,
joined by four loops, and measuring one cubit in length.
On the ground, there should be a space of one span, four finger-breadths, or six mātrās;
in whatever manner they may be, those two enclosures should be made extending from east to west.
One should imagine two pillars with a pinnacle joined to the northern door,
or alternatively, one may conceive of them as being joined from the middle of the *kumbha* and so forth.
Having dug a pit one man’s height deep and having placed a level stone slab at the bottom,
one should first place [the pillar] upon it and make it firm with sand.
Having thus completed everything, up to the final release of the artisans,
one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) in the well-decorated pavilion.
The wise one should cause a mandala known as Sarvatobhadra to be made, which is endowed with auspicious sprouts and possessed of various fruits.
From the vajra to the trident, [these are placed] in the eight directions of the pavilion;
and on the left side of the trident is a wheel, while on the right is a lotus.
Having worshipped the Lord of the Gods in the center and Gaurī accompanied by him on the left with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should worship Brahmā on the right.
One should worship Viṣṇu in the center and install the world-protectors (Lokapālas) around him;
one should place the Sun in the middle, or in the south-eastern direction, or alternatively in the south-west.
One should worship Bhānu in the northwest, Ravi in the northeast, and then Divākara;
likewise, one should worship Uṣā, Prabhā, Prajñā, Sandhyā, and Sāvitrī.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings from the center up to the northeast;
[one should place] the wide [altar] in the central region, and especially in the southeast.
Having worshipped the abundant, pure, essential, and adorable [deity] from the eastern direction, and having fully honored the northern limit, one should easily conquer the center.
The preeminent teacher should worship Bodhanī in the region of Vāyu, Īśānī and Āpyāyanī, and he should worship Ravi in the central region.
One should worship the Śaktis beginning with Dīptā, as they are said to extend from the east to the center;
one should then worship the eight planets, beginning with Soma and ending with Ketu.

Thereafter, the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed; its procedure is stated here: during the principal oblation, one should offer to the Lord of Devas and to the world-protectors (lokapālas) in the eight directions.
O best of the twice-born, one should perform oblations in the center with the Gāyatrī mantra, and in the directions with the mantras of the world-protectors (lokeśas),
using their respective names preceded by the syllable Om and ending with Svāhā.

Having prepared the Śiva-fire as prescribed by its own respective scripture, accompanied by the mouth of fire (agnimukha) and joined with the world-protectors (lokeśas), one should invoke the deity and worship him.
Combined with the *nāḍī-saṅghāna* [mantra] and endowed with the beginning and end of the *jayā* [mantras],
one should offer a thousand oblations— or half that number— of sacrificial rice (*samiccaru*) mixed with clarified butter.
Or else, one hundred and eight oblations should be offered by the elephants of the respective directions,
using pure milk-rice (pāyasa), meat (māṃsa), and sacrificial porridge (caru) as the three concluding offerings.
One should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with twenty-five blades of dūrvā grass smeared with milk, reciting the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra; then one should perform the Vāstuhoma.
One should perform the hundredfold Pārśvacita rite with many forms;
having worshipped all the deities honored within the mandala, one should offer oblations.
Having performed the *pūrṇāhuti* for the lords of the city, one should carry out the ritual here;
having bathed the Supreme Lord with a thousand jars of water, [one should proceed]. (39)
A great worship should be performed, provided with abundant sacrificial offerings;
or else, a ceremonial bath should be conducted with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), milk, and other substances.
Afterwards, he should feed the Brahmins and perform the ritual of ascending the scale;
having summoned the king, who has bathed and is dressed in white garments and anointed with unguents.
Adorned with all ornaments, decorated with white garlands, having performed the *pratisara* rite, peaceful, and bearing a sword and shield. (42)
Having summoned [the deity], one should sprinkle [it] with auspicious water while reciting the Śiva-mantra;
first, the sprinkling for the auspicious day (puṇyāha) is performed, preceded by the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa rite, he should plant [the seed] while reciting the mantra;
at that time, the patron (yajamāna) should mutter the one known as the Rudra-gāyatrī.
One should perform the seasonal rite (ayana) right there with either a ghaṭikā-arghya or half of that;
[the practitioner] should be situated in the eastern direction, standing in the middle, facing westward.
Beholding that golden [image] situated there, he— holding a tuft of grass in his hand and remembering Hara—
performed a Vedic musical performance accompanied by instrumental music, dance, and song.
If that [image] were equal in weight to gold and endowed with the auspiciousness of victory, then the weighing on the scales would have been performed by means of one's own body and wealth. || 47 ||
One hundred, fifty, or even half of that, or more for those of superior status and so forth, should be given as an excellent gift;
or one should perform the ritual of ascending the scales (tulārohaṇa) for the sake of the Lord of Gods or the Creator.
Afterwards, one should worship the preceptor with garments, gold, and ornaments;
and one should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests according to the prescribed rule.
One hundred niṣkas, or half of that, or even half of that amount of gold, should be given;
it is prescribed that ten niṣkas each should be given to all the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
One should cause whatever substance was used for the sacrifice to be given to the preceptor;
and the worship of the one who honors Śiva is declared by the Lord to be as before. (51)
The sacrificial fee for that rite is prescribed in the scripture as fifty niṣkas;
one should cause wealth equal to the weight of the balance to be given to the Brāhmaṇas.
One should especially bestow half of that upon my devotees, and endowed with faith, one should especially give it to the spiritual teachers (deśikas). || 53 ||
At that time, he should release those who have been imprisoned and confined in jails;
for those who perform labor there, he should impose a separate fine.
O best of the twice-born, this has been declared as the general rule regarding gifts.
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, the ritual for the offering of the weighing on the scales, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
84. In the eighty-fourth chapter: The Ritual for the Gift of the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha).
I shall describe the gift of the Golden Embryo, which bestows the accomplishment of all aims. One should fashion a vessel out of gold weighing one thousand *niṣkas*.
The upper vessel should be half of that, or two thousand [units],
or three-quarters, or half the measure, or one and a quarter, or even one and a half.
It should be made double that size, or according to what is available;
having fashioned it from wood, one should wrap it with gold bands.
The base should be twelve finger-breadths in length, increasing by one finger-breadth at each step;
the width of the base is desired to be twenty-nine units.
Starting from fifty-one and increasing by the measure of a single *vyoma* (zero) at each step,
its height is proclaimed to extend up to seventy-five measures.
Having divided that [measurement] into parts, by increasing each part one by one,
the width of the *dāsī* is desired to be half more than its width.
Now, when joined with the foot,
the projection of the foot from the wall is desired to have a measurement ranging from three *mātrās* up to nine *mātrās*.
The height of the pedestal (pāduka) should be one-half or one-quarter of that [the base], or three-quarters, or equal to it; this is desired as the measurement for the wooden plank and so forth.
In this scripture, the extent of the *phelā* (the pinnacle) is said to be either as long as the *pādukā* or as wide as the exterior of the wall;
it may extend up to the end of *māyā* or up to the end of *prakṛti*.
The upper vessel should extend as far as Śiva; in its center, it should have the form of Puruṣa.
The wise one should meditate upon the Self [in that manner]; the procedure for this is stated here.
Having prepared a site provided with an altar and endowed with a mandala,
one should, after performing the rites as before, scatter rice in its center.
Above that, one should place a vessel wrapped in new cloths;
having made it airtight by the method of using black gram, one should fill it with cow-products.
The wise and most excellent of gurus should fill each [vessel] with five [substances], or likewise with the five nectars, using the Brahma-mantras beginning with Īśāna.
O best of the twice-born, one should thereafter worship with the Gāyatrī so that [the deity] becomes identical with Śiva; one should perform the general worship as previously described.
Facing east, the performer should enter; he should mutter the Gaurī-Gāyatrī. The Guru, while recollecting the mantra of Śiva, should cover him with a cloth.
Then the Guru should perform the sixteen sacraments (saṃskāras), beginning with the rite of conception (garbhādhāna); or else, the specific details thereof are now being told.
Having brought the performer of the rite together with his wife, adorned with all ornaments,
he should perform for him the rites beginning with the impregnation (garbhādhāna).
One should perform the sprinkling of dūrvā grass juice into the hollow of the wife’s hands,
using twenty-one udumbara fruits.
Then, having brought kuśa grass according to one's ability, he should perform the *sīmantonnayana* rite;
[he should give] a girl weighing thirty *niṣkas*, adorned with all ornaments. (19)
Having placed [the child] at the side of his wife, he should offer it to Śiva and the other deities;
in the rite of the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana), he should feed the Brahmins with milk-rice (pāyasa).
Having uttered the Hṛllekhā mantra, one should perform all the rites;
whatever rite is not mentioned here, one should perform it according to the Tulārohaṇa [rite].
Thus, the mortal who performs this attains infinite fruit.
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, the procedure for the gift of Hiraṇyagarbha, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
85. In the eighty-fifth chapter, the procedure for the gift of a mountain of sesame seeds:
O best of the twice-born, the gift of a mountain of sesame seeds will now be described.
Having constructed a pavilion as before, it should be made without an altar (vedikā).
And one should lead the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) along the outer path according to the previously mentioned procedure;
having sprinkled the mandala prepared in the center with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having covered it with new cloths and scattered *droṇa* flowers,
he should perform the sprinkling for the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and [erect] a staff one hundred units in height.
There, the most excellent preceptor should place that which has been fashioned with bamboo as its frame,
and he should scatter sesame seeds there while reciting the Vyomavyāpin mantra.
The staff should be made one span (prādeśa) longer than [the body], or eight finger-breadths (aṅgula), or even more;
it should be made four finger-breadths longer by the virtuous. || 5 ||
One should not perform [the rite] with fewer [tilas] than the measure of the staff, nor should one do so with more;
one should wrap all the tilas in cloth while reciting the *sadyojāta* and other mantras.
Having prepared the site, it should especially be purified;
then one should place the image-makers together with the images at the edge of the mountain.
One should fashion images of Śarva and the others, preceded by Kṣmā (the Earth), out of three niṣkas of gold; there, one should worship the God situated in the midst of the mountain of sesame seeds.
The preceptor, knowing the ritual procedure, should be honored by the patron;
he should then show the God of gods, the Supreme Lord, situated in the midst of the sesame seeds.
For this Lord of the gods of gods, whose banner bears the bull, is the master of all; when worship is performed for him, every desired object certainly comes to pass. || 10 ||
Whatever worship or fire-oblation (homa) has not been mentioned here, as well as the bathing of the God of gods with a thousand pitchers and so forth—[all that is included]. (11)
One should perform everything according to the previously mentioned procedure, just as in the case of the weighing on the scales;
then, having bid farewell to the Lord of the Gods, one should offer [the merit] to Śiva, who possesses the nature of auspiciousness.
The maker of the sesame-egg should give it preceded by the offering of water;
there is no gift superior to this in these three worlds. (13)
Alternatively, another method for obtaining great fruit with little material is now described here, which should be performed at all times and on every occasion.
Having spread a cloth over a place smeared with cow dung, the preceptor should deposit there one *bhāra* of the best sesame seeds from among the ten types of seeds.
Having fashioned a lotus provided with a pericarp and filaments, endowed with eight petals,
and ten corners, one should then [construct] above that [the dome] at half the measurement.
In the center of that, one should place a lotus; in the center of that, one should worship Śiva. To the north of that, one should have the Manonmanī [image] made, measuring half its size.
Having fashioned the eight Śaktis, Vāmā and the others, with three niṣkas of gold,
one should likewise fashion the eight Vidyeśvaras on the outside with gold.
Having performed all that according to the rules and having honored it, the most excellent preceptor should cause the performer to give all of that, mixed with sesame seeds, to the devotees of Śiva.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, the procedure for the gift of a mountain of sesame seeds, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
86. In the eighty-sixth chapter, the procedure for the gift of golden land:
O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe the gift of golden land.
With a thousand pieces of gold, one should fashion the earth in the shape of a square and so forth.
Within the measure of a single hand, [the earth] is endowed with the seven continents, complete with oceans and mountains, and possessed of all sacred fords (tīrthas). || 2 ||
In the center, it should be made beautiful, joined with Mount Meru; one should contemplate it as consisting of nine divisions and inhabited by many sages.

As before, the most excellent of gurus should perform the worship of the deity and especially the fire-oblation (homa); he should worship Meru and the other [mountains] with their respective seed-syllables (bīja).
O best of the twice-born, one should bathe the Supreme Lord with a thousand jars and other vessels, and his worship should be performed as before.
The earth fashioned from gold should be offered to Śiva and the other deities.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, the ritual for the gift of the Golden Land, in the great tantra known as the *Uttarakāmika*.

87. In the eighty-seventh chapter, the ritual for the gift of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpapādapa*): O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe the gift of the wish-fulfilling tree. One should fashion the tree out of gold weighing one hundred *niṣkas*.
It was endowed with many scriptures and trees, provided with leaves and flowers, joined with various fruits, and possessed of every kind of beauty. || 2 ||
O twice-born ones, one should hang many strands of pearl necklaces upon the branches, and one should fashion variegated canopies with emeralds.
One should have foliage fashioned here especially from coral,
and one should provide various fruits made of rubies.
One should have the base of the staff made of sapphire, the trunk of diamond,
the top of the tree fashioned from beryl, and [the remainder] from topaz.
The head should be fashioned from gomedaka stone,
and the wise one, O observers of good vows, should indeed have the shoulders made from sūryakānta stone.
The altar for the tree should be made either of moonstone or crystal;
its length is prescribed to be one span.
One should establish the measurement and the height of the eight branches,
and at the root of the tree, one should install the Liṅga surrounded by the world-protectors (Lokapālas).
Having constructed a pavilion provided with an altar and endowed with a mandala as before— or even without that— having placed a tree in its center, || 9 ||
The preceptor should worship Īśāna, who is associated with the opening of the world;
O best of the twice-born, he should offer a tree to Īśvara and [offerings] to his attendants.
Whatever else has not been mentioned here, one should perform it according to the procedure for the Tulābhāra rite.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, the ritual for the gift of the Kalpapādapa tree, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
88. In the eighty-eighth chapter, the ritual for the gift of Gaṇeśa: I shall describe the gift of Gaṇeśa, which destroys all sins.
One should construct a pavilion as before, provided with an altar and a maṇḍala.
In the center of that, one should worship the Lord surrounded by the world-protectors (lokapālas);
outside of that, one should worship the eight lords of knowledge (vidyeśas) in the eight directions.
And all of them were fashioned individually out of gold;
the Guru [should worship] those provided with the third enclosure with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
One should offer oblations to Īśa in the primary [central] position and to the eight Vidyeśvaras in the eight directions;
having established the seven Brahmins in the directions beginning with Īśāna, one should worship them.
To the north, the preceptor should worship the maiden with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
he should then bestow the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) upon them, in due order, with their respective mantras.
Whatever else is not mentioned here should be performed like the ritual of ascending the scales.
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, the Ritual for the Gift of Gaṇeśa, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
89. In the eighty-ninth chapter: The Ritual for the Gift of a Golden Cow.
I shall now describe, in brief and in due order, the gift of a golden cow, which removes all sins and destroys all fears and famines. (1)
O twice-born ones, one should fashion it with a thousand gold pieces, or half of that,
or even half of that again, or with a hundred niṣkas.
The wise man should have an image of a cow fashioned, endowed with all the auspicious marks;
there should be a ruby on its horns, and a diamond is desired for the tips of its hooves.
The best of those skilled in ritual procedures should conceive of a pearl at the middle of the eyebrows, lapis lazuli in the region of the tail,
and topaz for the position of the teeth.
Having thus fashioned the form of a cow, and having likewise prepared a calf for it— one-tenth of its size— one should lead them to the pavilion as before.
The best of teachers should place the animal in the center of that [area] provided with a railing and a mandala; he should clothe it with a pair of garments along with its calf.
O best of the twice-born, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while reciting its Gāyatrī;
one should perform the ritual worship as before, and especially the fire-oblation (homa).
Then, either by means of the single-fire ritual (ekāgni-vidhāna) provided with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial oblations,
or with milk and other offerings, one should worship the Lord with a thousand jars and so forth.
Alternatively, when performing the single-fire rite for a preceptor, it should be understood that thirty niṣkas are required;
whatever else is not mentioned should be performed according to the procedure for ascending the scale.
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, the procedure for the gift of the Golden Cow, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.

90. In the ninetieth chapter, the ritual for the gift of Lakṣmī: For the sake of attaining great sovereignty, the gift of Lakṣmī is here described. [It is performed] with gold weighing one thousand [palas], or half of that, or half again.
Alternatively, one should fashion the Śrīdevī endowed with all auspicious marks using half of that amount;
or else, one should have her fashioned with one hundred and eight gold coins (niṣkas).
Having constructed a pavilion as before, complete with an altar and a mandala,
one should install Lakṣmī within the mandala so that she is situated to the left of Viṣṇu.
One should worship Lakṣmī with the Śrī-mantra, or otherwise one should honor her with the Śrī-sūkta;
and one should worship Viṣṇu with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, offering perfumes, flowers, and other such items.
One should perform the worship of Śiva and especially the fire-oblation (homa);
or the Guru may perform a single homa according to the previously mentioned procedure.

One should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) of the god of gods with a thousand jars and other vessels according to the previously mentioned procedure; whatever has not been stated here [should be understood from that].
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, the ritual for the bestowal of Lakṣmī, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
91. In the ninety-first chapter: The Ritual for the Gift of the Sesame-Cow.
I shall describe the ritual for the sesame-cow, which accomplishes all desired aims.
One should prepare a mandala as before, provided with an altar and a mandala.
In front of him, the wise man should have a beautiful lotus made of sesame seeds;
it should be fashioned with eight *droṇas*, or he may have it made with a *bhāra*.
Having covered it with cloths, one should place a golden lotus in its center;
it may be made of thirty niṣkas, or half of that, or even half of that again.
One should fashion [the image] with five *niṣkas*, adorned with a pericarp and a stalk;
to the north of that very [image], one should [honour] Brāhmaṇas equal in number to the Rudras.
Having recollected the eleven Rudras, one should invoke and worship them;
and previously, one should worship twelve Brahmins with the mantras of the twelve Ādityas.
To the south, one should worship the eight learned Brahmins who are masters of the sciences;
one should then contemplate sixteen [deities] in the four directions with perfumes and other offerings.
Then, having worshipped with those mantras the cloth and the coverings,
he spread them within that square, provided with the five-fold ornaments.
In each of those, one should place nine measures of sesame seeds, using a new cloth and a new fruit, within a bronze vessel.
A piece of sugarcane should be given to them, and a cow should be given to them in due order;
she should be one with golden horns, free from disease, and having silver hooves.
The pratiśaṅga should be one niṣka, and the khura should be twice that amount;
as before, one should construct a pavilion provided with an altar and a maṇḍala.
In the same way, worship, fire-offerings (homa), as well as bathing and so forth, or simply a gift to Rudra, or even a gift to Sūrya [should be performed]. || 11 ||
Or, one may arrange for the gift of an image of Vighneśa according to one's capacity;
here, one should provide five ornaments made of five *niṣkas* of gold.
One should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as before; whatever has not been mentioned should be as it was previously.
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Gift of a Sesame-Cow," in the great tantra known as the *Uttarakāmika*.
In the ninety-second chapter, the ritual for the gift of a thousand cows:
I shall describe the gift of a thousand cows for the sake of attaining success (*siddhi*).
Only those possessing all qualities and being more excellent in virtue should be accepted.
Having worshipped the eight [peaks], one should attach a niṣka of gold to each peak;
having fashioned a peak, one should then bind it, or likewise a silver one, to the hoof.
Then, having bound a necklace and a turban upon his neck, one should offer grass;
[he should enter] the pavilion provided with an altar and accompanied by a mandala.
As before, let the worship of Śiva and the fire-oblation (homa) be performed here;
then, let the ceremonial bathing of Śiva be carried out with a thousand pitchers and so forth.
For the sake of Śiva, he should give a cow along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to auspicious Brahmins;
[the fee] being ten niṣkas, or half of that, or even half of that, which is one niṣka.
One who recites this hymn at the time of giving is said to be a true donor:
"May cows always be before me; may cows be behind me. (6)
Cows are my heart forever; I dwell in the midst of cows.
Whatever ritual action has not been mentioned here, one should determine it by means of the weight on the scales.
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, the Ritual for the Gift of a Thousand Cows, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
In the ninety-third chapter, the Ritual for the Gift of a Golden Horse:
the bestowing of a golden horse is here described for the sake of victory.
This is considered superior to the fruit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices. || 1 ||
Having prepared a horse endowed with the auspicious marks, [one should perform the rite] with one thousand and eight repetitions, or half of that, or half again, or even with one hundred and eight.
One should have a beautiful image with five auspicious limbs fashioned out of silver,
endowed with all ornaments and possessed of the various artistic skills.
Having constructed a pavilion as before, provided with an altar and a mandala,
one should place within its center a horse known by the name Uccaiḥśravas.

Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should present [the gift] to the Brahmins; having honored them with the thought that they are the lords of the gods, and having given five *niṣkas* as a fee.
One should satisfy the poor, the blind, the wretched, and the helpless with food and other necessities;
likewise, one should perform the worship of the mandala, the fire sacrifice (homa), and the ritual bathing with the water-pot (kalaśa).
Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, the Ritual for the Gift of a Golden Horse, in the *Uttarakāmika Mahātantra*.
In the ninety-fourth chapter, the Ritual for the Gift of a Daughter:
"O best of the twice-born, I shall now describe the gift of a daughter, which is the supreme among all gifts."
Endowed with all auspicious marks and free from defects. || 1 ||
Having first obtained the consent of his parents and given wealth and other gifts, he gave her— who was born of a different lineage and born on an auspicious day— to him.
Having observed the minds of both and having adopted her as a daughter once more,
he bathed her with perfumes and garlands, and adorned her with ornaments and garments.
Having adorned the maiden, he should give her for the sacrifice according to this rite.
As before, he should construct a pavilion provided with an altar and a mandala. (24)
There, having fully worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) as before—a peaceful rite prescribed for occasional occasions, accompanied by devotion to Śiva. (25)
Having worshipped the Lord with devotion using perfumes, flowers, garlands, and other offerings,
he was adorned with the five-fold ornaments and provided with garments, land, and wealth.
Recalling Śiva with faith, she should give to the bridegroom excellent male and female servants, together with the necessary implements for the planets.
O twice-born ones, he who causes such a gift to be made for a maiden prospers in happiness for as many hundreds of years as there are hairs on that maiden's body.
Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, the Ritual for the Gift of a Daughter, in the great tantra known as the *Uttarakāmika*.
In the ninety-fifth chapter, the Ritual for the Gift of a Golden Ox:
now the gift of the golden ox is briefly described.
One should fashion it from gold weighing a thousand [units] or even half of that.
Or one may make it with half of that measure, or even half of that again;
one should fashion a bull endowed with all the auspicious marks, or [an image] measuring one hundred and eight [units].
On the forehead, there should be a silver crescent moon made of crystal, the ear should be of ruby, and the hump should be of *gomedaka* stone. (3)
The wise man should cause a bull-vehicle to be made, adorned with a garland of bells around its neck, variegated with jewels, and encircled by a string of small tinkling bells.
O best of the twice-born, having constructed a pavilion as before, complete with an altar and a mandala, one should place a bull in its center facing the west.
One should worship Ukṣuṅkṣa with the Gāyatrī mantra, and above that, the Supreme Lord;
and as before, there is the worship of Śiva and especially the fire-oblation (homa).

One should offer a magnificent bull to Śiva and to the devotees of Śiva, or else perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma) accompanied by sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and cooked rice oblations (caru). || 7 ||
Whatever has not been stated here should be understood as being as heavy as a burden on a scale.
Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, the ritual for the gift of the Golden Ox, in the *Uttarakāmika-mahātantra*.
96. In the ninety-sixth chapter is the ritual for the gift of an elephant.
Hereafter, O best of the twice-born, I shall proclaim the gift of an elephant.
One should fashion an elephant with the proper characteristics, either out of gold or silver.
The most excellent of teachers should cause it to be made with one thousand, half of that, half of that again, or half of that once more, or else with one hundred and eight.
One should construct a pavilion as before, provided with an altar and a mandala;
one should place a lordly elephant in the center and worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
As before, one should perform the worship of Śiva and especially offer oblations (homa);
one should give with faith to Śiva and to the devotees of Śiva.
Everything else that has not been specifically mentioned should be performed according to the rules for the Tulā and Bhāra rites.
Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, the ritual for the gift of an elephant, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
97. In the ninety-seventh chapter, the procedure for the gift of the eight world-protectors (*lokapāla*).
Hereafter, I shall describe the gift of the eight world-protectors;
it should be performed at the previously mentioned place and time, provided with an altar (*vedikā*) and a maṇḍala.
O best of the twice-born, the worship of Śiva and the fire-oblation (homa) are to be performed as before;
having invited eight Śaiva priests endowed with all auspicious characteristics, [one should proceed].
Seated facing north and draped in new garments,
one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while reciting mantras that invoke the lords of the world.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) either on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or in a fire-pit (kuṇḍa).
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall consist of ten niṣkas, accompanied by ornaments.
One should give clothing, an upper garment, a seat, or even a woolen blanket; whatever else is not mentioned here, one should perform according to the procedure for the Tulā and Bhāra [donations].
This very food of Lokeśa bestows all prosperity and abundance;
it crushes the armies of enemies and increases elephants and horses.
It bestows sons, secures the kingdom, and promotes the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Gift of the Eight World Guardians," in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
98. In the ninety-eighth chapter, the procedure for the supreme gift:
I shall now declare the foremost gift, known by the name *Sarvadānottama*.
One should construct a pavilion according to the rules, provided with an altar and a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
In the water-station (prapā), the ritual procedure should be as follows, accompanied by a mandala as before:
in the center, one should place the Lord of the God of Gods, together with Brahmā and Viṣṇu.
One should worship the Lord with perfumes and other offerings, [offering] again to Brahmā, to Viṣṇu,
to Brahmā who is the distinction of the Brāhmaṇas, and to Brahmā the giver of wealth.
To Śiva, to Hari, Svāhā! Svadhā! Vauṣaṭ! Vaṣaṭ! Namaḥ! We know Nārāyaṇa; we meditate upon Vāsudeva;
may that Viṣṇu inspire us.
Then, the remaining oblations (śeṣahoma) should be performed by those who are composed in the sacrificial pit;
indeed, three persons who are knowers of the four Vedas and reciters [of mantras] should be selected.
With reference to them, one should cause wealth to be given to the twice-born according to the rules—
one hundred and eight excellent items for each of them individually.
Adorned with the five-fold ornaments and endowed with excellent garments and coverings;
whatever has not been mentioned here, one should perform all that according to the previously stated rule.
Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, the ritual procedure, in the great tantra known as the Uttarakāmika.
